entries.nuance: ㄱㄱ is the texted form of 고고, Korea's reading of English 'go-go,' and it spread from gaming ('go go!' to launch a match) into all of casual life: heading out, ordering food, starting a task, kicking off a plan. It's energetic and breezy — closer to 'let's GO / let's do this' than a neutral 'okay.' The nearest sober alternatives are 가자 (let's go) and the work-safe 바로 진행하겠습니다 (I'll proceed right away). The big English-speaker pitfall is misreading the letters: ㄱㄱ is 고고 (go-go = let's go), NOT 'good good' — and especially NOT gaming's English 'gg = good game' (which Koreans write out as 'gg' or say 잘 쳤어, never ㄱㄱ); a learner who sees the letters and thinks 'good game / good job' will read the message backwards. Second pitfall is register/hype mismatch: that gamer energy is fun with friends but reads as flippant to a boss, so don't ㄱㄱ a superior's task request — write 바로 시작하겠습니다 instead. Third, it's a call to ACT, not a plain 'yes': use it for proposals to do something, not to answer a factual yes/no (that's ㅇㅇ). It loves to ride after ㅇㅋ or ㅇㅇ to seal a decision.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.

Using ㄱㄱ as a standalone 'yes' to a yes/no question — it specifically means 'let's go/start,' so it fits proposals to act, not factual questions (use ㅇㅇ for plain 'yeah')

structuredNuance.t: ㄱㄱ is the texted form of 고고, Korea's reading of English 'go-go.' It spread from gaming ('go go!' to launch a match) into all casual life: heading out, ordering, starting a task, kicking off a plan. Energetic and breezy — 'let's GO / let's do this,' not a neutral 'okay.'

Literally 'go go.' Real meaning: a call to START or MOVE NOW — let's head out / let's begin / let's commit. It carries hype, not just consent. Critically it is NOT 'good good' and NOT gaming's 'gg = good game' (Koreans keep that one in Latin letters); the Korean ㄱㄱ is 고고, an instruction to act.

Casual, friends and peers, with a gamer/hype flavor. Too breezy for anyone senior — to a boss it reads as flippant for a real task. Work-safe equivalents: 바로 진행하겠습니다 / 바로 시작하겠습니다 ('I'll proceed/start right away'). Save ㄱㄱ for plans with friends.

Sober alternatives: 가자 (banmal 'let's go'), 바로 진행하겠습니다 (formal 'I'll proceed'). And don't swap it for ㅇㅇ: ㄱㄱ proposes ACTION ('let's go/start'), ㅇㅇ answers a yes/no with 'yeah.' Use ㄱㄱ for 'let's do it,' ㅇㅇ for plain agreement.
ㄱㄱ (default) → ㄱㄱㄱ (extra hype). With lead-ins: 바로 ㄱㄱ (right now), ㄱㄱ? (proposing), ㅇㅋ ㄱㄱ / ㅇㅇ ㄱㄱ (agree-then-launch). Spelled out as 고고 / 고고씽 for playful emphasis.

(1) Misreading the letters as 'good good' or gaming's 'good game' — it's 고고 (let's go), a move-now instruction; Koreans write 'good game' in Latin 'gg.' (2) Hype/register mismatch: don't ㄱㄱ a boss's request — use 바로 진행하겠습니다. (3) It's a call to act, not a plain 'yes' — use ㅇㅇ for factual yes/no.

entries.nuance: ㅈㅅ is the initials of 죄송 (Sino-Korean 罪悚, literally 'sin + dread/fear' — i.e. 'I feel the weight of having done wrong'), the same word inside the full apology 죄송합니다/죄송해요. Shrinking that heavy word to two consonants is exactly what makes it casual: it deflates the seriousness into a light 'my bad,' fit only for trivial slips among friends — a late text, the wrong cup, a small bump. Its register-mates are 미안 (banmal sorry, also casual) and the proper 죄송합니다 (formal). The crucial English-speaker pitfall is thinking 'sorry is sorry' and using ㅈㅅ for anything real or to anyone senior: because the abbreviation strips out all gravity, sending ㅈㅅ to a boss, professor, or older person — or for an actual mistake — reads as careless and even insulting, like mumbling 'my bad' for breaking something important. For those, type the full 죄송합니다 (very formal) or 죄송해요 (polite). Note 미안 vs 죄송: 미안 is for equals/juniors, 죄송 outranks it in politeness, so even the full 미안해 wouldn't suit a boss. And the FORM itself signals SIZE — a two-letter ㅈㅅ inherently says 'this is small,' so it's wrong for anything that genuinely matters; for a real-but-casual apology, type at least 미안해/정말 미안해, not ㅈㅅ.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Sending ㅈㅅ to a boss/elder or for a serious mistake — abbreviating 죄송 strips out the gravity and reads as careless; write the full 죄송합니다 (formal) or 죄송해요 (polite)
Treating ㅈㅅ (죄송) and 미안 as the same level — both are casual, but 죄송 outranks 미안 in politeness; 미안 is only for equals/juniors, so don't use it 'up' even spelled out

Carrying over English where one 'sorry' covers all sizes of apology — in Korean the FORM signals the size; a two-letter ㅈㅅ inherently says 'this is small,' so it's wrong for anything that actually matters

structuredNuance.t: ㅈㅅ is the initials of 죄송, the same word inside the full apology 죄송합니다/죄송해요. Shrinking that heavy word to two consonants is what makes it casual: it deflates the seriousness into a light 'my bad,' fit only for trivial slips — a late text, the wrong cup, a small bump.

The root 죄송 is Sino-Korean 罪悚, literally 'sin + dread/fear' — 'I feel the weight of having done wrong,' a genuinely heavy word. But the two-letter ㅈㅅ form strips that gravity out: the real, lived meaning is a breezy 'oops, my bad' for something that doesn't actually matter.

Casual, friends and peers, trivial slips only. NEVER as a real apology and NEVER to a boss, professor, or elder — the abbreviation reads as careless, even insulting. For those, write it out: 죄송해요 (polite), 죄송합니다 (formal). Size of apology must match the size of the form.

Register-mates: 미안 (banmal sorry) and 죄송 (more polite). Key boundary: 죄송 OUTRANKS 미안 in politeness — 미안 is only for equals/juniors, so even the full 미안해 won't suit a boss. Ladder upward: 미안 → 미안해 → 죄송해요 → 정말 죄송합니다.
ㅈㅅ → ㅈㅅㅈㅅ (a bit more sorry) → 헐 ㅈㅅ / ㅈㅅㅠㅠ (softened). With reasons: 늦어서 ㅈㅅ. Spelled-out escalation for anything real: 미안 → 미안해 → 죄송해요 → 죄송합니다 → 정말 죄송합니다.

Thinking 'sorry is sorry.' In Korean the FORM signals the SIZE: a two-letter ㅈㅅ inherently says 'this is small.' Using it for a real mistake or to anyone senior reads as careless — like mumbling 'my bad' for breaking something important. Fix: 죄송합니다/죄송해요 spelled out for anything that matters.

entries.nuance: ㅊㅋ is the initials of 축하 (Sino-Korean 祝賀, 'celebrate + congratulate'), the noun inside 축하해 (banmal), 축하해요 (polite), and 축하드려요/축하드립니다 (humble-formal, with 드리다 'to give up to someone'). As an abbreviation it's bright and offhand — perfect for friends celebrating jobs, birthdays, moves, exams, or a new relationship. The English-speaker pitfall is the one that bites every abbreviation here: 'congrats' feels universally friendly in English, but ㅊㅋ to someone you respect (a boss, professor, older relative) can read as too breezy for a real milestone — the curt letters undercut the sincerity. For them, write it out and go UP a level with the humble form 축하드려요/축하드립니다, which literally offers the congratulations up to them. A subtler pitfall: don't attach ㅊㅋ to genuinely heavy life events even spelled-as-slang (a wedding, a 60th birthday, a new baby) — those want full, warm sentences, not abbreviations. And note the politeness climb isn't just 해요: superiors expect 드리다, the humble 'give upward,' which a plain 축하해요 doesn't supply — for a boss's promotion, 승진 축하드립니다 lands right where 축하해요 sounds flat.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Texting ㅊㅋ to a senior for an important milestone — the abbreviation reads as offhand; write the full 축하드려요/축하드립니다 (humble form) to show real sincerity
Stopping at the polite 축하해요 for a boss when 축하드려요 fits better — 드리다 humbly 'gives' the congratulations upward, which superiors expect for big news
Assuming any happy English 'congrats' transfers — for very weighty occasions (weddings, elders' big birthdays) even spelled-out slang feels thin; use a full warm sentence

structuredNuance.t: ㅊㅋ is the initials of 축하, the noun inside 축하해 (banmal), 축하해요 (polite), and 축하드려요/축하드립니다 (humble-formal). As an abbreviation it's bright and offhand — perfect for friends celebrating jobs, birthdays, moves, exams, or a new relationship.

Literally just the two initials of 축하 ('congratulation'). Real meaning is a quick, cheerful 'congrats!' — but the very shortness encodes 'this is a light, casual cheer.' For a sincere, weighty congratulation the abbreviation can't carry the warmth; the spelled-out humble form does.

Casual, friends and peers, for everyday good news. Too breezy for someone you respect — to a boss, professor, or older relative the curt letters undercut sincerity. Write it out, and for seniors climb to the HUMBLE form 축하드려요 / 축하드립니다 (offers the congratulations upward), not just 축하해요.

The ladder is one word at four heights: ㅊㅋ (slang) → 축하해 (banmal) → 축하해요 (polite) → 축하드려요/축하드립니다 (humble-formal). The jump that matters for seniors is to 드리다 — 축하해요 is merely polite, while 축하드립니다 humbly gives the congratulations up to them.
ㅊㅋ → ㅊㅋㅊㅋ (warmer) → 헐 ㅊㅋㅊㅋㅋ (excited). Slot after the occasion: 생일 ㅊㅋ, 졸업 ㅊㅋ, 합격 ㅊㅋ. Combo: ㅊㅋㅊㅋ 부럽다 (congrats + 'jealous,' a friendly compliment). Upward: 승진 축하드려요 / 진심으로 축하드립니다.

'Congrats' is universally friendly in English, but ㅊㅋ to someone you respect reads as too breezy for a real milestone. Worse, even spelled-out slang is thin for heavy events (weddings, elders' big birthdays, a new baby) — those need full warm sentences. Fix: 축하드립니다 for seniors; whole sentences for big occasions.

(casual slang — friends and peers; not for formal messages)" — that is ㅠㅠ (yuyu (the letters yu-yu; read as a crying-face emoticon, not spoken)). entries.nuance: ㅠㅠ is pure visual: the Korean vowel letter ㅠ is reused as a picture of two eyes with tears streaming down (its twin ㅜㅜ is the same face with eyes scrunched), so it's read with the EYES, not pronounced — there's no spoken 'yuyu.' It's one of the most common feeling-markers in Korean chat, and crucially its range runs from genuine sadness all the way to playful, exaggerated 'aw man / waaah' whining; more letters = more drama, often tongue-in-cheek. The English-speaker pitfalls are mostly mechanical and tonal. Mechanically: Koreans attach it with NO space, fused to the last word (취소됐어ㅠㅠ), where English would float an emoji after a space — a gap (휴무래 ㅠㅠ) reads slightly off. Tonally: because it's text and a little cute, English speakers sometimes drop it into semi-professional messages thinking it's neutral like 🙁 — but in a formal or work note it reads as childish and unprofessional, so leave it for friends and dating partners; to a boss, put the feeling in words (아쉽네요/속상하네요) instead. And don't read every ㅠㅠ as real tears; very often it's just light 'ugh, bummer.' Its blends ㅋㅋㅠㅠ / ㅎㅠ even mix laughing-while-crying ('I'm dying').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Putting ㅠㅠ in a formal email or message to a boss — it reads as childish/unprofessional there; keep emotional emoticons to casual chats with friends
Reading every ㅠㅠ as genuine crying — much of the time it's playful, exaggerated whining ('aw maaan'); tone depends on context and how many ㅠ there are
Writing it with a space like an English emoji ("오늘 휴무래 ㅠㅠ" feels off vs the natural 휴무래ㅠㅠ) — Koreans fuse it onto the preceding word with no gap

structuredNuance.t: ㅠㅠ is pure visual: the vowel letter ㅠ reused as two tear-streaming eyes (twin ㅜㅜ = eyes scrunched). Read with the EYES, never pronounced — there is no spoken 'yuyu.' One of the most common feeling-markers in Korean chat, signalling sadness, frustration, or whining.

There's no literal word at all — it's a drawing made of a vowel. So 'meaning' is tone, and the tone ranges wide: real sadness at one end, playful exaggerated 'aw maaan / waaah' at the other. More ㅠ usually = more drama, and much of the time it's tongue-in-cheek, not actual tears.

Casual only: friends, peers, dating partners. In a formal or work message it reads as childish and unprofessional — it is NOT a neutral 🙁. Keep all teary emoticons out of notes to a boss, client, or stranger; there, state the feeling in words (아쉽네요 / 속상하네요) instead.

ㅜㅜ is the same teary face, eyes scrunched (fully interchangeable). Mixed forms blend emotions: ㅋㅋㅠㅠ / ㅎㅠ = laughing-while-crying ('I'm dying'). For a plain neutral sad tone in polite text you wouldn't use any of these — you'd write 아쉬워요 / 속상해요.
ㅠ (small sigh) → ㅠㅠ (default) → ㅠㅠㅠㅠ (dramatic/sobbing). Variant ㅜㅜ; blends ㅋㅋㅠㅠ, ㅎㅠ, 헐ㅠㅠ. Fuses onto the prior word with no space: 취소됐어ㅠㅠ, 가고싶었는데ㅠㅠ.

(1) Spacing: attach it with NO space, fused to the last word (취소됐어ㅠㅠ); an English-style gap (휴무래 ㅠㅠ) reads off. (2) Register: it's not a neutral emoji — in work/formal messages it's childish; say 아쉽네요 instead. (3) Don't read every ㅠㅠ as real crying; it's often just light 'ugh, bummer.'

the ultra-common combo: hard agreement + laughing

entries.nuance: ㄹㅇ is the consonant skeleton of 리얼, Korea's borrowing of English 'real,' and it works two ways: as a reply it's emphatic agreement ('for real / no joke / facts'), and dropped inside a sentence it's an intensifier meaning 'genuinely/seriously' (이거 ㄹㅇ 웃겨 = 'this is genuinely funny'). It's very current 20-30s slang, at home in friend chats and comments, and frequently fused with ㅋㅋ as ㄹㅇㅋㅋ. Its native-Korean cousins are 진짜 and 정말 ('really/truly'), which carry the same meaning but sound a notch less slangy — and those are what you'd upgrade to in polite contexts (진짜요/정말요). Two English-speaker pitfalls: first, don't decode ㄹㅇ as 'right now' or any English-acronym guess — it's strictly '리얼/real (for real).' Second, ㄹㅇ overlaps heavily with the agreement word ㅇㅈ (인정, 'agreed'), but they aren't identical: ㄹㅇ asserts 'that's TRUE,' while ㅇㅈ concedes 'I ADMIT/agree' — close enough to stack (ㄹㅇ ㅇㅈ) but ㄹㅇ also works as a standalone intensifier where ㅇㅈ can't. And keep it casual: this is young-person slang, so with seniors say 진짜요/정말요, not ㄹㅇ. Note too that position rewrites the meaning — bare ㄹㅇ is 'true,' ㄹㅇ? is 'seriously?!', and mid-sentence ㄹㅇ is just 'really' — so the same two letters do three different jobs.

Treating ㄹㅇ and ㅇㅈ as identical — ㄹㅇ asserts 'that's true / genuinely' (and can intensify mid-sentence), while ㅇㅈ specifically means 'I agree/admit it'; only ㄹㅇ works as a plain intensifier

structuredNuance.t: ㄹㅇ is the consonant skeleton of 리얼 (Korea's borrowing of 'real'). It works two ways: as a reply, emphatic agreement ('for real / no joke / facts'); inside a sentence, an intensifier meaning 'genuinely/seriously' (이거 ㄹㅇ 웃겨 = 'genuinely funny'). Very current 20-30s slang.

Literally 'real' (리얼) reduced to two consonants. Real meaning splits by position: standalone it's 'for real / that's true,' a strong yes; with ? it's 'seriously?!'; mid-sentence it's just 'really/genuinely.' Same letters, three jobs — position tells you which.

Casual, young, friend chats and online comments. Not for work or formal messages — it's distinctly slangy and reads as too loose to a senior. Polite upgrades that mean the same thing: 진짜요 / 정말요 ('really'), 맞아요 ('that's right') for the agreement sense.

Native cousins 진짜/정말 mean the same but sound less slangy (and are the polite path: 진짜요/정말요). vs ㅇㅈ (인정): ㄹㅇ asserts 'that's TRUE,' ㅇㅈ concedes 'I ADMIT/agree.' They stack (ㄹㅇ ㅇㅈ), but only ㄹㅇ works as a plain mid-sentence intensifier.
ㄹㅇ (default) → ㄹㅇㅋㅋ (agree + laugh) → ㄹㅇ ㅇㅈ (double emphasis) → ㄹㅇ? (surprised). As intensifier: 이거 ㄹㅇ 맛있음, ㄹㅇ 대박. Spelled out: 리얼? / 리얼루 (playful). Polite swap: 진짜요 / 정말요.

(1) Don't decode ㄹㅇ as 'right now' or any English acronym — it's 리얼/real. (2) Don't treat it as identical to ㅇㅈ — ㄹㅇ is a truth-claim/intensifier, ㅇㅈ is agreement/admission; they pair but aren't swappable everywhere. (3) Keep it out of formal chats — use 진짜요/정말요 with seniors.

entries.nuance: ㅂㅂ is the consonant frame of 바이바이, Korea's reading of English 'bye-bye,' so it's a borrowed-word goodbye that feels breezy and a touch cute — fine for closing a casual chat with friends, peers, or a dating partner. Its register-mates run from the neutral 잘 가 / 또 봐 (banmal 'see ya') up to the polite parting set 들어가세요 / 안녕히 계세요 / 안녕히 가세요. The English-speaker pitfall is closing UP with it: in English 'bye!' ends a message to almost anyone, but ㅂㅂ to a boss, professor, or stranger reads as too informal to sign off a polite exchange — there you want a proper closing like 들어가세요 (go in well / take care) or, in a work context, 수고하셨습니다 (thank you for your hard work). A finer point most learners miss: Korean goodbyes split by who is leaving — 안녕히 가세요 to the person LEAVING, 안녕히 계세요 to the person STAYING — a distinction English's single 'bye' erases. ㅂㅂ sidesteps that only because it's casual; the moment you go polite, you must pick the right one. And note ㅂㅂ is just a sign-off, not a promise to meet — for a real next plan say 또 봐 / 담에 봐. One more trap: don't read the doubled letters as 'see you LATER (a set plan)'; the borrowed 바이바이 only ends the chat — it commits to nothing.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Ending a work or formal message with ㅂㅂ — it's too casual to close a polite exchange; use 들어가세요, 안녕히 계세요, or 수고하셨습니다 instead
Assuming one polite goodbye fits all like English 'bye' — Korean splits by who moves: 안녕히 가세요 to the one leaving, 안녕히 계세요 to the one staying
Using ㅂㅂ to mean 'see you (later, definite plan)' — it's just a sign-off; to confirm a next meeting say 또 봐 / 담에 봐 or spell out the plan

structuredNuance.t: ㅂㅂ is the consonant frame of 바이바이, Korea's reading of English 'bye-bye' — a breezy, slightly cute goodbye to end a chat. It closes a conversation casually; it does not by itself promise a next meeting.

Literally 'bye-bye' (a borrowed English word). Real use: a quick chat sign-off among friends, nothing more — it carries no warmth-of-promise and no politeness. The cuteness comes from the doubled borrowed sound, not from any added meaning.

Casual only: friends, peers, dating partners. Too informal to close a polite exchange — to a boss, professor, or stranger, end with a proper closing instead: 들어가세요 / 안녕히 계세요 / 안녕히 가세요, or in a work chat 수고하셨습니다 ('thank you for your hard work').

Banmal siblings: 잘 가 / 또 봐 ('see ya'). Polite set splits by who moves — 안녕히 가세요 to the one LEAVING, 안녕히 계세요 to the one STAYING — a split English 'bye' erases. ㅂㅂ dodges it only by being casual; once polite, you must pick the right one. For 'see you again,' 또 봐/담에 봐, not ㅂㅂ.
ㅂㅂ → ㅂㅂ! (cheerful) → ㅂㅂ2 ('bye-bye'). With wrap-up lead-ins: 그럼 ㅂㅂ, 나 갈게 ㅂㅂ. Caring combos: ㅂㅂ 조심히 가, ㅂㅂ 잘 자. Spelled out: 바이 / 바이바이. Polite replacements: 들어가세요 / 수고하셨습니다.

Closing UP with it. English 'bye!' ends a message to anyone; ㅂㅂ to a senior is too informal — use 들어가세요 / 수고하셨습니다. And don't read ㅂㅂ as 'see you (a definite plan)' — it's only a sign-off; confirm a next meeting with 또 봐 / 담에 봐 or by spelling the plan out.

entries.nuance: ㅇㅈ is the consonant frame of 인정 (Sino-Korean 認定, 'recognize + fix/settle'), literally 'to acknowledge/admit something as so' — and as slang it became young Koreans' punchy way to say 'agreed, that's facts.' Its polite equivalents are 맞아요 ('that's right'), 동의해요 ('I agree'), and very formal 동의합니다, which are what you'd use with seniors. Two English-speaker pitfalls. First, the literal core is 'acknowledge/admit,' so beyond cheerful agreement it can carry a faint flavor of conceding a point ('okay, I'll grant you that') — and the bare-noun 인정 even works as a real verb (그 실수는 인정 = 'I admit that mistake'); reading it as only upbeat 'yes!' misses that edge. Second, don't blur it with ㄹㅇ: ㅇㅈ = 'I agree/admit (인정),' a stance toward what you said; ㄹㅇ = 'for real/genuinely (리얼),' a claim about truth that can also intensify a sentence. They pair (ㄹㅇ ㅇㅈ) but aren't swappable everywhere. As always, keep ㅇㅈ casual — to a boss write 맞습니다 / 동의합니다. And mind the function: ㅇㅈ endorses an OPINION/take, so it fits 'good song / weekdays are better' — it is not a plain factual 'yeah' to a yes/no (that's ㅇㅇ).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using ㅇㅈ in formal writing or to a senior — it's slang; write 동의합니다 or 맞습니다 instead
Confusing ㅇㅈ with ㄹㅇ — ㅇㅈ (인정) = 'I agree/admit it,' a stance; ㄹㅇ (리얼) = 'for real/genuinely,' a truth-claim and intensifier; they stack but aren't interchangeable
Hearing ㅇㅈ as purely upbeat 'yes!' and missing the 'I'll admit/concede' shade — its root 인정 means acknowledge, so it can mark grudging agreement, not only enthusiastic

structuredNuance.t: ㅇㅈ is the consonant frame of 인정, literally 'to acknowledge/admit something as so' — young Koreans' punchy way to say 'agreed, that's facts.' A quick, emphatic 'I'm with you / true that' in friend chats and comments.

Literal root 인정 = 'acknowledge / admit / recognize as settled.' The slang sense is upbeat 'agreed!' — but the literal core leaves a faint shade of CONCEDING ('okay, I'll grant you that'). The bare noun even works as a verb: 그 실수는 인정 = 'I admit that mistake.' It's not purely cheerful.

Casual, young, friends and peers. Not for formal writing or seniors. Polite equivalents to use upward: 맞아요 / 맞습니다 ('that's right'), 동의해요 / 동의합니다 ('I agree'). In a work chat agree with 동의합니다, never ㅇㅈ.

Don't blur with ㄹㅇ: ㅇㅈ (인정) = 'I agree/admit it,' a stance toward what was said; ㄹㅇ (리얼) = 'for real/genuinely,' a truth-claim that can also intensify mid-sentence. They stack (ㄹㅇ ㅇㅈ) but aren't interchangeable — only ㄹㅇ works as a plain intensifier. And vs ㅇㅇ: ㅇㅈ endorses an opinion, ㅇㅇ just says 'yeah' to a yes/no. Polite path: 맞아요 / 동의해요.
ㅇㅈ → ㅇㅈㅇㅈ (strong) → ㄹㅇ ㅇㅈ (double). The set-phrase game ㅇㅈ? ㅇㅇㅈ (call-and-response 'right?'/'yeah agreed'). Spelled out: 인정 (also a standalone verb, 인정한다). Polite swap: 맞습니다 / 동의합니다.

(1) Hearing it as purely upbeat 'yes!' and missing the 'I'll admit/concede' shade from its root 인정 — it can mark grudging agreement. (2) Treating it as identical to ㄹㅇ — they're different (agreement vs truth-claim) and only ㄹㅇ intensifies. (3) Using it upward — write 동의합니다/맞습니다 to seniors.

entries.nuance: ㄱㅊ is the initials of 괜찮아 ('it's okay'), and it inherits that word's famously wide three-way range: (1) reassuring — 'it's fine, don't worry'; (2) self-report — 'I'm okay'; and (3) soft declining — 'I'm good' (i.e. 'no thanks'). Its polite forms are 괜찮아요 / 괜찮습니다, which is what seniors get. The standout English-speaker pitfall is sense (3): when someone offers you food or a drink and you reply 괜찮아요/ㄱㅊ, a Korean hears 'no thanks, I'm fine WITHOUT it' — a polite refusal — whereas English speakers, hearing 'it's okay,' often think they just ACCEPTED. So 'ㄱㅊ' to '커피 마실래?' means you're declining, not saying yes; if you actually want it, say 응 줘 / 네 주세요. The second pitfall is the usual register one: ㄱㅊ is friends-only, so don't reassure a boss with it — write 괜찮습니다. The near-synonyms for the decline sense are worth knowing: 됐어 is the blunter cousin ('no, that's enough,' can sound curt or annoyed), so ㄱㅊ/괜찮아 is the gentler way to turn something down. And the ? matters: ㄱㅊ states 'I'm fine,' but ㄱㅊ? flips it to 'are YOU okay?' It naturally follows apologies like ㅈㅅ/미안 to brush them off kindly.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Replying 괜찮아요/ㄱㅊ to an offer thinking you ACCEPTED — to a Korean it means 'no thanks, I'm fine without it' (a polite decline); to accept, say 응 줘 or 네 주세요
Reassuring a boss or elder with ㄱㅊ — it's casual; say 괜찮아요 or 괜찮습니다 to stay polite
Forgetting ㄱㅊ's three jobs and forcing one reading — depending on context it means 'don't worry,' 'I'm okay,' OR 'no thanks'; the ? (ㄱㅊ?) flips it to 'are YOU okay?'

structuredNuance.t: ㄱㅊ is the initials of 괜찮아 ('it's okay'), inheriting that word's wide three-way range: (1) reassuring — 'it's fine, don't worry'; (2) self-report — 'I'm okay'; (3) soft declining — 'I'm good / no thanks.' It naturally follows apologies (ㅈㅅ/미안) to brush them off kindly.

Literally just 'okay / fine' (괜찮아 abbreviated). But the real meaning depends entirely on context: as a reply to an apology it reassures, about yourself it's a status report, and — the tricky one — as a reply to an OFFER it's a polite REFUSAL ('I'm fine without it'), not acceptance.

Casual, friends and peers. Don't reassure or decline UP with it — to a boss or elder write 괜찮아요 (polite) / 괜찮습니다 (formal). The function (reassure / decline / self-report) stays the same at every level; only the form changes.

For the DECLINE sense, 아니야 괜찮아 / 됐어 are close kin — but 됐어 is blunter and can sound annoyed ('no, that's enough'), so ㄱㅊ/괜찮아 is the gentler turn-down. Crucially, ㄱㅊ is NOT how you accept: if you want the thing offered, say 응 줘 / 네 주세요, never ㄱㅊ. Polite forms: 괜찮아요 / 괜찮습니다.
ㄱㅊ → ㄱㅊㄱㅊ (warmly waving off) → 나 ㄱㅊ (I'm fine) → ㄱㅊ? (are YOU okay?). After apologies: ㅈㅅ → ㄱㅊㄱㅊ. Spelled out: 괜찮아 → 괜찮아요 → 괜찮습니다. The ? alone flips speaker from self to other.

Sense (3): replying ㄱㅊ/괜찮아요 to an offer means 'no thanks' to a Korean, but English speakers hear 'it's okay' and think they ACCEPTED. So ㄱㅊ to '커피 마실래?' DECLINES it — say 응 줘/네 주세요 to accept. Second: it's friends-only; reassure a boss with 괜찮습니다, not ㄱㅊ.

examples.note: a courteous full request-exchange to a stranger; note 여쭤보다 (ask, humble form)

entries.nuance: 실례지만 is the polite 'excuse me, but…' you put BEFORE a question that might intrude — asking a stranger's name, age, relationship status, or for directions. It is 실례(失禮) 'breach of etiquette' + 지만 'but', meaning 'it's a bit forward of me, but…'. This buffer is not optional small talk — it is culturally expected when your question crosses into personal territory, especially with someone you don't know. Register: 실례지만 is standard polite; 실례하지만 and 실례합니다만 are slightly more 격식; a softer, more casual variant is 실례인데. The nearest alternative is 죄송하지만 ('sorry, but…'), which leans more apologetic and frames asking a favor; the dividing line is that 실례지만 frames a social intrusion ('this question is a bit forward'), while 죄송하지만 frames an imposition ('I'm imposing on you'). Critical grammar rule English speakers miss: 실례지만 must attach to a following clause — it CANNOT end a sentence by itself like English 'excuse me'. To stand alone, say 실례합니다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 실례지만 alone like English 'excuse me' — it needs a following clause (실례지만, 누구세요?); to stand alone use 실례합니다.
Asking personal questions (age, name, marital status) with no cushion — Korean expects 실례지만/혹시 in front to soften.
Swapping it freely with 죄송하지만 — 실례지만 frames an intrusive question; 죄송하지만 leans toward asking a favor.

structuredNuance.t: 실례(失禮) 'breach of etiquette' + 지만 'but' = 'it's a bit forward of me, but…'. The real function is a social cushion that pre-apologizes for an intrusive question, signaling you are aware you might be crossing a line.

실례지만 is standard polite; 실례하지만 / 실례합니다만 are more 격식; 실례인데 is softer and slightly casual. Use any of these before personal questions to a stranger. Never drop the cushion — asking personal questions cold sounds blunt in Korean.

Nearest alternative is 죄송하지만 ('sorry, but…'), which leans apologetic and frames an imposition. The dividing line: 실례지만 = 'this question is a bit forward'; 죄송하지만 = 'I'm imposing on you / asking too much'. They can often swap, but 실례지만 is more about the question's intrusiveness.
Add 혹시 for extra softness: 실례지만 혹시 어디서 일하세요? Use 실례지만 말씀 좀 여쭙겠습니다 as a formal complete opener. In writing, 실례합니다만 is common.

English speakers drop the cushion entirely, firing 나이가 어떻게 되세요? cold — which sounds blunt and rude in Korean. Also, 실례지만 cannot end a sentence alone like English 'excuse me'; it must attach to a following clause. Use 실례합니다 to stand alone.

entries.english: The thing is… / Actually, the reason I'm asking is… (lead-in before getting to your real point/request)
entries.shortExplanation: 다름이 아니라 is a practical expression meaning "The thing is… / Actually, the reason I'm asking is… (lead-in before getting to your real point/request)".
entries.explanation: "The thing is… / Actually, the reason I'm asking is… (lead-in before getting to your real point/request)" — that is 다름이 아니라 (dareumi anira). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 다름이 아니라, 부탁이 하나 있어서요. ("The thing is, I have a favor to ask."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: The thing is, I have a favor to ask.
usagePhrases.note: Easing into a request; trailing -서요 leaves it softly open

usagePhrases.ko: 다름이 아니라 잠깐 드릴 말씀이 있어서요.
usagePhrases.romanization: dareumi anira jamkkan deuril malsseumi isseoseoyo.
usagePhrases.en: Actually, there's something I wanted to tell you.
usagePhrases.note: 드릴 말씀 = humble 'something to say to you'

usagePhrases.ko: 다름이 아니라, 다음 주 일정 때문에 연락드렸어요.
usagePhrases.romanization: dareumi anira, daeum ju iljeong ttaemune yeollakdeuryeosseoyo.
usagePhrases.en: I'm reaching out about next week's schedule, actually.
usagePhrases.note: Stating the purpose of a call/email

usagePhrases.ko: 다름이 아니고 돈 좀 빌릴 수 있을까 해서.
usagePhrases.romanization: dareumi anigo don jom billil su isseulkka haeseo.
usagePhrases.en: So, the thing is, I was wondering if I could borrow some money.
usagePhrases.note: 다름이 아니고 = looser spoken variant

examples.ko: 다름이 아니라, 시간 좀 있으세요?
examples.romanization: dareumi anira, sigan jom isseuseyo?
examples.en: The thing is — do you have a minute?
examples.note: Short build-up to a simple ask; the listener knows a real request is coming

examples.ko: A: 여보세요? 누구세요? / B: 저 민준이에요. 다름이 아니라 이번 주말에 시간 있으세요?
examples.romanization: A: yeoboseyo? nuguseyo? / B: jeo minjunieyo. dareumi anira ibeon jumare sigan isseuseyo?
examples.en: A: Hello? Who is this? / B: It's Minjun. The thing is, are you free this weekend?
examples.note: Phone call where 다름이 아니라 signals the speaker is now getting to the actual reason for calling

examples.ko: 과장님, 다름이 아니라 연차 하루만 쓸 수 있을까요?
examples.romanization: gwajangnim, dareumi anira yeoncha haruman sseul su isseulkkayo?
examples.en: Manager, the thing is, could I take just one day of leave?
examples.note: Real workplace request to a senior, fully polite — 다름이 아니라 softens the directness of asking a superior

entries.nuance: Polite set phrase literally meaning 'it's nothing other (than this)' — from 다르다 ('to differ') → 다름 ('difference') + 이 아니라 ('it's not that') — signaling 'I'm now about to get to the real reason.' It creates a small moment of suspense that primes the listener for a request or announcement, which is why it's so common before favors, phone call purposes, and workplace asks. The near-synonyms 저기요 and 저 ('um, hey') just flag the start of a turn, whereas 다름이 아니라 specifically promises 'here comes my actual point,' making it heavier and more formal. 다름이 아니고 is the slightly looser conversational variant. Because it is a lead-in, it cannot end the sentence — the real content must follow immediately. Pitch it at 존댓말 contexts: phone calls, emails, and talking to seniors. Among close friends it can feel unnecessarily stiff.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
It's a lead-in, not a full sentence — 다름이 아니라. on its own says nothing. Always attach your actual point: 다름이 아니라, 부탁이 하나 있어요.
Spelling: 다름이 (not 다림이). It comes from 다르다 (to differ), so the noun is 다름. 다림이 wrongly suggests 다리미 'an iron'.
Don't drop the connective and say 다름 아니라 in careful writing; standard is 다름이 아니라 with the subject 이.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'it's nothing different (from this)' — 다름 ('difference') + 이 아니라 ('it's not that'). In practice it means 'I'm now getting to the real reason I approached/called you,' priming the listener for a request or announcement.

Polite 존댓말, especially suited to phone calls, emails, and speaking to seniors at work or in service contexts. Among close friends it can feel unnecessarily stiff; replace with 있잖아 or 사실은 for casual speech.

vs 저기요 / 저: those just open a conversational turn ('um, hey'), whereas 다름이 아니라 specifically signals 'what follows is the whole point of this conversation,' so it carries more weight and formality. vs 사실은: 사실은 ('the truth is') reveals a contrast with what might be assumed; 다름이 아니라 simply frames the purpose of contact.
다름이 아니고 = slightly looser spoken variant, same meaning. The trailing sentence often ends in -서요 (e.g. 부탁이 있어서요) to keep the turn open and soft rather than closing it with a blunt demand.

It is a lead-in, NOT a complete sentence — never say 다름이 아니라. alone without your actual point. Spelling trap: it's 다름이 (noun from 다르다 'to differ'), never 다림이, which suggests 다리미 ('a clothes iron') and is simply wrong.

entries.english: Sorry, but… / Excuse me, but… (apologetic softener before a request, complaint, or refusal)
entries.shortExplanation: 죄송한데요 is a practical expression meaning "Sorry, but… / Excuse me, but… (apologetic softener before a request, complaint, or refusal)".
entries.explanation: 죄송한데요 (joesonghandeyo) = "Sorry, but… / Excuse me, but… (apologetic softener before a request, complaint, or refusal)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 죄송한데요, 이거 환불 가능할까요? ("Sorry, but is this refundable?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite complaint/request at a store

usagePhrases.ko: 죄송한데 조금만 조용히 해 주실 수 있어요?
usagePhrases.romanization: joesonghande jogeumman joyonghi hae jusil su isseoyo?
usagePhrases.en: Sorry, but could you keep it down a little?
usagePhrases.note: 죄송한데 (no 요) = slightly shorter, still polite

usagePhrases.ko: 죄송한데요, 지금은 좀 어려울 것 같아요.
usagePhrases.romanization: joesonghandeyo, jigeumeun jom eoryeoul geot gatayo.
usagePhrases.en: I'm sorry, but it'd be hard right now.
usagePhrases.note: Softening a refusal with 좀 + 것 같아요

usagePhrases.en: Excuse me, could you let me through?
usagePhrases.note: More apologetic in tone than 실례지만

examples.ko: 죄송한데요, 물 좀 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: joesonghandeyo, mul jom jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Sorry, could I get some water?
examples.note: Simple polite request to restaurant staff — 죄송한데요 keeps the tone warm even before 'could you'

examples.ko: A: 주문하시겠어요? / B: 죄송한데요, 주문한 거랑 다른 게 나왔어요.
examples.romanization: A: jumunhasigesseoyo? / B: joesonghandeyo, jumunhan georang dareun ge nawasseoyo.
examples.en: A: Are you ready to order? / B: Sorry, but this isn't what I ordered.
examples.note: Two-person restaurant exchange: 죄송한데요 opens the complaint without sounding accusatory

examples.ko: 죄송한데요, 제가 지금 통화가 좀 어려워서요.
examples.romanization: joesonghandeyo, jega jigeum tonghwaga jom eoryeowoseoyo.
examples.en: I'm sorry, but I can't really talk right now.
examples.note: Trailing -서요 leaves the refusal gently unfinished, making it softer than a full sentence

entries.nuance: Polite 존댓말 cushion built on 죄송 (罪悚: 罪 'sin/guilt' + 悚 'fear/trepidation') — originally a very strong apology implying guilt and awe — plus the ending -ㄴ데요 ('…, and so / …but'), turning it into a universal friction-reducer before a request, complaint, or soft refusal. Because it leads with an apology, it feels more deferential than 실례지만 (courteous but not guilty) — you'd say 죄송한데요 when complaining about your food or softly refusing a request, but 실례지만 when asking a stranger for directions. Koreans reach for this phrase constantly because leading with 죄송 keeps social friction very low. 죄송한데 (dropping -요) is the same phrase in slightly less formal speech. A critical distinction: this is a SOFTENING LEAD-IN, not a genuine apology for a real wrongdoing — if you actually hurt someone, you need a sincere 정말 죄송합니다, not this prefix.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't spell it 죄성한데요 — the word is 죄송 (罪悚). Listen for the ㅗ: 죄송.
It's a softener, not a real apology. If you genuinely wronged someone, 죄송한데요 sounds too light — use a full 정말 죄송합니다.
Avoid stacking it with a blunt demand: 죄송한데요, 빨리 해요 clashes. Keep the request equally polite: 죄송한데요, 조금만 빨리 해 주실 수 있을까요?

structuredNuance.t: 직역: '(I feel) guilty/fearful, but…' (罪悚 + -ㄴ데요). Real meaning: a universal friction-reducer placed before any request, complaint, or soft refusal. The apology-first structure keeps social harmony — Koreans use it constantly for exactly this reason.

Polite 존댓말. Works for requests to staff, complaints at stores, declining invitations, or asking a stranger to move. 죄송한데 (no -요) is slightly less formal but still polite. Do NOT use with close friends — just say 있잖아 or start directly.

vs 실례지만: 실례지만 is courteous-but-not-apologetic, good for asking strangers for information. 죄송한데요 leads with guilt and fits complaints and refusals too. vs 미안한데요: 미안한데요 is the casual-polite version for semi-formal situations; 죄송한데요 is the more formal, deferential choice.
죄송한데 (no 요) = slightly less formal. 정말 죄송한데요 = adds genuine weight ('I'm really sorry, but…'). For a full apology without a trailing request: 정말 죄송합니다.

Don't spell it 죄성한데요 — the word is 죄송 (罪悚); the second syllable ends in ㅇ. This is a SOFTENER, not a real apology for wrongdoing — using it alone after a serious mistake sounds too light. If you've genuinely wronged someone, use 정말 죄송합니다.

entries.english: Right? / exactly / I know, right — agreeing that you feel the same, often a bit helplessly.
entries.shortExplanation: 그러게요 is a practical expression meaning "Right? / exactly / I know, right — agreeing that you feel the same, often a bit helplessly.".
entries.explanation: "Right? / exactly / I know, right — agreeing that you feel the same, often a bit helplessly." — that is 그러게요 (geureogeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 그러게요 ("right? / I know"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: polite -요, agreeing with someone you respect

usagePhrases.en: yeah, right / tell me about it
usagePhrases.note: casual banmal, to a friend
fuller polite form, stronger agreement
casual emphatic, half-resigned agreement

examples.ko: A: 오늘 진짜 덥다 / B: 그러게.
examples.romanization: A: oneul jinjja deopda / B: geureoge.
examples.en: A: It's really hot today / B: Right?
examples.note: the bare agreement — echoing a shared feeling; you feel it too, so 그러게 is exactly right here

examples.ko: A: 요즘 왜 이렇게 시간이 빨라요 / B: 그러게요, 벌써 6월이에요.
examples.romanization: A: yojeum wae ireoke sigani ppallayo / B: geureogeyo, beolsseo 6worieyo.
examples.en: A: Why does time fly these days / B: I know, right — it's June already.
examples.note: everyday: polite agreement with a mutual observation; the 벌써 6월이에요 follow-up adds your own evidence of the shared feeling

examples.ko: A: 그때 그거 샀어야 했는데 / B: 그러게 말이에요. 지금은 품절이래요.
examples.romanization: A: geuttae geugeo sasseoya haenneunde / B: geureoge marieyo. jigeumeun pumjeoriraeyo.
examples.en: A: We should've bought it back then / B: Exactly. It's sold out now apparently.
examples.note: real situation: 그러게 말이에요 agreeing with a shared regret — the emphatic form feels more heartfelt than bare 그러게요

entries.nuance: 그러게(요) means 'right? / exactly / I know, I feel the same' — you agree with something the other person said, often with a faint helpless, resigned, or rueful tinge. It's built from 그러다 'to be/do like that' + the sentence-final 게/게요. Casual 그러게, polite 그러게요, emphatic 그러게 말이에요 'exactly, you said it.' The critical dividing line is against 그렇구나 / 그렇군요: 그러게(요) responds to a SHARED feeling or opinion you already hold ('I know, right'), while 그렇구나 / 그렇군요 reacts to NEW information you just learned ('oh, I see / I didn't know that'). Both respond to something the other person just said, but the agreement type is opposite. Saying 그러게요 to new facts implies you already knew and can sound dismissive. To a superior 그러게요 is acceptable but 맞아요 / 그러네요 can feel a touch more attentive and engaged. The English-speaker pitfall is using 그러게요 as a response to new information — e.g., someone tells you their hometown for the first time and you say 그러게요, which would mean 'I know' and imply you already knew. The second pitfall is misreading its tone as disagreement; it is agreement, just with a resigned or rueful undertone.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 그러게요 to react to brand-new information — that implies you already knew; for news you just learned use 그렇군요 / 그렇구나.
Saying plain 그러게 to a boss or elder — it's banmal; keep the polite 그러게요 (or 그러게 말이에요) with anyone you use 존댓말 with.
Reading 그러게요 as disagreement or doubt — it actually means 'right, I feel the same,' a soft, often resigned agreement.

structuredNuance.t: 그러게(요) means 'right? / I know / exactly' — you agree with something the other person just said, often with a faint resigned or rueful undertone ('yeah, I know, what can you do'). It is agreement, not disagreement.

그러게 (casual banmal to friends) → 그러게요 (polite, to seniors/coworkers) → 그러게 말이에요 (emphatic full agreement) → 그러게 말이야 (casual emphatic, half-resigned). With a superior, 맞아요 or 그러네요 can feel slightly more attentive.

그러게(요) = 'I know, right' — confirms shared feeling/opinion you already held. 그렇구나 / 그렇군요 = 'oh, I see' — reacts to NEW information you just learned. 맞아요 = 'that's right / correct' — cleaner factual agreement, less rueful. Swap 그러게요 for 그렇군요 with new info or you sound like you already knew.

Using 그러게요 to react to brand-new information — that implies you already knew and sounds dismissive. Misreading 그러게요 as doubt or disagreement — it is definitely agreement. Saying plain 그러게 to a boss or elder — banmal; use 그러게요 or 그러게 말이에요.

entries.english: It can't be helped / Nothing we can do / Oh well (accepting an unavoidable situation)
entries.shortExplanation: 어쩔 수 없죠 is a practical expression meaning "It can't be helped / Nothing we can do / Oh well (accepting an unavoidable situation)".
entries.explanation: "It can't be helped / Nothing we can do / Oh well (accepting an unavoidable situation)" — that is 어쩔 수 없죠 (eojjeol su eopjyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 비가 오니까 어쩔 수 없죠. ("Well, it's raining, so it can't be helped."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Well, it's raining, so it can't be helped.
usagePhrases.note: -(으)니까 gives the reason the situation is fixed

usagePhrases.en: Can't be helped — let's go next time.
usagePhrases.note: 어쩔 수 없지 = casual

usagePhrases.en: If it's sold out, oh well, nothing to do.
usagePhrases.note: Trailing 뭐 adds a resigned shrug

usagePhrases.en: I had no choice but to take a taxi.
usagePhrases.note: 어쩔 수 없이 = the adverb 'unavoidably'

examples.ko: A: 오늘 문 닫았네요. / B: 어쩔 수 없죠.
examples.romanization: A: oneul mun dadanneyo. / B: eojjeol su eopsjyo.
examples.en: A: They're closed today. B: Oh well, can't be helped.
examples.note: Quick, calm resignation — no blame, no distress, just acceptance

examples.ko: A: 기차표가 다 매진이에요. / B: 그래요? 어쩔 수 없죠, 버스 타죠 뭐.
examples.romanization: A: gichapyoga da maejinieyo. / B: geuraeyo? eojjeol su eopsjyo, beoseu tajyo mwo.
examples.en: A: The train tickets are all sold out. B: Oh well — let's just take the bus then.
examples.note: Graceful acceptance followed immediately by a practical fallback — the -죠 on 버스 타죠 recruits agreement

examples.ko: 몸이 안 좋으면 쉬어야죠, 어쩔 수 없어요.
examples.romanization: momi an joeumyeon swieoyajyo, eojjeol su eopseoyo.
examples.en: If you're not well you have to rest — there's no other way.
examples.note: 어쩔 수 없어요 = flatter, plainer final statement; used when the concession has already been discussed

entries.nuance: Casual-polite phrase for gracefully accepting something outside your control — a verbal shrug built from 어찌하다 ('to do how/what') contracted to 어쩌다 → 어쩔 수 없다 ('there's no way to do anything about it'). The -죠 softens the inevitability with 'right? / don't you agree?' — making the resignation feel communal rather than bitter. The closest near-synonym is 할 수 없죠, nearly interchangeable in most situations. The sharper contrast is with 포기하다 ('to give up'): 어쩔 수 없죠 is passive ACCEPTANCE of a situation that was never in your hands, while 포기하다 is an ACTIVE choice to stop something you could have continued. Tone is everything: said calmly it reads as mature and easygoing; said with a sharp sigh or flat affect, it tips into passive-aggressive 'fine, whatever.' The adverb variant 어쩔 수 없이 is a separate form that modifies verbs ('I unavoidably went') and cannot substitute for the standalone phrase.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't use it about things within your control. Saying 어쩔 수 없죠 about a choice you could make sounds like a dodge — it claims the situation is genuinely out of your hands.
Don't confuse the two forms: 어쩔 수 없죠 (a standalone 'it can't be helped') vs 어쩔 수 없이 (the adverb 'unavoidably' before a verb, e.g. 어쩔 수 없이 갔어요).
Watch the spelling/sound: it's 어쩔 (double ㅉ), not 어절. And 없죠 is pronounced 'eopjyo', a contraction of 없지요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'there is no way to do anything about it' (어쩌다 + -ㄹ 수 없다). Real meaning: a verbal shrug — calm, communal acceptance of something beyond your control. The -죠 ending invites the listener to agree, making the resignation feel shared.
Casual-polite 존댓말 (어쩔 수 없죠 / 없어요). Among friends: 어쩔 수 없지 / 어쩔 수 없어. Fits informal and semi-formal spoken situations. Tone matters: calm = easygoing; flat/sharp = passive-aggressive.

vs 할 수 없죠: nearly interchangeable; both mean 'nothing can be done.' vs 포기하다: 포기하다 is an active CHOICE to quit something you could have pursued; 어쩔 수 없죠 is passive acceptance of a situation that was never in your hands — so use 어쩔 수 없죠 for sold-out tickets, but 포기했어요 for a project you gave up on.

어쩔 수 없죠 (casual-polite) → 어쩔 수 없지 (casual) → 어쩔 수 없어요 (plainer polite statement). Trailing 뭐 (어쩔 수 없죠, 뭐) adds a resigned shrug. The adverb form 어쩔 수 없이 ('unavoidably') modifies verbs and cannot replace the standalone phrase.

Don't use it about situations you actually control — it claims helplessness, so applying it to a choice you could make sounds evasive. Don't swap the two forms: 어쩔 수 없죠 stands alone as an acceptance; 어쩔 수 없이 is an adverb that must precede a verb (어쩔 수 없이 갔어요).

entries.english: Oh, not at all / Don't mention it / Please, you're too kind (humbly deflecting thanks or praise)
entries.shortExplanation: 무슨 말씀을요 is a practical expression meaning "Oh, not at all / Don't mention it / Please, you're too kind (humbly deflecting thanks or praise)".
entries.explanation: 무슨 말씀을요 (museun malsseumeuryo) = "Oh, not at all / Don't mention it / Please, you're too kind (humbly deflecting thanks or praise)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 무슨 말씀을요, 당연히 도와드려야죠. ("Not at all, of course I should help."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Not at all, of course I should help.
usagePhrases.note: Deflecting thanks for a favor; 도와드리다 = humble 'help'

usagePhrases.en: Please, I'm the one who's grateful.
usagePhrases.note: 무슨 말씀을 (no 요) = slightly shorter, still polite

usagePhrases.en: Oh come on, don't say that.
usagePhrases.note: 에이 + the phrase brushes off excessive praise

usagePhrases.en: What do you mean — you're not late at all.
usagePhrases.note: 무슨 말씀이세요 = 'what are you saying?' to gently contradict

examples.ko: A: 감사합니다. / B: 무슨 말씀을요.
examples.romanization: A: gamsahamnida. / B: museun malsseumeuryo.
examples.en: A: Thank you. B: Oh, not at all.
examples.note: Shortest polite deflection — the brief reply conveys 'your thanks are unnecessary'

examples.ko: A: 음식 솜씨가 정말 좋으시네요. / B: 무슨 말씀을요, 별거 아니에요.
examples.romanization: A: eumsik somssiga jeongmal joeusineyo. / B: museun malsseumeuryo, byeolgeo anieyo.
examples.en: A: You're such a great cook. B: Oh, you're too kind — it's nothing really.
examples.note: Deflecting a compliment and adding a modest follow-up; the two moves must be consistent

examples.ko: A: 폐 끼쳐서 죄송해요. / B: 무슨 말씀을요, 괜찮아요. 또 오세요.
examples.romanization: A: pye kkichyeoseo joesonghaeyo. / B: museun malsseumeuryo, gwaenchanayo. tto oseyo.
examples.en: A: Sorry for being a bother. B: Not at all, it's fine — please come again.
examples.note: Host reassuring a guest who apologized; 또 오세요 turns the deflection into a warm invitation

entries.nuance: A polite, animated deflection of thanks or praise, literally 'what words (are you even saying)!' — built on the honorific 말씀 (the respectful elevated form of 말, 'speech/words') so the phrase shows deference to the person praising you. The full underlying structure is 무슨 말씀을 (하세요/하십니까) 'What are you saying?' with the verb dropped for rhetorical brevity. The near-synonym is a flat 아니에요 ('no, it's nothing'), but 무슨 말씀을요 is warmer, more animated, and more deferential — it actively protests on the other person's behalf, making it ideal when speaking to elders, customers, seniors, or anyone you're being especially courteous to. 아니에요 is the neutral everyday choice. After deflecting, the phrase must be followed by something modest (별거 아니에요, 당연한 거죠); deflecting and then accepting the compliment in the same breath is contradictory. Pitfall: you must use 말씀 (honorific), not plain 말 — 무슨 말을요 is awkward and under-polite here.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Use 말씀 (the honorific), not 말. 무슨 말을요 sounds under-polite and slightly wrong; the fixed phrase is 무슨 말씀을요.
Don't deflect and then accept. Saying 무슨 말씀을요 and then 네, 제가 좀 잘하죠 contradicts the humility — follow with modesty like 별거 아니에요.
Don't read it as a literal question demanding an answer. It's a rhetorical deflection, so the other person isn't expected to explain 'what they said.'

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'What words [are you saying]!' (무슨 말씀을 하세요? with verb dropped). Real meaning: 'Your thanks or praise is unnecessary — please don't.' The rhetorical force comes from pretending the thanks itself is so unwarranted it's hard to hear. Uses honorific 말씀 throughout.

Polite 존댓말; best used with elders, seniors, customers, or anyone you're being especially courteous to. 무슨 말씀을 (no 요) is slightly shorter but still polite. Do NOT substitute plain 말 — 무슨 말을요 is under-polite and sounds awkward.

vs 아니에요: 아니에요 is neutral, everyday deflection; 무슨 말씀을요 is warmer, more animated, and more deferential, actively protesting on the other person's behalf. vs 별말씀을요: 별말씀을요 ('don't say such a thing') is a near-equivalent set phrase with the same honorific 말씀; the two are interchangeable in most contexts.
무슨 말씀을요 (standard polite) → 무슨 말씀을 (shorter, still polite) → 무슨 말씀이세요 ('what are you saying?', slightly fuller, used to gently contradict). Pair with modest follow-ups: 별거 아니에요, 당연한 거죠, 제가 더 고맙죠.

You MUST use honorific 말씀, not plain 말 — 무슨 말을요 sounds off and under-polite. Because the phrase DEFLECTS, never immediately follow it by accepting the compliment — that's contradictory and reads as insincere. Always add a modest line after.

entries.english: Don't worry about it / Don't trouble yourself / Never mind it (telling someone to let something go)
entries.shortExplanation: 신경 쓰지 마세요 is a practical expression meaning "Don't worry about it / Don't trouble yourself / Never mind it (telling someone to let something go)".
entries.explanation: 신경 쓰지 마세요 (singyeong sseuji maseyo) means "Don't worry about it / Don't trouble yourself / Never mind it (telling someone to let something go)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 저는 괜찮으니까 신경 쓰지 마세요. ("I'm fine, so please don't worry about it."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: I'm fine, so please don't worry about it.
usagePhrases.note: Reassuring someone after their apology

usagePhrases.en: Don't worry about stuff like that.
usagePhrases.note: 신경 쓰지 마 = casual, to a friend

usagePhrases.ko: 제 건 신경 쓰지 마시고 먼저 드세요.
usagePhrases.romanization: je geon singyeong sseuji masigo meonjeo deuseyo.
usagePhrases.en: Don't bother about mine — go ahead and eat first.
usagePhrases.note: 신경 쓰지 마시고 = 'don't worry, and instead…'

usagePhrases.ko: 남들 말 너무 신경 쓰지 마세요.
usagePhrases.romanization: namdeul mal neomu singyeong sseuji maseyo.
usagePhrases.en: Don't pay so much attention to what others say.
usagePhrases.note: 신경(을) 쓰다 + object = 'mind/worry about X'

examples.ko: A: 제가 깜빡했어요, 죄송해요. / B: 신경 쓰지 마세요.
examples.romanization: A: jega kkamppakaesseoyo, joesonghaeyo. / B: singyeong sseuji maseyo.
examples.en: A: I totally forgot, sorry. B: Don't worry about it.
examples.note: Simple, warm reassurance — the clean short reply puts the other person at ease immediately

examples.ko: A: 자리까지 안 치워서 죄송해요. / B: 신경 쓰지 마세요, 제가 할게요.
examples.romanization: A: jarikkaji an chiwoseo joesonghaeyo. / B: singyeong sseuji maseyo, jega halgeyo.
examples.en: A: Sorry I didn't clear the table. B: Don't worry about it — I'll take care of it.
examples.note: Reassurance followed by a concrete offer; 제가 할게요 removes the obligation entirely

examples.ko: 사소한 일이니까 너무 신경 쓰지 마세요. 다 잘될 거예요.
examples.romanization: sasohan irinikka neomu singyeong sseuji maseyo. da jaldoel geoyeyo.
examples.en: It's a trivial thing, so don't dwell on it — it'll all work out.
examples.note: Comforting someone who's overthinking; 너무 softens the command and 다 잘될 거예요 adds forward reassurance

entries.nuance: Polite-casual reassurance built on the idiom 신경(을) 쓰다 — 신경 (神經: 神 'spirit/nerve' + 經 'channel,' i.e. the body's nerve pathways) + 쓰다 ('to use/expend') — literally 'don't expend your nerves on this.' It tells someone who is apologizing, fussing over you, or anxious about others' opinions to release the mental energy they're spending. The key contrast with 걱정하지 마세요 is temporal: 걱정 is future-facing anxiety ('don't be afraid something bad will happen'), while 신경 쓰다 is present-tense ATTENTION or fuss ('don't pay mental energy to this right now') — so say 걱정하지 마세요 before a frightening event, but 신경 쓰지 마세요 when someone is over-apologizing for a small spill. 신경 쓰지 마 for friends; 신경 쓰지 마시고 to continue into a next clause ('don't worry and [instead] do X'). Adding 너무 ('too much') softens the imperative toward a senior.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
In careful writing, space it: 신경 쓰지 마세요 (신경 and 쓰지 are separate words), not 신경쓰지.
Don't confuse it with 걱정하지 마세요. 신경 쓰지 마세요 = 'don't fuss/pay mind to this now'; 걱정하지 마세요 = 'don't be anxious about an outcome.' They aren't interchangeable.
To a senior, the bare command can sound curt. Soften it: add 너무 (너무 신경 쓰지 마세요) or pair with 괜찮으니까 / 괜찮아요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'don't expend your nerves on this' (神經 = nerve pathways + 쓰다 = to use/spend). Real meaning: 'stop spending mental energy on this — let it go.' Applies to fussing, over-apologizing, or anxiety about others' opinions.

신경 쓰지 마세요 = polite 존댓말. 신경 쓰지 마 = casual, close friends. 신경 쓰지 마시고 = polite, transitions to a follow-up action. To a senior, bare 마세요 can sound slightly curt — soften with 너무 (너무 신경 쓰지 마세요) or pair with 괜찮아요.

vs 걱정하지 마세요: 걱정 = future-facing anxiety about an outcome; 신경 쓰다 = present-tense mental attention or fuss. Say 걱정하지 마세요 before a scary test; say 신경 쓰지 마세요 when someone is over-apologizing for a small spill or dwelling on a trivial slight.
신경 쓰지 마세요 → 너무 신경 쓰지 마세요 (softer, 'don't worry too much') → 신경 쓰지 마시고 먼저 드세요 (chain into next action) → 신경 쓰지 마 (casual). Common collocates: 그런 거 신경 쓰지 마세요, 남들 말 신경 쓰지 마세요.

Standard spelling keeps 신경 and 쓰지 as two separate words (신경 쓰지), not 신경쓰지. Don't swap it with 걱정하지 마세요 in contexts about present fuss — the two aren't interchangeable. A bare command to a senior without 너무 can feel curt.

entries.english: Pretty much / More or less, yeah / You could say that (loosely confirming something as roughly true)
entries.shortExplanation: 그런 셈이죠 is a practical expression meaning "Pretty much / More or less, yeah / You could say that (loosely confirming something as roughly true)".
entries.explanation: "Pretty much / More or less, yeah / You could say that (loosely confirming something as roughly true)" — that is 그런 셈이죠 (geureon semijyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 뭐, 그런 셈이죠. ("Well, more or less, yeah."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Loose confirmation with the hedge 뭐
V-(으)ㄴ 셈이다 = 'amounts to having ~ed'
그런 셈 치다 = 'let's regard it as so', casual
N인 셈이다 = 'amounts to being N'

examples.ko: A: 그럼 거의 다 한 거예요? / B: 네, 그런 셈이죠.
examples.romanization: A: geureom geoui da han geoyeyo? / B: ne, geureon semijyo.
examples.en: A: So you're almost done? B: Yeah, pretty much.
examples.note: Soft 'basically yes' — B avoids an overconfident flat 맞아요

examples.ko: A: 그럼 두 분이 사귀는 거예요? / B: 뭐… 그런 셈이죠.
examples.romanization: A: geureom du buni sagwineun geoyeyo? / B: mwo… geureon semijyo.
examples.en: A: So you two are dating? B: Well… more or less, yeah.
examples.note: Half-admitting a relationship — the hedge 뭐 + 그런 셈이죠 deflects a direct yes while still confirming

examples.ko: 하루 종일 일했으니 쉰 날이 없는 셈이에요.
examples.romanization: haru jongil ilhaesseuni swin nari eopsneun semieyo.
examples.en: I worked all day, so it's basically like I had no day off.
examples.note: 셈이다 recalculates the situation: you 'count as' having had no break; this structure V-(으)ㄴ 셈이다 is extremely productive

entries.nuance: Casual-polite phrase for confirming something as approximately true when it isn't 100% exact — 'in effect, that's the case.' It comes from 셈, a native Korean noun meaning 'reckoning/calculation' (from 세다, 'to count'), so X인/은 셈이다 literally 'it counts/reckons as X.' The -죠 ending softens the assertion with a 'right? / would you agree?' feel. The critical contrast with 맞아요 is precision: 맞아요 asserts an exact factual 'that's correct,' while 그런 셈이죠 always signals 'for practical purposes, approximately' — use 맞아요 to confirm a street address, but 그런 셈이죠 to answer 'so you've basically settled in Korea now?' Saying 그런 셈이죠 when someone expects a definite yes sounds evasive. Pitfall: the phrase uses 셈 (reckoning), not the homophone 샘 (a spring, or jealousy) — writing 그런 샘이죠 is simply wrong.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
For a firm, exact 'yes,' use 맞아요 or 네 — 그런 셈이죠 always means 'roughly/effectively,' so it can sound evasive if the answer is actually definite.
Don't confuse 셈 (reckoning/count) with 샘 (a spring, or jealousy). The phrase is 그런 셈이죠, never 그런 샘이죠.
Keep the modifier 인/은: it's N인 셈이다 and V-(으)ㄴ 셈이다. Dropping it (그런 셈 vs 사장 셈) breaks the structure; say 사장님인 셈이죠.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'it is the reckoning/count of that' (셈 = reckoning, from 세다 'to count'). Real meaning: 'for practical purposes, you could say that' — agreement that holds approximately, not exactly. The -죠 softens the assertion into an invitation to concur.
Casual-polite; fits spoken conversations with colleagues, friends, or mild-formal contexts. 그런 셈이에요 is slightly flatter and less inviting than -죠. 그런 셈 치자 is casual — 'let's just count it as that.'

vs 맞아요: 맞아요 asserts a precise fact; 그런 셈이죠 acknowledges something as true only approximately or 'effectively.' vs 뭐, 그렇죠: 뭐, 그렇죠 is a bare casual 'well, yeah' with less grammatical commitment; 그런 셈이죠 uses the 셈이다 construction, giving it a slightly richer 'reckoning/counting' nuance.
그런 셈이죠 (casual-polite) → 그런 셈이에요 (plain polite) → 그런 셈이야 (casual) → 그런 셈 치자 (casual, 'let's just call it that'). Productive extension: V-(으)ㄴ 셈이다 (e.g. 다 끝난 셈이다), N인 셈이다 (e.g. 사장님인 셈이죠).

For a definite exact 'yes,' use 맞아요 or 네, not 그런 셈이죠 — the latter sounds evasive when precision is expected. Homophone trap: it's 셈 (reckoning), not 샘 (a water spring / jealousy); writing 그런 샘이죠 is simply incorrect.

entries.english: That's a bit… (uhh) / Hmm, that might be hard… (polite, trailing-off refusal or hesitation)
entries.shortExplanation: 그건 좀… is a practical expression meaning "That's a bit… (uhh) / Hmm, that might be hard… (polite, trailing-off refusal or hesitation)".
entries.explanation: 그건 좀… (geugeon jom…) = "That's a bit… (uhh) / Hmm, that might be hard… (polite, trailing-off refusal or hesitation)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 음… 그건 좀 어려울 것 같은데요. ("Umm… that might be a little difficult."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.ko: 음… 그건 좀 어려울 것 같은데요.
usagePhrases.romanization: eum… geugeon jom eoryeoul geot gateundeyo.
usagePhrases.en: Umm… that might be a little difficult.
usagePhrases.note: Spelling out the trailed-off hesitation in full
Left unfinished on purpose — the 'no' is implied

usagePhrases.en: That's kind of… not great, don't you think?
usagePhrases.note: 그건 좀 그렇다 = the set phrase 'that's kind of iffy'
Same trailing pattern with any noun + 좀

examples.ko: A: 이거 어때요? / B: 음, 그건 좀….
examples.romanization: A: igeo eottaeyo? / B: eum, geugeon jom….
examples.en: A: How about this one? B: Hmm, that's kind of…
examples.note: Softly signaling 'no' to a suggestion; the pause and trailing voice do the full communicative work

examples.ko: A: 오늘 밤에 시간 돼요? / B: 아, 오늘은 좀….
examples.romanization: A: oneul bame sigan dwaeyo? / B: a, oneureun jom….
examples.en: A: Are you free tonight? B: Ah, tonight is a bit…
examples.note: Declining an invite without a hard 'no'; A is expected to understand and drop it — pushing for a reason would be considered rude

examples.ko: A: 같이 투자하자는 건 좀… 죄송해요. / B: 아 네, 알겠어요.
examples.romanization: A: gachi tujahajaneun geon jom… joesonghaeyo. / B: a ne, algesseoyo.
examples.en: A: Investing together is, well… a bit hard. Sorry. / B: Ah, I see.
examples.note: Refusing a real proposal with 죄송해요 added for warmth; B's 알겠어요 shows the refusal was received without pressing

entries.nuance: A highly Korean indirect refusal: you trail off after 좀 ('a little') and let the silence and pause carry the 'no,' because saying it aloud (싫어요 'I don't like it' / 안 돼요 'can't do it') would feel confrontational and cause both sides to lose face. 좀 is a softened contraction of 조금 ('a little'), used here as a hedging cushion rather than a quantity. The fundamental contrast with 안 돼요 is the whole cultural lesson: 안 돼요 is a clear, direct refusal; 그건 좀… deliberately leaves the refusal unspoken to preserve harmony — in Korean communication, what you don't say is often as important as what you do. It works at all registers, with tone, a small wince or head-tilt, and the pause together doing the communicative work. Pitfall: English speakers often fail to register this as a refusal and keep pushing — in Korea that is considered pushy and awkward, because the message has already been delivered.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't finish it bluntly with 싫어요 ('I hate it') or a hard 안 돼요 — that defeats the whole face-saving point. The trailing silence IS the refusal.
Don't miss it as a refusal. English speakers hear an unfinished sentence and keep pushing; in Korea 그건 좀… reliably means 'no, but I'm being polite about it.'
Keep 좀 as the hinge: it's 그건 좀… (with 좀), not 그건… alone. The 좀 is what flags the soft, hedged tone.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'that is a little [left unsaid].' Real meaning: an indirect 'no' where the refusal is communicated through what is NOT said. The trailing sentence with 좀 is itself the complete message; face-saving silence replaces the explicit negative. 좀 = contraction of 조금 ('a little'), used here as a hedge.

Works at all speech levels — both casual and polite — because the softening comes from tone, pause, and facial expression, not from honorifics. Add 죄송해요 after the trail-off for extra warmth. Works best in spoken conversation; in writing it needs more spelling out.

vs 안 돼요: 안 돼요 is a clear, direct refusal; 그건 좀… preserves both sides' face by leaving the negative unspoken. vs 좀 어려울 것 같은데요: the 'spelled-out' version that names the difficulty explicitly, slightly softer than 안 돼요 but no longer a pure trail-off.

그건 좀… (the classic trail-off) → 그건 좀 어려울 것 같은데요 (fuller, less indirect) → 그건 좀 그렇지 않아요? (set phrase: 'that's a bit iffy, don't you think?') → [noun]이/가 좀… (same pattern applied to any subject: 가격이 좀…).

English speakers often don't recognize this as a refusal and push for clarification — in Korea that's considered rude, because the message has been delivered. Do NOT 'helpfully' finish the sentence with 싫어요 or 안 돼요; that bluntness destroys the face-saving purpose. The 좀 is load-bearing: 그건… alone without 좀 lacks the hedging signal.

entries.english: No way! / That's ridiculous / You've got to be kidding (disbelief, shock, or 'that makes no sense')
entries.shortExplanation: 말도 안 돼요 is a practical expression meaning "No way! / That's ridiculous / You've got to be kidding (disbelief, shock, or 'that makes no sense')".
entries.explanation: 말도 안 돼요 (maldo an dwaeyo) means "No way! / That's ridiculous / You've got to be kidding (disbelief, shock, or 'that makes no sense')". Say it as one set phrase — for example 진짜요? 말도 안 돼요! ("Really? No way!"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Shocked reaction to surprising news

usagePhrases.ko: 말도 안 돼, 그게 어떻게 가능해?
usagePhrases.romanization: maldo an dwae, geuge eotteoke ganeunghae?
usagePhrases.en: That's absurd — how is that even possible?
usagePhrases.note: 말도 안 돼 = casual
Calling something unreasonable; -죠 invites agreement

usagePhrases.ko: 말도 안 되는 소리 하지 마.
usagePhrases.romanization: maldo an doeneun sori haji ma.
usagePhrases.note: 말도 안 되는 + noun = 'nonsensical ~'

examples.ko: A: 내일 시험이래요. / B: 네? 말도 안 돼요!
examples.romanization: A: naeil siheomiraeyo. / B: ne? maldo an dwaeyo!
examples.en: A: They say the test is tomorrow. B: What? No way!
examples.note: Quick disbelief at bad news — 네? starts as an incredulous echo before the exclamation

examples.ko: A: 그 식당 한 시간 기다려야 한대요. / B: 한 시간이요? 말도 안 돼요!
examples.romanization: A: geu sikdang han sigan gidaryeoya handaeyo. / B: han siganiyo? maldo an dwaeyo!
examples.en: A: They say you wait an hour at that place. B: An hour? That's ridiculous!
examples.note: Indignant disbelief; the repeated noun echo (한 시간이요?) shows B can't process the information

examples.ko: 복권 당첨됐다고? 말도 안 돼! 진짜야?
examples.romanization: bokgwon dangcheomdwaetdago? maldo an dwae! jinjjaya?
examples.en: You won the lottery? No way! For real?
examples.note: Happy, excited shock with a close friend — tone here is delighted, not angry, showing the phrase covers both ends of the emotion spectrum

entries.nuance: A high-emotion exclamation literally meaning 'it doesn't even become words' — 말 ('words/speech') + 도 ('even') + 안 되다 ('doesn't come about/work') — i.e., something is so absurd or stunning it can't be processed into logical language. It spans happy shock, indignation, and 'that's nonsensical' depending entirely on tone and context. The contrast with 진짜요? / 정말요? is the dividing line: those phrases merely request confirmation ('really?'), while 말도 안 돼요 has already JUDGED the thing as impossible or outrageous — so you typically hear 진짜요? 말도 안 돼요! together, where 진짜요 checks and 말도 안 돼요 reacts. Speech level: 말도 안 돼 among friends; 말도 안 돼요 in polite speech. Pitfall: aim the phrase at a SITUATION or statement, never at a person — unlike English 'you're ridiculous,' which targets character, 말도 안 돼요 targets what was said.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spacing and spelling: it's 말도 안 돼요 with 안 written separately, and 돼요 (from 되다 + 어요), never 되요.

Don't aim it at a person ('you're ridiculous'). 말도 안 돼요 judges a statement or situation; pointing it at someone's character sounds like an insult — say 그건 말도 안 돼요 ('that's ridiculous') about the claim.
Don't use it as a neutral 'really?'. To simply confirm surprising news, use 진짜요? / 정말요?; 말도 안 돼요 already declares the thing impossible.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'words don't even come about (for this)' (말 + 도 + 안 되다). Real meaning: 'this is so absurd/stunning it defies language.' Covers both positive shock (winning the lottery) and negative indignation (outrageous prices) — tone and context decide which.

말도 안 돼 = casual, close friends. 말도 안 돼요 = polite speech. 말도 안 되죠 = polite with a 'right?' invitation for the listener to agree. 말도 안 되는 소리 = 'nonsensical talk,' noun-modifying form. Avoid using it toward a person's character — aim it at claims or situations.

vs 진짜요? / 정말요?: those just ask 'really?' (seeking confirmation); 말도 안 돼요 has already JUDGED the situation as impossible or outrageous. In practice they combine: 진짜요? 말도 안 돼요! vs 황당하다: 황당하다 ('absurd/preposterous') is more formal and literary; 말도 안 돼요 is the punchy everyday spoken reaction.
말도 안 돼 (casual) → 말도 안 돼요 (polite) → 말도 안 되죠 (polite + 'right?') → 말도 안 되는 소리 하지 마 ('don't talk nonsense'). Intensify: 이건 진짜 말도 안 돼요. Noun form: 말도 안 되는 일 ('an absurd thing').

Spelling/spacing: 말도 안 돼요 — 안 is a separate word and 돼요 comes from 되다 + 어요 (never 되요). Aim it at a situation or statement, not a person — 말도 안 돼요 said directly TO someone attacks a claim, not their character; using it like English 'you're ridiculous' sounds like an insult in Korean.

entries.english: I knew it / I figured as much / I had a feeling (this would happen)
entries.shortExplanation: 그럴 줄 알았어요 is a practical expression meaning "I knew it / I figured as much / I had a feeling (this would happen)".
entries.explanation: "I knew it / I figured as much / I had a feeling (this would happen)" — that is 그럴 줄 알았어요 (geureol jul arasseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 거봐요, 그럴 줄 알았어요. ("See? I knew it."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 거봐요 ('see, told you') pairs naturally

usagePhrases.ko: 그럴 줄 알았어, 네가 또 늦을 줄.
usagePhrases.romanization: geureol jul arasseo, nega tto neujeul jul.
usagePhrases.en: I knew it — that you'd be late again.
usagePhrases.note: 그럴 줄 알았어 = casual

usagePhrases.en: I knew it would turn out like this.
usagePhrases.note: V-(으)ㄹ 줄 알았다 = 'expected/knew that ~ would happen'
Opposite: 몰랐어요 = 'didn't know/expect'

examples.ko: A: 길이 막혀서 늦었어요. / B: 그럴 줄 알았어요.
examples.romanization: A: giri makyeoseo neujeosseoyo. / B: geureol jul arasseoyo.
examples.en: A: I was late because of traffic. B: I figured.
examples.note: Calm 'I expected that'; the flat delivery means sympathy, not accusation

examples.ko: A: 그 가게 망했대요. / B: 그럴 줄 알았어요, 손님이 없더라고요.
examples.romanization: A: geu gage manghaetdaeyo. / B: geureol jul arasseoyo, sonnimi eopsdeoragoyo.
examples.en: A: That shop went under. B: I figured — there were never any customers.
examples.note: -더라고요 adds recalled first-hand evidence that supports the prediction B had made

examples.ko: 역시 비가 오네, 그럴 줄 알았어. 우산 챙기길 잘했다.
examples.romanization: yeoksi biga one, geureol jul arasseo. usan chaenggigil jalhaetda.
examples.en: Of course it's raining — I had a feeling. Good thing I brought an umbrella.
examples.note: 역시 ('as expected') reinforces the sense of a confirmed prediction; 챙기길 잘했다 rewards the foresight

entries.nuance: Casual-polite phrase for 'this is exactly what I predicted,' built on the grammar V-(으)ㄹ 줄 알다 — 줄 here is a bound noun meaning roughly 'the fact/way that,' creating a structure 'I knew the way it would be.' The critical distinction to master is 그럴 줄 vs 그런 줄: 그럴 줄 알았어요 (future-oriented 그럴) = 'I correctly predicted this would happen'; 그런 줄 알았어요 (descriptive 그런) = 'I had assumed that was the case' — and the latter is very frequently used when the assumption was WRONG ('oh, I thought it was like that but…'). Pairs naturally with 거봐요 and 역시. Tone entirely controls reception: said gently it's knowing warmth or mild sympathy; said flatly after someone's bad news it becomes a smug 'told you so,' which in Korean social settings is considered cold — always add a warming element when the other person is hurting.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
줄 here means 'the fact/way that,' a grammar marker — not 줄 'a line/rope.' Don't translate 그럴 줄 알았어요 literally; it means 'I knew it would be so.'
Don't confuse 그럴 줄 알았어요 ('I correctly predicted this') with 그런 줄 알았어요 ('I'd assumed that — often mistakenly'). The 그럴 vs 그런 flips the meaning.
After someone's bad luck, a flat 그럴 줄 알았어 sounds like a smug 'told you so.' Add empathy (아이고, 그럴 줄 알았어요…) or soften it.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I knew the way/fact it would be so' (V-(으)ㄹ 줄 알다: 줄 = bound noun for 'the fact/way'). Real meaning: 'I had correctly predicted this outcome.' The 줄 is a grammar marker, NOT the homophone 줄 meaning 'rope/line.'

그럴 줄 알았어요 = casual-polite. 그럴 줄 알았어 = casual, close friends. 그럴 줄 알았죠 = polite, inviting light agreement. Pairs naturally with 거봐요 ('see?'), 역시 ('as expected'). Said after someone's misfortune without warmth = smug 'told you so' — add empathy or soften.

vs 그런 줄 알았어요: 그럴 줄 = predicted correctly; 그런 줄 = assumed (often mistakenly). These two are the most important pair to distinguish. vs 예상했어요: 예상했어요 ('I anticipated it') is more neutral and factual; 그럴 줄 알았어요 carries a warmer, more spoken 'I just knew it' feel.
그럴 줄 알았어요 (polite) → 그럴 줄 알았어 (casual) → 그럴 줄 알았죠 (polite + soft agreement-seek). Opposite: 그럴 줄 몰랐어요 ('I didn't expect that'). Extension: N/V이렇게 될 줄 알았어요 ('I knew it would end up like this').

줄 here is a grammar bound noun meaning 'the fact/way that' — NOT 줄 'a rope/line.' Don't confuse 그럴 줄 알았어요 (correct prediction) with 그런 줄 알았어요 (often a mistaken assumption). After someone's bad luck, flat delivery = smug 'told you so'; soften with 아이고, 그럴 줄 알았어요… + empathy.

entries.english: No pressure / Don't feel obligated / Please don't feel burdened (about a gift, favor, or invitation)
entries.shortExplanation: 부담 갖지 마세요 is a practical expression meaning "No pressure / Don't feel obligated / Please don't feel burdened (about a gift, favor, or invitation)".
entries.explanation: 부담 갖지 마세요 (budam gatji maseyo) = "No pressure / Don't feel obligated / Please don't feel burdened (about a gift, favor, or invitation)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 그냥 작은 선물이니까 부담 갖지 마세요. ("It's just a small gift, so please don't feel burdened."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.ko: 그냥 작은 선물이니까 부담 갖지 마세요.
usagePhrases.romanization: geunyang jageun seonmurinikka budam gatji maseyo.
usagePhrases.en: It's just a small gift, so please don't feel burdened.
usagePhrases.note: When handing someone a present

usagePhrases.en: Don't stress about it, just come comfortably.
usagePhrases.note: 부담 갖지 말고 = casual, inviting a friend

usagePhrases.en: If it feels like too much, you don't have to.
usagePhrases.note: 부담스럽다 = 'to feel burdensome'

usagePhrases.en: I'm not trying to pressure you.
usagePhrases.note: 부담(을) 주다 = 'to put pressure on'

examples.ko: 이거 받아요. 부담 갖지 마세요.
examples.romanization: igeo badayo. budam gatji maseyo.
examples.en: Here, take this. No pressure.
examples.note: Short, warm release when giving a gift; 받아요 is the gentle nudge, 부담 갖지 마세요 removes the sense of debt

examples.ko: A: 이렇게 비싼 걸 어떻게 받아요. / B: 부담 갖지 마세요, 제 마음이에요.
examples.romanization: A: ireoke bissan geol eotteoke badayo. / B: budam gatji maseyo, je maeumieyo.
examples.en: A: How can I accept something this expensive? B: No pressure — it's just my way of showing I care.
examples.note: Easing a reluctant gift recipient; 제 마음이에요 ('it's from my heart') reframes it as an expression of feeling, not an obligation

examples.ko: 식사 한번 대접하고 싶어서요. 부담 갖지 마시고 시간 되실 때 오세요.
examples.romanization: siksa hanbeon daejeopago sipeoseoyo. budam gatji masigo sigan doesil ttae oseyo.
examples.en: I'd like to treat you to a meal. No pressure — just come whenever you're free.
examples.note: Polite invitation that pre-empts the social obligation Korean dinners can carry; 부담 갖지 마시고 + action is a common chaining structure

entries.nuance: Polite-casual phrase that explicitly releases the other person from a sense of social debt, built on 부담 (負擔: 負 'to bear/carry' + 擔 'to shoulder a load' → burden/obligation) plus 갖다 ('to hold/have') — literally 'don't hold the burden.' This phrase matters in Korea because gifts, favors, and dinners automatically activate the expectation of reciprocity (정/체면/은혜 dynamics), and saying 부담 갖지 마세요 signals that the giver is NOT expecting anything back. The contrast with 걱정하지 마세요 is clean: 걱정하지 마세요 calms anxiety about a future OUTCOME, while 부담 갖지 마세요 lifts a feeling of OBLIGATION or indebtedness — a different social layer entirely. 부담 갖지 마 for friends; 부담 갖지 마시고 chains into what you should do instead. One important caution: saying it once warmly is enough — repeating it can ironically increase the other person's sense that they really owe you.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
The verb is 갖다 (to have/hold), so it's 부담 갖지 마세요, literally 'don't hold the burden.' 부담 하지 마세요 with 하다 is wrong.
Don't confuse it with 걱정하지 마세요. 부담 갖지 마세요 lifts a sense of obligation/debt; 걱정하지 마세요 calms anxiety about an outcome.
Don't over-insist. Repeating 부담 갖지 마세요 several times can ironically ADD pressure — say it once, warmly, and let it land.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'don't hold the burden' (負擔 = load one shoulders + 갖다 = to hold). Real meaning: 'don't feel socially indebted to me.' In Korean social culture, receiving a gift or favor can create an obligation to reciprocate — this phrase explicitly waives that expectation.

부담 갖지 마세요 = polite 존댓말, for elders, seniors, acquaintances. 부담 갖지 마 = casual, close friends. 부담 갖지 마시고 + V = polite chain: 'no pressure, and please [do X instead].' Most natural when giving gifts, extending invitations, or asking favors.

vs 걱정하지 마세요: 걱정하지 마세요 calms anxiety about a future outcome; 부담 갖지 마세요 lifts the feeling of obligation or debt — a different social concern. vs 편하게 생각하세요 ('think of it casually/comfortably'): similar purpose but softer and more general; 부담 갖지 마세요 is more direct about removing the sense of owing.

부담 갖지 마세요 (standard polite) → 부담 갖지 마 (casual) → 부담 갖지 마시고 먼저 [드세요/가세요] (chained) → 부담스러우시면 안 하셔도 돼요 (giving explicit permission to decline). Related: 부담(을) 주다 = 'to place a burden on someone'; 부담스럽다 = 'to feel burdensome.'
The verb is 갖다 ('hold'), so it's 부담 갖지 마세요, not 부담 하지 마세요 (wrong verb). Don't repeat it multiple times — saying it again and again paradoxically adds pressure. Say it once, sincerely, and move on.

entries.english: to be quick to read the room / perceptive about how others feel (lit. 'one's nunchi is fast')
