entries.shortExplanation: 눈치가 빠르다 is a practical expression meaning "to be quick to read the room / perceptive about how others feel (lit. 'one's nunchi is fast')".
entries.explanation: 눈치가 빠르다 (nunchiga ppareuda) means "to be quick to read the room / perceptive about how others feel (lit. 'one's nunchi is fast')". Say it as one set phrase — for example 눈치가 빠르다 ("to be quick on the uptake"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: to be quick on the uptake
usagePhrases.note: The whole idiom; 눈치 takes 가, never 를, with 빠르다. To pay a compliment to a friend: 너 진짜 눈치 빠르다 — to a senior: 눈치가 빠르시네요.

usagePhrases.en: to catch on / pick up on something
usagePhrases.note: Here 눈치 takes 를 — sensing a hidden fact, e.g. 선물인 걸 눈치챘어 ('I caught on it was a gift'). This is the moment of realizing, not the standing trait.
Watching a person's face to gauge their reaction; can sound timid or subservient, e.g. 상사 눈치를 보다 ('keep checking the boss's mood') — not a compliment.
The direct opposite — missing social cues entirely; 눈치 없이 끼어들다 = butt in without reading the room. 눈치(가) 보이다 is yet another: 'to feel self-conscious / sense I'm being judged.'

examples.ko: 우리 강아지는 눈치가 빨라.
examples.romanization: uri gangajineun nunchiga ppalla.
examples.en: Our dog is quick to read the mood.
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject + 눈치가 빨라; works even for pets, who sense your mood — shows the idiom isn't limited to clever people.

examples.ko: A: 나 아무 말도 안 했는데 어떻게 알았어? / B: 딱 보면 알지, 내가 눈치가 좀 빨라.
examples.romanization: A: na amu maldo an haenneunde eotteoke arasseo? / B: ttak bomyeon alji, naega nunchiga jom ppalla.
examples.en: A: I didn't say a word — how'd you know? / B: I can just tell; I'm pretty perceptive.
examples.note: A/B turn: 딱 보면 알지 ('I can tell at a glance') is the natural brag that pairs with 눈치가 빠르다 when someone reads you without being told.

examples.ko: 여기선 눈치가 빨라야 살아남아요.
examples.romanization: yeogiseon nunchiga ppallaya saranamayo.
examples.en: Around here you've got to be quick on the uptake to survive.
examples.note: Real office-survival nuance; 눈치가 빨라야 = 'you must be perceptive' (the -아야 'must' frame), hinting that Korean workplaces reward reading unspoken cues.

entries.nuance: 눈치 is the Korean 'social radar' for reading unspoken cues — the mood in a room, what someone really means, when to back off — and 빠르다 ('fast') frames you as catching all that quickly, so it's a warm compliment for being tactful and socially sharp. You say it about a friend, a sharp junior at work, even a perceptive child, and it is safe across registers: 너 눈치 빠르다 to a friend, 눈치가 빠르시네요 to someone you respect. Distinguish it from 똑똑하다 ('smart/book-clever'): 똑똑하다 is raw intelligence, while 눈치가 빠르다 is interpersonal sensitivity — a person can be 똑똑하지만 눈치가 없다 (brainy yet socially oblivious). Its nearest sibling expression 분위기 파악을 잘하다 ('reads the atmosphere well') overlaps but is more about group situations, whereas 눈치 빠르다 also covers reading one individual. Forms range from the bare brag 눈치 빠르다 up to honorific 눈치가 빠르시네요, and it pairs habitually with 금방 알아채다 (notice right away). The big English-speaker pitfall is treating 눈치 as eyesight because of 눈 ('eye') — it is social awareness, not vision — and using the wrong particle: it must be 눈치'가' 빠르다, whereas 'to catch on' is 눈치'를' 채다, and 'to anxiously gauge someone' is 눈치'를' 보다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't translate it as 'fast eyes' or link it to good vision — 눈치 means reading social atmosphere, despite containing 눈 ('eye'). It is mental/social, never about how well you physically see.
Particle error: people say 눈치를 빠르다, but the idiom is 눈치'가' 빠르다 because 빠르다 is an adjective. Use 를 only with the action verbs 채다/보다 (눈치를 채다 = catch on).

눈치가 빠르다 (perceptive, a compliment) ≠ 눈치를 보다 (nervously watching someone's reaction, often timid/subservient). They are not interchangeable and carry opposite vibes — one praises sharpness, the other hints at anxiety.

structuredNuance.t: 눈치 is the Korean 'social radar' for reading unspoken cues — the mood in a room, what someone really means, when to back off — and 빠르다 ('fast') frames you as catching all that quickly, so it's a warm compliment for being tactful and socially sharp. It pairs habitually with 분위기를 파악하다 (grasp the atmosphere) and 금방 알아채다 (notice right away).

Use it as praise — about a friend, a sharp junior, a perceptive child. It works at every level: casual 너 눈치 빠르다 to a friend, honorific 눈치가 빠르시네요 to someone senior. There is no register danger here; it is almost always welcome because it flatters someone's social intelligence. The only caution is tone — said sarcastically (눈치 빠르네…) about someone who exploited a cue, it can turn into a jab.

Distinguish it from 똑똑하다 ('smart/book-clever'): 똑똑하다 is raw intelligence, while 눈치가 빠르다 is interpersonal sensitivity — one can be 똑똑하지만 눈치가 없다 (brainy yet socially oblivious). Its sibling expression 분위기 파악을 잘하다 leans toward reading a group's mood, while 눈치 빠르다 also covers reading one person; 센스 있다 ('to have sense') is the warmer, more general cousin for thoughtful tact.

Scale from the bare brag 눈치 빠르다, to polite 눈치가 빨라요, to honorific 눈치가 빠르시네요. Switch the particle to shift meaning entirely: 눈치를 채다 (catch on to a fact), 눈치를 보다 (anxiously gauge someone), 눈치가 없다 (oblivious — the opposite), 눈치가 보이다 (feel self-conscious about onlookers).

The big pitfall is treating 눈치 as eyesight because of 눈 ('eye') — it is social awareness, not vision — and using the wrong particle: it must be 눈치'가' 빠르다, whereas 'to catch on' is 눈치'를' 채다, and 'to anxiously gauge someone' is 눈치'를' 보다. English has no single word for 눈치, so don't force 'tactful' or 'clever' onto it — it is its own concept of cue-reading.

entries.english: to be well-connected / know a lot of people (lit. 'one's feet are wide')
entries.shortExplanation: 발이 넓다 is a practical expression meaning "to be well-connected / know a lot of people (lit. 'one's feet are wide')".
entries.explanation: "to be well-connected / know a lot of people (lit. 'one's feet are wide')" — that is 발이 넓다 (bari neolda). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 발이 넓다 ("to be well-connected"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: The full idiom; 발 takes 이/은, and the adjective is 넓다 ('wide'). 발이 참 넓으시네요 = polite admiration of someone's reach.

usagePhrases.en: a well-connected person / a social hub
usagePhrases.note: Attributive 넓은 + noun; the go-to way to describe a networker who knows everybody and can connect people.
The opposite ('narrow feet') — knowing hardly anyone; 나는 발이 좁아서 = 'I don't know many people, so…' (a humble self-deprecation).
Near-synonym EXPRESSION using 인맥 (人脈, 'people-vein'); slightly more formal/business-flavored than the warmer, idiomatic 발이 넓다.

examples.ko: 우리 삼촌은 발이 넓어요.
examples.romanization: uri samchoneun bari neolbeoyo.
examples.en: My uncle knows a lot of people.
examples.note: Plain frame: subject + 발이 넓어요; states the trait neutrally as a simple fact about someone.

examples.ko: 일자리 알아보는 거면 발 넓은 선배한테 물어봐.
examples.romanization: iljari araboneun geomyeon bal neolbeun seonbaehante mureobwa.
examples.en: If you're job-hunting, ask that senior who knows everyone.
examples.note: Everyday: drop 이 in casual speech (발 넓은) and tap a connector for help — the idiom's most practical use is pointing to a useful person.

examples.ko: A: 그 사람 소개 좀 받을 수 있을까? / B: 민수한테 부탁해 봐, 걔가 발이 넓잖아.
examples.romanization: A: geu saram sogae jom badeul su isseulkka? / B: minsuhante butakae bwa, gyaega bari neolbjana.
examples.en: A: Could you get me an introduction to them? / B: Try asking Minsu — you know he's super well-connected.
examples.note: A/B turn: 걔가 발이 넓잖아 ('he's well-connected, you know') is exactly how Koreans steer you to the person who can introduce you.

entries.nuance: Literally 'wide feet,' the image is of feet that have walked into many circles, so it means having a broad social network — lots of acquaintances across different groups. It is a compliment about reach, used when someone seems to know people everywhere or could get you an introduction; register is neutral, fine in casual 발 넓네 and polite 발이 넓으시네요 alike, and there is no one you'd offend by saying it. Its sharper near-synonym expression is 인맥(人脈)이 넓다, where 인맥 ('person-vein,' a Sino-Korean word picturing connections as veins) names the network explicitly and sounds a touch more formal or business-flavored; 발이 넓다 is the warmer, more idiomatic everyday version, while 마당발 ('wide-foot person') is the noun nickname for such a connector. Natural partners: 모르는 사람이 없다 (there's nobody they don't know), 소개를 받다/시켜 주다 (get/give introductions). The key English-speaker pitfall is reading it literally (it has nothing to do with foot size) and confusing breadth with depth: 발이 넓다 means you know MANY people, not that you have many CLOSE friends — for true intimacy Koreans would say 친한 친구가 많다 instead. The opposite is 발이 좁다 ('narrow feet'), not 발이 작다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
It has nothing to do with literal foot size; never read 발이 넓다 as a physical description of someone's feet.
Don't use it for close friendships — it means a wide circle of ACQUAINTANCES, not many best friends. For that, say 친한 친구가 많다. Breadth, not depth.
The opposite is 발이 좁다 ('narrow feet'), not 발이 작다 ('small feet'). Picking the antonym by literal size breaks the idiom.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'wide feet,' the image is of feet that have walked into many circles, so it means having a broad social network — lots of acquaintances across different groups. It is a compliment about reach. Natural partners: 모르는 사람이 없다 (there's nobody they don't know), 소개를 받다/시켜 주다 (get/give introductions), 마당발이다 (be a connector).

Use it admiringly when someone seems to know people everywhere or could connect you to others. Register is neutral and safe: 발 넓네 to a friend, 발이 넓으시네요 to someone senior. It is a flattering observation, so there's no one it would offend — though if said with a wry tone it can imply 'always out networking,' so let context stay friendly.

Its sharper near-synonym expression is 인맥(人脈)이 넓다, where 인맥 ('person-vein') names the network explicitly and sounds more formal/business-flavored; 발이 넓다 is the warmer everyday version. The noun nickname for such a person is 마당발 ('wide-foot'), as in 걔는 완전 마당발이야. None of these imply close friendship — only reach.

Shift the adjective for the antonym: 발이 좁다 ('narrow feet' = few connections). Use the attributive 발 넓은 사람 to describe someone, the noun 마당발 to nickname them, and 인맥이 넓다 for a more formal phrasing. Honorific: 발이 넓으시다.

The key pitfall is reading it literally (it has nothing to do with foot size) and confusing breadth with depth: 발이 넓다 means you know MANY people, not that you have many CLOSE friends — for true intimacy say 친한 친구가 많다. The opposite is 발이 좁다, not 발이 작다 ('small feet').

entries.english: to be generous / cook or give in large quantities (lit. 'one's hands are big')
entries.shortExplanation: 손이 크다 is a practical expression meaning "to be generous / cook or give in large quantities (lit. 'one's hands are big')".
entries.explanation: 손이 크다 (soni keuda) = "to be generous / cook or give in large quantities (lit. 'one's hands are big')". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 손이 크다 ("to be generous (esp. with food/spending)"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Full idiom; 손 takes 이, adjective is 크다 ('big'). 우리 엄마 손 커 = my mom always makes/gives a lot of food.
Attributive 큰 + 사람; common compliment for a host who over-caters or a friend who always treats.

usagePhrases.en: to be stingy / always prepare too little
usagePhrases.note: Opposite ('small hands') — skimping on portions or money; 손이 작아서 늘 모자라 = always runs short at the table.
Verb collocation: 크게 쓰다 = lay out money freely on others, e.g. 오늘은 손 크게 쓸게 ('I'll splurge today / it's on me').

examples.ko: 우리 엄마는 손이 커요.
examples.romanization: uri eommaneun soni keoyo.
examples.en: My mom is generous (cooks a lot).
examples.note: Plain frame; defaults to the cooking-amount reading — she always makes far more than needed.

examples.ko: 손이 크신 분이라 선물도 늘 푸짐해요.
examples.romanization: soni keusin bunira seonmuldo neul pujimhaeyo.
examples.en: She's generous, so her gifts are always lavish.
examples.note: Everyday: honorific 크신 + 푸짐하다 (plentiful) — shows the idiom extends from food to gift-giving generosity.

examples.ko: A: 이걸 다 어떻게 먹어, 다섯 명인데! / B: 엄마가 손이 크셔서 항상 이래.
examples.romanization: A: igeol da eotteoke meogeo, daseon myeonginde! / B: eommaga soni keusyeoseo hangsang irae.
examples.en: A: How are we supposed to eat all this — there's only five of us! / B: Mom's so generous with food, it's always like this.
examples.note: A/B turn: the classic Korean dinner-table moment; 손이 크셔서 항상 이래 explains the overflowing table with fond exasperation.

entries.nuance: Literally 'big hands,' the picture is of hands that scoop out a lot at once, so it praises generosity — especially cooking in big batches or spending freely to feed and host others. It carries a warm, hospitable glow rooted in Korean food culture's love of abundance (a 손 큰 host would rather over-cater than run short), and you say it fondly about a mother, a relative, or a friend who always treats; register is neutral-to-positive, safe in 손 크다 with friends and 손이 크시다 with elders. Contrast it with 인심이 좋다 ('good 인심/人心, human-heartedness'), a near-synonym expression that stresses a kind, giving disposition in general, whereas 손이 크다 zooms in on the concrete scale of what you make or buy; 통이 크다 ('big container') is yet another sibling but means bold/big-spirited about money and decisions, not food portions. Natural partners: 음식이 넘쳐나다 (food overflows), 푸짐하다 (lavish/plentiful), 회식 때 많이 사 주다 (treats a lot at company dinners). The English-speaker pitfall: it is NOT about being a big spender on yourself or having literally large hands — it's generosity toward others; and don't confuse it with 손이 빠르다 ('fast hands' = a quick, efficient worker), which is unrelated. Opposite: 손이 작다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Not about literal hand size, and not about splurging on yourself — it's specifically generosity toward others (cooking/giving in big amounts). 'Big-handed' in English carries no such meaning.
Don't confuse it with 손이 빠르다 ('fast hands' = quick, efficient at a task). Different idiom, different meaning — speed, not generosity.
The opposite is 손이 작다 ('small hands' = stingy/under-prepares), not 손이 짧다 (which evokes 'short arms,' a separate image about being slow to give/help).

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'big hands,' the picture is of hands that scoop out a lot at once, so it praises generosity — especially cooking in big batches or spending freely to feed and host others. It carries a warm, hospitable glow rooted in Korean food culture's love of abundance. Natural partners: 음식이 넘쳐나다 (food overflows), 푸짐하다 (lavish/plentiful).

Said fondly about someone who feeds or gives generously — a mom who over-caters, a friend who always treats. Register is neutral-to-positive: casual 손 크다, honorific 손이 크시다 for an elder. It is praise, so it lands warmly in any company, and it's a graceful way to thank a generous host without sounding stiff.

Contrast it with the near-synonym expression 인심이 좋다 ('good human-heartedness'), which stresses a kind, giving disposition in general, whereas 손이 크다 zooms in on the concrete scale of what you make or buy. 통이 크다 ('big container') is a third sibling — bold/big-spirited about money and decisions, not food portions.
Flip to 손이 작다 ('small hands') for the stingy/under-preparing opposite. Use 손이 큰 사람 to describe a host, and the verb phrase 손 크게 쓰다 ('spend big') when picking up a generous tab. Honorific: 손이 크시다.

It is NOT about being a big spender on yourself or having literally large hands — it's generosity toward others. And don't confuse it with 손이 빠르다 ('fast hands' = a quick, efficient worker) or 손버릇이 나쁘다 ('bad hand-habit' = thieving), both unrelated body-part idioms.

entries.english: to be tight-lipped / good at keeping secrets (lit. 'one's mouth is heavy')
entries.shortExplanation: 입이 무겁다 is a practical expression meaning "to be tight-lipped / good at keeping secrets (lit. 'one's mouth is heavy')".
entries.explanation: 입이 무겁다 (ibi mugeopda) means "to be tight-lipped / good at keeping secrets (lit. 'one's mouth is heavy')". Say it as one set phrase — for example 입이 무겁다 ("to be tight-lipped / discreet"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Full idiom; 입 takes 이, adjective 무겁다 ('heavy'). 그 사람 입 무거워 = you can trust them with a secret.

usagePhrases.en: a discreet person you can trust with secrets
usagePhrases.note: Attributive 무거운 + 사람; the phrase that vouches for someone's reliability before you confide in them.
Opposite ('light mouth') — can't keep anything quiet; 걔 입 가벼워, 말하지 마 = don't tell, they'll leak it.

usagePhrases.en: to shut one's mouth / keep quiet
usagePhrases.note: Related verb; 다물다 = the concrete act of staying silent about a specific thing, e.g. 그 일은 입 다물고 있어 ('keep quiet about that').

examples.ko: 우리 형은 입이 무거워.
examples.romanization: uri hyeongeun ibi mugeowo.
examples.en: My older brother is tight-lipped.
examples.note: Plain frame; states a trustworthy trait — he won't repeat what you tell him.

examples.ko: 이건 비밀인데, 너 입 무거운 거 알아서 말하는 거야.
examples.romanization: igeon bimirinde, neo im mugeoun geo araseo malhaneun geoya.
examples.en: This is a secret, but I'm telling you because I know you're discreet.
examples.note: Everyday: drop 이 (입 무겁다) and use the phrase to vouch for the listener right before confiding.

examples.ko: A: 나 이거 말해도 돼? 소문나면 큰일인데. / B: 걱정 마, 나 입 진짜 무거워.
examples.romanization: A: na igeo malhaedo dwae? somunnamyeon keunirinde. / B: geokjeong ma, na ip jinjja mugeowo.
examples.en: A: Can I tell you this? It'll be a disaster if it gets around. / B: Don't worry — I'm really good at keeping secrets.
examples.note: A/B turn: 나 입 진짜 무거워 is the standard reassurance someone offers to be trusted with a secret.

entries.nuance: Literally 'a heavy mouth,' the image is that words are too heavy to spill out easily, so it means you can be trusted with secrets — discreet, reliable, not a gossip. It's a compliment, used to reassure someone before sharing something private (말해도 돼, 걔 입 무거워) or to vouch for a trustworthy colleague; register is neutral and works in both casual and polite settings, with no one it would offend. A crucial distinction: 입이 무겁다 is about confidentiality, NOT about being a quiet or shy personality in general — for that you'd say 말이 없다 ('has few words') or 과묵하다 (reserved, a literary-leaning word); a chatty, outgoing person can still be 입이 무거운 if they simply never leak. Its closest near-synonym expression is 입이 무거운 사람은 입단속을 잘한다 — the idiom 입단속을 잘하다 ('keep a tight lid on one's words'), which names the same discretion as an action, while the plain equivalent is simply 비밀을 잘 지키다. Natural partners: 비밀을 지키다 (keep a secret), 신뢰를 받다 (be trusted), 믿을 수 있다 (can be relied on). The English-speaker pitfall is mapping it onto general quietness and assuming the opposite is 입이 작다 — the true opposite is 입이 가볍다 ('light mouth' = a leaky gossip). Keep the body-part idioms straight: heavy/light mouth = discretion, not mouth size; and remember the particle is 이/은 (입이 무겁다), since 무겁다 is an adjective.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
It's about keeping SECRETS, not about being quiet or shy by nature. A chatty person can still be 입이 무거운 if they never leak confidences; for 'quiet,' use 말이 없다 or 과묵하다.
The opposite is 입이 가볍다 ('light mouth'), not 입이 작다. Don't pick the antonym by literal mouth size.
Don't say 입을 무겁다 — 무겁다 is an adjective describing 입, so the particle is 이/은 (입이 무겁다), never the object marker 을. Use 을 only with the action verb 다물다.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'a heavy mouth,' the image is that words are too heavy to spill out easily, so it means you can be trusted with secrets — discreet, reliable, not a gossip. Natural partners: 비밀을 지키다 (keep a secret), 신뢰를 받다 (be trusted), 믿을 수 있다 (can be relied on).

Use it to reassure someone before they confide (걔 입 무거우니까 말해도 돼) or to vouch for a trustworthy colleague. Register is neutral — casual 입 무거워, polite 입이 무거우세요 — and it works in both work and personal settings without offending anyone. It is genuine praise of reliability.

It is about confidentiality, NOT general quietness — for shy/reserved use 말이 없다 ('few words') or 과묵하다 (reserved). A chatty, outgoing person can still be 입이 무거운 if they never leak confidences. The true opposite is 입이 가볍다 ('light mouth'), not 입이 작다; 비밀을 잘 지키다 is the plain non-idiomatic equivalent.

Flip to 입이 가볍다 ('light mouth' = blabbermouth) for the opposite. Use 입이 무거운 사람 to describe someone, and the concrete verb 입을 다물다 ('shut one's mouth') for the act of staying silent about a specific thing. Honorific: 입이 무거우시다.

The pitfall is mapping it onto general quietness and assuming the opposite is 입이 작다 — the true opposite is 입이 가볍다 ('light mouth' = a leaky gossip). Also note the particle: 무겁다 is an adjective, so it's 입'이' 무겁다, never the object marker 을.

entries.english: to be easily swayed / quick to believe what others say (lit. 'one's ears are thin')
entries.shortExplanation: 귀가 얇다 is a practical expression meaning "to be easily swayed / quick to believe what others say (lit. 'one's ears are thin')".
entries.explanation: "to be easily swayed / quick to believe what others say (lit. 'one's ears are thin')" — that is 귀가 얇다 (gwiga yalda). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 귀가 얇다 ("to be easily swayed / gullible"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Full idiom; 귀 takes 가, adjective 얇다 ('thin'). 나 귀 얇아 = I cave to whatever I'm told.
Attributive 얇은 + 사람; mildly negative — they flip with the last opinion they heard.

usagePhrases.en: to be on the gullible side
usagePhrases.note: Softening 편이다 ('tend to be') makes the self-criticism gentler and less harsh — the polite way to admit it.

usagePhrases.en: to be won over / fall for it
usagePhrases.note: Frequent partner verb: 꼬시면 바로 넘어가 = caves the moment coaxed. It names the result of being 귀가 얇다.

examples.ko: 나 귀가 얇아.
examples.romanization: na gwiga yalba.
examples.en: I'm easily swayed.
examples.note: Simplest self-description with 귀가 얇다; often said half-jokingly to excuse an impulse purchase.

examples.ko: 친구가 좋다고 하니까 귀가 얇아져서 같은 걸 샀어.
examples.romanization: chinguga jotago hanikka gwiga yalbajyeoseo gateun geol sasseo.
examples.en: My friend said it was good, so I caved and bought the same thing.
examples.note: Everyday: 귀가 얇아지다 (become swayed) in a shopping moment — the inchoative shows the swaying happening in real time.

examples.ko: A: 너 그거 또 샀어? 광고 보고 산 거지? / B: 어... 내가 귀가 좀 얇잖아.
examples.romanization: A: neo geugeo tto sasseo? gwanggo bogo san geoji? / B: eo... naega gwiga jom yalbjana.
examples.en: A: You bought that too? You got it from an ad, didn't you? / B: Yeah… you know I'm a bit of a pushover.
examples.note: A/B turn: 내가 귀가 좀 얇잖아 is the sheepish self-admission after an impulse buy.

entries.nuance: Literally 'thin ears,' the image is ears so thin that whatever people say passes straight through and persuades you, so it describes someone easily swayed, quick to believe a recommendation, or talked into purchases. The tone is mildly negative or self-mocking, not a harsh insult — Koreans cheerfully admit 나 귀 얇아, and you can safely tease a close friend with 너 귀 얇잖아, but be gentler with someone you don't know well since it does imply weak judgment. Contrast it with 순진하다 ('naive/innocent'): 순진하다 is broad, often sympathetic innocence about the world, while 귀가 얇다 is specifically the trait of being persuaded by others' words — a 순진한 person may still hold firm, but a 귀 얇은 person flips with the last opinion they heard. Its closest near-synonym expression is the playful noun 팔랑귀 ('fluttering ear'), which names exactly this trait — 너 완전 팔랑귀야 = 'you cave to anything.' Natural partners: 광고 보면 자꾸 사다 (keep buying from ads), 남 말 듣고 (on others' say-so), 넘어가다 (be won over), 사기당하다 (get scammed). The English-speaker pitfall: it is NOT about hearing ability or literally thin ears, and it must NOT be read as a compliment for being 'open-minded' or 'flexible' — it always implies a lack of one's own judgment; for genuine flexibility say 생각이 유연하다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Not about hearing ability or physically thin ears — it means being easily influenced by what people say.
Don't use it as a compliment for being open-minded or flexible. 귀가 얇다 implies poor judgment/gullibility, which is negative; for genuine flexibility say 생각이 유연하다.
Particle: it's 귀'가' 얇다 (adjective describing the ears), not 귀를 얇다. 얇다 takes no object.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'thin ears,' the image is ears so thin that whatever people say passes straight through and persuades you, so it describes someone easily swayed, quick to believe a recommendation, or talked into purchases. Natural partners: 광고 보면 자꾸 사다 (keep buying from ads), 남 말 듣고 (on others' say-so), 넘어가다 (be won over).

The tone is mildly negative or self-mocking, not a cutting insult — Koreans freely say 나 귀 얇아 about themselves. You can tease a close friend (너 귀 얇잖아), but soften it (귀가 얇은 편이야) for someone you know less well, since it does imply weak judgment. Avoid saying it bluntly to a boss or stranger — it would sting.

Contrast it with 순진하다 ('naive/innocent'), which is broad, often sympathetic innocence about the world, while 귀가 얇다 is specifically being persuaded by others' words — a 순진한 person may hold firm, but a 귀 얇은 person flips with the last opinion they heard. 팔랑귀 ('fluttering ear') is the cuter noun nickname for exactly this trait.

Soften self-criticism with 귀가 얇은 편이다 ('tend to be on the gullible side'). Use the inchoative 귀가 얇아지다 ('got swayed') in the moment, the partner verb 넘어가다 ('be won over') for the result, and the playful noun 팔랑귀 to nickname someone.

It is NOT about hearing ability or literally thin ears, and it must NOT be read as a compliment for being 'open-minded' or 'flexible' — it always implies a lack of one's own judgment. For genuine flexibility, say 생각이 유연하다 instead. The particle is 귀'가' 얇다, never 귀를.

entries.english: to get stood up (when someone fails to show for a date/meeting) (lit. 'to be hit by the wind')
entries.shortExplanation: 바람을 맞다 is a practical expression meaning "to get stood up (when someone fails to show for a date/meeting) (lit. 'to be hit by the wind')".
entries.explanation: 바람을 맞다 (barameul matda) = "to get stood up (when someone fails to show for a date/meeting) (lit. 'to be hit by the wind')". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 바람(을) 맞다 ("to get stood up"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: You are the one left waiting; often written as one word 바람맞다. 나 바람맞았어 = I got stood up.
Causative 맞히다 — the subject is the no-show who ditched the other; 사람을 바람맞히면 안 돼 ('don't stand people up').
Totally different idiom! 피우다, not 맞다 — don't confuse the two; 바람피웠어 = 'I cheated,' a dangerous slip.

usagePhrases.en: a blind date (set up by someone)
usagePhrases.note: The classic setting where 바람맞다 happens, e.g. 소개팅에서 바람맞았어 ('got stood up at a blind date').

examples.ko: 나 또 바람맞았어.
examples.romanization: na tto barammajasseo.
examples.en: I got stood up again.
examples.note: Shortest form; 바람맞다 as one word, with 또 ('again') adding the sting of it happening repeatedly.

examples.ko: 한 시간 기다리다가 결국 바람맞았어요.
examples.romanization: han sigan gidaridaga gyeolguk barammajasseoyo.
examples.en: I waited an hour and ended up getting stood up.
examples.note: Everyday: 기다리다가 sets the scene before the no-show; 결국 = 'in the end,' marking the let-down conclusion.

examples.ko: A: 표정이 왜 그래? / B: 소개팅 나갔는데 바람맞았어, 연락도 없이.
examples.romanization: A: pyojeongi wae geurae? / B: sogaeting naganneunde barammajasseo, yeollakdo eopsi.
examples.en: A: Why the face? / B: I went to a blind date and got stood up — without even a text.
examples.note: A/B turn: 연락도 없이 ('without even a message') is the detail that makes being 바람맞다 feel especially rude.

entries.nuance: Literally 'to be hit by the wind,' the image is of someone left standing out in the wind, waiting for a person who never came — so it means getting stood up. It is most common for dates and 소개팅 (blind dates) but extends to any no-show, even a business meeting; register is casual, used among friends to vent (나 바람맞았어), and you'd phrase it more neutrally (약속이 펑크 났어 — 'the appointment fell through') in a formal context. The make-or-break point is the verb pairing: 바람(을) 맞다 = YOU got stood up (you are on the receiving end), while the causative 바람(을) 맞히다 = you stood SOMEONE ELSE up (you are the no-show) — swapping them reverses who is at fault. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is a near-homonym trap: 바람을 피우다 ('to raise/kindle wind') means to cheat on a romantic partner, a completely unrelated idea — saying 바람피웠어 instead of 바람맞았어 turns 'I got stood up' into 'I cheated,' a genuinely embarrassing slip. Natural partners: 한 시간(이나) 기다리다 (wait a whole hour), 연락도 없이 (without even a message), 소개팅 (blind date).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't confuse 바람을 맞다 (get stood up) with 바람을 피우다 (cheat on a partner). They share 바람 but the verbs and meanings are entirely different — a dangerous mix-up that can deeply embarrass you.
바람맞다 (you were stood up) vs 바람맞히다 (you stood someone up): the causative 히 flips who is to blame. Match the verb to who didn't show.
It's about a no-show for a meeting/date, not about literal wind or weather. Never read 바람 here as a breeze.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'to be hit by the wind,' the image is of someone left standing out in the wind, waiting for a person who never came — so it means getting stood up. Most common for dates and 소개팅 (blind dates) but extends to any no-show. Natural partners: 한 시간 기다리다 (wait a whole hour), 연락도 없이 (without even a message).

Register is casual — used among friends to vent (나 바람맞았어). In a formal or work context you'd phrase it more neutrally, e.g. 약속이 펑크 났어요 ('the appointment fell through') or 상대가 안 나왔어요 ('the other party didn't show'), rather than the playful 바람맞다. It carries a tone of being let down, not formal complaint.

Word-for-word it is 'to be hit by the wind,' which has nothing to do with weather — the picture is of someone abandoned outdoors, waiting in vain while the wind blows past. The real meaning is purely 'to be stood up' by a no-show; never read 바람 here as an actual breeze.

The make-or-break pair: 바람맞다 = YOU got stood up; causative 바람맞히다 = you stood SOMEONE up (the 히 flips the blame). The dangerous near-homonym is 바람피우다 ('to cheat on a partner') — entirely different; 바람피웠어 means 'I cheated,' not 'I got stood up.'

Besides the 피우다/맞다 mix-up, English speakers often invert blame by reaching for the wrong voice: if you didn't show, you 바람맞혔다 (caused it); if you were left waiting, you 바람맞았다 (suffered it). Match the verb to who failed to appear, and never read 바람 as literal wind.

entries.english: to lose track of time / not notice time passing (because you're absorbed/having fun)
entries.shortExplanation: 시간 가는 줄 모르다 is a practical expression meaning "to lose track of time / not notice time passing (because you're absorbed/having fun)".
entries.explanation: 시간 가는 줄 모르다 (sigan ganeun jul moreuda) means "to lose track of time / not notice time passing (because you're absorbed/having fun)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 시간 가는 줄 모르다 ("to lose track of time"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Fixed pattern; the 줄 모르다 frame = 'not realize that…'. Past: 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어 ('I lost track of time').

usagePhrases.en: to not realize that (something is the case)
usagePhrases.note: The grammar engine inside: verb + 는 줄 모르다, e.g. 비 오는 줄 몰랐어 ('didn't realize it was raining').

usagePhrases.en: to not even notice time passing
usagePhrases.note: Adding 도 ('even') intensifies the absorption — you were that lost in it that the clock vanished.
Natural partner adverb: 정신없이 놀다가 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어 = lost in fun, lost track of time.

examples.ko: 만화 보다가 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어.
examples.romanization: manhwa bodaga sigan ganeun jul mollasseo.
examples.en: I lost track of time reading comics.
examples.note: Simple: 보다가 + the pattern; an absorbed-in-fun excuse for being late, with a warm rather than careless tone.

examples.ko: 오랜만에 친구 만나서 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어요.
examples.romanization: oraenmane chingu mannaseo sigan ganeun jul mollasseoyo.
examples.en: I met a friend after ages and totally lost track of time.
examples.note: Everyday: explains a late return after catching up over hours — polite 요 form, safe to say to anyone.

examples.ko: A: 벌써 밤 열두 시야! / B: 헐, 얘기하느라 시간 가는 줄 몰랐네.
examples.romanization: A: beolsseo bam yeoldu siya! / B: heol, yaegihaneura sigan ganeun jul mollanne.
examples.en: A: It's already midnight! / B: Whoa, we were so caught up talking I lost all track of time.
examples.note: A/B turn: 얘기하느라 시간 가는 줄 몰랐네 is the natural reaction when a conversation runs way late and surprises you.

entries.nuance: Literally 'to not know that time is going,' it means you were so absorbed or having such a good time that you never noticed the hours slip by — English 'time flew.' The feel is warm and positive, so it doubles as a graceful, polite excuse for staying late or being late (게임하느라 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어요 softens a tardy arrival); register spans casual and polite, and it is safe to say to a boss or teacher precisely because it signals you were happily engaged, not careless. Note the contrast with 시간이 빨리 가다 ('time goes fast'): that simply observes speed, whereas 시간 가는 줄 모르다 adds the key nuance that you were unaware because you were engrossed — it's about your absorbed state, not just the clock. Its closest near-synonym expression is 정신없이 ~에 빠지다 ('get absorbed without noticing'), and 시간 가는 줄 모르고 (the -고 connective form) is how you chain it onto the next clause, e.g. 시간 가는 줄 모르고 게임했어 ('played games, losing all track of time'). The load-bearing grammar is the pattern -는 줄 모르다 ('to not realize that…'), so the structure 가는 줄 모르다 must stay intact, and you can swap the verb in (눈 오는 줄 몰랐어 = didn't realize it was snowing). The English-speaker pitfall: beginners drop 줄 (saying 시간 가는 모르다) and the 'didn't realize that…' meaning collapses; also avoid using it as an excuse for laziness or neglect — it implies you ENJOYED the time, not that you were careless. Natural partners: 정신없이 (absorbed), 수다 떨다가 (chatting away), 막차를 놓치다 (miss the last train).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Keep 줄 in the structure: it must be 가는 '줄' 모르다. Dropping 줄 (시간 가는 모르다) destroys the '-didn't realize that…' meaning.
It implies pleasant absorption, so don't use it to excuse laziness or neglecting something important — it says you were happily engrossed, not careless.
Don't swap in 시간을 모르다 (which would mean 'not know the time/clock'). The idiom needs the verb 가다: 시간 '가는' 줄 모르다.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'to not know that time is going,' it means you were so absorbed or having such a good time that you never noticed the hours slip by — English 'time flew.' The feel is warm and positive. Natural partners: 정신없이 (absorbed), 수다 떨다가 (chatting away), 막차를 놓치다 (miss the last train).

It doubles as a graceful excuse for being late or staying long, softening the apology (게임하느라 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어요). It spans casual and polite, and is safe even to a boss or teacher because it signals you were happily engaged, not careless or rude — far gentler than admitting 'I forgot the time.'

Contrast with 시간이 빨리 가다 ('time goes fast'), which merely observes speed, whereas 시간 가는 줄 모르다 adds that you were unaware because you were engrossed — it's about your absorbed state, not just the clock ticking. 푹 빠지다 ('be totally immersed') names the cause behind the lost time.

The load-bearing grammar is -는 줄 모르다 ('to not realize that…'), so 가는 줄 모르다 must stay intact; you can swap the verb (눈 오는 줄 몰랐어 = didn't realize it was snowing). Add 도 for emphasis: 시간 가는 줄'도' 몰랐어. Past tense is the most common form: 몰랐어/몰랐네.

Beginners drop 줄 (saying 시간 가는 모르다) and the 'didn't realize that…' meaning collapses; also avoid using it as an excuse for laziness or neglect — it implies you ENJOYED the time, not that you were careless. And don't say 시간을 모르다, which would mean 'not know the clock/time.'

entries.english: to have a hard/stressful time / sweat it out (lit. 'to drain greasy sweat')
entries.shortExplanation: 진땀을 빼다 is a practical expression meaning "to have a hard/stressful time / sweat it out (lit. 'to drain greasy sweat')".
entries.explanation: "to have a hard/stressful time / sweat it out (lit. 'to drain greasy sweat')" — that is 진땀을 빼다 (jinttameul ppaeda). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 진땀(을) 빼다 ("to sweat it out / struggle through"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: to sweat it out / struggle through
usagePhrases.note: Full idiom; 을 is often dropped in speech (진땀 빼다). 발표하다가 진땀 뺐어 = the talk was nerve-wracking.

usagePhrases.en: to break out in a cold sweat
usagePhrases.note: Near-synonym with 흘리다 ('shed'); heard just as often, same flustered struggle, image of sweat pouring.

usagePhrases.en: to break into a clammy sweat
usagePhrases.note: Intransitive variant: the sweat comes out on its own under pressure, no agent — 'I started sweating bullets.'
Cousin word; 식은땀 = literally 'cooled sweat,' from a scare or shock, not laborious struggle. 식은땀이 나다 = break into a fearful sweat.

examples.ko: 발표하다가 진땀 뺐어.
examples.romanization: balpyohadaga jinttam ppaesseo.
examples.en: I sweated it out during the presentation.
examples.note: Simple frame; casual 진땀 빼다 without 을 — recounting a nerve-wracking moment afterward.

examples.ko: 면접에서 어려운 질문 받고 진땀 뺐어요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeobeseo eoryeoun jilmun batgo jinttam ppaesseoyo.
examples.en: I got a tough question in the interview and sweated it out.
examples.note: Everyday: 어려운 질문을 받다 is the classic trigger; 받고 chains the cause to the struggle.

examples.ko: A: 통역 어땠어? / B: 말도 마, 전문 용어 나와서 진땀 뺐어.
examples.romanization: A: tongyeok eottaesseo? / B: maldo ma, jeonmun yongeo nawaseo jinttam ppaesseo.
examples.en: A: How was the interpreting? / B: Don't even ask — technical terms came up and I really sweated it out.
examples.note: A/B turn: 말도 마 ('don't even ask') + 진땀 뺐어 is the natural way to recount a stressful ordeal that's now over.

entries.nuance: 진땀 is the clammy, sticky 'cold sweat' you break into under pressure — not the healthy sweat of exercise — and 빼다 ('to extract/drain') frames you as having that stress wrung out of you, so 진땀을 빼다 means to struggle through something nerve-wracking, flustered and scrambling. It captures the emotional ordeal, not mere physical exertion, and you typically use it afterward to recount a tough moment (발표하다가 진땀 뺐어); register is casual-to-polite and fits both venting to friends and describing a hard meeting at work. Its closest near-synonym expression is 진땀(을) 흘리다 ('to shed cold sweat'); the meaning is essentially the same, with 빼다 leaning slightly more toward 'I got put through the wringer' and 흘리다 toward the image of sweat literally pouring. Mind the word itself: it must be 진땀 (the specific stress-sweat), not plain 땀 (ordinary sweat) — 땀을 빼다 would just mean working up a sweat or slimming down. Compare also 식은땀 ('cooled sweat'), which is the cold sweat of fear or shock specifically, while 진땀 is the sweat of laborious struggle. Natural partners: -느라 진땀 빼다 (sweat it out because of doing X), 어려운 질문을 받다 (get a tough question), 헤매다 (flounder/get lost).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't read it as literal sweating from heat or a workout — it's about a stressful, flustered struggle. For exercise sweat, plain 땀이 나다 fits, not 진땀을 빼다.
Use 진땀, not 땀: 땀을 빼다 means 'work up a sweat / lose weight,' a different idea. The 진 (clammy stress-sweat) is essential to the meaning.
Don't confuse 진땀 with 식은땀. Both are cold sweats, but 식은땀 is the sweat of fear/shock (식은땀이 나다 = break out in a fearful sweat), while 진땀 빼다 is about laborious, flustered struggle.

structuredNuance.t: 진땀 is the clammy 'cold sweat' you break into under pressure — not exercise sweat — and 빼다 ('to drain') frames you as having that stress wrung out of you, so 진땀을 빼다 means to struggle through something nerve-wracking, flustered and scrambling. It captures the emotional ordeal, not physical exertion. Partners: -느라 진땀 빼다, 어려운 질문을 받다, 헤매다.

Typically used afterward to recount a tough moment — a presentation, interview, or hard task that flustered you (발표하다가 진땀 뺐어). Register is casual-to-polite; it fits venting to friends and describing a stressful meeting at work alike. It frames the ordeal as survived, often with a touch of rueful humor.

Its closest near-synonym expression is 진땀(을) 흘리다 ('shed cold sweat'), essentially the same, with 빼다 leaning toward 'I got put through the wringer' and 흘리다 toward sweat literally pouring. Compare 식은땀 ('cooled sweat'), the cold sweat of fear/shock specifically, vs 진땀 = the sweat of laborious struggle. 진을 빼다 ('drain one's energy') is a related but broader exhaustion idiom.

Swap verbs: 진땀을 빼다 (struggle through), 진땀을 흘리다 (break out in cold sweat), 진땀이 나다 (the sweat comes on its own). Chain the cause with -느라/-다가, e.g. 통역하느라 진땀 뺐어. The 을 is usually dropped in casual speech.

Don't read it as literal sweating from heat — it captures the emotional ordeal, not physical exertion. Mind the word: it must be 진땀 (the specific stress-sweat), not plain 땀 (ordinary sweat) — 땀을 빼다 would just mean working up a sweat or slimming down.

entries.english: to catch one's breath / get a moment's relief after something hectic
entries.shortExplanation: 한숨 돌리다 is a practical expression meaning "to catch one's breath / get a moment's relief after something hectic".
entries.explanation: 한숨 돌리다 (hansum dollida) = "to catch one's breath / get a moment's relief after something hectic". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 한숨 돌리다 ("to catch one's breath / get a breather"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: to catch one's breath / get a breather
usagePhrases.note: Full idiom; 한숨 (one breath) + 돌리다 (let go round). No 을 — it's set as 한숨 돌리다, a fixed phrase.
Different idiom! Same 한숨 but 쉬다 = the act of sighing, often heavy with worry — not the relief of 돌리다.

usagePhrases.en: to put out the most urgent fire
usagePhrases.note: Natural lead-in: handle the emergency first, then 한숨 돌리다 once the crisis eases. 급한 불 끄고 한숨 돌렸어.
Frequent partner adverb: 겨우 한숨 돌렸다 = only just caught my breath after a frantic stretch.

examples.ko: 이제 좀 한숨 돌렸어.
examples.romanization: ije jom hansum dollyeosseo.
examples.en: I've finally caught my breath now.
examples.note: Simple frame with 이제 ('now') marking the relief point right after the stress lifts.

examples.ko: 시험 끝났으니까 좀 한숨 돌려.
examples.romanization: siheom kkeunnasseunikka jom hansum dollyeo.
examples.en: Exams are over, so take a breather.
examples.note: Everyday: imperative 돌려 gently telling someone to relax a bit now that the pressure is off — a kind thing to say.

examples.ko: A: 프로젝트 끝났어? / B: 응, 큰 고비는 넘겨서 이제 한숨 돌렸어.
examples.romanization: A: peurojekteu kkeunnasseo? / B: eung, keun gobineun neomgyeoseo ije hansum dollyeosseo.
examples.en: A: Is the project done? / B: Yeah, we got past the worst of it, so I can finally breathe now.
examples.note: A/B turn: 큰 고비는 넘겨서 한숨 돌렸어 is how you signal the pressure has just lifted after a crunch.

entries.nuance: Literally 'to send one breath around,' it means to finally catch your breath and feel relief the moment a hectic or stressful stretch eases — the pressure has just lifted, even if only briefly. It is one of the most useful everyday relief phrases at work and home, used right when a crunch ends (이제 한숨 돌렸어); register is casual-to-polite and carries no social risk. Beware the deceptive look-alike: 한숨(을) 쉬다 uses the SAME word 한숨 but means 'to sigh' out of worry, frustration, or weariness (그는 한숨을 쉬었다 = he heaved a sigh) — a heavy, negative breath, the near-opposite feeling. The dividing line is the verb: 돌리다 (relief, you got a breather) vs 쉬다 (a worried/tired sigh). Also distinguish the 쉬다 that means 'to rest': 한숨 돌리다 is a brief breather right after stress, not a long rest or vacation, for which you'd say 푹 쉬다 (rest fully). Its closest near-synonym expression is 한시름 놓다 ('set down a worry'), which adds the sense that a specific anxiety has lifted, while 숨을 돌리다 ('catch one's breath') is an almost interchangeable twin. A natural lead-in is 급한 불을 끄다 ('put out the urgent fire') — handle the emergency, then 한숨 돌리다. Other partners: 이제 (now), 겨우 (barely), 한고비 넘기다 (get past the crisis). The English-speaker pitfall is inserting 을 (it's idiomatically 한숨 돌리다, no object marker) and mixing it up with the worried 한숨을 쉬다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't confuse 한숨 돌리다 (relief, catch your breath) with 한숨을 쉬다 (to sigh out of worry/frustration). Same 한숨, opposite mood — the verb makes all the difference.
It means a BRIEF breather right after a hectic spell, not a long rest or vacation. For real rest, say 푹 쉬다.
Don't insert 을 here — it's idiomatically 한숨 돌리다 (no object marker), unlike 한숨'을' 쉬다 where 을 is natural.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'to send one breath around,' it means to finally catch your breath and feel relief the moment a hectic or stressful stretch eases — the pressure has just lifted, even if only briefly. It is one of the most useful everyday relief phrases. Partners: 이제 (now), 겨우 (barely), 급한 불을 끄다, 한고비 넘기다.

Use it right when a crunch ends — a deadline met, a crisis passed, a busy shift over (이제 한숨 돌렸어). Register is casual-to-polite and carries no social risk; you can say it to anyone, and the imperative 한숨 돌려 ('take a breather') is a kind thing to tell a tired friend or junior.

Beware the look-alike expression 한숨(을) 쉬다, same word 한숨 but meaning 'to sigh' out of worry/weariness (한숨을 쉬었다 = heaved a sigh) — the near-opposite mood. The verb decides it: 돌리다 = relief, 쉬다 = a worried sigh. And vs 푹 쉬다 (rest fully): 한숨 돌리다 is a brief breather, not a real rest.
Stays as 한숨 돌리다 (no 을). Common collocations: 겨우 한숨 돌리다 (barely got a breather), 이제 한숨 돌렸다 (now caught my breath), imperative 한숨 돌려 (take a breather). Lead in with 급한 불 끄고 한숨 돌리다.

Two traps: don't insert 을 — it's idiomatically 한숨 돌리다 (no object marker), unlike 한숨'을' 쉬다 where 을 is natural; and don't mix it up with 한숨을 쉬다 (sigh from worry), which carries the opposite, gloomy feeling. Same noun, opposite mood — the verb is everything.

entries.english: for excitement to fizzle / the mood to be killed (lit. 'the steam leaks out')
entries.shortExplanation: 김이 새다 is a practical expression meaning "for excitement to fizzle / the mood to be killed (lit. 'the steam leaks out')".
entries.explanation: 김이 새다 (gimi saeda) means "for excitement to fizzle / the mood to be killed (lit. 'the steam leaks out')". Say it as one set phrase — for example 김이 새다 ("for excitement/mood to fizzle out"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Full idiom; 김 (steam) + 새다 (leak); 김새다 is the contracted form you'll hear most in speech.

usagePhrases.en: for the buzz to go flat
usagePhrases.note: Near-synonym expression with 빠지다 ('drain out'); interchangeable with 김새다 in daily speech.
The everyday contracted spelling; 아, 김새 = 'ugh, that's a letdown,' a live reaction.
Common intensifier: 김이 팍 샜어 = the mood totally and abruptly deflated in one moment.

examples.ko: 미리 결말 말하지 마, 김새잖아.
examples.romanization: miri gyeolmal malhaji ma, gimsaejana.
examples.en: Don't spoil the ending — it ruins it.
examples.note: Simple: contracted 김새다 with 잖아 ('you know it does'), pushing back against a spoiler.

examples.ko: 기대했는데 취소돼서 김이 새 버렸어.
examples.romanization: gidaehaenneunde chwisodwaeseo gimi sae beoryeosseo.
examples.en: I was looking forward to it but it got canceled, so the excitement fizzled.
examples.note: Everyday: 새 버리다 ('end up fizzling') adds a note of finality and let-down to the deflation.

examples.ko: A: 나 그 영화 결말 알아, 사실은—— / B: 야! 말하지 마, 김새니까!
examples.romanization: A: na geu yeonghwa gyeolmal ara, sasireun—— / B: ya! malhaji ma, gimsaenikka!
examples.en: A: I know how that movie ends — actually—— / B: Hey! Don't say it, you'll ruin it!
examples.note: A/B turn: cutting someone off with 말하지 마, 김새니까 is the live reaction to an incoming spoiler.

entries.nuance: Literally 'the steam leaks out' — picture a hot 만두 or 김밥 going limp as its steam escapes — and it means built-up excitement or a good mood suddenly goes flat. You say it when something spoils the anticipation: a cancellation, a spoiler, a buzzkill comment, plans unraveling; register is casual, used freely among friends (아, 김새), and in a formal setting you'd reach for plainer wording like 흥미가 떨어졌어요 ('I lost interest'). Its near-synonym expression is 김(이) 빠지다 ('the steam drains out'), essentially interchangeable in everyday speech. Don't confuse it with 흥이 깨지다 ('the festive mood is broken') — that specifically describes a lively, party-like 흥 (merriment) being shattered, whereas 김이 새다 is the broader, quieter deflation of any built-up anticipation. The contracted 김새다 is the form you'll hear most, with 김 빠지다 as its twin. The English-speaker pitfall is a homonym trap: the 김 here is steam/vapor, NOT 김 the edible seaweed (laver) — there is no food in this idiom. And it describes deflated feeling, not a literal leak, so never use it for actual gas or air escaping (that's 새다 used plainly, e.g. 가스가 새다). Natural partners: 팍 (suddenly/totally), 미리 말하다 (spoil it in advance), 반응이 없다 (no reaction).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
The 김 here means steam/vapor, NOT 김 the edible seaweed (laver). No food is involved — it's about steam escaping from something hot.
It describes deflated excitement or mood, not a literal leak. Don't use 김이 새다 for actual gas, air, or water leaking (that's 새다 used plainly, e.g. 가스가 새다).
Don't over-narrow it to parties — for a shattered party mood specifically you can say 흥이 깨지다, but 김이 새다 covers any deflated anticipation, including quiet disappointment.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'the steam leaks out' — picture a hot 만두 going limp as its steam escapes — and it means built-up excitement or a good mood suddenly goes flat. You say it when something spoils the anticipation: a cancellation, a spoiler, a buzzkill comment. Partners: 팍 (suddenly/totally), 미리 말하다 (spoil in advance), 반응이 없다 (no reaction).

Register is casual, used freely among friends (아, 김새) and in texts. In a formal or work setting you'd choose plainer wording like 흥미가 떨어졌어요 ('I lost interest') rather than the playful 김새다. It vents mild disappointment, not anger — a deflated 'aw, never mind' feeling.

Its near-synonym expression is 김(이) 빠지다 ('the steam drains out'), essentially interchangeable. Don't confuse it with 흥이 깨지다 ('the festive mood is broken'), which specifically describes a lively, party-like 흥 being shattered, whereas 김이 새다 is the broader, quieter deflation of any built-up anticipation. 분위기 깨다 ('break the mood') is the agent-side version of killing it.

The contracted 김새다 is the everyday form; 김 빠지다 is its twin. Intensify with 김이 팍 새다 ('totally deflate'), and add finality with 김이 새 버리다 ('end up fizzling'). The exclamation 김새! ('what a buzzkill!') is common in speech. All stay casual.

A homonym trap: the 김 here is steam/vapor, NOT 김 the edible seaweed (laver) — there is no food in this idiom. And it describes deflated feeling, not a literal leak, so never use it for actual gas or air escaping (that's plain 새다, e.g. 가스가 새다).

entries.english: to be anxious/worried sick / eaten up with worry (lit. 'one's insides burn')
entries.shortExplanation: 속이 타다 is a practical expression meaning "to be anxious/worried sick / eaten up with worry (lit. 'one's insides burn')".
entries.explanation: "to be anxious/worried sick / eaten up with worry (lit. 'one's insides burn')" — that is 속이 타다 (sogi tada). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 속이 타다 ("to be eaten up with worry"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: to be eaten up with worry
usagePhrases.note: Full idiom; 속 (insides) takes 이, verb 타다 ('burn'). 연락이 안 돼서 속이 타 = sick with worry over no reply.

usagePhrases.en: to fret / to make someone worry
usagePhrases.note: Causative 태우다 — either you fret, or you cause others worry; 부모 속을 태우다 = worry one's parents.

usagePhrases.en: for worry to gnaw deeper and deeper
usagePhrases.note: Intensified 타들어 가다 = the burning spreads inward; stronger and more drawn-out, the worst phase of dread.
Close synonym idiom with 애 (one's innards/heart): 애가 타 죽겠어 = I'm dying of anxiety.

examples.ko: 연락이 안 돼서 속이 타.
examples.romanization: yeollagi an dwaeseo sogi ta.
examples.en: I can't reach them and I'm worried sick.
examples.note: Simple frame; 안 되다 (can't get through) triggers the worry — the unreachable-person scenario is the classic trigger.

examples.ko: 합격 발표 기다리느라 속이 타요.
examples.romanization: hapgyeok balpyo gidarineura sogi tayo.
examples.en: I'm on edge waiting for the results.
examples.note: Everyday: -느라 names the anxious waiting as the cause; polite 요 form fits sharing real distress with someone.

examples.ko: A: 왜 이렇게 안절부절못해? / B: 애가 시험 보러 갔는데 연락이 없어서 속이 타 죽겠어.
examples.romanization: A: wae ireoke anjeolbujeolmotae? / B: aega siheom boreo ganneunde yeollagi eopseoseo sogi ta jukgesseo.
examples.en: A: Why are you so on edge? / B: My kid went to take an exam and hasn't called, so I'm worried sick.
examples.note: A/B turn: 속이 타 죽겠어 ('dying of worry') is the hyperbolic peak you reach when waiting helplessly on someone.

entries.nuance: Literally 'the insides burn,' it conveys the gnawing, burning anxiety of worrying over something out of your control — waiting on news, an unreachable person, a sick family member. It is far stronger and more visceral than plain 걱정하다 ('to worry'): 걱정하다 is the everyday mental act of worrying, while 속이 타다 is the physical, churning agony of it, the way English 'worried SICK' outweighs 'worried.' Register is casual-to-polite and the feeling is genuine distress, so it's apt when you truly can't sit still, not for minor concerns. A close synonym idiom is 애가 타다 (애 = innards/heart-strings), nearly identical in force, while 발을 동동 구르다 ('stamp one's feet') adds the restless, can't-stay-put body language. The key grammar is the 이/을 voice pair: 속'이' 타다 = YOU feel the burning anxiety (it happens to you), whereas the causative 속'을' 태우다 = to fret, or to MAKE someone else worry (자식이 부모 속을 태운다 = a child makes the parents worry). Intensify with 속이 타들어 가다 ('burning deeper inward') or the hyperbolic 속이 타 죽겠어 ('dying of anxiety'). The English-speaker pitfall: don't read it as literal heartburn or indigestion — it's emotional anguish (for a stomach ailment use 속이 안 좋다 / 속이 쓰리다) — and don't swap the particles, or you reverse who is worrying and who is causing the worry.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't take it literally as heartburn or indigestion. 속이 타다 is emotional anxiety, not a stomach ailment (that would be 속이 안 좋다 / 속이 쓰리다).
Keep the 이/을 voice distinction: 속'이' 타다 = you feel anxious; 속'을' 태우다 = you cause worry (often to others). Swapping them flips who is at fault.
It's stronger than 걱정하다. Don't downgrade it to mere 'worry' in feel — 속이 타다 is 'worried sick,' the churning, can't-sit-still kind.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'the insides burn,' it conveys the gnawing, burning anxiety of worrying over something out of your control — waiting on news, an unreachable person, a sick family member. Intensify with 속이 타들어 가다 ('burning deeper inward') or the hyperbolic 속이 타 죽겠어 ('dying of anxiety').

Register is casual-to-polite, and the feeling is genuine distress — apt when you truly can't sit still (a child unreachable, results pending), not for trivial concerns. Saying it tells the listener your worry is serious and physical, so don't apply it to small everyday hassles, where 걱정돼요 fits better.

It is far stronger and more visceral than plain 걱정하다 ('to worry') — the churning agony, like 'worried SICK' vs 'worried.' A close synonym idiom is 애가 타다 (애 = innards), nearly identical in force; 발을 동동 구르다 ('stamp one's feet') adds the restless body language of helpless waiting.
The key voice pair: 속'이' 타다 = YOU feel the anxiety (happens to you); causative 속'을' 태우다 = to fret, or to MAKE someone worry (자식이 부모 속을 태운다). Stronger: 속이 타들어 가다; hyperbolic: 속이 타 죽겠어.

Don't read it as literal heartburn or indigestion — it's emotional anguish (for a stomach ailment use 속이 안 좋다 / 속이 쓰리다) — and don't swap the particles, or you reverse who is worrying (속이 타다) and who is causing the worry (속을 태우다).

entries.english: to be jam-packed / so crowded there's no room to step (lit. 'no gap to set a foot')
entries.shortExplanation: 발 디딜 틈이 없다 is a practical expression meaning "to be jam-packed / so crowded there's no room to step (lit. 'no gap to set a foot')".
entries.explanation: 발 디딜 틈이 없다 (bal didil teumi eopda) = "to be jam-packed / so crowded there's no room to step (lit. 'no gap to set a foot')". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 발 디딜 틈이 없다 ("to be jam-packed (no room to step)"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: to be jam-packed (no room to step)
usagePhrases.note: Full idiom; mind the spacing: 발 디딜 (to step) + 틈이 없다 ('no gap'). 가게가 발 디딜 틈이 없어 = the shop is mobbed.

usagePhrases.en: to have not even room to step
usagePhrases.note: Swapping 이→도 ('even') heightens the crowding to extreme — not a sliver of space left.
The verb core; 디디다 = to plant your foot down, here modifying 틈 as the attributive 발 디딜.
Sino-Korean near-synonym EXPRESSION (人山人海, 'people-mountain-people-sea'); punchier and more dramatic, common in news.

examples.ko: 가게가 발 디딜 틈이 없어.
examples.romanization: gagega bal didil teumi eopseo.
examples.en: The shop is jam-packed.
examples.note: Simple frame; subject + 발 디딜 틈이 없어 — the plainest way to say a place is mobbed.

examples.ko: 출근 시간 지하철은 발 디딜 틈도 없어요.
examples.romanization: chulgeun sigan jihacheoreun bal didil teumdo eopseoyo.
examples.en: The subway at rush hour has no room to even stand.
examples.note: Everyday: 틈도 없다 intensifies the rush-hour crush; polite 요 form works in description or report.

examples.ko: A: 주말에 그 카페 갈까? / B: 거기 주말엔 발 디딜 틈도 없어, 평일에 가자.
examples.romanization: A: jumare geu kape galkka? / B: geogi jumaren bal didil teumdo eopseo, pyeongire gaja.
examples.en: A: Want to go to that cafe on the weekend? / B: It's totally packed there on weekends — let's go on a weekday.
examples.note: A/B turn: 발 디딜 틈도 없어, 평일에 가자 is the real-life way to steer plans away from a crowded spot.

entries.nuance: Literally 'there's no gap to plant your foot,' it's a vivid hyperbole for a place so packed with people that you couldn't even find space to step. Use it for jammed streets, stores, subways, festivals — anywhere overflowing with a crowd — usually with a slightly overwhelmed tone; register is casual-to-polite and works fine in conversation and writing alike. Its Sino-Korean near-synonym expression is 인산인해 (人山人海, literally 'people-mountain, people-sea'), a punchier four-character idiom for an enormous throng often seen in news and dramatic description; 발 디딜 틈이 없다 is the more conversational, everyday way to say it, while 미어터지다 ('to be bursting at the seams') is an even more colloquial sibling. The single most important thing to get right is spacing and the verb: it is 발 디딜 틈이 없다, where 발 디딜 (from 발을 디디다, 'to set a foot down') modifies 틈 ('gap') — beginners wrongly fuse it as 발디딜. The English-speaker pitfall is scope: this idiom is specifically about a CROWD of people, so don't use it for a room cluttered with objects — for that you'd better say 어질러져 있다 (it's a mess). Natural partners: 주말 (weekend), 출근 시간 (rush hour), 축제 (festival), 발 디딜 틈도 없이 (so packed that…).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spacing/verb error: it's 발 디딜 틈이 없다 (발 디딜 = 'to step,' from 발을 디디다), not the fused 발디딜. Keep the space and the verb 디디다.
It's specifically about crowds of PEOPLE, not a room cluttered with objects. For a messy, cluttered space use 어질러져 있다, not this crowd idiom.
Don't drop 틈: 발 디딜 틈이 없다 needs 틈 ('gap'). 발 디딜 데가 없다 exists but shifts nuance toward 'nowhere to step/stand,' so keep 틈이 없다 for the 'jam-packed' meaning.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'there's no gap to plant your foot,' it's a vivid hyperbole for a place so packed with people that you couldn't even find space to step. Use it for jammed streets, stores, subways, festivals. Partners: 주말 (weekend), 출근 시간 (rush hour), 축제 (festival), 발 디딜 틈도 없이 (so packed that…).

Used with a slightly overwhelmed tone to describe a crush of people. Register is casual-to-polite and fits both speech and writing — you can warn a friend (거기 발 디딜 틈도 없어) or describe a festival in a polite report. It is hyperbole, so reserve it for genuinely heavy crowds, not a moderately busy room.

Its Sino-Korean near-synonym expression is 인산인해 (人山人海, 'people-mountain, people-sea'), punchier and more dramatic, common in news; 발 디딜 틈이 없다 is the more conversational version. An even more colloquial sibling is 미어터지다 ('bursting at the seams'); 북적북적하다 is the milder 'bustling' for moderate crowds.
Word-for-word 'no gap to step' = utterly packed. Heighten it with 발 디딜 틈'도' 없다 ('not even room to step') or the adverbial 발 디딜 틈도 없이. Keep the spacing 발 디딜 (from 발을 디디다) — never fuse to 발디딜.

Scope trap: this idiom is specifically about a CROWD of people, not a room cluttered with objects — for clutter say 어질러져 있다 ('it's a mess'). And don't fuse the spelling: it's 발 디딜 틈이 없다, with 발 디딜 (verb 디디다) kept separate, not 발디딜.

entries.english: Oh, I see / Ah, got it — a soft reaction when you just learned or understood something new.
entries.shortExplanation: 그렇구나 is a practical expression meaning "Oh, I see / Ah, got it — a soft reaction when you just learned or understood something new.".
entries.explanation: 그렇구나 (geureokuna) means "Oh, I see / Ah, got it — a soft reaction when you just learned or understood something new.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 그렇구나 ("oh, I see"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: casual banmal, to a friend — the bare two-syllable 'got it' you breathe out
polite -요 version, keeps respect — use this with anyone you'd use 요 with (coworker, staff, stranger)
with 아 as a natural lead-in breath that softens it and marks the realization landing
past form, reacting to a past event they told you — also carries quiet sympathy ('oh, you went through that')

examples.ko: 아, 그렇구나.
examples.romanization: a, geureokuna.
examples.en: Oh, I see.
examples.note: the bare reaction — just absorbing a new fact, no follow-up needed; 아 marks it clicking right now

examples.ko: A: 나 사실 부산 출신이야 / B: 아, 그렇구나. 어쩐지 사투리가.
examples.romanization: A: na sasil busan chulsiniya / B: a, geureokuna. eojjeonji saturiga.
examples.en: A: I'm actually from Busan / B: Oh, I see. No wonder the accent.
examples.note: A/B exchange: 그렇구나 receives the new fact, then pairs naturally with 어쩐지 when a clue suddenly clicks

examples.ko: A: 그 가게 월요일에 쉬어요 / B: 그렇군요. 알려주셔서 감사해요.
examples.romanization: A: geu gage woryoire swieoyo / B: geureokunyo. allyeojusyeoseo gamsahaeyo.
examples.en: A: That shop is closed on Mondays / B: I see. Thanks for letting me know.
examples.note: register lift: the polite 그렇군요 to a stranger who helped you — bare 그렇구나 here would sound too familiar

entries.nuance: 그렇구나 (casual) / 그렇군요 (polite) is the 'oh, I see — that's news to me' you breathe out the instant a new fact clicks. Literally it is 그렇다 'to be so' + the discovery ending -구나/-군요, which Korean reserves for something you have JUST taken in, so it always carries a faint flavor of fresh realization rather than neutral acknowledgment. The line to draw is against 그러게(요): 그렇구나 receives NEW information ('I didn't know that'), while 그러게 means 'right, I feel the same' about something you already shared — answer a surprising fact with 그러게요 and you sound like you knew all along. For a past event shift to 그랬구나 'oh, so that happened,' which also lets you show quiet sympathy. The English-speaker pitfall is register: 'I see' feels neutral in English, so learners drop plain 그렇구나 on a boss or elder, but the bare -구나 is banmal; with anyone you keep -요 with it must be 그렇군요, and to a senior even 그러시군요. A second trap is using it as filler — overusing 그렇구나 to every line can read as only half-listening, so reserve it for genuine new info.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 그렇구나 to a boss, teacher, or elder — the bare -구나 is casual banmal and sounds too familiar; use 그렇군요 (polite) or 그러시군요 (honorific) instead.
Answering surprising NEW info with 그러게요 instead of 그렇군요 — 그러게(요) means 'right, same here' about a shared feeling, so it implies you already knew; for genuinely new facts use 그렇구나/그렇군요.
Using present 그렇구나 for something that already happened — if a friend tells you about a past event, the natural reaction is the past form 그랬구나, not 그렇구나.

structuredNuance.t: 그렇구나 (casual) / 그렇군요 (polite) is the 'oh, I see — that's news to me' you breathe out the instant a new fact clicks. It always carries a faint flavor of fresh realization, not neutral acknowledgment. Reacting to a past event, shift to 그랬구나 'oh, so that happened,' which can also carry quiet sympathy.

Word by word it is 그렇다 'to be so' + the realization ending -구나, so it literally lands as 'ah, it IS so!' The real force is reactive discovery: 'oh, I didn't know that until just now.' It is not a statement of fact — it is the sound of new info settling in, which is why a flat present-tense statement can't replace it.

The line to draw is against 그러게(요): 그렇구나 receives NEW information ('I didn't know that'), while 그러게 means 'right, I feel the same' about something you already shared — answer a surprising fact with 그러게요 and you sound like you knew all along. Against 아 그래(요)?: that questions/checks the fact ('oh really?'), while 그렇구나 already accepts it and needs no answer.

Bare 그렇구나 is banmal — friends, juniors, kids only. With anyone you'd use 요 with (coworker, store staff, a stranger), use 그렇군요; to a clear senior or in deference, 그러시군요. The variant ladder is 그렇구나 → 그렇군요 → 그러시군요, each step adding respect; mismatching the step is the most common social slip.

'I see' feels register-neutral in English, so learners drop plain 그렇구나 on a boss or elder, but the bare -구나 is casual banmal and sounds too familiar. A second trap: sprinkling 그렇구나 on every line reads as half-listening — reserve it for genuinely new info, and for a past event use 그랬구나, not present 그렇구나.

entries.english: True / fair enough / come to think of it — used when you suddenly admit the other person has a point.
entries.shortExplanation: 하긴 is a practical expression meaning "True / fair enough / come to think of it — used when you suddenly admit the other person has a point.".
entries.explanation: "True / fair enough / come to think of it — used when you suddenly admit the other person has a point." — that is 하긴 (hagin). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 하긴 ("true, fair enough"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: conceding a point after a beat of reconsidering — almost always opens the reply
agreeing once you reconsider — the most common full form, lands the concession
-네 marks realizing they have a point just now, the fresh 'oh' moment
casual, half-resigned agreement, slightly trailing off into a shrug

examples.ko: 하긴, 그건 그래.
examples.romanization: hagin, geugeon geurae.
examples.en: Fair enough, that part's true.
examples.note: the bare concession — granting one specific point while you reconsider it on the spot

examples.ko: A: 지금 가도 차 막혀서 똑같아 / B: 하긴, 그냥 천천히 가자.
examples.romanization: A: jigeum gado cha makyeoseo ttokgata / B: hagin, geunyang cheoncheonhi gaja.
examples.en: A: Even if we leave now traffic's the same / B: Fair enough, let's just go slow.
examples.note: A/B exchange: conceding their logic and then changing the plan with a friend

examples.ko: A: 비 오는데 배달이 낫지 않아? / B: 하긴 그러네, 그냥 시키자.
examples.romanization: A: bi oneunde baedari natji ana? / B: hagin geureone, geunyang sikija.
examples.en: A: It's raining, isn't delivery better? / B: Huh, you're right, let's just order.
examples.note: the turn of mind: 하긴 그러네 marks the exact moment you switch your view to theirs

entries.nuance: 하긴 is a casual discourse opener that means 'now that you put it that way, you've got a point' — a small step back where you reconsider and half-concede. It is the frozen, idiomatic shortening of 하기는 (하다 'to do' + the topic-contrast -기는), and as a reaction it almost always opens the reply, usually as 하긴 그래 or 하긴 그러네. The contrast to keep clear is with 그러게(요): 그러게 means 'right, I already felt the same,' but 하긴 means 'I hadn't thought of it that way — but yes, fair'; that reconsideration nuance is the whole point. It also differs from a flat 맞아 'you're right,' which is plain agreement with no 'hmm, on reflection' beat. Register-wise it is firmly banmal-flavored — everywhere among friends and 20-30s coworkers off the clock — but in formal or business speech it sounds too offhand; there you say 그건 그렇네요 or 맞는 말씀이에요. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it as a full 'yes': 하긴 is a mild 'fair point,' not a strong agreement, and dropping it into a meeting reads as flippant. Stronger/softer variants: 하긴 그래 (settled) vs 하긴 뭐 (half-resigned shrug).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Treating 하긴 as full, firm agreement — it is a mild 'fair enough, you have a point,' not a strong yes; for committed agreement say 맞아 / 맞아요 or 그러게.
Using 하긴 in a formal meeting or with a superior — it sounds too offhand and casual; switch to 그건 그렇네요 or 맞는 말씀이에요.
Spelling or saying it as the full 하기는 in conversation — as a reaction it is the frozen short form 하긴; 하기는 in speech sounds stiff and unnatural.

structuredNuance.t: 하긴 is a casual discourse opener that means 'now that you put it that way, you've got a point' — a small step back where you reconsider and half-concede. It almost always opens the reply, usually as 하긴 그래 or 하긴 그러네. That 'I hadn't thought of it like that' reconsideration is the whole flavor.

Under the hood it is the frozen short form of 하기는 (하다 'to do' + contrast -기는), literally something like 'as for doing/it being so…'. But nobody hears the literal parts: as a reaction it just means 'true, fair enough, on second thought you're right.'

Against 그러게(요): 그러게 means 'right, I already felt the same,' but 하긴 means 'I hadn't thought of it that way — but yes, fair.' Against flat 맞아: 맞아 is plain agreement with no reconsidering beat, while 하긴 specifically marks a fresh concession after a pause. Against 하긴 한데, which concedes BUT then objects — 하긴 alone simply yields the point.

Firmly banmal-flavored — natural among friends and 20-30s coworkers off the clock. In a formal meeting or to a superior it sounds too offhand; switch to 그건 그렇네요 or 맞는 말씀이에요. Softer/stronger variants: 하긴 그래 (settled), 하긴 뭐 (half-resigned shrug).

Treating it as a full 'yes': 하긴 is a mild 'fair point,' not strong agreement, and dropping it into a meeting reads as flippant. Also don't expand it to 하기는 in speech as a reaction — the frozen 하긴 is what's natural.

entries.english: No wonder / that explains it — said when new info finally explains something you found odd.
entries.shortExplanation: 어쩐지 is a practical expression meaning "No wonder / that explains it — said when new info finally explains something you found odd.".
entries.explanation: 어쩐지 (eojjeonji) = "No wonder / that explains it — said when new info finally explains something you found odd.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 어쩐지 ("no wonder"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: reacting the moment an explanation lands and a small mystery resolves
with -더라 recalling the oddness you'd already noticed earlier

entries.nuance: 어쩐지 is the 'no wonder / that explains it' you say the moment a small mystery gets solved — you had quietly noticed something off, and the new fact snaps it into place. It is rooted in 어찌 'how/why' + the indefinite -ㄴ지, so under the hood it carries 'so THAT'S why,' and it loves to pair with the retrospective ending -더라 (어쩐지 …하더라) to replay what you had observed. The dangerous look-alike is 어쨌든 'anyway/regardless': they share the 어쩌- stem and beginners blur them, but 어쩐지 is causal ('that's the reason') while 어쨌든 dismisses the reason ('regardless of the reason'). A softer near-synonym is 그래서 그랬구나 'so that's why,' which is more explicit and complete; 어쩐지 keeps it punchy and can stand alone. It works in casual and softly polite speech alike — just surround it with 요-level verbs for politeness (어쩐지 …하더라고요). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'why' (왜): 어쩐지 is not a question, it is a satisfied 'ah, no wonder.' A second trap: leaving the verb in plain present (어쩐지 피곤해) loses the 'I'd noticed it earlier' nuance — the natural shape adds -더라/-더라고요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 어쩐지 (no wonder, causal) with 어쨌든 (anyway, regardless) — they share the 어쩌- root but are opposites: 어쩐지 embraces the reason, 어쨌든 sets it aside.
Treating 어쩐지 as a question like 왜 ('why?') — it is a reaction meaning 'ah, that explains it,' so it expects no answer.
Forgetting the -더라 that usually follows — saying just 어쩐지 피곤해 (present) loses the 'I'd noticed it earlier' feel; the natural form is 어쩐지 피곤해 보이더라.

structuredNuance.t: 어쩐지 is the 'no wonder / that explains it' you say the moment a small mystery gets solved — you had quietly noticed something off, and the new fact snaps it into place. It loves to pair with the retrospective ending -더라 (어쩐지 …하더라) to replay what you had observed.

Built from 어찌 'how/why' + the indefinite -ㄴ지, so literally it is 'somehow / for some reason.' In reaction use that flips to the satisfied 'so THAT'S why' — the reason that was missing has just been supplied, and you're confirming, not asking.

The dangerous look-alike is 어쨌든 'anyway/regardless': same 어쩌- stem, but 어쩐지 is causal ('that's the reason') while 어쨌든 dismisses the reason ('regardless of it'). Softer twin 그래서 그랬구나 'so that's why' is more explicit and complete; 어쩐지 stays punchy and can stand alone.

The word itself is register-neutral and works casual or polite — politeness comes from the verbs around it (어쩐지 피곤해 보이더라 to a friend, 어쩐지 …하더라고요 to someone you keep 요 with). On its own as a one-word 어쩐지, it's a light, everyday reaction fine with almost anyone.

Reaching for 'why' (왜): 어쩐지 is not a question, it is 'ah, no wonder.' Second trap: a flat present (어쩐지 피곤해) loses the 'I'd noticed it before' feel — the natural shape adds -더라/-더라고요 to replay the earlier observation.

entries.english: Anyway / by the way — used to change the subject or get back to what matters.
entries.shortExplanation: 그나저나 is a practical expression meaning "Anyway / by the way — used to change the subject or get back to what matters.".
entries.explanation: 그나저나 (geunajeona) means "Anyway / by the way — used to change the subject or get back to what matters.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 그나저나 ("anyway, by the way"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: dropping one thread for a new one you actually want to raise
leading warmly into the new topic — 말이야 softens the pivot
casual combo with 근데, doubling the 'shifting gears' feel
pivoting straight into a new question — a very common shape

examples.ko: 그나저나 저녁 뭐 먹지?
examples.romanization: geunajeona jeonyeong mwo meokji?
examples.en: Anyway, what should we eat for dinner?
examples.note: the bare pivot to a fresh topic — drops whatever came before

examples.ko: A: 그래, 그것도 맞아 / B: 그나저나 너 이사 준비는 잘 돼 가?
examples.romanization: A: geurae, geugeotdo maja / B: geunajeona neo isa junbineun jal dwae ga?
