examples.en: A: Enough about that / B: Anyway, are you free this weekend?
examples.note: deliberate drop: abandoning a topic to set up a plan

entries.nuance: 그나저나 means 'anyway / by the way' and its job is to DROP the current thread and bring up something else you actually want to talk about — a topic switch, not a wrap-up. It comes from 그러나저러나 'this way or that way,' so it literally shrugs off the previous talk to pivot. The contrast you must keep sharp is with 아무튼/어쨌든: those CONCLUDE the present topic and drive to its point, whereas 그나저나 abandons it for a NEW one — answer 'so what's the conclusion?' with 그나저나 and you've changed the subject instead of finishing. It also differs from 그건 그렇고 'that aside,' which is the slightly more composed, can-be-polite way to do the same pivot. It feels casual and warm, like a friendly nudge ('oh, by the way…'), and pairs habitually with 말이야 or a follow-up question (그나저나 밥은?). It is fine in everyday polite talk, but in formal writing or business email it is too chatty; there you use 그건 그렇고 or 다름이 아니라. English speakers map all of 'anyway / by the way / regardless' onto one word, so they reach for 그나저나 when they mean to conclude — that is the trap. A second trap: it is one word, 그나저나, not 그 나 저 나.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 그나저나 to wrap up and conclude the current topic — that is 아무튼/어쨌든's job; 그나저나 switches to a brand-new topic, so it derails a conclusion.
Putting 그나저나 in formal writing or a business email — it is conversational and too chatty there; use 그건 그렇고 or 다름이 아니라.
Confusing it with 그러나 'however' because they look alike — 그러나 contrasts ideas within one topic, while 그나저나 leaves the topic entirely.

structuredNuance.t: 그나저나 means 'anyway / by the way' and its job is to DROP the current thread and bring up something else you actually want to talk about — a topic switch, not a wrap-up. It feels casual and warm, like a friendly nudge ('oh, by the way…'), and pairs habitually with 말이야 or a follow-up question (그나저나 밥은?).

It is worn down from 그러나저러나 'this way or that way / whichever way,' so literally it brushes 'this or that' aside. The real use is purely functional: it signals 'leaving all that — new topic now,' regardless of where the previous talk was heading.

The sharp contrast is with 아무튼/어쨌든: those CONCLUDE the present topic and drive to its point, whereas 그나저나 abandons it for a NEW one. Closest twin is 그건 그렇고 'that aside,' which does the same pivot but is a touch more composed and can sit in polite/semi-formal talk.

Conversational and warm — fine in everyday polite talk and great between friends. In formal writing or a business email it is too chatty; there use 그건 그렇고 or 다름이 아니라 to change subject. Combine casually as 근데 그나저나 with friends for an even breezier pivot.

English maps 'anyway / by the way / regardless' onto one word, so learners reach for 그나저나 when they mean to conclude — but that's 아무튼/어쨌든. Also it is one word, 그나저나, and it is NOT 그러나 'however' (which contrasts ideas within one topic).

entries.english: Anyway / in any case — used to wrap up or push past a tangent to the main point.
entries.shortExplanation: 아무튼 is a practical expression meaning "Anyway / in any case — used to wrap up or push past a tangent to the main point.".
entries.explanation: "Anyway / in any case — used to wrap up or push past a tangent to the main point." — that is 아무튼 (amuteun). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 아무튼 ("anyway, in any case"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: wrapping up a tangent and driving to the point
closing a thought casually, letting the detail go
cutting past the explanation to land the warm message
slightly stronger 'regardless,' a firmer wrap-up

examples.ko: 아무튼 결론은 못 가.
examples.romanization: amuteun gyeolloneun mot ga.
examples.en: Anyway, the point is I can't go.
examples.note: the bare wrap-up to a conclusion — 결론은 underlines that you're landing the point

examples.ko: A: 설명하자면 길어 / B: 아, 그래? / A: 아무튼 도와줘서 진짜 고마워.
examples.romanization: A: seolmyeonghajamyeon gireo / B: a, geurae? / A: amuteun dowajwoseo jinjja gomawo.
examples.en: A: It's a long story / B: Oh yeah? / A: Anyway, thanks so much for the help.
examples.note: A/B exchange: brushing past details to land the real message

examples.ko: A: 그래서 어떻게 됐는데? / B: 아무튼 잘 끝났어.
examples.romanization: A: geuraeseo eotteoke dwaenneunde? / B: amuteun jal kkeunnasseo.
examples.en: A: So how did it turn out? / B: Anyway, it ended fine.
examples.note: glossing over the messy middle and giving the upshot

entries.nuance: 아무튼 means 'anyway / regardless' and is used to brush past the details and LAND on what counts — it concludes the current thread rather than opening a new one. It is built from 아무 'any' + the -튼/-든 'whichever' ending, so it literally says 'whatever the case, here's the point.' Two contrasts matter. First, against 그나저나: 그나저나 switches to a different topic, while 아무튼 wraps up THIS one — they are not interchangeable even though both translate as 'anyway.' Second, against its closest twin 어쨌든: the two are near-identical and usually swappable, but 어쨌든 leans a hair more on 'no matter what the situation,' often after weighing options, while 아무튼 is the everyday 'anyhow, moving on.' It rides from casual to polite comfortably; 아무튼 간에 adds a touch more 'no matter what.' The English-speaker pitfall is using one English 'anyway' to cover both the topic-switch and the wrap-up — in Korean those are 그나저나 and 아무튼, and mixing them confuses listeners. A second pitfall: leaning on 아무튼 to cut off someone mid-explanation can sound impatient, so save it for genuinely 'enough detail, here's the upshot.'
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 아무튼 to switch to a new topic — that is 그나저나; 아무튼 wraps up the current topic and drives to its point.
Assuming 아무튼 and 어쨌든 are always identical — they overlap heavily, but 어쨌든 leans more on 'regardless of the case,' often after weighing reasons, while 아무튼 is the plain 'anyhow, moving on.'
Stretching 아무튼 to mean 'either way both options are fine' — for genuinely weighing two outcomes, 어쨌든 fits better; 아무튼 just signals 'enough detail, here's the point.'

structuredNuance.t: 아무튼 means 'anyway / regardless' and is used to brush past the details and LAND on what counts — it concludes the current thread rather than opening a new one. It rides from casual to polite comfortably; 아무튼 간에 adds a touch more 'no matter what.'

It is 아무 'any' + the -든/-튼 'whichever' ending, so literally 'whichever way it is.' The real job is to signal 'setting all that aside, the point is…' — it drives toward a conclusion, not away from the topic, which is what separates it from 그나저나.

Against 그나저나: 그나저나 switches to a different topic, while 아무튼 wraps up THIS one. Against its closest twin 어쨌든: near-identical and usually swappable, but 어쨌든 leans a hair more on 'no matter what the situation,' often after weighing options, while 아무튼 is the everyday 'anyhow, moving on.'

Neutral and flexible — comfortable from casual chat (아무튼 그래) to polite speech, and acceptable in light writing. 아무튼 간에 bumps it toward a firmer 'regardless.' For very formal writing, 어쨌든 or 여하튼 can feel a touch more composed.

Using one English 'anyway' for both the topic-switch and the wrap-up — in Korean those are 그나저나 and 아무튼, and mixing them confuses listeners. Also, cutting someone off with 아무튼 mid-explanation can read as impatient, so reserve it for a genuine 'enough detail, here's the point.'

entries.english: Anyway / either way / regardless — moves on while setting aside whatever was just said.
entries.shortExplanation: 어쨌든 is a practical expression meaning "Anyway / either way / regardless — moves on while setting aside whatever was just said.".
entries.explanation: 어쨌든 (eojjaetdeun) = "Anyway / either way / regardless — moves on while setting aside whatever was just said.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 어쨌든 ("anyway, either way"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: setting the rest aside and proceeding to the outcome
stronger 'no matter what,' a firmer dismissal of the reason
interchangeable variant, handy for tone variety
leading to the outcome that stands regardless

examples.ko: 어쨌든 됐어.
examples.romanization: eojjaetdeun dwaesseo.
examples.en: Either way, it's fine.
examples.note: the bare 'regardless, that settles it' — closes off further debate

examples.ko: A: 그게 내 잘못은 아니잖아 / B: 이유야 어쨌든, 늦은 건 늦은 거야.
examples.romanization: A: geuge nae jalmoseun anijana / B: iyuya eojjaetdeun, neujeun geon neujeun geoya.
examples.en: A: That's not my fault, though / B: Whatever the reason, late is late.
examples.note: A/B exchange: acknowledging a reason but dismissing it as not changing the outcome

examples.ko: A: 환불은 어렵다고 하던데 / B: 어쨌든 한번 문의는 해 봐.
examples.romanization: A: hwanbureun eoryeopdago hadeonde / B: eojjaetdeun hanbeon munuineun hae bwa.
examples.en: A: They said a refund is hard / B: Either way, try asking once.
examples.note: pushing forward in spite of the obstacle

entries.nuance: 어쨌든 means 'either way / regardless' — you acknowledge what was just said, declare it doesn't change the outcome, and move on. It is 어찌하- 'however it be' + 었 + the -든 'whichever' ending, so it literally carries 'however things turned out.' Its near-twin is 아무튼, and in most sentences they swap freely; the fine line is that 어쨌든 leans harder on 'no matter what the situation/reason' — it often follows a reason you are setting aside (이유야 어쨌든) — while 아무튼 is the plainer 'anyhow, here's the point.' Keep it apart, too, from 그나저나, which abandons the topic for a new one rather than concluding it. It works in casual and polite speech alike, and 어쨌거나 is a fully interchangeable variant. Two English-speaker traps: spelling — it is 어쨌든, never 어쨋든 (the middle syllable is 쨌 with a double ㅆ batchim, not 쨋 with a single ㅅ); and overuse — leaning on 어쨌든 to wave away every objection can sound dismissive, so use it when you genuinely mean 'that aside, let's proceed.'
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spelling it 어쨋든 — the correct spelling is 어쨌든 (the middle syllable is 쨌, with a double ㅆ batchim, not 쨋 with a single ㅅ); 어쨋든 is a very common but wrong typo.
Treating 어쨌든 and 그나저나 as the same 'anyway' — 어쨌든 concludes/sets aside the current point, while 그나저나 switches to a new topic entirely.
Overusing 어쨌든 to brush off every counterpoint — repeated, it sounds dismissive; reserve it for genuinely 'regardless, let's move on,' not for ignoring valid objections.

structuredNuance.t: 어쨌든 means 'either way / regardless' — you acknowledge what was just said, declare it doesn't change the outcome, and move on. It works in casual and polite speech alike, and 어쨌거나 is a fully interchangeable variant.

It is 어찌하- 'however it be' + past 었 + the -든 'whichever' ending, so literally 'however it turned out.' Functionally it concedes the point ('whatever the case may be') and pivots to the outcome that stands regardless — a concession plus a push forward.

Near-twin 아무튼 usually swaps freely; the fine line is that 어쨌든 leans harder on 'no matter what the situation/reason,' often after a reason you are setting aside (이유야 어쨌든), while 아무튼 is the plainer 'anyhow, here's the point.' Keep it apart from 그나저나, which abandons the topic for a NEW one rather than concluding it.

Neutral — fine casual or polite, and 어쨌든 간에 adds a firmer 'no matter what.' Slightly more composed than 아무튼 in writing, so it sits comfortably in semi-formal speech and reports; 어쨌거나 is a free variant for tone variety.

Spelling — it is 어쨌든, never 어쨋든 (the middle syllable is 쨌 with a double ㅆ batchim, not 쨋 with a single ㅅ). And overuse — leaning on 어쨌든 to wave away every objection sounds dismissive; reserve it for genuine 'that aside, let's proceed.'

entries.english: That's true, but… — agreeing partly while raising a 'but' or hesitation.
entries.shortExplanation: 그렇긴 한데 is a practical expression meaning "That's true, but… — agreeing partly while raising a 'but' or hesitation.".
entries.explanation: 그렇긴 한데 (geureokin hande) means "That's true, but… — agreeing partly while raising a 'but' or hesitation.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 그렇긴 한데 ("that's true, but…"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: partial agreement before a reservation — the cushion goes first
conceding casually with -지, lightest concession on the ladder
trailing off into hesitation, objection left soft and unstated
polite agreement before the but — for a senior or coworker

examples.ko: 그렇긴 한데…
examples.romanization: geureokin hande…
examples.en: That's true, but…
examples.note: the bare concede-then-hedge, trailing off so the objection stays gentle

examples.ko: A: 거기 싸고 좋잖아 / B: 그렇긴 한데 너무 멀어.
examples.romanization: A: geogi ssago jochana / B: geureokin hande neomu meoreo.
examples.en: A: It's cheap and nice there / B: True, but it's too far.
examples.note: A/B exchange: granting the point, then the real objection after -ㄴ데

examples.ko: A: 운동 좀 해야 돼 / B: 그렇긴 해요. 시간이 없어서요.
examples.romanization: A: undong jom haeya dwae / B: geureokin haeyo. sigani eopseoseoyo.
examples.en: A: You should work out / B: That's true. It's just I have no time.
examples.note: polite half-agreement softening a 'but' with a senior or coworker

entries.nuance: 그렇긴 한데 means 'that's true, but…' — you grant the other person's point with 그렇긴 (그렇다 'be so' + the contrast-marking -긴), then -ㄴ데 swings the door open for your reservation. The whole move is a gentle, face-saving disagreement: concede first so the 'but' doesn't sting. The contrast to internalize is against a flat 아니 'no' or 그건 아니지 'that's not it': those reject head-on, while 그렇긴 한데 keeps the other person's dignity by agreeing partway first — Korean conversation strongly prefers this cushioned route. It also differs from plain 그런데/근데 'but,' which simply contrasts; the -긴 here adds a faint 'true ENOUGH, but…' reluctance that plain 그런데 lacks. It is casual; for polite speech say 그렇긴 한데요 or 그렇긴 해요 and continue. The English-speaker pitfalls are two: spacing — 긴 attaches to 그렇 (그렇긴), it is never 그렇 긴; and skipping the concession and jumping straight to the objection, which in Korean lands as blunt and a little cold. Softer/stronger range: 그렇긴 하지 (light concede) → 그렇긴 한데 (full concede + clear but) → 그렇긴 한데 좀… (concede, then trail off to keep it soft).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spacing it as 그렇 긴 한데 — 긴 attaches to the stem 그렇, so it is written 그렇긴 한데 (and 한데 is a separate chunk).
Dropping the concession and objecting head-on — Korean strongly prefers the cushion of 그렇긴 한데 before a 'but'; a flat 아니 or 그건 아니지 sounds blunt and cold.
Forgetting to make it polite when needed — to a senior, plain 그렇긴 한데 is banmal; use 그렇긴 한데요 or 그렇긴 해요 and then state your reservation.

structuredNuance.t: 그렇긴 한데 means 'that's true, but…' — you grant the other person's point with 그렇긴, then -ㄴ데 opens the door for your reservation. The whole move is a gentle, face-saving disagreement: concede first so the 'but' doesn't sting. It is casual; for polite speech say 그렇긴 한데요 or 그렇긴 해요 and continue.

Literally 'it IS so (그렇긴), but/and (한데)…'. The -긴 (from -기는) contrasts and concedes, so the real force is 'I'll give you that much, however…' — a built-in cushion, not a plain contrast. The listener hears the agreement first and the pushback as softened.

Against flat 아니 / 그건 아니지: those reject head-on, while 그렇긴 한데 keeps face by agreeing partway first — Korean strongly prefers this cushioned route. Against plain 그런데/근데 'but': 근데 just contrasts; the -긴 adds a faint 'true ENOUGH, but…' reluctance that 근데 lacks.

Plain 그렇긴 한데 is banmal — to a senior or in polite talk use 그렇긴 한데요 or 그렇긴 해요, then state the reservation. Softer/stronger ladder: 그렇긴 하지 (light) → 그렇긴 한데 (clear but) → 그렇긴 한데 좀… (concede then trail off).
Spacing — 긴 attaches to 그렇 (그렇긴), never 그렇 긴 (and 한데 is its own chunk). And skipping the concession to jump straight to the objection — in Korean that lands as blunt and a little cold.

entries.english: Of course / absolutely — a warm, emphatic 'yes, definitely' in polite speech.
entries.shortExplanation: 그럼요 is a practical expression meaning "Of course / absolutely — a warm, emphatic 'yes, definitely' in polite speech.".
entries.explanation: "Of course / absolutely — a warm, emphatic 'yes, definitely' in polite speech." — that is 그럼요 (geureomyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 그럼요 ("of course"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: warm, emphatic polite yes — radiates welcome, not mere consent
casual version to a friend (NOT the connective 그럼 'then')
doubling up for extra warmth and reassurance
granting permission graciously

examples.ko: 그럼요.

entries.nuance: 그럼요 is a warm, confident 'of course / absolutely' that reassures the listener you fully agree or gladly say yes — it radiates welcome, not mere consent. It is 그렇다 'to be so' contracted to 그럼 plus the polite -요, so it literally affirms 'it certainly IS so.' Its near-synonym is 당연하죠 'naturally/obviously,' and the two often stack (그럼요, 당연하죠) for extra warmth; the subtle difference is that 당연하죠 stresses 'that goes without saying,' while 그럼요 stresses friendly readiness. The plain-speech version is 그럼 for friends. The crucial English-speaker pitfall is a homograph clash: the SAME letters 그럼 also serve as the transition word 'then / in that case' (그럼 가자 'then let's go'). With the -요 attached, 그럼요 is almost always the emphatic 'of course'; the connective sense is the bare 그럼 plus a clause. Mixing them up makes you answer a yes/no question with 'well then…', which is confusing. A second pitfall: 그럼요 is emphatic and warm, so using it for a flat, lukewarm 'yes' overshoots — for a neutral factual yes use 네/예. Collocations: 그럼요 readily precedes 앉으세요 / 드세요 / 그렇게 하세요 when you grant something.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

Confusing 그럼요 (of course) with the transition 그럼 (then / in that case) — 그럼요 with -요 is an emphatic 'yes, of course,' while bare 그럼 + a clause means 'then…'; answering a question with the connective sense sounds off.
Saying plain 그럼 to a customer, senior, or stranger when you mean 'of course' — that is casual; the polite warm form is 그럼요.
Using 그럼요 to mean a neutral, lukewarm 'yes' — it is emphatic and warm ('absolutely!'); for a flat, factual yes use 네 / 예 instead.

structuredNuance.t: 그럼요 is a warm, confident 'of course / absolutely' that reassures the listener you fully agree or gladly say yes — it radiates welcome, not mere consent. The plain-speech version is 그럼 for friends. Collocations: 그럼요 readily precedes 앉으세요 / 드세요 / 그렇게 하세요 when you grant something.
It is 그렇다 'to be so' contracted to 그럼 + polite -요, so literally 'it IS so.' The real force is an emphatic, friendly 'of course! absolutely!' — affirmation with warmth, the opposite of a grudging yes.

Near-synonym 당연하죠 'naturally/obviously' often stacks with it (그럼요, 당연하죠); 당연하죠 stresses 'that goes without saying,' while 그럼요 stresses friendly readiness. Against a flat 네/예: those are neutral 'yes'; 그럼요 adds emphasis and warmth ('of course!').

그럼요 is the polite warm form — right for customers, seniors, strangers, hosting a guest. Plain 그럼 is the banmal version for friends. To a customer or elder, dropping to bare 그럼 for 'of course' sounds too casual; keep 그럼요.

Homograph clash: the same letters 그럼 also mean 'then / in that case' (그럼 가자). With -요, 그럼요 is the emphatic 'of course'; the connective sense is bare 그럼 + a clause. Mixing them makes you answer a yes/no question with 'well then…'. Also, 그럼요 is emphatic — for a flat factual yes use 네/예.

entries.english: Right? / I know / told you — sympathetic agreement, often with a hint of 'yeah, exactly.'
entries.shortExplanation: 그러게 is a practical expression meaning "Right? / I know / told you — sympathetic agreement, often with a hint of 'yeah, exactly.'".
entries.explanation: 그러게 (geureoge) = "Right? / I know / told you — sympathetic agreement, often with a hint of 'yeah, exactly.'". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 그러게 ("right? I know"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: casual sympathetic agreement to a shared feeling
polite -요 version for someone you keep 요 with
stronger 'totally, I feel it' — ramps the agreement up
emphatic 'see, I told you' — pairs with 내 말이

examples.ko: 그러게 말이야.
examples.romanization: geureoge mariya.
examples.en: Right, exactly.
examples.note: the bare strong 'totally, I feel the same' — full fellow-feeling

examples.ko: A: 날씨 진짜 춥다 / B: 그러게, 갑자기 겨울 됐어.
examples.romanization: A: nalssi jinjja chupda / B: geureoge, gapjagi gyeoul dwaesseo.
examples.en: A: It's so cold / B: I know, it suddenly turned winter.
examples.note: A/B exchange: warmly echoing a friend's complaint you already share

examples.ko: A: 진작 예약할걸 / B: 그러게, 자리가 없네.

entries.nuance: 그러게 is a sympathetic 'right? / I know' that signals you feel EXACTLY the same — most often about something mildly annoying, regrettable, or that you half-predicted, so it can carry a soft 'told you so.' It comes from 그러다 'to be/do so' + the -게 ending and works as a fellow-feeling echo. The contrast to fix is against 그렇구나: 그러게 agrees with a feeling you ALREADY share ('yeah, I know, right?'), while 그렇구나 receives a NEW fact you didn't know ('oh, I see') — answer 'it's freezing' with 그렇구나 and you sound like cold weather is breaking news. A second near-synonym is 내 말이(야) 'that's exactly what I'm saying,' which is even more emphatic and pairs with it (그러게, 내 말이). Use 그러게 with friends, 그러게요 with people you keep -요 with, and 그러게 말이야 to ramp the agreement up. The English-speaker pitfall is mishearing the rising tone as the question 'why did you do that?' — it is purely an agreeing reaction, not a 'why.' A second trap: because it can carry 'told you,' aiming it at a senior's mistake or complaint can sound smug, so keep it for shared feelings, not 'I-told-you-so' at someone above you.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Hearing 그러게 as the question 'why did you (do that)?' — it is an agreeing reaction meaning 'right, I know,' not an interrogative.
Using 그러게 to react to brand-new information — 그러게 echoes a feeling you ALREADY share; for news you just learned, use 그렇구나 / 그렇군요.
Saying plain 그러게 to a senior — it is banmal; with someone you keep -요 with, use 그러게요.

structuredNuance.t: 그러게 is a sympathetic 'right? / I know' that signals you feel EXACTLY the same — most often about something mildly annoying, regrettable, or that you half-predicted, so it can carry a soft 'told you so.' Use 그러게 with friends, 그러게요 with people you keep -요 with, and 그러게 말이야 to ramp the agreement up.

It is 그러다 'to be/do so' + the -게 ending — literally close to 'so it be / be that way.' The real force is fellow-feeling: 'right, I know, exactly — I felt the same.' It's an agreement noise, not a description, so don't parse it word-for-word.

Against 그렇구나: 그러게 agrees with a feeling you ALREADY share, while 그렇구나 receives a NEW fact ('oh, I see') — answer 'it's freezing' with 그렇구나 and cold weather sounds like breaking news. Near-synonym 내 말이(야) 'that's exactly what I'm saying' is more emphatic and pairs with it (그러게, 내 말이).

Plain 그러게 is banmal — friends and peers; with someone you keep 요 with use 그러게요. Because it can carry 'told you so,' it's best for shared feelings; aimed at a senior's complaint or mistake it can sound smug, so be careful upward.

Mishearing the rising tone as the question 'why did you do that?' — it is purely an agreeing reaction, not a 'why.' Second trap: its faint 'I-told-you-so' edge means it can read as smug if aimed at someone above you; reserve it for genuine shared feeling.

entries.english: Since you said so / because they were like that — explains why you acted, reacting to what someone said or did.
entries.shortExplanation: 그러길래 is a practical expression meaning "Since you said so / because they were like that — explains why you acted, reacting to what someone said or did.".
entries.explanation: 그러길래 (geureogillae) means "Since you said so / because they were like that — explains why you acted, reacting to what someone said or did.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 그러길래 ("since you said so"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: reacting to their words or actions as YOUR reason — the cause is them
naming who prompted you — the trigger is the other person
with 하도 for 'so insistently,' adding 'they wouldn't stop'
justifying your reaction — '(you prompted me) so I did, obviously'

examples.ko: 네가 그러길래 그랬지.
examples.romanization: nega geureogillae geuraetji.
examples.en: I did it because you said so.
examples.note: the bare 'you prompted me, so I acted' — note the cause is YOU, not me

examples.ko: 네가 먹고 싶다 그러길래 사 왔어.
examples.romanization: nega meokgo sipda geureogillae sa wasseo.
examples.en: You said you wanted some, so I bought it.
examples.note: your action explained by their words — quotative 다 + 그러길래

examples.ko: A: 왜 먼저 갔어? / B: 다들 바쁘다 그러길래.

examples.note: A/B exchange: the reason trails off, the result left implied

entries.nuance: 그러길래 explains YOUR own action as a reaction to what someone ELSE said or did — 'since you/they were like that, I…'. It is 그러다 'to do/be so' + the connective -길래, and the defining feature is that -길래 always points the cause at the other party, never at yourself: that is exactly what separates it from plain 그래서, a neutral 'so' that can take any subject. So 비가 와서 우산을 샀어 (it rained, neutral cause) is fine, but to say 'YOU kept saying it's good, so I tried it' you need 하도 맛있다고 그러길래 시켜 봤어 — the cause sits with them. It is casual and conversational, the reason frequently trailing off with the result left implied (다들 바쁘다 그러길래…). A close cousin is -기에, which means the same but is more written/formal; -길래 is the spoken form. The English-speaker pitfall: learners use 그러길래 for their own internal reason (because I was tired, because I wanted to) — for that you must use 그래서, since -길래 demands an external trigger from someone else. A second trap: when reporting speech, keep the quotative 다(고) — it is X-다고/-다 그러길래 ('they SAID X, so…'); dropping the 다 garbles the 'because they said' sense.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 그러길래 (or -길래) for your OWN reason — it must react to someone else's words or actions; for your own internal reason ('because I was tired') use 그래서, e.g. 피곤해서, not 피곤하길래.
Writing -길래 in a formal essay or report — there the more literary -기에 is expected; -길래 is the casual spoken form.
Forgetting the quotative 다(고) when reporting speech — it is X-다고/-다 그러길래 ('they SAID X, so…'); dropping it (X 그러길래 with no 다) garbles the 'because they said' meaning.

structuredNuance.t: 그러길래 explains YOUR own action as a reaction to what someone ELSE said or did — 'since you/they were like that, I…'. The defining feature is that -길래 always points the cause at the other party, never at yourself. It is casual and conversational, the reason frequently trailing off with the result left implied (다들 바쁘다 그러길래…).

It is 그러다 'to do/be so' + the reason connective -길래, so literally 'because (you/they) were doing/saying so.' Real use: 'since you said/did that, that's why I…' — your action framed as a direct response to their cue, with the spotlight on their prompt.

Against plain 그래서, a neutral 'so' that takes any subject: 비가 와서 우산을 샀어 (it rained) is fine, but -길래 must point the cause at the OTHER party. Close cousin -기에 means the same but is more written/formal; -길래 is the spoken form.

Spoken and casual — natural in everyday talk, often trailing off (그러길래…). For an essay or report, the more literary -기에 is expected instead. It's neutral in politeness: you can attach polite endings to the result clause (사 왔어요).

Using 그러길래/-길래 for your OWN reason — it needs an external trigger from someone else; for 'because I was tired' use 그래서 (피곤해서), not 피곤하길래. Second: keep the quotative 다(고) when reporting speech — X-다 그러길래 ('they SAID X, so…').

entries.english: I guess so / it seems so — a soft guess based on what you're seeing or hearing.
entries.shortExplanation: 그런가 봐요 is a practical expression meaning "I guess so / it seems so — a soft guess based on what you're seeing or hearing.".
entries.explanation: "I guess so / it seems so — a soft guess based on what you're seeing or hearing." — that is 그런가 봐요 (geureonga bwayo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 그런가 봐요 ("I guess so, seems so"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: soft polite inference from a clue you can see or hear
casual to a friend, same tentative hunch
negative version — 'seems like it's not the case'
hedging gently when unsure — stacks two softeners

examples.ko: 그런가 봐요.
examples.romanization: geureonga bwayo.
examples.en: I guess so.
examples.note: the bare soft guess from a hunch, no firm claim being made

examples.ko: 불이 꺼져 있네요. 오늘 쉬는 날인가 봐요.
examples.romanization: buri kkeojyeo inneyo. oneul swineun naringa bwayo.
examples.en: The lights are off. I guess they're closed today.
examples.note: inferring from a visible clue — the evidence (불이 꺼져 있네요) comes first

examples.ko: A: 비 오려나 / B: 하늘 보니까 그런가 봐.
examples.romanization: A: bi oryeona / B: haneul bonikka geureonga bwa.
examples.en: A: Is it going to rain / B: Looking at the sky, I guess so.
examples.note: A/B exchange: 보니까 + 그런가 봐 grounds the guess in evidence

entries.nuance: 그런가 봐요 means 'I guess so / it seems so' and is used to make a SOFT inference from something you observe rather than to state a fact outright. The engine is the ending -(으)ㄴ가/나 보다 'it looks like / I guess,' which marks a guess drawn from external evidence, so 그런가 봐요 = 'from what I can see, it seems to be so.' The contrast that matters is against -겠- and against 것 같다. -겠다 (그렇겠어요) is a quicker, more confident 'it must be so' from reasoning, while -나 보다 leans on observed evidence and stays more tentative; 그런 것 같아요 is very close but slightly more subjective ('I think so'), whereas 그런가 봐요 implies 'the signs suggest so.' Drop to 그런가 봐 with friends, and flip to 아닌가 봐요 for 'I guess not.' Two English-speaker pitfalls: spacing — standard is 그런가 봐요, with 봐요 written separately as the auxiliary (not 그런가봐요); and don't use -나 보다 about your OWN feelings or actions — you don't 'guess' your own state, so '배고픈가 봐요' about yourself is odd unless you mean it half-jokingly. Note the 봐 here is the verb 보다 in its inference sense, not 'look at it' — it is what makes this a hunch, not a command.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spacing it as 그런가봐요 — the standard is 그런가 봐요, with the auxiliary 봐요 written as a separate word.
Using -(으)ㄴ가/나 보다 about your OWN feelings or actions — you infer about others/the world, not yourself; for your own state say 그런 것 같아요 or just state it, not 그런가 봐요.
Swapping it for confident -겠어요 when you only have a hunch — 그런가 봐요 is tentative (evidence-based guess); 그렇겠어요 sounds like a firmer 'it must be so.'

structuredNuance.t: 그런가 봐요 means 'I guess so / it seems so' and is used to make a SOFT inference from something you observe rather than to state a fact outright, so it = 'from what I can see, it seems to be so.' Drop to 그런가 봐 with friends, and flip to 아닌가 봐요 for 'I guess not.'

Literally 'I look-and-see whether it is so' — the 봐(요) is 보다 in its inference sense, not the literal 'look at.' That's why the real meaning is a tentative, evidence-based 'I guess so,' not a statement and not a command to look.

Against -겠다 (그렇겠어요): a quicker, more confident 'it must be so' from reasoning, while -나 보다 leans on observed evidence and stays tentative. Against 그런 것 같아요: very close but slightly more subjective ('I think so'), whereas 그런가 봐요 implies 'the outward signs suggest so.'

그런가 봐요 is the polite form; 그런가 봐 is casual to friends. Tone is gentle and non-committal, which makes it useful for not sounding too sure — good with seniors when you'd rather hedge than assert. Stack 그런가 봐요, 잘 모르겠어요 to hedge further.

Spacing — standard is 그런가 봐요, with the auxiliary 봐요 written separately (not 그런가봐요). And don't use -나 보다 about your OWN feelings/actions — you don't 'guess' your own state, so '배고픈가 봐요' about yourself is odd; say 그런 것 같아요 or state it plainly.

entries.english: Now that you mention it / hearing you say that — you reconsider after listening to someone.
entries.shortExplanation: 듣고 보니 is a practical expression meaning "Now that you mention it / hearing you say that — you reconsider after listening to someone.".
entries.explanation: 듣고 보니 (deutgo boni) = "Now that you mention it / hearing you say that — you reconsider after listening to someone.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 듣고 보니 ("now that you mention it"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: reconsidering after listening — your view shifts on the spot
agreeing after a beat of reconsidering — 그렇네 marks the penny dropping
with -까 leading into a fuller clause that follows
after a second listen, re-judging with fresh ears

examples.ko: 듣고 보니 그러네.
examples.romanization: deutgo boni geureone.
examples.en: Now that you say it, yeah.
examples.note: the bare 'on hearing it, you're right' — the mind changes on the spot

examples.ko: A: 이 색이 너한테 더 어울려 / B: 듣고 보니 네 말이 맞는 것 같아.
examples.romanization: A: i saegi neohante deo eoullyeo / B: deutgo boni ne mari manneun geot gata.
examples.en: A: This color suits you better / B: Now that you mention it, I think you're right.
examples.note: A/B exchange: coming around to their view after listening

examples.ko: 듣고 보니까 그 식당 좀 비싸긴 했어.
examples.romanization: deutgo bonikka geu sikdang jom bissagin haesseo.

entries.nuance: 듣고 보니 literally stacks 듣다 'to hear' + -고 보니 'having done and then found,' so it means 'now that I've heard it (and looked back), I realize…' — you take in what someone said and reconsider, almost always ending up agreeing. The -고 보니 frame is a 'do X, then discover' construction (cf. 가 보니 'on going, I found,' 자고 보니 'after sleeping, I realized'), which is why it signals a fresh after-the-fact realization rather than a prior opinion. The contrast to keep is against 그러게: 그러게 means 'right, I already felt the same,' but 듣고 보니 means 'I hadn't seen it that way until you said it — and now I do,' so it foregrounds a CHANGE of mind. It also differs from 알고 보니 'as it turns out,' which reveals a hidden FACT rather than a shift in your opinion. It naturally flows into 그렇네 or 맞네 to mark that the penny dropped. It is comfortable in casual and polite speech; add -까 (듣고 보니까) before a longer follow-up clause. The English-speaker pitfall is reading -고 보니 as a plain 'after listening' time sequence — in conversation it specifically conveys 'on second thought, I now agree,' not just chronology. A second trap: 보니 here is 'I found/realized,' not the purpose '-(으)려고 to hear,' so don't read it as 'in order to hear.'
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Reading 듣고 보니 as merely 'after listening' (time order) — in conversation it specifically signals 'now that you mention it, I've reconsidered and tend to agree.'
Using 듣고 보니 when you already held that view — it marks a CHANGE of mind prompted by what you just heard; if you already agreed, use 그러게 or 내 말이.
Confusing the -고 보니 'discover after doing' frame with -고 (으)려고 'intending to' — 듣고 보니 means 'on hearing, I found,' not 'in order to hear.'

structuredNuance.t: 듣고 보니 means 'now that I've heard it (and looked back), I realize…' — you take in what someone said and reconsider, almost always ending up agreeing. It naturally flows into 그렇네 or 맞네 to mark that the penny dropped. It is comfortable in casual and polite speech; add -까 (듣고 보니까) before a longer follow-up clause.

It stacks 듣다 'hear' + -고 보니 'having done, then found' (cf. 가 보니 'on going I found'). So literally 'having heard, I find…'; the real force is 'on hearing it, I've reconsidered — and now I agree.' It marks a fresh realization, not a prior view.

Against 그러게 ('right, I already felt the same'): 듣고 보니 foregrounds a CHANGE of mind — 'I hadn't seen it that way until you said it.' Against 알고 보니 'as it turns out': that reveals a hidden FACT, while 듣고 보니 reports a shift in YOUR opinion after listening.

Register-neutral — works casual (듣고 보니 그러네) or polite (듣고 보니 맞는 것 같아요), and it's a graceful way to concede to a senior because it credits their point. Use -까 (듣고 보니까) when a longer clause follows; 다시 듣고 보니 for a second listen.

Reading -고 보니 as a plain 'after listening' time sequence — in conversation it specifically conveys 'on second thought, I now agree,' not mere chronology. Second: 보니 is 'I found/realized,' not purpose -(으)려고 'to hear,' so it does NOT mean 'in order to hear.'

entries.english: Tell me about it / I know, right? / Exactly what I was thinking (strong, sympathetic agreement)
entries.shortExplanation: 그러게 말이에요 is a practical expression meaning "Tell me about it / I know, right? / Exactly what I was thinking (strong, sympathetic agreement)".
entries.explanation: 그러게 말이에요 (geureoge marieyo) means "Tell me about it / I know, right? / Exactly what I was thinking (strong, sympathetic agreement)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 그러게 말이에요, 저도 딱 그 생각 했어요. ("Tell me about it — I was thinking the exact same thing."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.ko: 그러게 말이에요, 저도 딱 그 생각 했어요.
usagePhrases.romanization: geureoge marieyo, jeodo ttak geu saengga kaesseoyo.
usagePhrases.en: Tell me about it — I was thinking the exact same thing.
usagePhrases.note: Agreeing and confirming you felt it too

usagePhrases.en: I know, right? Isn't it just too much?
usagePhrases.note: 그러게 말이야 = casual form with friends

usagePhrases.en: Yeah, you can say that again.
usagePhrases.note: 그러게나 = slightly stronger/heavier sigh, implies deeper resignation
-ㅂ니다 form, polite to a senior or at work

examples.ko: A: 요즘 물가가 너무 올랐어요. B: 그러게 말이에요.
examples.romanization: A: yojeum mulgaga neomu ollasseoyo. B: geureoge marieyo.
examples.en: A: Prices have shot up lately. B: Tell me about it.
examples.note: Bare reaction — just the agreement, nothing added; simplest pattern

examples.ko: A: 주말마다 비가 오네요. B: 그러게 말이에요, 빨래를 못 하겠어요.
examples.romanization: A: jumalmada biga oneyo. B: geureoge marieyo, ppallaereul mo tagesseoyo.
examples.en: A: It rains every weekend. B: I know, right? I can't even do laundry.
examples.note: Agreement + piling on your own grievance — very natural extension

examples.ko: A: 그 사람 진짜 일을 잘하더라고요. B: 그러게 말이에요, 저도 보고 깜짝 놀랐어요.
examples.romanization: A: geu saram jinjja ireul jalhadeoragoyo. B: geureoge marieyo, jeodo bogo kkamjjang nollasseoyo.
examples.en: A: That person is really good at their job. B: Right? I was honestly surprised when I saw it.
examples.note: Works equally for positive remarks — the key is that BOTH speakers observed it from the outside

entries.nuance: Whole-hearted, sympathetic agreement that means far more than a flat 네 or 맞아요 — it carries the extra charge 'and I've felt exactly that myself.' The phrase is built from 그러게 ('right, isn't it') plus 말이에요 (literally 'it is [my] words'), making it the heavier, more emphatic cousin of plain 그러게요: where 그러게요 is a quick nod, 그러게 말이에요 is a shared sigh that says 'you took the words out of my mouth.' Contrast it with 맞아요, which simply confirms a fact ('that's correct'); 그러게 말이에요 instead bonds you emotionally over a shared feeling — usually a complaint or a 'what can you do' resignation, but also a mutual positive surprise. Register: casual-polite 해요체 is the default; drop to 그러게 말이야 with close friends and go up to 그러게 말입니다 with a boss or in formal settings. The English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for it to accept a compliment about yourself ('You're so good!' → 그러게 말이에요 sounds like you're agreeing you're great) — it only mirrors the other person's observation about something you both perceive from the outside.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

English speakers use it to accept praise ('You did great!' → 그러게 말이에요), which sounds like smug self-agreement. It's only for echoing a remark about something you both see, not about yourself — for praise say 감사합니다 instead.
It only confirms what was just said, so don't follow it with a counter-argument. To agree-then-disagree you need 그건 그런데… ('that's true, but…'), not 그러게 말이에요.
Don't shorten it to just 말이에요 hoping to keep the meaning — without 그러게 it just means 'I'm telling you / it's true,' losing the empathetic-agreement function.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'right, it is [my] words' (그러게 + 말이에요). The real meaning is 'you took the words out of my mouth' — a charged, emotionally resonant echo that signals you've been feeling the same thing all along. It goes well beyond a simple factual confirmation like 맞아요.

Best after shared complaints, mutual frustrations, or joint positive surprises — any situation where both of you have observed the same thing from the outside. Casual-polite 해요체 suits friends, coworkers, and acquaintances. Drop to 그러게 말이야 with close friends (반말); shift to 그러게 말입니다 with a senior colleague or boss (격식체). Safe with strangers at a polite register.

그러게요 is a quick, light nod ('yeah, right'); 그러게 말이에요 is the same emotion amplified into a shared sigh. 맞아요 confirms a fact ('that's correct') without the bonding warmth. 그렇군요 is the cool, detached 'I see,' used when processing new information rather than resonating with it.

그러게 말이야 (반말, friends) → 그러게 말이에요 (해요체, default) → 그러게 말입니다 (격식체, seniors). 그러게나 말이에요 adds a slightly heavier, more resigned sigh. You can extend: 그러게 말이에요, 저도 딱 그 생각 했어요 piles on your own confirmation.

Don't use it to accept a compliment directed AT yourself ('You're so talented!' → 그러게 말이에요 sounds like smug self-agreement). It only mirrors an observation you both see from the outside. For praise, say 감사합니다 or 과찬이세요. Also: it's not interchangeable with a counter-argument — you can't agree then disagree with it; for that, use 그건 그런데… ('that's true, but…').

entries.english: No, that's not it — / It's not that, it's… / What I mean is… (correcting a misunderstanding)
entries.shortExplanation: 그게 아니라 is a practical expression meaning "No, that's not it — / It's not that, it's… / What I mean is… (correcting a misunderstanding)".
entries.explanation: "No, that's not it — / It's not that, it's… / What I mean is… (correcting a misunderstanding)" — that is 그게 아니라 (geuge anira). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 그게 아니라, 제 말은 좀 다른 뜻이었어요. ("No, that's not it — what I meant was a bit different."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.ko: 그게 아니라, 제 말은 좀 다른 뜻이었어요.
usagePhrases.romanization: geuge anira, je mareun jom dareun tteusieosseoyo.
usagePhrases.en: No, that's not it — what I meant was a bit different.
usagePhrases.note: Clarifying after being misunderstood

usagePhrases.ko: 아니 그게 아니라, 시간이 없어서 그래.
usagePhrases.romanization: ani geuge anira, sigani eopseoseo geurae.
usagePhrases.en: No no, it's not that — it's because I don't have time.
usagePhrases.note: 그게 아니라 = casual; correcting a wrong assumption with the real reason

usagePhrases.ko: 그런 게 아니라 그냥 좀 피곤해서요.
usagePhrases.romanization: geureon ge anira geunyang jom pigonhaeseoyo.
usagePhrases.en: It's not like that, I'm just a bit tired.
usagePhrases.note: 그런 게 아니라 = 'it's not that KIND of thing' — denies a category, not just one claim

usagePhrases.en: That's not it — let me explain again.
usagePhrases.note: 그게 아니고 = looser spoken variant; softer, less urgent

examples.ko: A: 이거 싫어요? B: 그게 아니라 배가 불러서요.
examples.romanization: A: igeo sireoyo? B: geuge anira baega bulleoseoyo.
examples.en: A: You don't like this? B: It's not that — I'm just full.
examples.note: Short two-clause correction: denial + real reason in one breath

examples.ko: A: 저 싫어서 안 오시는 거예요? B: 아, 그게 아니라 오늘 진짜 바빠서 그래요.
examples.romanization: A: jeo sireoseo an osineun geoyeyo? B: a, geuge anira oneul jinjja bappaseo geuraeyo.
examples.en: A: Are you not coming because you don't like me? B: Oh, that's not it — it's just that I'm really busy today.
examples.note: Heading off a hurt feeling before it settles; 아, 그게 아니라 is a common spoken cluster

examples.ko: A: 환불해 달라는 거죠? B: 그게 아니라 사실은 교환을 하고 싶어서 말씀드린 거예요.
examples.romanization: A: hwanbulhae dallaneun geojyo? B: geuge anira sasireun gyohwaneul hago sipeoseo malsseumdeurin geoyeyo.
examples.en: A: So you want a refund? B: No — actually I brought it up because I'd like an exchange.
examples.note: Real service-desk correction: polite, clear, complete — the true intent follows right after

entries.nuance: An everyday repair phrase you fire off the instant someone misreads your words or your motive. Literally '그게 (that) + 아니라 (it is not, and so…)': 아니라 is the connective form of 아니다 ('to not be'), so the phrase is grammatically incomplete on purpose — it leans forward, pulling the correct version along behind it. Leading with 그게 아니라 softens a correction the way English 'no, what I mean is…' does: you're fixing a misunderstanding, not winning an argument, so it protects the other person's face. 그게 아니라요 (with 요 added to the phrase itself) adds extra politeness when you're in formal or cautious mode. Distinguish it carefully from 그게 아니면 (sounds nearly identical but means 'if not that, then…' — offers an alternative rather than denying) and from 그런 게 아니라 ('it's not that kind of thing' — rejects a whole category). The English-speaker pitfall is treating it as a standalone 'No.' and stopping; Korean listeners expect the real explanation to follow immediately, or the phrase sounds unfinished and slightly rude.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
English speakers use it as a complete reply ('That's not it.') and stop. Korean needs the real meaning attached: 그게 아니라 + your actual point. On its own it leaves the listener waiting.
Confusing 그게 아니라 (denying: 'it's not that') with 그게 아니면 (offering an alternative: 'if not that, then…'). One corrects, the other proposes a plan B — swapping them derails the conversation.
Saying 그것이 아니라 in casual speech sounds stiff and bookish; the natural spoken contraction is 그게 아니라. Reserve the full 그것이 for formal writing.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'that — it is not, and…' (그게 = 그것이 contracted; 아니라 = connective of 아니다). It's grammatically a dangling clause that REQUIRES the true statement to follow. In use it means 'No, you've misread me — here's what I actually meant.'

Use it the instant you feel misread — a wrong inference about your motive, a misheard request, or a badly landed joke. Works at every speech level: 그게 아니라 + 요 (그게 아니라요) is a standalone polite softener; 그게 아니라 (without 요) is casual-neutral; 그게 아니야 is pure 반말 with close friends. Safe with any interlocutor — it's explicitly face-saving. Avoid a harsh or loud delivery, which can make it sound like scolding.

그게 아니면 sounds almost identical but means 'if not that, then…' — it proposes a plan B rather than correcting. 그런 게 아니라 rejects a whole assumed category ('it's not that kind of situation') rather than one specific claim. 아니에요 is a plain flat denial with no built-in segue to your real meaning.

그게 아니라 (neutral) → 그게 아니라요 (extra-polite standalone) → 그게 아니라고요 (emphatic repeat, 'No — I said it's NOT that!') → 그런 게 아니라 (category denial) → 그게 아니고 (softer variant, 'it's not that and…'). In writing or formal speech: 그것이 아니라 (uncontracted, stiff).

Treating it as a complete sentence and stopping: 'That's not it.' In Korean, 그게 아니라 is a dangling clause — the real explanation MUST follow immediately, or you sound like you've cut yourself off and left the listener confused. Also: don't reach for 그것이 아니라 in spoken, casual conversation — it sounds overly formal and bookish.

entries.english: Now that you mention it / Come to think of it / Now that I think about it (realizing something mid-conversation)
entries.shortExplanation: 그러고 보니 is a practical expression meaning "Now that you mention it / Come to think of it / Now that I think about it (realizing something mid-conversation)".
entries.explanation: 그러고 보니 (geureogo boni) = "Now that you mention it / Come to think of it / Now that I think about it (realizing something mid-conversation)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 그러고 보니 오늘 점심을 안 먹었네요. ("Come to think of it, I haven't eaten lunch today."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.ko: 그러고 보니 오늘 점심을 안 먹었네요.
usagePhrases.romanization: geureogo boni oneul jeomsimeul an meogeonneyo.
usagePhrases.en: Come to think of it, I haven't eaten lunch today.
usagePhrases.note: Solo realization as you speak — nothing triggered it except the flow of thought

usagePhrases.en: Now that I look — did you get a haircut?
usagePhrases.note: 그러고 보니까 = -까 makes it more pointed, like 'wait, actually now that I think about it...'

usagePhrases.en: Now that you mention it, it's already December.
usagePhrases.note: Noticing the passage of time sparked by what someone just said

usagePhrases.en: Now that I hear it, you're right.
usagePhrases.note: Related: 듣고 보니 = 'now that I've heard it through' — specifically prompted by listening

examples.ko: 그러고 보니 우산을 안 가져왔네.
examples.romanization: geureogo boni usaneul an gajyeowanne.
examples.en: Come to think of it, I didn't bring an umbrella.
examples.note: Simple solo realization, one clause — the most common minimal pattern

examples.ko: A: 민수 씨 요즘 안 보이네요. B: 그러고 보니 진짜 한참 못 봤네요.
examples.romanization: A: minsu ssi yojeum an boineyo. B: geureogo boni jinjja hancham mot bwanneyo.
examples.en: A: I haven't seen Minsu lately. B: Now that you mention it, it really has been a while.
examples.note: Other person's remark sparks the realization — 그러고 보니 signals it's fresh, triggered by what B just heard

examples.ko: 그러고 보니 우리 처음 만난 지 벌써 일 년이나 됐네요, 시간 참 빠르다.
examples.romanization: geureogo boni uri cheoeum mannan ji beolsseo il nyeonina dwaenneyo, sigan cham ppareuda.
examples.en: Now that I think about it, it's already been a whole year since we first met — time really flies.
examples.note: Real reflection spun into a fuller thought; -네요 + 시간 참 빠르다 is a natural follow-through

entries.nuance: A connector for the exact moment a thought clicks into place mid-conversation. It breaks down as 그러고 ('having done/been so,' from 그러다) + 보니 ('upon looking/seeing,' from the -고 보니 pattern meaning 'do and then notice'), so literally 'looking at it that way, I now notice….' The realization is always FRESH — sparked by what someone just said or by something you just glimpsed; you can't use it for something you already knew. Compare three near-synonyms: 그러고 보니 is the broadest 'huh, now that I consider it'; 알고 보니 ('as it turns out') reveals a hidden truth that was previously unknown to both parties; 듣고 보니 ('now that I've heard it') is specifically triggered by what the other person said; and 생각해 보니 ('on reflection') implies deliberate thinking rather than a sudden click. Register is neutral — the form itself stays identical, only the ending verb changes (네요 for polite surprise, 네 for casual). Two critical pitfalls for English speakers: first, it marks new awareness — using it for known facts sounds odd; second, 그러고 is NOT 그리고 ('and') — one vowel separates them but the meaning is entirely different.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using it for something you already knew. 그러고 보니 specifically flags a fresh realization; for known facts use 사실은 ('actually') or just state it plainly.
Writing or saying 그리고 보니 instead of 그러고 보니. 그리고 means 'and'; 그러고 (from 그러다, 'to do so') is the correct base. The mix-up is the single most common slip here.
Jamming it into a single word (그러고보니). Standard spacing keeps 그러고 보니 as two words; the 보니 part is a separate verb.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'having done/been so (그러고) + upon seeing/noticing (보니)' — the -고 보니 pattern in Korean signals 'I did X, and THEN I noticed Y.' The real meaning is: 'I just connected the dots — here's something I've freshly realized.' The whole point is that the insight is new.

Use it at the moment a realization lands mid-conversation — your own thought or triggered by what someone just said. Extremely common in casual and casual-polite speech (반말 and 해요체 equally). Not used in formal written or presentation Korean; the form itself is invariant — only the following verb changes for register. Fine with anyone from close friends to polite acquaintances.

알고 보니 ('as it turns out') reveals a hidden truth now confirmed; 듣고 보니 ('now that I've heard it') specifically needs the other person's words as a trigger; 생각해 보니 ('on reflection') sounds more deliberate, implying you've actively thought it over. 그러고 보니 is the lightest and broadest — any fresh click, no deliberate effort required.

그러고 보니 (standard) → 그러고 보니까 (more emphatic/pointed) → 그러고 보면 ('if you think about it that way,' hypothetical) → 듣고 보니 (when the trigger is specifically something you heard) → 알고 보니 (when a hidden truth has now emerged).

Two traps: (1) Using it for facts you already knew — it specifically flags a NEW awareness; for known information just state it directly or use 사실은 ('actually'). (2) Writing or saying 그리고 보니 — 그리고 means 'and'; 그러고 comes from 그러다 ('to do so'). One vowel difference, entirely different meaning. Standard orthography also keeps it two words: 그러고 보니 (not 그러고보니).

entries.english: Maybe that's why / Perhaps because of that / That might be why (guessing a cause)
entries.shortExplanation: 그래서 그런지 is a practical expression meaning "Maybe that's why / Perhaps because of that / That might be why (guessing a cause)".
entries.explanation: 그래서 그런지 (geuraeseo geureonji) means "Maybe that's why / Perhaps because of that / That might be why (guessing a cause)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 어제 잠을 못 잤어요. 그래서 그런지 하루 종일 피곤하네요. ("I couldn't sleep last night. Maybe that's why I'm tired all day."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.ko: 어제 잠을 못 잤어요. 그래서 그런지 하루 종일 피곤하네요.
usagePhrases.romanization: eoje jameul mot jasseoyo. geuraeseo geureonji haru jongil pigonhaneyo.
usagePhrases.en: I couldn't sleep last night. Maybe that's why I'm tired all day.
usagePhrases.note: Classic two-sentence pattern: state the cause, then express the hedged result

usagePhrases.en: Maybe because it's the weekend, there are so many people.
usagePhrases.note: N(이)라 그런지 = 'perhaps because it's N' — noun-attached variant

usagePhrases.en: Perhaps because it's raining, the streets are quiet.
usagePhrases.note: V/A-아서/어서 그런지 = 'maybe because ~' — attaches directly to a verb/adjective

usagePhrases.ko: 요즘 운동을 해서 그런지 컨디션이 좋아요.
usagePhrases.romanization: yojeum undongeul haeseo geureonji keondisyeoni joayo.
usagePhrases.en: Maybe it's because I've been exercising — I feel great lately.
usagePhrases.note: Crediting a positive habit for a good result; the hedge signals you're not 100% sure

examples.ko: 피곤해서 그런지 자꾸 하품이 나와요.
examples.romanization: pigonhaeseo geureonji jakku hapumi nawayo.
examples.en: Maybe because I'm tired, I keep yawning.
examples.note: One cause, one observed symptom — the minimal, everyday pattern

examples.ko: A: 오늘따라 가게가 한가하네요. B: 평일이라 그런지 손님이 별로 없어요.
examples.romanization: A: oneulttara gagega hangahaneyo. B: pyeongirira geureonji sonnimi byeollo eopseoyo.
examples.en: A: The shop's unusually quiet today. B: Maybe because it's a weekday, there aren't many customers.
examples.note: Noun-attached 이라 그런지 in dialogue — speculating about a cause you can't confirm

examples.ko: 새 안경을 바꿔서 그런지 눈이 좀 피곤하고 머리도 살짝 아프네요.
examples.romanization: sae angyeongeul bakkwoseo geureonji nuni jom pigonhago meorido saljjak apeuneyo.
examples.en: Maybe because I changed to new glasses, my eyes feel tired and my head aches a little too.
examples.note: Tentative self-diagnosis stacking two noticed symptoms — note 살짝 ('slightly') matches the hedging tone

entries.nuance: A soft, speculative cause-marker meaning 'I suspect this is the reason, though I'm not certain.' The hedge is baked into the -ㄴ지 ending (from 그렇다, 'to be so'): 그런지 literally asks-to-itself 'whether it's so,' keeping the speaker from overcommitting. So 그래서 그런지 = 'so, [maybe] because of that…' and points back to a cause already stated, while the extended patterns -아서/어서 그런지 and -(이)라 그런지 attach the guess directly onto a cause clause. The sharpest contrast to master is against bare 그래서 ('so, therefore'), which states a cause you're SURE of: 비가 와서 길이 막혀요 ('traffic is jammed because it's raining' — definite) vs 비가 와서 그런지 길이 막히네요 ('maybe because it's raining, traffic seems jammed' — tentative). Using plain 그래서 when you're only guessing sounds overconfident; using 그래서 그런지 when the link is obvious can sound oddly wishy-washy. Because it introduces an OBSERVED result, English speakers sometimes try to bolt a request onto it (그래서 그런지 + 도와주세요) — that is grammatically and functionally wrong.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 그래서 그런지 for a cause you're certain of. It always carries a 'maybe' hedge; for a definite cause-effect, drop to plain 그래서 (e.g. 비가 와서 길이 막혀요).
Attaching a request or command after it ('그래서 그런지 좀 도와주세요'). It links a cause to an OBSERVED result, so it must end in a statement of what you noticed, not an imperative.
Mishandling the connector on a noun: it's 주말이라 그런지 (N+이라), not 주말이어서 그런지 in casual speech. With 이다, the natural form is N(이)라 그런지.

structuredNuance.t: 그런지 = '(I wonder) whether it's so' — the -ㄴ지 ending is a self-directed question that bakes uncertainty into the clause. So 그래서 그런지 literally means 'so, whether it's because of that…' and the real English sense is 'maybe that's why / perhaps that's the reason' — always hedged, never definite.

Use it when you notice a result and want to name a likely — but unconfirmed — cause. Extremely common in casual and casual-polite conversation, both spoken and texted. The pattern is neutral in register: 그래서 그런지 (standalone), -아서 그런지 (verb), -(이)라 그런지 (noun) all ride any speech level. Not typical in formal reports or academic writing, where you'd use 아마도 … 때문인 것으로 보인다 instead.

그래서 ('so, therefore') states a cause you're certain of — the result is definite. 그래서 그런지 adds a hedge — the result is observed but the causal link is your best guess. 덕분에 ('thanks to') credits a positive cause with gratitude and no uncertainty. 탓에 ('because of,' blame) attributes a negative result with certainty to a cause.

V/A-아서/어서 그런지 (cause = verb/adjective clause) → N(이)라 그런지 (cause = noun) → 그래서 그런지 (cause just stated in previous sentence). All share the same 그런지 hedge. The negative: 그래서 그런 건 아닌지 ('maybe it's NOT because of that') escalates the speculation.

Two traps: (1) Using plain 그래서 when you're only guessing — it sounds overconfident if the link is uncertain; add 그런지 to signal the hedge. (2) Trying to follow 그래서 그런지 with a request or command — it's a cause-to-observed-result connector, so only a statement of what you noticed can follow, never an imperative. And for nouns, use N(이)라 그런지, not 이어서 그런지, which is unnatural in everyday speech.

entries.english: Anyway / By the way / That aside (changing the subject)
entries.shortExplanation: 그건 그렇고 is a practical expression meaning "Anyway / By the way / That aside (changing the subject)".
entries.explanation: "Anyway / By the way / That aside (changing the subject)" — that is 그건 그렇고 (geugeon geureoko). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 그건 그렇고, 점심 뭐 먹을까요? ("Anyway, what should we eat for lunch?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Anyway, what should we eat for lunch?
usagePhrases.note: Pivoting cleanly from a closed topic to a new one

usagePhrases.ko: 그건 그렇고 너 요즘 회사는 어때?
usagePhrases.romanization: geugeon geureoko neo yojeum hoesaneun eottae?
usagePhrases.en: By the way, how's work these days?
usagePhrases.note: Casual subject change with a friend; signals 'I've set the previous thing aside'

usagePhrases.ko: 그건 그렇다 치고, 다음 얘기 해요.
usagePhrases.romanization: geugeon geureota chigo, daeum yaegi haeyo.
usagePhrases.en: Setting that aside, let's move on.
usagePhrases.note: 그건 그렇다 치고 = 'even granting that, anyway' — stronger, implies more deliberate shelving
그나저나 = close synonym; almost interchangeable but feels slightly more colloquial

examples.ko: 그건 그렇고, 너 밥은 먹었어?
examples.romanization: geugeon geureoko, neo babeun meogeosseo?
examples.en: Anyway, did you eat?
examples.note: Quickest possible pivot to a new question — one topic closed, one opened

examples.ko: A: 그 드라마 결말이 좀 아쉬웠어요. B: 그러게요. 그건 그렇고, 주말에 시간 돼요?
examples.romanization: A: geu deurama gyeolmari jom aswiwosseoyo. B: geureogeyo. geugeon geureoko, jumare sigan dwaeyo?
examples.en: A: That drama's ending was a bit disappointing. B: Right. Anyway, are you free this weekend?
examples.note: Acknowledge the previous point, then steer toward unrelated business — the two-step pivot

examples.ko: 회의 보고는 잘 끝났어요. 그건 그렇고, 아까 말씀하신 그 책 제목이 뭐였죠?
examples.romanization: hoeui bogoneun jal kkeunnasseoyo. geugeon geureoko, akka malsseumhasin geu chaek jemogi mwoyeotjyo?
examples.en: The meeting report wrapped up fine. By the way, what was the title of that book you mentioned earlier?
examples.note: Real situation: parking a work topic to reopen an earlier unrelated thread

entries.nuance: A friendly topic-switcher that literally says 'that — that's so, and…' (그건 = 그것은 contracted; 그렇고 = 그렇다 'to be so' + connective -고). It gently certifies the current topic as settled before swinging to a new one — you're acknowledging, not dropping, which is why it never sounds abrupt or rude. Compare three close neighbors: 그건 그렇고 closes a topic to open any new, unrelated one; 그나저나 ('anyway, be that as it may') is nearly interchangeable and equally common; but 말이 나왔으니까 ('since it's come up') does the OPPOSITE — it segues to a RELATED point, riding the current topic rather than leaving it. So the decision is: is your next remark connected to what's being discussed? Then use 말이 나왔으니까. Are you leaving the topic entirely? Use 그건 그렇고. Register is casual-polite, natural in both speech and written chat. Two English-speaker pitfalls: 'by the way' in English can preface a jab or a sudden challenge, but 그건 그렇고 only steers topics — never pushes back. And the spelling: 그렇고 keeps the ㅎ from 그렇다 (do NOT write 그러고, which comes from the different verb 그러다).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using it to disagree or push back, the way English 'by the way…' sometimes does. 그건 그렇고 only changes the topic; to object you'd say 그건 아니고 ('that's not it') or 그렇긴 한데 ('that may be, but…').
Spelling 그렇고 as 그러고. 그렇고 comes from 그렇다 ('to be so') and keeps the ㅎ; 그러고 comes from 그러다 ('to do so') and means something else. Different verb, different meaning.
Using it to introduce a closely RELATED follow-up. If the new remark grows out of the same topic, the natural choice is 말이 나왔으니까 ('since it came up'); 그건 그렇고 implies you're leaving the topic behind.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'that thing (그건 = 그것은) — it is so, and… (그렇고).' The real effect: a polite certification that the previous topic is accepted and closed, followed by an opening for something new. Not a dismissal — an acknowledgment, then a pivot.

Use when you want to leave a topic behind cleanly without the previous speaker feeling ignored — you've 'filed' their point before moving on. Casual-polite (해요체) in default use; works equally in 반말 between friends (그건 그렇고 너 밥은 먹었어?). Very common in spoken Korean and texted conversation. Polite formal registers tend to use 그 점은 그렇고 or 그 부분은 그렇다 치고 in meetings.

그나저나 is an almost interchangeable swap — slightly more colloquial, the same casual register, same function. 말이 나왔으니까 ('since it's come up') is the OPPOSITE: it leans INTO the current topic rather than switching away. 아무튼/어쨌든 ('anyway, in any case') can also switch topics but has a stronger 'regardless' flavor that can dismiss rather than acknowledge.
그건 그렇고 (standard) → 그건 그렇다 치고 (stronger: 'even granting that') → 그나저나 (near-synonym, slightly more colloquial) → 뭐 그건 그렇고 (softened with 뭐 for an even more casual pivot).

Two traps: (1) Using it to disagree or push back — English 'by the way' can preface a challenge, but 그건 그렇고 never does; for objection use 그건 아니고 or 그렇긴 한데. (2) Spelling 그렇고 as 그러고 — 그렇고 comes from 그렇다 (keeps the ㅎ); 그러고 comes from the different verb 그러다 and means something else entirely.

entries.english: Since we're on the subject / Now that it's come up / Speaking of which (segueing into a related point)
entries.shortExplanation: 말이 나왔으니까 is a practical expression meaning "Since we're on the subject / Now that it's come up / Speaking of which (segueing into a related point)".
entries.explanation: 말이 나왔으니까 (mari nawasseunikka) = "Since we're on the subject / Now that it's come up / Speaking of which (segueing into a related point)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데, 저도 그게 좀 불편했어요. ("Since it's come up, I'll say it — that bothered me a little too."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.ko: 말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데, 저도 그게 좀 불편했어요.
usagePhrases.romanization: mari nawasseunikka haneun marinde, jeodo geuge jom bulpyeonhaesseoyo.
usagePhrases.en: Since it's come up, I'll say it — that bothered me a little too.
usagePhrases.note: 말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데 = a set lead-in that signals an honest opinion is coming, softened by being 'invited' by the topic

usagePhrases.en: Since we're already on it, let's decide now.
usagePhrases.note: 말 나온 김에 = shorter, casual variant stressing convenient timing: 'while we're at it'

usagePhrases.ko: 여행 말이 나왔으니까 말인데, 다음에 같이 갈래요?
usagePhrases.romanization: yeohaeng mari nawasseunikka marinde, daeume gachi gallaeyo?
usagePhrases.en: Speaking of travel — want to go together next time?
usagePhrases.note: Topic-surfacing pattern: name the topic + 말이 나왔으니까 + request

usagePhrases.en: Since money came up, I'll be honest.
usagePhrases.note: 얘기가 나왔으니까 = 'since the talk (얘기) has come up' — 얘기 variant is equally natural

examples.ko: 말이 나왔으니까 하나만 더 물어볼게요.
examples.romanization: mari nawasseunikka hanaman deo mureobolgeyo.
examples.en: Since it's come up, let me ask just one more thing.
examples.note: Short segue into a single follow-up question — the follow-up must be genuinely related

examples.ko: A: 회식은 다음 주 금요일이에요. B: 아, 말이 나왔으니까 말인데, 저는 그날 좀 늦을 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: A: hoesigeun daeum ju geumyoirieyo. B: a, mari nawasseunikka marinde, jeoneun geunal jom neujeul geot gatayo.
examples.en: A: The team dinner is next Friday. B: Oh, since it's come up — I'll probably be a bit late that day.
examples.note: Adding relevant information while the topic is still live; 아, 말이 나왔으니까 말인데 is a very natural spoken cluster

examples.ko: 이사 말이 나왔으니까 말인데, 혹시 그 동네에 괜찮은 집 있으면 좀 소개해 줄 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: isa mari nawasseunikka marinde, hoksi geu dongnee gwaenchaneun jip isseumyeon jom sogaehae jul su isseoyo?
examples.en: Speaking of moving — if you happen to know a decent place in that neighborhood, could you put me onto it?
examples.note: Real situation: riding the current topic into a polite, related request — notice 혹시 and -아 줄 수 있어요? soften the ask

entries.nuance: A spoken segue that piggybacks on a topic SOMEONE JUST RAISED so your follow-up feels naturally invited rather than out of nowhere. It parses as 말이 ('the topic/word,' subject) + 나왔으니까 (나오다 'to come out,' past form 나왔다 + -(으)니까 'since/because'), literally 'since the subject has come out [just now].' The past tense is essential — the topic has ALREADY surfaced. The fuller idiom 말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데 ('since it's come up, this is what I want to say…') cushions a candid remark or a small request by framing it as triggered by the conversation, not by your own agenda. Two sharp contrasts: against 그건 그렇고, which switches AWAY to an unrelated topic — 말이 나왔으니까 leans INTO the current one; against 말 나온 김에 (using -(으)ㄴ 김에 'while we're at it'), which stresses opportune timing ('let's decide NOW while the subject is live') rather than the candid-addition flavor. English-speaker pitfall: 'speaking of which' in English can drift far from the original topic, but 말이 나왔으니까 requires a genuinely related thread that just surfaced. And like all these lead-ins, it's grammatically incomplete — the real remark must follow.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using it to jump to an unrelated topic, the way English 'speaking of which' can drift. 말이 나왔으니까 requires the point to be genuinely tied to what just came up; for an unrelated switch use 그건 그렇고.
Leaving it dangling as if it were a full sentence. It's a lead-in — you must follow it with the actual remark or request (often via …말인데, …할게요, …물어볼게요).
Mis-conjugating 나오다: it's 나왔으니까 (past + 으니까), not 나오니까. The topic has ALREADY come up, so the past tense is what makes the 'now that it's surfaced' meaning work.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'since the topic (말이) has come out (나왔으니까).' The past tense 나왔 is load-bearing: the topic has ALREADY surfaced in the conversation just now. Real meaning: 'I'm adding something related while the door is open — you opened this topic, not me, so my addition feels invited.' It frames your remark as a natural, non-pushy extension.

Use it when the other person has JUST mentioned a topic you have a related comment or question on — you ride their wave rather than changing the subject. Casual-polite 해요체 in default use. Short variant 말 나온 김에 (spoken, casual) is common with friends. The fuller 말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데 softens a candid remark or request especially well in semi-formal settings like team chats or with acquaintances. Not typical in formal writing or presentations.

그건 그렇고 ('anyway, by the way') does the OPPOSITE — it switches AWAY from the current topic to something unrelated; 말이 나왔으니까 stays ON the current topic. 말 나온 김에 shares the same base but stresses TIMING: 'let's do it now while the subject is live,' rather than 'I have something related to add.' 주제가 나온 김에 is a more formal variant with the same logic.
말이 나왔으니까 (standard) → 말이 나왔으니까 말인데 (softer, candid-remark version) → 말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데 (fullest version, most cushioned) → 말 나온 김에 (casual, timing-focused) → 얘기가 나왔으니까 (얘기 variant).

English 'speaking of which' can drift loosely from the original topic — Korean 말이 나왔으니까 demands the new point be genuinely tied to what JUST came up. For an unrelated topic switch, use 그건 그렇고. Also: it's incomplete on its own — the follow-up remark must come immediately (often via 말인데, 물어볼게요, 솔직히 말하면). And mis-conjugating: it's 나왔으니까 (past 나왔다 + 으니까), not 나오니까 — the past tense is what makes 'since it's surfaced' work.

entries.english: Oh good / What a relief / I'm glad to hear that (relieved that things turned out okay)
entries.shortExplanation: 다행이네요 is a practical expression meaning "Oh good / What a relief / I'm glad to hear that (relieved that things turned out okay)".
entries.explanation: 다행이네요 (dahaengineyo) means "Oh good / What a relief / I'm glad to hear that (relieved that things turned out okay)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 다 잘 끝났다니 다행이네요. ("I'm glad to hear it all worked out."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: I'm glad to hear it all worked out.
usagePhrases.note: Reacting with relief to good news you've just heard; -다니 = 'the fact that…'
다행이다 = casual; 정말 ('really') adds weight and sincerity

usagePhrases.en: It could've been worse / Silver lining.
usagePhrases.note: 불행 중 다행 = fixed idiom: '(something) fortunate amid (greater) misfortune'
V/A-아서/어서 다행이다 = 'lucky that ~' — attaches the relieving clause directly

examples.ko: A: 시험 통과했어요. B: 아, 다행이네요.
examples.romanization: A: siheom tonggwahaesseoyo. B: a, dahaengineyo.
examples.en: A: I passed the exam. B: Oh, what a relief.
examples.note: Bare relief reaction — the -네요 ending signals spontaneous, in-the-moment warmth

examples.ko: A: 검사 결과 괜찮대요. B: 아, 다행이네요. 저도 걱정 많이 했어요.
examples.romanization: A: geomsa gyeolgwa gwaenchantaeyo. B: a, dahaengineyo. jeodo geokjeong mani haesseoyo.
examples.en: A: The test results are fine. B: Oh, what a relief. I was really worried too.
examples.note: Relief on someone else's behalf + sharing your own worry — shows genuine care

examples.ko: 가방에 있을 줄은 몰랐어요. 진짜 잃어버린 줄 알고 한참 찾았는데, 있어서 정말 다행이에요.
examples.romanization: gabange isseul jureun mollasseoyo. jinjja ireobeorin jul algo hancham chajanneunde, isseoseo jeongmal dahaengieyo.
examples.en: I had no idea it was in my bag. I really thought I'd lost it and searched for ages — I'm so relieved it turned up.
examples.note: Real situation: the longer build-up ('I thought… I searched…') makes the 정말 다행이에요 payoff feel earned and natural

entries.nuance: A warm, sincere reaction of relief at a bad outcome that has been avoided. The core noun 다행 is Sino-Korean 多幸 — literally 'much (多) good fortune (幸)' — so the phrase means 'how fortunate' rather than just 'good.' When aimed at someone else's news it reads as caring ('I'm genuinely relieved FOR you'); about your own situation it's a heartfelt 'phew.' The -네요 ending (해요체) adds spontaneous, in-the-moment warmth — a beat more emotional than the flatter 다행이에요. The attached pattern -아서/어서 다행이에요 lets you name exactly what you're relieved about: 늦지 않아서 다행이에요 ('good thing we weren't late'), 없어서 다행이에요 ('lucky there wasn't any'). Two sharp neighbors: 잘됐네요 ('that turned out well / good for you') celebrates a positive OUTCOME, while 다행이에요 specifically exhales relief that something bad was AVOIDED; and 축하해요 ('congratulations') marks an earned achievement, not a near-miss someone survived. Casual form: 다행이다 (반말). Critical English-speaker spelling trap: 다행이네요 (noun 다행 + 이다) vs 다행히 (adverb 'fortunately') — only the noun form can end a sentence as a reaction.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 다행히네요 or ending a reaction with 다행히. 다행히 is the adverb 'fortunately' and modifies a verb; the relief reaction is 다행이에요/다행이네요 (noun 다행 + 이다).
Using it as congratulations for an achievement. 다행이에요 is relief that something bad was avoided; for an earned success say 축하해요, and for a happy outcome say 잘됐네요.
Saying 다행이네요 about a trivial non-event where nothing was ever at risk. The word implies there WAS a worry or danger that has now passed — without that tension it sounds odd.

structuredNuance.t: 다행 is Sino-Korean 多幸: 'much (多) good fortune (幸).' So 다행이네요 literally says 'it is much good fortune' — but the real meaning is an exhale of relief that something bad was narrowly avoided. It carries emotional warmth, not just a factual assessment.

Use it specifically when there WAS a real worry or danger that has now passed — good medical news, a found lost item, an escaped accident, a passed exam. Without that prior tension the word sounds hollow. Casual: 다행이다 (반말, close friends). Casual-polite: 다행이에요 / 다행이네요 (해요체, default). The -네요 form is more spontaneous and warm; 다행이에요 is slightly more composed. Safe with any interlocutor.

잘됐네요 ('that turned out well') celebrates a positive result; 다행이에요 exhales relief that a bad result was avoided — the underlying emotion is different. 축하해요 ('congratulations') marks an achievement earned through effort. 다행히 is the ADVERB form ('fortunately…') and modifies a verb in the middle of a sentence — it cannot end a sentence as a reaction.

다행이다 (반말) → 다행이에요 (polite, composed) → 다행이네요 (polite, spontaneous warmth) → 정말 다행이에요 (emphasis) → 진짜 다행이다 (casual emphasis) → V-아서/어서 다행이에요 (specifying what you're relieved about) → 불행 중 다행이에요 (fixed idiom: 'silver lining').

Two traps: (1) Spelling: 다행이네요 (noun 다행 + 이다 conjugated) vs 다행히 (adverb 'fortunately') — only 다행이에요/네요 ends a sentence as a standalone reaction; 다행히 must modify a verb. (2) Using it as congratulations for an achievement — 다행이에요 is relief that something bad was avoided, not praise for effort. For achievements, use 축하해요 or 잘했어요.

entries.english: Oh no, this is bad / We're in trouble / Uh-oh, big problem (reacting to something going wrong)
entries.shortExplanation: 큰일 났다 is a practical expression meaning "Oh no, this is bad / We're in trouble / Uh-oh, big problem (reacting to something going wrong)".
entries.explanation: "Oh no, this is bad / We're in trouble / Uh-oh, big problem (reacting to something going wrong)" — that is 큰일 났다 (keunil natda). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 큰일 났다, 지갑을 집에 두고 왔어. ("Oh no, I left my wallet at home."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.ko: 큰일 났다, 지갑을 집에 두고 왔어.
usagePhrases.romanization: keunil natda, jigabeul jibe dugo wasseo.
usagePhrases.en: Oh no, I left my wallet at home.
usagePhrases.note: Realizing a concrete problem mid-action; fully casual 반말

usagePhrases.en: What do I do, this is a disaster.
usagePhrases.note: 큰일 났어요 = polite; pairs naturally with 어떡해요 ('what do I do')

usagePhrases.en: At this rate something bad's going to happen.
usagePhrases.note: 큰일 나다 (future/conditional) = 'trouble will/might occur' — warning or prediction

usagePhrases.en: That was a close call — could've been a disaster.
usagePhrases.note: 큰일 날 뻔하다 = 'nearly went terribly wrong' — past near-miss

examples.ko: 큰일 났어, 늦었어!
examples.romanization: keunil nasseo, neujeosseo!
examples.en: Oh no, I'm late!
examples.note: Two-word alarm blurted in the heat of the moment — the simplest pattern

examples.ko: A: 기차 막차 끊겼대요. B: 헐, 큰일 났네요.
examples.romanization: A: gicha makcha kkeunkyeotdaeyo. B: heol, keunil nanneyo.
examples.en: A: They say the last train's gone. B: Oh no, we're in trouble.
