examples.romanization: A: dadeul oneul jeongmal yeolsimhi haesseoyo. / B: ne, dadeul sugohasyeosseoyo. deureogaseo swiseyo.
examples.en: A: Everyone really worked hard today. / B: Yes, everyone did. Go home and rest.
examples.note: A/B team wrap-up exchange; the team lead uses 수고하셨어요 with -시- to honor the group

examples.ko: 이사 도와줘서 정말 수고하셨어요.
examples.romanization: isa dowajwoseo jeongmal sugohasyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Thank you so much for helping me move.
examples.note: thanking someone after genuinely tiring, selfless help; the effort focus of 수고하셨어요 makes this feel more sincere than just 감사해요

entries.nuance: 수고 is Sino-Korean 受苦 (receive-suffering), so 수고했어요 literally acknowledges that someone has taken on toil and trouble on your behalf — it honors the effort itself, not whether the outcome was good. A project can fail and still earn a heartfelt 수고했어요 for the work poured in, which is what separates it from 잘했어요 (good result). It collocates naturally with 많이, 오늘도, and 정말. The register trap: a beginner often reads 'never say 수고 to a boss,' but the actual rule is more precise — bare 수고했어요 (peer-to-peer level) aimed upward is too familiar; the fully honorific 수고하셨습니다 or 수고하셨어요 is widely used to seniors in modern Korean workplaces and sounds respectful. What truly grates upward is 수고하세요 ('keep on working'), which can read as 'you keep slaving away' — never say this to a superior. The English-speaker pitfall is using the casual form everywhere after hearing it so often; always gauge the rank relationship first.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying bare 수고했어요 to a clear senior
Without -시- it carries a peer-to-junior tone that feels too familiar upward. Use 수고하셨습니다 or 수고하셨어요 for seniors.
Telling your boss 수고하세요 as you leave first
To a superior it can sound like 'you keep working away,' faintly cheeky. Better: 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다 / 먼저 가 보겠습니다.
Using 수고했어요 to praise the quality of a result
It thanks effort, not achievement; for a good result say 잘했어요 (downward) or 고생하셨습니다. Mixing the two blurs your meaning.

structuredNuance.t: 수고 (受苦) = 'receiving hardship'; the full expression thanks someone for the toil they took on, not the quality of the result. A failed project still earns a genuine 수고했어요 — this empathy-over-outcome sense is what makes it warm and distinct.

After a shared task ends — end of shift, end of a project, after someone helped you move or cook. Peer/junior: 수고했어요. Senior: 수고하셨어요 or 수고하셨습니다 (add -시-). Never use bare 수고했어요 to a boss; never say 수고하세요 to a superior as you leave.

잘했어요 judges the result (good outcome). 고생하셨어요 also means 'you went through hardship' and is slightly more sympathetic — often used after genuinely grueling work (moving, a long trip, overtime). 수고했어요 is the everyday catch-all for effort; 고생하셨어요 carries a slightly heavier weight of real struggle.
수고했어 (반말) → 수고했어요 (peer/junior) → 수고하셨어요 (honorific, safe) → 수고하셨습니다 (most formal) → 수고 많았어요 ('you worked really hard').

English 'thanks for your hard work' is socially flat. In Korean, the register split is sharp: using casual 수고했어요 to a senior is too familiar, and 수고하세요 to a departing boss can sound like 'you keep toiling.' When in doubt about rank, default to 수고하셨습니다.

entries.english: I wish you good luck.
entries.shortExplanation: 행운을 빌어요 is a practical expression meaning "I wish you good luck.".
entries.explanation: "I wish you good luck." — that is 행운을 빌어요 (haenguneul bireoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 행운을 빌어요 ("I wish you luck"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: warm and polite, said before a challenge
-ㅂ니다 for written notes or formal contexts
-ㄹ게요 promises ongoing support on your behalf
반말 to a close friend before an event

examples.ko: 내일 시험이지? 행운을 빌어!
examples.romanization: naeil siheomiji? haenguneul bireo!
examples.en: Your exam's tomorrow, right? Good luck!
examples.note: 반말 cheering on a friend the night before

examples.ko: A: 내일 면접인데 너무 떨려요. / B: 잘 하실 수 있어요. 행운을 빌어요!
examples.romanization: A: naeil myeonjeobinde neomu tteollyeoyo. / B: jal hasil su isseoyo. haenguneul bireoyo!
examples.en: A: I have an interview tomorrow and I'm so nervous. / B: You'll do great. I'm wishing you luck!
examples.note: A/B exchange — the natural context: one person shares anxiety, the other responds with encouragement + this phrase

examples.ko: 새 가게 잘되길 바라요. 진심으로 행운을 빕니다.
examples.romanization: sae gage jaldoegil barayo. jinsimeuro haenguneul bimnida.
examples.en: I hope your new shop thrives. I sincerely wish you good luck.
examples.note: formal, heartfelt send-off; 진심으로 elevates the sincerity for a big life milestone

entries.nuance: 행운 is Sino-Korean 幸運 ('fortunate-luck'), and 빌다 here means to pray or wish, so 행운을 빌어요 is literally 'I pray for your good fortune' — a sincere, warm hope that chance will favor someone before an exam, interview, audition, or big decision. The object particle 을 (행운을) is part of the set phrase and should not be dropped. Contrast it with 화이팅!/파이팅!, which is a breezy, energetic cheer focused on spirit and effort — Koreans actually shout 화이팅 far more often in everyday life; 행운을 빌어요 is gentler, more formal, and specifically about luck and outcome rather than hustle. Note that 빌다 also means 'to borrow' in the form 빌리다 — these are distinct verbs, so the sentence cannot be misread as 'I'll borrow your luck.' The timing is everything: 행운을 빌어요 belongs strictly before the event; after results are known, switch to 축하해요 (congratulations) or 아쉽네요 / 다음엔 잘 될 거예요 (too bad, better luck next time).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 행운을 빌어요 after the event is over
It hopes for a future outcome, so it only fits beforehand. After the fact use 축하해요 (good news) or 수고했어요 / 아쉽네요.
Dropping the particle: 행운 빌어요
The set phrase keeps the object marker — 행운을 빌어요. Omitting 을 sounds clipped and grammatically incomplete.
Confusing prayer-빌다 with borrow-빌리다
행운을 빌어요 uses 빌다 (to pray/wish for). 빌리다 means to borrow and is a completely different verb; don't blend them.

structuredNuance.t: 행운 (幸運) = 'fortunate luck'; 빌다 = 'to pray/wish.' Literally 'I pray for your good fortune.' The real use is a sincere, heartfelt pre-event wish — warmer and more formal than a casual cheer, genuinely pointing at luck and chance rather than just effort.

Use it the day before or moment before an exam, interview, audition, competition, or major decision. Polite 빌어요 for most situations; bump to 빕니다 in written messages or formal settings. Drop to 빌어 only with close friends. Always pre-event — it makes no sense once results are out.

화이팅!/파이팅! is a far more common spoken cheer, focused on effort, energy, and fighting spirit — it is casual and punchy. 행운을 빌어요 is quieter, points at luck/outcome, and sounds slightly more formal and sincere. 잘될 거예요 ('it'll go well') is reassurance based on optimism, not a luck-wish.
행운을 빌어 (반말) → 행운을 빌어요 (polite) → 행운을 빌게요 ('I'll keep wishing you luck') → 행운을 빕니다 (formal/written) → 진심으로 행운을 빕니다 (sincerest, for big milestones).

English 'good luck' can be casual, throwaway, or even sarcastic. 행운을 빌어요 is always genuinely sincere and can only precede the event — using it after results land sounds strange. Also, Koreans in daily speech much more often shout 화이팅! rather than 행운을 빌어요; over-relying on this phrase sounds bookish when a casual situation calls for 화이팅.

entries.english: Congratulations.
entries.shortExplanation: 축하드려요 is a practical expression meaning "Congratulations.".
entries.explanation: 축하드려요 (chukhadeuryeoyo) = "Congratulations.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 축하드려요 ("congratulations (humble-polite)"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: raises the listener — for elders, bosses, formal joy
warm and equal, to a peer or friend
진심으로 = sincerely, for big milestones like weddings or promotions
생신 is the honorific word for birthday

examples.ko: 합격 축하해! 한턱 쏴.
examples.romanization: hapgyeok chukahae! hanteok sswa.
examples.en: Congrats on passing! Treat us.
examples.note: 반말 ribbing a friend about standing a round

examples.ko: A: 오늘 아들이 대학에 합격했대요. / B: 어머, 정말요? 진심으로 축하드려요!
examples.romanization: A: oneul adeuri daehage hapgyeokaetdaeyo. / B: eomeo, jeongmaryo? jinsimeuro chukadeuryeoyo!
examples.en: A: I heard your son got into university today. / B: Oh my, really? Heartfelt congratulations!
examples.note: A/B exchange — sharing good family news; 드려요 is natural here because the parent being congratulated is an elder

examples.ko: 승진 축하드립니다, 부장님. 정말 잘되셨어요.
examples.romanization: seungjin chukadeurimnida, bujangnim. jeongmal jaldoesyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Congratulations on your promotion, sir. I'm so glad for you.
examples.note: to a superior, fully formal -ㅂ니다 + 부장님; 잘되셨어요 uses honorific -시-

entries.nuance: 축하 is Sino-Korean 祝賀 ('celebrate-congratulate'), and the critical split is in the verb: 축하해요 uses plain 하다 (to do), while 축하드려요 replaces it with 드리다 ('to humbly give/offer'), elevating the listener. So 축하드려요 is 'I humbly offer you my congratulations' — the humble verb lifts the other person socially. Use it without hesitation for bosses, parents, in-laws, teachers, and wedding guests who are your seniors. The event is fronted as a bare noun: 결혼 축하, 합격 축하, 승진 축하 — not 합격을 축하해요, which sounds overly grammatical. Remember to swap 생일 for the honorific 생신 when the birthday person is a senior. Contrast 축하드려요 with 잘됐어요 ('that worked out great'), which is informal celebration for a good outcome but not a formal congratulation. The English-speaker pitfall is using flat casual 축하해 with a senior or at a formal event — that sounds startlingly blunt; always ask yourself whether 드려요 or 합니다 is appropriate before speaking.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using casual 축하해 toward a senior or boss
반말-level 축하해 sounds disrespectful on a happy occasion. Use the humble 축하드려요 or 축하드립니다.
Saying 생일 축하드려요 to an elder
For a senior, 생일 becomes the honorific 생신: 생신 축하드려요. Using plain 생일 to an elder is a missed courtesy.
Inserting a particle: 합격을 축하해요
Colloquial Korean fronts the event directly without a particle — 합격 축하해요. Adding 을/를 here sounds stiff and textbook-like.

structuredNuance.t: 축하 (祝賀) = 'celebrate-congratulate'; 드리다 = 'to give humbly.' The real effect: by choosing 드리다 over 하다, you lower yourself and raise the listener — the same humble mechanism as 드세요 ('please eat') vs 먹어요. It transforms a peer-level phrase into a respectful one.

To a peer or friend: 축하해요 / 축하해. To a senior, boss, elder, or in a formal setting (wedding toast, promotion announcement): 축하드려요 or 축하드립니다. For a senior's birthday specifically: 생신 축하드려요 (생신, not 생일). Never use bare 축하해 upward.

축하해요 (plain, peer-level) vs 축하드려요 (humble, senior-level) — same warmth, different social altitude. 잘됐어요 ('great that it worked out') is casual celebration of a good outcome but not a formal congratulation. 수고하셨어요 thanks effort; 축하드려요 celebrates a positive result.
축하해 (반말) → 축하해요 (polite peer) → 축하드려요 (humble-polite, senior) → 축하드립니다 (most formal) → 진심으로 축하드립니다 (sincerest). Event noun fronted: 합격 / 결혼 / 승진 + 축하드려요.

English 'congratulations' is socially flat — you can say it to anyone at any register. In Korean, defaulting to casual 축하해 with a boss or elder is jarringly familiar. Also, Korean fronts the event (합격 축하해요), unlike English 'congrats on passing' — resist adding an extra particle between the event noun and 축하.

entries.english: It is cool. / You look great.
entries.shortExplanation: 멋있어요 is a practical expression meaning "It is cool. / You look great.".
entries.explanation: 멋있어요 (meosisseoyo) means "It is cool. / You look great.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 멋있어요 ("that's cool / impressive"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: praising style, skill, or character
정말 strengthens genuine admiration
반말 to a friend

usagePhrases.en: you're so impressive / you look wonderful
usagePhrases.note: honorific -시- about or to a respected person

examples.ko: 우와, 그 재킷 진짜 멋있어!
examples.romanization: uwa, geu jaekit jinjja meosisseo!
examples.en: Whoa, that jacket's seriously cool!
examples.note: 반말 complimenting a friend's outfit; 진짜 is the everyday intensifier

examples.ko: A: 저 오늘 발표 어땠어요? / B: 발표하시는 모습이 정말 멋있었어요.
examples.romanization: A: jeo oneul balpyo eottaesseoyo? / B: balpyohasineun moseubi jeongmal meosisseosseoyo.
examples.en: A: How was my presentation today? / B: You looked really impressive up there.
examples.note: A/B exchange — praising someone's manner and presence, not just the content; 모습 = 'the way they looked/appeared'

examples.ko: 혼자 세계여행을 하셨다니, 정말 멋있으세요.
examples.romanization: honja segyeyeohaengeul hasyeotdani, jeongmal meosisseuseyo.
examples.en: You traveled the world alone? You're genuinely amazing.
examples.note: admiring a person's life decision with honorific 멋있으세요 — the -시- is what makes it respectful rather than patronizing

entries.nuance: 멋있어요 comes from 멋 (style, flair, class) + 있어요 (to have), literally 'to have flair' — it praises whatever strikes you as stylish, impressive, admirable, or awe-inspiring: a look, a skill, a bold decision, a person's whole presence. Because it is built on 있다 (not 하다), its past is 멋있었어요 and the honorific is 멋있으세요 — knowing this pattern removes all conjugation worry. Contrast with 예뻐요 (pretty/cute-beautiful, focused on visual appeal) and 잘생겼어요 (good-looking/handsome, specifically about a person's face and physique): those judge surface appearance alone, while 멋있어요 also reaches inner character and competence — a wise speech or a courageous act is 멋있다 but not 예쁘다. In casual speech 멋지다 / 멋져요 is a common synonym, slightly more energetic in tone. The big English-speaker pitfall is the near-homophone 맛있어요 ('tasty,' from 맛 = taste): 멋 (first vowel ㅓ, 'uh') vs 맛 (first vowel ㅏ, 'ah') differ by one vowel and swapping them changes 'you're so cool' into 'you're so delicious.'
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 멋있어요 (cool) with 맛있어요 (tasty)
Only the vowel differs — 멋 (style) vs 맛 (taste). Say 멋있어요 to praise coolness; 맛있어요 is strictly for food.
Using 멋있어요 where you mean simply 'pretty'
멋있어요 admires style and impressiveness, not surface prettiness alone. For refined beauty use 예뻐요; for physical attractiveness use 잘생겼어요.
Conjugating it like a 하다 verb, e.g. 멋있해요
It follows the 있다 adjective pattern: present 멋있어요, past 멋있었어요. There is no 하다 in it.

structuredNuance.t: 멋 (flair/style) + 있어요 (to have) = 'to have flair.' The real scope is wide: you can call a stylish outfit, a skillful performance, a brave decision, or a person's whole aura 멋있다. It is admiration that goes beyond surface looks.

Use freely to peers and friends: 멋있어 (반말), 멋있어요 (polite). To a respected person you admire — a teacher, an older person, someone you look up to — use 멋있으세요 (honorific -시-). Calling a senior or boss 귀여워요 is condescending; 멋있으세요 to them is flattering.

예뻐요 = refined surface beauty (a flower, a dress, a woman's looks). 잘생겼어요 = physical attractiveness, mainly for men's faces. 멋있어요 = stylish coolness + impressiveness + inner character. 멋지다 / 멋져요 = casual synonym, slightly more energetic. Only 멋있어요 can praise a courageous decision or an impressive skill.
멋있어 (반말) → 멋있어요 (polite) → 멋있으세요 (honorific) → 정말 멋있어요 → 멋있었어요 (past). Synonym track: 멋지다 → 멋져요 (casual spoken).

Critical near-homophone: 맛있어요 ('tasty,' from 맛 = taste). The vowels differ — 멋 (ㅓ) vs 맛 (ㅏ) — but in fast speech they sound very close. Keep 멋 for style and impressiveness, 맛 for flavor and food. Swapping them turns a compliment into something very strange.

entries.english: It is cute.
entries.shortExplanation: 귀여워요 is a practical expression meaning "It is cute.".
entries.explanation: "It is cute." — that is 귀여워요 (gwiyeowoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 귀여워요 ("that's cute"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: polite reaction to something adorable
너무 = 'so/too,' the most natural intensifier here
반말 to a friend or about an animal
plain exclamation blurted aloud or in a chat caption

examples.ko: 어머, 너무 귀여워!
examples.romanization: eomeo, neomu gwiyeowo!
examples.en: Oh my, so cute!
examples.note: 반말 reaction on seeing a puppy; 어머 is a soft, affectionate 'oh my'

examples.ko: A: 조카가 말을 배우기 시작했대요. / B: 아, 그 나이가 제일 귀여워요!
examples.romanization: A: jokaga mareul baeugi sijakaetdaeyo. / B: a, geu naiga jeil gwiyeowoyo!
examples.en: A: My niece started learning to talk. / B: Oh, that age is the cutest!
examples.note: A/B exchange — sharing good family news; reacting with 귀여워요 about a toddler is the most typical daily use

examples.ko: 고양이가 발로 세수해요. 진짜 귀엽다.
examples.romanization: goyangiga ballo sesuhaeyo. jinjja gwiyeopda.
examples.en: The cat washes its face with its paw. So cute.
examples.note: plain-form 귀엽다 as a caption or a comment to oneself — very common in texting and social media

entries.nuance: 귀여워요 reacts to something small, charming, and lovable — babies, pets, plushies, a child's small actions. It is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: the stem 귀엽- drops its ㅂ before vowel endings and adds 워, giving 귀여워요 (never 귀엽어요) and past 귀여웠어요. The same flip happens with 춥다 → 추워요 (cold), 덥다 → 더워요 (hot), 무겁다 → 무거워요 (heavy) — mastering 귀엽다 unlocks a whole conjugation class. Contrast 귀엽다 with 예쁘다 (pretty, elegant beauty) and 아름답다 (beautiful, grand): 귀엽다 is specifically about adorable, often youthful or petite charm, while 예쁘다 covers refined loveliness. The key social caution: calling a senior or authority figure 귀여워요 is condescending — it infantilizes them. English 'cute' gets aimed at people of all ages casually, but in Korean that can land badly; keep 귀엽다 for children, pets, peers you're close to, and romantic partners.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 귀엽어요 instead of 귀여워요
귀엽다 is ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ becomes 우/워 before a vowel ending → 귀여워요, past 귀여웠어요. 귀엽어요 is incorrect.
Calling a senior or boss 귀여워요
To someone you should respect it sounds patronizing and infantilizing. Reserve 귀엽다 for kids, pets, peers, or a romantic partner.
Using 귀여워요 to mean elegant beauty
귀엽다 is adorable/endearing, not refined-pretty. For graceful beauty use 예뻐요; for grand or moving beauty use 아름다워요.

structuredNuance.t: 귀엽다 is a pure native Korean adjective meaning 'adorable/endearing.' The real range: small animals, babies, toddlers, tiny or petite things, and — in romantic contexts — a partner's charming behavior. It is about small-scale, youthful, lovable cuteness, not broad beauty.

Use freely for animals, children, plushies, and charming small actions. To a peer friend about their behavior it is affectionate. To a romantic partner it is a compliment. Never to a senior or someone you respect — it reads as condescending or infantilizing. 반말 귀여워 to a close friend is fine.

예쁘다 = refined, elegant beauty (a woman's looks, a flower, a dress). 아름답다 = grand, scenic, or deeply moving beauty. 귀엽다 = adorable, small-scale, youthful cuteness. These do not overlap much — a puppy is 귀엽다, not 아름답다; a mountain view is 아름답다, not 귀엽다.
ㅂ-irregular: 귀엽다 → 귀여워요 (present) → 귀여웠어요 (past) → 귀여울 것 같아요 ('seems like it'll be cute'). Same flip as 춥다 → 추워요, 덥다 → 더워요. Intensified: 너무 귀여워요, 정말 귀여워요.

Two traps: (1) conjugating it as 귀엽어요 — wrong, the ㅂ drops and becomes 워: 귀여워요; (2) directing it at a senior the way English 'cute' freely applies across ages — in Korean 귀여워요 to a boss or elder is patronizing. Also note: the wrong form 귀엽어요 is one of the most common written errors.

entries.english: How are you doing?
entries.shortExplanation: 잘 지내요? is a practical expression meaning "How are you doing?".
entries.explanation: 잘 지내요? (jal jinaeyo) means "How are you doing?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 잘 지내요? ("are you doing well?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: rising intonation = question; polite check-in with someone you know
honorific -시-, more deferential for seniors

usagePhrases.en: how are you getting on these days?
usagePhrases.note: 어떻게 asks 'how,' more open-ended, invites detail
falling intonation = the answer; same phrase, opposite tone

examples.ko: 야, 잘 지내? 요즘 어때?
examples.romanization: ya, jal jinae? yojeum eottae?
examples.en: Hey, doing okay? How are things lately?
examples.note: 반말 checking in on a friend; 요즘 어때? is the natural follow-up to invite sharing

examples.ko: A: 오랜만이에요! 그동안 잘 지내셨어요? / B: 네, 덕분에 잘 지냈어요. 선생님은요?
examples.romanization: A: oraenmanieyo! geudongan jal jinaesyeosseoyo? / B: ne, deokbune jal jinaesseoyo. seonsaengnimeunyo?
examples.en: A: Long time no see! Have you been well? / B: Yes, I've been fine, thanks. And you, teacher?
examples.note: A/B reunion exchange — honorific 지내셨어요 toward a teacher; answering with 덕분에 ('thanks to you') is the polite Korean formula

examples.ko: 부모님도 다 잘 지내시죠?
examples.romanization: bumonimdo da jal jinaesijyo?
examples.en: Your parents are doing well too, right?
examples.note: asking about someone's family; honorific 지내시죠 = 지내세요 + 죠 (seeking confirmation); shows warmth and care

entries.nuance: 잘 지내요 pairs 잘 (well) with 지내다, a verb meaning 'to get along / pass one's days / spend time living,' so it asks about a span of time — how has life been going lately? — not a single instant. It is far closer to 'how have you been keeping?' than a snapshot 'how do you feel right now?' Intonation alone turns question into answer: a rising pitch makes it 잘 지내요?, a falling pitch makes it 잘 지내요. Contrast it with 어떻게 지내요? (more open-ended, invites details, no built-in presumption) and 기분이 어때요? ('how do you feel?', probing mood in the moment, not life span). Because it implies a stretch of time, the past form 잘 지냈어요? is especially natural when reconnecting after a gap. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like American 'How are you?' which functions as a ritual greeting to strangers in English; in Korean 잘 지내요? implies you know the person and are genuinely reconnecting — directing it at a shop clerk or a stranger you just met sounds oddly familiar.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 잘 지내요? as a greeting to a stranger
It presumes prior acquaintance and reconnection. For someone you just met, 안녕하세요 is the right greeting; save 잘 지내요? for people you already know.
Saying 잘 있어요? when you mean 'how have you been?'
있다 asks location/existence ('are you there/around?'), not how life is going. The set phrase for well-being over time is 잘 지내요?
Dropping the honorific for a senior: plain 잘 지내요? to an elder
To someone you respect, add -시-: 잘 지내세요? / 잘 지내셨어요? Plain 잘 지내요? can feel a touch too casual upward.

structuredNuance.t: 잘 (well) + 지내다 (to pass one's days / get along in life). The real meaning spans a period of time — 'how has life been going?' — not a snapshot feeling. Intonation alone flips it: rising = question (잘 지내요?), falling = answer (잘 지내요.).

Use it when reconnecting with someone you already know — a friend you haven't seen in a while, a former colleague, a classmate. For a senior: 잘 지내세요? (with honorific -시-). After a long absence: past form 잘 지냈어요? To a stranger you have just met: don't use it; just say 안녕하세요.

어떻게 지내요? ('how are you getting on?') is more open-ended and invites a longer answer — no built-in presumption of 'fine.' 기분이 어때요? asks about mood right now, not life in general. 잘 있어요? ('are you okay?') checks whether someone is in a safe situation, not how life is going.
잘 지내? (반말) → 잘 지내요? (polite) → 잘 지내세요? (honorific, for seniors) → 잘 지냈어요? (past, after a gap) → 잘 지내셨어요? (past + honorific). Polite answer: 네, 덕분에 잘 지내요.

American 'How are you?' is a social ritual said to strangers and cashiers with no real expectation of an answer. 잘 지내요? implies prior acquaintance and genuine reconnection — using it with a stranger or a shop clerk sounds oddly intimate. With anyone unfamiliar, 안녕하세요 alone is the correct greeting.

entries.english: See you again.
entries.shortExplanation: 또 만나요 is a practical expression meaning "See you again.".
entries.explanation: 또 만나요 (tto mannayo) = "See you again.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 또 만나요 ("see you again"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: friendly, hopeful parting; implies you genuinely want to meet again
또 + 보다, the shorter casual version, slightly lighter
다음에 = next time; implies a real plan or intention
반말 to a close friend as you part

examples.ko: 오늘 진짜 재밌었어. 또 봐!
examples.romanization: oneul jinjja jaemisseosseo. tto bwa!
examples.en: Today was really fun. See ya!
examples.note: 반말 parting from a friend after a great time; 오늘 진짜 재밌었어 is the natural lead-in

examples.ko: A: 벌써 가요? 아쉽다. / B: 네, 다음에 또 만나요. 조심히 들어가세요.
examples.romanization: A: beolsseo gayo? aswipda. / B: ne, daeume tto mannayo. josimhi deureogaseyo.
examples.en: A: Are you leaving already? What a shame. / B: Yes, let's meet again next time. Get home safely.
examples.note: A/B farewell exchange — the most natural daily context for 또 만나요, paired with a safety send-off

examples.ko: 좋은 인연이었어요. 기회 되면 또 만나요.
examples.romanization: joeun inyeonieosseoyo. gihoe doemyeon tto mannayo.
examples.en: It was a good connection. Let's meet again if we get the chance.
examples.note: warm but open-ended farewell; 기회 되면 ('if the opportunity arises') softens it for situations where you genuinely hope to reconnect but have no fixed plan

entries.nuance: 또 만나요 joins 또 (again) with 만나다 (to meet, in the 요-form), meaning 'let's meet again' — a hopeful goodbye that implies you value this person and want to continue the relationship. 만나다 specifically means 'to meet up with a person' (a sought-out, intentional encounter), unlike 보다 ('to see/come across') which is lighter and more incidental; 또 봐요 uses 보다 and functions as the casual 'bye' with no specific plan behind it, while 또 만나요 feels a touch more intentional and warm. Compare 다음에 봐요 (vaguer 'see you next time'), 안녕히 가세요 (neutral farewell with no promise of reunion), and 또 만나요 (specifically projects a future meeting with genuine intent). Note 만나다 takes the person as a direct object or comitative: 친구를 만나요 / 친구와 만나요 — never 에서 for the person. The English-speaker pitfall is reflex-saying 'see you' to everyone, including strangers you will never see again; in Korean 또 만나요 genuinely implies an expectation of meeting, so for a one-off encounter where there is no plan to reconnect, the appropriate farewell is 안녕히 가세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 또 만나요 when you won't realistically meet again
It projects a genuine future meeting. For a one-time encounter with no plans, use 안녕히 가세요 / 안녕히 계세요 instead.
Using 보다 for arranging to meet a person, e.g. '친구를 봐요' for 'I'm meeting a friend'
보다 is 'see/look'; to actively arrange to meet a person use 만나다 — 친구를 만나요. (또 봐요 as a casual goodbye is fine, but for making plans, 만나다 is correct.)
Marking the person with 에서: 친구에서 만나요
에서 marks a location, not the person met. Use 친구를 만나요 or 친구와 만나요; 에서 is for the place (카페에서 만나요).

structuredNuance.t: 또 (again) + 만나요 (we meet, polite). Literally 'we meet again / let's meet again.' The real connotation: a genuine forward projection of wanting to see this person again — not a throwaway farewell. It sets an expectation of reunion.

Use when parting from a friend, acquaintance, or someone you've just had a positive meeting with — and genuinely expect or hope to meet again. 반말 또 만나 for close friends. For a one-off meeting with no realistic plan, use the neutral 안녕히 가세요 instead. To a senior you're parting from: 또 뵙겠습니다 (humble 뵙다).

또 봐요 = casual 'see you,' using the lighter 보다; the parting phrase with no specific expectation. 다음에 봐요 = 'see you next time,' slightly vaguer and time-delayed. 안녕히 가세요 = neutral goodbye, no promise of reunion. 또 만나요 is the most intentional among these — it specifically projects wanting to meet the person again.
또 만나 (반말) → 또 만나요 (polite) → 또 뵙겠습니다 (humble, for seniors) → 다음에 또 만나요 (adds next-time specificity). Casual synonym: 또 봐 / 또 봐요.

English 'see you' and 'see you again' are reflexive parting fillers that can be said to strangers you will genuinely never see again. 또 만나요 in Korean projects real intent to meet — using it with someone you just met briefly and will likely never see again can feel hollow or odd. For a one-time farewell, 안녕히 가세요 is the clean choice.

entries.english: I'd like to open an account
entries.shortExplanation: 계좌 만들고 싶어요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to open an account".
entries.explanation: 계좌 만들고 싶어요 (gyejwa mandeulgo sipeoyo) means "I'd like to open an account". Say it as one set phrase — for example 계좌 만들고 싶어요 ("I'd like to open an account"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to open an account
usagePhrases.note: Polite 존댓말, the everyday opening line at the bank counter

usagePhrases.en: I'm here to open an account
usagePhrases.note: 개설하다 is the formal/bank-form verb for 'open (an account)'; mirrors the teller's own register

usagePhrases.en: I came to open a bankbook
usagePhrases.note: 통장 (passbook) is what people say casually for a basic account; slightly more colloquial

usagePhrases.en: I'm looking to open an account
usagePhrases.note: -는데요 softens the request and invites the teller to guide you next

examples.ko: 계좌 만들고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: gyejwa mandeulgo sipeoyo.
examples.en: I'd like to open an account.
examples.note: Said to the teller as you sit down; the simplest, safest opener with any bank staff

examples.ko: A: 어떻게 오셨어요? / B: 계좌 만들고 싶어요. 외국인인데 어떤 서류 필요해요?
examples.romanization: A: eotteoke osyeosseoyo? / B: gyejwa mandeulgo sipeoyo. oegugininde eotteon seoryu piryohaeyo?
examples.en: A: How can I help you? / B: I'd like to open an account. I'm a foreigner — what documents do I need?
examples.note: Real two-turn exchange: state your purpose then immediately flag 외국인 status so the teller tells you what's required

examples.ko: 월급 받을 계좌 하나 개설하려고 왔는데요.
examples.romanization: wolgeup badeul gyejwa hana gaeseolharyeogo wanneundeyo.
examples.en: I came to open an account to receive my salary.
examples.note: State the purpose (월급 받을 'to receive a salary'); banks sometimes ask why, and giving a reason speeds things up

entries.nuance: 계좌 만들고 싶어요 is 계좌 (計座, 'account') + 만들다 ('to make') + -고 싶어요 ('I want to'): the plain spoken way to tell a teller you want to open an account. Two nouns are in play: 계좌 is the technical term — the account number used on forms, apps, and bank systems — while 통장 literally means the physical passbook but in everyday speech doubles as 'account' (so 통장 만들고 싶어요 sounds just as natural and a bit more colloquial). The bank's own paperwork and staff prefer the verb 개설하다 ('to establish/open'), so mirroring that verb in 계좌 개설하려고요 puts you on the right register. For a salary account specifically, say 급여 계좌 만들고 싶어요. The English-speaker trap is translating 'open' literally as 열다 ('to open a door') — 계좌 열고 싶어요 is wrong; an account is 만들다 or 개설하다, never 열다. This phrase is always addressed to staff, so 존댓말 is the only appropriate register here.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 계좌 열고 싶어요.
열다 ('to open') is for doors, lids, or shops — not bank accounts. You MAKE an account: 계좌 만들고 싶어요, or formally 계좌 개설하려고요.
Confusing 계좌 with 계산.
계좌 is a bank account; 계산 is 'calculation / paying a bill'. They sound close but 계산하고 싶어요 would mean 'I want to pay', not 'open an account'.
Using 통장 to mean the account number.
통장 is the physical passbook (and casually 'account'); the account NUMBER is 계좌번호. To give your number, say 계좌번호, not 통장.

structuredNuance.t: 계좌 (計座, 'account') + 만들다 ('to make') + -고 싶어요 ('I want to'). The verb is 만들다 — you literally 'make' an account, not 'open' one as in English. For a salary account say 급여 계좌 만들고 싶어요; for an account to receive transfers say 입금 받을 계좌요.

계좌 만들다 (plain speech) ≈ 계좌 개설하다 (formal, bank's own verb, better on paperwork). 통장 만들다 is the colloquial alternative — 통장 is the physical passbook but stands in for 'account' in casual talk. Choose 개설하다 at the counter for polish.
계좌 is Sino-Korean 計座, 'reckoning-seat → account'. 개설 is 開設, 'open + establish', the formal banking term.
Always addressed to bank staff, so 존댓말 is required. No 반말 version is appropriate here. You can soften with -려고 하는데요 to invite the teller to guide you, or be direct with 만들고 싶어요.

Saying 계좌 열고 싶어요 — 열다 means 'to open a door/lid/shop', never a bank account. An account is 만들다 (make) or 개설하다 (establish). Calquing 'open an account' word-for-word is the single most common error here.

entries.english: I'd like to check my balance
entries.shortExplanation: 잔액 확인하고 싶어요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to check my balance".
entries.explanation: "I'd like to check my balance" — that is 잔액 확인하고 싶어요 (janae kwaginhago sipeoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 잔액 확인하고 싶어요 ("I'd like to check my balance"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to check my balance
usagePhrases.note: Polite; said to a teller or narrated aloud before using an ATM
조회 ('inquiry/lookup') is the exact button label on ATMs and banking apps

usagePhrases.en: How much is in my account?
usagePhrases.note: 잔고 is the casual everyday synonym for 'balance' in spoken Korean
남다 ('to remain') framing — very natural in conversational speech

examples.ko: 잔액 확인하고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: janae kwaginhago sipeoyo.
examples.en: I'd like to check my balance.
examples.note: Said to a teller, or aloud to yourself before deciding whether to withdraw

examples.ko: A: 입금됐는지 확인해 주세요. / B: 네, 잔액 조회해 드릴게요. 잠깐만요.
examples.romanization: A: ipgeumdwaenneunji hwaginhae juseyo. / B: ne, janaek johoehae deurilgeyo. jamkkanmanyo.
examples.en: A: Please check if the deposit came in. / B: Of course, let me look up the balance for you. Just a moment.
examples.note: Two-turn exchange: customer requests balance check using 잔액 조회, the official ATM/app term the teller mirrors back

examples.ko: 이체하기 전에 잔액부터 확인할게요.
examples.romanization: ichehagi jeone janaekbuteo hwaginhalgeyo.
examples.en: Before transferring, let me check the balance first.
examples.note: 잔액부터 ('starting with the balance') — 부터 = 'starting from/first'; confirms you have enough before sending

entries.nuance: 잔액 확인하고 싶어요 is 잔액 (殘額, 'remaining amount = balance') + 확인하다 ('to check/confirm') + -고 싶어요. Two near-synonyms matter: 잔액 is the formal term printed on receipts, ATM menus, and statements, while 잔고 ('balance / what's left') is the warmer everyday word in casual speech ('통장에 잔고가 없어' = 'my account's empty'). On machines and in apps, the action is labeled 잔액 조회 ('balance inquiry'), where 조회 specifically means looking up stored information — so 조회 is the word you tap, and 확인 is the broader 'check/confirm' you say aloud. The particle trap: it's 잔액을 확인하다 (object particle 을), not 잔액에 확인하다 (location particle 에). To a teller use polite speech; with a friend drop to 잔고 얼마야? The English-speaker trap is reaching for 균형 ('equilibrium, physical balance') for a bank balance — 통장 균형 is meaningless to Koreans; the bank term is 잔액 or 잔고 only.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'balance' as 균형.
균형 is physical/abstract equilibrium ('keep your balance'). A bank balance is 잔액 (formal) or 잔고 (casual). 통장 균형 is meaningless to Koreans.
Saying 잔액에 확인하고 싶어요.
확인하다 takes the object particle 을/를: 잔액을 확인하고 싶어요. The particle 에 (location/time) is wrong here.
Mixing up 조회 and 충전.
조회 is 'inquiry/look up' (checking the balance); 충전 is 'top up/recharge' (adding money, e.g. to a transit card). Tap 조회 to SEE the balance, not 충전.

structuredNuance.t: 잔액 (殘額, 'remaining amount') + 확인하다 ('to verify/confirm') + -고 싶어요. 잔액 is formally 'the amount remaining', which is exactly what a bank balance is. With a teller use 잔액 확인; with a friend say 잔고 얼마야? The particle is 을: 잔액을 확인하다.

잔액 (formal, on receipts/ATMs) vs 잔고 (warmer casual, in chat: 잔고 없어). 확인하다 ('confirm/check') vs 조회하다 ('look up in a system') — 잔액 조회 is the ATM button; 잔액 확인 is what you say aloud. They overlap but 조회 is screen/app language.
잔액 is 殘額, '殘 remaining + 額 amount'. The partner term 잔고 (殘高) shares 殘 but uses 高 ('height/level') — both mean 'remaining balance' but at different registers.

Polite 존댓말 with any teller or ATM-screen context. Drop to 잔고 얼마야? with close friends checking their own account. This phrase would be odd in 반말 since you're always either speaking to staff or narrating to yourself.

Translating 'balance' as 균형 — 균형 is physical/abstract equilibrium ('keep your balance'). A bank balance is 잔액 (formal) or 잔고 (casual). Also watch the particle: 잔액을 확인하다 (object 을), not 잔액에 확인하다 (location 에 doesn't fit here).

entries.english: I'm going to withdraw some cash
entries.shortExplanation: 현금 좀 뽑으려고요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm going to withdraw some cash".
entries.explanation: 현금 좀 뽑으려고요 (hyeongeum jom ppobeuryeogoyo) = "I'm going to withdraw some cash". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 현금 좀 뽑으려고요 ("I'm going to take out some cash"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: I'm going to take out some cash
usagePhrases.note: Casual-polite; 뽑다 ('pull out') is the everyday verb specifically for ATM cash

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to make a withdrawal
usagePhrases.note: 출금 (出金) is the formal/screen word for 'withdrawal' — closer to what you say at a counter

usagePhrases.en: I'm going to withdraw some money
usagePhrases.note: 찾다 (lit. 'find/retrieve') is the standard neutral verb for getting your money out
Stating the amount upfront; 만 ('only/just') limits it

examples.ko: 현금 좀 뽑으려고요.
examples.romanization: hyeongeum jom ppobeuryeogoyo.
examples.en: I'm going to take out some cash.
examples.note: Said heading to the ATM, or telling a friend why you're stopping

examples.ko: A: 잠깐만요, 현금 좀 뽑고 올게요. / B: 아, ATM 저기 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: jamkkanmanyo, hyeongeum jom ppopgo olgeyo. / B: a, ATM jeogi isseoyo.
examples.en: A: Just a moment — I'll go take out some cash and be right back. / B: Oh, the ATM is right over there.
examples.note: A/B exchange: natural pre-errand announcement; B points you to the machine

examples.ko: 통장에서 십만 원 찾고 싶은데요.
examples.romanization: tongjangeseo simman won chatgo sipeundeyo.
examples.en: I'd like to withdraw 100,000 won from my account.
examples.note: 통장에서 ('from the account') — source takes 에서; 찾다 is the standard polite counter verb

entries.nuance: 현금 좀 뽑으려고요 is 현금 (現金, 'cash') + 좀 (softener) + 뽑다 ('to pull/draw out') + -으려고요 ('I intend to'). Korean has three verbs for getting money out, and choosing right matters: 뽑다 is the breezy spoken verb for pulling cash from an ATM (돈 뽑다 = 'hit the ATM'); 찾다 — which elsewhere means 'find' — is the neutral standard 'withdraw' used at a counter or machine (돈을 찾다); and 출금하다 (出金) is the formal Sino-Korean word on screens and forms. The opposite — depositing — is 입금하다 or 넣다; keep 출금 (money out) vs 입금 (money in) firmly apart, since swapping them at a teller causes real mistakes. With a friend you'd say 돈 좀 뽑을게. The English-speaker traps: calquing 'withdraw' as 철수하다 (military 'retreat') is wrong; and the word 찾다 in a banking context means 'withdraw', not 'look for' — 돈 찾으러 가요 = 'going to withdraw money', not 'going to search for it'.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'withdraw' as 철수하다 or 후퇴하다.
Those mean military/strategic withdrawal (retreat). For money it's 출금하다 / 돈을 찾다 / 돈을 뽑다.
Reading 돈 찾다 as 'look for money'.
In a banking context 찾다 means 'withdraw' (retrieve your money), not 'search'. 돈 찾으러 왔어요 = 'I came to withdraw money'.
Confusing 출금 and 입금.
출금 (出金) = money OUT (withdrawal); 입금 (入金) = money IN (deposit). Tell the teller 출금이요 to take cash out, 입금이요 to put money in.

structuredNuance.t: 현금 (現金, 'cash') + 좀 (softener) + 뽑다 ('to pull out') + -으려고요 ('I intend to'). 뽑다 is colloquial for ATM cash; the neutral verb for any withdrawal context is 찾다. Formal on forms and screens: 출금하다. With friends: 돈 좀 뽑을게.

뽑다 ('pull out', breezy/ATM-specific) vs 찾다 ('retrieve', neutral, counter or ATM) vs 출금하다 (出金, formal Sino-Korean on screens). Opposite: 입금하다 / 넣다 (deposit). 뽑다 sounds casual and vivid; 출금 is the official term.
현금 is 現金 ('cash'); 출금 is 出金 ('money out', formal withdrawal); 입금 is 入金 ('money in', deposit). The 出/入 pairing is the key to remembering which way money moves.
현금 좀 뽑으려고요 is casual-polite — fine with a colleague or when talking out loud. At a counter use 출금하려고 하는데요 or 돈 찾고 싶어요. With friends just say 돈 뽑을게. Never use 반말 with bank staff.

Two traps: (1) calquing 'withdraw' as 철수하다 — 철수 is military/strategic withdrawal (retreat), not money. (2) 찾다 in banking means 'retrieve/withdraw', not 'look for' — 돈 찾으러 가요 = going to withdraw, not going on a treasure hunt.

entries.english: Is there a fee?
entries.shortExplanation: 수수료 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Is there a fee?".
entries.explanation: 수수료 있어요? (susuryo isseoyo?) means "Is there a fee?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 수수료 있어요? ("Is there a fee?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; the basic question before any transaction — ATM, transfer, exchange
When you already expect a fee and want the exact amount
붙다 ('to be attached') is how Koreans say a fee is 'added on' — very idiomatic
면제되다 ('to be exempted') — asking if you qualify for free service

examples.ko: 수수료 있어요?
examples.romanization: susuryo isseoyo?
examples.en: Is there a fee?
examples.note: Asked before transferring money or using another bank's ATM

examples.ko: A: 다른 은행 ATM이라 수수료 붙어요? / B: 네, 800원 붙어요.
examples.romanization: A: dareun eunhaeng ATMira susuryo buteoyo? / B: ne, 800won buteoyo.
examples.en: A: It's another bank's ATM — will a fee get charged? / B: Yes, 800 won gets added.
examples.note: A/B exchange: the natural 붙다 verb in both question and answer — fee 'attaches' to the transaction

examples.ko: 이체 수수료는 면제고, 출금만 수수료 있어요.
examples.romanization: iche susuryoneun myeonjego, chulgeumman susuryo isseoyo.
examples.en: Transfer fees are waived; only withdrawals have a fee.
examples.note: Hear the teller distinguish 이체 vs 출금 fees; 면제 = exemption

entries.nuance: 수수료 있어요? is 수수료 (手數料, 'handling fee/commission') + 있어요? ('is there?'). 수수료 is the all-purpose word for a bank transaction fee — ATM fees, transfer fees, wire fees, exchange margins — making it the single most useful money word for navigating a Korean bank. The most idiomatic verb pairing is 붙다 ('to stick/attach'): Koreans say 수수료가 붙어요 ('a fee gets tacked on'), which sounds more natural than the textbook 수수료를 내다 ('to pay a fee'); both are correct, but 붙다 describes fees that appear automatically on a transaction. To ask about a fee waiver, use 면제되다: 수수료 면제돼요? The key dividing line from 요금: 요금 is a fare or utility charge (전기 요금, 택시 요금), while 수수료 is the bank's cut for handling your transaction. Don't ask a bank about 요금. The English-speaker trap is using 비용 or 가격 — too generic and off-register for a bank fee. Grammar note: 붙다 is intransitive, so the subject particle is 가: 수수료가 붙어요, not 수수료를 붙어요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 요금 for a bank transaction fee.
요금 is a fare/utility charge (택시 요금, 전기 요금). A bank's handling fee is 수수료: 송금 수수료, 출금 수수료.
Saying 가격 or 비용 for the fee.
가격 is the 'price' of a product; 비용 is general 'cost/expense'. The specific banking word is 수수료. Ask 수수료 얼마예요?, not 가격 얼마예요?.
Saying 수수료를 붙어요.
붙다 ('to be attached') is intransitive — the fee attaches itself: 수수료가 붙어요 (subject 가). With an object particle it'd be the transitive 붙이다. Use 수수료가 붙어요.

structuredNuance.t: 수수료 (手數料, 'handling fee/commission') + 있어요? ('is there?'). 수수료 covers all transaction fees at a bank: ATM, wire, exchange margin. The idiom: 수수료가 붙어요 ('a fee attaches/is added') — 붙다 is intransitive so the subject takes 가, never 를.

수수료 (bank/transaction fee, handling cut) vs 요금 (fare/utility charge: 택시 요금, 전기 요금). Ask 수수료 있어요? at a bank; ask 요금 얼마예요? for a cab or utility bill. Also: 수수료를 내다 (pay a fee, textbook) vs 수수료가 붙다 (fee attaches, idiomatic spoken).
수수료 is 手數料 — 手數 'the number of hand-moves (labor)' + 料 'charge'. A fee for the work of handling your transaction.

Used with tellers, ATMs, and exchange booths — always 존댓말. The question mark structure stays the same in casual speech (수수료 있어?) when talking to a friend about their bank, but you'd still use 있어요? with any staff.
Using 비용 ('cost/expense') or 가격 ('price') for a bank fee — both are too generic. The specific word is 수수료. Also: 붙다 is intransitive — 수수료가 붙어요 (subject 가), not 수수료를 붙어요 (object 를 is wrong here).

entries.english: Please enter your PIN/password
entries.shortExplanation: 비밀번호 입력해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please enter your PIN/password".
entries.explanation: "Please enter your PIN/password" — that is 비밀번호 입력해 주세요 (bimilbeonho imnyeokae juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 비밀번호 입력해 주세요 ("Please enter your PIN"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: What the teller or machine says TO you; 입력하다 = 'input' (formal screen term)
눌러 주세요 ('please press') — common spoken version a counter teller uses
자리 = 'digit/place'; Korean card PINs are almost always 네 자리 (4 digits)
What YOU say when you can't remember it — the situation is now reversed

examples.ko: 비밀번호 입력해 주세요.
examples.romanization: bimilbeonho imnyeokae juseyo.
examples.en: Please enter your PIN.
examples.note: The teller slides the keypad toward you and says this — it's directed at the customer

examples.ko: A: 비밀번호 네 자리 눌러 주세요. / B: 네. (누름) 됐어요?
examples.romanization: A: bimilbeonho ne jari nulleo juseyo. / B: ne. (nureum) dwaesseoyo?
examples.en: A: Please key in your 4-digit PIN. / B: Sure. (presses) Is that it?
examples.note: A/B counter exchange: teller requests, customer confirms — 됐어요? = 'is that done?'

examples.ko: 비밀번호 세 번 틀려서 카드가 잠겼어요.
examples.romanization: bimilbeonho se beon teullyeoseo kadeuga jamgyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I got the PIN wrong 3 times so my card got locked.
examples.note: 세 번 틀리다 ('wrong 3 times') triggers the standard lockout; explain this to the teller so they can unlock it

entries.nuance: 비밀번호 (秘密番號, lit. 'secret number') covers PIN, app password, and even door code — Korean does not split 'PIN' from 'password' the way English does. The same word serves your card PIN at the ATM, your banking app login, and the gym locker code. Two verbs go with it: 입력하다 ('to input', the formal screen word) and 누르다 ('to press', the spoken 'key it in'); 비밀번호 입력해 주세요 and 비밀번호 눌러 주세요 are interchangeable, the latter slightly warmer. This phrase is usually said TO you by staff or the machine — the honorific 주세요 makes it a polite request to the customer; when YOU forgot it you flip to 비밀번호 잊어버렸어요. Digit count uses 자리 ('place/digit'): 네 자리 = four digits. The English-speaker traps: calling it 패스워드 sounds IT/tech-only; using 암호 sounds like a spy cipher or encryption, not a bank PIN. Also don't confuse 비밀번호 (secret, never share) with 계좌번호 (account number, freely shared to receive money).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 비밀번호 with 계좌번호.
비밀번호 is your SECRET PIN/password (never share it); 계좌번호 is your account NUMBER (you give it out to receive money). Mixing them is a real security slip.
Using 암호 for a bank PIN.
암호 leans toward 'cipher/secret code/encryption'. Your everyday card PIN and app login are 비밀번호. Banks and ATMs all say 비밀번호.
Saying 비밀번호를 눌러요 to staff as a request.
As a polite request TO the customer it needs the favor form: 비밀번호 눌러 주세요 / 입력해 주세요. Bare 눌러요 sounds like a flat statement, not a courteous instruction.

structuredNuance.t: 비밀번호 (秘密番號, 'secret number') covers PIN, app password, and door code — Korean has one word for all. This phrase is usually said TO you by staff (주세요 = polite request to the customer). When YOU forgot it: 비밀번호 잊어버렸어요. Digits: 네 자리 = 4-digit PIN.
비밀번호 입력해 주세요 (formal, screen/teller) vs 비밀번호 눌러 주세요 (spoken, slightly warmer). Don't confuse 비밀번호 (secret PIN, never share) with 계좌번호 (account number, share freely to get paid).
비밀번호 is 秘密番號 — 秘密 'secret' + 番號 'number'. The bundling of PIN and password into one word reflects that Korean security culture uses one term for all personal access codes.

Always 존댓말 in a bank/ATM/shop context — you're speaking to or being addressed by staff. The phrase 비밀번호 입력해 주세요 is directed AT the customer (they are the subject of 'entering'). In casual tech talk 비번 is the shortened form (비밀번호 → 비번).

Using 패스워드 (tech-only loanword) or 암호 ('cipher/secret code' — sounds like spy terminology). The universal daily-life word is 비밀번호. Also: mixing up 비밀번호 with 계좌번호 is a genuine security slip — never give your 비밀번호 to receive money.

entries.english: I'd like to send money here
entries.shortExplanation: 여기로 송금하고 싶어요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to send money here".
entries.explanation: 여기로 송금하고 싶어요 (yeogiro songgeumhago sipeoyo) = "I'd like to send money here". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 여기로 송금하고 싶어요 ("I'd like to send money here"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to send money here
usagePhrases.note: Polite; 송금 (送金) is the formal word for 'remittance'; 여기로 marks the destination with 로

usagePhrases.en: I want to send money to this account
usagePhrases.note: 보내다 ('to send') is the plain everyday verb; account takes 로

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to do a bank transfer
usagePhrases.note: 계좌이체 = account-to-account electronic transfer (the standard app/ATM method)
해외 송금 = international remittance; ask if your account/bank supports it

examples.ko: 여기로 송금하고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: yeogiro songgeumhago sipeoyo.
examples.en: I'd like to send money here.
examples.note: Handing over a slip with the account details to the teller

examples.ko: A: 이 계좌로 삼십만 원 보내 주실 수 있어요? / B: 네, 계좌번호랑 예금주 성함 확인해 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: i gyejwaro samsimman won bonae jusil su isseoyo? / B: ne, gyejwabeonhorang yegeumju seongham hwaginhae deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: Could you send 300,000 won to this account? / B: Sure, let me confirm the account number and account holder's name.
examples.note: Full counter exchange: 이 계좌로 ('to this account', destination takes 로); teller cross-checks 예금주 name

examples.ko: 미국에 있는 가족한테 송금하려고 하는데요.
examples.romanization: miguge inneun gajokante songgeumharyeogo haneundeyo.
examples.en: I'm trying to send money to family in the US.
examples.note: 가족한테 ('to family') — person takes 한테; 미국에 marks the location; use 하는데요 to invite guidance

entries.nuance: 여기로 송금하고 싶어요 uses 송금 (送金, 'send-money = remittance') + 하다 + -고 싶어요. Three terms cluster here: 송금 is the formal umbrella for sending money to someone (especially overseas wire transfers, 해외 송금); 계좌이체 (or just 이체) is specifically account-to-account electronic transfer done via app or ATM; 보내다 ('to send') is the plain casual verb. For a teller, either 송금하고 싶어요 or 이체하고 싶어요 works. The make-or-break point is particles for the destination: an account/bank/place takes 로/으로 — 이 계좌로 보내다; a PERSON takes 한테/에게 — 친구한테 송금하다. English speakers overuse 에 here: 이 계좌에 보내다 sounds unnatural to Koreans; native is 이 계좌로. Also keep 송금 (sending OUT) apart from 입금 (money coming IN): if you want to receive money, share your 계좌번호 so someone else can 입금/송금 to you. Don't translate 'transfer' as 옮기다 — that means physically moving objects.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Marking the destination account with 에 instead of 로.
Money goes TO an account with 로/으로: 이 계좌로 보내 주세요. 이 계좌에 보내다 sounds unnatural to natives.
Using 한테/에게 for an account number.
한테/에게 are for PEOPLE (친구한테 송금). An account or bank takes 로/으로 (이 계좌로). Match the particle to person vs. thing.
Translating 'transfer' as 옮기다.
옮기다 means physically moving/relocating something. A money transfer is 이체하다 or 송금하다. 돈을 옮기다 sounds like carrying cash around.

structuredNuance.t: 송금 (送金, 'send-money') + 하다 + -고 싶어요. 송금 is the formal term, especially for overseas remittance. Destination particle rule: place/account takes 로 (이 계좌로); person takes 한테/에게 (친구한테). Either 송금 or 이체 is natural with a teller.

송금 (formal umbrella, esp. overseas) vs 계좌이체/이체 (account-to-account, in-app/ATM) vs 보내다 (casual spoken). Also: 송금 = outgoing (you send); 입금 = incoming (money arrives). They're opposite sides of the same transfer.
송금 is 送金, '送 send + 金 money'. 해외 송금 (海外送金) = overseas remittance. The partner term 입금 is 入金, 'money coming in'.

Always 존댓말 at a bank counter. In a banking app you tap through menus, but when you speak or message about it use the same polite forms. With friends texting 돈 보낼게 is casual and natural — no need for 송금 in casual chat.

Two traps: (1) using 에 for the destination account — native Korean is 이 계좌로 (direction particle 로), not 이 계좌에. (2) Translating 'transfer' as 옮기다 ('to move/relocate an object') — money transfer is 이체/송금, never 옮기다.

entries.english: I'll make a transfer
entries.shortExplanation: 이체할게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll make a transfer".
entries.explanation: 이체할게요 (ichehalgeyo) means "I'll make a transfer". Say it as one set phrase — for example 이체할게요 ("I'll make a transfer"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; announcing your own intended action with -ㄹ게요
Choosing transfer as the payment method over card or cash

usagePhrases.en: I've made the transfer / I sent it
usagePhrases.note: Past tense — telling someone the money has been sent on your side

usagePhrases.en: I'll transfer it to you right away
usagePhrases.note: -아/어 드리다 (humble favor form) when sending to someone you respect

examples.ko: 이체할게요.
examples.romanization: ichehalgeyo.
examples.en: I'll make the transfer.
examples.note: Said at the counter or aloud as you confirm in the banking app

examples.ko: A: 현금 없어서 계좌이체로 할게요. / B: 계좌번호 알려 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: hyeongeum eopseoseo gyejwaichero halgeyo. / B: gyejwabeonho allyeo juseyo.
examples.en: A: I have no cash so I'll pay by bank transfer. / B: Please give me your account number.
examples.note: Classic split-the-bill exchange: 계좌이체로 할게요 is the payment choice; B responds with the natural 계좌번호 알려 주세요

examples.ko: 방금 이체했는데 입금됐는지 확인 좀 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: banggeum ichehaenneunde ipgeumdwaenneunji hwagin jom hae juseyo.
examples.en: I just transferred it — please check if it arrived.
examples.note: 이체했다 (you sent) vs 입금됐다 (it landed on their end) — two different verbs for the same money moving

entries.nuance: 이체할게요 is 이체 (移替, 'account-to-account transfer') + -할게요, the -ㄹ게요 ending that announces your own intended action politely. 이체 is the precise word for moving money electronically between accounts; 계좌이체 spells it out fully and is the label for 'pay by bank transfer' as a payment method — standard in Korea for rent, large purchases, and splitting bills. The everyday alternative is 보내다 ('send'), so 돈 보낼게요 and 이체할게요 mean the same in casual use, with 이체 sounding a touch more official. The crucial paired vocabulary: when you've SENT money you say 이체했어요 (active, you transferred), but confirming it ARRIVED uses 입금됐어요? (passive, deposited on their side) — the two verbs describe the same money from opposite perspectives. The English-speaker trap is register: 이체할게요 is natural conversational speech; 이체하겠습니다 is stiff/overly formal for everyday use. To send to someone senior, add the humble 드리다: 이체해 드릴게요. Don't confuse 이체 with 환전 (currency exchange).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 이체했어요 to mean the recipient got it.
이체했어요 means YOU sent it. Whether it ARRIVED is 입금됐어요? (deposited on their end). The two sides have different verbs: 이체 (send) vs 입금 (receive).
Over-formalizing as 이체하겠습니다 in casual settings.
합쇼체 sounds stiff for an everyday transfer. The natural polite form is 이체할게요. Save 하겠습니다 for formal/business contexts.
Confusing 이체 with 환전.
이체 (移替) is account-to-account transfer; 환전 (換錢) is exchanging currency. Don't say 이체 when you mean to swap dollars for won.

structuredNuance.t: 이체 (移替, 'move-replace = account transfer') + -할게요 ('I will/intend to', speaker-side announcement). -ㄹ게요 signals your own decision; it's different from -겠어요 (more formal intent/presumption). 계좌이체 = the full compound used as a payment method label.

이체하다 ('transfer electronically', precise) vs 보내다 ('send', casual) vs 송금하다 (formal, esp. overseas). Crucial pair: 이체했어요 (I sent — your action) vs 입금됐어요 (it arrived — their side, passive). Don't swap them.
이체 is 移替 — 移 'move' + 替 'replace/switch'. The money moves and the ownership switches. Compare 환전 (換錢, 'swap-money'), which is a currency exchange, not an account transfer.

이체할게요 is natural polite speech at a counter or in chat. Upgrade to 이체해 드릴게요 (humble -드리다) when sending money to someone senior. Don't use 이체하겠습니다 casually — that -겠습니다 sounds unnatural in everyday situations.

Over-formalizing as 이체하겠습니다 in casual settings — 이체할게요 is the natural polite form. Also confusing 이체 (account transfer) with 환전 (currency exchange) — entirely different transactions. And mixing up 이체했어요 (I sent) with 입금됐어요 (it arrived).

entries.english: Could you give me your account number?
entries.shortExplanation: 계좌번호 좀 알려 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Could you give me your account number?".
entries.explanation: "Could you give me your account number?" — that is 계좌번호 좀 알려 주세요 (gyejwabeonho jom allyeo juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 계좌번호 좀 알려 주세요 ("Could you give me your account number?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Could you give me your account number?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking someone for their account details so you can pay them

usagePhrases.en: Please read out your account number
usagePhrases.note: 불러 주세요 ('read it aloud') when you'll type as they dictate
찍어 주세요 — casual 'shoot me' the account details (text it over)

usagePhrases.en: I'll give you my account number
usagePhrases.note: The reverse: humbly giving YOURS to someone; -드리다 for humility

examples.ko: 계좌번호 좀 알려 주세요.
examples.romanization: gyejwabeonho jom allyeo juseyo.
examples.en: Could you give me your account number?
examples.note: Asking a friend so you can send your share after splitting a meal

examples.ko: A: 계좌번호 좀 알려 주세요. / B: 국민은행이요, 0123-45-6789예요. 예금주는 김민준이에요.
examples.romanization: A: gyejwabeonho jom allyeo juseyo. / B: gungmineunhaengiyo, 0123-45-6789yeyo. yegeumjuneun gimminjunieyo.
examples.en: A: Could you give me your account number? / B: It's Kookmin Bank, 0123-45-6789. Account holder is Kim Min-jun.
examples.note: Full real exchange: B gives bank name first, then number, then 예금주 (holder) — the complete info needed to transfer

examples.ko: 계좌번호랑 예금주 성함 좀 알려 주세요.
examples.romanization: gyejwabeonhorang yegeumju seongham jom allyeo juseyo.
examples.en: Please tell me the account number and the holder's name.
examples.note: 예금주 ('account holder') name is checked by the banking app before you can confirm a transfer

entries.nuance: 계좌번호 좀 알려 주세요 is 계좌번호 ('account number') + 좀 (softener) + 알려 주세요 ('please let me know', from 알리다 'to inform' + 주다 favor). This phrase is used constantly in Korea, where splitting bills and paying back by instant transfer is the social norm — you ask for the other person's 계좌번호 and 이체 immediately. A complete transfer request also needs the bank name (은행 이름) and the account holder name (예금주 이름), since apps ask you to confirm the holder before sending. Three ways to request it: 알려 주세요 ('let me know', standard); 불러 주세요 ('read it aloud', when you'll type as they talk); 찍어 줘 ('text it to me', the casual message shorthand). Note the sharp contrast: 계좌번호 (account number, freely shared to receive money) vs 비밀번호 (PIN/password, never share). The English-speaker trap is using 가르쳐 주세요 — 가르치다 means 'to teach a skill', not 'to inform'; for giving information, the verb is 알리다 → 알려 주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 가르쳐 주세요 to ask for the number.
가르치다 = 'to teach (a skill)'. For sharing information like a number, use 알리다: 계좌번호 알려 주세요. 가르쳐 주세요 sounds like requesting instruction.
Confusing 계좌번호 with 비밀번호.
계좌번호 (account number) is shared so people can pay you; 비밀번호 (PIN/password) is secret. Never give your 비밀번호 to receive money — only your 계좌번호.
Forgetting to give the 은행 (bank name).
A 계좌번호 alone isn't enough — the sender needs the BANK too (예: 국민은행 123-45-6789). Say the 은행 first, then the number.

structuredNuance.t: 계좌번호 ('account number') + 좀 (softener) + 알리다 → 알려 주세요 ('please inform/let me know'). A full account hand-off includes: bank name (국민은행) + number + 예금주 (account holder). Apps verify the holder's name before confirming a transfer.
알려 주세요 ('inform me', standard) vs 불러 주세요 ('read aloud', for dictating) vs 찍어 줘 ('text it over', casual). Key contrast: 계좌번호 (share freely to get paid) ≠ 비밀번호 (secret PIN, never share).
Formal to anyone: 계좌번호 좀 알려 주세요. With friends: 계좌번호 좀 알려 줘 / 계좌 찍어 줘 (반말 text). Giving yours humbly: 제 계좌번호 알려 드릴게요. Asking for all details at once: 계좌번호랑 예금주 성함 알려 주세요.

Used in everyday bill-splitting situations between friends (casual 알려 줘) and at a bank or with a colleague (polite 알려 주세요). Always 존댓말 when dealing with staff or someone senior. This phrase is never used with a teller — you give YOUR number to others, not ask for the bank's.

Using 가르쳐 주세요 — 가르치다 means 'to teach a skill'; sharing a piece of information uses 알리다: 계좌번호 알려 주세요. 가르쳐 주세요 sounds like asking for a lesson, not data. Also forgetting the 은행 name — the account number alone is insufficient for a transfer.

entries.english: Please check if the deposit came in
entries.shortExplanation: 입금됐는지 확인해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please check if the deposit came in".
entries.explanation: 입금됐는지 확인해 주세요 (ipgeumdwaenneunji hwaginhae juseyo) = "Please check if the deposit came in". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 입금됐는지 확인해 주세요 ("Please check if it was deposited"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Please check if it was deposited
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking a teller or person to confirm money arrived on your side

usagePhrases.en: Did it come in? / Has it been deposited?
usagePhrases.note: Quick direct check that a transfer has landed
What you say when the expected money is still missing

usagePhrases.en: Let me know once you confirm the deposit
usagePhrases.note: Asking for a follow-up notification when it's confirmed

examples.ko: 입금됐는지 확인해 주세요.
examples.romanization: ipgeumdwaenneunji hwaginhae juseyo.
examples.en: Please check if the deposit came in.
examples.note: Asking the teller to verify an incoming transfer; -는지 = 'whether'

examples.ko: A: 방금 보냈는데 입금됐어요? / B: 잠시만요. 네, 방금 들어왔어요.
examples.romanization: A: banggeum bonaenneunde ipgeumdwaesseoyo? / B: jamsimanyo. ne, banggeum deureowasseoyo.
examples.en: A: I just sent it — did it come in? / B: One moment. Yes, it just came in.
examples.note: A/B exchange: 보냈다 (sent — sender's side) vs 들어왔어요 ('came in' — receiver's side); 들어오다 is the vivid casual alternative to 입금되다; 잠시만요 is the polite bank-staff form

examples.ko: 월급이 아직 입금 안 됐는데 언제 들어와요?
examples.romanization: wolgeubi ajik ipgeum an dwaenneunde eonje deureowayo?
examples.en: My salary hasn't come in yet — when will it arrive?
examples.note: 들어오다 ('to come in') is the casual spoken verb for money landing in an account

entries.nuance: 입금됐는지 확인해 주세요 is 입금 (入金, 'money in = deposit') + 되다 (passive 'be done') + -는지 ('whether') + 확인해 주세요 ('please check'). 입금 is the word for money ARRIVING in an account — the receiving side of any transfer. It pairs naturally with 송금/이체 (the sending side): the sender says 이체했어요 ('I sent it'), the receiver checks 입금됐어요? ('did it come in?'). A warmer, common alternative is 들어오다 ('to come in'): 돈 들어왔어요? and 월급 들어왔어요? are everyday spoken forms. The grammar point: 입금되다 (passive, money arrives on its own) vs 입금하다 (active, you deposit money) — 'did it arrive?' is passive 입금됐어요?, while 'I'll deposit it' is active 입금할게요. The -는지 structure makes an indirect question embedded in 확인해 주세요 and attaches to the verb stem (됐는지), not as a separate word. Casually: 입금됐어? or 돈 들어왔어?
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Mixing up 입금되다 and 입금하다.
입금되다 = 'be deposited / come in' (passive, money arrives): 입금됐어요?. 입금하다 = 'to deposit' (active, you put money in): 입금할게요. Use the passive for 'did it arrive'.
Confusing 입금 (in) with 출금 (out).
입금 (入金) is money coming IN; 출금 (出金) is money going OUT. 입금됐어요? asks if a deposit arrived; for a withdrawal you'd say 출금.
Saying 입금했는지 확인해 주세요 to check arrival.
That asks whether someone DEPOSITED (active). To check if money CAME IN, use the passive: 입금됐는지 확인해 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 입금 (入金, 'money in') + 되다 (passive) + -는지 ('whether') + 확인해 주세요 ('please check'). 입금 is the receiving side of a transfer. -는지 creates an embedded indirect question: it attaches to the verb stem (입금됐는지), not as a separate clause. Casual: 입금됐어? / 돈 들어왔어?

입금됐어요? (formal 'was it deposited?') vs 돈 들어왔어요? (casual 'did the money come in?'). Key grammar contrast: 입금되다 (passive, money arrives on its own) vs 입금하다 (active, you deposit). Use the passive to ask if money arrived; use the active when you're the one depositing.
입금 is 入金 — 入 'enter/in' + 金 'money'. Paired with 출금 (出金, 'money out = withdrawal'): 入 and 出 are the directional opposites that run through all banking vocabulary.
입금됐는지 확인해 주세요 is polite 존댓말 to a teller or someone you paid. Checking your own account informally: 입금됐어? or 돈 들어왔어? With salary: 월급 들어왔어? is what everyone says payday morning.

The passive/active confusion: 입금됐어요? (passive — did it arrive?) vs 입금했어요? (active — did you deposit it?). To ask if money has ARRIVED for you, use the passive 됐어요? If you accidentally use the active, you're asking if the other person did a manual deposit action, which is a different question.

entries.english: Please freeze/cancel my card
entries.shortExplanation: 카드 정지시켜 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please freeze/cancel my card".
entries.explanation: 카드 정지시켜 주세요 (kadeu jeongjisikyeo juseyo) means "Please freeze/cancel my card". Say it as one set phrase — for example 카드 정지시켜 주세요 ("Please freeze/block my card"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-urgent; 정지 (停止) = 'suspension/halt'; used when you notice the card missing

usagePhrases.en: I want to report my card lost
usagePhrases.note: 분실 신고 = 'loss report'; the formal procedure for a permanently lost/stolen card
막다 ('to block/plug') — urgent spoken version people blurt at the call center
재발급 = 'reissue' — the step you take after blocking to get a new card

examples.ko: 카드 정지시켜 주세요.
examples.romanization: kadeu jeongjisikyeo juseyo.
examples.en: Please freeze my card.
examples.note: Said urgently at the bank when you can't find your card or suspect fraudulent use

examples.ko: A: 카드를 잃어버린 것 같아요. 정지시켜 주세요. / B: 네, 바로 정지하겠습니다. 재발급도 원하세요?
examples.romanization: A: kadeureul ireobeorin geot gatayo. jeongjisikyeo juseyo. / B: ne, baro jeongjihagetseumnida. jaebalgeupdo wonhaseyo?
examples.en: A: I think I lost my card. Please freeze it. / B: Of course, I'll suspend it right away. Would you also like a replacement?
examples.note: Full urgent exchange: 정지 → B offers 재발급; B uses -하겠습니다 (bank staff's formal register)

examples.ko: 일단 카드 막아 주시고, 재발급도 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: ildan kadeu maga jusigo, jaebalgeupdo hae juseyo.
examples.en: First please block the card, then reissue it too.
examples.note: 일단 ('first of all') prioritizes the freeze before the replacement — natural two-step request

entries.nuance: 카드 정지시켜 주세요 is 카드 + 정지 (停止, 'suspension/halt') + 시키다 (causative, 'cause to happen') + 주세요. This is high-stakes vocabulary — get it right. 정지(시키다) means to SUSPEND/freeze the card (potentially reversible); for a lost or stolen card you'll also 분실 신고하다 ('file a loss report'), which permanently blocks it so you then 재발급 ('reissue') a new one. The spoken urgent verb is 막다 ('to block/stop up') — 카드 막아 주세요 is what a panicked person blurts at the call center. The grammar point: 정지하다 (intransitive, 'the card stops') vs 정지시키다 (causative, 'cause it to be stopped') — when asking the bank to freeze YOUR card, 정지시켜 주세요 is the cleaner choice. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'cancel' as 취소하다 — 취소하다 cancels a transaction or reservation, NOT a card; a card is 정지/해지/분실 신고, never 취소. Also distinguish 정지 (temporary freeze, reversible) vs 해지 (permanent termination of the card/account). Always 존댓말 to staff in this situation.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 카드 취소해 주세요 to block a card.
취소하다 cancels a transaction/order/reservation, not a card. To block a card say 카드 정지시켜 주세요, or for a lost card 분실 신고하려고요.
Using 정지하다 instead of 정지시키다.
정지하다 can sound like the card itself stops. To request the bank CAUSE it to be suspended, the causative 정지시키다 is clearer: 카드 정지시켜 주세요.
Confusing 정지 (suspend) with 해지 (terminate).
정지 is a (possibly temporary) freeze; 해지 permanently terminates the card/account. If you only lost it and want a new one, you 정지/분실 신고 + 재발급, not 해지.

structuredNuance.t: 카드 + 정지 (停止, 'stop/suspend') + 시키다 (causative, 'cause to happen') + 주세요. 정지 = temporary freeze (can be reversed); 분실 신고 = permanent block for lost/stolen cards; 재발급 = reissue a new card after blocking. The causative 시키다 is important: you're asking the bank to CAUSE the suspension.

카드 정지시키다 (formal, reversible suspend) vs 분실 신고하다 (formal procedure, permanently blocks for loss) vs 카드 막다 (spoken urgent 'block it'). Critical: 정지 (freeze, reversible) ≠ 해지 (terminate the card permanently). And: 취소하다 = cancel a transaction/reservation, NOT a card.
정지 is 停止 — 停 'stop/halt' + 止 'cease'. 분실 is 紛失 'loss/misplacement'. 재발급 is 再發給 're-issue/re-supply'.

Always 존댓말 — this is an urgent call-center or counter interaction. There is no casual version you'd realistically need; even with bank app chat support you use polite forms. Staff will respond in formal 합쇼체: 바로 정지하겠습니다.

Two traps: (1) using 취소하다 for 'cancel a card' — 취소 cancels a transaction/order, not a card; say 정지/해지/분실 신고. (2) using 정지하다 instead of 정지시키다 — 정지하다 can sound like 'the card stops on its own' (intransitive); the causative 시키다 makes your request clear: 'please MAKE it stop'.

entries.english: My card didn't work / got declined
entries.shortExplanation: 카드가 안 됐어요 is a practical expression meaning "My card didn't work / got declined".
entries.explanation: "My card didn't work / got declined" — that is 카드가 안 됐어요 (kadeuga an dwaesseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 카드가 안 됐어요 ("My card didn't go through"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the general catch-all 'it didn't work' at a register — covers any failure
결제 ('payment/settlement') is the precise noun at checkout; used when the card itself is fine but payment fails
거절되다 ('be rejected') — more explicit and formal, often mirrors error messages
한도 초과 = the exact on-screen error message you'll see for overspending

examples.ko: 카드가 안 됐어요.
examples.romanization: kadeuga an dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: My card didn't work.
examples.note: Said to the cashier when the terminal rejects the card; the all-purpose opening line

examples.ko: A: 결제가 계속 안 돼서요. 다시 한번 해 봐도 될까요? / B: 네, 카드 다시 대 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: gyeoljega gyesok an dwaeseoyo. dasi hanbeon hae bwado doelkkayo? / B: ne, kadeu dasi dae juseyo.
examples.en: A: The payment keeps failing. Could we try one more time? / B: Sure, please tap the card again.
examples.note: A/B exchange at a cashier: 결제가 안 되다 is the precise payment-failure framing; B asks to tap again (대다 = tap/present a card)

examples.ko: 카드 정지돼서 그런지 결제가 자꾸 거절돼요.
examples.romanization: kadeu jeongjidwaeseo geureonji gyeoljega jakku geojeoldwaeyo.
examples.en: Maybe because my card's frozen, payments keep getting declined.
examples.note: 정지돼서 그런지 ('maybe because it's frozen') — 그런지 expresses a tentative reason; 거절되다 is the more explicit 'declined'

entries.nuance: 카드가 안 됐어요 is 카드 + 가 (subject particle) + 안 ('not') + 되다 ('to work/function') in past polite. 되다 is the workhorse verb for 'something functions/goes through', so 안 되다 ('doesn't work') is the first thing to say whenever a card fails — it covers a declined card, a frozen card, a dead chip, or a bad terminal. For more precision at checkout the noun is 결제 ('payment/settlement'): 결제가 안 돼요 ('the payment won't go through'). For an explicit 'declined', 거절되다 mirrors the error message. A common real cause is 한도 초과 ('limit exceeded'). Grammar trap: it must be 카드가 안 됐어요 (subject particle 가, past 됐), not 카드를 안 했어요 (object particle 를 means 'I didn't do the card' — nonsense). The English-speaker trap is translating 'work' as 일하다 ('to labor') — 카드가 일 안 해요 is wrong and confusing; a device 'working' is 되다, never 일하다. Also: 카드가 틀렸어요 ('the card is incorrect', like a wrong answer) is wrong for a declined card; use 안 됐어요. Casual: 카드 안 돼.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'work' as 일하다.
일하다 means 'to do labor/have a job'. A card/machine functioning is 되다: 카드가 안 됐어요. 카드가 일 안 해요 is incorrect.
Saying 카드를 안 했어요.
With 를 it means 'I didn't do the card'. The card is the SUBJECT of failing, so use 가: 카드가 안 됐어요.
Using 틀리다 for a declined card.
틀리다 = 'to be wrong/incorrect (an answer)'. A card that won't process is 안 되다 / 거절되다, not 틀리다. Say 카드가 안 됐어요.

structuredNuance.t: 카드 + 가 (subject) + 안 ('not') + 되다 ('work/function'): 되다 is the Korean verb for 'something functions/goes through'. 안 되다 is the catch-all when a card fails for any reason. The past form 됐 → 안 됐어요 = 'didn't go through'. For an ongoing failure use the present: 카드가 안 돼요.

카드가 안 됐어요 (general 'didn't work', broadest) vs 결제가 안 돼요 ('payment fails', precise at a checkout) vs 거절됐어요 ('was declined', mirrors official error message). 한도 초과 = 'limit exceeded' (the specific cause if you've overspent).
Past (just happened): 카드가 안 됐어요. Present (still failing): 카드가 안 돼요. Guessing cause: 한도 초과인 것 같아요 ('I think it's over the limit'). Urgent re-try: 다시 한번 해 볼게요. Casual: 카드 안 돼.

Used with cashiers, tellers, or bank staff — always 존댓말. 되다/안 되다 is the appropriate register level: direct but polite. In casual chat with a friend you'd just say 카드 안 돼 or 카드 긁혔어? ('did the card go through?'). 긁히다 ('to be swiped') is the casual verb for a card transaction.

Two traps: (1) 일하다 for 'work' — 카드가 일 안 해요 is wrong and funny; a device/process working is 되다. (2) 틀리다 for a declined card — 틀리다 means 'to be incorrect (an answer)'; a non-functioning card is 안 되다 / 거절되다. Also: subject particle 가 (not object 를) is required.

entries.english: I'd like to exchange money
entries.shortExplanation: 환전하고 싶어요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to exchange money".
entries.explanation: 환전하고 싶어요 (hwanjeonhago sipeoyo) = "I'd like to exchange money". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 환전하고 싶어요 ("I'd like to exchange currency"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; 환전 (換錢) is the standard word for currency exchange at a bank or 환전소
Specifying the target currency with 로/으로 — direction particle for the result
-는데요 softens and opens the conversation with the teller
환율 ('exchange rate') is the partner word you'll always ask about before committing

examples.ko: 환전하고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: hwanjeonhago sipeoyo.
examples.en: I'd like to exchange money.
examples.note: Said at a bank counter or 환전소 (dedicated exchange booth)

examples.ko: A: 원화를 달러로 환전하고 싶어요. / B: 오늘 환율이 얼마예요?
examples.romanization: A: wonhwareul dalleoro hwanjeonhago sipeoyo. / B: oneul hwanyuri eolmayeyo?
examples.en: A: I'd like to exchange won into dollars. / B: What's today's exchange rate?
examples.note: A/B exchange: A states currencies with A를 B로 pattern; B asks the rate before quoting

examples.ko: 환율이 오늘 안 좋아서 조금만 환전할게요.
examples.romanization: hwanyuri oneul an joaseo jogeumman hwanjeonhalgeyo.
examples.en: The rate's bad today, so I'll only exchange a little.
examples.note: 환율이 안 좋다 ('the rate is unfavorable') — the natural everyday collocation for judging whether to exchange

entries.nuance: 환전하고 싶어요 is 환전 (換錢, 'exchange-money = currency exchange') + 하다 + -고 싶어요. Currency exchange is done at a bank or a 환전소 (dedicated booth, often better rates). The essential partner word is 환율 (換率, 'exchange rate') — ask 환율 어떻게 돼요? and judge with 환율이 좋다/안 좋다 ('the rate is good/bad'). To name currencies, use 로/으로 for the target: 달러로 환전하다 ('exchange INTO dollars'), 원화로 바꾸다. A plainer synonym is 바꾸다 ('change/swap') — 달러로 바꾸고 싶어요 is natural and slightly more colloquial. The critical confusion to avoid: 환전 (換錢, 'exchange money') vs 환불 (還拂, 'refund') — they look and sound similar but 환불 means getting your money back for a returned purchase; never say 환전 at a store return counter. Another trap: 교환하다 ('exchange goods, swap sizes') is for trading items, not currency. Also keep 환율 (the rate) distinct from 수수료 (the fee charged for the exchange), which is a separate cost worth asking about. To staff use 존댓말 throughout.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
