structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'body-ache arose'. 실제 뜻: 'I am aching all over / run down (from overwork or illness)'. 몸살 covers the whole cluster — muscle aches, fatigue, malaise — with no single English word. The past tense 났어요 expresses the current resulting state, like 감기에 걸렸어요.

몸살이 났어요 to a doctor or sympathetic colleague (존댓말). 몸살 났어 to a close friend (반말). 몸살이 났습니다 in a formal absence report. The typical cause to mention: 무리해서 (from overexerting), 일을 너무 많이 해서 (from working too much), 감기 때문에 (because of a cold).

몸살이 났어요 (body-ache/exhaustion cluster, often from overwork) vs 감기에 걸렸어요 (common cold, respiratory focus) vs 감기몸살이 났어요 (both combined). 온몸이 쑤셔요 ('my whole body aches') describes the sensation in more detail but lacks the exhaustion-fatigue component of 몸살.
몸살이 났어요 → 감기몸살이 났어요 (cold + body aches) → 몸살 기운이 있어요 (early signs) → 몸살이 다 나았어요 (all recovered).

Two traps: (1) no English equivalent — learners describe it piecemeal ('I'm tired and my body hurts'); 몸살이 났어요 does this in one phrase. (2) wrong verb — 몸살을 했어요 is wrong; the collocation is 몸살이 나다, and the past 났어요 expresses the present state.

entries.english: Do I need to get a shot?
entries.shortExplanation: 주사 맞아야 해요? is a practical expression meaning "Do I need to get a shot?".
entries.explanation: 주사 맞아야 해요? (jusa majaya haeyo?) = "Do I need to get a shot?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 주사 맞아야 해요? ("Do I have to get a shot?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Do I have to get a shot?
usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; patient asking the doctor or nurse

usagePhrases.en: Do I have to get a shot?
usagePhrases.note: 반말; a child asking a parent, or a friend
Formal register; 합니까 = formal question ending

usagePhrases.ko: 주사 안 맞고 약만 먹으면 안 돼요?
usagePhrases.romanization: jusa an matgo yangman meogeumyeon an dwaeyo?
usagePhrases.en: Can't I just take pills instead of a shot?
usagePhrases.note: Extension negotiating the alternative; very natural to a doctor

examples.ko: A: 주사 맞아야 해요? / B: 아니요, 약만 드시면 될 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: A: jusa majaya haeyo? / B: aniyo, yangman deusimyeon doel geot gatayo.
examples.en: A: Do I need a shot? / B: No, I think you just need to take the medicine.
examples.note: Classic reassuring A/B at the clinic — the doctor's 약만 드시면 돼요 is the most welcome answer

examples.ko: 독감 예방 주사 맞아야 해요? 해마다 맞아야 하나요?
examples.romanization: dokgam yebang jusa majaya haeyo? haemada majaya hanayo?
examples.en: Should I get the flu vaccine? Do I need to get it every year?
examples.note: Everyday preventive context; 예방 주사 = preventive shot / vaccination; 해마다 = every year

examples.ko: 열이 사흘째 안 떨어지는데 주사 맞아야 해요? 솔직히 주사는 좀 무서워서요.
examples.romanization: yeori saheuljjae an tteoreojineunde jusa majaya haeyo? soljiki jusaneun jom museowoseoyo.
examples.en: My fever hasn't broken for three days — do I need a shot? Honestly I'm a bit scared of needles.
examples.note: Fuller, authentic patient exchange; 사흘째 = going on three days; 무섭다 = scared — the hesitation is very real

entries.nuance: 주사 맞아야 해요? asks whether you need an injection, and the verb choice is the essential learning point: you 'get hit by' a shot — 주사를 맞다 — using 맞다 ('to be struck/get hit'). NOT 주사를 받다 (받다 = receive a handed object) and NOT 주사를 하다 (하다 = do; this is what the nurse does TO you, from the nurse's perspective). This is one of the most universal English-speaker errors in Korean medical language. The ~아야 하다 frame means 'have to/must': 맞아야 해요? = 'do I have to get (hit/struck)'? In casual speech 해요 swaps to 돼요 (맞아야 돼요?) — both are fine and natural. The Sino-Korean word 주사 (注射) covers both the injection and the needle/syringe. Two practical extensions: 예방 주사 맞다 (get vaccinated), and 수액 맞다 (get an IV drip) — 맞다 governs all of them. Pair with 약만 먹으면 돼요? when you want to avoid needles.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 주사를 받아야 해요 with 받다.
받다 = receive a handed object. An injection uses 맞다 ('be struck'): 주사 맞아야 해요?
Saying 주사를 해야 해요 as the patient.
주사를 하다 is what the medical staff does (administers). As the one getting it, you say 주사를 맞다.
Confusing 맞다 'be hit' here with 맞다 'be correct'.
Same spelling, but 주사를 맞다 specifically means 'get an injection'. Context (주사) makes it the shot meaning.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'do I have to be hit by a shot?' 실제 뜻: 'do I need to get an injection?' The surprising verb is 맞다 ('to be struck/hit') — you are the passive recipient of the needle. The ~아야 하다 frame = 'must/have to'. In casual speech 해요 → 돼요: 맞아야 돼요?

주사 맞아야 해요? to a doctor or nurse (존댓말). 주사 맞아야 돼? to a parent or friend (반말). 주사 맞아야 합니까? in a formal context. A useful follow-up to signal fear or preference: 주사 안 맞고 약만 먹으면 안 돼요? ('Can I just take pills instead?').

주사를 맞다 (get an injection — patient) vs 주사를 놓다 (give an injection — nurse/doctor) vs 주사를 맞히다 (cause someone to get a shot — e.g. parent talking about a child). This matched-pair structure (맞다/놓다/맞히다) is unique to injection vocabulary.

주사 = 注射 — 注 (pour in) + 射 (shoot/inject). A Sino-Korean medical term. 맞다 is pure native Korean meaning 'to be hit' — the pairing of a Chinese medical noun with a native verb for being struck reflects how Korean absorbed medical vocabulary.
Two traps: (1) 주사를 받다 — 받다 = receive a handed object; needles aren't handed to you, they are inserted; use 맞다. (2) 주사를 하다 — 하다 is from the nurse's perspective (administering); as the patient, say 맞다.

entries.english: Are you okay?
entries.shortExplanation: 괜찮아요? is a practical expression meaning "Are you okay?".
entries.explanation: 괜찮아요? (gwaenchanayo?) means "Are you okay?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 괜찮아요? ("Are you okay?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; the first thing you ask someone who's hurt or upset
반말, to a friend or someone younger/close
Honorific 으세요, to an elder, a customer, or a stranger
Follow-up when they may be physically injured

examples.ko: A: 괜찮아요? / B: 네, 괜찮아요. 잠깐 놀랐을 뿐이에요.
examples.romanization: A: gwaenchanayo? / B: ne, gwaenchanayo. jamkkan nollasseul ppunieyo.
examples.en: A: Are you okay? / B: Yes, I'm fine. I was just startled for a moment.
examples.note: Rising intonation on 괜찮아요? is the question; the exact same words with falling intonation in B's reply mean 'I'm fine' — tone does all the work

examples.ko: 많이 놀랐죠? 괜찮아요?
examples.romanization: mani nollatjyo? gwaenchanayo?
examples.en: That must have been a shock — are you okay?
examples.note: 놀랐죠 acknowledges the fright before checking on them; pair recognition of the feeling with the welfare check

examples.ko: 얼굴이 안 좋아 보여요. 무슨 일 있어요? 괜찮으세요?
examples.romanization: eolguri an joa boyeoyo. museun il isseoyo? gwaenchaneuseyo?
examples.en: You don't look well. Is something wrong? Are you all right?
examples.note: Pairing 괜찮으세요? with 무슨 일 있어요? opens the door gently — use 으세요 any time you'd use honorifics (elder, stranger, boss, customer)

entries.nuance: 직역: 괜찮다 = 'to be fine/acceptable' + 아요? = polite question marker, so literally 'is it fine?' used as welfare-check 'are you okay?'. The real force is checking the person's state after a stumble, bad news, a fright, or an upset — it is the all-purpose first-response comfort question. Register is the critical skill: 괜찮아? (반말, friend/younger), 괜찮아요? (polite-neutral, peer, most situations), 괜찮으세요? (honorific -으세요, elder/boss/stranger). The nearest near-synonym is 어디 다친 데 없어요? ('are you hurt anywhere?'), which narrows to physical injury; 괜찮아요? covers physical AND emotional. The biggest English-speaker trap is adding 당신 ('you') — 당신 괜찮아요? sounds cold or even confrontational; Korean drops the subject entirely and lets context fill it. Also never use 너 괜찮아요? (mixing 반말 pronoun with polite ending) — if you add any pronoun at all to a polite form, use 선생님, a name, or omit it.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 당신 괜찮아요? to someone's face.
당신 ('you') sounds distant or even confrontational when spoken directly. Korean drops the subject: just 괜찮아요? The 'you' is understood.
Using 괜찮아요? (rising) and 괜찮아요 (falling) interchangeably.
Rising intonation asks 'are you okay?'; falling intonation states 'I'm fine / it's all right'. Same words, opposite roles — control your tone.
Asking an elder 괜찮아? without the honorific.
괜찮아? is 반말 and too casual for an elder, customer, or stranger. Use 괜찮으세요? to show respect when checking on them.

structuredNuance.t: 괜찮다 literally means 'to be fine/acceptable' — as a rising-tone question it becomes the all-purpose welfare check 'are you okay?', covering physical injury, emotional upset, shock, or looking unwell. The same words with falling intonation shift to the reassuring reply 'I'm fine / it's all right / no thank you'. Intonation is the only signal.

Use any time someone stumbles, cries, looks pale, gets bad news, or seems off. Register ladder: 괜찮아? (반말 — friend or someone younger/very close) → 괜찮아요? (polite-neutral — peer, acquaintance, most everyday situations) → 괜찮으세요? (honorific — elder, boss, customer, stranger). The honorific -으세요 is obligatory when you'd normally use 존댓말.

어디 다친 데 없어요? ('are you hurt anywhere?') is the closest near-synonym but narrows to physical injury. 괜찮아요? is broader — it covers emotional upset, shock, and general distress as well. Use 어디 다친 데 없어요? as a follow-up when physical harm is possible.

Stack with 많이 놀랐죠? for 'that must have been a shock — are you okay?'. Chain 괜찮아요? with 무슨 일 있어요? to gently invite them to share. When offering reassurance, the same words with falling tone become the reply: 괜찮아요 = 'I'm fine'.

Adding 당신 ('you') — 당신 괜찮아요? — sounds cold or confrontational; Koreans drop the subject and let context supply it. Also do NOT mix pronouns and endings: 너 괜찮아요? pairs 반말 너 with a polite ending — awkward and inconsistent. With an elder, a plain 괜찮아? (no honorific) can come across as rude.

entries.english: Cheer up / Hang in there
entries.shortExplanation: 힘내 is a practical expression meaning "Cheer up / Hang in there".
entries.explanation: "Cheer up / Hang in there" — that is 힘내 (himnae). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 힘내 ("Hang in there / You got this"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Hang in there / You got this
usagePhrases.note: 반말; to a close friend or someone younger
Polite; to a peer or someone you're not super close with
Honorific; to an elder, a coworker, or a customer

usagePhrases.en: Stay strong, it'll all work out
usagePhrases.note: Pairing it with reassurance about the future

examples.ko: A: 시험이 너무 걱정돼. / B: 힘내! 잘할 수 있어.
examples.romanization: A: siheomi neomu geokjeongdwae. / B: himnae! jalhal su isseo.
examples.en: A: I'm so worried about the exam. / B: Hang in there! You can do it.
examples.note: 힘내 is future-facing encouragement — said before or during a challenge, not as a response to fresh grief

examples.ko: 요즘 많이 힘들지? 힘내.
examples.romanization: yojeum mani himdeulji? himnae.
examples.en: Things are rough lately, huh? Hang in there.
examples.note: 힘들지 acknowledges the struggle before the encouragement; validate first, then encourage

examples.ko: 많이 지치셨죠. 그래도 힘내세요. 제가 응원할게요.
examples.romanization: mani jichisyeotjyo. geuraedo himnaeseyo. jega eungwonhalgeyo.
examples.en: You must be worn out. Still, please hang in there — I'm rooting for you.
examples.note: 응원할게요 ('I'll cheer you on') backs the encouragement with concrete support; note 힘내세요 for someone you respect

entries.nuance: 직역: 힘 ('strength/energy') + 내다 ('to put out/summon') — imperative 'put out your strength'. The real use is encouragement aimed at FUTURE effort — pushing through an exam, a rough patch, a job hunt, a hard week. It is not sympathy for what has already happened. The key near-synonym contrast is 화이팅 (an energetic pep-rally cheer, often for sports or go-get-em moments) vs. 힘내 (warmer, more tender support for someone who is genuinely hurting or depleted). A huge English-speaker trap is using 힘내세요 at a funeral or for a death — it can sound like 'snap out of it', because the person is not facing a hurdle to overcome, they are grieving; use 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 or 마음이 아프네요 instead. Register ladder: 힘내 (반말) → 힘내요 (polite) → 힘내세요 (honorific). Another confusion to avoid: 힘내 ('summon strength', imperative) vs. 힘들어 ('it's tough', a state) — they share 힘 but mean opposite things.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 힘내세요 to someone who is grieving a death.
For a challenge ahead, 힘내 fits; for a death it can sound like 'cheer up', which is jarring. At a funeral say 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 or 얼마나 힘드세요.
Confusing 힘내 with 힘들어.
힘내 = 'summon your strength' (encouragement to them); 힘들어 = 'it's hard / I'm struggling' (a state). Don't tell a tired friend 힘들어 when you mean 힘내.
Treating 화이팅 and 힘내 as identical.
화이팅 is energetic pep ('go go go!'); 힘내 carries gentle, caring support for someone who's down. To comfort a struggling friend, 힘내 lands warmer than 화이팅.

structuredNuance.t: 힘 ('strength/energy') + 내다 ('to summon/put out') → literally 'put out your strength'. The real meaning is warm encouragement to keep going — aimed at future effort, not past suffering. It tells someone to push forward through an exam, a rough patch, or a hard season.

Use before an exam, during a job hunt, mid-way through a tough project, or when a friend is drained but still going. Do NOT use at a funeral or for irreversible loss — it reads as 'snap out of it'. Register: 힘내 (반말 — friend/younger) → 힘내요 (polite — peer) → 힘내세요 (honorific — elder/coworker/customer).

화이팅 is upbeat pep-rally energy ('go go go!') — sports, pre-game, celebrations. 힘내 is softer, more personal warmth for someone who is genuinely hurting or depleted. For a struggling friend, 힘내 lands warmer than 화이팅. Neither is appropriate at a funeral; use 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 there.

Pair with a concrete promise: 힘내요, 제가 응원할게요 ('hang in there, I'm rooting for you'). Add a future reassurance: 힘내요, 다 잘될 거예요 ('stay strong, it'll all work out'). For a friend who needs both validation and a lift: 많이 힘들지? 힘내.

Using 힘내세요 at a funeral or for a death sounds like 'cheer up / snap out of it' — jarring and hurtful. For loss say 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 or 마음이 아프네요. Also do not confuse 힘내 ('summon strength', a command to them) with 힘들어 ('it's tough', describing a state) — they share 힘 but point in opposite directions.

entries.english: It'll be okay
entries.shortExplanation: 괜찮아질 거예요 is a practical expression meaning "It'll be okay".
entries.explanation: 괜찮아질 거예요 (gwaenchanajil geoyeyo) = "It'll be okay". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 괜찮아질 거예요 ("It'll get better / be okay"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; reassuring a peer or someone you respect
반말; comforting a close friend
Add 다 ('all') to widen the reassurance
곧 ('soon') when you want to promise it won't last

examples.ko: A: 이 상황이 너무 힘들어. / B: 괜찮아질 거야. 시간이 지나면 달라져.
examples.romanization: A: i sanghwangi neomu himdeureo. / B: gwaenchanajil geoya. sigani jinamyeon dallajyeo.
examples.en: A: This situation is so hard. / B: It'll be okay. Things will change with time.
examples.note: 괜찮아질 거야 for a friend; note the -아질 change verb rather than just -을 거야 — emphasizing the process of getting better

examples.ko: 지금은 힘들어도 곧 괜찮아질 거예요.
examples.romanization: jigeumeun himdeureodo got gwaenchanajil geoyeyo.
examples.en: Even if it's hard now, it'll be okay soon.
examples.note: Contrast 지금은 힘들어도 ('though hard now') with the hopeful future — acknowledge the current pain before reassuring

examples.ko: 시간이 좀 걸리겠지만, 다 괜찮아질 거예요. 너무 걱정 마요.
examples.romanization: sigani jom geolligetjiman, da gwaenchanajil geoyeyo. neomu geokjeong mayo.
examples.en: It may take some time, but everything will be okay. Don't worry too much.
examples.note: Add 너무 걱정 마요 to round out the comfort; 다 괜찮아질 거예요 is the widest, most all-encompassing form

entries.nuance: 직역: 괜찮아지다 = 괜찮다 ('to be okay') + -아지다 (the becoming/change suffix), so 'to become okay'; -ㄹ 거예요 = future 'will' — literally 'it will become okay'. The crucial difference from the simpler 괜찮을 거예요 ('it will be okay') is the -아지- change verb: 괜찮아질 거예요 specifically promises IMPROVEMENT from the current bad state, while 괜찮을 거예요 just predicts a future state without necessarily implying movement from now. Use this for illness, breakups, work crises, anything time can heal. Do NOT use for a death or irreversible loss — 'it'll get better' rings hollow for grief; say 마음이 아프네요 instead. Register: 괜찮아질 거야 (반말) → 괜찮아질 거예요 (polite). The classic English-speaker conjugation error is inserting 하: 괜찮해질 거예요 is wrong — 괜찮다 has no 하. Pair with 너무 걱정 마요 for a complete, warm comfort.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 괜찮할 거예요 or 괜찮해질 거예요.
괜찮다 has no 하/해 in it. The future is 괜찮을 거예요; the 'get better' form is 괜찮아질 거예요. Never insert 하.
Using 괜찮을 거예요 when you mean 'it'll improve'.
괜찮을 거예요 = 'it'll be okay'; 괜찮아질 거예요 = 'it'll BECOME okay (from now)'. For 'things will get better', keep the change verb 괜찮아지다.
Saying 괜찮아질 거예요 about a death.
For irreversible loss this can sound dismissive. Reserve it for things time can heal; for a death, offer 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 or 마음이 아프네요 instead.

structuredNuance.t: 괜찮아지다 = 괜찮다 ('to be okay') + -아지다 (become/change suffix) + -ㄹ 거예요 (future 'will') — literally 'it will become okay'. The real meaning is forward-looking reassurance: things will improve FROM their current state. The -아지- is what signals change, not merely prediction.

Use for illness, a breakup, a work crisis, a ruined plan — anything time can genuinely heal. Do NOT use for a death or irreversible loss (sounds dismissive). Register: 괜찮아질 거야 (반말 — close friend) → 괜찮아질 거예요 (polite — peer or respectful). Soften with 너무 걱정 마요 as a closer.

괜찮을 거예요 ('it will be okay') is common and fine, but doesn't carry the CHANGE meaning — it predicts a future state. 괜찮아질 거예요 specifically says 'it will get BETTER from now', which is more comforting when someone is currently struggling. For 'things will improve', keep the change verb 괜찮아지다.

Widen with 다 ('all'): 다 괜찮아질 거예요 ('everything will be okay'). Add urgency or hope with 곧 ('soon'): 곧 괜찮아질 거예요. Frame with 지금은 힘들어도 ('even if it's hard now') before the reassurance for a more empathetic structure.

The most common error is inserting 하: 괜찮해질 거예요 is wrong — 괜찮다 has no 하 in it. Also, using 괜찮아질 거예요 for a death or permanent loss sounds dismissive ('it'll get better'); reserve it for situations that genuinely can improve over time.

entries.english: Don't worry
entries.shortExplanation: 걱정하지 마 is a practical expression meaning "Don't worry".
entries.explanation: 걱정하지 마 (geokjeonghaji ma) means "Don't worry". Say it as one set phrase — for example 걱정하지 마 ("Don't worry"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 반말; to a close friend or someone younger
Polite; to a peer or acquaintance
Honorific; to an elder, customer, or boss
Add 너무 to soften an outright 'don't'

examples.ko: A: 결과가 어떻게 될지 너무 걱정돼. / B: 걱정하지 마. 최선을 다했잖아.
examples.romanization: A: gyeolgwaga eotteoke doelji neomu geokjeongdwae. / B: geokjeonghaji ma. choeseoneul dahaetjana.
examples.en: A: I'm so worried about the outcome. / B: Don't worry. You did your best.
examples.note: 걱정하지 마 is the warm command; back it up with a reason — 최선을 다했잖아 ('you did your best, remember') makes it convincing

examples.ko: 내가 도와줄게. 걱정하지 마.
examples.romanization: naega dowajulge. geokjeonghaji ma.
examples.en: I'll help you, so don't worry.
examples.note: Pair 도와줄게 ('I'll help') with 걱정하지 마 — always more convincing with a concrete offer of support

examples.ko: 잘 해결될 테니까 너무 걱정하지 마세요. 제가 옆에 있잖아요.
examples.romanization: jal haegyeoldoel tenikka neomu geokjeonghaji maseyo. jega yeope itjanayo.
examples.en: It'll work out, so please don't worry too much. I'm right here with you.
examples.note: 옆에 있잖아요 ('I'm beside you, you know') makes the reassurance personal; note 마세요 for honorific register

entries.nuance: 직역: 걱정하다 ('to worry') + -지 마 (negative imperative 'don't') — literally 'don't do worrying'. The real function is calming someone who is anxious or fretting; it works for exam stress, relationship worries, or general anxiety. The crucial conjugation point is that -지 마 is the COMMAND form ('don't do X'), while -지 않아 is a STATEMENT ('I/you don't do X') — 걱정하지 않아 means 'I don't worry' (declarative), not 'don't worry'. The near-synonym 걱정 마요 (dropping 하) is conversational shorthand fine for friends but sounds abrupt with elders — always keep the full 걱정하지 마세요 for respectful speech. Adding 너무 ('too much') is a small but powerful softener: a bare 걱정하지 마세요 can sound like an order, but 너무 걱정하지 마세요 says 'don't worry EXCESSIVELY' — kinder and more realistic. Register: 걱정하지 마 (반말) → 걱정하지 마요 (polite) → 걱정하지 마세요 / 너무 걱정하지 마세요 (honorific).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 걱정하지 않아 to mean 'don't worry'.
걱정하지 않아 is a statement ('I don't worry'), not a command. The imperative is 걱정하지 마(요/세요). Use -지 마, not -지 않아, to tell someone not to do something.
Confusing 걱정하지 마 with 걱정돼.
걱정하지 마 tells the other person not to worry; 걱정돼 means 'I'm worried (about you/it)'. Don't say 걱정돼 when you mean to reassure them.
Using a curt 걱정 마! with an elder.
걱정 마 (dropping 하) is friendly-casual, fine for friends but too blunt for an elder or boss. Say 너무 걱정하지 마세요 to stay respectful and gentle.

structuredNuance.t: 걱정하다 ('to worry') + -지 마 (negative imperative 'don't') — literally 'don't do worrying'. The real function is calming someone anxious, stressed, or fretting. The -지 마 form is the only proper imperative; -지 않아 is declarative, not a command.

Use when someone is anxious about an exam, a medical result, a relationship, or any future uncertainty. Register: 걱정하지 마 (반말 — friend/younger) → 걱정하지 마요 (polite — peer) → 걱정하지 마세요 / 너무 걱정하지 마세요 (honorific — elder/boss/customer). Add 너무 ('too much') to soften the command.

걱정하지 마 ('don't worry' — to the other person) vs. 걱정돼 ('I'm worried' — describing your own feeling, from 걱정되다). Same root 걱정, opposite direction. Do not say 걱정돼 when you mean to reassure them — that reports your anxiety, not theirs.

Make it more convincing by adding a reason or support: 내가 도와줄게, 걱정하지 마 ('I'll help, don't worry'). For an elder: 너무 걱정하지 마세요 + 잘 해결될 거예요 ('don't worry too much, it'll work out'). Short form: 걱정 마 (to a friend, very casual — dropping 하).

The command 'don't worry' requires -지 마, NOT -지 않아. 걱정하지 않아 is a statement ('I/you don't worry'), not an instruction. Another trap: using the shortened 걱정 마 (dropping 하) with an elder — it sounds blunt. Always use 걱정하지 마세요 for anyone you'd address with honorifics.

entries.english: Is something wrong?
entries.shortExplanation: 무슨 일 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Is something wrong?".
entries.explanation: "Is something wrong?" — that is 무슨 일 있어요? (museun il isseoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 무슨 일 있어요? ("Is something wrong? / What happened?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; opening when someone looks upset
반말; to a close friend
Honorific; to an elder, customer, or boss
혹시 ('perhaps') makes the question gentler, less prying

examples.ko: A: (looking worried) ... / B: 혹시 무슨 일 있어요?
examples.romanization: A: (looking worried) ... / B: hoksi museun il isseoyo?
examples.en: A: (looking worried) ... / B: Is something maybe wrong?
examples.note: 혹시 softens the question to 'by any chance' — use it when you're not sure something is wrong; it feels caring rather than prying

examples.ko: 표정이 안 좋네요. 무슨 일 있어요?
examples.romanization: pyojeongi an jonneyo. museun il isseoyo?
examples.en: You look down. Is something wrong?
examples.note: 표정이 안 좋다 ('your expression is not good') observes the signal before the gentle probe; pairing a specific observation makes the question warmer

examples.ko: 혹시 무슨 일 있으세요? 제가 도울 일 있으면 말씀하세요.
examples.romanization: hoksi museun il isseuseyo? jega doul il isseumyeon malsseumhaseyo.
examples.en: Is something the matter? If there's anything I can do, please tell me.
examples.note: Offer help with 도울 일 있으면 말씀하세요 to show you mean it; 있으세요 for honorific — 있다 → 있으세요 with -으세요

entries.nuance: 직역: 무슨 ('what kind of') + 일 ('matter/event') + 있어요 ('is there') — literally 'is there some matter?'. The real use is a gentle probe when someone looks troubled and you want to invite them to open up, without forcing it. Note that 일 here means 'a happening/issue', not 'work' (same word, different context). The key near-synonym split: 무슨 일 있어요? checks WHETHER something is wrong (probing); 무슨 일이에요? asks WHAT a problem is (assuming something's already up). The golden softener is 혹시 ('perhaps, by any chance'): 혹시 무슨 일 있어요? feels caring and tactful, not intrusive. Register: 있어? (반말) → 있어요? (polite) → 있으세요? (honorific, where 있다 becomes 있으세요). The particle pitfall: 있다 ('to exist') takes a subject or nothing — never the object marker 을. So it is 무슨 일(이) 있어요?, never 무슨 일을 있어요?.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 무슨 일을 있어요?
있다 ('to exist') never takes the object marker 을. It's 무슨 일(이) 있어요? — subject marker or nothing, because the matter EXISTS, it isn't an object you act on.
Mixing up 무슨 일 있어요? and 무슨 일이에요?
무슨 일 있어요? checks IF something's wrong; 무슨 일이에요? asks WHAT a known matter is. Use 있어요? to gently probe when you're not sure anything happened.
Asking an elder 무슨 일 있어? without honorifics.
있어? is 반말. For an elder, customer, or boss, lift it to 무슨 일 있으세요?, where 있다 becomes the honorific 있으세요.

structuredNuance.t: 무슨 ('what kind of') + 일 ('matter/event') + 있어요 ('is there') — literally 'is there some matter?'. The real function is a gentle invitation to open up when you've noticed someone looks troubled. 일 here is 'a happening/issue', not 'work'.

Use when someone looks upset, quiet, or off — you notice but don't want to pry. Add 혹시 ('perhaps, by any chance') for maximum tact: 혹시 무슨 일 있어요? Register: 무슨 일 있어? (반말 — friend) → 있어요? (polite) → 있으세요? (honorific — elder/boss/customer).

무슨 일 있어요? checks IF something is wrong (probing). 무슨 일이에요? asks WHAT a known problem is (assuming something's already up). Use 있어요? to gently test whether anything happened; switch to 일이에요? once you know something did.
Lead with an observation: 표정이 안 좋네요, 무슨 일 있어요? ('you look down — is something wrong?'). Follow up with an offer: 제가 도울 일 있으면 말씀하세요. Softest form: 혹시 무슨 일 있으세요?
chips: 표정이 안 좋네요. 무슨 일 있어요?

structuredNuance.t: 있다 ('to exist') never takes the object marker 을. It's 무슨 일(이) 있어요? — subject marker 이 or nothing, never 일을 있어요. Another trap is translating 'what's wrong WITH you' literally and sounding accusatory — 무슨 일 있어요? is warm and open; don't add 너 (you) to a stranger.

entries.english: Oh no, what do we do
entries.shortExplanation: 어떡해요 is a practical expression meaning "Oh no, what do we do".
entries.explanation: 어떡해요 (eotteokaeyo) = "Oh no, what do we do". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 어떡해요 ("Oh no / what'll you do"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; a sympathetic reaction to someone's bad news
반말; to a close friend, often half-gasped

usagePhrases.en: Oh dear, what should we do
usagePhrases.note: Polite -죠, drawing the listener in

usagePhrases.en: Oh, what a thing / good heavens
usagePhrases.note: A warmer, slightly older-flavored variant

examples.ko: A: 지갑을 잃어버렸어요. / B: 어머, 어떡해요!
examples.romanization: A: jigabeul ireobeoryeosseoyo. / B: eomeo, eotteokaeyo!
examples.en: A: I lost my wallet. / B: Oh my, that's awful!
examples.note: 어머 + 어떡해요 is the instinctive reaction to bad news — it signals shared dismay, not a request for a plan; do not wait for instructions after hearing it

examples.ko: 면접에 떨어졌다고요? 어떡해요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeobe tteoreojyeotdagoyo? eotteokaeyo.
examples.en: You failed the interview? Oh no.
examples.note: Echo their problem, then 어떡해요 to share the dismay — the whole expression means 'oh no, what a shame' in this context

examples.ko: 저런, 그렇게 됐다니 정말 어떡해요. 많이 놀라셨겠어요.
examples.romanization: jeoreon, geureoke dwaetdani jeongmal eotteokaeyo. mani nollasyeotgesseoyo.
examples.en: Oh dear, to think it turned out that way — what a thing. You must have been so shaken.
examples.note: Chain with 놀라셨겠어요 ('you must have been shaken') to deepen the sympathy; 저런 is the natural lead-in

entries.nuance: 직역: 어떡해요 is a contraction of 어떻게 해요 ('how do (we/you) do?'), but as a set exclamation it has bleached into 'oh no / what a shame / what'll you do' — pure sympathetic reaction to bad news, not an actual request for a plan. The most important spelling split in Korean emotional vocabulary: 어떡해 (standalone exclamation, contracted, takes NO following verb) vs. 어떻게 (the adverb 'how', must pair with a verb — 어떻게 해요, 어떻게 가요). Writing 어떡해 가요 is a common error; it's 어떻게 가요. Register: 어떡해 (반말) → 어떡해요 (polite). For an elder you'd often shift to 이를 어째요 or 저런 or 얼마나 놀라셨어요. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 어떡해요 literally as 'how should I do it?' and either waiting for instructions or answering it — in sympathy it's simply 'oh no'. Reserve it for genuine bad news, not a trivial mishap (there, use 아이고 or 어머).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 어떡해 when you mean 어떻게 ('how').
어떻게 is the question word and pairs with a verb (어떻게 해요). 어떡해 is the standalone exclamation ('oh no') and takes no following verb. 어떡해 가요 is wrong; say 어떻게 가요.
Treating 어떡해요 as a literal request for a plan.
In sympathy it means 'oh no / what a shame', not 'tell me how'. Don't wait for or expect instructions — it's an expression of shared dismay.
Using 어떡해요 for trivial mishaps.
It carries genuine concern. For a tiny slip (spilled coffee) say 아이고 or 어머; reserve 어떡해요 for real bad news so it doesn't sound melodramatic.

structuredNuance.t: 어떡해요 contracts from 어떻게 해요 ('how do we do?'), but as a set exclamation it has fully bleached into 'oh no / what a shame / what'll you do' — pure sympathetic reaction. It signals 'I feel for you, this is awful', not a literal request for a plan of action.

Use as an immediate reaction when someone shares genuine bad news — a lost item, a failed exam, an accident, bad luck. Register: 어떡해 (반말 — friend) → 어떡해요 (polite). For an elder, 이를 어째요 or pairing with 얼마나 놀라셨겠어요 ('you must have been so shocked') is more natural.

이를 어째요 is a warmer, slightly more formal/older-generation variant with the same 'oh dear, what a thing' meaning. 어머 or 아이고 are lighter exclamations for smaller mishaps. 어떡해요 carries genuine concern — reserve it for real bad news, not a spilled coffee.

The key variant to know is 어떡하죠 (polite -죠, 'what are we to do?') — pulls the listener in to shared concern. Lead with 어머 or 저런 for a natural flow: 어머, 어떡해요. Follow up with 많이 놀라셨겠어요 to deepen sympathy.

The critical spelling trap: 어떡해 (exclamation, standalone) vs. 어떻게 (adverb 'how', must pair with a verb). You CANNOT say 어떡해 가요 — it's 어떻게 가요. Also do not take 어떡해요 literally as a question expecting a plan — in this sympathy context it means 'oh no'. Avoid using it for trivial mishaps; it implies real dismay.

entries.english: You worked hard / Thanks for your effort
entries.shortExplanation: 고생했어요 is a practical expression meaning "You worked hard / Thanks for your effort".
entries.explanation: 고생했어요 (gosaenghaesseoyo) means "You worked hard / Thanks for your effort". Say it as one set phrase — for example 고생했어요 ("You've worked hard / Thanks for the effort"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: You've worked hard / Thanks for the effort
usagePhrases.note: Polite; to a peer or someone junior after hard work
반말; to a close friend or someone younger

usagePhrases.en: Thank you for your hard work
usagePhrases.note: Honorific; to an elder, senior, or someone you respect

usagePhrases.en: You've been through so much / worked so hard
usagePhrases.note: Add 많다 to stress just how much effort it took

examples.ko: A: 드디어 끝났어요. / B: 고생하셨어요. 정말 수고 많으셨어요.
examples.romanization: A: deudieo kkeunnasseoyo. / B: gosaenghasyeosseoyo. jeongmal sugo maneusyeosseoyo.
examples.en: A: It's finally done. / B: Thank you for your hard work. You really put in so much effort.
examples.note: 고생하셨어요 for a senior (note -시-); this is the end-of-project acknowledgment — never use 고생했어요 without -시- toward a boss or elder

examples.ko: 먼 길 오느라 고생하셨어요. 좀 쉬세요.
examples.romanization: meon gil oneura gosaenghasyeosseoyo. jom swiseyo.
examples.en: Thank you for coming all this way — you must be tired. Please rest.
examples.note: 오느라 ('in the course of coming') ties the effort to a specific act; follow with 쉬세요 as natural comfort

examples.ko: 힘든 일 겪으시느라 고생 많으셨어요. 이제 좀 나아지셨어요?
examples.romanization: himdeun il gyeokkeusineura gosaeng maneusyeosseoyo. ije jom naajisyeosseoyo?
examples.en: You've been through so much — are you feeling a bit better now?
examples.note: 겪으시느라 ('in going through it') turns it into sympathy for endured hardship; 고생 많으셨어요 is the deepest form

entries.nuance: 직역: 고생 ('hardship/toil', Sino-Korean 苦生) + 했어요 (past tense of 하다) — literally 'you did hardship'. Despite the seemingly negative 苦 ('suffering'), this is a warm acknowledgment and compliment, equivalent to 'you worked so hard, thank you for your effort'. It does double duty: it thanks someone for difficult work AND sympathizes with someone who's been through a hard time. Register is critical: to a senior, elder, or anyone you respect you MUST include the honorific -시-: 고생하셨어요 / 고생 많으셨어요. A plain 고생했어요 to your boss is like patting them on the head — disrespectful. The key near-synonym split: 수고했어요 ('good work, thanks') is lighter and travels DOWNWARD (to staff, a clerk, a delivery worker); 고생하셨어요 implies harder, more draining toil and is safer upward. Saying 수고하세요 to a senior can feel condescending — use 고생하셨어요 to honor their effort properly.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 고생했어요 (no -시-) to your boss or an elder.
To a superior you must honorify: 고생하셨어요. Plain 고생했어요 to someone senior sounds like praising a junior — add -시- to show respect.
Using 수고하세요 to an elder or boss.
수고하다 is lighter and often directed downward (to staff). To a senior it can feel condescending; 고생하셨어요 or 고생 많으셨어요 conveys respect for their effort better.
Reading 고생 as purely negative and avoiding the phrase.
Though 고생 means 'hardship', 고생했어요 is a warm thank-you/compliment for someone's effort. Don't shy away from it; it's exactly what Koreans say to honor hard work.

structuredNuance.t: 고생 ('hardship/toil', 苦生) + 했어요 (past 하다) — literally 'you did hardship'. Despite the seemingly dark character 苦 ('suffering'), this is a warm compliment: 'you worked so hard, thank you'. It covers both work effort (thanks for the effort) and endured hardship (you've been through so much).

Use at the end of a long day, project, event, or difficult period. CRITICAL: to anyone senior or older, add -시-: 고생하셨어요 / 고생 많으셨어요. Using 고생했어요 without -시- to your boss sounds like you're patting a junior on the back. Register: 고생했어 (반말 — friend/younger) → 고생했어요 (peer/junior) → 고생하셨어요 / 고생 많으셨어요 (elder/senior).

수고했어요 ('good work / thanks for the effort') is lighter and typically travels DOWNWARD — you say it to staff, a delivery person, a service worker. 고생하셨어요 implies harder, more draining toil and is appropriate upward or laterally. Critically, 수고하세요 to an elder or boss can feel condescending; 고생하셨어요 is the safer respectful choice.

Deepen with 많다: 고생 많으셨어요 ('you went through so much hardship'). Tie to a specific act with -느라: 먼 길 오시느라 고생하셨어요 ('thank you for coming all this way'). Natural follow-up: 오늘은 푹 쉬세요 ('please rest well today').

The direct-translation trap is reading 고생 ('hardship/suffering') as negative and shying away from the phrase — it's actually a warm, respectful acknowledgment, not a complaint. The bigger error is dropping -시- with a superior: always 고생하셨어요 to an elder or boss, never 고생했어요.

entries.english: Get some good rest
entries.shortExplanation: 푹 쉬어요 is a practical expression meaning "Get some good rest".
entries.explanation: "Get some good rest" — that is 푹 쉬어요 (puk swieoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 푹 쉬어요 ("Rest up well"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; to a peer who's tired or unwell
반말; to a close friend or someone younger
Honorific; to an elder, boss, or customer

usagePhrases.en: Take good care of yourself (recover well)
usagePhrases.note: Specifically when someone is sick or recovering

examples.ko: A: 오늘 정말 힘들었어요. / B: 고생하셨어요. 오늘은 푹 쉬세요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul jeongmal himdeureosseoyo. / B: gosaenghasyeosseoyo. oneureun puk swiseyo.
examples.en: A: Today was really exhausting. / B: You worked so hard. Please rest well tonight.
examples.note: Pair 고생하셨어요 + 푹 쉬세요 — acknowledging the effort then sending them to rest is the natural two-step comfort sequence

examples.ko: 감기 빨리 나으려면 푹 쉬어요.
examples.romanization: gamgi ppalli naeuryeomyeon puk swieoyo.
examples.en: Rest up well so your cold gets better fast.
examples.note: Tie the rest to recovery with 나으려면 ('to get better'); note 나으려면 from 낫다 (ㅅ-irregular)

examples.ko: 많이 힘드셨을 텐데 오늘은 아무 생각 말고 푹 쉬세요.
examples.romanization: mani himdeusyeosseul tende oneureun amu saenggang malgo puk swiseyo.
examples.en: It must have been so hard — today, don't think about anything, just rest well.
examples.note: 아무 생각 말고 ('without thinking of anything') deepens the care; 푹 쉬세요 is the gracious close

entries.nuance: 직역: 푹 ('deeply/soundly/thoroughly', a mimetic adverb) + 쉬다 ('to rest') — literally 'rest deeply/soundly'. 푹 is the key flavor word: same as in 푹 자다 ('sleep soundly') and 푹 삶다 ('boil thoroughly'). It upgrades a plain 쉬어요 ('rest') to 'really rest, recharge fully'. The natural near-synonym is 몸조리 잘하세요 ('take good care of your body / recover well'), which is specifically for someone SICK or post-surgery/postpartum — when illness is the issue, 몸조리 잘하세요 is more precise. 푹 쉬세요 is for general fatigue, stress, or as a caring goodbye. Register: 푹 쉬어 (반말) → 푹 쉬어요 (polite) → 푹 쉬세요 (honorific). The natural pairing: after 고생하셨어요, add 오늘은 푹 쉬세요. Do NOT use it mid-task when the person cannot actually stop — the implication is that they now have time to rest. The English-speaker pitfall is the formal 직역 'take a rest' → 휴식을 취하세요, which is stiff HR-memo Korean, not warm spoken comfort.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 휴식을 취하세요 to comfort someone.
That's stiff, written-style Korean (like an HR memo). In warm spoken comfort, say 푹 쉬세요 — natural and caring, not bureaucratic.
Writing 폭 쉬어요 instead of 푹 쉬어요.
The adverb is 푹 ('soundly, deeply'), not 폭. 폭 means something else (width/explosion sounds). For 'rest well' it's 푹 쉬어요.
Using 푹 쉬세요 for someone who's sick when 몸조리 fits better.
푹 쉬세요 is general fatigue/stress. For illness or recovery specifically, 몸조리 잘하세요 ('recover well, take care of your body') is the precise, caring phrase.

structuredNuance.t: 푹 ('deeply/soundly/thoroughly', mimetic adverb) + 쉬다 ('to rest') — literally 'rest deeply'. 푹 is the intensity marker: same sound-symbol as in 푹 자다 ('sleep soundly'). It transforms a plain 'rest' into 'really recharge, rest fully'. The real function is a caring farewell or comfort after hard work or illness.

Use as a caring close when someone is exhausted, sick, or grieving. Natural sequence: 고생하셨어요 → 오늘은 푹 쉬세요. Do NOT say it mid-task when the person cannot stop — it implies they now have free time to rest. Register: 푹 쉬어 (반말 — friend) → 푹 쉬어요 (polite — peer) → 푹 쉬세요 (honorific — elder/boss).

몸조리 잘하세요 ('recover well, take care of your body') is the near-synonym for someone who is ill or recovering from surgery/postpartum. 푹 쉬세요 is broader: general fatigue, stress, emotional exhaustion. When someone has a cold or just left the hospital, reach for 몸조리 잘하세요 first.
Pair with acknowledgment: 고생하셨어요, 오늘은 푹 쉬세요. For illness, combine: 얼른 나으세요, 푹 쉬어요. Deepen care: 아무 생각 말고 푹 쉬세요 ('rest without thinking about anything'). Do not confuse 푹 with 폭 — different words.

The direct-translation 'take a rest' → 휴식을 취하세요 is stiff, written-register Korean (like a memo). In warm spoken comfort, say 푹 쉬세요. Also, do not write 폭 쉬어요 — the adverb is 푹 (soft u-sound), not 폭 (a different word meaning width or explosion sound).

entries.english: Get well soon
entries.shortExplanation: 얼른 나으세요 is a practical expression meaning "Get well soon".
entries.explanation: 얼른 나으세요 (eolleun naeuseyo) = "Get well soon". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 얼른 나으세요 ("Get well soon"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Honorific; to anyone who's sick (the everyday go-to)
반말; to a close friend or someone younger
Honorific with 빨리, interchangeable with 얼른
Formal-written; for a card, text, or to a senior

examples.ko: A: 오늘 몸이 너무 안 좋아요. / B: 얼른 나으세요. 오늘은 푹 쉬세요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul momi neomu an joayo. / B: eolleun naeuseyo. oneureun puk swiseyo.
examples.en: A: I'm feeling really unwell today. / B: Get well soon. Please rest up well today.
examples.note: 얼른 나으세요 + 푹 쉬세요 is the natural two-phrase sequence — recovery wish followed by how to get there; note 나으세요 from 낫다 (ㅅ-irregular: ㅅ drops before vowel)

examples.ko: 감기 조심하시고 얼른 나으세요.
examples.romanization: gamgi josimhasigo eolleun naeuseyo.
examples.en: Take care of that cold and get well soon.
examples.note: 조심하시고 ('take care, and') leads into the wish for recovery; 얼른 adds warm urgency ('soon') slightly softer than 빨리

examples.ko: 입원하셨다는 소식 들었어요. 쾌차하시길 바랍니다. 푹 쉬세요.
examples.romanization: ibwonhasyeotdaneun sosik deureosseoyo. kwaechahasigil baramnida. puk swiseyo.
examples.en: I heard you were hospitalized. Wishing you a swift recovery. Please rest well.
examples.note: For serious illness or a written message, 쾌차하시길 바랍니다 (Sino-Korean 快瘥, formal) fits; switch from 얼른 나으세요 to this in cards or messages to seniors

entries.nuance: 직역: 얼른 ('quickly/soon') + 낫다 ('to heal/recover') in the honorific imperative 나으세요 — literally 'please recover quickly'. The critical grammar is 낫다's ㅅ-irregular: the final ㅅ drops before a vowel, so 낫다 → 나아요 / 나으세요 / 나았어요, never 낫아요 or 낫으세요. Three near-identical-sounding verbs trip learners: 낫다 ('to heal') → 나으세요; 낮다 ('to be low') → 낮으세요; 낳다 ('to give birth') → 낳으세요. Saying 낳으세요 bizarrely tells someone to give birth. The register ladder: 빨리 나아 (반말 — friend) → 얼른/빨리 나으세요 (honorific — everyday polite) → 쾌차하시길 바랍니다 (快瘥, 'swift recovery', formal-written — card, message, hospitalization, senior). Contrast with 푹 쉬세요: 나으세요 specifically wishes RECOVERY from illness; 푹 쉬세요 is broader rest — they pair naturally. Do NOT use 나으세요 for emotional grief; it is for physical illness and injury only.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Conjugating 낫다 as 낫으세요 or 낫아요.
낫다 is a ㅅ-irregular: the ㅅ drops before a vowel. Correct forms are 나으세요, 나아요, 나았어요 — not 낫으세요, 낫아요.
Saying 낳으세요 instead of 나으세요.
낳다 means 'to give birth'; 낫다 means 'to heal'. 낳으세요 tells someone to give birth! For 'get well', it's 나으세요 (from 낫다).
Translating 'get well' as 잘 되세요.
잘 되세요 means 'may things go well / may you succeed', not recover from illness. The verb for healing is 낫다: 얼른 나으세요.

structuredNuance.t: 얼른 ('quickly/soon') + 낫다 ('to heal/recover') in honorific imperative 나으세요 — literally 'please recover quickly'. The real use is the standard 'get well soon' for anyone physically ill or injured, from a friend with a cold to a hospitalized coworker. Only for physical illness; do NOT use for emotional grief.

Use whenever someone is sick, injured, or recovering. Register ladder: 빨리 나아 (반말 — friend/younger) → 얼른/빨리 나으세요 (honorific — everyday spoken) → 쾌차하시길 바랍니다 (快瘥 — formal-written: card, message to a senior, serious illness). Pair with 푹 쉬세요 as a natural follow-up.

쾌차하시길 바랍니다 (快瘥 'swift recovery') is the formal-written near-synonym — appropriate in condolence/recovery cards, messages to seniors, or for hospitalization. 몸조리 잘하세요 ('take care of your body') emphasizes ongoing self-care over speed. 얼른 나으세요 and 빨리 나으세요 are interchangeable; 얼른 is slightly warmer and softer.
ㅅ-irregular conjugation set of 낫다: 나아요 (present polite), 나으세요 (honorific imperative), 나았어요 (past), 나을 거예요 (future). Natural pairing: 얼른 나으세요, 몸조리 잘하세요. Tie to self-care: 감기 조심하시고 얼른 나으세요.

Three homophones: 낫다 ('to heal') → 나으세요; 낮다 ('to be low') → 낮으세요; 낳다 ('to give birth') → 낳으세요. Saying 낳으세요 means 'please give birth' — not what you want. Also, translating 'get well' as 잘 되세요 means 'may you succeed/prosper', not recover. The verb for healing is always 낫다.

entries.english: Don't push yourself too hard
entries.shortExplanation: 너무 무리하지 마세요 is a practical expression meaning "Don't push yourself too hard".
entries.explanation: 너무 무리하지 마세요 (neomu murihaji maseyo) means "Don't push yourself too hard". Say it as one set phrase — for example 너무 무리하지 마세요 ("Don't overdo it"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Honorific; to an elder, boss, or someone you respect
Polite; to a peer
반말; to a close friend

usagePhrases.en: Don't overdo it — take a break
usagePhrases.note: Pair with 쉬어요 to offer the alternative

examples.ko: A: 이번 주도 매일 야근했어요. / B: 너무 무리하지 마세요. 건강이 제일이에요.
examples.romanization: A: ibeon judo maeil yageunhaesseoyo. / B: neomu murihaji maseyo. geongangi jeirieyo.
examples.en: A: I did overtime every day this week again. / B: Don't push yourself too hard. Health comes first.
examples.note: This is the right phrase when someone is OVEREXERTING — contrast with 힘내세요 ('push harder'), which would be the wrong choice here for someone already depleted

examples.ko: 몸도 안 좋은데 너무 무리하지 마요.
examples.romanization: momdo an joeunde neomu murihaji mayo.
examples.en: You're not even well — don't push yourself too hard.
examples.note: 몸도 안 좋은데 ('you're unwell, and yet...') gives the specific reason for concern; 마요 for polite peer register

examples.ko: 일도 중요하지만 너무 무리하지 마세요. 건강이 제일이에요.
examples.romanization: ildo jungyohajiman neomu murihaji maseyo. geongangi jeirieyo.
examples.en: Work matters, but don't overdo it. Health comes first.
examples.note: 건강이 제일이에요 ('health is number one') is the natural framing companion — together they make a complete, caring message for overworkers

entries.nuance: 직역: 너무 ('too much') + 무리하다 ('to overdo/strain oneself', from Sino-Korean 無理 'unreasonable, beyond one's limits') + -지 마세요 ('please don't') — literally 'please don't do the unreasonable'. The real meaning is 'ease up on yourself; don't strain past what your body or situation can bear'. 무리하다 specifically means pushing past reasonable physical or situational limits, pairing naturally with 몸 ('body'), 건강 ('health'), and overwork. The essential contrast with 힘내세요: they are nearly OPPOSITE — 힘내세요 urges MORE effort; 무리하지 마세요 urges LESS. Using 힘내세요 on someone already overexerting is tone-deaf; 무리하지 마세요 shows you truly see their depletion. Register: 무리하지 마 (반말) → 무리하지 마요 (polite) → 무리하지 마세요 (honorific). Keep 너무 in front; bare 무리하지 마세요 is fine but 너무 makes it gentler. English-speaker pitfall: 밀다 ('to push an object') is NOT the word for overexerting — 무리하다 carries the whole concept.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 힘내세요 to someone who's already overworking.
힘내세요 pushes for MORE effort; an exhausted person needs the opposite. Say 너무 무리하지 마세요 ('don't overdo it') to tell them to ease off.
Translating 'don't push yourself' as 너 자신을 밀지 마세요.
밀다 is physical 'to push (an object)'. The idea of overexerting is carried by 무리하다. Correct: 너무 무리하지 마세요.
Confusing the verb 무리하다 with the noun 무리 ('a group').
They're homonyms. 무리 can mean 'a herd/crowd', but 무리하다 means 'to strain beyond one's limits'. Context (the verb form) makes it 'overdo it' here.

structuredNuance.t: 무리하다 comes from 無理 ('unreasonable/beyond limits') — literally 'to do the unreasonable'. The real meaning: 'to overexert, to push past what your body or situation can bear'. 너무 + -지 마세요 = 'please don't strain yourself beyond your limits'. It is caring restraint, not encouragement.

Use when someone is overworking, pushing through illness, or carrying too heavy a load — you see they are depleted. Register: 무리하지 마 (반말 — friend) → 무리하지 마요 (polite — peer) → 무리하지 마세요 (honorific — elder/boss). Keep 너무 in front to soften; bare 무리하지 마세요 sounds slightly more direct.

힘내세요 ('stay strong, push harder') is nearly the OPPOSITE: it urges more effort, while 무리하지 마세요 urges less. For someone already overexerting or depleted, 무리하지 마세요 is the caring choice. Saying 힘내세요 in that situation can feel dismissive or counterproductive.
Pair with the alternative: 무리하지 말고 좀 쉬어요 ('don't overdo it — take a break'). Give context: 몸도 안 좋은데 너무 무리하지 마세요. Close with a value: 건강이 제일이에요 ('health comes first').

Do NOT translate 'push yourself' as 너 자신을 밀다 — 밀다 is physical pushing of objects. The concept 'overexert yourself' is entirely captured by 무리하다. Also, the homonym 무리 (noun: 'a herd/group') has nothing to do with 무리하다 (verb: 'to overexert') — context (the verb form -하다) makes the meaning clear.

entries.english: It breaks my heart / I feel for you
entries.shortExplanation: 마음이 아프다 is a practical expression meaning "It breaks my heart / I feel for you".
entries.explanation: "It breaks my heart / I feel for you" — that is 마음이 아프다 (maeumi apeuda). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 마음이 아파요 ("It breaks my heart / I'm so sorry to hear that"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: It breaks my heart / I'm so sorry to hear that
usagePhrases.note: Polite; expressing your own ache at someone's pain
반말; to a close friend
Polite with -네요, a softer 'I'm feeling this right now'

usagePhrases.en: Your heart must be aching so much
usagePhrases.note: Turn it toward THEM: 'you must be hurting' (honorific)

examples.ko: A: 강아지가 어제 무지개다리를 건넜어요. / B: 어머, 마음이 아프네요. 얼마나 힘드세요.
examples.romanization: A: gangajiga eoje mujigaedarireul geonneosseoyo. / B: eomeo, maeumi apeuneyo. eolmana himdeuseyo.
examples.en: A: My dog crossed the rainbow bridge yesterday. / B: Oh, my heart aches. How hard this must be for you.
examples.note: 마음이 아프네요 = your own heartache at their news; follow with 얼마나 힘드세요 to acknowledge their pain — both together show deep empathy without making it about yourself

examples.ko: 많이 힘드시죠. 옆에서 보는 저도 마음이 아프네요.
examples.romanization: mani himdeusijyo. yeopeseo boneun jeodo maeumi apeuneyo.
examples.en: It must be so hard. Even watching from beside you, my heart aches.
examples.note: 옆에서 보는 저도 ('even I, watching from the side') shows shared grief without centering your own feelings above theirs

examples.ko: 얼마나 마음이 아프시겠어요. 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없네요.
examples.romanization: eolmana maeumi apeusigesseoyo. mwora deuril malsseumi eopsneyo.
examples.en: How much your heart must be aching. I'm at a loss for words.
examples.note: Flipping to 아프시겠어요 (with -시겠) acknowledges THEIR heartache; 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없다 ('I have no words to offer') is the set sympathy line for deep loss

entries.nuance: 직역: 마음 ('heart/mind/feelings') + 이 (subject) + 아프다 ('to hurt/ache') — literally 'the heart hurts'. The real meaning is emotional heartbreak or deep sympathy when hearing something sad. Critical distinction: 마음 is the EMOTIONAL heart (feelings, mind), NOT the physical organ 심장. 심장이 아파요 = literal chest pain (see a doctor). Use 마음이 아파요 about YOUR OWN ache at their news; flip with -시겠어요 to acknowledge THEIR pain: 마음이 아프시겠어요 ('your heart must ache'). Near-synonym: 가슴이 아프다 ('the chest/breast aches') — equally natural for heartbreak. Key contrast: 속상하다 ('upset/distressed') is lighter and everyday; 마음이 아프다 is heavier, for genuine sorrow or loss — don't use 속상해요 for a death. Particle rule: 마음이 아파요 (subject -이, never object -을) — 아프다 is an adjective; the heart is the SUBJECT that aches.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 심장이 아파요 to mean 'heartbroken'.
심장 is the physical heart organ — 심장이 아파요 means literal chest pain (see a doctor!). Emotional heartbreak is 마음이 아파요 or 가슴이 아파요.
Saying 마음을 아파요 with the object marker.
아프다 is an adjective; the heart is what hurts, so it's the subject: 마음이 아파요. You can't take 마음 as an object with 을.
Using 속상해요 for a serious loss like a death.
속상하다 is everyday 'upset/bummed' — too light for grief. For real sorrow or a death, 마음이 아파요 (heartbroken) carries the proper weight.

structuredNuance.t: 마음 ('heart/feelings/mind') + 이 (subject) + 아프다 ('to hurt') — literally 'the heart hurts'. The real meaning is emotional heartbreak or the deep ache of sympathy. 마음이 아파요 = your own heartache at their news; 마음이 아프시겠어요 = acknowledging their heartache (projecting with -시겠어요).

Use for genuine sorrow, loss, or hearing something deeply sad — a pet's death, a family illness, serious hardship. Register: 마음이 아파 (반말 — friend) → 마음이 아파요 / 아프네요 (polite) → 마음이 아프시겠어요 (turning sympathy toward THEM, honorific). The -네요 ending adds 'I'm feeling this right now as I hear it'.

가슴이 아프다 ('the chest/breast aches') is an interchangeable near-synonym for heartbreak. 속상하다 ('upset/distressed') is lighter — everyday frustration; do NOT use 속상해요 for a death or serious loss, it's too light. 마음이 아프다 carries proper weight for genuine sorrow.

Flip toward them: 마음이 아프시겠어요 (honorific, 'your heart must ache'). Intensify: 너무 마음이 아파요. Pair for deep loss: 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없네요 ('I'm at a loss for words'). The -네요 variant adds a 'realizing it as I hear it' quality.

Critical mix-up: 심장이 아파요 means PHYSICAL chest pain (see a doctor), not emotional heartbreak. For a broken heart, it's 마음이 아파요 or 가슴이 아파요. Particle error: 마음을 아파요 (object -을) is wrong — 아프다 is an adjective; the heart is the SUBJECT that aches, so it takes subject marker -이: 마음이 아파요.

entries.english: You must be so upset
entries.shortExplanation: 속상하시겠어요 is a practical expression meaning "You must be so upset".
entries.explanation: 속상하시겠어요 (soksanghasigesseoyo) = "You must be so upset". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 속상하시겠어요 ("You must be so upset"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Honorific; empathizing with an elder or someone you respect
Polite; to a peer, imagining their feelings

usagePhrases.en: That must suck / you must be bummed
usagePhrases.note: 반말; to a close friend

usagePhrases.en: How upset you must have been
usagePhrases.note: Stress the depth with 얼마나 ('how much'), past tense

examples.ko: A: 열심히 준비했는데 갑자기 취소됐어요. / B: 저런, 정말 속상하시겠어요.
examples.romanization: A: yeolsimhi junbihaenneunde gapjagi chwisodwaesseoyo. / B: jeoreon, jeongmal soksanghasigesseoyo.
examples.en: A: I prepared so hard and it got suddenly cancelled. / B: Oh no, you must be so upset.
examples.note: 저런 ('oh dear') + 속상하시겠어요 is the natural pair; the -겠어요 projects the feeling ONTO THEM — this is how Korean empathizes, not 속상해요 which reports your own state

examples.ko: 애써 준비했는데 안 됐다니, 정말 속상하겠어요.
examples.romanization: aesseo junbihaenneunde an dwaetdani, jeongmal soksanghagesseoyo.
examples.en: You worked so hard to prepare and it fell through — that must be really upsetting.
examples.note: Name the cause (애써 준비했는데 — 'you tried so hard, and yet') before the empathy to show you truly understand what happened

examples.ko: 그렇게 믿었던 사람한테 그런 일을 당하셨으니 얼마나 속상하셨어요.
examples.romanization: geureoke mideotdeon saramhante geureon ireul danghasyeosseuni eolmana soksanghasyeosseoyo.
examples.en: To have that happen from someone you trusted so much — how upset you must have been.
examples.note: 당하셨으니 ('having suffered that, honorific') validates the hurt; 얼마나 is rhetorical — an expression of empathy, not a question seeking an answer

entries.nuance: 직역: 속상하다 ('to be upset/distressed') + -겠- (projecting/guessing suffix) + -시- (honorific) + -어요 — literally 'you must be upset'. The real function is projecting a feeling onto the listener: -겠- transforms 속상해요 ('I am upset') into 속상하시겠어요 ('you must be feeling upset'). This is the single most important Korean empathy move — use -겠어요 to project feelings onto them. 속상하다 itself: 속 ('insides') + 상하다 ('to be spoiled/damaged') = 'my insides are spoiled', vivid for everyday distress. The contrast: 속상하다 fits everyday upset (a cancelled plan, a betrayal, bad luck); 마음이 아프다 is heavier, for genuine sorrow. For a death, use 마음이 아프시겠어요 instead. Register: 속상하겠다 (반말) → 속상하겠어요 (polite) → 속상하시겠어요 (honorific with -시-). Lead with 저런 or 아이고 for natural warmth.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 속상해요 to empathize with someone else.
속상해요 means 'I'M upset'. To acknowledge THEIR feeling, use the guessing -겠-: 속상하시겠어요 ('you must be upset'). That's how Korean shows empathy.
Dropping -시- with an elder: 속상하겠어요.
To an elder or someone you respect, include the honorific: 속상하시겠어요. The -시- shows you're respecting whose feelings you're imagining.
Using 속상하다 for a death or deep grief.
속상하다 is everyday distress/frustration — too light for grief. For profound sorrow or loss, 마음이 아프시겠어요 carries the right weight.

structuredNuance.t: 속상하다 ('to be upset') + -겠- (projecting/guessing) + -시- (honorific) + -어요. The -겠- is the key: it projects the feeling onto THEM ('you must be feeling upset'), not reporting your own state. This is how Korean expresses empathy — project with -겠어요, rather than saying how you feel with -해요.

Use for everyday misfortune: a cancelled event, a failed exam, a betrayal, bad luck, a ruined plan. Not heavy enough for a death — use 마음이 아프시겠어요 there. Register: 속상하겠다 (반말 — friend) → 속상하겠어요 (polite — peer) → 속상하시겠어요 (honorific — elder, must include -시-). Lead with 저런 or 아이고 for warmth.

마음이 아프시겠어요 ('your heart must ache') is the heavier near-synonym — for genuine sorrow, loss, death. 속상하시겠어요 is for everyday upset and frustration. The dividing line: 속상하다 for a ruined trip or bad grade; 마음이 아프다 for bereavement or deep grief.
Intensify with 얼마나: 얼마나 속상하셨어요 ('how upset you must have been') — rhetorical, not a real question. Use past tense for things they've already endured. Name the cause first: 애써 준비했는데 안 됐다니, 속상하시겠어요.

Saying 속상해요 (without -겠-) to empathize means 'I AM upset' — reporting your own feeling, not acknowledging theirs. To show empathy, include the projecting -겠-: 속상하시겠어요. Dropping -시- with an elder is also a register error.

entries.english: You must be going through so much
entries.shortExplanation: 얼마나 힘드세요 is a practical expression meaning "You must be going through so much".
entries.explanation: 얼마나 힘드세요 (eolmana himdeuseyo) means "You must be going through so much". Say it as one set phrase — for example 얼마나 힘드세요 ("How hard this must be for you"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: How hard this must be for you
usagePhrases.note: Honorific; deep sympathy to an elder or anyone suffering
Polite; to a peer going through a lot

usagePhrases.en: You must be going through so much
usagePhrases.note: 반말; to a close friend

usagePhrases.en: How hard it must have been
usagePhrases.note: Past tense, for hardship they've already endured

examples.ko: A: 6개월째 병원에 계세요. / B: 얼마나 힘드세요. 제가 뭐라도 돕고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: A: 6gaewoljjae byeongwone gyeseyo. / B: eolmana himdeuseyo. jega mworado dopgo sipeoyo.
examples.en: A: She's been in the hospital for six months. / B: How hard this must be. I want to help however I can.
examples.note: 얼마나 힘드세요 is rhetorical — do NOT wait for a quantified answer; it expresses 'I can only imagine how much you are suffering'; follow with an offer of help

examples.ko: 혼자 그 일을 다 감당하시느라 얼마나 힘드셨어요.
examples.romanization: honja geu ireul da gamdanghasineura eolmana himdeusyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Bearing all of that alone — how hard it must have been for you.
examples.note: 감당하시느라 ('in shouldering all of it, honorific') honors the specific struggle; past -셨어요 for hardship already endured

examples.ko: 말 안 해도 알아요. 요즘 얼마나 힘드세요. 제가 뭐라도 돕고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: mal an haedo arayo. yojeum eolmana himdeuseyo. jega mworado dopgo sipeoyo.
examples.en: I know without you saying. How hard things are for you lately. I want to help however I can.
examples.note: 뭐라도 돕고 싶다 ('want to help with anything') turns validation into support — the ideal sequence: acknowledge the pain, then offer help

entries.nuance: 직역: 얼마나 ('how much') + 힘들다 ('to be hard/difficult/draining') + honorific -으세요. Used as a RHETORICAL EXCLAMATION of sympathy, not a question: 'how hard this must be for you!' The 얼마나 ... -세요 structure is a Korean sympathy idiom meaning 'I can only imagine how much you're suffering'. The ㄹ-irregular conjugation matters: 힘들다 → ㄹ drops before -세요 → 힘드세요 (not 힘들으세요). Register: 얼마나 힘들어 (반말) → 얼마나 힘들어요 (polite) → 얼마나 힘드세요 / 힘드셨어요 (honorific present/past). The essential contrast: 힘내세요 ('stay strong') pushes them FORWARD; 얼마나 힘드세요 SITS with the pain and validates it first. For deep hardship, lead with validation — then you may offer encouragement. Do not confuse 힘들다 ('hard/draining') with 힘세다 ('physically strong').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Treating 얼마나 힘드세요 as a literal question.
It's a rhetorical exclamation of sympathy ('how hard this must be!'), not a request for information. Don't wait for them to quantify it — it's empathy, not an inquiry.
Saying 힘들으세요 instead of 힘드세요.
힘들다 is a ㄹ-irregular verb: the ㄹ drops before -세요, giving 힘드세요. 힘들으세요 is incorrect.
Jumping straight to 힘내세요 with someone deep in grief or hardship.
Validating first lands better. Lead with 얼마나 힘드세요 (acknowledging their pain), then optionally 힘내세요 — not the reverse.

structuredNuance.t: 얼마나 ('how much') + 힘들다 ('to be hard/draining') + honorific -으세요. Literally 'how hard is it for you?' but used as a RHETORICAL EXCLAMATION of sympathy — not a question seeking a number. The real meaning: 'I can only imagine how much you are suffering right now.'

Use for genuine heavy hardship: long illness, caregiving, bereavement, crisis. This validates pain before any encouragement — lead with 얼마나 힘드세요, then optionally 힘내세요. Register: 얼마나 힘들어 (반말 — friend) → 얼마나 힘들어요 (polite — peer) → 얼마나 힘드세요 / 힘드셨어요 (honorific — elder, present/past).

힘내세요 ('stay strong') is nearly the opposite in purpose: it pushes forward, while 얼마나 힘드세요 sits with the pain and validates it. For someone deep in hardship, leading with 얼마나 힘드세요 then following with 힘내세요 is the mature comfort sequence. Skipping straight to 힘내세요 can feel dismissive.

Past tense for endured hardship: 얼마나 힘드셨어요 ('how hard it must have been'). Follow with an offer: 제가 뭐라도 돕고 싶어요 ('I want to help however I can'). Add the cause: 혼자 감당하시느라 얼마나 힘드셨어요 ('bearing it all alone — how hard it must have been').

Two errors: (1) treating it as a literal question and pausing for an answer — it's rhetorical empathy; (2) mis-conjugating 힘들다 as 힘들으세요 instead of 힘드세요 — 힘들다 is ㄹ-irregular: ㄹ drops before -세요. Do not confuse 힘들다 ('to be hard/draining') with 힘세다 ('to be physically strong').

entries.english: It's such a shame / heartbreaking
entries.shortExplanation: 안타깝다 is a practical expression meaning "It's such a shame / heartbreaking".
entries.explanation: "It's such a shame / heartbreaking" — that is 안타깝다 (antakkapda). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 안타깝네요 ("What a shame / how unfortunate"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite with -네요; reacting to sad or regrettable news
Polite; expressing your regret over their misfortune
반말; to a friend, or muttered to yourself
Fuller, more formal: 'a truly unfortunate matter'

examples.ko: A: 결승까지 갔는데 마지막에 졌어요. / B: 저런, 정말 안타깝네요.
examples.romanization: A: gyeolseungkkaji ganneunde majimage jyeosseoyo. / B: jeoreon, jeongmal antakkamneyo.
examples.en: A: We made it to the finals and lost at the very last moment. / B: Oh no, that's truly heartbreaking.
examples.note: 안타깝다 is perfect for near-misses — the helpless feeling that something SHOULD have worked out but didn't; 저런 is the natural lead-in

examples.ko: 그렇게 열심히 했는데 떨어졌다니 너무 안타까워요.
examples.romanization: geureoke yeolsimhi haenneunde tteoreojyeotdani neomu antakkawoyo.
examples.en: To work that hard and still not make it — it's such a shame.
examples.note: Name the effort (열심히 했는데) to make the regret heartfelt; 안타까워요 is the polite present-tense reaction form (ㅂ-irregular: 안타깝 → 안타까워요)

examples.ko: 젊은 나이에 그런 일을 겪으셨다니, 듣는 제가 다 안타깝습니다.
examples.romanization: jeolmeun naie geureon ireul gyeokkeusyeotdani, deunneun jega da antakkapseumnida.
examples.en: To go through that at such a young age — even hearing it, I feel the sorrow of it.
examples.note: 듣는 제가 다 ('even I, just hearing it') shows the news moves you; 안타깝습니다 is formal register for serious contexts

entries.nuance: 안타깝다 is an adjective: 'to be regrettable / heartbreaking / sorrowful', the feeling of helpless sympathy when something sad happens that you wish were otherwise — a near-miss, a young person's suffering, bad luck, an unfair outcome. It carries a tinge of 'what a shame, if only things had gone differently'. The ㅂ-irregular conjugation: ㅂ → 워/운 before vowels — 안타깝다 → 안타까워요 / 안타까웠어요 / 안타까운, never 안타깝아요. Key contrast with 불쌍하다 ('pitiful/pathetic'): 불쌍하다 looks DOWN with pity and can feel condescending if said about an adult's face-to-face hardship ('poor thing'); 안타깝다 expresses sympathetic regret about a SITUATION — respectful, not pitying. 아쉽다 ('disappointing/too bad') is much lighter (a sold-out dish, a rained-out picnic) — not for genuine misfortune. English-speaker pitfall: reaching for 불쌍하다 where 안타깝다 belongs, and mis-conjugating the ㅂ-irregular.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 불쌍해요 to someone's face about their hardship.
불쌍하다 ('pitiful') looks down with pity and can offend an adult. To express sympathetic regret about their situation, use 안타까워요 — kinder and not condescending.
Conjugating it as 안타깝아요.
안타깝다 is a ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 워, giving 안타까워요 (and 안타까운 for the modifier). Never 안타깝아요.
Using 아쉽다 for a serious misfortune.
아쉽다 is light 'too bad / disappointing' (a sold-out dish, a rained-out picnic). For genuine, heavier misfortune, 안타깝다 carries the real weight of sympathy.

structuredNuance.t: 안타깝다 is an adjective: 'to be regrettable / heartbreaking / sorrowful (about a situation)'. The real feeling is helpless sympathy — the ache when something bad happens that you wish were otherwise. Said ABOUT a situation or someone's plight, not as a pity label for the person.

Use for near-misses, bad luck, unfair suffering, outcomes you wish had gone differently. Reactive forms fit any register; just change endings: 안타깝다 (반말/self) → 안타깝네요 / 안타까워요 (polite reactive) → 안타깝습니다 (formal). The -네요 ending adds 'I'm feeling this right now'.

불쌍하다 ('pitiful/pathetic') looks DOWN with pity and can be condescending about an adult's hardship said to their face. 안타깝다 expresses sympathetic regret about the situation — gracious, not pitying. 아쉽다 ('disappointing/too bad') is lighter and smaller — for minor letdowns, not misfortune.
ㅂ-irregular conjugation: 안타깝다 → 안타까워요 (present polite) / 안타까웠어요 (past) / 안타까운 (modifier). Fuller form: 참 안타까운 일이네요. Intensify: 너무 안타까워요 / 듣는 제가 다 안타깝습니다.

Reaching for 불쌍하다 where 안타깝다 belongs — 불쌍해요 to someone's face about their adult hardship can feel condescending or infantilizing. Use 안타까워요 about the situation instead. Conjugation error: 안타깝아요 is wrong (ㅂ-irregular → 안타까워요). Do NOT insert 하: 안타깝해요 is also wrong.

entries.english: Cheer up / Lift your spirits
entries.shortExplanation: 기운 내요 is a practical expression meaning "Cheer up / Lift your spirits".
entries.explanation: 기운 내요 (giun naeyo) = "Cheer up / Lift your spirits". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 기운 내요 ("Cheer up / Perk up"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; gently lifting a downcast peer
반말; to a close friend who's low
Honorific; to an elder or someone you respect

usagePhrases.en: Come on, cheer up a little
usagePhrases.note: Add 좀 to soften it into a gentle nudge

examples.ko: A: 요즘 너무 축 처지네. / B: 기운 내. 맛있는 거 먹으러 가자.
examples.romanization: A: yojeum neomu chuk cheojine. / B: giun nae. masinneun geo meogeureo gaja.
examples.en: A: I've been feeling really down lately. / B: Cheer up. Let's go eat something tasty.
examples.note: 기운 내 for a friend emotionally low; follow with a concrete pick-me-up — this is the key distinction: 기운 내 lifts MOOD while 힘내 pushes through a TASK

examples.ko: 그렇게 축 처져 있지 말고 기운 좀 내요.
examples.romanization: geureoke chuk cheojyeo itji malgo giun jom naeyo.
examples.en: Don't be so down in the dumps — come on, cheer up a little.
examples.note: 축 처져 있다 ('drooping/dejected', the body-language word for being emotionally sunken) names the mood vividly; 좀 softens the request

examples.ko: 많이 속상하시겠지만 기운 내세요. 좋은 날도 올 거예요.
examples.romanization: mani soksanghasigetjiman giun naeseyo. joeun naldo ol geoyeyo.
examples.en: I know you must be upset, but please cheer up. Good days will come too.
examples.note: Always acknowledge first (속상하시겠지만 = 'though you must be upset'), then offer the lift — validation before encouragement

entries.nuance: 직역: 기운 ('energy/spirits/vitality', Sino-Korean 氣運) + 내다 ('to summon/put out') — literally 'summon your spirits'. The real meaning is a gentle 'cheer up, perk up' for someone emotionally low or deflated. Close sibling of 힘내요, with a key nuance: 힘내요 summons STRENGTH to push through a challenge (exam, tough task); 기운 내요 lifts MOOD and emotional energy when someone is feeling down or drained. For someone emotionally low with no specific hurdle ahead, 기운 내요 fits better. Register: 기운 내 (반말) → 기운 내요 (polite) → 기운 내세요 (honorific). Do NOT say 기운 내세요 at a funeral — it reads as 'snap out of it'. Critical vocabulary trap: 기운 ('spirits/energy', 氣運) vs. 기분 ('mood/feeling') — 기운(을) 내다 = summon energy; 기분 내다 = splurge/treat yourself (a completely different idiom, nothing to do with cheering up).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 기분 내요 to mean 'cheer up'.
기분 내다 actually means 'to splurge / live it up'. 'Cheer up' is 기운 내요 (summon your spirits). Don't swap 기운 (energy) and 기분 (mood).
Inventing the verb 기운하다.
There's no 기운하다. It's 기운(을) 내다 — the noun 기운 plus the verb 내다. Say 기운 내요, 기운 내세요.
Telling the recently bereaved 기운 내세요.
For fresh grief, 'cheer up' can feel premature or dismissive. Offer 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 or 얼마나 힘드세요 first; save 기운 내세요 for later, lighter lows.

structuredNuance.t: 기운 ('energy/spirits/vitality', 氣運) + 내다 ('to summon/put out') — literally 'put out/summon your spirits'. The real meaning is a gentle 'cheer up, perk up' for someone emotionally deflated or low-energy. It is not for tasks or challenges — that's 힘내요.

Use when someone is emotionally down, drooping, or lacking energy with no particular hurdle ahead. Do NOT use for fresh bereavement — sounds like 'snap out of it'. Register: 기운 내 (반말 — friend) → 기운 내요 (polite — peer) → 기운 내세요 (honorific — elder). Soften with 좀: 기운 좀 내요 ('come on, perk up a little').

힘내요 summons STRENGTH to push through a challenge (exam, project). 기운 내요 lifts MOOD/emotional spirits when feeling low. They're often interchangeable, but 기운 내요 fits better when the person is emotionally drained with no specific task ahead. For a pre-exam send-off, 힘내요 is sharper.
Soften: 기운 좀 내요. Pair with a plan: 기운 내, 맛있는 거 먹으러 가자. Always validate first: 속상하시겠지만 기운 내세요. Follow with hope: 좋은 날도 올 거예요 ('good days will come too').

Critical vocabulary trap: 기분 내다 means 'to splurge / live it up / treat yourself' — NOT 'cheer up'. Do NOT swap 기운 (spirits/energy) for 기분 (mood/feeling). Also, 기운하다 does not exist — it's 기운(을) 내다 (noun + verb). And do not say 기운 내세요 at a funeral.

entries.english: You've got me / I'm here for you
entries.shortExplanation: 내가 있잖아 is a practical expression meaning "You've got me / I'm here for you".
entries.explanation: 내가 있잖아 (naega itjana) means "You've got me / I'm here for you". Say it as one set phrase — for example 내가 있잖아 ("You've got me, you know"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 반말; reassuring a close friend you're there
Polite; to a peer or someone you respect a bit

usagePhrases.en: I'll be right here beside you
usagePhrases.note: A promise to stay present (반말)
Reassurance that they have support

examples.ko: A: 너무 외롭고 힘들어. / B: 걱정 마. 내가 있잖아. 언제든 연락해.
examples.romanization: A: neomu oeropgo himdeureo. / B: geokjeong ma. naega itjana. eonjedeun yeollakae.
examples.en: A: I feel so lonely and it's so hard. / B: Don't worry. You've got me. Call me anytime.
examples.note: 내가 있잖아 is the intimate reassurance of non-aloneness; 언제든 연락해 ('call me anytime') makes it concrete — the -잖아 reminder + a real promise

examples.ko: 무슨 일 있으면 언제든 말해. 내가 있잖아.
examples.romanization: museun il isseumyeon eonjedeun malhae. naega itjana.
examples.en: If anything's wrong, tell me anytime. You've got me.
examples.note: 언제든 말해 ('tell me anytime') makes the support open-ended; 내가 있잖아 is the warm close — note bare 내가 있어 without -잖아 would be much flatter

examples.ko: 힘들 때 혼자 끙끙대지 마요. 제가 있잖아요.
examples.romanization: himdeul ttae honja kkeungkkeungdaeji mayo. jega itjanayo.
examples.en: Don't suffer alone when things are hard. You've got me.
examples.note: 끙끙대다 ('to agonize/struggle alone') sets up the offer of support; 제가 있잖아요 — note 제가 not 내가 for polite register

entries.nuance: 직역: 내가 ('I') + 있다 ('to be/exist') + -잖아 ('you know / remember / after all') — literally 'I'm here, you know'. The entire emotional payload is in -잖아: it gently reminds the listener of a comforting fact they should hold onto ('don't forget — I'm right here for you'). Without -잖아, bare 내가 있어 ('I'm here') is flat and almost like answering a roll call; the -잖아 is what makes it comfort. This is intimate, close language — for friends, family, or a partner — NOT appropriate with a boss or stranger, where it would be oddly intrusive. Register: 내가 있잖아 (반말 — 내가 is the casual 'I') → 제가 있잖아요 (polite — 제가 is the humble 'I', plus 요). The key pitfall: 내가 있잖아요 mixes the casual 반말 pronoun 내가 with the polite ending 요 — inconsistent. Always switch to 제가 있잖아요 with anyone you'd address respectfully. The -잖아 ender is not argumentative ('but I AM here!') — in this context it's gentle, carried by soft intonation.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 내가 있잖아요 to someone you respect.
내가 is the casual 'I'; polite speech uses the humble 제가. To a peer or senior it's 제가 있잖아요 — don't mix casual 내가 with the polite 요.
Dropping -잖아 and saying just 내가 있어.
Bare 내가 있어 ('I'm here') is flat, almost like a roll-call answer. The ender -잖아 ('you know') makes it a warm, comforting reminder: 내가 있잖아.
Using 내가 있잖아 with a boss or stranger.
This is intimate, affectionate reassurance for friends/family/partners. To a boss or stranger it sounds oddly close. For them, keep comfort more formal (예: 제가 도와드릴게요).

structuredNuance.t: 내가 ('I') + 있다 ('to be/exist') + -잖아 ('you know / remember / after all') — literally 'I'm here, you know'. The real meaning is a tender reminder that they are not alone. The -잖아 is the warm payload: it doesn't just state presence, it says 'don't forget — I'm right here for you'.

Use with close friends, family, or a partner when they feel lonely, overwhelmed, or unsupported. Too intimate for a boss or stranger. Register: 내가 있잖아 (반말 — 내가, casual 'I') → 제가 있잖아요 (polite — 제가, humble 'I' + 요). Do NOT say 내가 있잖아요 — mixing casual pronoun with polite ending is inconsistent.

내가 있어 ('I'm here' — bare statement) is flat and can sound like responding to a roll call. The -잖아 ender transforms it into reassurance: 'I'm here, and you should take comfort in that'. 혼자가 아니에요 ('you're not alone') is slightly more explicit, slightly less intimate — appropriate when you want to be warm without being quite as personal.
Extend to a promise: 내가 옆에 있을게 ('I'll be right here beside you'). Make it open: 언제든 연락해, 내가 있잖아. Polite version: 제가 있잖아요, 너무 힘들면 말씀하세요.

Register mismatch: 내가 is the casual 반말 pronoun — pairing it with 요 (내가 있잖아요) is inconsistent. For polite speech, switch to 제가 있잖아요. Also, misreading -잖아 as confrontational is wrong — in this caring context it's a gentle, warm reminder, not a retort. Soft, caring intonation is everything.

entries.english: I don't know if this is any comfort, but...
entries.shortExplanation: 위로가 될지 모르겠지만 is a practical expression meaning "I don't know if this is any comfort, but...".
entries.explanation: "I don't know if this is any comfort, but..." — that is 위로가 될지 모르겠지만 (wiroga doelji moreugetjiman). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 위로가 될지 모르겠지만 ("I don't know if this helps, but..."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: I don't know if this helps, but...
usagePhrases.note: Polite-formal; humble lead-in before offering comfort

usagePhrases.en: Not sure this comforts you, but...
usagePhrases.note: 반말 flavor with 말이야 tacked on, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: I hope my words are some comfort
usagePhrases.note: A warm closing wish after speaking

usagePhrases.en: I hardly know what words of comfort to offer
usagePhrases.note: When you're lost for words at deep grief

examples.ko: A: 회사에서 잘렸어요. / B: 위로가 될지 모르겠지만, 제가 늘 응원하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: hoesaeseo jallyeosseoyo. / B: wiroga doelji moreugetjiman, jega neul eungwonhago isseoyo.
examples.en: A: I got fired. / B: I don't know if it's any comfort, but I'm always rooting for you.
