examples.note: 위로가 될지 모르겠지만 cushions whatever follows — it says 'I know words may not fix this, but let me try'; always follow with something genuine and specific

examples.ko: 위로가 될지 모르겠지만, 시간이 약이라고 하잖아요.
examples.romanization: wiroga doelji moreugetjiman, sigani yagirago hajanayo.
examples.en: I don't know if this helps, but they say time heals, right?
examples.note: 시간이 약 ('time is medicine') is a classic Korean comfort saying; -잖아요 softens it from advice to gentle shared wisdom

examples.ko: 뭐라 위로의 말씀을 드려야 할지 모르겠습니다. 그저 마음이 아플 뿐입니다.
examples.romanization: mwora wiroui malsseumeul deuryeoya halji moreugetseumnida. geujeo maeumi apeul ppunimnida.
examples.en: I hardly know what words of comfort to offer. I just feel the pain of it deeply.
examples.note: 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없다 + 그저 마음이 아플 뿐 is the set combination for situations too heavy for words; -ㅂ니다 is the formal register for solemn occasions

entries.nuance: 직역: 위로 ('comfort/consolation', Sino-Korean 慰勞) + 가 (subject) + 되다 ('to become') + -ㄹ지 모르겠다 ('I'm not sure whether') + -지만 ('but') — literally 'I'm not sure whether this will become comfort, but...'. The real function is a humble, gracious preface before offering comfort to someone in genuine pain. It signals 'I know words cannot fix this, but let me try' — emotional tact and maturity. Core vocabulary: 위로하다 ('to console'), 위로가 되다 ('to be comforting'). The near-synonym for when you're truly at a loss: 뭐라 위로의 말씀을 드려야 할지 모르겠습니다 ('I hardly know what words of comfort to offer') — use this when words themselves have run out, vs. 위로가 될지 모르겠지만 when you DO have something to say but want to humble-preface it. Grammar trap: the structure is -ㄹ지 모르겠지만; saying 될지 몰라서 changes the meaning (because/since I don't know) and breaks the set phrase. English-speaker pitfall: 당신을 위로하고 싶어요 ('I want to console you') sounds clinical and presumptuous — the natural Korean move is this humble opener + your words.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 당신을 위로하고 싶어요 to a grieving person.
It's grammatical but sounds clinical and presumptuous ('I want to console you'). The natural, humble move is 위로가 될지 모르겠지만... followed by your actual words of comfort.
Mangling the structure as 될지 몰라서 or 되는지 모르겠지만.
The set polite preface is 위로가 될지 모르겠지만 (-ㄹ지 모르겠지만 = 'I'm not sure whether..., but'). Keep the 지 and the 지만.
Leading with 힘내세요 or advice at deep grief.
Charging in can feel insensitive. Cushion it: open with 위로가 될지 모르겠지만 (or 뭐라 위로의 말씀을 드려야 할지) to show tact before saying anything else.

structuredNuance.t: 위로 ('comfort/consolation', 慰勞) + 가 + 되다 + -ㄹ지 모르겠다 + -지만 — literally 'I'm not sure whether this will become comfort, but...'. The real meaning: a humble preface that says 'I know my words may not fix this, but I want to try anyway'. It shows emotional tact and respect for the depth of their pain.

Use with anyone facing heavy hardship: grief, job loss, serious illness, a devastating setback. Emotionally mature register, appropriate for peers and seniors alike. Always follow this opener with something genuine — it's a preface, not a standalone statement.

뭐라 위로의 말씀을 드려야 할지 모르겠습니다 ('I hardly know what words of comfort to offer') is the near-synonym for when words have completely run out — for the most devastating grief. 위로가 될지 모르겠지만 implies you HAVE something to say but humbly aren't sure it helps; 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없다 is for when you are truly speechless.
Close with the paired wish: 제 말이 위로가 됐으면 좋겠어요 ('I hope my words were some comfort'). Casual version with a friend: 위로가 될지 모르겠지만 말이야. Formal: 위로가 될지 모르겠지만 말씀드리고 싶었습니다.

Direct translation 'I want to comfort you' → 당신을 위로하고 싶어요 is grammatical but sounds clinical and presumptuous. The natural Korean move is this humble opener + your actual comforting words. Grammar: -ㄹ지 모르겠지만 must keep the 지; 될지 몰라서 means 'because/since I don't know' — different grammar, different meaning.

entries.english: My deepest condolences (may the deceased rest in peace)
entries.shortExplanation: 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 is a practical expression meaning "My deepest condolences (may the deceased rest in peace)".
entries.explanation: 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 (samga goinui myeongbogeul bimnida) means "My deepest condolences (may the deceased rest in peace)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 ("May the deceased rest in peace"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: May the deceased rest in peace
usagePhrases.note: Formal set phrase; the standard thing said/written at a funeral

usagePhrases.en: May the departed rest in peace
usagePhrases.note: Slightly shorter; still formal and correct

usagePhrases.en: I'm at a loss for words
usagePhrases.note: Said directly to the bereaved family, expressing helpless sorrow
A gentler, spoken comfort to a grieving friend (less formal)

examples.ko: 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다.
examples.romanization: samga goinui myeongbogeul bimnida.
examples.en: My deepest condolences.
examples.note: The phrase you say while bowing at the 빈소, or write on the condolence envelope and funeral wreath — nearly always used as a complete utterance

examples.ko: A: 갑작스러운 비보에 정말 놀랐어요. / B: 정말요. 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다.
examples.romanization: A: gapjakseureoun biboe jeongmal nollasseoyo. / B: jeongmaryo. samga goinui myeongbogeul bimnida.
examples.en: A: I was truly shocked by the sudden sad news. / B: Indeed. My deepest condolences.
examples.note: Natural exchange between two people who both knew the deceased — 비보 ('sad news') opens the condolence naturally

examples.ko: 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다. 얼마나 힘드세요.
examples.romanization: samga goinui myeongbogeul bimnida. eolmana himdeuseyo.
examples.en: My condolences. This must be so hard for you.
examples.note: After the formal phrase, switch to 얼마나 힘드세요 to comfort the living family — the two serve different purposes

entries.nuance: This is the Korean funeral phrase, and it is almost entirely fixed — memorize it as one unit. Breaking it down: 삼가 ('respectfully/humbly'), 고인 (故人 = 'the deceased'), 명복 (冥福 = 'happiness/blessing in the afterlife'), 빌다 ('to pray/wish') → 'I respectfully pray for the deceased's blessing in the next life'. You say it and write it on the plain white condolence envelope and on funeral wreaths (근조화환) at a 빈소/장례식장. The phrase is for the DECEASED — it is not addressed to the grieving person as a greeting. To the bereaved family you offer 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다 ('I don't know what to say') or 얼마나 힘드세요 ('how hard this must be for you'). The single biggest English-speaker error is saying 죄송합니다 or 미안해요 as 'I'm sorry (for your loss)' — those mean 'I apologize for a fault' and are completely wrong here. Korean condolence is the 명복을 빕니다 formula. A second pitfall: saying anything cheerful (축하, upbeat 힘내세요 before acknowledging grief). The phrase has no 반말 version; register stays formal throughout. Do not smile; tone is everything.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 죄송합니다 or 미안해요 to mean 'sorry for your loss'.
Those mean 'I apologize (for a fault)'. Korean condolence isn't an apology — say 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다, or to the family 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다.
Saying 축하해요 or anything upbeat by reflex.
축하하다 ('congratulate') is for happy events; at a funeral it's deeply offensive. Keep to the solemn 명복을 빕니다 formula.
Directing 명복을 빕니다 at the living as a hello.
That phrase prays for the DECEASED. To comfort the grieving person, say 얼마나 힘드세요 or 힘내세요; reserve 명복을 빕니다 for the deceased.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I respectfully pray for the deceased's 명복 (冥福 = happiness/blessing in the afterlife)'. 삼가 adds the humble, solemn tone. The phrase directs good wishes toward the soul of the deceased, not toward the living mourner — that distinction is essential.

고인 (故人) = 'the late/deceased person'; 명복 (冥福) = 'blessing in the underworld/afterlife' (冥 = dark/underworld, 福 = blessing); 빌다 = 'to pray/wish'. The Sino-Korean layer makes it formal and irreplaceable with everyday words.

Used exclusively at funerals (장례식장/빈소) — said aloud while bowing, written on condolence envelopes, and inscribed on funeral wreaths. Always formal; no 반말 version exists. The phrase goes toward the DECEASED; to the grieving person you say 얼마나 힘드세요 or 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다.
chips: 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다 (to the bereaved)

structuredNuance.t: 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 (for the deceased, always formal) vs 얼마나 힘드세요 (directed at the living mourner, empathetic) vs 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다 (loss for words, for the bereaved). These serve different recipients — do not conflate them.

The critical trap: translating English 'I'm sorry' as 죄송합니다 or 미안해요 — both mean apologizing for a fault, not condolence. Korean condolence has no apology structure; use 명복을 빕니다. A second trap: using 축하해요 or any cheerful phrase by social reflex. A third: directing 명복을 빕니다 at the living mourner as a greeting — it is only for the deceased.

entries.english: Here's the receipt
entries.shortExplanation: 영수증 여기 있어요 is a practical expression meaning "Here's the receipt".
entries.explanation: 영수증 여기 있어요 (yeongsujeung yeogi isseoyo) means "Here's the receipt". Say it as one set phrase — for example 영수증 여기 있어요 ("Here's the receipt"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; handing over your receipt at the counter
반말, to a friend helping you return something
Formal 합쇼체, stiffer or to a manager
Saying you have it before you hand it over

examples.ko: 영수증 여기 있어요.
examples.romanization: yeongsujeung yeogi isseoyo.
examples.en: Here's the receipt.
examples.note: The most basic form — said as you place the receipt on the counter; no extra words needed.

examples.ko: 환불하려고요. 영수증 여기 있어요.
examples.romanization: hwanbulharyeogoyo. yeongsujeung yeogi isseoyo.
examples.en: I'd like a refund. Here's the receipt.
examples.note: State your purpose first, then offer proof — this sequence signals you came prepared.

examples.ko: A: 혹시 영수증 있으세요? / B: 네, 영수증 여기 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: hoksi yeongsujeung isseuseyo? / B: ne, yeongsujeung yeogi isseoyo.
examples.en: A: Do you happen to have the receipt? / B: Yes, here's the receipt.
examples.note: Classic staff-customer exchange; B's reply is the natural beat after A's polite 있으세요? request.

entries.nuance: 영수증 여기 있어요 is 영수증 ('receipt', Sino-Korean 領收證) + 여기 있어요 ('it is here / here it is'). 여기 있어요 is the natural Korean phrase for 'here you go / here it is' when presenting an object — it literally says 'it exists here', and the offering sense comes from context and gesture. Keep the receipt, because almost every Korean store requires 영수증 for a refund or exchange; without it you may only get 교환 (store exchange) or be refused entirely. The nearest near-synonym is 영수증 드릴게요 ('I'll give it to you'), which actively announces you're handing it over and feels slightly more deferential; 여기 있어요 simply presents it — both are natural, but 여기 있어요 is the everyday default. Stronger/softer variants: 영수증 여기 있습니다 (formal), 여기 있어 (반말). The English-speaker trap is translating 'here you go' word-for-word as 여기 가요, which means 'here I go / I'm going here' — the correct presenting phrase is 여기 있어요 (존재동사 있다, not 가다). A second common confusion: 영수증 (receipt, proof of payment already made) vs 계산서 (the bill/statement, often before paying) — for a return you need 영수증.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 여기 가요 for 'here you go'.
여기 가요 means 'I'm going here / here I go', not 'here it is'. To present an object, say 여기 있어요 — the existence verb 있다, not the motion verb 가다.
Confusing 영수증 with 계산서.
영수증 is the receipt (proof you paid); 계산서 is the bill/itemized statement before paying. For a refund or exchange the staff want the 영수증.
Attempting a return with no receipt and expecting a full refund.
Most Korean stores require 영수증 for a cash refund; without it you may get only 교환 (exchange) or store credit. Keep and present it: 영수증 여기 있어요.

structuredNuance.t: 영수증 ('receipt', 領收證) + 여기 있어요 ('it exists here'). The presenting force — 'here you go' — comes from context and gesture, not from a separate giving verb. It is the standard counter phrase when handing staff any document.

Used at any retail or service counter: refund desks, pharmacy pick-ups, parcel offices. Speech-level is 해요체 (polite-neutral). Upgrade to 여기 있습니다 (합쇼체) with a manager; drop to 여기 있어 (반말) with a friend helping you. Safe for strangers and staff.

영수증 드릴게요 ('I'll give you the receipt') actively announces the handover and is a touch more deferential; 여기 있어요 just presents it. Both are fine — 여기 있어요 is the unmarked everyday default. Distinguish 영수증 (paid receipt) from 계산서 (itemized bill, often before payment); for returns you need 영수증.
여기 있어요 → 여기 있습니다 (stiffer/formal) → 여기 있어 (반말). Add lead-in: 영수증 가지고 왔어요 ('I brought the receipt') to say you have it before presenting it.

'Here you go' → 여기 가요 is the classic trap. 가요 means 'I go/am going'; the presenting verb is 있어요 (existence). A second trap: using 계산서 instead of 영수증 for a return — 계산서 is the bill, not proof of payment.

entries.english: Please give me a refund
entries.shortExplanation: 환불해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please give me a refund".
entries.explanation: 환불해 주세요 (hwanbulhae juseyo) = "Please give me a refund". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 환불해 주세요 ("Please give me a refund"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the standard request to be refunded
반말, to a friend or very casual seller

usagePhrases.en: Could you give me a refund, please?
usagePhrases.note: More polite/formal with -주시겠어요

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to request a refund
usagePhrases.note: Softer, deferential with 부탁드리다 ('to request a favor')

examples.ko: 환불해 주세요.
examples.romanization: hwanbulhae juseyo.
examples.en: Please give me a refund.
examples.note: Said once you've confirmed a refund is possible and shown the receipt — this is your actual request.

examples.ko: 사이즈가 안 맞아서요. 환불해 주세요.
examples.romanization: saijeuga an majaseoyo. hwanbulhae juseyo.
examples.en: The size doesn't fit — please refund it.
examples.note: Give the reason with -아서요 first, then the request; this soft reason-first structure is natural Korean complaint phrasing.

examples.ko: A: 어떻게 해 드릴까요? / B: 이거 카드로 결제했는데 환불해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: eotteoke hae deurilkkayo? / B: igeo kadeuro gyeoljehaenneunde hwanbulhae juseyo.
examples.en: A: How would you like to proceed? / B: I paid for this by card — please refund it.
examples.note: B mentions payment method so staff refund to the right channel (card, not cash); the A/B format mirrors a real service-desk exchange.

entries.nuance: 환불해 주세요 is 환불 ('refund') + 해 주세요 ('please do for me', from 해 주다, the favor-verb pattern). The 해 주다 is what turns it into a courteous request for the staff's help rather than a flat command: bare 환불하세요 would be an order ('you refund!'), which sounds bossy and rude. Use this AFTER you've confirmed a refund is possible with 환불돼요?; if you jump straight to 환불해 주세요 without the preamble, it can seem aggressive. 환불 is a 하다-noun — it needs the verb 하다, so you cannot say 환불 주세요 ('please give a refund') as though 환불 is a physical object you can hand over. To de-escalate when staff resist, soften to 환불해 주시겠어요? or 환불 부탁드려요. Korean law requires card purchases to be refunded back to the same card (카드 취소), not in cash — always mention 카드로 결제했어요 so staff process it correctly. The English-speaker error is the missing favor verb (환불하세요, too blunt) or the ungrammatical 환불 주세요. Another pitfall is register mismatch: 환불 부탁드립니다 in a casual market stall sounds oddly stiff, while plain 환불 in a department store sounds rude — default to 환불해 주세요 and calibrate.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 환불하세요 to the staff.
Bare 환불하세요 is an imperative ('you, refund!') and sounds commanding. The polite favor form is 환불해 주세요, asking them to do it for you.
Saying 환불 주세요 without 하다.
환불 is a 하다-noun and can't be 'given' directly. It needs 하다 + the favor 주다: 환불해 주세요, not 환불 주세요.
Demanding cash back for a card purchase.
By card you're refunded to the same card, not in cash (카드 결제는 카드로 환불). Say 카드로 결제했어요, 환불해 주세요, and expect the card to be credited.

structuredNuance.t: 환불(還拂) + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'). Literally 'please do the refund for me' — the favor-verb 주다 signals a polite request for the other person's help, not a command. Use AFTER confirming 환불돼요? — this is the execution step.

Stage two at the counter — after feasibility is confirmed. 해요체 (polite-neutral) with all staff. Upgrade to 환불해 주시겠어요? or 환불 부탁드려요 if the clerk is reluctant or you're at a formal department-store service desk. Do not use bare 환불하세요 — it is imperative and rude to staff.

환불해 주세요 (general request, any stage) vs 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 (specifically 'please execute/process it now', once agreed). 환불 부탁드려요 is softer and more face-saving when staff are reluctant. 환불 주세요 is wrong — 환불 is not a physical object you can give.
환불해 주세요 → 환불해 주시겠어요? → 환불 부탁드려요 → 환불 부탁드립니다 (most formal). Casual: 환불해 줘 (반말). Add reason: 사이즈가 안 맞아서 환불해 주세요.

Two errors: (1) 환불하세요 — the bare imperative is a command, not a request; add 주세요. (2) 환불 주세요 — 환불 is a 하다-noun and can't be 'given'; it needs 하다: 환불해 주세요. Also: card refunds go back to the card (카드 취소), not in cash — state your payment method.

entries.english: I'd like to exchange this
entries.shortExplanation: 교환하고 싶어요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to exchange this".
entries.explanation: 교환하고 싶어요 (gyohwanhago sipeoyo) means "I'd like to exchange this". Say it as one set phrase — for example 교환하고 싶어요 ("I'd like to exchange this"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; stating you want to swap the item
반말, to a friend or casual seller
교환하려고요 ('intending to exchange'), softer announcement
Asking first whether an exchange is possible

examples.ko: 이거 교환하고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: igeo gyohwanhago sipeoyo.
examples.en: I'd like to exchange this.
examples.note: Stated while presenting the item; combines purpose with politeness — no need to explain yet.

examples.ko: 사이즈가 작아서 한 치수 큰 걸로 교환하고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: saijeuga jagaseo han chisu keun geollo gyohwanhago sipeoyo.
examples.en: It's too small, so I'd like to exchange it for one size up.
examples.note: 한 치수 큰 걸로 ('for one size up') specifies exactly what you want; -아서 gives the reason without sounding accusatory.

examples.ko: A: 어떻게 오셨어요? / B: 색깔이 마음에 안 들어서 교환하고 싶은데요.
examples.romanization: A: eotteoke osyeosseoyo? / B: saekkkari maeume an deureoseo gyohwanhago sipeundeyo.
examples.en: A: How can I help? / B: I don't like the colour, so I'd like an exchange.
examples.note: B uses the soft -ㄴ데요 ender, which is warmer than a flat statement and naturally invites the staff to respond.

entries.nuance: 교환하고 싶어요 is 교환 ('exchange', Sino-Korean 交換) + 하고 싶어요 ('want to do'), 'I want to exchange (this)'. Unlike ordering food — where 먹고 싶어요 can sound bluntly desire-focused — for returns and exchanges 하고 싶어요 is perfectly polite, because you're stating your purpose to staff who'll then guide you. Many Korean learners soften this further to 교환하고 싶은데요… (trailing -ㄴ데요) to invite the staff's response. The crucial distinction: 교환돼요? checks IF an exchange is possible; 교환하고 싶어요 declares that you WANT one — always check first if unsure. Know the three-way split: 교환 (swap for another item) vs 환불 (money back) vs 반품 (physically sending back the goods). When naming the replacement, use -로/-으로: 큰 사이즈로 교환, 다른 색으로 교환. The English-speaker error is confusing 교환 with 변경 ('change/alter', used for reservations, plans, or settings) — you 교환 a product but 변경 a booking. Forgetting -로/-으로 on the replacement target makes the request vague: 큰 거 교환 is incomplete; 큰 걸로 교환 is correct.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 변경하고 싶어요 to swap a product.
변경 is for changing plans, reservations, or settings; a physical product swap is 교환. Say 교환하고 싶어요, not 변경하고 싶어요.
Forgetting -로/-으로 on the replacement.
To name what you're swapping for, use -로: 큰 걸로 교환, 다른 색으로 교환. Without it (큰 거 교환) the target item is unclear.
Saying 교환하고 싶어요 when you actually want money back.
교환 gets you a different item, not cash. If you want your money, say 환불해 주세요, not 교환하고 싶어요.

structuredNuance.t: 교환(交換) + 하고 싶어요 → 'I want to do an exchange'. The -고 싶어요 desire form is entirely natural here; staff read it as a polite statement of purpose, not a brash want. Softening option: 교환하고 싶은데요… (trailing -ㄴ데요).
Said at the counter when you want a different item, not a refund. 해요체 (polite-neutral). Can say it to any staff member. If you haven't yet confirmed an exchange is allowed, open with 교환돼요? first.
교환하고 싶어요 (want an exchange) vs 교환돼요? (is it possible?) vs 환불해 주세요 (want money back) vs 반품하고 싶어요 (want to physically return the goods). 교환 ≠ 변경 — 변경 is for reservations/plans/settings, not products.
교환하고 싶어요 → 교환하고 싶은데요… → 교환하려고요 ('I'm here to exchange'). Add target with -로: 큰 사이즈로 교환하고 싶어요 / 다른 색으로 교환해 주세요.
두 함정: (1) 교환 vs 변경 — products use 교환, reservations/plans use 변경. (2) Missing -로/-으로 on the target: 큰 거 교환 is vague; 큰 걸로 교환 ('exchange for a big one') is the correct form marking what you swap INTO.

entries.english: Please swap it for a different one
entries.shortExplanation: 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please swap it for a different one".
entries.explanation: "Please swap it for a different one" — that is 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요 (dareun geollo bakkwo juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요 ("Please swap it for a different one"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Please swap it for a different one
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking to exchange for another item

usagePhrases.en: Swap it for a different one
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend or casual stall

usagePhrases.en: Could you swap it for a different one?
usagePhrases.note: More polite/formal with -주시겠어요

usagePhrases.en: Please swap it for a different color
usagePhrases.note: 다른 색으로 ('for a different color') when only the color is off

examples.ko: 이거 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요.
examples.romanization: igeo dareun geollo bakkwo juseyo.
examples.en: Please swap this for a different one.
examples.note: The everyday counter request when the item itself is fine but you want a clean replacement.

examples.ko: 이거 흠집 있어서 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요.
examples.romanization: igeo heumjip isseoseo dareun geollo bakkwo juseyo.
examples.en: This has a scratch — please swap it for a different one.
examples.note: 흠집 있다 ('has a scratch') names the defect; -아서 links reason to request without hostility.

examples.ko: A: 뭐가 문제예요? / B: 여기 실밥 풀렸어요. 같은 걸로 새 거 있으면 바꿔 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: mwoga munjeyeyo? / B: yeogi silbap pullyeosseoyo. gateun geollo sae geo isseumyeon bakkwo juseyo.
examples.en: A: What's the problem? / B: The stitching came loose here. If you have a new one of the same, please swap it.
examples.note: B points to the exact flaw (실밥 풀리다 = stitching unraveled), then qualifies with 새 거 있으면, making the request realistic.

entries.nuance: 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요 is 다른 ('different/other') + 걸로 (걸 = 거 'thing' + -로 'into/for') + 바꿔 주세요 ('please change it for me'). 바꾸다 is the native Korean verb 'to change/swap', warmer and more everyday than the Sino-Korean 교환하다 — both work at a counter, but 바꿔 주세요 is what most people say naturally. The -로 on 다른 걸로 is essential: it marks the target you're swapping INTO ('for a different one'); drop it and 다른 거 바꿔 주세요 sounds incomplete. The dividing line from 환불해 주세요 is outcome: 바꿔 주세요 gets you a replacement item; 환불해 주세요 gets you your money back. Specify what's wrong or what you want (다른 색으로, 큰 사이즈로, 새 걸로) so staff know whether it's a defect swap or a preference swap. The English-speaker error is saying 다른 거 주세요 ('give me a different one') without the exchange framing — that sounds like you're starting a fresh purchase, not swapping the item you hold. Another pitfall: 바꾸다 works for physical items; don't use it for changing a reservation (use 변경하다) or changing money (use 환전하다).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Dropping -로 and saying 다른 거 바꿔 주세요.
The -로 marks what you swap INTO; without it the sentence dangles. Say 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요.
Saying 다른 거 주세요 to mean 'exchange this'.
That sounds like asking for a different item as a new request, not swapping the one you hold. For an exchange, use 바꿔 주세요: 이거 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요.
Using 바꿔 주세요 when you want money back.
바꾸다 swaps one item for another; it doesn't return money. If you want a refund, say 환불해 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 다른 ('different') + 걸로 (thing + -로 'into/for') + 바꿔 주세요 ('please swap for me'). 바꾸다 is native Korean for 'swap/change'; -로 marks the target. Without -로, the sentence is incomplete.

Used when you want a physical replacement, not a refund. Natural at any retail counter. 해요체 (polite-neutral). With a manager or when being persistent, upgrade to 다른 걸로 바꿔 주시겠어요?. Dropping to 바꿔 줘 (반말) is only for close friends or an unusually casual seller.

바꿔 주세요 (swap item, native verb, warm) vs 교환해 주세요 (exchange, Sino-Korean, slightly more formal) — both get you a replacement. Neither returns money: for money back, say 환불해 주세요. 다른 거 주세요 (just 'give me a different one') has no exchange framing and sounds like a new purchase.
다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요 → 큰 사이즈로 바꿔 주세요 → 새 걸로 바꿔 주세요 → 같은 거 새 걸로 바꿔 주세요. The -로 slot accepts any target: 다른 색으로, 다른 사이즈로.
Saying 다른 거 주세요 sounds like a new purchase, not an exchange. The swap framing requires 바꿔: 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요. Also: 바꾸다 is for physical items; reservations use 변경하다, currency exchange uses 환전하다.

entries.english: This one's defective
entries.shortExplanation: 이거 불량인데요 is a practical expression meaning "This one's defective".
entries.explanation: 이거 불량인데요 (igeo bullyangindeyo) = "This one's defective". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 이거 불량인데요 ("This one's defective"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; flagging a faulty product gently
반말, to a friend or casual seller
Flat statement, a touch more direct

usagePhrases.en: I think it's a defective item
usagePhrases.note: Softer, hedged with -것 같아요 ('seems')

examples.ko: 이거 불량인데요.
examples.romanization: igeo bullyangindeyo.
examples.en: This one's defective.
examples.note: Said while showing the faulty item to staff; the trailing -ㄴ데요 invites their response rather than accusing.

examples.ko: 새로 샀는데 이거 불량인데요. 작동이 안 돼요.
examples.romanization: saero sanneunde igeo bullyangindeyo. jakdongi an dwaeyo.
examples.en: I just bought it, but it's defective — it doesn't work.
examples.note: 작동이 안 되다 ('doesn't operate') names the specific malfunction; saying 새로 샀는데 heads off any suggestion you broke it through use.

examples.ko: A: 어디가 문제예요? / B: 박스 열자마자 봤는데 이거 불량인데요. 사진 찍어 뒀어요.
examples.romanization: A: eodiga munjeyeyo? / B: bakseu yeoljamaja bwanneunde igeo bullyangindeyo. sajin jjigeo dwosseoyo.
examples.en: A: What's the problem? / B: I noticed it the moment I opened the box — this is defective. I took photos.
examples.note: B's 박스 열자마자 ('the instant I opened the box') makes a strong case that the defect is pre-existing, not user-caused; 사진 찍어 뒀어요 offers proof.

entries.nuance: 이거 불량인데요 is 이거 ('this') + 불량 ('defect/defective', Sino-Korean 不良) + 인데요 (copula 이다 + soft ender -ㄴ데요). 불량 means the product is functionally faulty from the maker — a manufacturing defect — and 불량품 is the noun form 'a defective item'. The -ㄴ데요 ender is the politeness engine: it raises the problem as 'here's the situation…' and invites the staff to respond, so it's far gentler than a flat 이거 불량이에요, which can sound like an accusation. The dividing line from 하자 ('flaw/blemish', Sino-Korean 瑕疵) is function vs condition: 불량 implies it doesn't work right (functional fault), while 하자 is a visible blemish — a scratch, crack, or tear. For electronics that won't turn on, 불량 fits; for a visible blemish on packaging, 하자 있어요 is more precise. The English-speaker error is reaching for 'broken' and saying 고장났어요 for a brand-new item — 고장 implies it broke down after some use, whereas a product faulty out of the box is 불량. Note: 불량 is also slang for a 'delinquent person' (불량 학생), but with a product it unambiguously means defective.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 고장났어요 for a brand-new faulty item.
고장 means it broke down (usually after use). A product faulty from the start is 불량: 이거 불량인데요 / 불량품이에요.
Dropping -ㄴ데요 and stating flat 이거 불량이에요.
The bare statement can sound accusatory. The soft ender raises it gently: 이거 불량인데요 lets staff respond without feeling blamed.
Confusing 불량 (faulty function) with 하자 (blemish/flaw).
불량 = doesn't work right; 하자 = a flaw like a scratch or crack. For a non-working item say 불량, for a visible blemish say 하자 있어요.

structuredNuance.t: 이거 + 불량(不良) + 인데요 → 'this is [a case of] poor quality / defective — here's the situation'. 불량 = a manufacturing fault (functional). The -ㄴ데요 ender softens the claim into a situation-framer that invites the staff's response, rather than a blunt accusation.

Used when a brand-new item doesn't function correctly. 해요체 (polite-neutral) — appropriate with all staff. Softer option: 불량품인 것 같아요 (hedge with 것 같다). Point at the defect as you speak to make it concrete. Avoid being in 반말 with staff even if frustrated.

불량 (functional fault, from factory) vs 하자 (blemish/flaw in condition: scratch, crack, tear) vs 고장 (breakdown after some use). For a never-worked item: 불량. For a visible mark: 하자 있어요. For a phone that stopped working after a week: 고장 났어요.
이거 불량인데요 (soft) → 이거 불량이에요 (direct) → 불량품인 것 같아요 (hedged) → 불량품이에요 (noun form). Escalate: 불량품이라서 교환해 주세요 / 환불해 주세요.

'Broken' → 고장났어요 is wrong for a brand-new faulty item. 고장 = broke down after use; 불량 = defective from the start. Also: 불량 is also slang for a delinquent person, but in a product context it always means defective.

entries.english: There's a flaw here
entries.shortExplanation: 여기 하자 있어요 is a practical expression meaning "There's a flaw here".
entries.explanation: 여기 하자 있어요 (yeogi haja isseoyo) means "There's a flaw here". Say it as one set phrase — for example 여기 하자 있어요 ("There's a flaw here"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; pointing out a blemish on the product
반말, to a friend or casual seller
흠집 ('scratch') for a surface mark specifically

usagePhrases.en: It seems to have a bit of a flaw
usagePhrases.note: Softer, hedged with -것 같다 ('seems')

examples.ko: 여기 하자 있어요.
examples.romanization: yeogi haja isseoyo.
examples.en: There's a flaw here.
examples.note: Said while pointing directly at the blemish — the 여기 + gesture combination makes the complaint concrete and hard to dismiss.

examples.ko: 여기 보세요, 하자 있어요. 박음질이 터졌어요.
examples.romanization: yeogi boseyo, haja isseoyo. bageumjiri teojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Look here — there's a flaw. The stitching's come apart.
examples.note: 박음질이 터지다 ('the stitching burst') names the exact defect; 보세요 invites the staff to verify rather than just trust your word.

examples.ko: A: 언제 발견하셨어요? / B: 살 때는 몰랐는데 집에서 보니까 여기 하자 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: eonje balgyeonhasyeosseoyo? / B: sal ttaeneun mollanneunde jibeseo bonikka yeogi haja isseoyo.
examples.en: A: When did you notice? / B: I didn't see it when buying, but at home I noticed a flaw here.
examples.note: B's 집에서 보니까 explains why it wasn't caught in-store, making the late complaint more credible.

entries.nuance: 여기 하자 있어요 is 여기 ('here') + 하자 ('flaw/blemish', Sino-Korean 瑕疵) + 있어요 ('there is'). 하자 is the precise term for a defect in condition — a scratch, crack, tear, stain, or other blemish — as opposed to 불량, which leans toward a functional fault (it doesn't work). Pointing with 여기 ('here') as you say it makes the complaint concrete and helps staff see exactly what you mean. For an everyday surface mark, the native 흠집 ('scratch/nick') is even more specific: 여기 흠집 났어요. The dividing line: 하자 있어요 is calm and somewhat formal (it's the word used in warranties and consumer-protection law), 흠집 났어요 is plainer and very visual, while 불량이에요 says the thing fails to function. The English-speaker error is using 'have' literally and saying 이거 하자를 가지고 있어요 — Korean expresses 'there is a flaw' with the existence verb 있다, not 가지다; say 하자 있어요. Another pitfall is the particle: 하자 있어요 (or 하자가 있어요), never 하자를 있어요 — 있다 takes 이/가, not 을/를. Pair it with a defect word (터지다 'burst', 깨지다 'cracked', 찢어지다 'torn') to be unambiguous.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 하자를 가지고 있어요.
Korean uses the existence verb for 'there is a flaw': 하자 있어요, not the 'possess' verb 가지다. 가지고 있어요 sounds like a translation of English 'have'.
Using 하자를 있어요 with the object particle.
있다 takes 이/가, not 을/를. Say 하자 있어요 or 하자가 있어요, never 하자를 있어요.
Using 하자 for something that simply doesn't work.
하자 is a blemish/flaw in condition. If the item won't function at all, that's 불량 or 고장 — say 작동이 안 돼요 or 불량이에요.

structuredNuance.t: 여기 ('here') + 하자(瑕疵, 'flaw/blemish') + 있어요 ('there is'). The existence verb 있다 is what 'there is a flaw' maps to in Korean — not 가지다 ('have/possess'). Pointing as you speak makes the complaint specific and hard to argue with.

Used at a counter or on the phone when reporting a visible defect: scratch, crack, tear, stain. 해요체 (polite-neutral). 하자 is also the term used in consumer-protection policies, so staff recognize it immediately. For a casual market, 여기 흠집 났어요 (native word) is equally natural.

하자 있어요 (formal, in policies/law, blemish in condition) vs 흠집 났어요 (native, 'got scratched', very visual) vs 불량이에요 (functional fault — won't work). Don't use 하자 for things that simply don't function: that's 불량 or 고장.
여기 하자 있어요 → 여기 하자가 있어요 (subject particle added, same meaning) → 하자가 좀 있는 것 같은데요 (hedged). Add specifics: 여기 깨져 있어요 (cracked), 여기 찢어져 있어요 (torn), 여기 흠집 났어요 (scratched).
Two errors: (1) 하자를 가지고 있어요 ('it possesses a flaw') — use the existence verb: 하자 있어요. (2) Particle error: 하자를 있어요 is wrong; 있다 takes the subject particle 이/가, not the object particle 을/를.

entries.english: This is broken
entries.shortExplanation: 이거 고장 났어요 is a practical expression meaning "This is broken".
entries.explanation: "This is broken" — that is 이거 고장 났어요 (igeo gojang nasseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 이거 고장 났어요 ("This is broken / It broke down"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: This is broken / It broke down
usagePhrases.note: Polite; reporting that something stopped working
반말, to a friend or casual seller
Softer, hedged with -것 같아요 ('seems')

usagePhrases.en: It doesn't work / won't turn on
usagePhrases.note: Describing the symptom instead of naming 'broken'

examples.ko: 이거 고장 났어요.
examples.romanization: igeo gojang nasseoyo.
examples.en: This is broken.
examples.note: Said while showing the device that won't work; clear, matter-of-fact, no blame implied.

examples.ko: 산 지 일주일밖에 안 됐는데 고장 났어요.
examples.romanization: san ji iljuilbakke an dwaenneunde gojang nasseoyo.
examples.en: It's only been a week since I bought it, and it broke.
examples.note: 산 지 일주일밖에 안 됐다 emphasizes how recently it was bought, implying the fault isn't from extended use.

examples.ko: A: 어디가 안 되세요? / B: 전원이 안 켜져요. 이거 고장 난 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: A: eodiga an doeseyo? / B: jeonwoni an kyeojyeoyo. igeo gojang nan geot gatayo.
examples.en: A: What seems to be the problem? / B: It won't power on. I think it's broken.
examples.note: B describes the symptom (전원이 안 켜지다 'won't power on') before naming 고장, which helps staff diagnose before asserting a defect.

entries.nuance: 이거 고장 났어요 is 이거 ('this') + 고장 ('breakdown/malfunction', Sino-Korean 故障) + 났어요 (past of 나다, here 'to occur/arise'). The fixed collocation is 고장이 나다 — literally 'a breakdown occurs' — so 'it's broken' comes out as 고장 났어요, NOT 고장했어요 (고장 is not a 하다-verb) or 고장됐어요. This phrasing is for machines, devices, and appliances that stop working. The dividing line from 불량 is timing/cause: 고장 means it broke down, usually after some use, while 불량 means it was faulty from the factory; a phone that worked for a week and then died can use either depending on emphasis, but a never-worked item leans 불량. Don't apply 고장 to non-mechanical 'broken': a cracked screen is 깨졌어요; a torn bag is 찢어졌어요; a snapped cable is 끊어졌어요; a broken zipper is 지퍼가 고장 났어요 or 지퍼가 안 잠겨요. The English-speaker error is the wrong verb pairing: 고장했어요 or 고장됐어요 are not standard; the correct pairing is 고장 + 나다. Another pitfall is using 고장 for a torn or shattered item — those use different Korean verbs.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 고장했어요 or 고장됐어요.
고장 pairs with the verb 나다: the correct form is 고장 났어요 ('a breakdown occurred'). 고장하다/고장되다 are not standard.
Using 고장 for non-machines.
고장 is for devices/machinery. A snapped pencil is 부러졌어요, shattered glass is 깨졌어요, a torn bag is 찢어졌어요 — not 고장 났어요.
Confusing 고장 (broke down) with 불량 (faulty from the start).
If it worked then failed, 고장 났어요; if it never worked out of the box, 불량이에요. Pick based on whether it ever functioned.

structuredNuance.t: 고장(故障) + 났어요 ('occurred/arose') → 'a breakdown occurred'. 고장 is a noun; it collocates with 나다, not 하다 or 되다. Think of it as 'a malfunction happened' rather than 'it did a breakdown'.

For machines, electronics, appliances — things that stop functioning. Not for physical breakage (snapping, shattering). 해요체 (polite-neutral). When unsure, describe the symptom instead: 작동이 안 돼요 / 전원이 안 켜져요.
고장 났어요 (machine broke down after use) vs 불량이에요 (faulty from the factory) vs 작동이 안 돼요 (symptom description: doesn't operate). For physical damage: 깨졌어요 (shattered), 찢어졌어요 (torn), 부러졌어요 (snapped).
이거 고장 났어요 → 고장 난 것 같아요 (hedged) → 고장이 난 건 아닌데 작동이 안 돼요 (softer: 'not sure it's broken but it won't work'). Also: 고장 수리 맡기다 ('send for repair'), A/S 신청하다 ('apply for after-sales service').
고장했어요 and 고장됐어요 are both wrong — 고장 pairs with 나다. Say 고장 났어요. Also: 고장 is only for machines; for a torn/shattered/snapped item use the correct breakage verb (깨지다, 찢어지다, 부러지다).

entries.english: What's the refund policy?
entries.shortExplanation: 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "What's the refund policy?".
entries.explanation: 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? (hwanbul gyujeongi eotteoke dwaeyo?) = "What's the refund policy?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? ("What's the refund policy?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; asking how returns work here
반말, to a friend who works there

usagePhrases.en: How does the refund policy work?
usagePhrases.note: Softer, slightly more polite with -나요
환불 정책 ('refund policy'), a near-synonym of 규정

examples.ko: 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요?
examples.romanization: hwanbul gyujeongi eotteoke dwaeyo?
examples.en: What's the refund policy?
examples.note: Asked before buying — the smartest time, since you'll know your options before any problem arises.

examples.ko: 혹시 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? 며칠 안에 가능한가요?
examples.romanization: hoksi hwanbul gyujeongi eotteoke dwaeyo? myeochil ane ganeunghangayo?
examples.en: What's the refund policy — how many days do I have?
examples.note: 혹시 ('by any chance') softens the inquiry; 며칠 안에 가능한가요? drills down to the time limit immediately.

examples.ko: A: 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? / B: 7일 이내에 영수증 지참하시면 가능해요.
examples.romanization: A: hwanbul gyujeongi eotteoke dwaeyo? / B: 7il inaee yeongsujeung jichamhasimyeon ganeunghaeyo.
examples.en: A: What's the refund policy? / B: Within 7 days with the receipt, it's possible.
examples.note: B's reply is the typical staff formula — 이내에 ('within'), 영수증 지참 ('with receipt in hand'); learning this means you'll understand the answer too.

entries.nuance: 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? is 환불 ('refund') + 규정 ('regulation/policy', Sino-Korean 規定) + 이 어떻게 돼요? ('how does it go / what is it?'). The set frame …이/가 어떻게 돼요? is the natural Korean way to ask 'what is X / how does X work' for policies, fees, schedules, and personal details — it's softer and more conversational than a blunt 뭐예요?. This question asks the store to explain its full return rules: time limits, receipt requirements, sale-item exclusions. The dividing line from 환불돼요? is scope: 환불돼요? is about one specific item right now; 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? asks for the store's general policy. 규정 and 정책 are interchangeable here, with 규정 sounding slightly more like 'the official rules'. The English-speaker error is translating 'what is the policy' as 환불 규정이 뭐예요? — grammatically possible but blunt and survey-like; natives prefer the 어떻게 돼요? frame. The particle trap: 규정이 어떻게 돼요 (subject particle 이), never 규정을 어떻게 돼요. Mastering 어떻게 돼요? unlocks many polite info questions: 가격이 어떻게 돼요? (price), 영업시간이 어떻게 돼요? (hours).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 환불 규정이 뭐예요?.
Grammatically fine but abrupt and survey-like. The natural, polite frame is 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요?.
Using the object particle: 환불 규정을 어떻게 돼요?.
되다 takes the subject particle here: 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요?. 규정을 is wrong with 되다.
Confusing the general policy with one item.
환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? asks the overall rules. To ask about the specific thing in your hand, say 이거 환불돼요?.

structuredNuance.t: 환불 + 규정(規定, 'regulation/policy') + 이 어떻게 돼요? ('how does it become?'). 어떻게 돼요? is a versatile information frame meaning 'what/how is X' — softer than 뭐예요?, more open-ended than a yes/no. It asks staff to explain the full policy.

Ask before buying (ideally) or before the return attempt. 해요체 (polite-neutral) — correct with all staff. In writing/email, 환불 규정이 어떻게 되나요? or 환불 정책을 안내해 주시겠어요? is more formal. Don't use 반말 with staff.
환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? (general policy, open) vs 이거 환불돼요? (this one specific item, closed yes/no) vs 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? (the time-limit sub-question). 규정 ≈ 정책 in this context — both natural.
어떻게 돼요? transfers across topics: 교환 규정이 어떻게 돼요? / 반품 규정이 어떻게 돼요? / 가격이 어떻게 돼요?. For a specific follow-up: 며칠 이내예요? ('within how many days?').
환불 규정이 뭐예요? is grammatically fine but sounds abrupt — use 어떻게 돼요?. Particle error: 규정을 어떻게 돼요? is wrong; 되다 takes the subject particle: 규정이 어떻게 돼요?.

entries.english: By how many days do I have to get a refund?
entries.shortExplanation: 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "By how many days do I have to get a refund?".
entries.explanation: 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? (myeochil ane hwanbulhaeya dwaeyo?) means "By how many days do I have to get a refund?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? ("Within how many days do I have to refund it?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Within how many days do I have to refund it?
usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; asking the return deadline

usagePhrases.en: How many days do I have to refund?
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend or casual seller

usagePhrases.en: How many days is the refund window?
usagePhrases.note: 환불 기간 ('refund period'), asking the window directly

usagePhrases.en: Until when is a refund possible?
usagePhrases.note: 언제까지 ('by when'), asking the cutoff date

examples.ko: 이거 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요?
examples.romanization: igeo myeochil ane hwanbulhaeya dwaeyo?
examples.en: By how many days do I have to get this refunded?
examples.note: The smart follow-up to ask at the moment of buying so you know your exact deadline before any problem arises.

examples.ko: 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? 일주일 지나면 안 돼요?
examples.romanization: myeochil ane hwanbulhaeya dwaeyo? iljuil jinamyeon an dwaeyo?
examples.en: How many days do I have? Is it no good after a week?
examples.note: 일주일 지나면 ('if a week passes') probes the boundary; this two-beat structure is natural in real negotiation.

examples.ko: A: 선물할 건데요, 혹시 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? / B: 14일 이내에 영수증 있으시면 가능해요.
examples.romanization: A: seonmulhal geondeyo, hoksi myeochil ane hwanbulhaeya dwaeyo? / B: 14il inaee yeongsujeung isseusimyeon ganeunghaeyo.
examples.en: A: I'm buying this as a gift — within how many days must it be refunded? / B: Within 14 days, with the receipt.
examples.note: A's 선물할 건데요 explains why the window matters; B's reply gives the standard Korean policy formula — 14일 이내, 영수증.

entries.nuance: 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? is 며칠 ('how many days') + 안에 ('within') + 환불하다 ('to refund') + -아야 되다 ('have to / must'). The core grammar -아/어야 되다 expresses obligation or a deadline: 'within how many days must the refund be done?'. 안에 ('within') takes a time noun directly: 일주일 안에, 14일 안에, 한 달 안에. Korean stores typically allow returns within 7 or 14 days (7일/14일 이내), so knowing this is genuinely practical. The dividing line from 환불 기간이 며칠이에요? ('how long is the refund period?') is angle: 며칠 안에 …해야 돼요? frames it as your obligation/deadline, while 환불 기간 asks for the policy window as a plain fact — both yield the same answer. Two spelling traps for English speakers: 며칠 ('how many days', one word) is often misspelled 몇 일 even by native speakers; the correct spelling is 며칠 — write it as one word. Second: 안에 ('within') and 안 ('not') look similar but are entirely different — 며칠 안에 = 'within how many days'; 안 would negate a verb. The obligation ending is 돼요 (from 되다), not 해요, so 환불해야 돼요?, not 환불해야 해요? (though -아야 하다 is also used in formal contexts).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spelling it 몇 일 안에.
The question word for 'how many days' is written 며칠, one word — not 몇 일. So it's 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요?.
Confusing 안에 ('within') with 안 ('not').
안에 sets a time/space frame ('within'); 안 negates a verb. 며칠 안에 = 'within how many days'; 며칠 안 환불해요 would be nonsense.
Mixing up 얼마 안에 and 며칠 안에.

얼마 안에 means 'within a short while' (vague); the correct deadline question word is 며칠 ('how many days'): 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요?. Saying 얼마 안에 환불해야 돼요? asks 'must I refund within a short time?' rather than asking how many days.

structuredNuance.t: 며칠 ('how many days') + 안에 ('within') + 환불해야 ('must refund') + 돼요? → 'within how many days must the refund happen?'. Frames it as your obligation/deadline — subtly implying you want to comply, which is politer than demanding to know if you can still get one.

Ask at point of purchase, not when you already have a problem. 해요체 (polite-neutral). Gifts and online orders especially warrant this question. If you've missed the window, it's better to ask 지금도 환불 가능한가요? ('is a refund still possible?') rather than this form.

며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? (deadline as obligation) vs 환불 기간이 며칠이에요? (window as fact) vs 언제까지 환불 가능해요? (cutoff date). All three ask for the same information from different angles — 며칠 안에 is the most natural spoken form.
-아야 되다 transfers: 교환해야 돼요? (exchange deadline), 반품해야 돼요? (return deadline). Also: 며칠 이내예요? ('within how many days?', shorter). The time noun slot: 며칠 / 일주일 / 14일 / 한 달.

두 함정: (1) 며칠 spelling — the correct form is 며칠, NOT 몇 일; even many native speakers misspell this. (2) 안에 vs 안 — 안에 = 'within' (a time/space frame); 안 = 'not' (negation). They look similar but are unrelated.

entries.english: I'd like to return this
entries.shortExplanation: 이거 반품하고 싶어요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to return this".
entries.explanation: "I'd like to return this" — that is 이거 반품하고 싶어요 (igeo banpumhago sipeoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 이거 반품하고 싶어요 ("I'd like to return this"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; sending an item back (esp. online orders)
반말, to a friend or casual seller
반품하려고요 ('intending to return it'), softer announcement
반품 신청 ('return application'), the online/app step

examples.ko: 이거 반품하고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: igeo banpumhago sipeoyo.
examples.en: I'd like to return this.
examples.note: In a physical store, stating your purpose clearly at the start; staff will then guide you through the process.

examples.ko: 온라인에서 샀는데 반품하고 싶어요. 어떻게 해요?
examples.romanization: ollaineseo sanneunde banpumhago sipeoyo. eotteoke haeyo?
examples.en: I bought it online — I'd like to return it. How do I do that?
examples.note: 온라인에서 샀다 ('bought online') is key context since the process (app, courier) differs from in-store.

examples.ko: A: 네, 어떻게 오셨어요? / B: 마음에 안 들어서 반품하고 싶은데, 택배비는 누가 내요?
examples.romanization: A: ne, eotteoke osyeosseoyo? / B: maeume an deureoseo banpumhago sipeunde, taekbaebineun nuga naeyo?
examples.en: A: How can I help you? / B: I don't like it and want to return it — who pays the shipping?
examples.note: B immediately asks the critical online-return question: 택배비 누가 내요? ('who pays shipping?'). The answer depends on 단순 변심 (buyer pays) vs 불량 (seller pays).

entries.nuance: 이거 반품하고 싶어요 is 이거 ('this') + 반품 ('returning goods', Sino-Korean 返品) + 하고 싶어요 ('want to do'). 반품 is specifically the act of sending the product back — the physical/logistical return — which then results in a 환불 (refund) or sometimes 교환 (exchange). This word dominates online shopping, where you 반품 신청 ('file a return request') through an app and arrange for a courier pickup. The three-way distinction: 반품 = give the goods back physically; 환불 = get your money back; 교환 = swap for another item. They're related but not interchangeable: saying 환불하고 싶어요 when the agent needs to arrange a courier pickup can confuse things. For online 단순 변심 ('simple change of mind') returns you pay return shipping 택배비; for 불량 ('defect') returns the seller typically pays — always ask 택배비는 누가 내요?. Don't confuse 반품 with 반납 ('returning something borrowed or rented', like a library book or a rental car) — you 반품 a purchase but 반납 a rental. For in-store, 반품 works, but people often just say 환불해 주세요 directly.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 환불 when you mean sending the item back.
환불 is the money refund; the act of returning the goods is 반품. For online orders especially, say 반품하고 싶어요, then sort out the 환불.
Confusing 반품 (return a purchase) with 반납 (return a rental/borrowed item).
반품 is for goods you bought; 반납 is for things you borrowed or rented (books, equipment). Don't say 반납하고 싶어요 for a store purchase.
Forgetting to ask about 택배비 (shipping) on online returns.
For 단순 변심 ('change of mind') the buyer usually pays return shipping; for 불량 ('defect') the seller does. Ask 택배비는 누가 내요? when you say 반품하고 싶어요.

structuredNuance.t: 반품(返品) = 'returning goods' + 하고 싶어요 ('want to do'). 반품 is the logistics of sending the product back — it's the first step; 환불 (money) or 교환 (replacement) is the result. Dominant in online commerce; in-store people often skip to 환불해 주세요.

Use when the item actually needs to go back — especially for online orders where a courier must be arranged. 해요체 (polite-neutral). Online: 반품 신청하다 (apply through the app). In-store: 반품하고 싶어요 or 환불해 주세요. Always ask 택배비 누가 내요? for online returns.
반품하고 싶어요 (send the item back, logistics) vs 환불해 주세요 (get money back) vs 교환하고 싶어요 (swap for different item). 반품 ≠ 반납 — 반납 is for borrowed/rented items (도서관 책 반납, 렌터카 반납).
반품하고 싶어요 → 반품하려고요 (softer announcement) → 반품 신청할게요 ('I'll file a return request', online). Lead-in: 단순 변심인데 반품하고 싶어요 / 불량인데 반품하고 싶어요 (state reason, as it affects shipping cost).

'Return' maps to both 반품 and 환불 in English — but they are different steps in Korean. 반품 is the physical return; 환불 is the money. Mixing them can cause confusion. Also: 반납 (return a rental/borrowed item) ≠ 반품 (return a purchase). For 단순 변심 online returns, you (the buyer) pay 택배비.

entries.english: Can I get a refund even without the receipt?
entries.shortExplanation: 영수증 없이도 환불돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I get a refund even without the receipt?".
entries.explanation: 영수증 없이도 환불돼요? (yeongsujeung eopsido hwanbuldwaeyo?) = "Can I get a refund even without the receipt?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 영수증 없이도 환불돼요? ("Can I refund it even without the receipt?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Can I refund it even without the receipt?
usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; checking the no-receipt case
반말, to a friendly seller

usagePhrases.en: Is there no refund without a receipt?
usagePhrases.note: Phrased as 'won't it work without one?'

usagePhrases.en: Do I absolutely need the receipt?
usagePhrases.note: Asking directly if the receipt is mandatory

examples.ko: 영수증 없이도 환불돼요?
examples.romanization: yeongsujeung eopsido hwanbuldwaeyo?
examples.en: Can I get a refund even without the receipt?
examples.note: When you've lost or thrown away the receipt; the -도 ('even') acknowledges you know it's normally required.

examples.ko: 영수증을 잃어버렸는데, 영수증 없이도 환불돼요?
examples.romanization: yeongsujeungeul ireobeoryeonneunde, yeongsujeung eopsido hwanbuldwaeyo?
examples.en: I lost the receipt — can I still get a refund?
examples.note: 영수증을 잃어버리다 ('lost the receipt') explains the situation upfront, making the follow-up question less awkward.

examples.ko: A: 영수증 있으세요? / B: 카드로 샀는데 영수증 없이도 환불돼요? 카드 내역 있잖아요.
examples.romanization: A: yeongsujeung isseuseyo? / B: kadeuro sanneunde yeongsujeung eopsido hwanbuldwaeyo? kadeu naeyeok itjanayo.
examples.en: A: Do you have the receipt? / B: I paid by card — can I refund without the receipt? There's a card record.
examples.note: B pivots to 카드 내역 (card transaction record) as an alternative to the receipt — this often works and is a genuinely useful tactic.

entries.nuance: 영수증 없이도 환불돼요? is 영수증 ('receipt') + 없이 ('without', the adverb derived from 없다) + -도 ('even/also') + 환불돼요? ('is a refund possible?'). The key element is 없이도 — 없이 means 'without', and -도 adds 'even', so together it asks 'is a refund possible EVEN without the receipt?'. The -도 is crucial: it implicitly acknowledges you know the receipt is normally required, which is more face-saving and polite than just asking as if the rule doesn't exist. Because Korean stores usually require 영수증, knowing alternatives is practically important: a card purchase (카드 결제) leaves a 카드 내역 (card transaction record) that can often substitute. The dividing line from 영수증 없으면 환불 안 돼요? is framing: 없이도 …돼요? hopefully asks 'can it still be done?', while 없으면 …안 돼요? pessimistically asks 'is it impossible without one?' — both are polite, 없이도 sounds more constructive. The English-speaker error is forming 'without' with a clunky negative clause like 영수증 안 가지고 환불돼요? — the clean adverb is 없이. Dropping -도 (영수증 없이 환불돼요?) is fine but slightly loses the 'even/acknowledging the norm' nuance.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 영수증 안 가지고 환불돼요? for 'without the receipt'.
That's clumsy. The clean way to say 'without' is the adverb 없이: 영수증 없이(도) 환불돼요?.
Confusing 없이 (without) with 없으면 (if there isn't).
없이 = 'without' (adverb); 없으면 = 'if there's none' (conditional). Both work but differ: 영수증 없이도 환불돼요? vs. 영수증 없으면 환불 안 돼요?.
Forgetting you paid by card.
A card purchase leaves a 카드 내역 that can stand in for the receipt. Mention 카드로 샀어요 — it often unlocks a refund even 영수증 없이.

structuredNuance.t: 영수증 + 없이 ('without', adverb of 없다) + 도 ('even') + 환불돼요? → 'even without the receipt, is a refund possible?'. The -도 politely signals you know the receipt is normally required — you're asking about the exception, not ignoring the rule.

When you've lost the receipt or it was a gift. 해요체 (polite-neutral). Strengthen your case by mentioning your payment method: 카드로 샀어요, 영수증 없이도 환불돼요? — card records often substitute. Don't use 반말 with staff.
없이도 …돼요? (constructive: 'can it still be done?') vs 없으면 …안 돼요? (pessimistic: 'is it impossible?') vs 영수증 꼭 있어야 돼요? ('is the receipt absolutely required?'). All three are polite; choose based on tone.
없이도 환불돼요? → 없이도 교환돼요? → 없이도 반품돼요?. Add alternatives: 카드 내역으로 가능해요? ('is the card record enough?'), 앱 구매 내역으로 가능해요? ('can the app purchase history work?').

없이 (adverb: 'without') is the clean form — don't substitute 안 가지고 ('without bringing'). Dropping -도 gives 영수증 없이 환불돼요? which is fine but loses the face-saving 'even though I know it's needed' nuance that -도 carries.

entries.english: I'd just like a refund (not an exchange)
entries.shortExplanation: 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd just like a refund (not an exchange)".
entries.explanation: 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 (geunyang hwanbulbatgo sipeoyo) means "I'd just like a refund (not an exchange)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 ("I'd just like a refund"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; declining exchange, wanting money back
반말, to a friend or casual seller

usagePhrases.en: A refund, not an exchange, please
usagePhrases.note: 교환 말고 ('not an exchange') makes the contrast explicit

usagePhrases.en: Could I possibly get a refund?
usagePhrases.note: Softer, tentative with -ㄹ 수 있을까요

examples.ko: 그냥 환불받고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: geunyang hwanbulbatgo sipeoyo.
examples.en: I'd just like a refund.
examples.note: Said when staff offer an exchange but you want money back; 그냥 keeps the refusal gentle.

examples.ko: 교환은 됐고요, 그냥 환불받고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: gyohwaneun dwaetgoyo, geunyang hwanbulbatgo sipeoyo.
examples.en: Never mind the exchange — I'd just like a refund.
examples.note: 교환은 됐다 ('I'm done with the exchange [idea]') politely closes off the staff's alternative offer;됐다 here means 'no thanks, that's enough' not 'it worked'.

examples.ko: A: 교환해 드릴까요? / B: 아니요, 그냥 환불받고 싶어요. 교환 말고요.
examples.romanization: A: gyohwanhae deurilkkayo? / B: aniyo, geunyang hwanbulbatgo sipeoyo. gyohwan malgoyo.
examples.en: A: Shall I arrange an exchange? / B: No, I'd just like a refund. Not an exchange.
examples.note: B uses 그냥 + 교환 말고요 together — the double-emphasis politely but unmistakably insists on money, not a replacement.

entries.nuance: 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 is 그냥 ('just/simply') + 환불받다 ('to receive a refund', 환불 + 받다 'receive') + 고 싶어요 ('want to'). The 그냥 does crucial social work: it signals 'just / never mind the alternatives', which is how you politely decline a pushy exchange offer without sounding aggressive. Korean staff often steer you toward 교환 (exchange) or store credit first, and 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 gently but firmly insists on money back. Note the giver/receiver verb distinction: 환불받다 (receive a refund, customer's perspective) vs 환불해 주다 / 환불하다 (issue a refund, staff's action); as the customer wanting your money returned, 환불받고 싶어요 is the natural form — 환불해 주고 싶어요 ('I want to give a refund') reverses the roles. The dividing line from bare 환불해 주세요 is softness: adding 그냥 frames it as 'I'd simply prefer a refund', de-escalating — useful when staff push back. For maximum clarity, combine: 교환 말고 그냥 환불받고 싶어요. The English-speaker error is omitting 그냥 and repeating a flat 환불해 주세요 under pressure, which can sound confrontational.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 환불해 주고 싶어요 to mean 'I want a refund'.
환불해 주다 is to GIVE a refund (the staff's action). As the customer receiving money, say 환불받고 싶어요.
Dropping 그냥 when declining an exchange.
Without 그냥, repeating 환불해 주세요 can sound blunt under pressure. 그냥 softens it to 'I'd simply prefer a refund' while staying firm.
Assuming a refund is automatic over an exchange.
Staff often push 교환 or store credit first. Be explicit: 교환 말고 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 ('not an exchange — just a refund').

structuredNuance.t: 그냥 ('just, simply') + 환불받다 ('receive a refund') + 고 싶어요 ('want to'). 그냥 is the softener that says 'I'm not being difficult — I simply want my money back'. It de-escalates a potentially tense pushback.
Used when staff offer 교환 (exchange) or 적립금 (store credit) but you want cash/card credit back. 해요체 (polite-neutral). Appropriate with any staff. Combine with 교환 말고 for emphasis: 교환 말고 그냥 환불받고 싶어요.

그냥 환불받고 싶어요 (soft, declining alternatives) vs 환불해 주세요 (direct request, no implicit decline of alternatives) vs 교환 말고 환불해 주세요 (explicit contrast). 환불받다 (customer receives) ≠ 환불해 주다 (staff gives) — don't swap the verb.
그냥 환불받고 싶어요 → 교환 말고 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 → 적립금 말고 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 (declining store credit). Softer: 그냥 환불받을 수 있을까요?

두 함정: (1) 환불해 주고 싶어요 reverses the roles — 해 주다 = 'give', so you'd be saying 'I want to give a refund'. Say 환불받고 싶어요 (receive). (2) Dropping 그냥 when declining an exchange makes 환불해 주세요 sound blunt under pressure; 그냥 keeps it gentle.

entries.english: It's unused
entries.shortExplanation: 안 쓴 거예요 is a practical expression meaning "It's unused".
entries.explanation: "It's unused" — that is 안 쓴 거예요 (an sseun geoyeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 안 쓴 거예요 ("It's unused"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; assuring staff the item wasn't used
반말, to a friend or casual seller
한 번도 ('not even once') for stronger emphasis

usagePhrases.en: I didn't even open the packaging
usagePhrases.note: 포장 안 뜯다 ('didn't tear the wrapping'), the strongest proof

examples.ko: 이거 안 쓴 거예요.
examples.romanization: igeo an sseun geoyeyo.
examples.en: This is unused.
examples.note: Reassuring staff during a return so they accept it; the adnominal construction describes the item's condition, not just your past action.

examples.ko: 택도 안 뗐고 안 쓴 거예요.
examples.romanization: taekdo an ttetgo an sseun geoyeyo.
examples.en: The tag's still on and it's unused.
examples.note: 택 안 떼다 ('tag not removed') is physical, verifiable proof; stacking it with 안 쓴 거예요 makes a much stronger case.

examples.ko: A: 왜 반품하시려고요? / B: 선물 받았는데 저한테 안 맞아서요. 안 쓴 거예요.
examples.romanization: A: wae banpumhasiryeogoyo? / B: seonmul badanneunde jeohante an majaseoyo. an sseun geoyeyo.
examples.en: A: Why do you want to return it? / B: I received it as a gift but it doesn't suit me. It's unused.
examples.note: B's 선물 받았다 explains the absence of a receipt; 안 쓴 거예요 confirms the item's condition, which together is the best case for a gift return.

entries.nuance: 안 쓴 거예요 is 안 ('not') + 쓴 (past adnominal of 쓰다 'to use') + 거예요 ('it is the thing that…'), literally 'it's a not-used thing' → 'it's unused'. 쓰다 here means 'to use' (쓰다 is polysemous: also 'to write', 'to wear glasses/hat', 'to be bitter' — context disambiguates; with a product it clearly means 'use'). This phrase matters because Korean return policies hinge on condition: 미개봉 (unopened packaging), 미사용 (unused), 택 그대로 (tag intact) all strengthen your claim. The dividing line: 안 쓴 거예요 is the everyday spoken form of the formal 미사용 (未使用) printed in policies; 포장 안 뜯었어요 ('packaging not opened') and 택 안 뗐어요 ('tag not removed') are even more concrete and persuasive. The English-speaker error is reaching for the perfect tense and saying 안 사용했어요 — that's fine as 'I didn't use it', but to DESCRIBE the item as unused, the adnominal form 안 쓴 거예요 is more native. The critical verb-confusion trap: 쓰다 'use' vs 사다 'buy' — 안 산 거예요 means 'something I didn't buy' (the opposite of helpful). Also, the past adnominal of 쓰다 is simply 쓴 (not 쓰은), so 안 쓴 거예요, never 안 쓰은 거예요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 안 쓰은 거예요.
The past adnominal of 쓰다 is 쓴, not 쓰은. Say 안 쓴 거예요.
Confusing 쓰다 'use' with 사다 'buy'.
안 쓴 거 = unused; 안 산 거 = not bought. To say the item is unused, it's 안 쓴 거예요, not 안 산 거예요.
Thinking 'unused' alone guarantees a return.
Stores also check 택 (tag), 포장 (packaging), and time limits. Reinforce with 택도 안 뗐어요 / 포장도 안 뜯었어요 alongside 안 쓴 거예요.

structuredNuance.t: 안 + 쓴 (past adnominal of 쓰다 'use') + 거예요 ('it's the thing that…') → 'it's an unused thing'. The adnominal form describes the ITEM's condition, not just your past action — more natural than the plain-past 안 썼어요 in this context.

Essential to say during any return to confirm the item's condition. 해요체 (polite-neutral). Back it up with physical evidence: 택도 안 뗐어요 (tag on), 포장도 안 뜯었어요 (packaging sealed). Staff will often check before accepting.
안 쓴 거예요 (spoken, describes item) vs 미사용 제품이에요 (formal, label language) vs 한 번도 안 썼어요 (emphasizes how often: 'not even once'). Stack for impact: 포장도 안 뜯었고 안 쓴 거예요 ('packaging intact and unused').
안 쓴 거예요 → 한 번도 안 썼어요 → 포장도 안 뜯었어요 → 택도 안 뗐어요. Formal: 미사용 상태예요. The past adnominal is 쓴 (not 쓰은): 안 쓴 거예요.
두 함정: (1) 쓰다 'use' vs 사다 'buy' — 안 산 거예요 = 'something I didn't buy', not 'unused'. (2) Adnominal form: 쓰다 → 쓴 (not 쓰은). Say 안 쓴 거예요, never 안 쓰은 거예요.

entries.english: I bought it not long ago
entries.shortExplanation: 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요 is a practical expression meaning "I bought it not long ago".
entries.explanation: 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요 (san ji eolma an dwaesseoyo) = "I bought it not long ago". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요 ("I bought it not long ago"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: I bought it not long ago
usagePhrases.note: Polite; stressing the purchase was recent
반말, to a friend or casual seller

usagePhrases.en: It's only been a few days
usagePhrases.note: 며칠 ('a few days') pins it down more
Naming the exact day, the most concrete version

examples.ko: 이거 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요.
examples.romanization: igeo san ji eolma an dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: I bought this not long ago.
examples.note: Establishing you're within the return window — the first thing staff mentally calculate when you walk in.

examples.ko: 산 지 얼마 안 됐는데 벌써 고장 났어요.
examples.romanization: san ji eolma an dwaenneunde beolsseo gojang nasseoyo.
examples.en: I bought it recently and it's already broken.
examples.note: 벌써 ('already') highlights how premature the failure is, implying it's a quality issue, not normal wear.

examples.ko: A: 언제 구매하셨어요? / B: 산 지 일주일도 안 됐어요. 영수증도 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: eonje gumaehasyeosseoyo? / B: san ji iljuildo an dwaesseoyo. yeongsujeungdo isseoyo.
examples.en: A: When did you buy it? / B: It hasn't even been a week. I have the receipt too.
examples.note: B answers the staff's standard question precisely (일주일도 안 됐어요 = 'not even a week') and proactively adds 영수증도 있어요 — the two things staff always need.

entries.nuance: 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요 is 산 (past adnominal of 사다 'to buy') + 지 (bound noun marking elapsed time SINCE an action) + 얼마 안 됐어요 ('not much has become' → 'not long has passed'). The construction -ㄴ 지 + time + 되다 is the standard Korean way to say 'it's been [time] since I did X': 산 지 일주일 됐어요 = 'it's been a week since I bought it'. 얼마 안 됐어요 means 'not much time has passed', i.e. 'it was recent'. This is crucial to establish because refund/exchange eligibility depends on the purchase date, and staff will ask 언제 사셨어요? ('when did you buy it?'). The dividing line from 어제 샀어요 ('I bought it yesterday') is precision: 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요 is vaguer ('recently'), while naming the day is more concrete and convincing if you're close to the deadline. Two traps: the 지 marking elapsed time is written with a SPACE (산 지), unlike the connective -는지 ('whether', written attached: 샀는지); confusing them changes the meaning. Also: don't say 산 지 얼마 안 했어요 — time passing uses 되다, not 하다. And it must be the past adnominal 산 (not 사는 지, present), because the buying is complete.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 산지 (no space) or confusing it with -는지.
The elapsed-time 지 is a separate bound noun, spaced: 산 지. The connective -는지 ('whether') is different: 샀는지 몰라요 means 'I don't know whether I bought it'.
Saying 산 지 얼마 안 했어요.
Time passing uses 되다, not 하다: 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요 ('not long has passed'). 안 했어요 is wrong here.
Using the wrong tense: 사는 지 얼마 안 됐어요.
The purchase is finished, so use the past adnominal 산: 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요, not 사는 지.

structuredNuance.t: 산 (past adnominal of 사다) + 지 (elapsed-time noun) + 얼마 안 됐어요 ('not much time has become') → 'not long has passed since I bought it'. The -ㄴ 지 되다 construction is the standard 'it's been X time since' frame. Staff use this to assess whether you're in the return window.

Say this the moment you approach the counter — it's the first data point staff need. 해요체 (polite-neutral). If you know the exact date, name it (어제 산 거예요, 이틀 전에 샀어요) for a more convincing case. Pair with 영수증 여기 있어요 for maximum impact.
산 지 얼마 안 됐어요 (vague 'recently') vs 산 지 며칠 안 됐어요 ('only a few days') vs 어제 산 거예요 (exact day, most concrete). More precise is more persuasive when you're near the deadline.
-ㄴ 지 되다 with time: 산 지 일주일 됐어요 / 산 지 이틀 됐어요 / 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요. Stress: 산 지 일주일도 안 됐어요 ('not even a week'). The -도 adds 'not even', intensifying the recency claim.
두 함정: (1) 산지 (no space) vs 산 지 (space required — this 지 is a separate bound noun). 산지 merged is wrong. (2) 산 지 얼마 안 했어요 is wrong — elapsed-time uses 되다, not 하다: 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요.

entries.english: It was already like this when I got it
entries.shortExplanation: 받았을 때부터 이랬어요 is a practical expression meaning "It was already like this when I got it".
entries.explanation: 받았을 때부터 이랬어요 (badasseul ttaebuteo iraesseoyo) means "It was already like this when I got it". Say it as one set phrase — for example 받았을 때부터 이랬어요 ("It was like this from when I got it"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: It was like this from when I got it
usagePhrases.note: Polite; insisting the fault wasn't your doing

usagePhrases.en: It was like this when I got it
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend or casual seller

usagePhrases.en: It was like this from the start
usagePhrases.note: 처음부터 ('from the beginning'), a simpler version

usagePhrases.en: I'm not the one who did it
usagePhrases.note: Stating directly that it wasn't your fault

examples.ko: 이거 받았을 때부터 이랬어요.
examples.romanization: igeo badasseul ttaebuteo iraesseoyo.
examples.en: It was already like this when I got it.
examples.note: Defending against the implicit assumption you caused the damage — 받았을 때부터 pins the fault to before you ever touched it.

examples.ko: 저 안 떨어뜨렸어요. 받았을 때부터 이랬어요. 사진도 있어요.
examples.romanization: jeo an tteoreotteuryeosseoyo. badasseul ttaebuteo iraesseoyo. sajindo isseoyo.
examples.en: I didn't drop it — it was like this when I got it. I have photos too.
examples.note: 안 떨어뜨렸다 ('didn't drop it') heads off the most common counter-accusation; 사진도 있어요 offers the decisive evidence.

examples.ko: A: 이거 고객님이 사용하시다가 그러신 거 아닌가요? / B: 아니요, 박스 열자마자 봤는데 받았을 때부터 이랬어요.
examples.romanization: A: igeo gogaengnimi sayonghasidaga geureosin geo aningayo? / B: aniyo, bakseu yeoljamaja bwanneunde badasseul ttaebuteo iraesseoyo.
examples.en: A: Isn't this damage from how you used it? / B: No — I noticed it the moment I opened the box. It was like this when I got it.
examples.note: This is the most realistic dispute scenario: A's 사용하시다가 그러신 거 아닌가요? is the staff deflection; B counters with 박스 열자마자 ('the instant I opened the box'), the strongest possible claim of pre-existing fault.

entries.nuance: 받았을 때부터 이랬어요 is 받다 ('to receive/get') + -았을 때 ('at the time when [past action completed]') + 부터 ('from/since') + 이랬어요 (contracted past of 이렇다 'to be like this'). It means 'it was already like this from the very moment I received it'. This is the line you use when staff suspect you caused the damage and you need to insist the fault is pre-existing (not 사용자 과실, 'user's fault'). Proving it's pre-existing is what secures a free refund or exchange, as opposed to a repair cost being charged to you. 이랬어요 is the contracted spoken past of 이렇다 (이러했어요 → 이랬어요); attempting 이렇었어요 is wrong. The dividing line from 처음부터 이랬어요 ('it was like this from the beginning') is specificity: 받았을 때부터 pins it to the exact moment of receipt — especially powerful for online orders where there's a delivery record — while 처음부터 is a looser 'from the start'. The English-speaker error is tense mismatch: 받을 때 이래요 (present tense on both verbs) misses that both the receiving and the state are past. Another pitfall is the confrontational route of saying 제 잘못 아니에요 ('it's not my fault') — stating facts (받았을 때부터 이랬어요) is calmer, harder to argue with, and more persuasive.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 받을 때 이래요 (present tense).
Both the receiving and the condition are in the past: 받았을 때 ('when I received it') + 이랬어요 ('was like this'). Present tense misses that it was already faulty.
Trying to say 이랬어요 as 이렇었어요.
이렇다 contracts in the past to 이랬어요 (from 이러했어요), not 이렇었어요. Use 이랬어요.
Leading with 제 잘못 아니에요 ('it's not my fault').
That's confrontational. Stating the fact — 받았을 때부터 이랬어요 — makes the same point more calmly and is harder to argue with, especially with 사진 (photos).

structuredNuance.t: 받았을 때 ('at the time I received it') + 부터 ('from/since') + 이랬어요 ('was like this'). 'From the very moment I got it, it was in this state.' 부터 anchors the fault before you, ruling out user damage — that's the legal/practical force of this phrase.

Used when staff challenge whether you caused the damage. 해요체 (polite-neutral). Point at the defect as you speak. Strengthen with 사진도 있어요 (unboxing photos) or 박스 열자마자 봤어요 ('I saw it the moment I opened the box'). Never drop to 반말 with staff, even under frustration.

받았을 때부터 이랬어요 (pinned to moment of receipt — strong for online delivery) vs 처음부터 이랬어요 ('from the beginning' — vaguer, works for any purchase) vs 제가 그런 거 아니에요 ('I didn't do it' — direct but confrontational). Factual > accusatory.

이랬어요 (contracted form, natural) — don't say 이렇었어요. Add evidence: 박스 열자마자 이랬어요 / 사진 찍어 뒀어요 ('I took photos'). For online orders: 배송받자마자 확인했는데 이랬어요 ('I checked as soon as it arrived and it was like this').

두 함정: (1) Tense — both the receiving and the state are past: 받았을 때 + 이랬어요, NOT 받을 때 이래요 (present). (2) 이랬어요 is the correct contracted past; 이렇었어요 is wrong. Also: 제 잘못 아니에요 is confrontational — stating facts is more persuasive.

entries.english: Please process the refund
entries.shortExplanation: 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please process the refund".
entries.explanation: "Please process the refund" — that is 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 (hwanbul cheori jom hae juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 ("Please process the refund"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking staff to carry out the refund
반말, to a friend or casual seller

usagePhrases.en: Could you process the refund, please?
usagePhrases.note: More polite/formal with -주시겠어요

usagePhrases.en: I'd appreciate it if you'd process the refund
usagePhrases.note: Very polite/formal, useful in writing or to a manager

examples.ko: 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: hwanbul cheori jom hae juseyo.
examples.en: Please process the refund.
examples.note: Once the reason is accepted and the details are confirmed — this is the final execution step, asking them to push it through.

examples.ko: 확인되셨으면 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: hwagindoesyeosseumyeon hwanbul cheori jom hae juseyo.
examples.en: If you've confirmed everything, please process the refund.
examples.note: 확인되셨으면 ('if/once you've checked') acknowledges the staff's verification step and moves the conversation forward.

examples.ko: A: 네, 환불 가능하세요. 어떻게 해 드릴까요? / B: 카드 취소로 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: ne, hwanbul ganeunghaseyo. eotteoke hae deurilkkayo? / B: kadeu chwisoro hwanbul cheori jom hae juseyo.
examples.en: A: Yes, a refund is possible. How would you like to proceed? / B: Please process it as a card cancellation.
examples.note: B specifies 카드 취소 (card cancellation) — the correct channel for card purchases — ensuring the staff process it to the right account.

entries.nuance: 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 is 환불 ('refund') + 처리 ('processing/handling', Sino-Korean 處理) + 좀 (softener) + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'). Adding 처리 makes it about completing the administrative action — running the card cancellation, logging the return in the system — rather than just the concept of a refund. This is the natural register at a service desk where the refund is a procedure. The 좀 cushions the request and is almost always present in spoken Korean requests. The dividing line from bare 환불해 주세요 is stage: 환불해 주세요 works at any point ('please refund me'), while 환불 처리를 해 주세요 specifically says 'please execute the refund now' — you use it once the reason is accepted. 처리 is productive and transfers: 교환 처리 (process the exchange), 취소 처리 (process the cancellation), A/S 처리 (handle after-sales service). The particle: it's 환불 처리(를) 해 주세요 — 처리 is the object of 하다 — not 환불 처리가 해 주세요. The English-speaker error is treating 처리 as optional formality and either over-formalizing in a tiny shop (where 환불해 주세요 is warmer) or being too casual at a department-store counter (where 환불 처리 부탁드립니다 fits better). Always state the refund method (카드 취소 / 현금).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 환불 처리가 해 주세요.
처리 is the object of 하다, so it takes 를 (often dropped), not 가: 환불 처리(를) 해 주세요.
Over-formalizing in a tiny shop.
At a small market stall, 환불 처리 부탁드립니다 can sound stiff. A warm 환불해 주세요 fits better; save 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 for service desks and counters.
Not stating the refund method.
Refunds go back by the original method (카드 결제 → 카드 취소). Say 카드 취소로 / 현금으로 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 so it's done correctly.

structuredNuance.t: 환불 + 처리(處理, 'processing/handling') + 좀 (softener) + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'). The addition of 처리 shifts the request from the concept of a refund to the execution of a procedure. Use it once everything is agreed — this is the 'now do it' step.

At a service desk or customer center once the refund eligibility is confirmed. 해요체 (polite-neutral). For a tiny market stall, 환불해 주세요 is warmer. For a department-store service desk or writing to customer service: 환불 처리 부탁드립니다 / 환불 처리해 주시면 감사하겠습니다.

환불 처리 해 주세요 (execute the refund now, procedural) vs 환불해 주세요 (general request, any stage). 처리 is productive: 교환 처리 (exchange), 취소 처리 (cancellation), 반품 처리 (return). Mention method: 카드 취소로 처리해 주세요 / 현금으로 처리해 주세요.
환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 → 환불 처리 좀 해 주시겠어요? → 환불 처리 부탁드려요 → 환불 처리해 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (most formal/written). Add method: 카드 취소로 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요.
