두 함정: (1) 환불 처리가 해 주세요 is wrong — 처리 is the object: 환불 처리(를) 해 주세요. (2) Over-formalizing: in a casual market 처리 sounds stiff; save it for service desks. Also: always state the refund method (카드 취소 / 현금) so it's processed correctly.

entries.english: So you're saying this can't be refunded?
entries.shortExplanation: 이거 환불이 안 된다고요? is a practical expression meaning "So you're saying this can't be refunded?".
entries.explanation: 이거 환불이 안 된다고요? (igeo hwanburi an doendagoyo?) = "So you're saying this can't be refunded?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 이거 환불이 안 된다고요? ("So this can't be refunded?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; pushing back / confirming a refusal
반말, to a friend or casual seller

usagePhrases.en: Do you mean it can't be refunded?
usagePhrases.note: Very polite, honorific 말씀 + 이세요
Asking directly for the reason

examples.ko: 네? 이거 환불이 안 된다고요?
examples.romanization: ne? igeo hwanburi an doendagoyo?
examples.en: Sorry? This can't be refunded?
examples.note: 네? (rising intonation: 'sorry?') + the echo signals genuine surprise; it politely forces the staff to re-explain rather than simply accepting the refusal.

examples.ko: 불량인데도 환불이 안 된다고요?
examples.romanization: bullyangindedo hwanburi an doendagoyo?
examples.en: Even though it's defective, it can't be refunded?
examples.note: 불량인데도 ('even though it's defective') names the concrete reason why the refusal seems unreasonable; this kind of pushback often prompts a manager referral.

examples.ko: A: 세일 상품은 환불이 안 됩니다. / B: 그럼 교환은 되는데 환불이 안 된다고요?
examples.romanization: A: seil sangpumeun hwanburi an doemnida. / B: geureom gyohwaneun doeneunde hwanburi an doendagoyo?
examples.en: A: Sale items cannot be refunded. / B: So an exchange is fine but no refund?
examples.note: B doesn't argue with the policy directly but clarifies the exact scope of the refusal — this is a smart pivot that often reveals an exchange option you hadn't been offered.

entries.nuance: 이거 환불이 안 된다고요? is 이거 ('this') + 환불이 안 되다 ('a refund isn't possible') + -다고요? (a quotative ending that echoes back the other person's statement with rising intonation). The -다고요? is the core of this phrase: it repeats what was just said to confirm or gently challenge it — 'you're telling me…?' — and is the polite, non-aggressive way to push back when a store refuses. The rising intonation signals surprise/disbelief without accusation, which often prompts staff to re-explain or escalate to a manager. The dividing line from 왜 안 돼요? ('why not?') is tone: 안 된다고요? mirrors their own words and sounds like incredulous confirmation rather than a demand, keeping the exchange civil while making clear you're not satisfied. To go fully polite (e.g. to a manager), use 환불이 안 된다는 말씀이세요? ('are you saying it can't be refunded?', with honorific 말씀). The English-speaker error is dropping the quotative and saying 환불 안 돼요? again — that just re-asks the yes/no question and loses the 'wait, are you telling me that…' pushback force. The final 요 is non-negotiable: 환불 안 된다고? without 요 is 반말 and sounds confrontational or rude to staff. Particle: 환불이 안 돼요 (subject 이/가), never 환불을.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Re-asking 환불 안 돼요? instead of echoing.
That just repeats the plain question. To push back / confirm a refusal, use the quotative echo: 환불이 안 된다고요? ('you're saying it can't be refunded?').
Dropping the 요: 환불 안 된다고?.
Without the final 요, -다고 is 반말 and sounds curt or confrontational to staff. Keep it polite: 환불이 안 된다고요?.
Using 환불을 안 돼요.
되다 takes the subject particle: 환불이 안 돼요 / 환불이 안 된다고요?. 환불을 is wrong with 되다.

structuredNuance.t: 이거 + 환불이 안 된다 ('a refund is not possible') + -고요? (quotative echo, rising). Literally: 'you're saying a refund is not possible for this?' The -다고요? is a polite echo-back frame, not a new question — it signals surprise and invites re-explanation or escalation.

When staff refuse a refund and you want to push back without escalating. 해요체 (polite-neutral) — the 요 is essential. Upgrade to 환불이 안 된다는 말씀이세요? (honorific 말씀) when addressing a manager. Never drop to 반말 with staff even under frustration.

-다고요? (echo-back, polite disbelief/confirmation) vs 왜 안 돼요? (direct demand for reason) vs 환불이 안 된다는 말씀이세요? (fully honorific version). -다고요? is the most tactically useful: it keeps tone calm while clearly not accepting the refusal.
-다고요? is versatile: 교환도 안 된다고요? / 영수증 있어도 안 된다고요?. Escalate: 환불이 안 된다는 말씀이세요? → 담당자분을 불러 주시겠어요? ('could you get the person in charge?'). Always include 요 with staff.

두 함정: (1) Re-asking 환불 안 돼요? just restates the question — it loses the 'wait, are you telling me that…' pushback force of -다고요?. (2) Dropping 요: 환불 안 된다고? (no 요) is 반말 and rude to staff. Always keep 요.

entries.english: You're really good at this!
entries.shortExplanation: 잘하시네요 is a practical expression meaning "You're really good at this!".
entries.explanation: "You're really good at this!" — that is 잘하시네요 (jalhasineyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 잘하시네요 ("you're good at it (admiring)"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: honorific -시-, to someone you respect
banmal, to a friend
-는데요 adds a surprised, leaning-in tone
진짜 boosts the admiration

examples.ko: A: (그림을 보여주며) / B: 와, 잘하시네요!
examples.romanization: A: (geurimeul boyeojumyeo) / B: wa, jalhasineyo!
examples.en: A: (showing a painting) / B: Wow, you're really talented!
examples.note: the bare admiring reaction to a skill on display right now

examples.ko: 요리 한 입 먹고 "어머, 요리 잘하시네요" 했어요.
examples.romanization: yori han im meokgo "eomeo, yori jalhasineyo" haesseoyo.
examples.en: After one bite I said, 'Oh my, you're a wonderful cook.'
examples.note: complimenting a host's cooking mid-experience — the -시- signals upward respect

examples.ko: 한국어로 인사하니까 직원분이 "한국말 진짜 잘하시네요" 하고 놀랐어요.
examples.romanization: hangugeoro insahanikka jigwonbuni "hangungmal jinjja jalhasineyo" hago nollasseoyo.
examples.en: When I greeted in Korean the staff was surprised: 'Your Korean is really good.'
examples.note: the go-to compliment Koreans give learners; respond modestly with 아니에요, 아직 멀었어요 — not 감사합니다 alone

entries.nuance: 잘하시네요 is the present-tense 'you're good at this' said WHILE observing or experiencing someone's skill — 잘하다 'to be good at doing' + honorific -시- + the noticing ending -네요 ('oh, I notice'). Unlike 잘했어요, which judges a finished result, 잘하시네요 praises ABILITY in the moment. Because -시- and -네요 are baked in, it safely aims upward or sideways — toward an elder, a stranger, a host. The English-speaker pitfall is double: dropping the -시- (so 잘하네 alone to an elder is too casual), and treating the ubiquitous 한국말 잘하시네요 as a literal assessment of fluency — it is really a warm social icebreaker, and agreeing proudly with 네, 잘해요 sounds arrogant; the right reply is modest deflection such as 아니에요, 아직 멀었어요. Register: 잘하네 (banmal) ↔ 잘하네요 (polite) ↔ 잘하시네요 (honorific).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Answering 한국말 잘하시네요 with 네, 감사합니다 and a proud face — Korean modesty expects 아니에요 / 아직 멀었어요; agreeing sounds boastful.
Saying 잘하네 to someone older — the bare -네 is banmal; toward a senior you need the honorific 잘하시네요.
Using 잘했어요 when you mean present skill — 잘했어요 judges a finished act, while admiring live ability is 잘하시네요.

structuredNuance.t: 잘하다 = 'to do well' + -시- (honorific) + -네요 ('I notice'). Literally 'I notice you do it well (respectfully).' In use, it is a present-tense admiration of live skill — 'you're really good at this' — aimed at what you are watching or tasting right now.

Say it while watching or experiencing a skill: a host's cooking, a colleague's calligraphy, a learner's pronunciation. With -시- it is safe toward elders and strangers. To a close friend, trim to 잘하네. The famous 한국말 잘하시네요 to a foreign speaker is social warmth, not a grammar report.

The dividing line from 잘했어요: 잘했어요 judges a past completed act ('you did well'), while 잘하시네요 notices present ability ('you're good at this'). Against 대단하시네요: 잘하시네요 credits a specific skill; 대단하시네요 expresses broad awe at a person's achievement or character.
Register: 잘하네 (banmal) → 잘하네요 (polite) → 잘하시네요 (honorific). Intensify with 진짜/정말: 진짜 잘하시네요. The variant -는데요 ending (잘하시는데요) adds a surprised, leaning-in admiration.

Two traps: (1) using 잘하네 to an elder (too casual — add -시-); (2) responding to 한국말 잘하시네요 with 네, 감사합니다 and a proud nod — Korean modesty convention expects 아니에요 or 아직 멀었어요; accepting the compliment openly reads as boastful.

entries.english: It's pretty / You're lovely.
entries.shortExplanation: 예뻐요 is a practical expression meaning "It's pretty / You're lovely.".
entries.explanation: 예뻐요 (yeppeoyo) means "It's pretty / You're lovely.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 예뻐요 ("it's pretty / you're pretty"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: polite -요, to a peer or younger
banmal, to a close friend
honorific -으시-, to an older woman
exclamatory -다, admiring something out loud

examples.ko: A: (새 옷 입고) 어때요? / B: 우와, 너무 예뻐요!
examples.romanization: A: (sae ot ipgo) eottaeyo? / B: uwa, neomu yeppeoyo!
examples.en: A: (in new clothes) How does it look? / B: Wow, it's so pretty!
examples.note: the bare compliment on someone's outfit or appearance

examples.ko: 꽃다발 받고 "꽃이 너무 예쁘다" 하면서 좋아했어요.
examples.romanization: kkotdabal batgo "kkochi neomu yeppeuda" hamyeonseo joahaesseoyo.
examples.en: Getting the bouquet I said happily, 'The flowers are so pretty.'
examples.note: everyday: 예쁘다 covers objects — flowers, rooms, handwriting — not just people

examples.ko: 아기 사진 보고 "어머, 정말 예뻐요" 했더니 엄마가 좋아했어요.
examples.romanization: agi sajin bogo "eomeo, jeongmal yeppeoyo" haetdeoni eommaga joahaesseoyo.
examples.en: After seeing the baby photo I said, 'Oh, so adorable,' and the mom was delighted.
examples.note: real situation: 예쁘다 for cute babies is a safe, warm compliment to a parent — much safer than complimenting a stranger's own face

entries.nuance: 예뻐요 means 'pretty / lovely / adorable' and applies to people, clothes, flowers, babies, handwriting — anything visually pleasing or cute. The base 예쁘다 is a 으-irregular: drop 으 and add 어요 → 예뻐요 (never 예쁘어요). The three-way split learners miss: 예쁘다 = pretty/lovely, 귀엽다 = cutely endearing (puppies, a giggling toddler), 멋있다 = cool/impressive — a strong, handsome man is 멋있어요, not 예뻐요, as the latter implies a more feminine, delicate beauty. The English-speaker pitfall is the conjugation (writing 예쁘어요) and aiming compliments at strangers: in Korean, commenting on a stranger's face unprompted can feel forward, so 예뻐요 lands most warmly on friends, children, and objects; complimenting an outfit is less invasive than a face. Register: 예뻐 (banmal) ↔ 예뻐요 (polite) ↔ 예쁘세요 (honorific).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Conjugating it 예쁘어요 — 예쁘다 is a 으-irregular, so 으 drops before 어요: the correct form is 예뻐요.
Calling a cool, manly guy 예뻐요 — it implies pretty/feminine; use 멋있어요 for cool or handsome men.
Complimenting a stranger's face with 예뻐요 out of nowhere — it can feel forward; aim it at friends, kids, or objects, or compliment an outfit instead.

structuredNuance.t: 예쁘다 literally means 'pretty / beautiful (in a gentle, lovely way).' In use, it covers any visually pleasing thing: a person's face, a dress, a flower arrangement, neat handwriting. The prettiness it describes leans feminine and delicate rather than bold or impressive.

Freely used for objects, clothes, flowers, and children. For people, it is warmest between friends or toward younger people. Complimenting a stranger's face directly can feel forward; complimenting their outfit (그 옷 예뻐요) is less intrusive. For elders, soften with 예쁘세요.

Three-way split: 예쁘다 (pretty/lovely, people/things), 귀엽다 (cute/endearing, puppies, toddlers, something charming), 멋있다 (cool/impressive, bold actions, stylish men). A strong man is 멋있어요, not 예뻐요; a puppy is 귀여워요, not 예뻐요 — though 예쁘다 can stretch to puppies colloquially.
Irregular conjugation: 예쁘다 → 예뻐요 (not 예쁘어요), 예뻐, 예쁘세요. Intensify with 너무/진짜/정말: 너무 예뻐요, 진짜 예뻐. Exclamatory: 진짜 예쁘다 (said to yourself).

Two traps: (1) conjugating it 예쁘어요 — the 으-irregular drops 으, giving 예뻐요; (2) complimenting a stranger's face out of nowhere — it can feel forward; aim 예뻐요 at friends, kids, or objects, or comment on an outfit rather than physical features.

entries.english: You're amazing / That's really impressive.
entries.shortExplanation: 대단하세요 is a practical expression meaning "You're amazing / That's really impressive.".
entries.explanation: "You're amazing / That's really impressive." — that is 대단하세요 (daedanhaseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 대단하세요 ("you're amazing (respectful)"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: honorific -세요, to someone you admire
banmal, to a friend
-시네요 adds fresh admiration upon noticing
정말 deepens the awe

examples.ko: A: 마라톤 완주했어요! / B: 와, 대단하세요!
examples.romanization: A: maraton wanjuhaesseoyo! / B: wa, daedanhaseyo!
examples.en: A: I finished the marathon! / B: Wow, that's amazing!
examples.note: the bare awe-reaction to an impressive achievement

examples.ko: 혼자 아이 셋 키운다는 말에 "진짜 대단하세요" 하고 감탄했어요.
examples.romanization: honja ai set kiundaneun mare "jinjja daedanhaseyo" hago gamtanhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Hearing she raises three kids alone I said, 'You're truly remarkable.'
examples.note: everyday: admiring someone's endurance or effort over a long period

examples.ko: 사장님이 맨손으로 회사를 일으킨 얘기를 듣고 "정말 대단하십니다" 했어요.
examples.romanization: sajangnimi maensoneuro hoesareul ireukin yaegireul deutgo "jeongmal daedanhasimnida" haesseoyo.
examples.en: Hearing the CEO built the company from nothing I said, 'That is truly remarkable, sir.'
examples.note: real situation: the formal -십니다 form for a respected senior; 대단하다 fits whole-life achievements

entries.nuance: 대단하세요 expresses genuine AWE at someone's achievement, effort, or character — 대단하다 'to be remarkable' + honorific -세요. It is heartfelt admiration for something impressively hard ('I could never do that'), which is why its default form already points upward with -세요. The dividing line from 잘하시네요 is scale: 잘하시네요 praises a specific SKILL ('you're good at this'), while 대단하세요 expresses being overwhelmed by the WHOLE accomplishment or person ('that's incredible'). The English-speaker pitfall is the bare 대단해 toward an elder — natural between friends, but to a senior it sounds flippant; use 대단하세요 or formal 대단하십니다. A subtler trap: 대단하다 can flip to sarcasm with a flat tone ('oh, wonderful...'), so deliver it with clear warmth. Register: 대단해 (banmal) ↔ 대단해요 (polite) ↔ 대단하세요 / 대단하십니다 (honorific/formal).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 대단해 to an elder or boss — the bare banmal can sound flippant; admire a senior with 대단하세요 or 대단하십니다.
Using 대단하세요 for a minor everyday compliment — it carries real awe, so reserve it for genuinely impressive feats, not 'nice shoes'.
Delivering it flatly — 대단하다 can read as sarcasm ('oh, wonderful'); say it with clear warmth so it lands as praise.

structuredNuance.t: 대단하다 literally means 'to be great/remarkable' (not from a 한자 compound most learners recognize). In use, it conveys genuine awe — 'I'm blown away by what you did or who you are.' The honorific -세요 is the default because the expression naturally points at someone admirable.

Use it for genuinely impressive feats — raising three children alone, building a company from scratch, finishing a marathon at 70. It aims naturally upward or sideways. Toward an elder or boss use 대단하세요 or 대단하십니다. The banmal 대단해 is warm between friends but sounds flippant to a senior.

대단하세요 vs 잘하시네요: 잘하시네요 praises a skill ('you're good at this'), while 대단하세요 expresses awe at a whole accomplishment ('incredible'). Against 존경스러워요 ('I respect/admire you'): 존경스럽다 is more formal reverence toward a person's overall stature; 대단하다 reacts to a specific feat.
Register: 대단해 (banmal) → 대단해요 (polite) → 대단하세요 (honorific) → 대단하십니다 (formal). Noticing variant: 대단하시네요. Intensified: 정말/진짜 대단하세요.

Two traps: (1) saying bare 대단해 to an elder — use 대단하세요 or 대단하십니다; (2) delivering it flatly — 대단하다 can read as sarcasm ('oh, how wonderful...'), so lean into warm delivery. Also: reserve it for genuinely impressive things; using it for minor tasks (nice soup!) dilutes it.

entries.english: Go for it! / You can do it! / Good luck!
entries.shortExplanation: 화이팅 is a practical expression meaning "Go for it! / You can do it! / Good luck!".
entries.explanation: 화이팅 (hwaiting) = "Go for it! / You can do it! / Good luck!". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 화이팅 ("go for it / you got this"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: go for it / you got this
usagePhrases.note: casual cheer, any close relationship
the officially correct Korean spelling, same word and meaning
polite -하세요 toward someone you respect
rallying a group together before a shared challenge

examples.ko: A: 나 이제 면접 보러 가! / B: 화이팅!
examples.romanization: A: na ije myeonjeop boreo ga! / B: hwaiting!
examples.en: A: I'm off to my interview! / B: Go get 'em!
examples.note: the bare one-word cheer just before a challenge — often with a raised fist gesture

examples.ko: 시험 앞둔 친구한테 "내일 시험 화이팅!" 하고 메시지 보냈어요.
examples.romanization: siheom apdun chinguhante "naeil siheom hwaiting!" hago mesiji bonaesseoyo.
examples.en: I texted my friend, 'Good luck on tomorrow's exam!'
examples.note: everyday: the standard pre-exam text; you can add 너 할 수 있어 for extra encouragement

examples.ko: 마라톤 나가는 선배께 "선배님, 화이팅 하세요!" 하고 응원했어요.
examples.romanization: maraton naganeun seonbaekke "seonbaenim, hwaiting haseyo!" hago eungwonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Since my senior was running a marathon I cheered, 'Go for it, sunbae!'
examples.note: real situation: add 하세요 to make the cheer politely address someone older — bare 화이팅 alone to a much older person is too light

entries.nuance: 화이팅 (borrowed from English 'fighting') is Korea's universal pre-effort cheer — 'go for it, you've got this, I believe in you' — shouted before exams, interviews, games, or any challenge, often with a raised fist. By itself it is casual and friendly; toward someone you respect, attach a verb: 화이팅 하세요. The dividing line is against 힘내세요: 화이팅 pumps up ENERGY before an effort that has not started yet ('push!'), while 힘내세요 comforts someone who is already in the middle of a struggle ('hang in there'). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: never read it as 'let's fight' — it was borrowed purely as encouragement; and the bare 화이팅 in a formal or very hierarchical setting feels too light, so use 화이팅 하세요 or 잘하시길 바랍니다. Spelling note: 파이팅 is the officially standardized form, but 화이팅 is what most Koreans actually write.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Reading 화이팅 as 'let's fight / I'll fight you' — it is borrowed to mean encouragement ('go for it'), never literal fighting.
Shouting bare 화이팅 at a senior in a formal setting — soften it to 화이팅 하세요 or 잘하시길 바랍니다.
Assuming 파이팅 is wrong — it is actually the standardized spelling; both are accepted, with 화이팅 more common in casual writing.

structuredNuance.t: 화이팅 looks like the English word 'fighting' but it was borrowed purely as an encouragement cheer — 'go for it / push hard / I believe in you.' There is no aggression implied. Think of it as Korea's 'allez' or 'vamos': pure forward energy.

Ideal before any challenge: an exam, a job interview, a first day at work, a sports match, a presentation. Between friends and peers, bare 화이팅 is perfect. To a senior or in a formal setting, attach a verb: 화이팅 하세요. There is no honorific form of the cheer-noun itself — politeness rides on the attached verb.

화이팅 vs 힘내세요: 화이팅 fires before the effort starts ('go!'), while 힘내세요 comforts someone already struggling ('hang in there'). Against 잘될 거예요: that reassures about the outcome ('it'll be fine'), while 화이팅 charges up the person's energy.

Both spellings are accepted: 화이팅 (common casual writing) and 파이팅 (official standard). Polite form: 화이팅 하세요. Group cheer: 우리 화이팅! Combo: 화이팅, 잘할 수 있어! Written online as 핫팅 or 팅 (very informal shorthand).

Two traps: (1) reading 화이팅 as 'let's fight' or 'I'll fight you' — it is borrowed encouragement, not aggression; (2) shouting bare 화이팅 at a much older person or in a formal setting — it feels too light; use 화이팅 하세요 or 잘하시길 바랍니다 instead.

entries.english: It'll work out / Things will be fine.
entries.shortExplanation: 잘될 거예요 is a practical expression meaning "It'll work out / Things will be fine.".
entries.explanation: "It'll work out / Things will be fine." — that is 잘될 거예요 (jaldoel geoyeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 잘될 거예요 ("it'll work out fine"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: polite -요, reassuring a peer or younger
banmal, to a close friend
honorific -시-, reassuring an elder
다 'all' makes the comfort broader and warmer

examples.ko: A: 합격할 수 있을까요? / B: 물론이죠, 잘될 거예요.
examples.romanization: A: hapgyeokal su isseulkkayo? / B: mullonijyo, jaldoel geoyeyo.
examples.en: A: Do you think I'll pass? / B: Of course — it'll work out.
examples.note: the bare reassurance about an uncertain outcome — 물론이죠 adds confidence

examples.ko: 걱정하는 친구한테 "너무 걱정 마, 다 잘될 거야" 했어요.
examples.romanization: geokjeonghaneun chinguhante "neomu geokjeong ma, da jaldoel geoya" haesseoyo.
examples.en: To my worried friend I said, 'Don't worry too much, everything will work out.'
examples.note: everyday: pairs naturally with 너무 걱정 마 — one phrase addresses the worry, the other addresses the outcome

examples.ko: 수술을 앞두신 분께 "분명히 잘되실 거예요. 제가 응원할게요" 하고 위로했어요.
examples.romanization: susureul apdusin bunkke "bunmyeonghi jaldoesil geoyeyo. jega eungwonhalgeyo" hago wirohaesseoyo.
examples.en: To someone facing surgery I said, 'It will surely go well. I'm rooting for you.'
examples.note: real situation: honorific 잘되실 거예요 for a senior + 응원할게요 for deeper comfort

entries.nuance: 잘될 거예요 ('it will go well', 잘되다 'to turn out well' + future -ㄹ 거예요) reassures an anxious person about a FUTURE OUTCOME — a test result, a job application, a surgery, a new relationship. It calms worry about how things will turn out, which is its clear dividing line from 힘내세요 (strength for the present struggle) and 화이팅 (energy for the effort itself). The three smooth stacking: 너무 걱정 마세요 → 잘될 거예요 → 응원할게요. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb choice: 잘되다 is intransitive 'turn out well', so 잘될 거예요 ≠ 잘할 거예요 ('will perform well' — active doer). Also the spelling: it is 거예요, never 꺼에요 or 거에요. To an elder, add honorific -시-: 잘되실 거예요. Register: 잘될 거야 (banmal) ↔ 잘될 거예요 (polite) ↔ 잘되실 거예요 (honorific).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 잘할 거예요 to comfort someone — that means 'will perform well' (active doer); the reassurance about how things turn out is 잘될 거예요 (intransitive).
Spelling the ending 잘될 꺼에요 / 거에요 — the standard future form is 거예요: 잘될 거예요.
Using bare 잘될 거야 to an elder — add the honorific -시-: 잘되실 거예요.

structuredNuance.t: 잘되다 = 'to turn out well' (intransitive — things go well by themselves). 잘될 거예요 = 'it will turn out well.' In use, it is the 'don't worry, it'll be fine' reassurance about an outcome the listener is anxious about — not a promise about their performance, but about how things will unfold.

Use it when someone is anxious about a result or outcome: an exam result, a job interview, a medical procedure, starting over. It looks FORWARD to how things will resolve. To a peer or younger person: 잘될 거예요. To an elder: 잘되실 거예요 (with honorific -시-). Banmal to close friends: 잘될 거야.

잘될 거예요 (outcome: 'it'll turn out fine') vs 힘내세요 (strength for the current struggle: 'hang in there') vs 화이팅 (energy pump-up for the effort: 'go for it'). These three layer beautifully: 힘내세요, 화이팅, 잘될 거예요 — covering the present, the push, and the outcome.
Register: 잘될 거야 (banmal) → 잘될 거예요 (polite) → 잘되실 거예요 (honorific). Warmer: 다 잘될 거예요, 분명히 잘될 거예요. Stacks with: 너무 걱정 마세요, 잘될 거예요.

Two traps: (1) confusing 잘될 거예요 (things will turn out well — intransitive) with 잘할 거예요 (you/I will perform well — active doer); the verbs are different; (2) misspelling the future as 꺼에요 or 거에요 — the standard written form is 거예요: 잘될 거예요.

entries.english: Don't worry too much.
entries.shortExplanation: 너무 걱정 마세요 is a practical expression meaning "Don't worry too much.".
entries.explanation: 너무 걱정 마세요 (neomu geokjeong maseyo) = "Don't worry too much.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 너무 걱정 마세요 ("don't worry too much"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: polite -세요, to a peer or someone you respect
banmal, to a close friend
the uncontracted form — identical meaning, slightly softer and more careful
reassurance plus a concrete offer — far more comforting than the phrase alone

examples.ko: A: 일이 잘못될까 봐 불안해요 / B: 너무 걱정 마세요, 잘될 거예요.
examples.romanization: A: iri jalmotdoelkka bwa buranhaeyo / B: neomu geokjeong maseyo, jaldoel geoyeyo.
examples.en: A: I'm anxious it'll go wrong / B: Don't worry too much — it'll work out.
examples.note: the bare reassurance; stacking with 잘될 거예요 is the natural complete comfort phrase

examples.ko: 시험 걱정하는 동생에게 "너무 걱정 마, 충분히 준비했잖아" 했어요.
examples.romanization: siheom geokjeonghaneun dongsaengege "neomu geokjeong ma, chungbunhi junbihaetjana" haesseoyo.
examples.en: To my anxious younger sibling I said, 'Don't worry — you've prepared enough, haven't you?'
examples.note: everyday: comfort in banmal, grounded with a reminder of their effort

examples.ko: 환자 보호자분께 "너무 걱정 마세요. 최선을 다하겠습니다" 하고 안심시켰어요.
examples.romanization: hwanja bohojabunkke "neomu geokjeong maseyo. choeseoneul dahagetseumnida" hago ansimsikyeosseoyo.
examples.en: To the patient's guardian I said, 'Please don't worry. We will do our very best,' as reassurance.
examples.note: real situation: professional reassurance, softened with 너무, followed by a commitment — the formula in medical or care settings

entries.nuance: 너무 걱정 마세요 means 'don't worry too much' — 너무 'too (much)' + 걱정 'worry' + 마세요 'please don't.' The 너무 is essential: without it, bare 걱정 마세요 is correct but can sound slightly blunt ('stop worrying'), while 너무 softens it to 'don't worry SO much', acknowledging the concern is understandable. Grammatically, 마세요 is the polite prohibitive of 말다, not 안 + verb; the common English-learner error 안 걱정하세요 is wrong. The dividing line from 잘될 거예요 is direction: 걱정 마세요 addresses the WORRY itself ('ease up on the fretting'), while 잘될 거예요 addresses the OUTCOME ('it'll be fine') — they pair beautifully and almost always appear together. Register: 걱정 마 (banmal) ↔ 걱정 마세요 (polite) ↔ 걱정 마십시오 (formal).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Forming the negative as 안 걱정하세요 — a prohibition uses 말다: 걱정하지 마세요 / 걱정 마세요, never 안 + verb here.
Saying bare 걱정 마 to an elder or boss — use 걱정 마세요 or 걱정 마십시오.
Confusing 걱정 마세요 (address the worry) with 잘될 거예요 (address the outcome) — natural comfort uses both together.

structuredNuance.t: 너무 'too much' + 걱정 'worry' + 마세요 'please don't' = 'please don't worry too much.' The 너무 is a softener — it acknowledges the person's concern is understandable, it just asks them not to worry EXCESSIVELY. Without 너무, the phrase is fine but a touch more direct.

Use it when someone is clearly anxious about an outcome, situation, or decision. Polite -세요 works for peers and can be used toward seniors who are worried. Banmal 걱정 마 is warm for friends. In professional settings (medical, legal, service), 걱정 마세요 + a commitment (제가 도와드릴게요 / 최선을 다하겠습니다) is a complete, reassuring phrase.

걱정 마세요 (target: the worry — 'ease up') vs 잘될 거예요 (target: the outcome — 'it'll be fine'). Natural pair: 너무 걱정 마세요, 잘될 거예요. Against 괜찮아요 ('it's okay / don't worry'): 괜찮아요 is shorter and more all-purpose; 걱정 마세요 specifically addresses an anxious person's ongoing worry.
Prohibitive forms: 걱정 마 (banmal) → 걱정 마세요 (polite) → 걱정 마십시오 (formal). Full uncontracted: 걱정하지 마세요. With 너무: 너무 걱정 마세요. Softer still: 너무 걱정하지 않으셔도 돼요.

Two traps: (1) building the prohibition with 안: 안 걱정하세요 is wrong; use 말다 → 걱정하지 마세요 / 걱정 마세요; (2) using bare 걱정 마 with an elder or in a serious context — 걱정 마세요 is the right polite form, and for real formality, 걱정 마십시오.

entries.english: I'm proud (of you).
entries.shortExplanation: 자랑스러워요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm proud (of you).".
entries.explanation: 자랑스러워요 (jarangseureowoyo) means "I'm proud (of you).". Say it as one set phrase — for example 자랑스러워요 ("I'm proud of you"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: polite -요, to a peer or younger
banmal, to a close friend or child
격식 -습니다, a speech, award ceremony, or formal note
네가 identifies the person you're proud of — natural in banmal

examples.ko: A: 저 전국 1등 했어요! / B: 우와, 정말 자랑스러워요!
examples.romanization: A: jeo jeonguk 1deung haesseoyo! / B: uwa, jeongmal jarangseureowoyo!
examples.en: A: I came in first in the whole country! / B: Wow, I'm so proud of you!
examples.note: the bare expression of pride at a remarkable achievement

examples.ko: 졸업식 날 딸에게 "우리 딸, 진짜 자랑스러워" 했어요.
examples.romanization: joreopsing nal ttarege "uri ttal, jinjja jarangseureowo" haesseoyo.
examples.en: On graduation day I told my daughter, 'I'm so proud of you, my girl.'
examples.note: everyday: a parent's pride in banmal toward a child — the most natural direction for this expression

examples.ko: 후배가 큰 상을 받았을 때 "네가 우리 팀의 자랑이야. 정말 자랑스러워" 했어요.
examples.romanization: hubaega keun sangeul badasseul ttae "nega uri timui jarangiya. jeongmal jarangseureowo" haesseoyo.
examples.en: When the junior won a major award I said, 'You're our team's pride. I'm truly proud of you.'
examples.note: real situation: pairs with 자랑이야 ('you're our pride/glory') for a fuller compliment; senior → junior direction

entries.nuance: 자랑스러워요 ('to feel proud', from 자랑 'pride/boasting' + -스럽다 'to feel like') expresses pride in someone's achievement or in who they are. The DIRECTION rule is crucial and uniquely Korean: pride flows DOWNWARD or sideways — a parent to a child, a senior to a junior, or between peers. Telling a teacher, boss, or elder 자랑스러워요 sounds odd and presumptuous, as if you are positioned above them evaluating their worth; toward a respected senior, 존경스러워요 ('I admire/respect you') or 대단하세요 is far more natural. The dividing line: 자랑스럽다 (pride, looking down or across) vs 존경스럽다 (respect, looking up). The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this cultural gap — English 'I'm proud of you' is freely said to anyone, including a teacher, so learners aim 자랑스러워요 at their Korean tutor and it lands awkwardly. Note the ㅂ-irregular conjugation: 자랑스럽다 → 자랑스러워요. Register: 자랑스러워 (banmal) ↔ 자랑스러워요 (polite) ↔ 자랑스럽습니다 (formal).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 자랑스러워요 to a teacher, boss, or elder — pride implies a higher position; toward a senior use 존경스러워요 or 대단하세요.
Conjugating it 자랑스럽어요 — 자랑스럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular: 자랑스러워요.
Confusing 자랑스럽다 (proud of someone) with 자랑하다 (to boast/show off) — 자랑하지 마 means 'don't brag', a different sense of 자랑.

structuredNuance.t: 자랑 means 'something one boasts about with pride.' -스럽다 means 'to feel like, to be full of.' So 자랑스럽다 = 'feels like something to be proud of / makes me feel proud.' In practice, it says 'I'm proud of you' — the speaker's internal feeling of pride at someone else's achievement.

Crucially flows DOWNWARD or sideways — a parent to a child, a teacher to a student, a senior to a junior, or between close peers. Do NOT say it upward to a teacher or boss — it implies you are positioned above them. To an elder you admire, use 존경스러워요 or 대단하세요 instead.

자랑스럽다 (pride, pointing downward/sideways) vs 존경스럽다 (respect/admiration, pointing upward). Confusingly similar: 자랑스럽다 (I feel proud OF someone) vs 자랑하다 (to brag/show off — 자랑하지 마 = 'don't brag', a negative sense of 자랑).
ㅂ-irregular: 자랑스럽다 → 자랑스러워요 (not 자랑스럽어요). Register: 자랑스러워 (banmal) → 자랑스러워요 (polite) → 자랑스럽습니다 (formal). Intensify: 정말/진짜 자랑스러워요, 네가 자랑스러워.

The English-speaker pitfall is the direction rule — English 'I'm proud of you' is used freely toward anyone including a teacher or boss. In Korean, 자랑스러워요 upward at a senior sounds presumptuous ('I'm proud of you' implies you are grading them from above). Say 존경스러워요 or 대단하세요 instead.

entries.english: That looks nice / It's good to see.
entries.shortExplanation: 보기 좋아요 is a practical expression meaning "That looks nice / It's good to see.".
entries.explanation: "That looks nice / It's good to see." — that is 보기 좋아요 (bogi joayo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 보기 좋아요 ("it looks nice / good to see"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: it looks nice / good to see
usagePhrases.note: polite -요, to a peer or younger
banmal, to a close friend

usagePhrases.en: you look great / it's lovely to see (respectful)
usagePhrases.note: honorific -으시-, noticing tone, to an elder
-네요 adds a warm, observational noticing tone

examples.ko: A: (커플 사진을 보여주며) / B: 와, 두 분 정말 보기 좋아요.
examples.romanization: A: (keopeul sajineul boyeojumyeo) / B: wa, du bun jeongmal bogi joayo.
examples.en: A: (showing a couple photo) / B: Wow, you two really look great together.
examples.note: the warm approval of a wholesome scene — not just prettiness, but a good-to-witness sight

examples.ko: 살 빠진 친구한테 "얼굴도 좋아 보이고 보기 좋다" 했어요.
examples.romanization: sal ppajin chinguhante "eolguldo joa boigo bogi jota" haesseoyo.
examples.en: To my friend who lost weight I said, 'Your face looks well, and you look good.'
examples.note: everyday: 보기 좋다 approves a healthier, happier appearance — wholesome rather than merely pretty

examples.ko: 오랜만에 만난 두 분이 사이좋게 계셔서 "두 분 보기 좋으시네요" 했어요.
examples.romanization: oraenmane mannan du buni saijoke gyesyeoseo "du bun bogi joeusineyo" haesseoyo.
examples.en: Seeing the two of them getting along so warmly, I said, 'It's truly lovely to see you two together.'
examples.note: real situation: honorific 보기 좋으시네요 toward elders, expressing warm approval of their relationship or wellbeing

entries.nuance: 보기 좋아요 (보다 'to see' + -기 nominalizer + 좋다 'good' = 'good to look at') is the warm 'that looks nice / it's heartwarming to see' you say about a pleasing or wholesome sight — a happy couple, someone glowing with health, people getting along beautifully, a tidy home. It often carries APPROVAL of a wholesome scene rather than just visual prettiness, which is its dividing line from 예뻐요 (purely visual prettiness) and 멋있어요 (cool/impressive): 보기 좋다 = 'this is a beautiful thing to witness.' The English-speaker pitfall is the fixed structure: learners try 좋게 보여요 or 좋아 보기, but the correct nominalized form is 보기 좋다. Also, 보기 좋아요 ('nice to see') differs from 좋아 보여요 ('looks good / appears to be in good condition') — the word order is reversed and the meaning shifts. Register: 보기 좋아 (banmal) ↔ 보기 좋아요 (polite) ↔ 보기 좋으세요 (honorific).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Restructuring it as 좋게 보여요 or 좋아 보기 — the fixed expression is 보기 좋다: 보기 좋아요.
Mixing it up with 좋아 보여요 — 보기 좋아요 = 'nice to see', while 좋아 보여요 = 'looks good/well' (condition); related but not identical.
Using bare 보기 좋아 toward an elder you're complimenting — use the honorific 보기 좋으세요 / 보기 좋으시네요.

structuredNuance.t: 보기 = 'the act of seeing' (보다 'see' + -기 nominalizer); 좋아요 = 'is good.' Literal: 'the seeing of it is good' = 'it's good to look at.' In use, it is the warm 'looks nice / heartwarming to see' — applies to wholesome scenes, not just visual beauty.

Use it when a scene or person gives you a warm, positive feeling: a happy couple, someone looking healthy, two friends getting along, a nicely arranged space. It is warmer and more approving than just 예뻐요. To an elder, use 보기 좋으시네요. Between friends, bare 보기 좋아 feels natural and genuine.

보기 좋아요 vs 예뻐요: 예뻐요 says the thing itself is pretty; 보기 좋아요 says it is good/wholesome to witness. Against 좋아 보여요: 좋아 보여요 = 'looks good (in condition/health)' — reversed word order, different meaning. Against 멋있어요: 멋있어요 = cool/impressive; 보기 좋아요 = heartwarming/wholesome to see.
Register: 보기 좋아 (banmal) → 보기 좋아요 (polite) → 보기 좋으세요 (honorific). Noticing tone: 보기 좋네요, 보기 좋으시네요. For two people: 두 분 보기 좋으세요 / 보기 좋아요.

Two traps: (1) restructuring it as 좋게 보여요 or 좋아 보기 — the fixed expression is 보기 좋다, with 보기 (nominalizer) first; (2) confusing it with 좋아 보여요 — the reversed word order shifts the meaning from 'nice to see' to 'looks to be in good condition'; they are related but not interchangeable.

entries.english: I'm jealous / I envy you (the nice kind)
entries.shortExplanation: 부러워요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm jealous / I envy you (the nice kind)".
entries.explanation: 부러워요 (bureowoyo) = "I'm jealous / I envy you (the nice kind)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 부러워요 ("I'm so envious"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the everyday warm way to say you wish you had what someone has
반말, said freely to a friend
Half-to-yourself exclamation; the most natural spoken form, even around elders
완전 ('totally') boosts the warmth — common in chat messages

examples.ko: A: 다음 주에 제주도 가요! / B: 와, 진짜요? 부러워요!
examples.romanization: A: daeum jue jejudo gayo! / B: wa, jinjjayo? bureowoyo!
examples.en: A: I'm going to Jeju next week! / B: Wow, really? I'm so jealous!
examples.note: A/B exchange showing the natural warm reaction to good news; 진짜요? adds genuine surprise

examples.ko: A: 집이 회사랑 걸어서 5분이에요. / B: 아… 너무 부럽다.
examples.romanization: A: jibi hoesarang georeoseo 5bunieyo. / B: a… neomu bureopda.
examples.en: A: My place is five minutes' walk from work. / B: Ahh… I'm so jealous.
examples.note: 반말 mutter 부럽다 as pure wistful reaction — the most natural everyday form

examples.ko: 휴가 간다고요? 진짜 부러워요. 저는 방학이 없어서요.
examples.romanization: hyuga gandagoyo? jinjja bureowoyo. jeoneun banghagi eopseoseoyo.
examples.en: You're going on vacation? I'm really jealous — I don't get time off.
examples.note: Adding your own situation (저는 방학이 없어서요) makes the envy sound sincere, not bitter

entries.nuance: 부러워요 comes from the adjective 부럽다 ('to be envious'), and it captures the GOOD, warm kind of envy — 'lucky you, I wish that were me.' Koreans say it constantly as a friendly compliment on good news: a trip, a new phone, a five-minute commute. It is never hostile. Keep it far from 질투 / 질투하다 ('jealousy'), which is the dark, possessive jealousy of a romantic rival or someone who resents your success — saying 질투나요 to a friend's vacation news sounds creepy or bitter, so 부러워요 is the safe everyday choice. For register: 부러워요 is polite, 부러워 is 반말, and 부럽다 is the bare adjective exclamation Koreans mutter even around elders — because the plain-form exclamatory 다 functions like thinking aloud rather than 반말 aimed at someone. The number-one English-speaker pitfall is the particle and direction: you do NOT say 당신을 부러워요 ('I envy YOU' with an object) — mark what is envied with 이/가 (가방이 부러워요 'I envy your bag', 네가 부러워 'I envy you/your situation'), or simply say 부러워요 about the whole thing. A look-alike trap: 부럽다 ('envious') vs. 부끄럽다 ('shy/embarrassed') — they share 부 but are opposite-feeling words.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 질투나요 to react to a friend's good news.
질투 is dark, possessive jealousy (a love rival, resentment). Friendly 'lucky you' envy is 부러워요. 질투나요 to a friend's vacation sounds hostile, not warm.
Marking the person as an object: 너를 부러워.
부럽다 takes the envied thing/situation with 이/가, not a person with 을/를. Say 네가 부러워 ('I envy you/your situation') or just 부러워.
Translating 'I'm jealous OF your car' as 차에 부러워요.
Don't use 에. The envied thing takes 이/가: 차가 부러워요, or simply 부러워요 about the whole thing.

structuredNuance.t: 직역 would be 'I am envious.' But in practice 부러워요 functions as a warm COMPLIMENT — 'lucky you, I wish that were me' — not a statement of bitterness. The feeling is openly shared and affectionate, not hidden or hostile.

Use freely to friends, family, coworkers of similar rank, even casual strangers, whenever you hear good news — a trip, a deal, a short commute. It is the natural warm reaction. 부러워요 is polite-casual; 부러워 is 반말; 부럽다 works as an exclamation even around seniors. Avoid it only when the context is competitive or you're already tense with someone (there 질투 might apply).

vs. 질투(나다): 질투 is dark, possessive jealousy — the resentment of a love rival. Saying 질투나요 to a friend's good news sounds hostile. vs. 부끄럽다: looks similar (부) but means 'shy/embarrassed' — completely different. 부러워요 = warm envy; 부끄러워요 = I'm embarrassed. Keep them separate.

완전 부러워요 ('totally jealous'), 진짜 부러워요 ('really jealous'), 부럽네요 (soft polite observation, '~must say I envy you'), 부러우면 지는 거예요 (joke: 'if you're jealous, you lose'). Name the envied thing with 이/가: 네 휴가가 부러워요.

Do NOT mark the person with 을/를: 너를 부러워요 is wrong. The envied thing/situation takes 이/가: 네가 부러워, 그 가방이 부러워요. Also don't confuse 부럽다 ('envious') with 부끄럽다 ('embarrassed') — they sound alike but mean opposite things.

entries.english: I'll be rooting for you / I've got your back.
entries.shortExplanation: 응원할게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll be rooting for you / I've got your back.".
entries.explanation: 응원할게요 (eungwonhalgeyo) means "I'll be rooting for you / I've got your back.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 응원할게요 ("I'll cheer you on"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: polite -요, to a peer or younger
banmal, to a close friend
격식 -겠습니다, a formal pledge of support

usagePhrases.en: I'll always be rooting for you
usagePhrases.note: 항상 makes it a lasting, ongoing promise — not just for this one event

examples.ko: A: 저 이번에 도전해 보려고요! / B: 응원할게요, 잘할 수 있어요!
examples.romanization: A: jeo ibeone dojeonhae boryeogoyo! / B: eungwonhalgeyo, jalhal su isseoyo!
examples.en: A: I'm going to give it a try this time! / B: I'm rooting for you — you can do it!
examples.note: the bare pledge of personal support, combined with belief in them

examples.ko: 시험 앞둔 친구에게 "내가 응원할게, 분명 잘될 거야" 했어요.
examples.romanization: siheom apdun chinguege "naega eungwonhalge, bunmyeong jaldoel geoya" haesseoyo.
examples.en: To my friend before the exam I said, 'I'm rooting for you — it'll definitely work out.'
examples.note: everyday: banmal support pledge, paired with reassurance — 응원할게 feels like a personal promise

examples.ko: 퇴사하고 창업한다는 선배께 "새로운 도전 진심으로 응원하겠습니다" 하고 인사드렸어요.
examples.romanization: toesahago changeopandaneun seonbaekke "saeroun dojeon jinsimeuro eungwonhagetseumnida" hago insadeuryeosseoyo.
examples.en: To the senior starting a business after leaving I said, 'I sincerely support your new challenge.'
examples.note: real situation: formal 응원하겠습니다 for a serious life step by a senior — the -겠- signals earnest commitment

entries.nuance: 응원할게요 (應援, 응원 'support/cheering' + -ㄹ게요 'I will, for you') is a personal pledge — 'I'll cheer you on / I'm in your corner' — that promises ongoing backing for someone's effort or challenge. The -ㄹ게요 ending is the key: it is a speaker's promissory 'I commit to this, for your sake', not just a flat prediction, which is the dividing line from 응원할 거예요 ('I will cheer', a neutral future statement). It is also warmer and more committed than 화이팅: 화이팅 is a quick shout in the moment, while 응원할게요 promises you personally will keep backing them over time. The English-speaker pitfall is the spelling: learners write 응원할께요 (wrong — the standard promissory ending is -ㄹ게요, though pronounced tensely as 께). Register: 응원할게 (banmal) ↔ 응원할게요 (polite) ↔ 응원하겠습니다 (formal).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spelling it 응원할께요 — the standard promissory ending is -ㄹ게요: 응원할게요 (pronounced with a tense 께 sound but written 게).
Using 응원할 거예요 instead — that is a flat prediction 'I will cheer'; the warm promise to the listener is 응원할게요.
Treating it as identical to 화이팅 — 화이팅 is an in-the-moment shout, while 응원할게요 pledges ongoing, personal support.

structuredNuance.t: 응원 (應援) = 'support, cheering, backing.' -ㄹ게요 = promissory future: 'I will (for you).' So 응원할게요 = 'I commit to rooting for you.' In use, it is a warm personal pledge — 'I've got your back, I'll keep cheering you on' — more than just saying 'good luck.'

Use it when someone is taking on a challenge, starting something new, or needs sustained encouragement: a job change, a hard exam season, a creative project, a difficult relationship. It implies ongoing support, not just a one-time cheer. To peers and younger people: 응원할게요. To a senior or in formal settings: 응원하겠습니다.

응원할게요 (personal ongoing pledge: 'I'll keep rooting for you') vs 화이팅 (immediate in-the-moment cheer: 'go!'). Against 잘될 거예요 (outcome reassurance: 'it'll work out'): these three layer naturally — 화이팅, 응원할게요, 잘될 거예요 — to cover the push, the backing, and the outcome.
Register: 응원할게 (banmal) → 응원할게요 (polite) → 응원하겠습니다 (formal). Durational: 항상 응원할게요, 끝까지 응원할게요. Intensified: 진심으로 응원할게요.

Two traps: (1) spelling it 응원할께요 — the standard promissory ending is -ㄹ게요 (written 게, though it sounds tense like 께); (2) substituting 응원할 거예요 — that is a flat prediction ('I will cheer') with no warmth or commitment to the listener; 할게요 carries the personal, promissory weight.

entries.english: It suits you / It looks good on you.
entries.shortExplanation: 잘 어울려요 is a practical expression meaning "It suits you / It looks good on you.".
entries.explanation: "It suits you / It looks good on you." — that is 잘 어울려요 (jal eoullyeoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 잘 어울려요 ("it suits you well"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: polite -요, to a peer or younger
banmal, to a close friend
honorific -으시-, to an elder
너무 boosts the compliment — the natural intensifier for this expression

examples.ko: A: (새 안경 쓰고) 어때요? / B: 진짜 잘 어울려요, 완전 잘 맞는 것 같아요!
examples.romanization: A: (sae angyeong sseugo) eottaeyo? / B: jinjja jal eoullyeoyo, wanjeon jal manneun geot gatayo!
examples.en: A: (in new glasses) How is it? / B: It really suits you — looks like it was made for you!
examples.note: the go-to reaction to a new look; 완전 잘 맞는 것 같아요 adds extra warmth

examples.ko: 원피스 입은 친구에게 "그 원피스 색깔이 너랑 진짜 잘 어울려" 했어요.
examples.romanization: wonpiseu ibeun chinguege "geu wonpiseu saekkkari neorang jinjja jal eoullyeo" haesseoyo.
examples.en: To my friend in a dress I said, 'That dress color really suits you.'
examples.note: everyday: name the specific item/color + 너랑 잘 어울려 — the natural collocation pattern

examples.ko: 머리 자른 부장님께 "새로 하신 머리 스타일 잘 어울리세요" 했어요.
examples.romanization: meori jareun bujangnimkke "saero hasin meori seutail jal eoulliseyo" haesseoyo.
examples.en: To the manager with a new haircut I said, 'That new hairstyle suits you well, sir.'
examples.note: real situation: honorific 잘 어울리세요 toward a senior's new look — head straight to this form with anyone older

entries.nuance: 잘 어울려요 (잘 'well' + 어울리다 'to match/go together') is the everyday 'it suits you / it looks good on you' for clothes, glasses, a new haircut, a makeup style, or a color — and the single most natural thing to say when someone shows off a new look. The key dividing line from 예뻐요/멋있어요: 예뻐요 judges the THING itself ('that outfit is pretty'), while 잘 어울려요 says it MATCHES THE PERSON ('that outfit fits you'), which flatters the wearer directly and is why Koreans reach for it constantly as a compliment. The English-speaker pitfall is the grammar: 어울리다 is INTRANSITIVE, so you never attach an object particle; and the natural partner is the particle 랑/이랑/하고 ('goes WITH' the person) — 그 색이 너랑 잘 어울려, not 너를. Also: drop 잘 and bare 어울려요 sounds neutral 'it matches', not a compliment. Register: 잘 어울려 (banmal) ↔ 잘 어울려요 (polite) ↔ 잘 어울리세요 (honorific).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using an object particle (그 옷을 잘 어울려요) — 어울리다 is intransitive; the thing 'goes with' you: 그 옷이 너랑/너한테 잘 어울려요.
Dropping 잘 and saying bare 어울려요 — the compliment keeps 잘 ('suits you well'); without it, it sounds like a flat 'it matches'.
Saying 예뻐요 when you mean it flatters the person — 예뻐요 praises the item itself, while 잘 어울려요 says it suits the wearer.
Using bare 잘 어울려 to an elder — raise it to the honorific 잘 어울리세요 when complimenting a senior's outfit or hair.

structuredNuance.t: 잘 = 'well'; 어울리다 = 'to match, go together harmoniously.' 잘 어울려요 literally 'goes together well' — in practice it means 'it suits you / it looks great on you.' The compliment is about the FIT between person and item, not the item in isolation.

Use it when someone tries on or shows off a new outfit, glasses, hairstyle, hair color, or makeup. It is the warmest, most direct compliment on a new look. To peers and younger people: 잘 어울려요. To an elder: 잘 어울리세요. You can also use it for two people who look good together: 두 분 잘 어울리세요.

잘 어울려요 (suits the person — the fit between person and item) vs 예뻐요 (the item itself is pretty, not about the wearer) vs 멋있어요 (it's cool/impressive, not about fit). 어울리다 vs 맞다: 잘 어울려요 is about harmonious matching (style, color); 잘 맞아요 is about physical fit (size).
Register: 잘 어울려 (banmal) → 잘 어울려요 (polite) → 잘 어울리세요 (honorific). Intensified: 너무/진짜 잘 어울려요, 완전 잘 어울려. For two people: 두 사람 잘 어울려요.

Two traps: (1) adding an object particle (그 옷을 잘 어울려요) — 어울리다 is intransitive; the thing goes WITH you: 그 옷이 너랑/너한테 잘 어울려요; (2) dropping 잘 (bare 어울려요 sounds neutral 'it matches' — the warm compliment keeps 잘 'suits you WELL').

entries.english: Do you have a boyfriend?
entries.shortExplanation: 남자친구 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Do you have a boyfriend?".
entries.explanation: 남자친구 있어요? (namjachingu isseoyo?) = "Do you have a boyfriend?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 남자친구 있어요? ("Do you have a boyfriend?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; the standard way to ask if someone's taken
반말 + the clipped 남친; among friends or once you're close
Same frame, swap to 여자친구 / 여친
Softer, less direct — 'someone you're meeting' rather than a labeled partner

examples.ko: 혹시 남자친구 있어요?
examples.romanization: hoksi namjachingu isseoyo?
examples.en: Do you maybe have a boyfriend?
examples.note: 혹시 ('by any chance') cushions what would otherwise be a blunt personal question — always add it with strangers

examples.ko: 실례지만 남자친구 있으세요? 소개해 주고 싶은 사람이 있어서요.
examples.romanization: sillyejiman namjachingu isseuseyo? sogaehae jugo sipeun sarami isseoseoyo.
examples.en: Sorry to ask, but do you have a boyfriend? I've got someone I'd like to introduce you to.
examples.note: Honorific 있으세요 + giving a reason makes blind-intro territory feel polite and harmless, not creepy

examples.ko: A: 남자친구 있어요? B: 아니요, 솔로예요. 왜요?
examples.romanization: A: namjachingu isseoyo? B: aniyo, solloyeyo. waeyo?
examples.en: A: Do you have a boyfriend? B: No, I'm single. Why do you ask?
examples.note: The natural A/B exchange; 솔로 (solo, single) is the common self-label, and 왜요 ('why?') is the expected curious reply

entries.nuance: 남자친구 있어요? is 남자친구 ('boyfriend') + 있다 ('to exist/have') — the everyday way to find out whether someone is romantically taken. Korean uses 있다, never 가지다 ('possess'): 남자친구를 가지고 있어요? sounds like you own a person and will earn puzzled looks. The clipped forms 남친/여친 are ubiquitous in casual speech and texting but sound too breezy in a first polite conversation, so use the full form. The gentler near-synonym 만나는 사람 있어요? ('are you seeing someone?') sidesteps the committed-relationship label and feels less presumptuous — smart when you're hinting at your own interest. Raise the ending to 있으세요? for older or higher-status people. The biggest English-speaker trap is the particle: never 남자친구를 있어요? because 있다 is not a transitive verb — it takes 이/가 or nothing in speech, never 을/를. Even asking the bare question of a near-stranger without cushioning it with 혹시 can feel nosy.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 남자친구를 있어요? with the object particle.
있다 ('to have/exist') is not a transitive verb; it takes 이/가 or nothing, not 을/를. Say 남자친구 있어요? (or 남자친구가 있어요?).
Translating 'have a boyfriend' as 남자친구를 가지고 있어요?
가지다 ('to possess') is for objects; using it for a person sounds like ownership. Korean 'has' people and relationships with 있다: 남자친구 있어요?
Confusing 남자친구 with 남자 사람 친구.
남자친구 by default means a romantic boyfriend. A male friend (just a friend) is 남사친 (남자 사람 친구). Saying 남자친구 about a buddy implies you're dating.

structuredNuance.t: 남자친구 ('boyfriend') + 있다 ('to exist/have') — literally 'does a boyfriend exist (for you)?'. Korean frames possession of people with 있다, not 가지다 ('possess objects'). The everyday reading is simply 'are you taken / do you have a boyfriend?'

Safe and natural in polite conversation (존댓말) among peers, but add 혹시 with a near-stranger and give a reason (소개해 주고 싶어서요) to soften it. Use 있으세요? with someone older. The clipped 남친 있어? (반말) is only for close friends. Never ask a coworker or much older acquaintance without a clear reason — it can feel intrusive.

만나는 사람 있어요? ('are you seeing someone?') avoids labeling the relationship and feels less loaded — better when you don't know whether they're attached or you're feeling out the situation. 남자친구 있어요? implies you expect a potential boyfriend label, while 만나는 사람 is a neutral 'is there anyone?'
남자친구 있어요? (neutral polite) → 혹시 남자친구 있으세요? (deferential softened) → 남친 있어? (반말, friends) → 만나는 사람 있어요? (non-labeling softer). The clipped 남친/여친 in texting is standard among friends.

Two particle traps: (1) 남자친구를 있어요? — 있다 is not transitive, it never takes 을/를; use 남자친구 있어요? or 남자친구가 있어요?. (2) 남자친구를 가지고 있어요? — 가지다 ('to hold/possess') is for objects, not people. Both errors mark you as a very early learner.

entries.english: What's your type?
entries.shortExplanation: 이상형이 어떻게 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "What's your type?".
entries.explanation: 이상형이 어떻게 돼요? (isanghyeongi eotteoke dwaeyo?) means "What's your type?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 이상형이 어떻게 돼요? ("What's your ideal type?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; the go-to get-to-know-you question asking what someone finds attractive
반말, among friends gossiping about crushes

usagePhrases.en: What kind of person do you like?
usagePhrases.note: Plainer version, less jargon than 이상형, and slightly more casual

usagePhrases.en: What's your ideal type, may I ask?
usagePhrases.note: Honorific 되세요 for someone older or on a first meeting

examples.ko: 이상형이 어떻게 돼요? 저는 유머 있는 사람이요.
examples.romanization: isanghyeongi eotteoke dwaeyo? jeoneun yumeo inneun saramiyo.
examples.en: What's your type? Mine's someone with a sense of humor.
examples.note: Answer with 속성 + 사람 + 이요; 유머 있는 사람 is a natural answer pattern

examples.ko: 완전 제 이상형이에요.
examples.romanization: wanjeon je isanghyeongieyo.
examples.en: You're totally my type.
examples.note: The compliment form; 완전 ('totally') + 제 이상형 + 이에요 — smooth and direct

examples.ko: A: 이상형이 어떻게 돼요? B: 음... 눈이 크고 다정한 사람이요.
examples.romanization: A: isanghyeongi eotteoke dwaeyo? B: eum... nuni keugo dajeonghan saramiyo.
examples.en: A: What's your type? B: Hmm... someone with big eyes and a warm personality.
examples.note: Typical A/B exchange; listing two traits with 고 ('and') is the natural format

entries.nuance: 이상형이 어떻게 돼요? is 이상형 (理想型, 'ideal type') + 이/가 + 어떻게 돼요 ('how is it?') — the standard question for 'what kind of person are you into romantically?'. The chunk 어떻게 돼요? is the polite, idiomatic Korean frame for asking about personal specifics (name, age, type, job); it's softer than blunt 뭐예요? ('what is it?'), which sounds like reading a form. Don't swap in 이상형이 뭐예요? unless you're already being casual. The contrast: 이상형 is specifically about your romantic ideal and carries a flirty charge, whereas 어떤 사람 좋아해요? ('what kind of person do you like?') is milder and could be asked platonically. 제 이상형이에요 is the compliment — natural and warm; compare with the slangy 타입 (loanword 'type') which younger Koreans use but sounds less standard. Origin note: 이상형 is Sino-Korean 理想型. Particle trap: the expression headword takes 이/가 as subject — 이상형이 어떻게 돼요; don't drop the 이 or mis-attach 을.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'you're my type' literally as 당신은 제 타입이에요.
당신 sounds stiff/confrontational in real speech, and 타입 is slangy. Natural Korean is 완전 제 이상형이에요, dropping the pronoun.
Using 뭐예요 and asking 이상형이 뭐예요? to someone you just met.
It's grammatical but blunt. The polite, idiomatic frame for personal questions is 어떻게 돼요?: 이상형이 어떻게 돼요?
Reading 어떻게 돼요 as 'how does it become'.
As a set phrase it just asks 'what is it / how is it'. 이상형이 어떻게 돼요 means 'what's your type', not 'how does your ideal type become'.

structuredNuance.t: 이상형 ('ideal type', 理想型) + 이 + 어떻게 돼요 (lit. 'how does it turn out?'). The chunk 어떻게 돼요 is a fixed, softened frame Koreans use for personal info questions — think of it as 'and what would that be?'. The whole phrase means 'what kind of person are you into?'

A natural icebreaker over drinks or on a blind date (소개팅); it signals romantic interest without being too forward. Use -어떻게 돼요? with peers; -어떻게 되세요? with someone older. Asking in a work meeting or to a much senior person would be odd unless you're setting up a 소개팅 for them.

이상형이 어떻게 돼요? (specific romantic ideal, slightly loaded) vs. 어떤 사람 좋아해요? (neutral 'what kind of person do you like?', can be platonic). To compliment someone, 제 이상형이에요 is natural and direct; the loanword 제 타입이에요 is also used colloquially but sounds younger/slangy.
이상형이 어떻게 돼요? (polite) → 이상형이 뭐야? (반말) → 이상형이 어떻게 되세요? (deferential). The compliment form: 제 이상형이에요 / 완전 제 이상형이에요.

Replacing 어떻게 돼요 with 뭐예요?: 이상형이 뭐예요? is grammatical but blunt, like demanding an answer. The polite idiomatic frame is 어떻게 돼요. Also don't say 당신은 제 타입이에요 — 당신 sounds confrontational; drop the pronoun and say 완전 제 이상형이에요.

entries.english: I fell for you at first sight
entries.shortExplanation: 첫눈에 반했어요 is a practical expression meaning "I fell for you at first sight".
entries.explanation: "I fell for you at first sight" — that is 첫눈에 반했어요 (cheonnune banhaesseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 첫눈에 반했어요 ("I fell for you at first sight"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: I fell for you at first sight
usagePhrases.note: Polite; a sweet confession of instant attraction

usagePhrases.en: I fell for you at first sight
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a partner or crush you're already comfortable with

usagePhrases.en: I was smitten at one glance
usagePhrases.note: 한눈에 ('in one look') — a near-identical variant, slightly more poetic
완전 ('totally') for emphasis without the 'first sight' framing — can be said later too

examples.ko: 사실 처음 봤을 때 첫눈에 반했어요.
examples.romanization: sasil cheoeum bwasseul ttae cheonnune banhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Actually, the first time I saw you, I fell for you instantly.
examples.note: 처음 봤을 때 ('the first time I saw you') makes the timeline explicit; 사실 softens it as a confession

examples.ko: 그 사람한테 완전 반해서 잠도 안 와요.
examples.romanization: geu saramhante wanjeon banhaeseo jamdo an wayo.
examples.en: I'm so smitten with them I can't even sleep.
examples.note: 반하다 + 한테 marks the target; 잠도 안 와 ('can't even sleep') — intensity collocate

examples.ko: A: 언제부터 좋았어? B: 솔직히 첫눈에 반했어.
examples.romanization: A: eonjebuteo joasseo? B: soljiki cheonnune banhaesseo.
examples.en: A: When did you start liking me? B: Honestly, I fell for you at first sight.
examples.note: Natural A/B where 첫눈에 반했어 is the punchline confession answer

entries.nuance: 첫눈에 반하다 is 첫눈에 (첫 'first' + 눈 'eye/look' + 에 'at') + 반하다 ('to fall for / be smitten') — the set phrase for instant infatuation, love at first sight. The core verb 반하다 means to be captivated; its target takes 에게/한테 ('by/to'), never 을/를. The form is almost always past — 반했어요, because 반하다 describes a state already entered, so 반했어요 means 'I've fallen for you (and remain so)'. Saying 반해요 in present sounds unfinished or odd. The crucial contrast: 반하다 (the sudden spark, surface attraction) is not yet 좋아하다 ('to like', more intentional) or 사랑하다 ('to love', deep and earned). 첫눈에 / 한눈에 are interchangeable ('first sight' vs. 'one glance'). Careful not to confuse 반하다 ('be smitten') with unrelated homophones, or with 반갑다 ('glad to meet you') — totally different verbs. Register: 반했어요 (polite) makes a beautiful confession line; 반했어 in 반말 with someone close.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Marking the person with 을/를: 너를 반했어.
반하다 takes 에게/한테 ('to/by'): 너한테 반했어 ('I fell for you'). The one you're smitten by is not a direct object.
Using present 반해요 for the feeling.
반하다 describes a state already entered, so it's normally past: 반했어요 ('I've fallen for you'). Present 반해요 sounds unfinished.
Swapping in 사랑해요 for instant attraction.
사랑하다 is deep, serious love. The sudden crush/smitten feeling is 반하다. 'I fell for you at first sight' is 첫눈에 반했어요, not 첫눈에 사랑했어요.

structuredNuance.t: 첫눈에 = 'at first eye/glance' (첫 first + 눈 eye + 에 at); 반하다 = 'to be captivated, fall for'. Together: 'I was captivated at the first glance' = 'I fell for you at first sight'. It is a fixed idiom — don't decode it piece by piece.

Said as a romantic confession to a crush, a new partner, or retrospectively to a long-term partner ('remember when I fell for you instantly?'). 반했어요 (polite) is a lovely confession line safe even early on; 반했어 is intimate 반말 for someone close. Not used in professional or formal settings.

반하다 (the sudden smitten spark — can be surface-level charm) vs. 좋아하다 ('to like', more deliberate feeling) vs. 사랑하다 ('to love', deep and serious). 첫눈에 반하다 is the spark moment; don't substitute 사랑하다 for this feeling — 첫눈에 사랑했어요 sounds strange. 첫눈에 vs. 한눈에: both mean 'at first sight / at one glance' and are interchangeable.

반하다 → 반했어요 (polite past, most common) / 반했어 (반말 past) / 반해서 (cause: 'because I fell for you...') / 완전 반했어요 (intensified). The present 반해요 is rare; the past is the default because 반하다 marks a state already entered.
Particle error: 반하다 takes 에게/한테 for the target, NOT 을/를 — 너한테 반했어 ('I fell for you'), never 너를 반했어. Also don't confuse 반하다 ('be smitten') with 반갑다 ('glad to meet someone') — completely unrelated.

entries.english: Are we, like, a thing?
entries.shortExplanation: 우리 썸 타는 거야? is a practical expression meaning "Are we, like, a thing?".
entries.explanation: 우리 썸 타는 거야? (uri sseom taneun geoya?) = "Are we, like, a thing?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 우리 썸 타는 거야? ("Are we kind of a thing?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Are we kind of a thing?
usagePhrases.note: 반말; the playful question between two people in the gray zone — half-joking, half-sincere

usagePhrases.en: Are we sort of seeing each other?
usagePhrases.note: Polite version if you're still on 존댓말 with each other
Describing the relationship status to a third party

usagePhrases.en: Are you and them a thing?
usagePhrases.note: Asking a friend about their gray-zone someone; 걔 = 'that person'

examples.ko: 요즘 누구 썸 타는 사람 있어?
examples.romanization: yojeum nugu sseom taneun saram isseo?
examples.en: Are you talking to anyone these days?
examples.note: Friend gossip; 썸 타는 사람 = 'someone you're in the gray zone with' — the standard way to probe

examples.ko: 썸만 타다가 결국 흐지부지됐어요.
examples.romanization: sseomman tadaga gyeolgu keujibujidwaesseoyo.
examples.en: We were just in that talking stage and it fizzled out without ever becoming official.
examples.note: 썸만 타다 ('only ever 썸, never went official') + 흐지부지되다 ('fizzle out')

examples.ko: A: 우리 썸 타는 거야? B: 글쎄... 뭐가 되고 싶은데.
examples.romanization: A: uri sseom taneun geoya? B: geulsse... mwoga doego sipeunde.
examples.en: A: So, are we a thing? B: Well... I want us to be something.
examples.note: The classic gray-zone confrontation; 뭐가 되고 싶다 = 'I want us to become something'

entries.nuance: 썸 타다 is 썸 (from English 'something') + 타다 (lit. 'to ride') — the wildly popular slang for the ambiguous pre-dating stage where two people are clearly interested, flirting, and texting, but no one has confessed or made things official. There is no clean English equivalent; 'talking' or 'situationship' comes close. The verb is locked as 타다 ('ride', the same 타다 as buses): 썸을 타다 is correct, 썸 하다 is not — memorize 썸(을) 타다 as one unit. The crucial line: 썸 타다 is BEFORE official dating, 사귀다 is AFTER the 고백 (confession) and agreement — calling an official couple 썸 타는 사이 implies it's still ambiguous, which could offend. This is casual/young register — never in formal contexts or with older people who may not recognize the term. Pitfall: don't back-translate 'something' as 뭔가; the slang noun is the loanword 썸 itself.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 썸 하다 instead of 썸 타다.
The fixed verb is 타다 ('to ride'): 썸을 타다. 썸 하다 is not how Koreans say it. Memorize the collocation 썸 타다.
Using 썸 타다 for an official couple.
썸 is the stage BEFORE dating. Once you've confessed and agreed, you're 사귀다 ('dating'). Calling a committed couple 썸 implies it's still unofficial.
Translating 'something' word-for-word as 뭔가 타다.
The slang comes from English 'something' but is borrowed as the noun 썸. It's 썸 타다, not 뭔가 타다 or any literal rendering.

structuredNuance.t: 썸 = loanword from English 'something'; 타다 = 'to ride'. Literally 'to ride something'. The actual meaning is the pre-dating ambiguous stage: mutual interest is clear but no one has confessed or committed. Think 'we're in the grey zone' or 'we're talking'.

Said between the two people in the gray zone to half-jokingly name what's happening, or by a third party asking about someone's romantic status. Pure casual/반말 register — you'd never say this to a boss or older relative. Older Koreans may not know the term; it skews under-40.

썸 타다 (pre-official, ambiguous) vs. 사귀다 (officially dating, both parties have agreed). 썸 타다 PRECEDES 사귀다 — asking 우리 사귀어? when you mean 썸 jumps the gun and can make things awkward. 연애하다 ('to date / have a relationship') also implies an established relationship, not the gray zone.

썸(을) 타다 (verb) → 썸 타는 사이 ('a 썸-stage relationship') → 썸남 (썸 stage guy, 썸 + 남자) / 썸녀 (썸 stage girl) → 썸타다가 사귀다 ('go from 썸 to official'). The noun 썸 alone is used freely: 썸인 것 같아 ('I think we're in the 썸 zone').

The verb is fixed as 타다: 썸 하다 is wrong, 썸 타다 is correct. Also never literally render 'something' as 뭔가 (뭔가 타다 is nonsense). And don't use 썸 for an official couple — it implies the relationship is still ambiguous.

entries.english: Will you go out with me?
entries.shortExplanation: 우리 사귈래요? is a practical expression meaning "Will you go out with me?".
entries.explanation: 우리 사귈래요? (uri sagwillaeyo?) means "Will you go out with me?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 우리 사귈래요? ("Want to go out (with me)?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-casual; the classic ask to make it official, safe on 존댓말
반말, once you're close or both young

usagePhrases.en: Let's date / let's be a couple
usagePhrases.note: A statement-style ask, gentle and warm — almost a declaration
Earnest, even humble; 주세요 makes it a heartfelt request

examples.ko: 나 너 좋아해. 우리 사귈래?
examples.romanization: na neo joahae. uri sagwillae?
examples.en: I like you. Want to go out?
examples.note: The classic one-two: 고백 (좋아해) immediately followed by the ask — standard structure

examples.ko: 우리 오늘부터 1일이에요.
examples.romanization: uri oneulbuteo 1irieyo.
examples.en: Today is day one for us.
examples.note: Said the moment someone says yes; Korean couples count from 1일 (day one) and celebrate milestones religiously

examples.ko: A: 저랑 사귀어 주실래요? B: 네, 저도 좋아요.
examples.romanization: A: jeorang sagwieo jusillaeyo? B: ne, jeodo joayo.
examples.en: A: Would you please go out with me? B: Yes, I feel the same.
examples.note: Slightly deferential ask with -주실래요? — genuine earnestness in a polite register; B's 저도 좋아요 = 'I like you too'

entries.nuance: 사귀다 means 'to date / be in a committed relationship', and 우리 사귈래요? is the ritual question that converts 썸 into official couplehood. The ending -ㄹ래요? asks for the listener's willingness ('do you want to?'), exactly the soft, inviting register you want — not a command. The key contrast: 사귀다 (official, labeled, 'boyfriend/girlfriend') vs. 만나다 ('to meet/see' — can mean casual going-out or just meeting up without the committed label). Confessing with 사귀다 is the moment a couple becomes 'official'. After a yes, couples announce 오늘부터 1일 ('day one starts today') and count anniversaries. English-speaker traps: (1) the spelling — 사귀다 → 사귀어요, past 사귀었어요 (NOT 사겨요, an extremely common mistake). (2) The particle: 사귀다 takes the comitative 랑/와 ('with') — 나랑 사귈래? — never the object 을/를. Register note: -ㄹ래요? is warm and friendly; move to 사귈래? only once you're already using 반말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing/saying 사겨요 instead of 사귀어요.
사귀다 keeps the 위: present polite is 사귀어요. 사겨요 is a frequent misspelling. Conjugate it as 사귀어요, 사귀었어요.
Using 만나다 to mean 'be my official partner'.
만나다 ('to meet/see') is vaguer and can mean casual dating or just meeting up. To ask for a committed relationship, use 사귀다: 우리 사귈래요?
Attaching 을/를: 너를 사귈래?
사귀다 takes the comitative 랑/와 ('with'), not the object 을/를. Say 나랑 사귈래? ('go out WITH me?'), not 너를 사귈래?

structuredNuance.t: 우리 ('we/us') + 사귀다 ('to make friends, to socialize with → to date in romantic sense') + -ㄹ래요? ('want to?'). Literal reading: 'Do we want to go together?'. Actual meaning: 'Will you be my boyfriend/girlfriend?' — the formal-commitment ask.

Said after a period of 썸 (pre-dating ambiguity) or after a 고백 (confession of feelings) to officially become a couple. Use -ㄹ래요? with someone you're on 존댓말 with; drop to 사귈래? in 반말. This is a serious, sincere question — don't throw it around casually or it loses meaning.

사귀다 (committed relationship, 'boyfriend/girlfriend') vs. 만나다 ('to date casually / to meet up' — vaguer). Asking 우리 만나는 거야? can mean 'are we an item?' but 만나다 alone implies less commitment. 사귀다 is the clear, official step.
사귈래요? (polite ask) → 사귈래? (반말) → 사귀자 (반말 'let's date') → 사귀어 주실래요? (humble earnest) → 사귀었어요 (past: 'we dated') → 사귀고 있어요 (currently dating). Spelling: always 사귀-, never 사겨-.

Spelling/conjugation: 사귀다 → 사귀어요 (NOT 사겨요). Particle: it's 나랑 사귈래? ('go out WITH me?') using 랑/와, never 너를 사귈래? with the object marker. The comitative 랑/와 is essential — 사귀다 is about being-with, not doing-to.

entries.english: I'm going to confess (my feelings)
entries.shortExplanation: 고백할 거예요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm going to confess (my feelings)".
entries.explanation: "I'm going to confess (my feelings)" — that is 고백할 거예요 (gobaekal geoyeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 고백할 거예요 ("I'm going to confess my feelings"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: I'm going to confess my feelings
usagePhrases.note: Polite; telling a friend your plan before you do it
반말, to a friend you're confiding in
Past tense — you already did it and are reporting
The receiving side; 받다 ('to receive') flips the direction completely

examples.ko: 용기 내서 고백했는데 차였어요.
examples.romanization: yonggi naeseo gobaekaenneunde chayeosseoyo.
examples.en: I worked up the courage and confessed, but got rejected.
examples.note: 용기 내다 ('gather courage') is the natural lead-in; 차이다 ('get rejected/dumped') is the feared outcome

examples.ko: 어제 고백받았는데 어떡하지?
examples.romanization: eoje gobaekbadanneunde eotteokaji?
examples.en: Someone confessed to me yesterday — what do I do?
examples.note: 고백받다 = you are the one confessed to; completely different from 고백하다

examples.ko: A: 나 오늘 고백할 거야. B: 진짜? 잘 될 거야!
examples.romanization: A: na oneul gobaekal geoya. B: jinjja? jal doel geoya!
examples.en: A: I'm going to confess today. B: Really? It'll go well!
examples.note: The pep-talk A/B exchange; B's 잘 될 거야 ('it'll work out') is the standard encouragement

entries.nuance: 고백하다 is 고백 (告白, 'white confession' → declaring something openly) + 하다, and in a dating context it specifically means declaring your romantic feelings — the pivotal event that makes 썸 official and precedes 사귀다. This is NOT the English 'confess' in the guilty-admission sense; a romantic 고백 is hopeful and nervous, not shameful. For admitting a fault, Koreans use 자백하다 or 털어놓다 — don't mix them up. Direction is critical: 고백하다 = YOU confess TO someone; 고백받다 = someone confesses TO YOU. The target of your confession takes 에게/한테 ('to'), never 을/를: 그 사람한테 고백했어요. After a 고백 the outcome is either a yes (→ 사귀다) or rejection (차이다). 고백 is the noun, so it needs a verb: 고백하다 (to confess), 고백받다 (to receive a confession) — you can't say 고백 주세요. Register is flexible: 고백 is everyday vocabulary, equally natural in 존댓말 or 반말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 고백하다 to mean 'admit I did something wrong'.
Romantic 고백 = declaring feelings, not owning up to a fault. For confessing a mistake, use 자백하다 or 솔직히 말하다 / 털어놓다.
Mixing up 고백하다 and 고백받다.
고백하다 = YOU confess to them; 고백받다 = THEY confess to you. 'I got confessed to' is 고백받았어요, not 고백했어요.
Marking the person with 을/를: 그 사람을 고백했어요.
The confession target takes 에게/한테 ('to'): 그 사람한테 고백했어요. The person you confess to is not a direct object.

structuredNuance.t: 고백 (告白) literally means 'white/open declaration'. In a dating context, 고백하다 = 'to declare romantic feelings openly to someone'. It is the formal-yet-emotional step of stating your feelings and inviting a relationship — not a guilty admission.

Typically done after a period of 썸 (ambiguous closeness), often in a one-on-one setting. Koreans often plan the moment carefully — 언제 고백하지? ('when should I confess?') is a real anxiety. Said to the person you like (+ 한테/에게), or reported to friends after the fact. Register is flexible.

고백하다 (romantic declaration) vs. 자백하다 (confess a crime/misdeed, in court or to someone you wronged) vs. 털어놓다 (open up/unburden, more emotional). Don't reach for 자백 when you mean a romantic confession — the connotations are guilt-crime, not love.
고백하다 → 고백할 거야/거예요 (plan) → 고백했어/했어요 (past, reported) → 고백받았어요 (was confessed to) → 고백 성공/실패 ('confession succeeded/failed'). The noun 고백 alone works in compound phrases: 고백하러 가다 ('go to confess').

Romantic 고백 is NOT guilty admission. For owning up to a fault, say 자백하다 or 솔직히 말하다. Also watch direction: 고백하다 (I confess) ≠ 고백받다 (I receive a confession). And the target takes 한테/에게, never 을/를: 그 사람한테 고백했어요.

entries.english: I'd like to ask you out (on a date)
entries.shortExplanation: 데이트 신청하고 싶어요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to ask you out (on a date)".
entries.explanation: 데이트 신청하고 싶어요 (deiteu sincheonghago sipeoyo) = "I'd like to ask you out (on a date)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 데이트 신청하고 싶어요 ("I'd like to ask you out"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to ask you out
usagePhrases.note: Polite; expressing the wish to ask for a date — earnest and slightly formal
반말, declaring your intention to a friend or to the crush directly

usagePhrases.en: Want to go on a date?
usagePhrases.note: The direct invite itself — skips the 신청 and just asks
The soft indirect opener that typically leads into asking someone out

examples.ko: 저 사실 데이트 신청하고 싶었어요.
examples.romanization: jeo sasil deiteu sincheonghago sipeosseoyo.
examples.en: I actually wanted to ask you out.
examples.note: 사실 ('actually/honestly') makes it a slightly hesitant but sweet reveal; -었어요 past = 'I'd been wanting to'

examples.ko: 우리 이번 주말에 데이트할래요?
examples.romanization: uri ibeon jumare deiteuhallaeyo?
examples.en: Want to go on a date this weekend?
examples.note: 데이트하다 + -ㄹ래요 for the actual invitation; 이번 주말에 is the natural time anchor

examples.ko: A: 주말에 시간 있어요? B: 네, 왜요? A: 같이 밥 먹으러 갈래요?
examples.romanization: A: jumare sigan isseoyo? B: ne, waeyo? A: gachi bam meogeureo gallaeyo?
examples.en: A: Are you free this weekend? B: Yes, why? A: Want to grab a meal together?
examples.note: The real-world indirect ask; Koreans rarely say '데이트하자' out of nowhere to a near-stranger — they ease in like this

entries.nuance: 데이트 is the loanword 'date', and there are two key verb patterns: 데이트하다 ('to go on a date', the activity) and 데이트 신청하다 ('to ask someone out', lit. 'to submit a date application', 신청 申請 = applying/requesting). Using 신청하다 frames the ask as a formal request — the same verb you use to register for a class or apply for a scholarship, which makes it endearing in Korean. Contrast: 데이트하다 (the act of going on the date itself) vs. 사귀다 (being in a committed relationship) — you can 데이트 with someone before you're officially together. Koreans often avoid announcing '데이트하자' bluntly to someone they barely know; instead they float 주말에 시간 있어요? ('free this weekend?') and work up to it. Pitfall: saying 데이트를 물어보다 ('ask about a date') for 'ask out' is wrong — the idiom is 데이트 신청하다. 데이트 is a noun and needs a verb: 데이트하다 or 데이트 신청하다; you can't conjugate the noun alone.
