Register: 데이트 itself is casual-neutral; keep the sentence ending polite with someone new.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 데이트를 물어보고 싶어요 for 'I want to ask you out'.
물어보다 means 'ask a question'. To ask someone ON a date, the set phrase is 데이트 신청하다: 데이트 신청하고 싶어요.
Treating the loanword 데이트 as a verb on its own.
데이트 is a noun; the verb needs 하다: 데이트하다. 'Let's go on a date' is 데이트하자/데이트할래요 — you can't conjugate the noun directly (no 데이트자 / 데이트요 to mean 'let's date').
Assuming 데이트 means you're officially a couple.
데이트 is the activity of going out; you can date casually before being official. The committed-couple status is 사귀다, a separate step.

structuredNuance.t: 데이트 (loanword 'date') + 신청하다 (申請: 'to apply for / submit a request'). Literally 'to apply for a date'. The real meaning: 'to ask someone out on a date'. The 신청 framing — borrowed from formal application vocabulary — gives the phrase a slightly earnest, respectful tone.

Used after some 썸 or at least a few friendly encounters — not the first words to a stranger. Say 데이트 신청하고 싶어요 (polite) to someone you're on 존댓말 with; 데이트 신청할게 (반말) to a friend or once you're close. Koreans typically ease in with 시간 있어요? first rather than blurting the 데이트 ask.

데이트하다 (going on a date, the experience) vs. 사귀다 (being a couple, the ongoing status). You can go on a 데이트 with someone you're not yet officially dating. 데이트 신청하다 = inviting them to that experience; 사귀다 = the committed step that may come after.
데이트 신청하고 싶어요 (polite wish) → 데이트 신청할게요 (I'll ask you out) → 우리 데이트할래요? (direct invite) → 데이트하자 (반말 'let's date'). Indirect opener: 주말에 시간 있어요? → 같이 뭔가 할까요?

데이트를 물어보다 ('ask about a date') does NOT mean 'ask someone out' — use 데이트 신청하다. Also 데이트 is a noun; don't try to conjugate it directly (no 데이트요 / 데이트자 as verbs). And 데이트 ≠ 사귀다 — going on a date doesn't mean you're an official couple.

entries.english: Let's keep in touch / Text me
entries.shortExplanation: 연락해요 is a practical expression meaning "Let's keep in touch / Text me".
entries.explanation: 연락해요 (yeollakaeyo) means "Let's keep in touch / Text me". Say it as one set phrase — for example 연락해요 ("Let's stay in touch / text me"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Let's stay in touch / text me
usagePhrases.note: Polite-casual; said when parting, hoping to talk again — warm but non-committal
반말, to a friend or someone you're close with
Promising YOU will reach out first — -ㄹ게요 commits your own action
Asking THEM to reach out; 주다 puts the action on the other person

examples.ko: 조심히 들어가고 연락해요.
examples.romanization: josimhi deureogago yeollakaeyo.
examples.en: Get home safe and text me.
examples.note: 조심히 들어가다 ('get home safely') + 연락해요 is the warm standard farewell in early dating

examples.ko: 왜 연락 안 했어? 기다렸잖아.
examples.romanization: wae yeollak an haesseo? gidaryeotjana.
examples.en: Why didn't you text? I was waiting for you.
examples.note: 연락 안 하다 ('not contact') is the root of 연락 없음 anxiety; 기다렸잖아 ('I was waiting, you know') is a gentle complaint

examples.ko: A: 나중에 연락할게요. B: 네, 기다릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: najunge yeollakalgeyo. B: ne, gidarilgeyo.
examples.en: A: I'll be in touch later. B: Okay, I'll wait.
examples.note: Direction contrast in one exchange: A promises their own action (-ㄹ게요); B accepts with 기다리다

entries.nuance: 연락하다 is 연락 (連絡, 'contact/communication') + 하다 — the all-purpose verb for reaching out via any channel: calling, texting, messaging. In the dating world, it carries outsized weight: 연락 잘 하는 사람 ('someone who texts back reliably') is a highly prized quality, and 연락이 뜸해지다 ('contact grows sparse') is often the first sign a relationship is cooling. The critical distinctions are in verb form and direction: 연락할게요 = 'I'LL contact you' (-ㄹ게 promises your OWN action); 연락해요 = 'let's stay in touch / you contact me' (imperative/suggestion); 연락 주세요 = 'please reach out to me' (you put the action on them with 주다). Mixing these sends opposite messages. Particle trap: the target takes 에게/한테, not 을/를 — 나한테 연락해 ('contact ME'), never 나를 연락해. Also note you can say 연락해 주세요 (verb + 주다 favor) or 연락 주세요 (noun + 주다), but NOT 연락하 주세요 (broken split).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 연락할게 when you mean 'you text me'.
연락할게(요) promises YOUR own action ('I'll reach out'). To ask them to contact you, say 연락해(요) or 연락 줘(요)/연락 주세요.
Marking the person with 을/를: 너를 연락해.
The contact target takes 한테/에게 ('to'): 나한테 연락해 ('contact me'). 연락하다 doesn't take a direct-object person.
Translating 'keep in touch' literally with unrelated idioms.
There's no body-part idiom; the verb is simply 연락하다. 'Let's keep in touch' = 연락해요 / 연락하고 지내요.

structuredNuance.t: 연락 (連絡: 'contact/communication') + 하다. Literally 'do contact'. Used for any channel — call, text, KakaoTalk message. In dating it is loaded: frequent mutual 연락 is the lifeblood of a budding relationship.

Said at the end of a date or a first meeting to express you want to continue the interaction. 연락해요 (polite) is safe with someone new; 연락해 (반말) for friends. The direction the action flows — toward you or them — is set entirely by the verb form, so choose carefully.

연락할게요 ('I'll contact you' — you initiate) vs. 연락해요 / 연락해 ('contact me / let's be in touch' — they initiate or mutual) vs. 연락 주세요 ('please reach out to me' — clearly requesting they act). Mixing them reverses who is supposed to text first.

연락해요 (let's be in touch, polite) → 연락해 (반말) → 연락할게요 (I'll reach out) → 연락 주세요 (please reach out to me) → 연락해 주세요 (please reach out to me, verb form) → 연락하고 지내요 ('let's stay in contact and get along').

Particle: the person you contact takes 한테/에게, not 을/를 — 나한테 연락해, never 나를 연락해. Don't literally translate 'keep in touch' as anything involving hands (손 잡고 있어 etc.) — the Korean is simply 연락하다. And 연락하 주세요 is broken; use 연락해 주세요 or 연락 주세요.

entries.english: I miss you
entries.shortExplanation: 보고 싶어요 is a practical expression meaning "I miss you".
entries.explanation: "I miss you" — that is 보고 싶어요 (bogo sipeoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 보고 싶어요 ("I miss you / I want to see you"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: I miss you / I want to see you
usagePhrases.note: Polite; tender, said to someone you care about romantically or as a close friend
반말, to a partner or very close friend — intimate

usagePhrases.en: I missed you / I've been missing you
usagePhrases.note: Past: best said at the moment of reunion, 'I was missing you'
많이 ('a lot') adds genuine warmth and longing — lovely for long-distance moments

examples.ko: 오늘 하루 종일 보고 싶었어요.
examples.romanization: oneul haru jongil bogo sipeosseoyo.
examples.en: I missed you all day today.
examples.note: 하루 종일 ('all day long') intensifies the longing; past tense is the most natural form

examples.ko: 멀리 있으니까 더 보고 싶네요.
examples.romanization: meolli isseunikka deo bogo simneyo.
examples.en: Being far apart makes me miss you even more.
examples.note: Long-distance context; 더 ('even more') + the gentle surprise/realization ending -네요

examples.ko: A: 나 도착했어. B: 잘 왔어, 보고 싶었어!
examples.romanization: A: na dochakaesseo. B: jal wasseo, bogo sipeosseo!
examples.en: A: I arrived. B: Welcome, I missed you!
examples.note: The reunion exchange; B's 보고 싶었어 lands warm the instant the person appears

entries.nuance: 보고 싶다 is literally 보다 ('to see') + -고 싶다 ('want to'), so it means BOTH 'I want to see you' and 'I miss you' — Korean fuses the two ideas because missing someone IS wanting to see them. It is the standard romantic and close-friendship 'I miss you', warmer and lighter than any clinical translation. The key contrast: don't use 그립다 / 그리워하다 ('to long for, to miss deeply') for everyday 'I miss you' to a partner you'll see soon — 그립다 is a heavy, often nostalgic longing for something distant, lost, or past (a hometown, a late grandparent, childhood), so 당신이 그리워요 to a partner you're meeting tomorrow sounds dramatic or song-lyric. Also distinguish 보고 싶다 (emotional 'miss you' — about the person) from 만나고 싶다 ('I want to meet up' — more about logistics). Particle trap: the person you miss takes SUBJECT marking — 네가/당신이 보고 싶어 (lit. 'YOU are want-to-see'), not the object 너를 보고 싶어 which learners reach for instinctively.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 그리워요 / 그립다 for someone you'll see soon.
그립다 is a heavy, nostalgic longing (for the lost or distant). Everyday 'I miss you' to a partner is 보고 싶어요. 그리워요 sounds melodramatic for a quick reunion.
Marking the person with 을/를: 너를 보고 싶어.
With -고 싶다 the desired object takes 이/가 (or 을/를 is debated, but for people the natural choice is 가): 네가 보고 싶어. Many learners over-apply 를.
Treating 보고 싶다 as only 'want to see', missing the 'miss you' sense.
Context makes it emotional: to a loved one, 보고 싶어요 means 'I miss you', not a neutral 'I'd like to see you'. Read it as the warm idiom.

structuredNuance.t: 보다 ('to see') + -고 싶다 ('want to'). Literally 'I want to see'. In emotional context to a loved one, this IS 'I miss you' — Korean collapses the two feelings because missing = wanting to see. Context makes the warm reading automatic.

Said to a romantic partner, a close friend, or family member. 보고 싶어요 (polite) works even with someone you're not yet deeply intimate with; 보고 싶어 (반말) is the tender form between partners. Most naturally in past tense 보고 싶었어요 when you reunite, or in ongoing statements ('I keep missing you').

그립다 / 그리워하다 = deep nostalgic longing for something distant, lost, or past (hometown, late relative, a past era). 보고 싶다 = everyday 'miss you' to a person you care about and will see again. Using 그리워요 to a partner you're seeing tomorrow sounds melodramatic. 만나고 싶다 leans toward logistics ('want to meet up'), while 보고 싶다 is purely the emotional 'I miss you'.

보고 싶어요 (polite) → 보고 싶어 (반말) → 보고 싶었어요 (past, at reunion) → 많이 보고 싶었어 (intensified) → 너무 보고 싶어서 못 참겠어 ('I miss you so much I can't stand it'). 빨리 보고 싶어 ('I want to see you soon') is the impatient variant.

Particle error: the person you miss takes 이/가 (subject), not 을/를 (object) — 네가 보고 싶어 ('YOU are want-to-see'), never 너를 보고 싶어. This feels backwards to English speakers. Also don't reach for 그립다 for an everyday 'I miss you' — reserve it for heavy nostalgic longing.

entries.english: Honey / babe
entries.shortExplanation: 자기야 is a practical expression meaning "Honey / babe".
entries.explanation: 자기야 (jagiya) = "Honey / babe". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 자기야 ("Honey / babe"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 반말; the go-to pet name between Korean couples, replacing the partner's name
The same word used as a subject or reference — '자기 오늘 어때?' ('how are you today, babe?')
A woman addressing an older boyfriend; romantic when directed at a partner
The married-couple equivalent — sweet but strictly for spouses; never for a dating partner

examples.ko: 자기야, 뭐 해?
examples.romanization: jagiya, mwo hae?
examples.en: Babe, what are you doing?
examples.note: The everyday couple opener replacing the name; 뭐 해? is the casual 'what are you up to?'

examples.ko: 자기야~ 나 이거 사 줘.
examples.romanization: jagiya~ na igeo sa jwo.
examples.en: Babe~ buy me this.
examples.note: Drawn-out 자기야~ + a request signals 애교 (cute wheedling behavior); the tilde shows the drawn-out vowel

examples.ko: A: 자기야, 오늘 너무 보고 싶었어. B: 나도 자기 보고 싶었어.
examples.romanization: A: jagiya, oneul neomu bogo sipeosseo. B: nado jagi bogo sipeosseo.
examples.en: A: Babe, I missed you so much today. B: I missed you too, babe.
examples.note: Couple exchange; B uses 자기 (without 야) as a softer reference — both forms natural

entries.nuance: 자기 (自己, lit. 'oneself') is repurposed as a romantic pet name; 자기야 adds the vocative particle 야 (used after vowel-ending words). As a couple term, it entirely replaces the partner's name in address — you stop calling your boyfriend 민준 and start calling him 자기야. It is exclusively couple language in 반말 register and would be bizarre said to anyone else. The stage and gender contrast is critical: 자기야 is gender-neutral and works at the dating stage; a woman often calls an older boyfriend 오빠 ('older brother') — affectionate and common; 여보 / 당신 are for MARRIED couples only. Using 여보 with a new partner is either a joke ('let's play house') or an odd misfire. Note: 자기 does mean 'oneself' grammatically (자기 자신 'oneself'), but between lovers the pet-name reading is unmistakable by context. English-speaker trap: don't try to use 당신 ('you/dear') as a neutral second-person pronoun in couple talk — 당신 to a stranger is aggressive; to a partner in everyday speech it's either formal-lyrical or married-register, not what couples actually say.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Calling a new girlfriend/boyfriend 여보.
여보 is the MARRIED couples' term ('dear'). For dating, the pet name is 자기야. 여보 to a new partner sounds like playing house.
Using 당신 as a casual 'you' to your partner.
당신 to a stranger is aggressive; to a partner it's married/lyrical register. In everyday couple talk use 자기 or their name, not 당신.
Reading 자기 only as the reflexive 'oneself'.
자기 does mean 'oneself' grammatically, but as a vocative to a lover it's 'babe/honey': 자기야. Context flips the meaning.

structuredNuance.t: 자기 (自己) literally means 'oneself, self' in grammar. Between couples, the same word is completely repurposed as 'babe/honey'. 자기야 adds the vocative 야 (used after vowel-ending words). Context makes it unmistakably the pet name.

Strictly for your romantic partner, in 반말. Calling anyone other than your partner 자기야 is jarring. Start using it once you're officially a couple (사귀다). Women often alternate 자기야 with 오빠 for an older boyfriend; men use 자기야 universally regardless of the partner's age relative to theirs.

자기야 (dating couples, gender-neutral) vs. 오빠 (woman to older boyfriend — affectionate but gendered) vs. 여보/당신 (married couples only). Don't use 여보 for a dating partner — it sounds like you're roleplaying being married. 여보 said in jest is funny; said seriously it confuses.

자기야 (vocative call) → 자기 (mid-sentence reference: '자기는 뭐 먹을 거야?') → 자기야~ (with drawn-out vowel for 애교) → 우리 자기 ('my babe', emphatic). Some couples switch to names or 오빠/자기 interchangeably once comfortable.

Don't read 자기 as the reflexive 'oneself' in couple context — between partners it's purely 'babe'. Don't use 당신 as a casual 'you' for your partner — 당신 is confrontational to strangers and lyrical/married-register to a partner; use 자기 or their name in everyday couple talk.

entries.english: Do you like me, or your friend(s) more?
entries.shortExplanation: 내가 좋아? 친구가 좋아? is a practical expression meaning "Do you like me, or your friend(s) more?".
entries.explanation: 내가 좋아? 친구가 좋아? (naega joa? chinguga joa?) means "Do you like me, or your friend(s) more?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 내가 좋아? 친구가 좋아? ("Me, or your friends — who do you like more?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Me, or your friends — who do you like more?
usagePhrases.note: 반말; a half-pouting, playful jealous question in a couple or close friendship
Polite, gentler version of fishing for reassurance

usagePhrases.ko: 나랑 친구 중에 누가 더 좋아?
usagePhrases.romanization: narang chingu junge nuga deo joa?
usagePhrases.en: Between me and your friend, who do you like more?
usagePhrases.note: Spelled-out 'between X and Y, who' version — slightly more direct
The expected reassuring comeback; 당연히 ('of course') + 너

examples.ko: 내가 좋아, 게임이 좋아?
examples.romanization: naega joa, geimi joa?
examples.en: Do you like me more, or your games?
examples.note: Swap 친구 for any rival (게임, 축구, etc.) to tease about divided attention — a widely used playful structure

examples.ko: 에이, 그걸 말이라고 해? 당연히 너지.
examples.romanization: ei, geugeol marirago hae? dangyeonhi neoji.
examples.en: Come on, you even have to ask? You, obviously.
examples.note: The reassuring comeback: 그걸 말이라고 해 ('is that even a question?') + 당연히 너 — textbook couple banter

examples.ko: A: 내가 좋아? 친구가 좋아? B: 아, 진짜! ...당연히 자기지.
examples.romanization: A: naega joa? chinguga joa? B: a, jinjja! ...dangyeonhi jagiji.
examples.en: A: Me or your friends? B: Ugh, seriously! ...You, obviously, babe.
examples.note: Real couple exchange; B's mock-exasperation then warm 자기 makes it cute

entries.nuance: 내가 좋아? 친구가 좋아? is the playful 'who do you like more, me or ___?' question a partner asks to fish for reassurance — equal parts 애교 (cute behavior) and 질투 (jealousy). It fits any rivalry slot: 내가 좋아? 게임이 좋아? / 내가 좋아? 축구가 좋아? — the structure is X가 좋아? Y가 좋아?. The verb is 좋다 ('to be good/likable'), an ADJECTIVE in Korean, so the liked thing takes the subject marker 이/가 — 내가 좋아? literally 'am I good (to you)?' = 'do you prefer me?'. This is the single biggest grammar trap: English speakers reach for 좋아하다 ('to like', a transitive verb) + 을/를, producing 나를 좋아해? — grammatical and understandable, but the comparison frame uses 좋다 + 이/가, not 좋아하다 + 를. The 'I' pronoun shifts: 나 → 내가 with the subject marker. Register is 반말; this is intimate couple-talk, never a question for coworkers or strangers.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 좋아하다 + 를 in the comparison: 나를 좋아해, 친구를 좋아해?
The teasing frame uses the adjective 좋다 with 가: 내가 좋아? 친구가 좋아? Using 좋아해 here breaks the idiom (though it's understandable).
Marking 'me' with 를: 내를 좋아?
좋다 is an adjective; what's liked takes 이/가, and 'I' becomes 내가. So it's 내가 좋아?, never 내를.
Saying it in 존댓말 to a non-partner.
This is intimate, teasing couple-talk. Asking a coworker or stranger 내가 좋아, 친구가 좋아? is bizarre. Keep it for someone you're dating.

structuredNuance.t: 내가 ('I/me' + 이/가 subject) + 좋아? ('am I good to you?'). 좋다 is an adjective meaning 'to be good/likable'; what is liked takes 이/가, not 을/를. The literal meaning 'am I good? is your friend good?' translates into 'do you prefer me or your friend?' — the comparison frame is built into the repeated 좋아.

Quintessential couple banter in 반말, usually said when a partner feels the other is spending too much time with friends, gaming, or anything that isn't them. Works as a gentle jealous tease, not a serious accusation. Only between romantic partners or very close friends; asking a coworker 내가 좋아? 친구가 좋아? would be bizarre.
좋다 + 가 (adjective frame, 내가 좋아?) vs. 좋아하다 + 를 (verb frame, 나를 좋아해?). Both mean 'do you like me?', but the comparison pattern uses 좋다: 내가 좋아? 친구가 좋아?. 더 좋다 ('like more') is the comparative: 내가 더 좋아?
내가 좋아? 친구가 좋아? → 내가 좋아? 게임이 좋아? → 내가 더 좋아? (simpler comparative) → 내가 더 좋아요? (polite). The reassuring answer pattern: 당연히 너지 / 당연히 자기지.

좋다 is an adjective; what's liked takes 이/가, and 'I' becomes 내가 — so 내가 좋아? (correct) vs. 나를 좋아해? (uses the verb 좋아하다, grammatical but breaks the comparison-frame idiom). Never 내를 (impossible: 나 + 를 would be me as direct object, and 'I' contracted is 내, not 내를).

entries.english: I'm jealous
entries.shortExplanation: 질투 나요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm jealous".
entries.explanation: "I'm jealous" — that is 질투 나요 (jiltu nayo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 질투 나요 ("I'm jealous"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; admitting jealousy, often with a half-playful smile in a relationship
반말, to a partner or close friend you can be honest with
Telling someone to stop acting jealous; 질투하다 = the active behavior
Owning it openly and a bit cutely; -는 거야 = 'it's that I'm doing'

examples.ko: 솔직히 말하면 질투 나.
examples.romanization: soljiki malhamyeon jiltu na.
examples.en: If I'm honest, I'm jealous.
examples.note: 솔직히 말하면 ('if I'm honest') is the natural lead-in for admitting feelings you'd normally hide

examples.ko: 다른 사람이랑 웃으니까 질투 났어.
examples.romanization: dareun saramirang useunikka jiltu nasseo.
examples.en: I got jealous when you laughed with someone else.
examples.note: Naming the specific trigger: 다른 사람이랑 웃다 ('laughing with another person') + 질투 나다 past

examples.ko: A: 왜 그래? B: 질투하는 거 아니야! ...조금 질투 나긴 해.
examples.romanization: A: wae geurae? B: jiltuhaneun geo aniya! ...jogeum jiltu nagin hae.
examples.en: A: What's wrong? B: I'm not jealous! ...Okay, maybe a little.
examples.note: Classic deny-then-admit pattern; 질투 나긴 해 = 'I am, to some extent, jealous' — the 긴 qualifies

entries.nuance: 질투 나다 is 질투 (嫉妬, 'jealousy') + 나다 ('to arise/come out') — jealousy framed as a feeling that wells up in you rather than something you actively do. The same 나다 appears in 화나다 ('get angry'), 짜증 나다 ('get annoyed'), 겁나다 ('be scared') — Korean systematically treats emotions as arising events. The key contrast: 질투 나다 (feeling wells up) vs. 질투하다 (the behavior, what you do with that feeling or how you act it out). 'I feel jealous' = 질투 나(요); 'stop being jealous' = 질투하지 마 (active verb, commanding behavior). There is also 부럽다 ('to envy', wanting what someone has with no romantic sting): your friend's new phone makes you 부럽다, not 질투. English blurs 'jealous' and 'envious'; Korean separates them sharply. The particle trap: 질투(가) 나다 takes the feeling as grammatical subject — never force a 'I jealous YOU' structure like 너를 질투해. Register: 질투 나요 is fine and even endearing with a partner when said semi-playfully; in serious accusation it escalates.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 부럽다 when you mean romantic jealousy.
부럽다 is envy (wanting what someone has, no romance). Feeling jealous about a partner is 질투 나다. 'I'm jealous (of who you're with)' = 질투 나, not 부러워.
Saying 질투해요 to describe your own feeling.
질투하다 leans toward the behavior/accusation ('to act jealous'). To say you FEEL jealous, the natural phrase is 질투 나요 (the feeling arises).
Forcing an English structure like 너를 질투해 for 'I'm jealous of you'.
질투(가) 나다 takes the feeling as subject: 질투 나. To say you got jealous over a situation, name the trigger + 질투 났어, e.g. 다른 사람이랑 있어서 질투 났어 ('I got jealous because you were with someone else').

structuredNuance.t: 질투 ('jealousy', 嫉妬) + 나다 ('to arise/come out'). Literally 'jealousy arises [in me]'. This framing treats emotions as events that visit you — the same pattern as 화나다 ('anger comes out') and 짜증 나다 ('annoyance arises'). The real meaning: 'I feel jealous'.

Said to a romantic partner when they interact with someone in a way that stirs possessive feelings. 질투 나요 (polite) is safe even in early dating; 질투 나 (반말) is more intimate. Said semi-playfully it's cute and endearing; said as a serious confrontation it changes the dynamic significantly.

질투 나다 (feeling arises — 'I feel jealous') vs. 질투하다 (acting jealous — 'to be jealous, to act on it'): 나는 질투 나 = 'I feel jealous inside'; 질투하지 마 = 'stop acting jealous'. Also: 부럽다 ('I envy you/them' — coveting what someone has, zero romantic possessiveness). Korean separates 질투 (romantic/possessive jealousy) and 부럽다 (envy over someone's advantage).
질투 나요 (polite present) → 질투 나 (반말) → 질투 났어 (past: jealousy arose) → 질투하지 마 (stop it) → 질투 나는 거야? (are you jealous?). Intensified: 진짜 질투 나 / 너무 질투 나.

English blurs 'jealous' and 'envious'; Korean splits them (질투 vs. 부럽다). Particle trap: 질투(가) 나다 takes the emotion as subject — don't say 너를 질투해 ('I jealous you') — instead name the trigger: 네가 그 사람이랑 있어서 질투 났어 ('I got jealous because you were with that person').

entries.english: Don't cheat (on me)
entries.shortExplanation: 바람피우지 마 is a practical expression meaning "Don't cheat (on me)".
entries.explanation: 바람피우지 마 (barampiuji ma) = "Don't cheat (on me)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 바람피우지 마 ("Don't cheat"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 반말; said to a partner, either as a half-joking caution or in deadly seriousness
Polite-formal version; the topic is heavy so the -요 softens the confrontation
The accusing question, past tense; 설마 바람피운 거야? ('don't tell me you cheated?') is also common

usagePhrases.en: Apparently they cheated / are having an affair
usagePhrases.note: Gossip form; 바람나다 = the affair happened, 대 = 'I heard/apparently'

examples.ko: 설마 바람피운 거야?
examples.romanization: seolma barampiun geoya?
examples.en: Don't tell me you cheated?
examples.note: 설마 ('surely not' / 'don't tell me') signals shocked suspicion — the accusation is still being denied mentally

examples.ko: 걔네 헤어졌대, 한 명이 바람났대.
examples.romanization: gyaene heeojyeotdae, han myeongi baramnatdae.
examples.en: They broke up — apparently one of them cheated.
examples.note: 바람나다 in gossip: 바람나다 = the affair surfaced; 헤어지다 = broke up

examples.ko: A: 바람피우지 마. B: 무슨 말이야, 내가 왜?
examples.romanization: A: barampiuji ma. B: museun mariya, naega wae?
examples.en: A: Don't cheat on me. B: What are you talking about, why would I?
examples.note: The cautionary warning and the defensive reply; -지 마 is 반말 command, B's 내가 왜 is the protest

entries.nuance: 바람피우다 is a fixed idiom for cheating / having an affair: 바람 ('wind') + 피우다 ('to cause/give off') — 'to kick up wind', meaning to stray or be unfaithful. It is the standard, everyday word for romantic infidelity. Two related but distinct forms confuse learners: 바람피우다 (active verb, 'to cheat' — what the cheater intentionally does: 바람피우지 마) vs. 바람나다 (inchoative, 'an affair occurred / got swept into one' — describes the event or situation: 바람났대 'I heard they had an affair'). Command/accusation form is always 바람피우다; the gossip/news form uses 바람나다. 속이다 ('to deceive/lie') is general deception — romantic infidelity specifically is 바람피우다, so 속이다 sounds too mild or generic. Particle: if you name the affair partner, use 랑/하고 ('with') — 다른 사람이랑 바람피우다; you don't mark anyone with 를 in this structure. Register: 바람피우지 마 is 반말 and heavy; even joking about it carries real emotional weight.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 바람 literally as 'wind' and getting lost.
바람피우다 is a fixed idiom for cheating; 바람 here is not weather. Learn the whole phrase as 'to cheat', don't decode it word-by-word.
Confusing 바람피우다 and 바람나다.
바람피우다 = the active 'to cheat' (what one does); 바람나다 = 'an affair occurred / got swept into one' (the event). Command form is 바람피우지 마.
Using 속이다 for cheating on a partner.
속이다 is general 'to deceive/lie'. Romantic infidelity is specifically 바람피우다. 'He cheated' = 바람피웠어, not 속였어 (which just means 'lied').

structuredNuance.t: 바람 ('wind') + 피우다 ('to give off, produce'). Literally 'to kick up wind'. This is a fixed idiom for romantic infidelity — do not decode it word by word. The actual meaning is 'to cheat on a partner / have an affair'.

Said to a partner as a half-joking preemptive warning ('just don't cheat!') or as a serious confrontation. Always between people in a romantic relationship — not a topic for strangers or casual acquaintances. 바람피우지 마 is 반말 command; use 바람피우지 마세요 if you want to soften the confrontation with politeness.

바람피우다 (active 'to cheat', what one intentionally does) vs. 바람나다 (inchoative 'an affair occurred / was swept into one' — describes the event/state). Use 바람피우지 마 for the command; use 바람났대 for gossip/reporting. Also 속이다 ('to deceive/lie') is generic; romantic infidelity specifically is 바람피우다.
바람피우다 → 바람피우지 마 (command) → 바람피웠어? (past accusation) → 바람피운 것 같아 ('seems like they cheated'). 바람나다 → 바람났어 (past, stated) → 바람났대 (reported hearsay).

The literal trap: 바람 means 'wind' but the idiom has nothing to do with weather — never translate it piece by piece. The verb trap: using 속이다 ('to lie/deceive') for cheating — 속이다 is too generic; 바람피우다 is the specific romance-infidelity word.

entries.english: We go well together
entries.shortExplanation: 우리 잘 어울려요 is a practical expression meaning "We go well together".
entries.explanation: 우리 잘 어울려요 (uri jal eoullyeoyo) means "We go well together". Say it as one set phrase — for example 우리 잘 어울려요 ("We suit each other well"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; saying a couple looks/fits good together — lovely early-dating or compliment line
반말, to your partner — warm and affirming

usagePhrases.en: You two really suit each other
usagePhrases.note: Said about a couple by an onlooker; 진짜 ('really') — a compliment from the outside looking in

usagePhrases.en: You're a match made in heaven
usagePhrases.note: Stronger praise; 천생연분 = destined pair — for a couple that clearly fits perfectly

examples.ko: 우리 진짜 잘 어울리는 것 같아.
examples.romanization: uri jinjja jal eoullineun geot gata.
examples.en: I think we really go well together.
examples.note: -는 것 같다 ('I think/seems like') sweetly softens what might sound overconfident — it's a modest hedge

examples.ko: 이 옷 색이 너한테 잘 어울려요.
examples.romanization: i ot saegi neohante jal eoullyeoyo.
examples.en: This outfit's color really suits you.
examples.note: 어울리다 for clothes suiting a person — same verb, shows the word's dual use for couples AND style

examples.ko: A: 우리 잘 어울리지? B: 응, 완전 잘 어울려!
examples.romanization: A: uri jal eoulliji? B: eung, wanjeon jal eoullyeo!
examples.en: A: We go well together, right? B: Yes, totally!
examples.note: Fishing for reassurance and the enthusiastic confirmation — natural couple micro-conversation

entries.nuance: 어울리다 means 'to match / suit / go well together', and 우리 잘 어울려요 conveys that a couple is a good fit — looks good together, has chemistry. The same verb covers clothing ('this color suits you') and interpersonal compatibility, so it spans both the visual ('you look great together') and the relational ('we click'). The crucial contrast: 어울리다 (compatibility/fit) vs. 사귀다 (official relationship status) — saying 잘 어울려요 doesn't mean you're an official couple, only that you'd be a good one. For destiny-level praise, escalate to 천생연분 ('heaven-made match') or 잘 맞다 ('we click'). The difference between 어울리다 and 맞다: 잘 어울리다 leans toward the visual and social fit ('you look right together, you complement each other'), while 잘 맞다 ('to click') is about personality alignment and compatibility from the inside. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) 어울리다 is intransitive — 'it suits you' is 너한테 잘 어울려 (한테/에게 for the target), never 너를 어울려. (2) Don't mangle the stem — it is 어울리다, conjugating 어울려요; not 어울다 or 어우르다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Marking the person with 를: 너를 잘 어울려.
어울리다 is intransitive; the one something suits takes 한테/에게: 너한테 잘 어울려 ('it suits you'). For a couple, just use a plural subject: 우리 잘 어울려.
Thinking 잘 어울려 means 'we're officially dating'.
어울리다 = compatible / go well together (fit), not relationship status. To say you're a couple, that's 사귀다. You can suit each other without being official.
Confusing 어울리다 with 어울다/어우르다.
The verb is 어울리다 ('to match/suit'). 'It suits you' = 잘 어울려요. Don't mangle the stem; conjugate 어울리다 → 어울려요.

structuredNuance.t: 어울리다 = 'to go together harmoniously, to match, to suit'. 우리 잘 어울려요 = 'we (잘 well) go together'. The literal meaning is already the real meaning, but the word covers both the visual (this outfit suits you) and the relational (we are a good match as a couple).

Said to a partner or about a couple (by a third party). 우리 잘 어울려요 (polite) is a warm, early-dating affirmation; 우리 잘 어울려 (반말) is the intimate version. 두 사람 잘 어울려요 is the compliment a matchmaker, friend, or family member gives when seeing a couple together.

어울리다 (visual + social fit: 'go together, look right') vs. 잘 맞다 ('click', personality compatibility from within). A couple can 잘 어울리다 without 잘 맞다 (look perfect but have friction) or vice versa. 천생연분 ('destined pair', heaven-made match) is the superlative for both.

우리 잘 어울려요 → 우리 잘 어울려 → 잘 어울리는 커플 ('a well-matched couple') → 너한테 잘 어울려 (clothes suit you) → 천생연분이에요 (you're a perfect match). The compliment 잘 어울린다 (dictionary form -ㄴ다) is the casual declarative used observationally.

(1) 어울리다 is intransitive — use 한테/에게 for who something suits (너한테 잘 어울려), never 너를 어울려. (2) Stem confusion: the verb is 어울리다 → 어울려요; don't substitute 어울다 or 어우르다 (different or non-existent). (3) Don't confuse 잘 어울리다 ('good fit, look right together') with 잘 맞다 ('click in personality').

entries.english: Stop playing hard to get
entries.shortExplanation: 밀당하지 마 is a practical expression meaning "Stop playing hard to get".
entries.explanation: "Stop playing hard to get" — that is 밀당하지 마 (mildanghaji ma). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 밀당하지 마 ("Stop playing hot and cold / stop the push-pull"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Stop playing hot and cold / stop the push-pull
usagePhrases.note: 반말; calling out someone's calculated hot-and-cold behavior

usagePhrases.en: Please don't play hard to get
usagePhrases.note: Polite version of the same plea — softens a potentially confrontational topic

usagePhrases.en: Are you playing hard to get?
usagePhrases.note: Asking half-amused or half-frustrated if this is a deliberate tactic

usagePhrases.en: You're really good at the push-pull game
usagePhrases.note: A teasing remark about someone's skill at it; 잘하다 ('good at')

examples.ko: 솔직하게 말해, 밀당하지 마.
examples.romanization: soljikage malhae, mildanghaji ma.
examples.en: Just be honest with me, stop playing games.
examples.note: 솔직하게 ('honestly') is directly contrasted with the game-playing — be real instead

examples.ko: 답장 일부러 늦게 해? 밀당하는 거야?
examples.romanization: dapjang ilbureo neutge hae? mildanghaneun geoya?
examples.en: Are you texting back late on purpose? Is this push-pull?
examples.note: 일부러 ('on purpose') names the calculated tactic behind delayed replies

examples.ko: A: 밀당도 적당히 해야지. B: 나 밀당 같은 거 안 해!
examples.romanization: A: mildangdo jeokdanghi haeyaji. B: na mildang gateun geo an hae!
examples.en: A: You should keep the push-pull in moderation. B: I don't play those games!
examples.note: 적당히 해야지 ('do it in moderation') + the defensive denial — typical back-and-forth

entries.nuance: 밀당 is a slangy contraction of 밀고 당기기 ('pushing and pulling'), from 밀다 ('push') + 당기다 ('pull') — the calculated pre-dating game of alternating interest and coolness to keep the other person hooked. 밀당하다 = to play this game. It covers deliberate mixed signals: texting enthusiastically then going quiet, seeming available then suddenly busy. Very current Korean slang, dominant among young adults (roughly under 40); older Koreans may not use the term. The important contrast is 밀당 (ongoing strategic push-pull pattern) vs. 튕기다 ('to bounce / play coy', specifically feigning reluctance or disinterest at a single moment to seem less eager — like declining the first ask-out to appear hard-to-get). 밀당 is a repeated pattern; 튕기다 is a one-time coy refusal. English-speaker pitfall: there is no word-by-word route — 게임 하다 literally means playing a videogame; the dating game is 밀당하다. And it's a 하다-compound: 밀당하다, 밀당하지 마, never 밀당 주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'play games' as 게임 하다.
게임 하다 means playing a (video)game. The dating push-pull is 밀당하다. 'Stop playing games (with my feelings)' = 밀당하지 마, not 게임 하지 마.
Using 밀당 in formal or professional settings.
밀당 is casual slang for romance/relationships. It sounds out of place in formal speech or non-dating contexts. Keep it to friends and partners.
Confusing 밀당 (ongoing strategy) with 튕기다 (feigning reluctance once).
밀당하다 is the continuous hot-and-cold game; 튕기다 is acting coy/refusing at a moment to seem less eager. Related but not identical — pick by whether it's a one-time coyness or a pattern.

structuredNuance.t: 밀당 = contraction of 밀고 당기기 ('pushing and pulling'), from 밀다 (push) + 당기다 (pull). Literally 'pushing and pulling'. The real meaning: the calculated dating tactic of hot-and-cold behavior — showing interest then pulling back, to keep someone invested.

Used in casual conversation between people in the 썸 or early-dating stage when one person perceives the other's behavior as strategically inconsistent. Pure informal/반말 register — said to a crush, partner, or a friend describing someone else's behavior. Don't use in formal speech or around older people unfamiliar with the slang.

밀당하다 (ongoing push-pull strategy, a repeated pattern) vs. 튕기다 ('play coy / bounce', a single moment of feigning reluctance — e.g. turning down a first ask-out to seem less eager). 밀당 is the continuous game; 튕기다 is one strategic refusal. Related but not the same.
밀당 (noun) → 밀당하다 (verb) → 밀당하지 마 (stop it, command) → 밀당하는 거야? (are you doing this?) → 밀당 고수 ('push-pull expert'). Related compound: 썸과 밀당 ('the 썸 stage and the push-pull game').
게임 하다 = playing a (video)game, NOT playing romantic games. The dating game is 밀당하다. Also 밀당 is a 하다-noun: 밀당하다, 밀당하지 마 — never 밀당 주세요 or 밀당 줘.

entries.english: We've hit a rough patch / lost the spark
entries.shortExplanation: 권태기가 왔어요 is a practical expression meaning "We've hit a rough patch / lost the spark".
entries.explanation: 권태기가 왔어요 (gwontaegiga wasseoyo) = "We've hit a rough patch / lost the spark". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 권태기가 왔어요 ("We've hit a slump in our relationship"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: We've hit a slump in our relationship
usagePhrases.note: Polite; describing a stale phase in an established relationship — confiding to anyone
반말, confiding to a close friend

usagePhrases.en: I think we're in a slump
usagePhrases.note: Tentative -ㄴ/ㄹ 것 같다 ('seems like') — not yet sure, testing the idea

usagePhrases.en: We got through the rough patch
usagePhrases.note: 극복하다 ('to overcome') — came out the other side, now stronger

examples.ko: 요즘 권태기 온 것 같아. 예전 같지 않아.
examples.romanization: yojeum gwontaegi on geot gata. yejeon gatji ana.
examples.en: I think the slump has hit lately. It doesn't feel like before.
examples.note: -ㄴ 것 같아 (tentative 'seems like') + 예전 같지 않다 ('not like before') — two natural ways to voice the feeling

examples.ko: 3년 사귀다 보니까 권태기가 오더라고요.
examples.romanization: 3nyeon sagwida bonikka gwontaegiga odeoragoyo.
examples.en: Dating for 3 years, the slump eventually set in.
examples.note: -더라고요 reports a realized, experienced truth — 'I noticed that...' — very natural in this frame

examples.ko: A: 요즘 권태기야? B: 글쎄... 권태기 극복하고 싶어.
examples.romanization: A: yojeum gwontaegiya? B: geulsse... gwontaegi geukbokago sipeo.
examples.en: A: Are we in a slump these days? B: I don't know... I want to work through it.
examples.note: Naming the phase and immediately pivoting to 극복 ('overcoming') — the hopeful couple response

entries.nuance: 권태기 (倦怠期, 'weariness period') is the relationship slump — the stage in a long-term couple when excitement fades and daily life feels routine, like 'the honeymoon's over' or 'we've lost the spark'. The fixed collocation is 권태기가 오다 ('the slump arrives/comes') — Korean frames emotional phases as visitors that come to you, the same structure as 사춘기가 오다 ('puberty hits') and 감기가 오다 ('a cold comes'). This framing is important: learners wrongly try 권태기를 하다 or 가지다 (to have/do it as an object), but it 'arrives'. The contrast: 권태기 (a phase within an ongoing relationship, with the possibility of 극복 'overcoming') is entirely different from 헤어지다 (actually breaking up). Saying 권태기 왔어 does NOT mean the couple is over. Also 권태기 implies a relationship of some duration — you wouldn't use it for a two-week fling; for something that fizzled fast, say 흐지부지됐어 instead. Register: 권태기 is everyday vocabulary, equally natural in polite speech or 반말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 권태기를 해요 / 권태기를 가지고 있어요.
권태기 collocates with 오다 ('to come'): 권태기가 왔어요. You don't 'do' or 'possess' it as an object. The slump 'arrives'.
Thinking 권태기 means you broke up.
권태기 is a stale/bored phase WITHIN a relationship, often overcome (권태기 극복). Breaking up is 헤어지다. 권태기 왔어 means the spark faded, not that it's over.
Using 권태기 for a brand-new fling.
권태기 presupposes a longer relationship that's gone stale. For a short thing losing steam, you'd say it fizzled (흐지부지됐어), not 권태기.

structuredNuance.t: 권태기 (倦怠期) = 倦 (weary) + 怠 (sluggish/idle) + 期 (period). Literally 'the period of weariness'. In relationship terms: the phase where excitement fades and things feel routine. 오다 ('come') treats it as a visiting phase — 'the slump arrived'.

Used to describe a stale phase in an established relationship — implies the couple has been together long enough to have developed routine. Said to a close friend you're confiding in, or between partners acknowledging the phase. Not a term for a new relationship or casual fling.

권태기 (boredom/stale phase within a relationship — can be overcome) vs. 헤어지다 (breaking up, the relationship ends). 권태기 came = still together but struggling; 헤어졌어 = it's over. Also 흐지부지되다 ('fizzle out', for short things that never built momentum) is for new/casual things losing steam, not for an established relationship.
권태기가 오다 (arrive) → 권태기인 것 같다 (seems like we're in it) → 권태기를 극복하다 (overcome the slump) → 권태기가 풀리다 ('the slump loosens/resolves'). Intensified: 심한 권태기 ('a severe slump').

(1) Verb error: 권태기가 오다 (it 'comes') — never 권태기를 하다 or 가지다. (2) Don't assume 권태기 means they broke up — it's a phase within the relationship. (3) Don't use 권태기 for a brand-new or short relationship; the word implies established history.

entries.english: Let's break up
entries.shortExplanation: 우리 헤어져요 is a practical expression meaning "Let's break up".
entries.explanation: 우리 헤어져요 (uri heeojyeoyo) means "Let's break up". Say it as one set phrase — for example 우리 헤어져요 ("Let's break up"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the breakup line said gently but with finality — heavy even with -요
반말, to a partner; 헤어지자 ('let's') is the slightly softer 반말 version
A softer phrasing — 'stop meeting' rather than the blunt 헤어지다; somewhat kinder
Reporting the breakup to a third party, past tense — what you tell friends

examples.ko: 미안해. 우리 헤어지자.
examples.romanization: mianhae. uri heeojija.
examples.en: I'm sorry. Let's break up.
examples.note: -자 ('let's') is 반말; 미안해 cushions the blow — the standard Korean breakup structure leads with an apology

examples.ko: 우리 그만 만나는 게 좋겠어요.
examples.romanization: uri geuman mannaneun ge jokesseoyo.
examples.en: I think it'd be better for us to stop seeing each other.
examples.note: -는 게 좋겠어요 ('I think it'd be better to') — a gentle, indirect breakup phrasing Koreans use to soften the blow

examples.ko: A: 우리 헤어지자. B: 왜? 무슨 일이야?
examples.romanization: A: uri heeojija. B: wae? museun iriya?
examples.en: A: Let's break up. B: Why? What's going on?
examples.note: The shocked B response — 왜? 무슨 일이야? is the natural reply when a partner suddenly says this

entries.nuance: 헤어지다 means 'to break up / part ways', and 우리 헤어져요 is the direct breakup line. Crucially, 헤어지다 is reciprocal and intransitive — both people part, so the partner is marked with 와/랑/하고 ('with'), NOT 을/를: 남자친구랑 헤어졌어요 ('I broke up WITH my boyfriend'). The single most common learner error is 남자친구를 헤어졌어요 with the object particle — you part WITH someone, you don't 'break up someone'. Note 헤어지다 also means simply 'to part ways' in a neutral, non-romantic sense (after meeting a friend: 여기서 헤어져요 'let's say goodbye here'), so context determines the weight. For a gentler breakup, Koreans reach for 그만 만나다 ('stop seeing each other') rather than the blunt 헤어지다. Don't confuse 헤어지다 (mutual parting) with 차다 (one person dumps the other) and 차이다 (to get dumped). Register: even the polite 헤어져요 is a heavy line; the word itself signals the end.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Marking the partner with 을/를: 남자친구를 헤어졌어요.
헤어지다 is reciprocal ('part WITH'): the partner takes 랑/와/하고. Say 남자친구랑 헤어졌어요. You don't break someone up as a direct object.
Confusing 헤어지다 with 차다/차이다.
헤어지다 = mutually parted. 차다 = 'to dump (someone)'; 차이다 = 'to get dumped'. 'I got dumped' is 차였어요, not 헤어졌어요 (which is neutral 'we broke up').
Using only the blunt 헤어져 when you want to soften it.
헤어지자 is direct. To be gentler, Koreans say 우리 그만 만나자 / 그만 만나는 게 좋겠어 ('let's stop seeing each other'), which lands softer.

structuredNuance.t: 헤어지다 = 'to come apart, to part ways'. In dating context, 우리 헤어져요 = 'let's break up'. The verb is reciprocal (both people part), not one-directional. The same word is used neutrally after any meeting ('let's say goodbye here'), so context carries the romantic weight.

Said to a partner to end a romantic relationship. 우리 헤어져요 (polite) is the slightly gentler form; 우리 헤어지자 (반말, 'let's') is the standard direct form between couples. Koreans typically lead with 미안해 ('I'm sorry') before the actual line. This is never a casual or public conversation.

헤어지다 (mutual parting, neutral as to who ended it) vs. 차다 ('to dump', one-directional — the dumper's act) vs. 차이다 ('to get dumped' — the dumpee's experience). For softer phrasing: 그만 만나다 / 그만 만나는 게 좋겠어. 헤어지자 is blunter; 그만 만나자 sounds slightly kinder.
우리 헤어져요 (polite) → 우리 헤어지자 (반말 suggestion 'let's') → 우리 그만 만나요 (softer) → 헤어졌어요 (past, reporting) → 헤어지고 싶어요 ('I want to break up'). The comitative: 남자친구랑 헤어졌어요.
헤어지다 is intransitive and reciprocal — the partner takes 랑/와/하고 ('with'), NOT 을/를. 남자친구랑 헤어졌어요 is correct; 남자친구를 헤어졌어요 is the #1 learner error. You part WITH someone, you don't 'break up someone'.

entries.english: I want to get back together
entries.shortExplanation: 재회하고 싶어요 is a practical expression meaning "I want to get back together".
entries.explanation: "I want to get back together" — that is 재회하고 싶어요 (jaehoehago sipeoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 재회하고 싶어요 ("I want to get back together"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: I want to get back together
usagePhrases.note: Polite-formal; earnest and slightly literary — wanting to reunite with an ex

usagePhrases.en: I want to see you / be together again
usagePhrases.note: 반말, warmer and plainer than the formal 재회 — what you'd actually whisper to an ex
A tender, hopeful invitation to restart; 다시 시작하다 ('start again') feels fresh and forward-looking

usagePhrases.en: I got back together with my ex-boyfriend
usagePhrases.note: Reporting it to a friend; 전 남자친구 ('ex-boyfriend') + 랑

examples.ko: 헤어졌지만 아직도 재회하고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: heeojyeotjiman ajikdo jaehoehago sipeoyo.
examples.en: We broke up, but I still want to get back together.
examples.note: 헤어졌지만 ('though we split') sets up the longing; 아직도 ('still') intensifies the lingering feeling

examples.ko: 우리 다시 만날 수 있을까? 한 번만 더 해보자.
examples.romanization: uri dasi mannal su isseulkka? han beonman deo haeboja.
examples.en: Can we get back together? Let's try just one more time.
examples.note: 다시 만나다 + 한 번만 더 ('just once more') — the emotionally raw appeal; -ㄹ 수 있을까 adds uncertain hope

examples.ko: A: 재회해도 똑같을까 봐 무서워요. B: 이번엔 다를 거야.
examples.romanization: A: jaehoehaedo ttokgateulkka bwa museowoyo. B: ibeonen dareul geoya.
examples.en: A: I'm scared it'll be the same even if we reunite. B: This time will be different.
examples.note: -ㄹ까 봐 ('afraid that') voices the core reunion fear; B's 이번엔 다를 거야 is the classic reassurance

entries.nuance: 재회하다 (再會 + 하다) means 'to reunite / get back together' after an actual breakup. It is the formal-ish or literary word for rekindling; in everyday speech Koreans almost always say the simpler 다시 만나다 ('meet again') — 전 남친이랑 다시 만나요 is what someone tells a friend, while 재회하고 싶어요 is more earnest/formal, like something from a drama monologue. Don't confuse 재회 ('reunite after a breakup') with 화해하다 ('to make up / reconcile after a fight while still together') — 화해 is for in-relationship disputes, 재회 is for after 헤어지다. Also 다시 만나다 carries ambiguity in context: with an ex it naturally reads as romantic reunion, but without context it can simply mean 'let's meet again sometime' — context resolves it. Particle: the ex takes 랑/와 ('with'), not 를 — 전 여자친구랑 재회했어요. 재회 is a 하다-noun: 재회하다, 재회하고 싶다, never 재회 주세요 or 재회를 원해요 (unnatural). Register: 재회하고 싶어요 (polite-earnest); 다시 만나고 싶어 (intimate 반말, what you'd actually say).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Marking the ex with 을/를: 전 남자친구를 재회했어요.
재회/만나다 take 랑/와 ('with'): 전 남자친구랑 재회했어요. The reunion partner is not a direct object.
Confusing 재회 (get back together) with 화해 (reconcile after a fight).
화해하다 = make up while still together after an argument. 재회하다 = reunite after an actual breakup. Use 재회 only if you'd split up.
Overusing formal 재회 in casual conversation.
재회 sounds literary. In everyday speech Koreans say 다시 만나다: 전 남친이랑 다시 만나기로 했어 ('decided to get back with my ex'). Save 재회하다 for earnest/formal moments.

structuredNuance.t: 재회 (再會) = 再 (again) + 會 (meet/gather). Literally 're-meet'. 재회하다 = 'to reunite'. In a dating context this specifically means getting back together with an ex after a breakup — not just seeing someone again socially.

Said after a real breakup when feelings linger and you want to try again. 재회하고 싶어요 is more earnest/formal — works in a sincere face-to-face moment with the ex or when reporting to someone. 다시 만나고 싶어 is the warmer 반말 you'd say directly to an ex late at night over the phone.

재회하다 (reunite after a breakup — formal, literary) vs. 다시 만나다 (everyday 'get back together' OR just 'see each other again' — context-dependent) vs. 화해하다 ('reconcile after a fight while still together' — NOT after a breakup). Use 화해 for in-relationship conflict; 재회 only after 헤어지다.
재회하다 → 재회하고 싶어요 (I want to reunite) → 재회했어요 (we got back together) → 전 남자친구랑 재회했어 (reported). Casual equivalent: 다시 만나고 싶어 → 다시 시작하자 ('let's start over').
(1) Partner takes 랑/와, not 를: 전 남자친구랑 재회했어요. (2) 재회 is a 하다-noun — 재회하다 / 재회하고 싶다, never 재회 주세요. (3) Overusing formal 재회 in casual conversation — 다시 만나다 sounds far more natural in real speech.

entries.english: No really, I'm fine
entries.shortExplanation: 아니에요, 괜찮아요 is a practical expression meaning "No really, I'm fine".
entries.explanation: 아니에요, 괜찮아요 (anieyo, gwaenchanayo) means "No really, I'm fine". Say it as one set phrase — for example 아니에요, 괜찮아요 ("No really, it's fine"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; a firmer, warmer double 'no thanks'
반말, refusing a friend
Formal 합쇼체, to staff or in business
Add 진짜 ('really') to insist when they keep offering

examples.ko: 아니에요, 괜찮아요.
examples.romanization: anieyo, gwaenchanayo.
examples.en: No really, I'm fine.
examples.note: Said while gently pushing back when someone insists

examples.ko: 이거 가져가세요. — 아니에요, 괜찮아요. 마음만 받을게요.
examples.romanization: igeo gajyeogaseyo. — anieyo, gwaenchanayo. maeumman badeulgeyo.
examples.en: Take this. — No really, I'm fine. I appreciate the thought.
examples.note: 마음만 받을게요 ('I'll just take the thought') softens the refusal

examples.ko: 제가 도와드릴게요. — 아, 아니에요, 괜찮아요. 혼자 할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: jega dowadeurilgeyo. — a, anieyo, gwaenchanayo. honja hal su isseoyo.
examples.en: Let me help you. — Oh no, it's fine. I can do it alone.
examples.note: Declining offered help while reassuring them

entries.nuance: 아니에요, 괜찮아요 stacks 아니에요 ('it's not so / no') in front of 괜찮아요 to make a refusal that is both clear and warm — the 아니에요 firmly turns down the offer while 괜찮아요 reassures 'I'm okay, don't worry about me.' Koreans typically offer two or three times out of politeness, so you often need this stronger version when one 괜찮아요 isn't taken. Register: 아니에요, 괜찮아요 is polite; 아니야, 괜찮아 with friends; 아닙니다, 괜찮습니다 formally. The key learner point is that 아니에요 (the soft 'it's not / no') is the natural refusal particle here, NOT 아니요 — though both exist, 아니에요 flows better before 괜찮아요 and sounds gentler. A trap: do NOT decline a gift or kindness with a cold single 싫어요 ('I don't like/want it'), which is for genuine dislike and sounds harsh; 싫어요 to a host's food can be offensive. Another English-speaker error is over-insisting in a Western way ('no, no, I really couldn't') with literal translations; the natural Korean cushions are 마음만 받을게요 ('I'll accept just the thought') or 부담스러워요 ('it makes me feel indebted').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Refusing food or a gift with 싫어요.
싫어요 means 'I dislike/don't want it' and sounds harsh or ungrateful about someone's kindness. Use 아니에요, 괜찮아요 to decline warmly.
Confusing 아니에요 with 아니요 and overusing the curt form.
아니요 is a plain 'no'; 아니에요 ('it's not so') is the softer refusal that pairs naturally here: 아니에요, 괜찮아요. Lead with 아니에요 to sound gentle.
Giving up after one 괜찮아요 and accepting because they offered again.
Re-offering is Korean politeness, not pressure. If you truly don't want it, repeat 아니에요, 괜찮아요 or 진짜 괜찮아요 — repetition is expected, not rude.

structuredNuance.t: 아니에요, 괜찮아요 stacks 아니에요 ('it's not so / no') in front of 괜찮아요 to make a refusal that is both clear and warm — the 아니에요 firmly turns down the offer while 괜찮아요 reassures 'I'm okay, don't worry about me.' Koreans typically offer two or three times out of politeness, so you often need this stronger version when one 괜찮아요 isn't taken.

Do NOT decline a gift or kindness with a cold single 싫어요 ('I don't like/want it'), which is for genuine dislike and sounds harsh; 싫어요 to a host's food can be offensive. The natural Korean cushions instead are 마음만 받을게요 ('I'll accept just the thought') or 부담스러워요 ('it makes me feel indebted').
Register: 아니에요, 괜찮아요 is polite; 아니야, 괜찮아 with friends; 아닙니다, 괜찮습니다 formally.

The key learner point is that 아니에요 (the soft 'it's not / no') is the natural refusal particle here, NOT 아니요 — though both exist, 아니에요 flows better before 괜찮아요 and sounds gentler. Another error is over-insisting in a Western way ('no, no, I really couldn't') with literal translations.

entries.english: Right now isn't great for me
entries.shortExplanation: 지금은 좀 그래요 is a practical expression meaning "Right now isn't great for me".
entries.explanation: "Right now isn't great for me" — that is 지금은 좀 그래요 (jigeumeun jom geuraeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 지금은 좀 그래요 ("Now isn't a great time"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; vague soft refusal without giving a reason
반말, to a friend
Formal, to a senior or in business
Swap 지금은 for 그건 to call a specific thing awkward

examples.ko: 지금은 좀 그래요.
examples.romanization: jigeumeun jom geuraeyo.
examples.en: Now isn't really a good time.
examples.note: Declining an invite or request without spelling out why

examples.ko: 오늘 같이 술 한잔 어때요? — 아, 오늘은 좀 그래요. 다음에요.
examples.romanization: oneul gachi sul hanjan eottaeyo? — a, oneureun jom geuraeyo. daeumeyo.
examples.en: How about a drink today? — Ah, today's not great for me. Another time.
examples.note: Softly declining tonight while leaving the door open with 다음에요

examples.ko: 이 가격에 어떠세요? — 음… 그건 좀 그런데요.
examples.romanization: i gagyeoge eotteoseyo? — eum… geugeon jom geureondeyo.
examples.en: How about this price? — Hmm… that's a bit much.
examples.note: Using 그건 좀 그런데요 to push back on an offer without flat rejection

entries.nuance: 좀 그래요 is one of the most Korean phrases there is: literally '(it's) a bit like that', it deliberately leaves the negative UNSAID. 그렇다 ('to be so/like that') stands in for an awkward, uncomfortable, or undesirable quality the speaker won't name, and 좀 ('a bit') softens it further — so the whole thing means 'it's kind of… not ideal' without you ever having to say why. This indirectness is the point: it declines or expresses reluctance while saving everyone's face. Register: polite 좀 그래요, casual 좀 그래, formal 좀 그렇습니다 / 좀 그런데요. The dividing line from 안 돼요 ('it's not possible / no') is bluntness — 안 돼요 is a hard no, while 좀 그래요 is a soft, deniable 'eh, not really.' The huge English-speaker trap is treating 그래요 as 'yes, that's right' (its other meaning, as agreement) — but 좀 그래요 with a hesitant tone is the OPPOSITE: a polite refusal. Another error is demanding or expecting a reason; Korean culture accepts 좀 그래요 as a complete, reason-free decline, and pressing 'why?' (왜요?) can feel pushy. Deliver it with a slight trailing tone and maybe 좀 그런데요 to invite the other person to back off gracefully.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

Plain 그래요 can mean 'that's so/okay', but 좀 그래요 with a hesitant tone is a soft refusal meaning 'it's kind of not great'. Read the 좀 and the tone.
Demanding a reason after someone says 좀 그래요.
It's intentionally vague to save face. Pressing 왜요? ('why?') feels pushy. Accept it as a polite 'no', or offer an alternative like 다음에요.
Using 좀 그래요 for a hard, non-negotiable no.
It signals mild reluctance, not a firm refusal. If you absolutely cannot, say 안 돼요 or 어려울 것 같아요; 좀 그래요 may sound like you could still be persuaded.

entries.english: I'll do it next time
entries.shortExplanation: 다음에 할게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll do it next time".
entries.explanation: 다음에 할게요 (daeume halgeyo) = "I'll do it next time". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 다음에 할게요 ("I'll do it next time"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; declines now but promises later
반말, to a friend
Formal 합쇼체, to a senior or at work
Short form; just 'next time' as a gentle pass

examples.ko: 다음에 할게요.
examples.romanization: daeume halgeyo.
examples.en: I'll do it next time.
examples.note: Politely passing on something offered now

examples.ko: 같이 점심 어때요? — 오늘은 약속이 있어서, 다음에 할게요.
examples.romanization: gachi jeomsim eottaeyo? — oneureun yaksogi isseoseo, daeume halgeyo.
examples.en: Lunch together? — I have plans today, so let's do it next time.
examples.note: Give a light reason, then defer with 다음에 할게요

examples.ko: 멤버십 가입하시겠어요? — 아, 다음에 할게요. 오늘은 그냥 살게요.
examples.romanization: membeosip gaipasigesseoyo? — a, daeume halgeyo. oneureun geunyang salgeyo.
examples.en: Would you like to sign up for membership? — Ah, maybe next time. I'll just buy it today.
examples.note: Declining a sales pitch politely while still making the purchase

entries.nuance: 다음에 할게요 is 다음에 ('next time') + 할게요 (the -ㄹ게요 promise/intention form of 하다 'to do'), meaning 'I'll do it next time' — a soft refusal that declines the present offer while leaving the relationship warm by implying you'll come back to it. The -ㄹ게요 ending is key: it frames the deferral as YOUR own intention/promise, which feels considerate. Often it's just politeness, not a real commitment — both sides understand 다음에 ('next time') may never come, like the English 'maybe some other time.' Register: 다음에 할게요 polite, 다음에 할게 casual, 다음에 하겠습니다 formal. The dividing line from 안 할게요 ('I won't do it') is that 안 할게요 closes the door, while 다음에 할게요 keeps it ajar — much softer for declining invitations, sign-ups, or offers. The English-speaker trap is using 다음에 합시다 ('let's do it next time') when YOU are the one declining: 합시다 ('let's') is a suggestion/command to the group and can sound like you're scheduling them, whereas 할게요 humbly states your own choice. Another error is over-promising — Koreans read 다음에 할게요 as a polite brush-off, so don't be hurt if a 다음에 plan never materializes, and don't feel you broke a promise if yours doesn't either.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 다음에 합시다 when you're the one declining.
-합시다 ('let's') suggests/orders the group and can sound presumptuous. To politely defer your own participation, say 다음에 할게요 (your intention), not 합시다.

다음에 할게요 is often a gentle brush-off, like 'some other time'. Don't treat it as a scheduled commitment, and don't feel guilty if it doesn't happen.

하고 싶어요 means 'I want to do it'. To politely defer doing it now, say 다음에 할게요. Saying 다음에 하고 싶어요 sounds like expressing a wish, not declining the present offer.

entries.english: I'll go next time
entries.shortExplanation: 다음에 갈게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll go next time".
entries.explanation: 다음에 갈게요 (daeume galgeyo) means "I'll go next time". Say it as one set phrase — for example 다음에 갈게요 ("I'll go next time"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; declines an outing but stays friendly
반말, to a friend inviting you out
Formal, to a senior or boss
다음 기회에 ('next opportunity') sounds a touch warmer/sincerer

examples.ko: 다음에 갈게요.
examples.romanization: daeume galgeyo.
examples.en: I'll go next time.
examples.note: Turning down an invitation to go somewhere together

examples.ko: 회식 오실 거죠? — 오늘은 몸이 안 좋아서, 다음에 갈게요.
examples.romanization: hoesik osil geojyo? — oneureun momi an joaseo, daeume galgeyo.
examples.en: You're coming to the work dinner, right? — I'm not feeling well today, so I'll go next time.
examples.note: Declining a 회식 (company dinner) with a health reason

examples.ko: 노래방 갈래요? — 저는 먼저 갈게요. 다음에 같이 가요.
examples.romanization: noraebang gallaeyo? — jeoneun meonjeo galgeyo. daeume gachi gayo.
examples.en: Wanna go to noraebang? — I'll head off first. Let's go together next time.
examples.note: Bowing out now while proposing a real future plan with 다음에 같이 가요

entries.nuance: 다음에 갈게요 is 다음에 ('next time') + 갈게요 (-ㄹ게요 form of 가다 'to go'), the standard soft way to decline an invitation to go somewhere — a meal, a 회식 (work dinner), a 노래방 trip — while signalling goodwill ('I'll join next time'). Like 다음에 할게요, it is often a courteous brush-off rather than a firm plan, especially for the near-obligatory Korean 회식 culture where bowing out gracefully matters. Register: 갈게요 polite, 갈게 casual, 가겠습니다 formal. A warmer, more sincere upgrade is 다음 기회에 꼭 갈게요 ('I'll definitely go next chance'), where 꼭 ('for sure') signals you really mean it. The dividing line from 안 갈게요 ('I won't go') is openness — 안 갈게요 flatly refuses, which can feel cold for a group invite, while 다음에 갈게요 declines without rejecting the relationship. The English-speaker trap is pairing it with the wrong particle on the place: Korean marks the destination with -에 (회식에 갈게요), and learners often misuse -에서 (which is for the location of an action, not the destination). Another error is treating a refused 회식 lightly in a strict workplace; even with 다음에 갈게요, add a real reason (몸이 안 좋아서, 선약이 있어서) to soften it.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Marking the destination with -에서 instead of -에.
Destination of 가다 takes -에: 회식에 갈게요. -에서 marks where an action happens, so 회식에서 갈게요 is wrong for 'go to the dinner'.
Declining a 회식 with a bare 안 갈게요 and no reason.
In many Korean workplaces a flat refusal sounds cold. Soften with a reason plus 다음에 갈게요: 오늘은 선약이 있어서 다음에 갈게요.
Promising 다음에 꼭 갈게요 you don't mean.
꼭 ('definitely') raises the commitment. If it's really just a polite pass, plain 다음에 갈게요 is enough; over-promising with 꼭 can create expectations.

entries.english: Today won't work for me, I think
entries.shortExplanation: 오늘은 안 될 것 같아요 is a practical expression meaning "Today won't work for me, I think".
entries.explanation: "Today won't work for me, I think" — that is 오늘은 안 될 것 같아요 (oneureun an doel geot gatayo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 오늘은 안 될 것 같아요 ("Today probably won't work"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; softened 'no' using '~것 같다' (it seems)
반말, to a friend
Formal, swapping in 어렵다 for the workplace
힘들다 ('to be hard') variant, very common spoken hedge

examples.ko: 오늘은 안 될 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: oneureun an doel geot gatayo.
examples.en: I don't think today will work.
examples.note: Turning down a same-day plan gently

examples.ko: 이따 잠깐 볼 수 있어요? — 죄송한데 오늘은 안 될 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: itta jamkkan bol su isseoyo? — joesonghande oneureun an doel geot gatayo.
examples.en: Can we meet briefly later? — Sorry, but today probably won't work.
examples.note: 죄송한데 ('sorry, but') + the hedge makes a courteous refusal

examples.ko: 내일까지 끝낼 수 있을까요? — 음, 솔직히 내일까지는 힘들 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: naeilkkaji kkeunnael su isseulkkayo? — eum, soljiki naeilkkajineun himdeul geot gatayo.
examples.en: Could you finish it by tomorrow? — Hmm, honestly by tomorrow seems tough.
examples.note: Hedging on a deadline you can't meet without a flat 'no'

entries.nuance: 오늘은 안 될 것 같아요 wraps a refusal in the hedge -ㄹ 것 같다 ('it seems / I think'), turning a flat 안 돼요 ('it's not possible') into the much gentler 'I don't think it'll work.' That -것 같다 is the single most important softening tool in Korean: by framing the 'no' as your tentative impression rather than a hard fact, you avoid sounding blunt or final. 오늘은 ('as for today', with the topic particle 은 implying contrast) hints 'maybe another day', which softens further. Register: 안 될 것 같아요 polite, 안 될 것 같아 casual, 어려울/안 될 것 같습니다 formal. Common swap-ins are 어렵다 ('to be difficult') and 힘들다 ('to be hard/tough') — 어려울 것 같아요 and 힘들 것 같아요 are slightly more graceful than the plain 안 되다. The English-speaker trap is dropping the hedge and saying a bald 오늘 안 돼요, which is grammatically fine but socially harder; Koreans almost always cushion refusals with 것 같다. Another error is mixing the form up as 안 될 거 같아요 vs the textbook 안 될 것 같아요 — both are heard (거 is the casual contraction of 것), so don't be thrown. Adding 죄송한데 ('sorry, but') at the front is the natural, polite opener for declining.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Declining with a bald 오늘 안 돼요 and no hedge.
It's correct but blunt. Soften with -것 같다: 오늘은 안 될 것 같아요. The hedge frames it as your impression, not a hard refusal, which is far more polite.

The pattern is verb-stem + -ㄹ/을 것 같다. From 안 되다 you get 안 될 것 같아요 (future-leaning) — not 안 돼 것 같아요. Keep the -ㄹ 것 같다 frame.
Forgetting 오늘은 leaves no 'maybe later' nuance.
The topic 은 in 오늘은 implies contrast ('today specifically'), hinting another day is fine. Dropping it (오늘 안 될 것 같아요) is okay but loses that soft, door-open feeling.

entries.english: I'll think about it
entries.shortExplanation: 생각해 볼게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll think about it".
entries.explanation: 생각해 볼게요 (saenggakae bolgeyo) = "I'll think about it". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 생각해 볼게요 ("I'll think about it"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; non-committal, often a soft no
반말, to a friend
Formal 합쇼체, business or to a senior

usagePhrases.en: Let me think a bit more
usagePhrases.note: Add 좀 더 ('a bit more') to ask for time / hedge harder

examples.ko: 생각해 볼게요.
examples.romanization: saenggakae bolgeyo.
examples.en: I'll think about it.
examples.note: Non-committal reply to an offer or a sales pitch

examples.ko: 이 제품 어떠세요? — 음, 생각해 볼게요. 좀 둘러보고 올게요.
examples.romanization: i jepum eotteoseyo? — eum, saenggakae bolgeyo. jom dulleobogo olgeyo.
examples.en: How about this product? — Hmm, I'll think about it. Let me look around.
examples.note: Politely escaping a pushy salesperson

examples.ko: 주말에 등산 같이 갈래요? — 오, 좋은데… 생각해 볼게요. 일정 보고 연락드릴게요.
examples.romanization: jumare deungsan gachi gallaeyo? — o, joeunde… saenggakae bolgeyo. iljeong bogo yeollakdeurilgeyo.
examples.en: Want to hike this weekend? — Oh, sounds good… I'll think about it. I'll check my schedule and let you know.
examples.note: Buying time on an invite while leaving it genuinely open

entries.nuance: 생각해 볼게요 is 생각하다 ('to think') + -아/어 보다 ('to try doing') + -ㄹ게요 (intention), literally 'I'll try thinking about it' — i.e. 'I'll consider it.' The -어 보다 ('give it a try') makes it tentative, and like in English, 'I'll think about it' is frequently a polite, face-saving NO, especially toward salespeople and pushy invitations. But it can also be a genuine 'let me check' — context and tone decide. Register: 생각해 볼게요 polite, 생각해 볼게 casual, 생각해 보겠습니다 formal/business. The dividing line from 안 살게요 / 안 할게요 ('I won't buy/do it') is that those are clear refusals, while 생각해 볼게요 declines softly and defers, avoiding an awkward direct 'no.' The English-speaker trap is treating it as a firm commitment to genuinely deliberate and then feeling obligated — in Korean service contexts it's understood as a graceful exit. Another error is omitting the -어 보다 and saying 생각할게요, which sounds more like 'I will think (definitely)' and is heavier; the natural hedge keeps 보다. To buy time more explicitly, add 좀 더 ('a bit more') or follow with 둘러보고 올게요 ('I'll look around and come back'), the classic line for leaving a shop without buying.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Dropping 보다 and saying 생각할게요.
생각할게요 sounds like a firmer 'I will think (about it)'. The natural non-committal hedge keeps -어 보다: 생각해 볼게요 ('I'll try to think it over').

Toward salespeople and many invites it's a polite 'no'. Don't feel bound to actually decide, and don't expect a definite yes when someone says it to you.
Confusing 생각해 볼게요 with 생각이 나요.
생각이 나요 means 'it comes to mind / I remember'. To say 'I'll consider it', use 생각해 볼게요. They share 생각 but mean different things.

structuredNuance.t: 생각해 볼게요 literally 'I'll try thinking about it' — i.e. 'I'll consider it.' The -어 보다 ('give it a try') makes it tentative, and like in English, 'I'll think about it' is frequently a polite, face-saving NO, especially toward salespeople and pushy invitations. But it can also be a genuine 'let me check' — context and tone decide. To buy time more explicitly, add 좀 더 ('a bit more') or follow with 둘러보고 올게요 ('I'll look around and come back'), the classic line for leaving a shop without buying.
The dividing line from 안 살게요 / 안 할게요 ('I won't buy/do it') is that those are clear refusals, while 생각해 볼게요 declines softly and defers, avoiding an awkward direct 'no.'
생각해 볼게요 is 생각하다 ('to think') + -아/어 보다 ('to try doing') + -ㄹ게요 (intention).
Register: 생각해 볼게요 polite, 생각해 볼게 casual, 생각해 보겠습니다 formal/business.

The trap is treating it as a firm commitment to genuinely deliberate and then feeling obligated — in Korean service contexts it's understood as a graceful exit. Another error is omitting the -어 보다 and saying 생각할게요, which sounds more like 'I will think (definitely)' and is heavier; the natural hedge keeps 보다.

entries.english: It feels like too much / It makes me uncomfortable
entries.shortExplanation: 좀 부담스러워요 is a practical expression meaning "It feels like too much / It makes me uncomfortable".
entries.explanation: 좀 부담스러워요 (jom budamseureowoyo) means "It feels like too much / It makes me uncomfortable". Say it as one set phrase — for example 좀 부담스러워요 ("It's a bit much for me"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: It's a bit much for me
usagePhrases.note: Polite; declining because it feels like too big a favor/gift
반말, to a friend
Formal, in business or to a senior
Flip side: what you say to relieve someone else's pressure

examples.ko: 좀 부담스러워요.
examples.romanization: jom budamseureowoyo.
examples.en: It feels like a bit much.
examples.note: Declining an over-generous gift or gesture

examples.ko: 이거 받으세요. — 아유, 이렇게까지… 좀 부담스러워요.
examples.romanization: igeo badeuseyo. — ayu, ireokekkaji… jom budamseureowoyo.
examples.en: Please take this. — Oh, you didn't have to… this is a bit much.
examples.note: 이렇게까지 ('to go this far') + 부담스러워요 to refuse an extravagant gift

examples.ko: 제가 다 계산할게요. — 아니에요, 그러면 제가 너무 부담스러워요. 더치페이해요.
examples.romanization: jega da gyesanhalgeyo. — anieyo, geureomyeon jega neomu budamseureowoyo. deochipeihaeyo.
examples.en: I'll pay for everything. — No, then I'd feel too indebted. Let's split it.
examples.note: Declining to be treated, proposing 더치페이 (Dutch pay) instead

entries.nuance: 부담스럽다 means 'to feel burdened / pressured / indebted' — it describes the uncomfortable feeling of receiving something so generous that you feel you owe the giver. 좀 부담스러워요 ('it's a bit much for me') is the polite way to decline an over-the-top gift, an offer to pay, or a favor that feels too big, precisely BECAUSE Korean relationships track reciprocity (정 and obligation). Saying it signals 'your kindness is so great it makes me uneasy' — a culturally fluent, face-saving refusal. Register: 부담스러워요 polite, 부담스러워 casual, 부담스럽습니다 formal. The flip side is 부담 갖지 마세요 ('don't feel obligated'), what the GIVER says to put you at ease — knowing both lets you navigate the back-and-forth. The dividing line from 싫어요 ('I dislike it') is crucial: 싫어요 rejects the THING, which is rude about a gift, while 부담스러워요 praises the gesture as too generous — it declines while honoring the giver. The English-speaker trap is mistranslating 부담 as merely 'pressure/stress' and missing the indebtedness nuance, or using 스트레스 받아요 ('I'm stressed'), which is about general stress, not the specific 'this is too much kindness' feeling. Pair it with 마음만 받을게요 ('I'll accept just the thought') for the most graceful refusal.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Declining a gift with 싫어요 instead of 부담스러워요.
싫어요 rejects the item and sounds ungrateful. 부담스러워요 declines by honoring the gesture as too generous — the polite, relationship-safe choice.
Translating 부담스럽다 as plain 'stressful' and using 스트레스 받아요.
스트레스 받아요 is general stress. 부담스럽다 specifically means feeling indebted by someone's kindness. Use 부담스러워요 to decline over-generosity.
Saying 부담돼요 instead of 부담스러워요.
The adjective for the feeling is 부담스럽다 → 부담스러워요. 부담이 되다 ('to become a burden') is also valid but conjugated 부담이 돼요; don't blend them into the non-standard 부담돼요 in this slot.

entries.english: I'll just accept the thought
entries.shortExplanation: 마음만 받을게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll just accept the thought".
entries.explanation: "I'll just accept the thought" — that is 마음만 받을게요 (maeumman badeulgeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 마음만 받을게요 ("I'll accept just the thought"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; graciously refuses a gift while honoring the giver
반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: I shall accept your kind thought
usagePhrases.note: Formal 합쇼체, very gracious

usagePhrases.en: Just the thought is more than enough
usagePhrases.note: Warmer expansion stressing gratitude

examples.ko: 마음만 받을게요.
examples.romanization: maeumman badeulgeyo.
examples.en: I'll just accept the thought.
examples.note: Refusing a gift kindly without seeming ungrateful

examples.ko: 이거 작은 거예요, 받으세요. — 아유, 마음만 받을게요. 정말 감사해요.
examples.romanization: igeo jageun geoyeyo, badeuseyo. — ayu, maeumman badeulgeyo. jeongmal gamsahaeyo.
examples.en: It's just a small thing, please take it. — Oh, I'll just accept the thought. Thank you so much.
examples.note: The standard warm refusal of a gift, capped with thanks

examples.ko: 용돈 좀 드릴게요. — 아니에요, 어머니. 마음만 받을게요. 저 충분해요.
examples.romanization: yongdon jom deurilgeyo. — anieyo, eomeoni. maeumman badeulgeyo. jeo chungbunhaeyo.
examples.en: Let me give you some pocket money. — No, mother. I'll just accept the thought. I have enough.
examples.note: Declining money from an elder while honoring their care

entries.nuance: 마음만 받을게요 is 마음 ('heart/thought/intention') + 만 ('only') + 받을게요 ('I'll receive', -ㄹ게요 form of 받다), literally 'I'll receive only the heart' — i.e. 'I appreciate the gesture, but I can't take the gift itself.' It is the most graceful, culturally fluent way to refuse a present, money, or a favor: you accept the GIVER'S kindness (마음) while declining the object, so no one loses face. The particle 만 ('only') is the whole engine — it narrows acceptance to the intention. Register: 받을게요 polite, 받을게 casual, 받겠습니다 formal. The dividing line from a flat 안 받을게요 ('I won't take it') is warmth — 안 받을게요 can sound like rejecting the person, while 마음만 받을게요 explicitly cherishes their thought. The English-speaker trap is having no direct equivalent and resorting to literal 'it's the thought that counts' translations that don't exist idiomatically; just memorize 마음만 받을게요 as a set phrase. Another error is misreading 마음 as only 'mind/heart' in the emotional sense — here it means the giver's caring intention. Pair it with 부담스러워요 ('it's too much') and 감사해요 for a complete, gracious refusal.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

Dropping 만 and saying 마음 받을게요.
The 만 ('only') is essential: it means you take ONLY the thought, not the gift. Without it, 마음 받을게요 loses the whole 'just the gesture' meaning.
Trying to translate 'it's the thought that counts' literally.
Korean has no word-for-word version; the set phrase is 마음만 받을게요. Don't construct 생각이 중요해요 — memorize this idiom for refusing gifts.
