In a legal or bureaucratic context, 서명 is cleaner; 사인 is understood but sounds informal. The question 도장 없는데 서명해도 돼요? covers the most common scenario foreigners face.

여기 서명하면 돼요? (confirm spot + permission) → 어디에 서명해요? (open: where to sign at all) → 서명만 하면 돼요? (is signing the only thing left?). Combining: 이름 쓰고 여기 서명하면 돼요? ('write name and sign here?'). Staff may say: 여기 서명해 주세요 or 도장 찍어 주세요 ('please stamp here').

두 가지 함정: (1) 서명해야 돼요? vs 서명하면 돼요? — 해야 돼요 asks 'must I?' (obligation); 하면 돼요 asks 'is it okay if I?' (confirmation of spot). For confirming the location, use 하면 돼요. (2) Not knowing 도장 — many Korean forms still expect a seal, not a signature. Learn 도장 없는데 서명해도 돼요? as a ready-made fallback.

entries.english: Do you need a copy of my passport?
entries.shortExplanation: 여권 사본 필요해요? is a practical expression meaning "Do you need a copy of my passport?".
entries.explanation: 여권 사본 필요해요? (yeogwon sabon piryohaeyo?) means "Do you need a copy of my passport?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 여권 사본 필요해요? ("Do you need a passport copy?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Do you need a passport copy?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking if a photocopy is required
Stating you already have one ready

usagePhrases.en: Do you need the original too?
usagePhrases.note: 원본 ('original') vs 사본, a key document pair

usagePhrases.en: Where can I make a copy?
usagePhrases.note: 떼다 ('to issue/make a copy'), where to get one

examples.ko: 여권 사본 필요해요?
examples.romanization: yeogwon sabon piryohaeyo?
examples.en: Do you need a copy of my passport?
examples.note: Ask proactively before handing over documents to avoid needing an extra trip; note 필요하다 takes 사본이 as subject, not object

examples.ko: A: 여권 원본도 가져오셨어요? / B: 네, 사본이랑 원본 둘 다 가져왔어요.
examples.romanization: A: yeogwon wonbondo gajyeoosyeosseoyo? / B: ne, sabonirang wonbon dul da gajyeowasseoyo.
examples.en: A: Did you bring the original passport too? / B: Yes, I brought both the copy and the original.
examples.note: A/B exchange: staff confirm both documents; 둘 다 ('both') is the natural way to confirm you have the pair

examples.ko: 사본이 없는데 여기서 떼도 돼요?
examples.romanization: saboni eopsneunde yeogiseo ttedo dwaeyo?
examples.en: I don't have a copy — can I make one here?
examples.note: 떼도 돼요 asks if copying on-site is allowed; 없는데 ('I don't have one, but…') frames the problem before the request

entries.nuance: 여권 사본 필요해요? is 여권 ('passport', 旅券) + 사본 ('copy/duplicate', 寫本) + 필요해요 ('is needed'), asking whether a photocopy is required. The crucial pair is 사본 ('a copy') vs 원본 ('the original', 原本): immigration often wants both your passport 원본 (to verify) and a 사본 (to keep on file), so knowing both words prevents a wasted trip. The verb for obtaining an official copy or certificate is 떼다 (literally 'to detach/peel') — 사본 떼다 ('make/get a copy'), 등본 떼다 ('get a certified register extract') — baffling to English speakers because 떼다 usually means 'peel off'; just learn 떼다 = 'obtain an official paper at a counter'. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'copy' as 카피, which Koreans don't use for documents (카피 sounds like advertising copy or computer copy); the document word is 사본. Another trap is the verb 'need': learners say 필요로 해요 (over-literal), but natural Korean is simply 필요해요 ('is needed') — note 필요하다 makes the needed thing the SUBJECT (여권 사본이 필요해요), so 여권 사본을 필요해요 is a particle error. Register plain 존댓말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 여권 사본을 필요해요.
필요하다 makes the needed thing the SUBJECT: 여권 사본이 필요해요. Marking it with object 을/를 is ungrammatical.
Using 카피 for a document copy.
카피 reads as 'advertising copy' in Korean. A photocopy/duplicate of a document is 사본: 여권 사본 필요해요?
Not knowing 떼다 for making copies/certificates.
To get an official copy you 떼다 it: 사본 떼다, 등본 떼다. Saying 사본 만들다 is understandable but 떼다 is the natural office verb.

structuredNuance.t: Word-for-word: 여권(passport) + 사본(copy) + 필요해요(is needed). The real function: proactively checking the document checklist before handing anything over, avoiding the common frustration of being told mid-process that you need a copy you don't have. Note: 필요하다 makes the thing needed the SUBJECT — 사본'이' 필요해요, never 사본'을'.

Said at the counter when presenting documents, or before visiting if you're preparing your packet. Register is plain 존댓말. You can confirm you brought both with 사본이랑 원본 둘 다 가져왔어요 ('I brought both copy and original'). Ask about on-site copying with 여기서 사본 뗄 수 있어요? ('can I make a copy here?').

사본 (copy of a document) vs 원본 (the original) — always learn these as a pair. The verb 떼다 ('to obtain an official paper') is the natural action verb: 사본 떼다, 등본 떼다. Saying 사본 만들다 ('make a copy') is understandable but 떼다 is what office Korean sounds like.

여권 사본 필요해요? → 원본도 필요해요? (asking about the original too) → 사본 몇 장 필요해요? (how many copies?). If you need to find the copier: 사본 어디서 떼요? or 복사기 어디 있어요? ('where's the copier?'). Staff may say: 사본 한 장 주세요 ('please give one copy').

두 가지 함정: (1) saying 카피 for a document copy — 카피 sounds like advertising copy; the correct word is 사본. (2) 여권 사본을 필요해요 — 필요하다 takes the subject particle, not object: 여권 사본이 필요해요. The 을/를 particle error is very common.

entries.english: I've prepared all these documents
entries.shortExplanation: 이 서류 다 준비했어요 is a practical expression meaning "I've prepared all these documents".
entries.explanation: "I've prepared all these documents" — that is 이 서류 다 준비했어요 (i seoryu da junbihaesseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 이 서류 다 준비했어요 ("I've prepared all these documents"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; showing you brought everything
Simpler 'they're all here' phrasing

usagePhrases.en: These are all the documents — is that right?
usagePhrases.note: 이게 다인데 ('this is everything') asks for confirmation

usagePhrases.en: Is there any more document I need?
usagePhrases.note: Checking if anything is still missing

examples.ko: 이 서류 다 준비했어요.
examples.romanization: i seoryu da junbihaesseoyo.
examples.en: I've prepared all these documents.
examples.note: Set your papers on the counter; the past tense 준비했어요 ('I have prepared') signals completion — staff know to begin checking

examples.ko: A: 서류 다 준비하셨어요? / B: 네, 말씀하신 서류 다 준비했는데 확인해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: seoryu da junbihasyeosseoyo? / B: ne, malsseumhasin seoryu da junbihaenneunde hwaginhae juseyo.
examples.en: A: Have you prepared all your documents? / B: Yes, I prepared everything you mentioned — please check.
examples.note: A/B exchange: staff ask with honorific -셨어요; you reply confirming and adding 확인해 주세요 ('please check') to invite verification

examples.ko: 서류 다 준비했는데 혹시 빠진 거 있어요?
examples.romanization: seoryu da junbihaenneunde hoksi ppajin geo isseoyo?
examples.en: I prepared everything — is anything possibly missing?
examples.note: 혹시 빠진 거 ('anything possibly left out') invites the clerk to double-check; 혹시 softens the concern and 빠진 거 ('missing thing') is the natural way to ask about gaps

entries.nuance: 이 서류 다 준비했어요 is 이 ('this/these') + 서류 ('documents/paperwork', 書類) + 다 ('all') + 준비하다 ('to prepare', 準備) in past tense, the line that says you've brought everything required. 서류 is the all-purpose word for official papers (forms, certificates, copies) treated as a mass noun — you don't pluralize it, and one paper or a whole stack is still 서류. The verb 준비했어요 (past of 준비하다) is exactly right for 'I have prepared/got ready'. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'documents' as 다큐먼트 or even 문서 in the wrong place: 문서 ('a document/text file') is more about a written document or computer file, while the packet you bring to a government office is 서류 — say 서류 at immigration. Another trap is 다 ('all') placement: 다 goes right before the verb (다 준비했어요), not before the noun as English 'all the documents' might tempt you (it's not 다 서류). The natural softener when handing them over is the -는데 lead-in: 다 준비했는데 확인해 주세요 ('I've prepared everything, so please check'), pairing your statement with a polite request to verify. Register plain 존댓말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 문서 for the papers at immigration.
문서 leans toward a written document or file. The packet of official papers is 서류: 이 서류 다 준비했어요.
Placing 다 before the noun: 다 서류 준비했어요.
다 ('all') normally sits right before the verb: 서류 다 준비했어요. Fronting it onto the noun sounds off.
Saying 준비해요 (present) for 'I have prepared'.
Completed preparation is past tense: 준비했어요. 준비해요 sounds like a general/habitual 'I prepare', not 'I've got it ready'.

structuredNuance.t: Word-for-word: 이 서류(these documents) + 다(all) + 준비했어요(I have prepared). The real function: signaling to the clerk that you believe your document packet is complete so they can begin the intake process — while also opening the door for them to flag anything missing.

Said at the intake window when you place your documents on the counter or slide them through the slot. Register plain 존댓말. The most useful follow-up is 혹시 빠진 거 있어요? ('is anything missing?') — clerks appreciate when applicants actively invite a check rather than assuming everything is correct.

서류 (the official papers you bring to an office — a mass noun) vs 문서 (a written document or computer file). At immigration always say 서류. Also: 이 서류 다 준비했어요 (past, completed action) vs 이 서류 다 있어요 ('all the documents are here', present state) — both work; past 준비했어요 emphasizes your preparation effort.

다 준비했어요 → 다 준비했는데 확인해 주세요 (adds a polite verification request) → 서류 이게 다인데 맞아요? (asks if this is the complete set) → 서류 더 필요한 거 있어요? (checks for gaps). 말씀하신 서류 다 준비했어요 ('I prepared all the documents you mentioned') references the checklist the clerk gave you.

두 가지 함정: (1) 다큐먼트/문서 for the office packet — use 서류. (2) 다 ('all') placement: English places 'all' before the noun ('all the documents'), tempting 다 서류 준비했어요 — but in Korean 다 modifies the verb and goes right before it: 서류 다 준비했어요.

entries.english: to apply (for a job)
entries.shortExplanation: 지원하다 is a practical expression meaning "to apply (for a job)".
entries.explanation: 지원하다 (jiwonhada) = "to apply (for a job)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 지원했어요 ("I applied"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite past; the everyday way to say you submitted an application
Polite; stating your intention with -려고요

usagePhrases.en: I will apply / I am applying
usagePhrases.note: Formal 합쇼체, for the cover letter or a formal email
반말, telling a friend

examples.ko: 저 그 회사에 지원했어요.
examples.romanization: jeo geu hoesae jiwonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I applied to that company.
examples.note: Mark the company with 에, not 를: 회사에 지원하다 — the particle 에 is non-negotiable here

examples.ko: A: 마케팅 팀에 지원하려고 하는데 자격 요건이 어떻게 돼요? / B: 공고 보셨어요? 거기 다 나와 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: maketing time jiwonharyeogo haneunde jagyeok yogeoni eotteoke dwaeyo? / B: gonggo bosyeosseoyo? geogi da nawa isseoyo.
examples.en: A: I'm thinking of applying to the marketing team — what are the requirements? / B: Have you seen the job posting? It's all listed there.
examples.note: 지원하려고 하다 = 'be about to / planning to apply'; 공고 = job announcement

examples.ko: 귀사의 영업직에 지원하게 되어 영광입니다.
examples.romanization: gwisaui yeongeopjige jiwonhage doeeo yeonggwangimnida.
examples.en: It is an honor to apply for the sales position at your company.
examples.note: 귀사 ('your esteemed company') + 지원하게 되어 + 영광입니다 is cover-letter register — the -게 되어 adds humble indirectness

entries.nuance: 지원하다 here is Sino-Korean 志願 ('aspire + wish') and is THE verb for applying to a job, school, or program — you put yourself forward as a candidate. The make-or-break grammar point for English speakers is the particle: the target you apply TO takes 에, NOT 을/를. So it is 회사에 지원하다, never 회사를 지원하다 — and that wrong particle is doubly dangerous because there is a homophone 지원(支援)하다 meaning 'to support/sponsor', which IS transitive, so 회사를 지원하다 reads as 'I sponsor the company'. Two different Hanja, same sound: 志願 = apply, 支援 = support. Do not confuse 지원하다 with 신청하다 ('to sign up / request', used for courses, refunds, cards): you 지원 for a competitive position where you might be rejected, but 신청 for a service you simply request. From 지원하다 you can build: 지원했어요 (polite past) → 지원하겠습니다 (formal intent) → 지원하게 되어 영광입니다 (humble cover-letter register). A direct-translation trap is calling the document an '어플리케이션' — Koreans hear that as a smartphone app; the application document is 지원서 and the act is 지원하다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 회사를 지원했어요.
The object particle 를 makes it sound like 'I supported/sponsored the company' (支援). Apply TO takes 에: 회사에 지원했어요.
Using 신청하다 to apply for a competitive job.
신청하다 is 'to request/sign up' (a course, a card, a refund). For a job where you compete and can be rejected, use 지원하다.
Calling the application an 어플 / 어플리케이션.
That means a smartphone app in Korean. The application document is 지원서; the action is 지원하다.

structuredNuance.t: 지원하다 is THE verb for applying to a job, school, or program — you put yourself forward as a candidate. 지원했어요 is the safe spoken default; a cover letter wants 지원하겠습니다 or the humble 지원하게 되어 영광입니다. Derived noun: 지원서 (the application document itself).

Sino-Korean 志願 ('aspire + wish'). Beware the homophone 지원(支援)하다 'to support/sponsor', which is transitive (정부 지원 = 'government aid'). Two different Hanja, same sound: 志願 = apply, 支援 = support. The particle 에 is your safety rail for telling them apart.

지원하다 vs 신청하다: you 지원 for a competitive position where you can be rejected; you 신청 for a service or slot you simply request (강의 신청 = sign up for a class, 카드 신청 = apply for a card). The competitive-vs-request dividing line is the key.
지원했어요 (polite past) → 지원하려고요 (polite intent) → 지원하겠습니다 (formal commitment) → 지원하게 되어 영광입니다 (humble cover-letter close). Noun form: 지원서 (application document), 지원자 (applicant).
Particle trap: 회사를 지원했어요 sounds like 'I sponsored the company' (支援). Always 회사에 지원했어요. Also, a job application document is 지원서, not 어플리케이션 (which Koreans hear as a phone app); the act is 지원하다.

entries.english: to have / take a job interview
entries.shortExplanation: 면접 보다 is a practical expression meaning "to have / take a job interview".
entries.explanation: 면접 보다 (myeonjeop boda) means "to have / take a job interview". Say it as one set phrase — for example 면접 봐요 ("I have an interview / I'm interviewing"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: I have an interview / I'm interviewing
usagePhrases.note: Polite; the everyday phrasing from the candidate's side
Polite; -러 가다 = 'go in order to'
Polite past, after it's done
반말, to a friend

examples.ko: 내일 면접 봐요.
examples.romanization: naeil myeonjeop bwayo.
examples.en: I have an interview tomorrow.
examples.note: From the candidate's side the verb is 보다 ('see/take'), not 하다 — lock this in from the start

examples.ko: A: 오후에 면접 보러 가는데 너무 떨려요. / B: 잘 할 수 있어! 연습 많이 했잖아.
examples.romanization: A: ohue myeonjeop boreo ganeunde neomu tteollyeoyo. / B: jal hal su isseo! yeonseum mani haetjana.
examples.en: A: I'm going to an interview this afternoon and I'm so nervous. / B: You can do it! You've practiced a lot.
examples.note: 면접 보러 가다 = heading off to interview; 떨리다 = 'to be nervous/trembling inside'

examples.ko: 1차 면접 봤는데 분위기 괜찮았어요. 2차 기다리는 중이에요.
examples.romanization: 1cha myeonjeop bwanneunde bunwigi gwaenchanasseoyo. 2cha gidarineun jungieyo.
examples.en: I had the first-round interview and the vibe was okay. I'm waiting for the second round.
examples.note: 1차 면접 = first-round; companies often run 2차, 3차 too — 차 (次) is 'round/step'

entries.nuance: 면접 (Sino-Korean 面接, 'face + meet') is the job interview, and the verb that pairs with it from YOUR side as the candidate is 보다 — literally 'to see/take', the same 보다 used in 시험 보다 ('take an exam'). This collocation is the single biggest pitfall for English speakers, who calque 'do an interview' into 면접 하다 — but 면접하다 sounds like the COMPANY is conducting/administering the interview, so a candidate saying 저 면접 해요 sounds off. Think of an interview as a test you 'take'. From the employer's angle they 면접을 진행하다 ('conduct the interview'). The role words: 면접관 = interviewer (관 官 means 'official'); 지원자/면접자 = the candidate. Don't confuse 면접 (the job interview event) with 인터뷰 — the loanword 인터뷰 leans toward a media/press interview. Register: 면접 봐요 is the polite everyday form, 면접 봐 is 반말. Variant scale: 면접 봐 → 면접 봐요 → 면접을 보겠습니다 (most formal). In practice 면접(을) is often said without the object particle in speech.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 면접 해요 for taking an interview.
면접하다 sounds like the company is conducting it. The candidate 'takes' the interview: 면접 봐요 (like 시험 보다).
Using 인터뷰 for a job interview.
인터뷰 suggests a press/media interview. A hiring interview is 면접. Say 면접 보다.
Marking it 면접에 봐요.
면접 takes the object particle (often dropped in speech): 면접을 봐요 or just 면접 봐요, not 면접에 봐요.

structuredNuance.t: 면접 is the job interview, and the verb that pairs with it from YOUR side as the candidate is 보다 — literally 'to see/take', the same 보다 you use for 시험 보다 ('take an exam'). Lock in 면접 봐요 (polite everyday); 반말 is 면접 봐. 면접관 = interviewer (관 = 'official/officer'); 지원자/면접자 = the candidate.
면접 is Sino-Korean 面接, 'face + meet' — you meet face-to-face for evaluation.

면접 (hiring interview) vs 인터뷰 (media/press interview): don't use 인터뷰 when you mean a job interview. Also 면접 보다 (candidate's perspective) vs 면접을 진행하다 (interviewer's perspective, 'conduct the interview').
면접 봐 (반말) → 면접 봐요 (polite) → 면접을 보겠습니다 (formal). With a modifier: 1차 면접, 2차 면접 ('first/second round interview'), 최종 면접 ('final interview'), 화상 면접 ('video interview').

Calquing 'do an interview' into 면접 하다 — but 면접하다 sounds like the company is conducting it, not the candidate taking it. Candidate always uses 보다: 면접 봐요. Also don't mark it 면접에 봐요 — the particle is 을 (often dropped): 면접(을) 봐요.

entries.english: résumé / CV
entries.shortExplanation: 이력서 is a practical expression meaning "résumé / CV".
entries.explanation: "résumé / CV" — that is 이력서 (iryeokseo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 이력서 냈어요 ("I submitted my résumé"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite past; 내다 ('to hand in') is the natural verb for submitting

usagePhrases.en: Could you look over my résumé?
usagePhrases.note: Polite request to have it reviewed; 봐 주다 = 'look at for me'
Polite; 쓰다 = 'to write/fill out'
Casual pairing; 자소서 = 자기소개서 shortened

examples.ko: 이력서 어디로 보내면 돼요?
examples.romanization: iryeokseo eodiro bonaemyeon dwaeyo?
examples.en: Where should I send my résumé?
examples.note: 보내다 ('send') for email; 내다 ('submit') for physically handing in — both natural

examples.ko: A: 이력서에 경력 사항을 더 자세히 적어야 할까요? / B: 네, 구체적인 성과를 숫자로 보여 주면 좋아요.
examples.romanization: A: iryeokseoe gyeongnyeok sahangeul deo jasehi jeogeoya halkkayo? / B: ne, guchejeogin seonggwareul sutjaro boyeo jumyeon joayo.
examples.en: A: Should I write my work history in more detail on the résumé? / B: Yes, showing concrete achievements with numbers is good.
examples.note: 경력 사항 = 'career/work-history section'; numbers-based achievements are valued in Korean 이력서

examples.ko: 이력서랑 자기소개서 같이 첨부해서 메일로 보내 주세요.
examples.romanization: iryeokseorang jagisogaeseo gachi cheombuhaeseo meillo bonae juseyo.
examples.en: Please attach both your résumé and cover letter and email them.
examples.note: 첨부하다 = 'to attach (a file)'; 이력서 and 자기소개서 are almost always submitted together

entries.nuance: 이력서 (Sino-Korean 履歷書, 'career-record document') is your résumé/CV — the form listing your education and work history. Verb choices matter: you SUBMIT it with 내다 ('hand in') or 보내다 ('send'), and WRITE or fill it out with 쓰다 or 적다. The big content note for English speakers is that a Korean 이력서 traditionally pairs with a separate 자기소개서 ('self-introduction document', the cover-letter-style essay, often shortened to 자소서) — the 이력서 is the fact sheet (dates, titles, scores), the 자기소개서 is the narrative ('why me'). Many applications expect BOTH. Culture point: traditional Korean 이력서 often included a photo, birth date, and personal details that Western résumés omit, though modern/international companies have dropped some of these. The nearest synonym confusion: 경력 is the experience itself, 이력서 is the document recording it. Avoid calling it '씨브이' (CV), '레쥬메', or '어플리케이션' — none of these is the Korean word used in hiring; the real word is 이력서 throughout.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 씨브이 or 레쥬메 for a résumé.
Everyday Korean hiring uses 이력서. The English loans are not standard; say 이력서를 내다 / 보내다.
Assuming the 이력서 includes your self-introduction.
The narrative 'about me' is a separate 자기소개서 (자소서). The 이력서 is just facts; many applications require both.
Using 만들다 as 이력서를 만들다 only.
만들다 ('make') is okay for creating the file, but to submit it use 내다/보내다, and to fill it in use 쓰다/적다.

structuredNuance.t: 이력서 is your résumé/CV — the form listing education and work history. Submit it with 내다 ('hand in') or 보내다 ('send'); fill it out with 쓰다 or 적다. Always distinguish: the 이력서 is facts, the 자기소개서 (자소서) is the narrative essay — most Korean applications require both.
이력서 is Sino-Korean 履歷書, 'career-record document'. 履歷 means 'things walked through / career path'; 書 means 'document/letter'.

이력서 (the document) vs 경력 (the career experience itself — what the document records). Also: 이력서 (fact sheet) vs 자기소개서/자소서 (narrative essay). Don't call it 이력서 when you mean only your work history bullet points — 경력 사항 ('career items/section') is the term for those.
이력서를 쓰다 / 작성하다 ('write/compose') → 내다 / 보내다 ('submit/send') → 검토하다 ('review'). Shortened speech: '이력서 냈어요?' is all a recruiter needs to hear. Related: 자기소개서 (자소서), 포트폴리오, 자격증 사본 ('certificate copy').

Don't say 씨브이, 레쥬메, or 어플리케이션 — none is standard Korean hiring vocabulary; say 이력서. Don't merge the 이력서 with the 자기소개서 (they are separate documents). Culture note: traditional 이력서 included a photo and personal details Western résumés omit — be prepared for this difference.

entries.english: Please introduce yourself (a little)
entries.shortExplanation: 자기소개 좀 해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please introduce yourself (a little)".
entries.explanation: 자기소개 좀 해 주세요 (jagisogae jom hae juseyo) = "Please introduce yourself (a little)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 자기소개 좀 해 주세요 ("Please introduce yourself"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; what the interviewer typically says to open
Formal; very common opening line from an interviewer
Polite, slightly encouraging; 한번 ... 보세요 = 'give it a try'
Adds 간단하게 ('briefly/simply'), a frequent real instruction that sets a time frame

examples.ko: 먼저 자기소개 좀 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: meonjeo jagisogae jom hae juseyo.
examples.en: First, please introduce yourself.
examples.note: 먼저 ('first') signals this is the opening question — prepare the full mini-pitch, not just your name

examples.ko: A: 그럼 1분 정도로 자기소개 한번 해 보시겠어요? / B: 네, 안녕하세요. 저는 이수진이라고 합니다.
examples.romanization: A: geureom 1bun jeongdoro jagisogae hanbeon hae bosigesseoyo? / B: ne, annyeonghaseyo. jeoneun isujinirago hamnida.
examples.en: A: Then could you introduce yourself in about a minute? / B: Yes, hello. My name is Lee Sujin.
examples.note: 1분 정도로 ('in about a minute') — interviewers often set a time; answer name + background + role + strength + 잘 부탁드립니다

examples.ko: 자기소개는 간단하게 부탁드릴게요. 지원 동기는 따로 여쭤볼게요.
examples.romanization: jagisogaeneun gandanhage butakdeurilgeyo. jiwon donggineun ttaro yeojjwobolgeyo.
examples.en: A brief self-introduction please. I'll ask about your motivation for applying separately.
examples.note: 부탁드릴게요 softens the request; shows 자기소개 and 지원 동기 are separate questions in Korean interviews

entries.nuance: 자기소개 (Sino-Korean 自己紹介, 'self-introduction') is the opening ritual of nearly every Korean interview, and 자기소개 좀 해 주세요 is what the INTERVIEWER says to you — so you'll mostly HEAR this and need to respond, not say it yourself. The verb is 소개하다 ('to introduce'); note 자기소개하다 can be one word, or split as 자기소개(를) 해 주세요. The 좀 here is the politeness softener, not 'a little bit of', and 해 주세요 frames it as a courteous request. English speakers make two errors: first, answering by literally translating 'My name is...' and stopping — but a Korean 자기소개 is expected to be a mini-pitch: name, background, role applied for, a strength, and 잘 부탁드립니다 to close; just stating your name feels incomplete. Second, reusing 자기소개 to introduce someone else — but 자기소개 is reflexive ('introduce ONESELF'); to introduce another person use 소개하다 (제 친구를 소개할게요). Register: the interviewer uses 해 주세요 / 부탁드립니다 / 해 보세요; your reply stays in 존댓말 (-습니다 or -요) throughout. Scale of formality: 해 주세요 → 부탁드립니다 → 해 주시겠습니까.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Answering with only your name.
A Korean 자기소개 is a mini-pitch: name + background + the role + a strength + 잘 부탁드립니다. Stopping at 저는 ...입니다 feels unfinished.
Reusing 자기소개 to introduce another person.
자기소개 is reflexive ('introduce oneself'). For someone else, use 소개하다: 제 동료를 소개하겠습니다.
Saying 자기소개를 만들어 주세요.
You don't 'make' a self-intro on the spot; you 'do/give' it: 자기소개 좀 해 주세요 / 자기소개해 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 자기소개 is the opening ritual of nearly every Korean interview, and 자기소개 좀 해 주세요 is what the INTERVIEWER says — you'll mostly HEAR this and respond. The verb is 소개하다; 자기소개하다 can be one word or split. The 좀 is a politeness softener, not 'a little bit'. Your reply stays in 존댓말 (-습니다 or -요).
자기소개 is Sino-Korean 自己紹介 — 자기 自己 'oneself' + 소개 紹介 'introduction'. Because 자기 means 'oneself', this is a REFLEXIVE expression; it cannot be used to introduce another person.

자기소개 (introduce yourself) vs 소개하다 (introduce someone/something). To introduce a colleague: 제 동료를 소개하겠습니다, NOT 제 동료 자기소개. Also: 자기소개 (the full ritual) vs 인사 ('greeting/hello') — they overlap in context but 자기소개 carries the structured content expectation.
Interviewer's prompts: 자기소개 좀 해 주세요 → 자기소개 부탁드립니다 → 간단하게 자기소개해 주세요 → 1분 자기소개 부탁드립니다. The content formula: 이름 + 배경 + 지원 직무 + 강점 + 잘 부탁드립니다. The closer 이상입니다 + 잘 부탁드립니다 caps it neatly.

Answering with only your name ('저는 제인이에요') feels unfinished — a Korean 자기소개 is a mini-pitch with name, background, role, strength, and 잘 부탁드립니다. Also, reusing 자기소개 to introduce someone else is wrong — it's reflexive; use 소개하다 for others. And don't say 자기소개를 만들어 주세요 ('make a self-intro') — you 하다 (do/give) it.

entries.english: What's your reason for applying? (motivation)
entries.shortExplanation: 지원 동기가 뭐예요? is a practical expression meaning "What's your reason for applying? (motivation)".
entries.explanation: "What's your reason for applying? (motivation)" — that is 지원 동기가 뭐예요? (jiwon donggiga mwoyeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 지원 동기가 뭐예요? ("What's your reason for applying?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; a slightly casual phrasing of the classic question

usagePhrases.en: What is your motivation for applying?
usagePhrases.note: Polite-formal; the smoother, more common interview wording

usagePhrases.en: Is there a reason you applied to our company?
usagePhrases.note: Softer, indirect interviewer phrasing using 이유 ('reason')

usagePhrases.en: Was there something that led you to apply?
usagePhrases.note: 계기 ('trigger/occasion') — asks for the specific spark behind it

examples.ko: 저희 회사에 지원한 동기가 뭐예요?
examples.romanization: jeohui hoesae jiwonhan donggiga mwoyeyo?
examples.en: What's your motivation for applying to our company?
examples.note: 동기 is the subject (가), the answer is 존댓말; 저희 회사 = 'our company' (humble, used by company staff)

examples.ko: A: 지원 동기가 어떻게 되세요? 편하게 말씀해 주세요. / B: 네, 저는 귀사의 글로벌 사업 확장에 기여하고 싶어서 지원했습니다.
examples.romanization: A: jiwon donggiga eotteoke doeseyo? pyeonhage malsseumhae juseyo. / B: ne, jeoneun gwisaui geullobeol saeo pwakjange giyeohago sipeoseo jiwonhaetseumnida.
examples.en: A: What's your reason for applying? Please speak comfortably. / B: Yes, I applied because I want to contribute to your company's global business expansion.
examples.note: 어떻게 되세요 is the polished way; answer frame: ...에 기여하고 싶어서 지원했습니다

examples.ko: 솔직히 지원 동기가 궁금해서요. 왜 이 직무를 택하셨어요?
examples.romanization: soljiki jiwon donggiga gunggeumhaeseoyo. wae i jingmureul taekasyeosseoyo?
examples.en: Honestly, I'm curious about your motivation — why this particular role?
examples.note: 직무 = 'job role/duties'; 택하다 = 'to choose'; 솔직히 signals a candid follow-up

entries.nuance: 지원 동기 (Sino-Korean 志願動機; 지원 志願 'apply' + 동기 動機 'motive') is the reason you applied, and 'What's your 지원 동기?' is the single most predictable interview question in Korea — prepare a full answer in 존댓말. Two phrasings matter: the textbook 지원 동기가 뭐예요? and the smoother, very common 지원 동기가 어떻게 되세요? — the latter uses 어떻게 되다, a polite formula for asking someone's info (also used for name, age, contact), and sounds more courteous than the blunt 뭐예요 in a formal setting. English speakers stumble in two ways: first, confusing 동기 ('motive', 動機) with its homonym 동기 (同期, 'same-year cohort-mate') — same sound, different Hanja; context disambiguates, but be aware. Second, giving a self-centered answer ('good salary', 'it's near my house') — Korean interview culture expects you to frame motivation around fit with the company and role (회사의 비전, 직무 적합성); a purely personal-benefit answer reads as immature. The answer frame is: [company/role strength]에 기여하고 싶어서 지원했습니다 ('I applied because I want to contribute to...'). Don't translate 'motivation' as 모티베이션; the word is 동기.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 동기 (motive) with 동기 (cohort-mate).
동기 (動機) is 'motivation'; the homonym 동기 (同期) means a same-year colleague/classmate. Context decides — in 지원 동기 it's always 'motive'.
Answering with purely personal benefits.
Saying '월급이 높아서' or '집이 가까워서' sounds immature. Frame your 지원 동기 around fit with the company/role: ...에 기여하고 싶어서 지원했습니다.
Using 뭐예요 in a very formal interview.
지원 동기가 뭐예요 is fine but blunt. The polished interviewer/answer register prefers 어떻게 되세요 / ...때문에 지원했습니다.

structuredNuance.t: 지원 동기 is the reason you applied — the single most predictable Korean interview question. You will HEAR it constantly, so prepare to answer in 존댓말. Two phrasings: 지원 동기가 뭐예요? (slightly casual) and 지원 동기가 어떻게 되세요? (polished, common). Answer frame: ...에 기여하고 싶어서 지원했습니다 ('I applied because I want to contribute to...').

Sino-Korean 志願動機; 지원 志願 'apply/aspire' + 동기 動機 'motive/trigger'. Beware the homonym 동기 (同期) = 'same-year cohort-mate/classmate' — different Hanja, same pronunciation; in 지원 동기 it always means 'motive'.

지원 동기 ('motive for applying') vs 지원 이유 ('reason for applying') — nearly synonymous, but 동기 implies a deeper inner drive while 이유 can be a surface reason. Interviewers prefer to hear 동기 because it invites a richer answer about fit and aspiration rather than circumstance.
Question variants: 동기가 뭐예요? → 동기가 어떻게 되세요? → 지원하게 된 계기가 있나요? → 이 회사를 선택한 이유가 있으실까요? Answer templates: ...때문에 지원했습니다 (reason-first) / ...에 기여하고 싶어 지원했습니다 (contribution-first, more impressive).

Two traps: (1) 동기 (動機, motive) vs 동기 (同期, cohort-mate) — same sound, different meaning; in 지원 동기 it is always 'motive'. (2) Giving a self-centered reason ('salary is good', 'location is convenient') — Korean interview culture expects motivation framed around company/role fit. Don't translate 'motivation' as 모티베이션; say 동기.

entries.english: What's your work experience?
entries.shortExplanation: 경력이 어떻게 되세요? is a practical expression meaning "What's your work experience?".
entries.explanation: 경력이 어떻게 되세요? (gyeongnyeogi eotteoke doeseyo?) = "What's your work experience?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 경력이 어떻게 되세요? ("What is your work experience?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-formal; the natural way an interviewer asks — uses the courteous info-asking formula
Polite; a simpler yes/no version, often asked of new graduates

usagePhrases.en: How much relevant experience do you have?
usagePhrases.note: 관련 ('related') narrows it to experience in the same field

usagePhrases.en: How many years of experience do you have?
usagePhrases.note: Asks specifically for the number of years

examples.ko: 혹시 경력이 어떻게 되세요?
examples.romanization: hoksi gyeongnyeogi eotteoke doeseyo?
examples.en: May I ask about your work experience?
examples.note: 혹시 softens a potentially sensitive question about whether someone has experience at all

examples.ko: A: 이 분야에서 경력이 얼마나 되세요? / B: 3년 정도 있어요. 주로 B2B 영업 쪽이었어요.
examples.romanization: A: i bunyaeseo gyeongnyeogi eolmana doeseyo? / B: 3nyeon jeongdo isseoyo. juro B2B yeongeop jjogieosseoyo.
examples.en: A: How much experience do you have in this field? / B: About three years. It was mainly B2B sales.
examples.note: 분야 = 'field'; 경력이 3년 있다 = 'to have 3 years of career experience'

examples.ko: 신입이라 경력은 없지만 관련 인턴 경험은 있어요.
examples.romanization: sinibira gyeongnyeogeun eopsjiman gwallyeon inteon gyeongheomeun isseoyo.
examples.en: I'm entry-level so I have no career experience, but I do have related internship experience.
examples.note: 신입 = entry-level; highlights the critical 경력 (formal paid career) vs 경험 (any experience) distinction

entries.nuance: 경력 (Sino-Korean 經歷, 'things one has gone through') means professional work experience / career history — the years and roles you've held. 경력이 어떻게 되세요? again uses the polite info-asking formula 어떻게 되세요, making it the courteous interview standard. The crucial distinction for English speakers is 경력 vs 경험: 경력 specifically means formal, usually paid, career experience that 'counts' (jobs, professional roles, measured in years), while 경험 (經驗) is any experience broadly (an internship, a project, travel, life experience). A new grad correctly says 경력은 없지만 경험은 있어요. This maps onto the hiring split between 신입 (新入, entry-level) and 경력직 (經歷職, experienced hire) — job posts are labeled 신입 채용 vs 경력 채용. A second pitfall: 경력 is the experience itself, while 이력 (履歷) is the documented record of it — your 이력서 lists your 이력/경력. For counting years, say 경력이 3년 됐어요 ('my career reached 3 years') or 3년 경력이 있어요. Verb: 경력이 있다/없다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 경험 when you mean professional career.
경험 is any experience; 경력 is formal/paid career history counted in years. For job experience say 경력이 3년 있어요, not 경험이 3년.
A new grad calling themselves 경력직.
No career yet = 신입 (entry-level). 경력직 means an experienced hire. Say 저는 신입이에요 / 경력은 없어요.
Confusing 경력 with 이력.
경력 is the experience itself; 이력 is the written record of it (in your 이력서). Ask 경력이 어떻게 되세요, not 이력이 어떻게 되세요.

structuredNuance.t: 경력 means professional work experience / career history — the years and roles you've held. 경력이 어떻게 되세요? uses the polite info-asking formula 어떻게 되다. For counting years: 경력이 3년 됐어요 or 3년 경력이 있어요. Verb pattern: 경력이 있다/없다.
경력 is Sino-Korean 經歷 — 經 'to pass through/experience' + 歷 'track record/history'. Note how the 이력 (履歷) in 이력서 overlaps — 이력 is the written record, 경력 is the lived experience.

경력 (formal paid career, counted in years, the basis of 경력직) vs 경험 (any experience broadly, including internships, volunteer work, life events). A new grad says 경력은 없지만 경험은 있어요. Also: 경력 (the experience) vs 이력 (the written record of it in 이력서).

경력이 있다 / 없다 / 있어요 → 경력이 3년 됐어요 / 3년 경력이 있어요 → 관련 경력이 있어요 ('have relevant experience'). Compound: 경력직 (experienced hire), 경력 사항 (career section on 이력서), 경력 단절 (career interruption, e.g. after childcare leave).

Don't use 경험 when you mean professional career years (경력이 3년 있어요, not 경험이 3년). Don't call yourself 경력직 if you're a new grad — 신입 is correct. And don't use 경험이 어떻게 되세요 in a hiring context when asking years on the job — ask 경력.

entries.english: What's your strength?
entries.shortExplanation: 강점이 뭐예요? is a practical expression meaning "What's your strength?".
entries.explanation: 강점이 뭐예요? (gangjeomi mwoyeyo?) means "What's your strength?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 강점이 뭐예요? ("What's your strength?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; slightly casual interview phrasing, acceptable but direct

usagePhrases.en: What do you think your strength is?
usagePhrases.note: Formal-polite; 본인 ('oneself', referring to 'you') is typical interview wording
Uses 장점 (everyday 'good point') instead of 강점 — slightly less formal

usagePhrases.en: What would you say your strengths are?
usagePhrases.note: Polished info-asking register with 어떻게 되다

examples.ko: 본인의 강점이 뭐라고 생각하세요?
examples.romanization: boninui gangjeomi mworago saenggakaseyo?
examples.en: What do you consider your strength?
examples.note: 본인 + 라고 생각하세요 is textbook interviewer phrasing — 본인 ('oneself') is how the interviewer politely refers to 'you'

examples.ko: A: 강점이 어떻게 되세요? / B: 제 강점은 어떤 일이든 끝까지 책임지고 해낸다는 거예요.
examples.romanization: A: gangjeomi eotteoke doeseyo? / B: je gangjeomeun eotteon irideun kkeutkkaji chaegimjigo haenaendaneun geoyeyo.
examples.en: A: What would you say your strengths are? / B: My strength is that I take responsibility and see any task through to the end.
examples.note: ...다는 거예요 nominalizes a whole behavior as a strength — a high-value interview structure

examples.ko: 제 강점은 꼼꼼함이에요. 덕분에 실수를 잘 안 해요.
examples.romanization: je gangjeomeun kkomkkomhamieyo. deokbune silsureul jal an haeyo.
examples.en: My strength is being meticulous. As a result, I rarely make mistakes.
examples.note: 제 강점은 X이에요 = clean answer frame; 덕분에 ('thanks to that') shows the concrete benefit

entries.nuance: 강점 (Sino-Korean 強點, 'strong point') is your strength, the positive half of the inevitable interview pair 강점/약점 (strengths/weaknesses). The answer frame is 제 강점은 ___이에요/입니다. The subtle distinction: 강점 vs 장점. 장점 (長點, 'good point') is the broad everyday word for any merit (of a person, product, or plan), while 강점 leans toward a competitive/professional strength you bring — interviewers often specifically ask 강점, and answering with 장점 is fine but slightly more casual/general. Opposites differ too: 강점↔약점, 장점↔단점. The classic pitfall is the 직역 of 'strength' as 힘 ('physical force/power') — 제 힘은... means 'my physical strength is...', which is comically wrong in an interview context. When you describe the strength as a behavior rather than a single noun, use the nominalizer: 끝까지 해내는 거 ('the fact that I see things through'). Another trap is humility miscalibration: Korean interview culture rewards confident-but-not-arrogant phrasing, so state your 강점 plainly (제 강점은 ...입니다) rather than over-hedging with 별로 없는데요 ('I don't really have one'), which reads as a non-answer. Register stays 존댓말 throughout; 본인 is how the interviewer refers to 'you'.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'strength' as 힘.
힘 is physical force. A character/professional strength is 강점 (or 장점). Say 제 강점은..., never 제 힘은...
Answering 강점이 별로 없어요.
Excessive humility reads as a non-answer. State it plainly: 제 강점은 ...입니다. Confidence (not arrogance) is expected.
Mixing the opposites: pairing 강점 with 단점.
강점 pairs with 약점; 장점 pairs with 단점. Keep the sets straight: 강점/약점, 장점/단점.

structuredNuance.t: 강점 is your strength, the positive half of the interview pair 강점/약점. Answer frame: 제 강점은 ___이에요/입니다. When describing a behavior not a noun, nominalize: 끝까지 해내는 거예요 ('the fact that I see things through'). State it confidently — over-hedging sounds like a non-answer. 본인 is how the interviewer refers to 'you' in polite wording.

강점 is Sino-Korean 強點 — 강 強 'strong' + 점 點 'point'. The matching opposite is 약점 (弱點, 'weak point'). Their everyday lookalikes — 장점 (長點, 'long/good point') and 단점 (短點, 'short/bad point') — are a separate pair.

강점 (competitive strength, interview-register) vs 장점 (any merit, everyday register). Keep the pairs intact: 강점↔약점 / 장점↔단점. Mixing them (e.g. 강점과 단점) marks you as a learner. 장점 is fine but 강점 fits interviews better.
제 강점은 [명사]이에요 → 제 강점은 [동사-는 거]예요 (behavior) → 제 가장 큰 강점은 ...이라고 생각합니다 (most emphatic). Scale: 강점이에요 → 강점이라고 생각해요 → 강점이라고 자부합니다 (proudest, reserved for confident moments).

Classic trap: translating 'strength' as 힘 ('physical force') — 제 힘은... means 'my physical strength is...', wrong in any interview. Answer with 강점. Also avoid excessive humility: 별로 없는데요 ('I don't really have any') reads as unprepared; state your 강점 plainly and confidently.

entries.english: What's your weakness?
entries.shortExplanation: 약점이 뭐예요? is a practical expression meaning "What's your weakness?".
entries.explanation: "What's your weakness?" — that is 약점이 뭐예요? (yakjeomi mwoyeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 약점이 뭐예요? ("What's your weakness?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; slightly casual interview phrasing

usagePhrases.en: What do you think your weakness is?
usagePhrases.note: Formal-polite; standard interviewer wording with 본인
Uses everyday 단점 ('flaw') in place of 약점 — slightly softer

usagePhrases.en: Is there anything you'd like to improve?
usagePhrases.note: Gentlest phrasing; 보완하다 = 'to supplement/shore up'

examples.ko: 본인의 약점은 뭐라고 생각하세요?
examples.romanization: boninui yakjeomeun mworago saenggakaseyo?
examples.en: What do you consider your weakness?
examples.note: The matched pair to the 강점 question — prepare both before every interview

examples.ko: A: 약점이 뭐예요? / B: 약점은 거절을 잘 못 하는 건데, 요즘 고치려고 노력 중이에요.
examples.romanization: A: yakjeomi mwoyeyo? / B: yakjeomeun geojeoreul jal mo taneun geonde, yojeum gochiryeogo noryeok jungieyo.
examples.en: A: What's your weakness? / B: My weakness is that I can't say no well, but I'm working on fixing it lately.
examples.note: The expected structure: weakness + 고치려고/보완하려고 노력 중이에요 ('working to fix/improve it')

examples.ko: 제 약점은 가끔 너무 완벽하게 하려는 거예요. 그래서 시간 배분을 더 신경 쓰고 있어요.
examples.romanization: je yakjeomeun gakkeum neomu wanbyeokage haryeoneun geoyeyo. geuraeseo sigan baebuneul deo singyeong sseugo isseoyo.
examples.en: My weakness is that I sometimes try too hard to do things perfectly. So I'm paying more attention to time management.
examples.note: Frame a 'weakness' that doubles as effort; 시간 배분 ('time allocation') as the concrete improvement shows self-awareness

entries.nuance: 약점 (Sino-Korean 弱點, 'weak point') is your weakness, the flip side of 강점. The expected Korean interview answer structure is: 약점을 말하고 (state the weakness) → 개선 노력을 더하기 (add how you're improving it): 제 약점은 ___인데, 고치려고/보완하려고 노력하고 있어요. This structure is nearly a formula, and skipping the improvement part makes your answer feel unfinished. Like the strengths pair, watch 약점 vs 단점: 단점 (短點) is the everyday word for any flaw, 약점 is the more interview-flavored 'weak point/vulnerability'; opposites are 약점↔강점, 단점↔장점. The English-speaker pitfalls: (1) the 직역 of 'weakness' as 약함 ('weakness' as an abstract noun, awkward in this context) or 힘이 없다 ('to lack physical strength') — wrong register entirely; the noun is 약점. (2) Cultural over-honesty: English coaching says 'give a real weakness', but in Korea a brutally honest fatal flaw (저는 게을러요 = 'I'm lazy') with no fix can sink you — the norm is a manageable weakness plus a clear improvement effort. The polished verb 보완하다 ('to supplement/shore up') sounds more sophisticated than the plainer 고치다 ('fix'). Nominalizer pattern: 약점은 [동사]-는 거예요 for behavior-style weaknesses.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'weakness' as 약함 or 힘이 없어요.
Those mean abstract/physical weakness. The interview noun is 약점: 제 약점은 ...이에요.
Naming a fatal flaw with no fix.
저는 게을러요 ('I'm lazy') with nothing more reads badly in Korea. Give a manageable weakness + 고치려고/보완하려고 노력하고 있어요.
Pairing 약점 with 단점 as if synonyms in one set.
약점 pairs with 강점; 단점 pairs with 장점. Don't list '강점과 단점' — say 강점과 약점 or 장점과 단점.

structuredNuance.t: 약점 is your weakness, the flip side of 강점. Korean interviews expect the two-part structure: state the weakness + how you're improving it: 제 약점은 ___인데, 고치려고/보완하려고 노력하고 있어요. Skipping the improvement part makes the answer feel incomplete. Keep it 존댓말; for behavior-style weaknesses use the nominalizer: 못 하는 거예요.
약점 is Sino-Korean 弱點 — 약 弱 'weak' + 점 點 'point'. Its pair is 강점 (強點). The everyday lookalike 단점 (短點, 'short/lacking point') pairs with 장점, not 강점.

약점 (interview-register 'weak point/vulnerability') vs 단점 (everyday 'shortcoming/flaw of any kind'). Keep pairs intact: 약점↔강점 / 단점↔장점. Also: 보완하다 ('to supplement/shore up', polished) vs 고치다 ('to fix', plainer) — interviewers appreciate hearing 보완하려고 노력 중이에요.
Simple: 제 약점은 X예요. With improvement: 제 약점은 X인데, 보완하려고 노력하고 있어요. Behavior-style: 제 약점은 [동사]-는 거예요. Scale of hedges: 약점이에요 → 약점이라고 할 수 있어요 → 보완해야 할 점이 있다면 ...이에요.

Two traps: (1) 직역 of 'weakness' as 약함 or 힘이 없다 — wrong register; the interview noun is 약점. (2) Cultural over-honesty: naming a fatal flaw (게을러요 = 'I'm lazy') with no improvement effort can hurt you in Korea. The expected move is a manageable weakness + 보완하려고 노력 중이에요.

entries.english: personality strengths and weaknesses
entries.shortExplanation: 성격의 장단점 is a practical expression meaning "personality strengths and weaknesses".
entries.explanation: 성격의 장단점 (seonggyeogui jangdanjeom) = "personality strengths and weaknesses". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 성격의 장단점이 뭐예요? ("What are your personality's pros and cons?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: What are your personality's pros and cons?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; the classic combined question — note it asks for BOTH

usagePhrases.en: Please tell me your personality's strengths and weaknesses
usagePhrases.note: Formal-polite request; 말씀해 주세요 = 'please tell me' (humble listening)

usagePhrases.en: And your personality's pros and cons?
usagePhrases.note: Casual-polite follow-up with -은요?, softly inviting your answer

usagePhrases.en: What's your personality like, would you say?
usagePhrases.note: Softer opener than장단점; ...편이세요 = 'tend to be' — less confrontational

examples.ko: 성격의 장단점을 말씀해 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: seonggyeogui jangdanjeomeul malsseumhae jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Could you tell me the pros and cons of your personality?
examples.note: 장단점 = 장점 + 단점 fused into one compound word — you MUST address both halves

examples.ko: A: 성격의 장단점이 뭐예요? / B: 제 성격의 장점은 밝은 거고, 단점은 좀 급한 거예요.
examples.romanization: A: seonggyeogui jangdanjeomi mwoyeyo? / B: je seonggyeogui jangjeomeun balgeun geogo, danjeomeun jom geupan geoyeyo.
examples.en: A: What are your personality's strengths and weaknesses? / B: My personality's strength is being cheerful, and the weakness is being a bit hasty.
examples.note: 장점은 ... 단점은 ... lets you answer both in one breath — clean and complete

examples.ko: 성격이 꼼꼼한 편이라 장점이자 단점이 될 때도 있어요.
examples.romanization: seonggyeogi kkomkkomhan pyeonira jangjeomija danjeomi doel ttaedo isseoyo.
examples.en: I tend to be meticulous, so it can be both a strength and a weakness at the same time.
examples.note: 장점이자 단점 uses -이자 ('being both A and B') — a high-value reframing that shows self-awareness

entries.nuance: 성격의 장단점 means 'the strong and weak points of one's personality (성격)', and 장단점 is the fused noun 장점 + 단점 — Korean loves these compressed pairs (장단점, 찬반, 손익). Interviewers very often ask the combined question, so you answer BOTH halves: 제 성격의 장점은 ___이고, 단점은 ___이에요. The high-value move is the -이자 structure: 꼼꼼한 게 장점이자 단점이에요 ('being meticulous is both a strength and a weakness'), which reframes one trait as double-edged — interviewers reward this as showing nuanced self-awareness. Learners who don't know -이자 clumsily repeat the trait twice instead. The genitive 의: 성격의 장단점 links 성격 to 장단점; 의 is often pronounced '에' and in speech 성격 장단점 without 의 is also natural. Don't confuse 성격 ('personality/temperament') with 성질 — 성질 can imply a bad temper (성질부리다 = throw a tantrum), so always describe yourself with 성격. Register: keep 존댓말 throughout; 본인 성격의 장단점은요? is the interviewer's softened version.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Treating 장단점 as 'choose pros OR cons'.
장단점 is one compound = 'pros and cons'. The question wants BOTH: 장점은 ...이고, 단점은 ...이에요.
Describing yourself with 성질 instead of 성격.
성질 often implies a bad temper (성질부리다 = throw a fit). Your character is 성격: 제 성격은...
Repeating the trait instead of using -이자.
To say one trait is both, use -이자: 꼼꼼한 게 장점이자 단점이에요, rather than awkwardly stating it twice.

structuredNuance.t: 성격의 장단점 asks for BOTH halves of your personality — 장점 (strengths) and 단점 (weaknesses). Answer both: 제 성격의 장점은 ___이고, 단점은 ___이에요. Keep 존댓말. The interviewer's soft version: 성격이 어떤 편이세요? (What's your personality like?).

장단점 is the compressed pair: 장점 (長點, 'good/long point') + 단점 (短點, 'bad/short point'). 성격 (性格) = 'personality/character'. The -이자 structure ('being both A and B simultaneously') is the high-value reframing tool: 장점이자 단점이에요.

성격 ('personality/character', neutral to positive) vs 성질 (can imply bad temper; 성질부리다 = throw a fit). Always self-describe with 성격. Also: 성격의 장단점 (specifically about personality traits) vs 강점/약점 (professional competency strengths/weaknesses) — different question, different focus.
장단점이 뭐예요? → 장단점을 말씀해 주세요 → 성격이 어떤 편이세요? (softer opener). Answer frames: 장점은 X이고 단점은 Y예요 / 장점이자 단점은 Z예요 (double-edged reframe with -이자). 의 can be dropped in speech: 성격 장단점 = 성격의 장단점.

Misreading 장단점 as choose-one: it's ONE compound meaning 'pros AND cons' — answer both. Don't use 성질 to describe yourself. Missing the -이자 structure makes answers sound flat; 장점이자 단점이에요 is the smooth and impressive move. The genitive 의 is often dropped in natural speech — 성격 장단점 is fine.

entries.english: What's the salary (annual)?
entries.shortExplanation: 연봉이 어떻게 되나요? is a practical expression meaning "What's the salary (annual)?".
entries.explanation: 연봉이 어떻게 되나요? (yeonbongi eotteoke doenayo?) means "What's the salary (annual)?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 연봉이 어떻게 되나요? ("What is the annual salary?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; careful, indirect way to ask about pay — 어떻게 되다 softens a sensitive topic

usagePhrases.en: What salary range are you thinking of?
usagePhrases.note: What the employer asks YOU about your expectation; 어느 정도 = 'what range'
희망 연봉 = 'desired/expected annual salary' — the standard term on Korean job applications

usagePhrases.en: How much is the monthly pay?
usagePhrases.note: 월급 = monthly wage; more casual and direct — less appropriate in a formal interview

examples.ko: 혹시 연봉이 어떻게 되나요?
examples.romanization: hoksi yeonbongi eotteoke doenayo?
examples.en: May I ask what the annual salary is?
examples.note: 혹시 + 어떻게 되나요 keeps a money question polite — always use this buffer, not 얼마예요?

examples.ko: A: 희망 연봉은 어느 정도세요? / B: 4,500만 원 정도 생각하고 있는데, 협의 가능합니다.
examples.romanization: A: huimang yeonbongeun eoneu jeongdoseyo? / B: 4,500man won jeongdo saenggakago inneunde, hyeobui ganeunghamnida.
examples.en: A: What's your desired salary range? / B: I'm thinking around 45 million won, but it's negotiable.
examples.note: 희망 연봉 is your expected yearly figure; 협의 가능합니다 ('it's negotiable') is the polished add-on

examples.ko: 연봉은 협의 가능한가요? 복지 혜택도 궁금해서요.
examples.romanization: yeonbongeun hyeobui ganeunghangayo? bokji hyetaekdo gunggeumhaeseoyo.
examples.en: Is the salary negotiable? I'm also curious about benefits.
examples.note: 협의 가능 = 'negotiable'; 복지 혜택 = 'welfare/benefits' — asking about both shows full-picture thinking

entries.nuance: 연봉 (Sino-Korean 年俸, 'yearly stipend') is ANNUAL salary, and Korea quotes pay annually by default — a job post saying 연봉 4,000 means 40 million won PER YEAR, not per month. This is a major trap for English speakers, who may hear a number and think monthly. Distinguish 연봉 (yearly) from 월급 (月給, monthly wage). Asking about pay is delicate; the polite formula 연봉이 어떻게 되나요? / 어떻게 되세요? far outperforms the blunt 얼마예요? ('how much?'), which can sound money-first in a formal interview. From the employer's side you'll be asked your 희망 연봉 ('desired annual salary') — answer with a yearly range and add 협의 가능합니다 ('negotiable'). Cultural note: raising salary TOO early or aggressively reads poorly in Korea; many candidates wait until the employer raises it or until a later round. Know the cluster: 복지 (benefits/welfare), 인센티브, 성과급 ('performance pay'), 4대 보험 (the four major social insurances), and 세전/세후 (before/after tax) — 연봉 figures are usually 세전 ('before tax'). Don't translate 'salary' as 샐러리; the words are 연봉 (annual) and 월급 (monthly).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Hearing a 연봉 figure as monthly.
연봉 is ANNUAL. 연봉 3,600 means 36 million won per year (≈ 300/month). Monthly pay is 월급.
Asking 얼마예요? bluntly in a formal interview.
Money questions need cushioning. Use 연봉이 어떻게 되나요? or 협의 가능한가요?, and ideally let the employer raise it first.
Stating your 희망 연봉 as a monthly number.
Desired salary is quoted yearly: 희망 연봉은 4,000만 원 정도입니다. Giving a monthly figure confuses the negotiation.

structuredNuance.t: 연봉 is ANNUAL salary — Korea quotes pay yearly by default. A figure of 연봉 4,000 means 40 million won per year, not per month. Polite ask: 연봉이 어떻게 되나요? Your expected salary: 희망 연봉은 [X]만 원 정도입니다. Always add 협의 가능합니다 ('negotiable'). Related cluster: 복지, 인센티브, 성과급, 4대 보험, 세전/세후.
연봉 is Sino-Korean 年俸 — 년/연 年 'year' + 봉 俸 'stipend/salary'. 월급 (月給) = month + pay/supply. The difference in base nouns reflects the different time units.

연봉 (annual, formal job-offer context) vs 월급 (monthly wage, casual everyday context). Don't quote monthly when asked 희망 연봉 — it confuses negotiations. Also: 연봉 (fixed annual figure) vs 성과급/인센티브 (variable performance pay on top).
연봉이 어떻게 되나요? → 희망 연봉이 어떻게 되세요? → 연봉은 협의 가능한가요? Answer scale: [X]만 원 생각하고 있어요 → [X]만 원 정도 희망합니다 → 회사 기준에 맞추겠습니다 (deferential, lets the company lead).

Hearing a 연봉 figure as monthly: 연봉 3,600 means 36 million won per YEAR (≈3 million/month). Stating your 희망 연봉 as a monthly number confuses the whole negotiation. Don't ask 얼마예요? bluntly — use 어떻게 되나요? / 어느 정도세요?. Don't say 샐러리; say 연봉 or 월급.

entries.english: When can you start (come to work)?
entries.shortExplanation: 언제부터 출근 가능하세요? is a practical expression meaning "When can you start (come to work)?".
entries.explanation: "When can you start (come to work)?" — that is 언제부터 출근 가능하세요? (eonjebuteo chulgeun ganeunghaseyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 언제부터 출근 가능하세요? ("When can you start working?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-formal; what the interviewer asks near the end — a positive signal

usagePhrases.en: From when are you available to start?
usagePhrases.note: Reordered, equally common interviewer wording
Your reply; 바로 = 'right away/immediately' — the eagerness answer

usagePhrases.en: I can start from next week
usagePhrases.note: Your reply with a specific time; 부터 = 'from/starting'

examples.ko: 혹시 언제부터 출근 가능하세요?
examples.romanization: hoksi eonjebuteo chulgeun ganeunghaseyo?
examples.en: When would you be able to start?
examples.note: Hearing this is usually a GOOD sign — they're mentally placing you on the team

examples.ko: A: 언제부터 출근 가능하세요? / B: 지금 회사 일 정리할 게 있어서 2주 정도 후에 가능할 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: A: eonjebuteo chulgeun ganeunghaseyo? / B: jigeum hoesa il jeongnihal ge isseoseo 2ju jeongdo hue ganeunghal geot gatayo.
examples.en: A: When can you start? / B: I have some things to wrap up at my current job, so I think I can start in about 2 weeks.
examples.note: 지금 회사 일 정리 = 'wrapping up things at my current job' — a realistic reason; 2주 정도 후 = 'in about 2 weeks'

examples.ko: 다음 달 1일부터 출근 가능합니다.
examples.romanization: daeum dal 1ilbuteo chulgeun ganeunghamnida.
examples.en: I can start on the 1st of next month.
examples.note: Give a concrete date: 부터 ('from') marks the start point — never 까지, which means 'until'

entries.nuance: 언제부터 출근 가능하세요? means 'from when are you able to come to work?' — 출근 (Sino-Korean 出勤, 'go to work/report for duty') + 가능하다 ('to be possible'). Hearing this question is usually a GOOD sign; it implies they're picturing you on the team. The key vocabulary point: 출근 specifically means going TO work / starting work (its opposite is 퇴근, 退勤, 'leaving work') — it's the right word for 'start the job' here, not 시작하다 ('to begin') in the abstract. So you answer 다음 주부터 출근 가능합니다, not 일을 시작할 수 있어요 (understandable but less idiomatic). The particle is 부터 ('from/starting'): 언제부터, 다음 주부터, 1일부터. Common pitfalls: (1) confusing 부터 ('from') with 까지 ('until') — 'starting from Monday' is 월요일부터, never 월요일까지; (2) honorific direction — the interviewer asks with 가능하세요 (honoring YOU), but YOU answer about yourself with plain 가능합니다/가능해요, not 가능하세요; (3) calquing 'start' and saying 일을 시작할 수 있어요 — use 출근 가능합니다. A polished, face-saving reason for a delay is 인수인계 ('handover') at your current job.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 부터 and 까지.
부터 = 'from/starting'; 까지 = 'until'. 'From next week' is 다음 주부터, not 다음 주까지 (which means 'by next week').
Answering about yourself with 가능하세요.
-세요 honors the other person. For your own availability use plain forms: 다음 주부터 가능합니다 / 가능해요.
Saying 일을 시작할 수 있어요 instead of 출근.
For starting a job, the idiomatic word is 출근: 언제부터 출근 가능하세요 / 바로 출근 가능합니다.

structuredNuance.t: 언제부터 출근 가능하세요? = 'From when can you report for work?' Hearing it is a positive sign. Answer: 다음 주부터 출근 가능합니다 / 바로 가능합니다. The particle is 부터 ('from'); for delays, 인수인계 ('handover') is the polished reason. Keep answer in plain polite forms (가능합니다/가능해요), not honorific.

출근 is Sino-Korean 出勤 — 출 出 'go out' + 근 勤 'work/duty'. Its opposite is 퇴근 (退勤, 'leave work'). 가능 (可能) = 'possible'. The 出 already implies direction 'out to work', reinforcing why 부터 ('from') fits naturally.

출근하다 (reporting for work on a given day — daily) vs 입사하다 (joining the company — one-time event). On your first day you both 입사 AND 출근, but daily commuting is only 출근. For 'start the job' use 출근 in this context, not the more abstract 시작하다.
Question variants: 언제부터 출근 가능하세요? → 출근 가능한 날짜가 어떻게 되세요? → 빠르면 언제 가능하세요? Answers: 바로 가능합니다 → 다음 주부터 가능합니다 → 인수인계 후 [X]주 후에 가능할 것 같습니다.

Three traps: (1) 부터 vs 까지 — 부터 = 'from (start)', 까지 = 'until (end)'; 'starting Monday' is 월요일부터, never 월요일까지. (2) Mirroring the interviewer's honorific: they say 가능하세요 to honor you, but you answer about yourself with plain 가능합니다/가능해요, not 가능하세요. (3) Saying 일을 시작할 수 있어요 instead of 출근 가능합니다 — use 출근.

entries.english: Do you have any questions?
entries.shortExplanation: 궁금한 점 있으세요? is a practical expression meaning "Do you have any questions?".
entries.explanation: 궁금한 점 있으세요? (gunggeumhan jeom isseuseyo?) = "Do you have any questions?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 궁금한 점 있으세요? ("Do you have any questions?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-formal; the interviewer's standard closing invitation — do NOT answer 없어요
Slightly more direct version; 질문 (質問) = question/inquiry
마지막으로 ('lastly') signals the interview is wrapping up — a final cue to engage

usagePhrases.en: Yes, may I ask one thing?
usagePhrases.note: Your reply; 여쭤보다 = humble 'to ask' (much more polished than 물어보다 to an interviewer)

examples.ko: 혹시 저희한테 궁금한 점 있으세요?
examples.romanization: hoksi jeohuihante gunggeumhan jeom isseuseyo?
examples.en: Do you happen to have any questions for us?
examples.note: 저희한테 = 'to/for us (the company)' — your cue to ask a thoughtful question, not to say 없어요

examples.ko: A: 마지막으로 궁금한 점 있으세요? / B: 네, 여쭤봐도 될까요? 입사하면 어떤 업무를 먼저 맡게 되나요?
examples.romanization: A: majimageuro gunggeumhan jeom isseuseyo? / B: ne, yeojjwobwado doelkkayo? ipsahamyeon eotteon eommureul meonjeo matge doenayo?
examples.en: A: Lastly, do you have any questions? / B: Yes, may I ask — if I join, what tasks would I take on first?
examples.note: 여쭤봐도 될까요 = humble 'may I ask?'; 업무 = 'duties'; 맡다 = 'to take charge of' — shows role-specific curiosity

examples.ko: 팀 분위기가 궁금한데, 여쭤봐도 될까요?
examples.romanization: tim bunwigiga gunggeumhande, yeojjwobwado doelkkayo?
examples.en: I'm curious about the team atmosphere — may I ask?
examples.note: Asking about the work environment shows genuine interest without seeming demanding

entries.nuance: 궁금한 점 있으세요? ('do you have anything you're curious about?') is the interviewer's standard closing line — 궁금하다 ('to be curious') + 점 ('point/thing') + 있으세요 (honorific 'do you have'). The hidden rule English speakers miss is cultural: answering 아니요, 없어요 ('no, none') is a soft red flag in Korean interviews — it signals low interest in the company. You're expected to have a prepared 역질문 (reverse question) about the role, team, or growth opportunities. Treat this as your final impression opportunity. When YOU ask, use the humble verb 여쭤보다 rather than the plain 물어보다 (묻다): 하나 여쭤봐도 될까요? sounds far more polished than 하나 물어봐도 돼요?. Grammar pitfalls: 있으세요 honors the listener (the interviewer is honoring YOU), so don't echo it about yourself — say 궁금한 게 있습니다 / 질문 있습니다 for your own questions. Also, 점 here means an abstract 'point/matter' (not a physical dot); 것/거 is also fine (궁금한 거) but 점 is the crisp interview register. Don't translate 'question' rigidly as 질문 every time; 궁금한 점/거 ('something I'm curious about') is softer and more natural here.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Answering '없어요' with nothing to ask.
In Korea, no questions signals low interest. Prepare a 역질문 about the role/team: 입사하면 어떤 업무를 맡게 되나요?
Using 물어봐도 돼요 to the interviewer.
물어보다 is plain; the humble verb is 여쭤보다. Say 하나 여쭤봐도 될까요? to sound respectful.
Echoing 있으세요 about your own questions.
-으세요 honors the other person. For yourself: 궁금한 게 있습니다 / 질문 있습니다, not 저는 궁금한 점 있으세요.

structuredNuance.t: 궁금한 점 있으세요? is the interviewer's standard closing line. NEVER answer 없어요 — it signals low interest. You're expected to have a prepared 역질문 (reverse question) about the role, team, or growth. When asking, use the humble verb 여쭤보다: 하나 여쭤봐도 될까요? is far more polished than 물어봐도 돼요?. Keep everything in 존댓말.

궁금하다 is a native Korean expressive word — its etymology is uncertain and it is NOT a Hanja compound. It appears early in written Korean as an affective/sensory root meaning an itching or restless curiosity. The 점 in 궁금한 점 is Sino-Korean 點 ('point/matter'), not a physical dot — this 점 abstracts any concrete question into a polite 'point of curiosity', which is softer than demanding a 질문 ('formal question').

궁금한 점 ('a point of curiosity', soft/natural interview register) vs 질문 ('a formal question' — more direct). 궁금한 게 있습니다 is softer and often better than 질문 있습니다. Also: 여쭤보다 (humble ask, for seniors/interviewers) vs 물어보다 (plain ask, peer level).
Interviewer: 궁금한 점 있으세요? → 질문 있으세요? → 마지막으로 궁금한 거 있으세요? Your opener for the question: 하나 여쭤봐도 될까요? → 한 가지 말씀드려도 될까요? → 궁금한 점이 있는데 여쭤봐도 되겠습니까? (most formal).

Answering 없어요 sends the wrong signal in Korean interviews — always have a 역질문 ready. Honorific trap: 있으세요 honors you (the interviewee); about yourself say 궁금한 게 있습니다, not 저는 궁금한 점 있으세요. Using 물어봐도 돼요? to an interviewer misses the humility register — use 여쭤봐도 될까요?.

entries.english: I passed / I got in (got the job)
entries.shortExplanation: 합격했어요 is a practical expression meaning "I passed / I got in (got the job)".
entries.explanation: 합격했어요 (hapgyeokaesseoyo) means "I passed / I got in (got the job)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 합격했어요 ("I passed / I got accepted"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite past; the standard happy announcement in polite speech
Formal; for an announcement to a superior or a company notification

usagePhrases.en: I got in / I made it
usagePhrases.note: Casual everyday synonym; 붙다 literally 'to stick/adhere'
반말, telling a close friend the good news

examples.ko: 저 그 회사 합격했어요!
examples.romanization: jeo geu hoesa hapgyeokaesseoyo!
examples.en: I got accepted at that company!
examples.note: 합격하다 takes the target with 에 (not 을/를): 그 회사에 합격했어요

examples.ko: 최종 합격해서 다음 주부터 출근해요.
examples.romanization: choejong hapgyeokaeseo daeum jubuteo chulgeunhaeyo.
examples.en: I passed the final round, so I start next week.
examples.note: 최종 합격 = 'final acceptance' (after all rounds); 출근 = 'start commuting/working'

examples.ko: A: 서류는 붙었는데 면접에서 떨어졌어요. / B: 아쉽다. 다음엔 꼭 합격할 거야!
examples.romanization: A: seoryuneun buteonneunde myeonjeobeseo tteoreojyeosseoyo. / B: aswipda. daeumen kko kapgyeokal geoya!
examples.en: A: I passed the document screening but got rejected at the interview. / B: That's a shame. You'll definitely get it next time!
examples.note: 붙다 ('pass') paired with 떨어지다 ('fail/fall') — the natural everyday pair

entries.nuance: 합격하다 (Sino-Korean 合格, 'meet the standard') means to pass / be accepted — for an exam, a school, or a job. 합격했어요 is how you announce you got in. The everyday casual synonym is 붙다 (literally 'to stick/adhere', as if sticking to the position), and its opposite 떨어지다 ('to fall', i.e. to fail/be rejected) — this 붙다/떨어지다 pair is extremely common in speech (서류 붙었어 / 면접 떨어졌어). English speakers trip on: (1) 합격하다 is intransitive — you say 시험에 합격하다 (with 에), and 'I passed' is 합격했어요, NOT 시험을 합격했어요 with 을 in standard grammar (though spoken Korean sometimes bends this). (2) Keep 합격 (you meet the bar) apart from 채용 (採用, 'hiring', the employer's act of taking you on) — you 합격, the company 채용한다 / 뽑는다. (3) Keep 합격 apart from 통과 (通過, 'get through', the casual verb for clearing one stage, e.g. 서류 통과); 합격 is the formal verdict, 통과 is 'made it past'. (4) The 직역 trap: 'I won the job' → there's no 이기다 ('win') here; you 합격했어요. Register: 합격했어요 (polite) is safe; 붙었어요 is fine with peers/friends but a touch casual for a senior, where 합격했습니다 fits. Stages: 서류 합격 → 면접 → 최종 합격.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 시험을 합격했어요 with the object particle.
합격하다 is intransitive; the standard pattern is 시험에 합격하다. Spoken Korean sometimes uses 을, but the safe form is 시험에 합격했어요 or simply 합격했어요.
Translating 'win the job' with 이기다.
There's no 'winning' here. Getting the job is 합격하다 / 붙다: 합격했어요, not 일을 이겼어요.
Using 합격 for the company's action.
You 합격 (pass); the company 채용한다 (hires) or 뽑는다 (picks). Don't say 회사가 저를 합격했어요 — say 회사가 저를 뽑았어요 / 채용했어요.

structuredNuance.t: 합격하다 means to pass / be accepted — for an exam, school, or job. 합격했어요 is the polite announcement; 합격했습니다 is formal; 붙었어요 is the casual everyday synonym. Stages: 서류 합격 (passed résumé screen) → 면접 → 최종 합격 (final acceptance).
합격 is Sino-Korean 合格 — 합 合 'meet/fit' + 격 格 'standard/criterion'. The opposite 불합격 (不合格) adds 불 不 ('not'). The casual pair 붙다 ('stick') / 떨어지다 ('fall') carries the same pass/fail meaning.

합격 (formal 'passed/accepted') vs 붙다 (casual 'stuck to it, made it') vs 통과하다 (casual 'got through one stage'). On the other side: 합격 (you pass) vs 채용 (採用, the company hires you) vs 뽑다 (the company 'picks' you). You always 합격; the company 채용하다 or 뽑는다.
붙었어 (반말) → 합격했어요 (polite) → 합격했습니다 (formal). With stages: 서류 합격 / 1차 합격 / 최종 합격. Negative: 떨어졌어요 / 불합격했어요. Good-news framing: 합격하게 됐어요 (humble, 'it came to pass that I was accepted').

합격하다 is intransitive — the target takes 에: 시험에 합격했어요, not 시험을 합격했어요. 'Win the job' has no 이기다 in Korean — say 합격했어요. Don't say 회사가 저를 합격했어요; the company 뽑았어요 / 채용했어요 (they pick/hire); you 합격했어요 (you pass).

entries.english: I didn't get it / I was rejected
entries.shortExplanation: 불합격했어요 is a practical expression meaning "I didn't get it / I was rejected".
entries.explanation: "I didn't get it / I was rejected" — that is 불합격했어요 (bulhapgyeokaesseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 불합격했어요 ("I didn't pass / I was rejected"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: I didn't pass / I was rejected
usagePhrases.note: Polite; the neutral, formal way to state rejection — relatively clinical

usagePhrases.en: I got rejected / I didn't make it
usagePhrases.note: Casual everyday phrasing; 떨어지다 = 'to fall/drop' — far more common in speech
Softer, face-saving; 안 되다 = 'it didn't happen/go through'
반말, to a close friend

examples.ko: 이번엔 불합격했어요.
examples.romanization: ibeonen bulhapgyeokaesseoyo.
examples.en: I didn't pass this time.
examples.note: 이번엔 ('this time') frames it as one attempt among many, not the end of the road

examples.ko: A: 면접까지 갔는데 아쉽게 떨어졌어요. / B: 힘내요. 다음 기회도 있을 거예요.
examples.romanization: A: myeonjeopkkaji ganneunde aswipge tteoreojyeosseoyo. / B: himnaeyo. daeum gihoedo isseul geoyeyo.
examples.en: A: I made it to the interview stage but sadly didn't get it. / B: Cheer up. There will be other chances.
examples.note: 아쉽게 ('regrettably') softens the bad news; 힘내요 = 'hang in there'

examples.ko: 불합격 통보를 받아서 좀 속상하지만 다시 도전하려고요.
examples.romanization: bulhapgyeok tongboreul badaseo jom soksanghajiman dasi dojeonharyeogoyo.
examples.en: I got a rejection notification and I'm a bit upset, but I'm going to try again.
examples.note: 불합격 통보 = 'rejection notice'; 도전하다 = 'to take on the challenge'; framing it as one attempt keeps motivation positive

entries.nuance: 불합격 (불 不 'not' + 합격) is the formal 'fail/rejection', the direct opposite of 합격. But in real speech Koreans far more often say 떨어졌어요 ('I fell' = I got rejected) than the clinical 불합격했어요 — 떨어지다 is the everyday counterpart to 붙다 ('to pass'). For softening bad news, 안 됐어요 ('it didn't work out') or 아쉽게 안 됐어요 is gentle and face-saving, useful when telling a mentor or senior. English speakers stumble on: (1) reaching for 실패하다 ('to fail') — but 실패하다 implies a broad failure of a venture or project; using it for a single job rejection (면접에 실패했어요) sounds heavier and odd; the right verbs are 떨어지다 / 불합격하다. (2) Saying 거절하다 for 'they rejected me' — 거절하다 means to decline an OFFER or request (you 거절 a confession, an invitation), so 회사가 저를 거절했어요 misframes the situation; from your side say 떨어졌어요. (3) Particle/voice trap: 떨어지다 is intransitive ('I fell/was dropped'), so use 에서 (떨어진 장소): 면접에서 떨어졌어요, not 면접을 떨어졌어요. Register: 불합격했어요 is neutral-formal; 떨어졌어요 is natural spoken; with a senior who asked, 아쉽게 안 됐습니다 is graceful.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 실패하다 for a single rejection.
실패하다 = a broad failure of a plan/venture. For one job rejection use 떨어지다 / 불합격하다: 면접에서 떨어졌어요.
Saying 회사가 저를 거절했어요.
거절하다 is declining an offer/request. A company turning you down: 떨어졌어요 (your side) or 불합격시켰어요. You 거절 an offer; you don't get 거절-ed as a candidate.
Marking it 면접을 떨어졌어요.
떨어지다 is intransitive. Use 에서 for where you were dropped: 면접에서 떨어졌어요, not 면접을 떨어졌어요.

structuredNuance.t: 불합격 is the formal rejection, the opposite of 합격. In real speech use 떨어졌어요 ('I fell/dropped') far more often — it's the everyday counterpart to 붙었어요. To soften with a senior: 아쉽게 안 됐습니다. Register: 불합격했어요 (neutral-formal), 떨어졌어요 (natural spoken), 아쉽게 안 됐어요 (gentle/face-saving).

불합격 = 불 不 ('not') + 합격 (合格, 'meet the standard'). The casual metaphor pair: 붙다 ('to stick' = pass) / 떨어지다 ('to fall' = fail/be rejected). These physical metaphors of sticking vs falling are deeply embedded in everyday Korean.

떨어지다 (natural everyday 'get rejected') vs 불합격하다 (formal) vs 실패하다 (broad 'fail a venture/project' — too heavy for a single rejection). Also: 떨어지다 (intransitive, your side) vs 떨어뜨리다 / 불합격시키다 (the company's action, 'to drop/reject someone'). 거절하다 is 'to decline an offer/request' — not for a company rejecting a candidate.
떨어졌어 (반말) → 떨어졌어요 (polite) → 불합격했습니다 (formal). Softer forms: 아쉽게 안 됐어요 → 이번엔 인연이 아니었나 봐요 ('it seems it wasn't meant to be this time'). Notification noun: 불합격 통보 ('rejection notice').

Don't use 실패하다 for a single rejection — it implies a large-scale failure. Don't use 거절하다 for 'they rejected me' — that's declining an offer; the company 불합격시켰어요 and you 떨어졌어요. Particle trap: 떨어지다 is intransitive — use 에서 for the stage you fell at: 면접에서 떨어졌어요, NOT 면접을 떨어졌어요.

entries.english: to join a company (start employment)
entries.shortExplanation: 입사하다 is a practical expression meaning "to join a company (start employment)".
entries.explanation: 입사하다 (ipsahada) = "to join a company (start employment)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 입사했어요 ("I joined the company"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite past; you've started working there — one-time event

usagePhrases.en: I ended up joining / I'm joining
usagePhrases.note: Polite; -게 되다 = 'it came about that', adds humble and modest nuance favored when sharing good news
States a scheduled future start; 예정 (豫定) = 'scheduled/planned'
Asking someone their start date; honorific -세요 honors the listener

examples.ko: 다음 달에 새 회사에 입사해요.
examples.romanization: daeum dare sae hoesae ipsahaeyo.
examples.en: I'm joining a new company next month.
examples.note: Mark the company with 에: 회사에 입사하다 — 入 already means 'enter', so you enter INTO (에) the company

examples.ko: A: 입사한 지 일주일 됐는데 아직 적응 중이에요. / B: 다들 처음엔 그래요. 금방 익숙해질 거예요.
examples.romanization: A: ipsahan ji iljuil dwaenneunde ajik jeogeung jungieyo. / B: dadeul cheoeumen geuraeyo. geumbang iksukaejil geoyeyo.
examples.en: A: It's been a week since I joined and I'm still adjusting. / B: Everyone's like that at first. You'll get used to it quickly.
examples.note: 입사한 지 ...됐다 = 'it's been [time] since joining' — a very useful time-since-event pattern

examples.ko: 정규직으로 입사하게 돼서 정말 기뻐요.
examples.romanization: jeonggyujigeuro ipsahage dwaeseo jeongmal gippeoyo.
examples.en: I'm thrilled to be joining as a full-time permanent employee.
examples.note: 정규직 = 'permanent/full-time position' (vs 계약직 'contract position'); -게 돼서 shows humble gratitude

entries.nuance: 입사하다 (Sino-Korean 入社, 'enter the company') means to join a company / begin employment — the formal counterpart to 'start a job'. Its opposite is 퇴사하다 (退社, 'to leave/resign from a company'), and the pair 입사/퇴사 is everyday office vocabulary. The crucial grammar point: the company you join takes 에, not 을/를 — 회사에 입사하다 ('enter INTO the company'), never 회사를 입사하다, because 입사 already contains 'enter'. Distinctions to keep straight: 입사 is joining a COMPANY specifically; joining a school is 입학 (入學), joining the military is 입대 (入隊). Also separate 입사 (the one-time act of joining) from 출근 (出勤, commuting to work on a given day): your first day you 입사 AND 출근, but daily commuting is only 출근. The 직역 trap: 'I got the job' is 취직했어요/취업했어요 ('became employed', the broad state), while 입사했어요 zooms in on joining that PARTICULAR company. Register: 입사했어요 is polite; the humble 입사하게 됐어요 ('it came about that I'm joining') sounds gracious and modest. Key collateral: 정규직 (permanent), 계약직 (contract), 수습 기간 (probation period), 신입 사원 (new employee).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 회사를 입사했어요.
입사하다 already means 'enter the company', so the target takes 에: 회사에 입사했어요, never 회사를 입사했어요.
Using 입사 for school or the army.
입사 is for a company. School = 입학, military = 입대. Match the 입- word to the institution.
Confusing 입사 (joining) with 출근 (commuting to work).
입사 is starting at the company (a one-time event); 출근 is going to work each day. Don't say 매일 입사해요 — that's 매일 출근해요.

structuredNuance.t: 입사하다 = to join a company / begin employment (one-time event). Its opposite is 퇴사하다 (resign/leave). Polite: 입사했어요; humble/modest: 입사하게 됐어요 (favored when sharing good news). Key collateral: 정규직 (permanent), 계약직 (contract), 수습 기간 (probation), 신입 사원 (new employee).

입사 is Sino-Korean 入社 — 입 入 'enter' + 사 社 'company/organization'. Because 入 already means 'enter', the target logically takes 에 (direction into): 회사에 입사하다. The opposite 퇴사 (退社) = 退 'retreat/leave' + 社.

입사 (joining this specific company) vs 취직/취업 (broad state of gaining employment anywhere). Also: 입사 (one-time joining event) vs 출근 (daily commute/report for work). And domain-specific: 입학 (入學, join a school), 입대 (入隊, join the military) — don't generalize 입사 to these.

입사했어요 (polite) → 입사했습니다 (formal) → 입사하게 됐어요 (humble, 'it came about'). With modifiers: 내일 입사해요 / 입사 첫날이에요 ('first day of joining') / 입사 1주년이에요 ('one year since joining'). Noun: 입사일 ('start date'), 입사 지원 ('applying for the position').
Particle trap: never 회사를 입사하다 — 입사 already contains 'enter', so use 에: 회사에 입사하다. Don't confuse 입사 with 출근 — you 입사 once, you 출근 every day. Don't use 입사 for school (입학) or military (입대).

entries.english: document screening (résumé round)
entries.shortExplanation: 서류 전형 is a practical expression meaning "document screening (résumé round)".
entries.explanation: 서류 전형 (seoryu jeonhyeong) means "document screening (résumé round)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 서류 전형에 합격했어요 ("I passed the document screening"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; 합격하다 takes 에 — the first hurdle before interviews
Casual everyday phrasing; 통과하다 = 'to pass through' — takes 을 as object
States your current application status

usagePhrases.en: I got cut at the résumé stage
usagePhrases.note: The unhappy outcome; 떨어지다 = 'to be dropped' — takes 에서, not 에

examples.ko: 일단 서류 전형부터 통과해야 해요.
examples.romanization: ildan seoryu jeonhyeongbuteo tonggwahaeya haeyo.
