examples.en: First I have to get past the document screening.
examples.note: 일단 ('first of all') + 부터 ('starting with') orders the hiring stages — 서류 전형 is always step one

examples.ko: A: 서류 전형 결과는 언제쯤 나와요? / B: 보통 2주 안에 연락 온대요.
examples.romanization: A: seoryu jeonhyeong gyeolgwaneun eonjejjeum nawayo? / B: botong 2ju ane yeollak ondaeyo.
examples.en: A: When do the document-screening results come out? / B: Usually they contact you within 2 weeks.
examples.note: 결과가 나오다 = 'results come out'; 언제쯤 = 'around when' — this is the anxious waiting stage

examples.ko: 서류 전형은 붙었는데 인적성에서 떨어졌어요.
examples.romanization: seoryu jeonhyeongeun buteonneunde injeokseongeseo tteoreojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I passed the document screening but failed the aptitude test.
examples.note: 인적성 = 인성(人性, personality) + 적성(適性, aptitude) test — a key stage many large Korean companies (대기업) add between 서류 and 면접

entries.nuance: 서류 전형 is the document-screening round: 서류 ('documents', your 이력서 + 자기소개서) + 전형 (銓衡, 'screening/selection stage'). It's the FIRST gate in a typical Korean hiring process — 서류 전형 → 인적성/필기 (aptitude or written test) → 면접 (interview) → 최종 합격. The verb pairings are the learner trap: to PASS this stage you use 전형에 합격하다 (합격 takes 에) or the very common 서류 통과하다 / 서류 붙다; to FAIL it, 서류에서 떨어지다 (떨어지다 takes 에서). English speakers mishandle 전형 in two ways: (1) treating 전형 as if it meant the documents themselves — but 전형 is the SCREENING PROCESS ('the evaluation done via documents'), so you don't 'submit a 전형', you 지원하다 and then pass/fail the 전형. (2) Confusing 전형 with 서류 alone: 서류 are the papers, 전형 is the evaluation round. Particle precision: 합격 takes 에 (전형에 합격), 떨어지다 takes 에서 (전형에서 떨어지다), 통과하다 takes 을/를 (전형을 통과하다). Know the bigger hiring context: 공채 (公採, open mass recruitment, seasonal, typical of 대기업) vs 수시 채용 (rolling/as-needed hiring, typical of startups and smaller firms).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Treating 전형 as the documents themselves.
전형 is the screening PROCESS; 서류 are the documents. You don't submit a 전형 — you 지원하다, then pass the 서류 전형: 서류 전형에 합격했어요.
Saying 서류 전형을 합격했어요 with 을.
합격하다 is intransitive and takes 에: 서류 전형에 합격했어요. To use an object particle, switch verbs: 서류 전형을 통과했어요 (통과하다 can take 을).
Marking the failure with 에 not 에서.
You're dropped FROM a stage: 서류에서 떨어졌어요 (에서), not 서류에 떨어졌어요. Pass uses 에 (합격), fail uses 에서 (떨어지다).

structuredNuance.t: 서류 전형 is the document-screening round — always the first gate. Hiring order: 서류 전형 → 인적성/필기 → 면접 → 최종 합격. Pass verbs: 전형에 합격하다 or 서류 통과하다 / 서류 붙다. Fail verb: 서류에서 떨어지다. Note: 통과하다 takes 을 (전형을 통과), 합격하다 takes 에 (전형에 합격).
서류 전형 = 서류 ('documents') + 전형 (銓衡, 'screening/selection') — 銓 means 'to weigh/evaluate' and 衡 means 'balance/measure'. The word carries the sense of weighing candidates against a standard.

서류 전형 (the evaluation round) vs 서류 (the documents themselves). You submit 서류, then pass/fail the 전형. Also: 공채 (公採, open mass recruitment, seasonal, large companies) vs 수시 채용 (rolling hiring, startups/SMEs). 인적성 시험 = the aptitude/personality test stage often inserted between 서류 전형 and 면접 at large Korean firms.
서류 전형에 합격하다 → 서류 전형을 통과하다 → 서류에 붙다 (casual). Fail: 서류에서 떨어지다 → 서류 전형에서 탈락하다 (formal, 탈락 = 'elimination'). Results notification: 합격 통보 ('pass notice') / 불합격 통보 ('rejection notice').

전형 is the PROCESS, not the documents — you 지원하다 (submit) the 서류, then pass/fail the 전형. Particle precision: 합격 needs 에 (not 을) — 서류 전형에 합격했어요; 떨어지다 needs 에서 — 서류에서 떨어졌어요; 통과하다 takes 을 — 서류 전형을 통과했어요. Don't say 전형을 이겼어요 ('won the screening').

entries.english: That concludes my answer / That's all
entries.shortExplanation: 이상입니다 is a practical expression meaning "That concludes my answer / That's all".
entries.explanation: "That concludes my answer / That's all" — that is 이상입니다 (isangimnida). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 이상입니다 ("That concludes it / That's all"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Formal; caps off your self-intro or an answer — the crisp stop signal
Very formal; ends a presentation or a longer prepared statement
Slightly softer way to signal you're done — 여기 = 'here (up to this point)'
Casual-polite; fine for a relaxed panel or informal interview setting

examples.ko: 제 소개는 여기까지입니다. 이상입니다.
examples.romanization: je sogaeneun yeogikkajiimnida. isangimnida.
examples.en: That's the end of my introduction. That concludes it.
examples.note: Pair 여기까지 with 이상입니다 to double-close cleanly — signals a well-rehearsed structure

examples.ko: A: 이상으로 자기소개를 마치겠습니다. 감사합니다. / B: 네, 감사합니다. 그럼 다음 질문으로 넘어갈게요.
examples.romanization: A: isangeuro jagisogaereul machigetseumnida. gamsahamnida. / B: ne, gamsahamnida. geureom daeum jilmuneuro neomeogalgeyo.
examples.en: A: With that, I'll conclude my self-introduction. Thank you. / B: Yes, thank you. Let's move to the next question.
examples.note: 이상으로 ... 마치겠습니다 is the polished closing frame — -겠습니다 marks it as formal and deliberate

examples.ko: 답변은 이상입니다. 추가로 궁금한 점 있으실까요?
examples.romanization: dapbyeoneun isangimnida. chugaro gunggeumhan jeom isseusilkkayo?
examples.en: That's my full answer. Is there anything else you'd like to know?
examples.note: 답변은 이상입니다 = 'that completes my response'; flipping it with a question invites follow-up naturally

entries.nuance: 이상입니다 literally is 이상 (以上, 'the above / that much') + 입니다 ('it is'), meaning 'that is the extent of it' — the crisp, formal way to signal you've FINISHED speaking. It tells the listener 'I'm done, your turn', which is crucial in interviews because trailing off ambiguously leaves the interviewer unsure whether to jump in. English speakers underuse this because English has no exact single-word equivalent (you'd just stop talking), and the result is awkward dead air; landing on 이상입니다 or 여기까지입니다 makes you sound composed and structured. Two pitfalls: (1) the homonym confusion — 이상 also appears in 이상하다 ('to be weird/abnormal') and as 'more than' (3개 이상 = 'three or more'); but as a standalone closing 이상입니다 it purely means 'that's all'; don't avoid it from fear of sounding strange. (2) The 직역 trap: 'that's all' → 그게 다예요 is fine in casual speech but too light for a formal interview close; 이상입니다 carries the right businesslike register. Scale: 이상입니다 (formal single-sentence close) → 이상으로 마치겠습니다 (formal close for a longer prepared talk). Register: casual equivalent 이게 다야 (반말); 이상이에요 (polite but slightly softer). Always follow with 감사합니다 and a slight bow.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Letting it bleed into 이상하다 ('to be strange').
Standalone 이상입니다 means 'that's all/that concludes it'. It is unrelated to 이상하다 ('weird'). Don't avoid it for fear of sounding 'strange'.
Using casual 그게 다예요 to close a formal interview.
그게 다예요 is fine casually but too light for an interview. The composed close is 이상입니다 (or 이상으로 마치겠습니다).
Trailing off with no closing signal.
Silence leaves the interviewer unsure you're finished. Mark the end clearly: 이상입니다. 감사합니다.

structuredNuance.t: 이상입니다 is the crisp formal stop signal — 'that is the extent of it, I'm done speaking.' Used to cap a 자기소개, an interview answer, or a presentation. Trailing off without it leaves the interviewer unsure you're finished; 이상입니다 + 감사합니다 + slight bow is the composed, polished close.

이상 is Sino-Korean 以上 — 이 以 'using/with' + 상 上 'above/the foregoing'. Literally 'the above (statement) is it'. Distinguish from: 이상하다 (異常, 'unusual/strange') — different Hanja; and 이상 (以上) as 'more than/at least' in counting (3개 이상 = 'three or more').

이상입니다 (most formal, cleanest interview close) vs 여기까지입니다 ('up to here', slightly softer) vs 이상으로 마치겠습니다 ('with that I'll conclude', for longer prepared talks) vs 그게 다예요 / 이게 다예요 (casual, not interview-register). The scale: 그게 다예요 < 여기까지입니다 < 이상입니다 < 이상으로 마치겠습니다.

이상입니다 (single-answer close) → 이상으로 자기소개를 마치겠습니다 (자기소개-specific) → 이상으로 마치겠습니다 (presentation-level). Follow-up formula: 이상입니다. 감사합니다. + slight bow. Optional additions: 추가로 궁금한 점 있으시면 말씀해 주세요 ('if there are further questions, please let me know').

Two traps: (1) 이상하다 bleed — standalone 이상입니다 means 'that's all/concludes it' and is completely unrelated to 이상하다 ('weird'). Don't avoid it. (2) 직역 trap: 'that's all' → 그게 다예요 is too casual for a formal interview; use 이상입니다. Trailing off without any close creates awkward dead air — mark the end deliberately.

entries.english: Please change the diaper
entries.shortExplanation: 기저귀 좀 갈아 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please change the diaper".
entries.explanation: 기저귀 좀 갈아 주세요 (gijeogwi jom gara juseyo) = "Please change the diaper". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 기저귀 좀 갈아 주세요 ("Please change the diaper"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; what you ask the daycare teacher or a helper
반말, to your partner or family at home

usagePhrases.en: Could you change the diaper, please?
usagePhrases.note: More polite/formal with -주시겠어요, to staff you don't know well
Stating it about the baby's routine, not a direct request

examples.ko: 기저귀 좀 갈아 주세요.
examples.romanization: gijeogwi jom gara juseyo.
examples.en: Please change the diaper.
examples.note: Handing the baby (or a fresh diaper) to the teacher at drop-off

examples.ko: A: 애기 기저귀 찼는데요. / B: 네, 바로 갈아 줄게요.
examples.romanization: A: aegi gijeogwi channeundeyo. / B: ne, baro gara julgeyo.
examples.en: A: The baby's diaper is wet. / B: Sure, I'll change it right away.
examples.note: 찼다 ('it's wet/full') tells them why; B confirms with 바로 ('right away')

examples.ko: 등원할 때 기저귀 여유분 가방에 넣어 뒀어요. 필요하면 갈아 주세요.
examples.romanization: deungwonhal ttae gijeogwi yeoyubun gabange neoeo dwosseoyo. piryohamyeon gara juseyo.
examples.en: I put spare diapers in the bag for daycare. Please change him if needed.
examples.note: Real handoff: 여유분 ('spares') + 갈아 주세요 for the teacher to use as needed

entries.nuance: 기저귀 좀 갈아 주세요 is the standard polite request to change a diaper — 기저귀 ('diaper') + 좀 (politeness softener, never translate as 'a little') + 갈아 주세요, from 갈다 ('to replace/swap one thing with another') + -아 주세요 ('please do it for me as a favor'). Use 존댓말 to daycare teachers (선생님), babysitters (이모님/베이비시터), or any relative who's helping; with your spouse drop to 기저귀 좀 갈아 줘. The key verb is 갈다 meaning 'replace' — this is the word for swapping out a soiled diaper, not 바꾸다 ('exchange/return') or 변경하다 ('modify formally'). The softened variants scale with familiarity: 갈아 줘 (반말) → 갈아 주세요 (존댓말) → 갈아 주시겠어요? (formal). To describe a wet/dirty diaper, use 차다 (기저귀 찼어요, 'the diaper's full/wet'), then follow with 갈아 주세요. In natural speech the object particle 을/를 is usually dropped: 기저귀 갈아 주세요, not 기저귀를 갈아 주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 기저귀 바꿔 주세요.
바꾸다 means 'exchange/swap' (like returning a product). Changing a dirty diaper uses 갈다 ('replace'): 기저귀 좀 갈아 주세요.
Saying 기저귀 변경해 주세요.
변경하다 is bureaucratic 'modify/alter' (a reservation, a plan). It never applies to a diaper. Use the everyday 갈다: 기저귀 갈아 주세요.
Describing a wet diaper with 젖었어요 only and expecting it to sound natural.
젖다 ('to get wet') works for clothes, but for a diaper Koreans say 기저귀 찼어요 ('the diaper's full'). Then ask 갈아 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'diaper + (softener) + replace-and-give-me'. 기저귀 = diaper; 좀 = politeness softener; 갈아 주세요 = please replace (one soiled thing with a clean one as a favor to me). The verb 갈다 means 'swap out / replace', not 'change' in the sense of altering.

존댓말 to daycare teachers, babysitters, helpers, or in-laws you're not close to. With your partner at home: 기저귀 좀 갈아 줘 (반말). Do not use 변경하다 or 바꾸다 with a daycare teacher — those words signal a product exchange, not a diaper change.

갈아 주세요 vs 갈아 주시겠어요? — both polite, but -주시겠어요? is more formally deferential, suited for a teacher you've just met. In practice parents mainly use 갈아 주세요 because -주시겠어요? can sound a touch stiff for this everyday request.
Softest (반말): 기저귀 갈아 줘. Standard polite: 기저귀 좀 갈아 주세요. Formal: 기저귀 갈아 주시겠어요? You can add urgency: 빨리 갈아 주세요 ('please change it quickly') or add a why: 기저귀 찼으니까 갈아 주세요.

English speakers reach for 바꾸다 or 변경하다 (both meaning 'change/alter'). Neither fits: 기저귀 바꿔 주세요 sounds like returning a diaper for a different brand; 기저귀 변경해 주세요 sounds like filing a formal modification. The correct verb is always 갈다 ('replace'): 갈아 주세요.

entries.english: He pooped
entries.shortExplanation: 응가했어요 is a practical expression meaning "He pooped".
entries.explanation: 응가했어요 (eunggahaesseoyo) means "He pooped". Say it as one set phrase — for example 응가했어요 ("He pooped"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; baby-talk word, what you say to the teacher
반말, to your partner or the baby
Clinical/neutral; what you'd say to a doctor
The pee counterpart; 쉬 = baby-talk for pee

examples.ko: 애기 응가했어요. 기저귀 갈아 주세요.
examples.romanization: aegi eunggahaesseoyo. gijeogwi gara juseyo.
examples.en: The baby pooped. Please change the diaper.
examples.note: 응가 + the diaper-change request, the natural pair

examples.ko: A: 오늘 응가 두 번 했어요? / B: 네, 점심 먹고 나서 두 번 했어요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul eungga du beon haesseoyo? / B: ne, jeomsim meokgo naseo du beon haesseoyo.
examples.en: A: Did he poop twice today? / B: Yes, twice after lunch.
examples.note: Count check with the daycare teacher; natural A/B handoff at pickup

examples.ko: 요즘 변비라서 응가를 며칠째 못 했어요. 이유식 바꿔 볼까 봐요.
examples.romanization: yojeum byeonbiraseo eunggareul myeochiljjae mo taesseoyo. iyusik bakkwo bolkka bwayo.
examples.en: He's constipated lately and hasn't pooped for days. I might change his solids.
examples.note: 변비 ('constipation') is the clinical word; 며칠째 ('for several days now')

entries.nuance: 응가했어요 means '(he) pooped' — 응가 (baby-talk/nursery word for poop, like English 'poo-poo') + 했어요 (past of 하다), so 응가하다 is the verb. This is the word adults use WITH or ABOUT babies and toddlers in warm, non-clinical speech: 존댓말 to a daycare teacher (애기 응가했어요) and 반말 to a spouse (응가했어). Its pee-counterpart is 쉬(하다). The full register spectrum matters: 응가 is nursery language, 똥 is the plain blunt adult word (a bit crude to announce to a teacher about a baby), and 변(便)/대변 is clinical ('stool/bowel movement', for the pediatrician). Pick by audience: teacher/baby → 응가, doctor → 변/대변. The idiom split is important: 응가하다 uses 하다, but the clinical form uses 보다 — it's 변을 보다 ('to have a bowel movement', literally 'to see stool'), never 변 했어요. Constipation is 변비, diarrhea is 설사. 응가 is also used as a noun you can point to ('there's an 응가!') and as a verb, giving parents flexibility.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Announcing 똥 쌌어요 to the daycare teacher.
똥 is the blunt word and 싸다 is coarse. For a baby in polite talk use the nursery word: 응가했어요. Save 똥 for casual adult joking.
Saying 변 했어요 for 'had a bowel movement'.
변(stool) pairs with 보다 ('to see'), not 하다: 변 봤어요. The 하다 verb goes with the baby-word 응가 (응가했어요).
Using clinical 배변했어요 with a teacher.
배변하다 ('to defecate') is medical/stiff. With a daycare teacher about a baby, 응가했어요 is the natural register; 변 봤어요 if you want neutral.

structuredNuance.t: 응가 is a soft nursery-register noun meaning poop (no adult literal translation). 했어요 is past of 하다 ('to do'). So literally 'did a poo-poo'. The whole form 응가하다 = 'to poop' — only usable about/with babies and small children; sounds wrong about adults.

존댓말 to daycare teacher or babysitter about the baby. 반말 to your partner or when talking to the baby itself. NOT to a doctor — use 변 봤어요 or 대변을 봤어요 with medical staff. Never use 똥 쌌어요 to staff — it's the blunt/crude adult register.
응가했어요 (nursery, to teacher) vs 변 봤어요 (clinical, to doctor) vs 똥 쌌어요 (blunt adult, inappropriate for teacher). The pee parallel is 쉬했어요. For constipation status, add 변비라서 아직 못 했어요.
응가했어요 (polite statement) → 응가했어 (반말) → 응가했어요? (question: 'did he poop?') → 응가 아직 안 했어요 ('hasn't pooped yet'). Clinical upgrade: 변 봤어요 / 대변 봤어요. Quantity: 응가 두 번 했어요.

Two traps: (1) defaulting to 똥 쌌어요 in polite childcare talk — 똥 is the blunt word and 싸다 is coarse; use 응가했어요 with teachers. (2) Saying 변 했어요 for 'had a bowel movement' — the clinical verb is 보다, not 하다: it's 변 봤어요, not 변 했어요.

entries.english: Did he take a nap?
entries.shortExplanation: 낮잠 잤어요? is a practical expression meaning "Did he take a nap?".
entries.explanation: "Did he take a nap?" — that is 낮잠 잤어요? (natjam jasseoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 낮잠 잤어요? ("Did he take a nap?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking the teacher at pickup how naptime went

usagePhrases.en: Did you nap? / Did he nap?
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to the child or your partner
Add 잘 ('well') to ask about quality, not just yes/no

usagePhrases.en: Did you put him down for a nap?
usagePhrases.note: Causative 재우다 — asking if SOMEONE made the baby sleep

examples.ko: 오늘 낮잠 잤어요?
examples.romanization: oneul natjam jasseoyo?
examples.en: Did he nap today?
examples.note: A simple pickup question to the daycare teacher

examples.ko: A: 우리 애 낮잠 잘 잤어요? / B: 네, 오늘은 한 시간 반 잤어요.
examples.romanization: A: uri ae natjam jal jasseoyo? / B: ne, oneureun han sigan ban jasseoyo.
examples.en: A: Did my child nap well? / B: Yes, he slept an hour and a half today.
examples.note: Natural pickup exchange; B gives duration which parents always want to know

examples.ko: 낮잠 안 자고 계속 울었다고요? 아이고, 집에서도 그래요.
examples.romanization: natjam an jago gyesok ureotdagoyo? aigo, jibeseodo geuraeyo.
examples.en: He didn't nap and kept crying? Oh dear, he's like that at home too.
examples.note: Reacting to a teacher's report; 안 자고 ('without sleeping') + 울었다

entries.nuance: 낮잠 잤어요? means 'did (he) take a nap?' — 낮잠 (낮 'daytime' + 잠 'sleep' = 'nap') + 잤어요 (past of 자다 'to sleep'). It's the daily pickup question to a daycare teacher, in 존댓말; to your own child or spouse it drops to 낮잠 잤어?. Adding 잘 gives quality — 잘 잤어요? asks not just 'did he nap' but 'did he nap well'. The crucial distinction is 자다 vs 재우다: 자다 = the child sleeps (낮잠 잤어요? = 'did he sleep?'), while 재우다 is the causative 'to put someone to sleep' (낮잠 재웠어요? = 'did you put him down?'). Mixing them flips who's doing the action. Korean uses the cognate-object construction 낮잠을 자다 ('sleep a nap') — you never say 낮잠을 하다 or 낮잠을 가지다 the way English 'take a nap' might tempt you; drop the particle in speech: 낮잠 잤어요. For 'he fell asleep' use 잠들었어요, not 잤어요. Scalar forms: 낮잠 못 잤어요 ('didn't nap'), 낮잠 조금 잤어요 ('napped a little'), 두 번 잤어요 ('napped twice').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 낮잠 했어요? using 하다.
낮잠 pairs with the verb 자다 ('to sleep'), not 하다. The natural form is 낮잠 잤어요? Korean never says 낮잠을 하다.
Confusing 잤어요 (slept) with 재웠어요 (put to sleep).
자다 = the child sleeps; 재우다 = an adult makes the child sleep. Ask 낮잠 잤어요? for whether he slept, 재웠어요? for whether you/someone got him down.
Using 자다 for 'fell asleep'.
잤어요 = 'slept'; 'fell asleep / drifted off' is 잠들었어요. 'He finally fell asleep' is 드디어 잠들었어요, not 잤어요.

structuredNuance.t: 낮잠 = nap (낮 'daytime' + 잠 'sleep'); 잤어요 = slept (past of 자다). So literally 'slept a daytime-sleep?' The cognate-object structure 낮잠을 자다 ('sleep a nap') is Korean's idiomatic form — not 낮잠을 하다 or 낮잠을 취하다.

존댓말 (낮잠 잤어요?) to the daycare teacher at pickup. 반말 (낮잠 잤어?) to your child or partner. This is the most common question at 하원 time and teachers expect it. If the answer surprises you — 안 잤어요, 못 잤어요 — you naturally follow up about mood or next steps.
낮잠 잤어요? (yes/no) vs 낮잠 잘 잤어요? (quality) vs 낮잠 재웠어요? (causative — did YOU put him down?). The causative 재우다 asks about the caregiver's action; 자다 asks about the child's.
낮잠 잤어요? → 낮잠 잘 잤어요? ('nap well?') → 낮잠 얼마나 잤어요? ('how long did he nap?') → 낮잠 못 잤어요? ('couldn't nap?'). To say he fell asleep: 잠들었어요. To say you put him down: 낮잠 재웠어요.
Two traps: (1) 낮잠 하다 / 낮잠 가지다 from English 'take a nap' — the verb is always 자다. (2) Confusing 잤어요 (slept) with 재웠어요 (put someone to sleep) — different subjects, different verbs, don't mix them.

entries.english: We've started solids (baby food)
entries.shortExplanation: 이유식 시작했어요 is a practical expression meaning "We've started solids (baby food)".
entries.explanation: 이유식 시작했어요 (iyusik sijakaesseoyo) = "We've started solids (baby food)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 이유식 시작했어요 ("We've started solids"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; telling the teacher or pediatrician about the baby's stage
반말, to a friend or family
Stating the current routine with 먹이다 ('to feed')
The negative, when the baby is still on milk only

examples.ko: 저희 애기 이유식 시작했어요.
examples.romanization: jeohui aegi iyusik sijakaesseoyo.
examples.en: Our baby has started solids.
examples.note: A simple update to the daycare teacher at enrollment

examples.ko: A: 이유식은 언제부터 시작하셨어요? / B: 6개월 됐을 때부터 시작했어요. 지금은 중기예요.
examples.romanization: A: iyusigeun eonjebuteo sijakasyeosseoyo? / B: 6gaewol dwaesseul ttaebuteo sijakaesseoyo. jigeumeun junggiyeyo.
examples.en: A: When did you start solids? / B: We started at 6 months. Now we're in the mid stage.
examples.note: Parent-to-parent or doctor conversation; 중기 ('mid stage')

examples.ko: 이유식 알레르기 때문에 계란이랑 우유는 아직 안 줬어요. 어린이집에서 주의해 주세요.
examples.romanization: iyusik allereugi ttaemune gyeranirang uyuneun ajik an jwosseoyo. eorinijibeseo juuihae juseyo.
examples.en: Because of allergies we haven't given egg or milk yet. Please be careful at daycare.
examples.note: Real allergy handoff; 주의해 주세요 ('please be cautious')

entries.nuance: 이유식 시작했어요 means 'we've started baby food / solids' — 이유식 (離乳食, Sino-Korean: 離 'separate' + 乳 'milk' + 食 'food', literally 'weaning food') + 시작했어요 (past of 시작하다 'to begin'). Korean weaning culture is highly stage-conscious: 초기 (early, ~6 months, thin purée), 중기 (mid, ~7–8 months), 후기 (late, ~9–11 months), 완료기 (finishing, ~12 months+) — parents routinely report which stage they're in. Say this in 존댓말 to the daycare teacher or pediatrician; casually to friends it's 이유식 시작했어. The crucial distinction: 이유식 is transitional purée (babies ~6 months on), not 아기 음식 (unnatural calque) and not 유아식 — which is toddler food (소금/양념 lightly added, ~15 months+). Calling a 2-year-old's meal 이유식 is wrong; that's 유아식. The feed verb is 먹이다 (causative of 먹다): 이유식 먹여요, never 이유식 먹어요 (which means the baby feeds itself).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 아기 음식 instead of 이유식.
아기 음식 is a literal calque of 'baby food' and sounds unnatural. The real term for weaning purée is 이유식: 이유식 시작했어요.
Calling toddler meals 이유식.
이유식 is purée for babies starting solids (~6mo). Toddler food (~15mo+, lightly seasoned) is 유아식. Don't call a toddler's rice-and-soup 이유식.
Saying 이유식 먹어요 to mean 'I feed him'.
먹다 = 'to eat' (the baby does it). To say YOU feed the baby, use the causative 먹이다: 이유식 먹여요. 이유식 먹어요 means the baby eats it himself.

structuredNuance.t: 이유식 is 離乳食 ('weaning food' — separating from milk). 시작했어요 = started (past). The phrase reports that a baby has moved from milk-only to purée feeding. It carries cultural weight because Korean weaning is staged: 초기/중기/후기/완료기, and daycare teachers need to know the stage.

존댓말 to daycare teacher, pediatrician, or 어린이집 enrollment staff. 반말 to friends or family. Very often the next sentence specifies the stage: 지금 초기예요 / 중기예요. Allergy info always follows: 계란, 우유, 땅콩 아직 안 줬어요.

이유식 (transitional baby purée, ~6 months on) vs 유아식 (toddler food, ~15 months+, lightly seasoned). These are not interchangeable. 아기 음식 is an unnatural direct calque of 'baby food'; always use 이유식 for the weaning stage.
이유식 시작했어요 → 이유식 먹이고 있어요 ('currently feeding solids') → 이유식 초기/중기/후기예요 ('early/mid/late stage') → 이유식 끝내고 유아식으로 넘어갔어요 ('moved to toddler food'). Negative: 아직 이유식 안 해요.

Two traps: (1) Translating 'baby food' literally as 아기 음식 — unnatural; always 이유식. (2) Saying 이유식 먹어요 to mean 'I feed him' — 먹다 is intransitive (the baby eats). To say YOU feed him, use the causative 먹이다: 이유식 먹여요.
離乳食 — 離 'separate', 乳 'milk/breast', 食 'food'. Literally 'food for separating from breast milk' — the purpose of weaning is encoded in the word itself.

entries.english: What time should I come pick him up?
entries.shortExplanation: 몇 시에 데리러 가면 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "What time should I come pick him up?".
entries.explanation: 몇 시에 데리러 가면 돼요? (myeot sie derireo gamyeon dwaeyo?) means "What time should I come pick him up?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 몇 시에 데리러 가면 돼요? ("What time should I pick him up?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: What time should I pick him up?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking the daycare about pickup time

usagePhrases.en: What time are you picking him up?
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to your partner

usagePhrases.en: By what time do I need to be there?
usagePhrases.note: Asking the deadline with -까지 ('by') + 가야 돼요
Stating you'll do the pickup; -ㄹ게요 announces your intention

examples.ko: 오늘 몇 시에 데리러 가면 돼요?
examples.romanization: oneul myeot sie derireo gamyeon dwaeyo?
examples.en: What time should I come pick him up today?
examples.note: Confirming pickup time with the teacher

examples.ko: A: 회사가 좀 늦게 끝날 것 같아요. 6시에 데리러 가도 될까요? / B: 네, 6시까지는 괜찮아요.
examples.romanization: A: hoesaga jom neutge kkeunnal geot gatayo. 6sie derireo gado doelkkayo? / B: ne, 6sikkajineun gwaenchanayo.
examples.en: A: Work will run a bit late. Can I pick him up at 6? / B: Yes, 6 o'clock is fine.
examples.note: Asking for a later pickup with -도 될까요? — a very common parent situation

examples.ko: 오늘은 할머니가 데리러 가실 거예요. 다른 사람이 가도 괜찮죠?
examples.romanization: oneureun halmeoniga derireo gasil geoyeyo. dareun sarami gado gwaenchanchyo?
examples.en: Grandma will pick him up today. It's okay if someone else comes, right?
examples.note: Notifying that a different guardian will collect; 가실 거예요 honorifies grandma

entries.nuance: 몇 시에 데리러 가면 돼요? means 'what time should I come pick (him) up?' — 몇 시 ('what time') + 에 (time particle) + 데리러 (purpose form of 데리다 'to take/bring a person') + 가면 돼요 ('is it okay if I go', from -면 되다 'it suffices to / should'). This is the core daycare pickup question, in 존댓말 to the teacher; with your partner it drops to 몇 시에 데리러 가?. The first big pitfall: 데리러 가다 = 'go to fetch a PERSON' (데리다 is only for living people you accompany), while 가지러 가다 = 'go to fetch a THING'. Saying 애기 가지러 갈게요 treats the baby like a package — always use 데리러 가다 for a child. The second pitfall: 데리러 가다 means going TO collect them (they're elsewhere), while 데리고 가다 means TAKING them ALONG somewhere (you leave together). Don't swap these: for daycare pickup it's 데리러 가다. The -러 ending attaches to a motion verb (가다/오다) and marks the purpose of movement.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 애 가지러 갈게요 for picking up a child.
가지러 가다 is for fetching THINGS. A child is a person, so use 데리러 가다: 애 데리러 갈게요. 가지러 treats the child like an object.
Confusing 데리러 가다 with 데리고 가다.
데리러 가다 = go TO COLLECT someone (they're elsewhere). 데리고 가다 = TAKE someone ALONG (going together). For daycare pickup it's 데리러 가다.
Saying 픽업하러 가요 and assuming it's the only option.
픽업 (the loanword) exists but in daycare context the natural verb is 데리러 가다. 'I'll go pick him up' is 데리러 갈게요.

structuredNuance.t: 몇 시에 = at what time; 데리러 = in order to fetch (a person); 가면 돼요 = is it okay if I go? So literally 'at what time is it okay if I go in order to fetch (him)?'. The -면 되다 form softens a question that could otherwise sound demanding.

존댓말 to the daycare teacher when confirming pickup time. 반말 to your partner when coordinating. Often paired with a reason: 회사 때문에 늦어요 ('work is running late') or 병원 때문에 일찍 갈게요 ('I'll come early for a doctor's visit').
몇 시에 데리러 가면 돼요? (open question about time) vs 몇 시까지 가야 돼요? (asking the deadline, -까지 'by') vs 제가 데리러 갈게요 (stating intent). For 'may I come at X time?', use -에 가도 될까요?

데리러 가다 → 데리러 오다 (teacher 'comes' to get the child from inside; parent 'goes' to get) → 데리고 가다 (take along). Add time: 5시에 데리러 갈게요. Add reason: 일이 생겨서 일찍 데리러 갈게요 ('something came up so I'll pick him up early').

English 'pick up' covers both persons and things. Two Korean traps: (1) 가지러 가다 is for things, not people — always 데리러 가다 for a child. (2) 데리고 가다 ≠ picking up — that means taking someone WITH you, not going to fetch them.

entries.english: What time is drop-off?
entries.shortExplanation: 등원 시간이 몇 시예요? is a practical expression meaning "What time is drop-off?".
entries.explanation: "What time is drop-off?" — that is 등원 시간이 몇 시예요? (deungwon sigani myeot siyeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 등원 시간이 몇 시예요? ("What time is drop-off?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking the daycare's morning arrival time
반말, to your partner

usagePhrases.en: By what time do we need to arrive?
usagePhrases.note: Asking the deadline with -까지 + 해야 돼요

usagePhrases.en: We're not sending him in today
usagePhrases.note: The negative, using causative 등원시키다

examples.ko: 등원 시간이 보통 몇 시예요?
examples.romanization: deungwon sigani botong myeot siyeyo?
examples.en: What time is drop-off usually?
examples.note: Asking the daycare's normal morning schedule

examples.ko: A: 내일 병원 때문에 좀 늦게 등원할 것 같아요. / B: 네, 오전 중으로만 오시면 돼요.
examples.romanization: A: naeil byeongwon ttaemune jom neutge deungwonhal geot gatayo. / B: ne, ojeon jungeuroman osimyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: A: We'll probably arrive a bit late tomorrow because of a doctor's visit. / B: That's fine, just come before noon.
examples.note: Notifying a late arrival; teacher responds with a gentle deadline

examples.ko: 아침마다 등원 전쟁이에요. 애가 안 가려고 울어서요.
examples.romanization: achimmada deungwon jeonjaengieyo. aega an garyeogo ureoseoyo.
examples.en: Every morning is a drop-off battle — he cries and won't go.
examples.note: 등원 전쟁 ('drop-off war') is a real parent idiom for the morning struggle

entries.nuance: 등원 시간이 몇 시예요? means 'what time is drop-off at daycare?' — 등원 (登園, Sino-Korean: 登 'go up to/attend' + 園 'garden', for 어린이집/유치원) + 시간 ('time') + 몇 시예요? ('what time is it?'). 등원 is the specialized verb/noun for arriving at a 어린이집 or 유치원 (both contain 園 'garden'), and its opposite is 하원 ('leaving daycare'). This pair — 등원/하원 — is the daily vocabulary of Korean childcare; for elementary school and up the parallel is 등교/하교 (校 'school'). Using 등교 for a 3-year-old is a clear word mismatch. Note 등원하다 is intransitive (the child arrives); to say you're taking/sending the child, use the causative 등원시키다 (애 등원시켰어요 = 'I dropped the kid off'). Don't confuse 등원 with 출근 (adult going to work) — the morning routine typically combines both: 애 등원시키고 출근했어요 ('dropped the kid off then went to work'). The English-speaker pitfall is over-building the expression as 어린이집에 데려다 주는 시간 — the precise word is 등원 시간.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 등교 for a daycare/kindergarten child.
등교/하교 (校 'school') are for elementary school and up. For 어린이집/유치원 use 등원/하원 (園 'garden'). A 4-year-old 등원s, not 등교s.
Saying 등원하다 when you mean 'I drop him off'.
등원하다 is intransitive — the CHILD arrives. For 'I take/send him', use the causative 등원시키다: 애 등원시키고 출근했어요.
Confusing 등원 with 출근.
등원 = a young child going to daycare; 출근 = an adult going to work. 'I dropped off the kid then went to work' is 애 등원시키고 출근했어요 — two different verbs.

structuredNuance.t: 등원 = 登園, 'ascend to the garden/daycare'. 시간 = time. Literally 'the time of ascending to the garden'. In practice it simply means drop-off time at daycare or kindergarten. It carries no literal meaning in everyday speech — it's just the standard term.

존댓말 to daycare staff when asking about schedule. 반말 to your partner when coordinating mornings. Both 등원하다 (intransitive: child arrives) and 등원시키다 (causative: parent sends/brings child) are needed — distinguish them carefully.

등원 (arriving at daycare/kindergarten) vs 등교 (arriving at elementary school+). 등원 ↔ 하원 (leave daycare) vs 등교 ↔ 하교 (leave school). 출근 (adult going to work) is a completely separate word. Don't mix these across age groups.
등원하다 (child arrives) → 등원시키다 (parent drops off) → 등원 못 했어요 (couldn't make it in) → 늦게 등원했어요 (arrived late). Common phrase: 애 등원시키고 출근했어요 ('dropped kid off then went to work').

Two traps: (1) Over-building 'drop-off time' as 어린이집에 데려다 주는 시간 — clunky; the crisp word is 등원 시간. (2) Using 등교 for a daycare/kindergarten child — 등교 is for elementary school and up; use 등원 for 원 (garden-based) institutions.
登園 — 登 'ascend/attend', 園 'garden'. Both 어린이집 and 유치원 are 원-based institutions. The kanji 園 ('garden/park') is the unifying element; 등원 specifically applies to them.

entries.english: He keeps crying
entries.shortExplanation: 애가 자꾸 울어요 is a practical expression meaning "He keeps crying".
entries.explanation: 애가 자꾸 울어요 (aega jakku ureoyo) = "He keeps crying". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 애가 자꾸 울어요 ("He keeps crying"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; reporting to the teacher or doctor
반말, to your partner or a friend

usagePhrases.en: I don't know why he's crying
usagePhrases.note: Expressing you can't find the cause; 우는지 ('whether/why he cries')

usagePhrases.en: Please soothe him when he cries
usagePhrases.note: Asking staff to comfort a crying child; 달래다 = 'to soothe'

examples.ko: 애가 아까부터 자꾸 울어요.
examples.romanization: aega akkabuteo jakku ureoyo.
examples.en: He's been crying over and over since a while ago.
examples.note: 아까부터 ('since earlier') + 자꾸 ('repeatedly') describe ongoing crying

examples.ko: A: 밤에 자다가 자꾸 깨서 울어요. 어디 아픈 걸까요? / B: 이앓이 시기라서 그럴 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: bame jadaga jakku kkaeseo ureoyo. eodi apeun geolkkayo? / B: iari sigiraseo geureol su isseoyo.
examples.en: A: He keeps waking up crying at night. Could he be sick? / B: He might be teething — that's common.
examples.note: Doctor/parent exchange; 이앓이 ('teething') is the natural answer

examples.ko: 등원할 때마다 우는 애를 떼어 놓고 오는 게 너무 힘들어요.
examples.romanization: deungwonhal ttaemada uneun aereul tteeo noko oneun ge neomu himdeureoyo.
examples.en: Leaving my crying child every drop-off is so hard.
examples.note: 우는 애 ('crying child') as a modifier; 떼어 놓다 = 'pry away/leave behind'

entries.nuance: 애가 자꾸 울어요 means 'the child keeps crying' — 애 (casual short form of 아이 'child') + 가 (subject particle) + 자꾸 ('repeatedly, again and again') + 울어요 (from 울다 'to cry'). Say this in 존댓말 to a teacher or pediatrician about a pattern; to your spouse it's 애가 자꾸 울어. The adverb 자꾸 is the key — it signals frustrated repetition ('keeps on, won't stop'), which is exactly the parenting complaint. It's more vivid than 계속 ('continuously', one unbroken stretch): 자꾸 implies stopping and starting again, which is what a baby does. A crucial vocabulary set for English speakers: 울다 = 'to cry (shed tears)', 징징대다 = 'to whine/fuss', 떼쓰다 = 'to throw a tantrum (willful demanding)'. English 'crying' blurs all three, but Koreans keep them separate — a screaming-for-candy toddler is 떼쓰다, a tired whimperer is 징징대다, and genuine wet-eyed crying is 울다. To ask staff to soothe, the verb is 달래다 ('to comfort/soothe'): 달래 주세요. Don't use 진정시키다 ('calm down'), which sounds clinical for a baby.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 울다 for a whining/nagging toddler.
울다 is shedding tears. A toddler fussing/whining for something is 징징대다, and a willful tantrum is 떼쓰다. 'He's whining' is 징징대요, not 울어요.
Saying 애는 울어요 with the topic particle by default.
To report what's happening now, mark the subject: 애'가' 울어요. 애'는' shifts to contrast ('as for the kid…'), which sounds off in a plain report.
Translating 'calm him down' as 진정시켜 주세요 for a baby.
진정시키다 (calm an agitated adult) sounds clinical for a baby. The warm word for soothing a child is 달래다: 좀 달래 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 애가 자꾸 울어요 = 'the kid cries again and again'. 자꾸 is the load-bearing adverb — it conveys frustrated, recurring action (stopping and starting), not one continuous stream (which would be 계속). The subject particle 가 on 애 is required: it marks who is performing the crying.

존댓말 to a daycare teacher or pediatrician when reporting the pattern. 반말 to your partner. The phrase signals that you've noticed a pattern, not a one-off event — it naturally invites the listener's advice or investigation. To ask staff to comfort: 달래 주세요 (warm, childcare-appropriate) not 진정시켜 주세요 (clinical).

울다 (cry/weep) vs 징징대다 (whine/fuss, less intense) vs 떼쓰다 (tantrum, willful demanding). These are not interchangeable. 자꾸 울다 = keeps crying (genuine); 자꾸 징징대다 = keeps whining; 자꾸 떼쓰다 = keeps throwing fits.
애가 자꾸 울어요 → 왜 우는지 모르겠어요 ('I don't know why') → 달래도 울음을 그치지 않아요 → 울다가 잠들어요 ('cries and falls asleep'). Intensify: 엄청 울어요, 하루 종일 울어요. Soften: 조금 칭얼대요.

Three traps: (1) Flattening 울다/징징대다/떼쓰다 all into 'crying' — each is distinct. (2) Using 진정시켜 주세요 for a baby instead of 달래 주세요. (3) Dropping the subject particle: 애'가' 울어요, not 애'는' (the 는 implies a contrast/topic shift).

entries.english: I'm planning to send him to daycare
entries.shortExplanation: 어린이집 보내려고요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm planning to send him to daycare".
entries.explanation: 어린이집 보내려고요 (eorinijip bonaeryeogoyo) means "I'm planning to send him to daycare". Say it as one set phrase — for example 어린이집 보내려고요 ("I'm planning to send him to daycare"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: I'm planning to send him to daycare
usagePhrases.note: Polite; stating your plan, -려고요 ('intending to')

usagePhrases.en: I'm gonna send him to daycare
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend
Earlier stage: 알아보다 = 'to look into / research'
Done: 등록하다 = 'to enroll/register'

examples.ko: 내년부터 애를 어린이집에 보내려고요.
examples.romanization: naenyeonbuteo aereul eorinijibe bonaeryeogoyo.
examples.en: I'm planning to send my child to daycare starting next year.
examples.note: 보내다 ('send') + -려고요 states the plan; 에 marks the destination

examples.ko: A: 복직은 언제 하세요? / B: 다음 달에 복직해야 해서 어린이집 보내려고요. 대기 걸어 놨어요.
examples.romanization: A: bokjigeun eonje haseyo? / B: daeum dare bokjikaeya haeseo eorinijip bonaeryeogoyo. daegi georeo nwasseoyo.
examples.en: A: When are you going back to work? / B: I have to go back next month, so I'm sending him to daycare. I'm on the waitlist.
examples.note: Real conversation about return-to-work driving daycare enrollment; 대기 걸다 = 'put in a waitlist'

examples.ko: 국공립 어린이집은 대기가 너무 길어서 가정 어린이집부터 보내려고요.
examples.romanization: gukgongnip eorinijibeun daegiga neomu gireoseo gajeong eorinijipbuteo bonaeryeogoyo.
examples.en: Public daycare waitlists are too long, so we'll start with a home daycare.
examples.note: 국공립 (public) vs 가정 (home) 어린이집 — the real types parents weigh

entries.nuance: 어린이집 보내려고요 means 'I'm planning to send (my child) to daycare' — 어린이집 (어린이 'children' + 집 'house', daycare for ages ~0–5) + 보내려고요 (보내다 'to send' + -(으)려고 'intending to' + 요). The -려고(요) ending signals a personal plan you're sharing; it sounds natural when chatting about decisions and isn't as blunt as -겠어요. The verb 보내다 ('send someone off to attend') is the standard verb for putting a child in any institution: 어린이집/유치원/학교/학원 보내다. The key institutional trio English speakers must learn: 어린이집 = daycare (run under the welfare ministry, ages 0–5, all-day care), 유치원 = kindergarten (educational, ages 3–5, shorter hours), 학교 = school (age 6+, elementary). 'Daycare' in the Western sense maps to 어린이집. The particle pitfall: it's 어린이집'에' 보내다 ('send TO daycare', 에 = directional destination). Learners sometimes use 한테/에게 (person recipients) — wrong; a place takes 에. Also don't substitute 어린이집 가게 하다 ('make him go') — 보내다 is the idiomatic, caring-sounding choice.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 어린이집한테 보내요.
한테/에게 mark a person recipient. A place/institution takes 에: 어린이집'에' 보내요. You send the child TO the daycare (a location).
Confusing 어린이집 with 유치원.
어린이집 = daycare (0–5, welfare/all-day). 유치원 = kindergarten (3–5, educational). 'Daycare' is 어린이집. Picking the wrong one misnames the institution.
Using 학교 보내다 for a toddler.
학교 is for ages 6+. A toddler goes to 어린이집 or 유치원, not 학교. 'I'm sending my 2-year-old' is 어린이집에 보내요, never 학교에 보내요.

structuredNuance.t: 어린이집 = 'children's house' (daycare). 보내다 = 'to send (someone to a place)'. -려고요 = expressing intent. So literally 'intending to send to the children's house'. The phrase is softer than 'I will' because -려고요 signals a plan being formed, not a firm decision.

존댓말 (-려고요) to teachers, doctors, or neighbors when sharing your childcare plan. 반말 (-려고) to friends or family. Often paired with a reason: 복직 때문에 ('returning to work'), 사회성 키우려고 ('to build social skills'). The next sentence is often about the waitlist: 대기 걸었어요.
어린이집 보내려고요 (planning) vs 알아보고 있어요 (still researching) vs 등록했어요 (already enrolled) vs 대기 중이에요 (on the waitlist). These are the four stages of the enrollment journey in Korea.
보내려고요 (polite intent) → 보낼 거예요 (definite plan) → 보내고 있어요 (currently attending) → 보냈어요 (sent, done). Institution variants: 유치원 보내려고요, 학원 보내려고요.

Two traps: (1) Particle error — 어린이집'한테' 보내요 is wrong; a place takes 에: 어린이집'에' 보내요. (2) Confusing 어린이집 (daycare, 0–5) with 유치원 (kindergarten, 3–5) — they're different institutions serving different hours and regulatory frameworks.

entries.english: He's not feeling well today
entries.shortExplanation: 오늘 컨디션이 안 좋아요 is a practical expression meaning "He's not feeling well today".
entries.explanation: "He's not feeling well today" — that is 오늘 컨디션이 안 좋아요 (oneul keondisyeoni an joayo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 오늘 컨디션이 안 좋아요 ("He's not in good shape today"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: He's not in good shape today
usagePhrases.note: Polite; telling the teacher the child is off
반말, to your partner

usagePhrases.ko: 몸이 좀 안 좋은 것 같아요
usagePhrases.romanization: momi jom an joeun geot gatayo
usagePhrases.note: Softer guess with -ㄴ 것 같아요 ('seems')
Past, giving the onset

examples.ko: 애가 오늘 컨디션이 좀 안 좋아요.
examples.romanization: aega oneul keondisyeoni jom an joayo.
examples.en: He's a little off today.
examples.note: A heads-up to the daycare teacher at drop-off

examples.ko: A: 오늘 좀 안 좋아 보이는데 괜찮아요? / B: 새벽에 열이 났는데 지금은 좀 나아졌어요. 그래도 컨디션이 안 좋아요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul jom an joa boineunde gwaenchanayo? / B: saebyeoge yeori nanneunde jigeumeun jom naajyeosseoyo. geuraedo keondisyeoni an joayo.
examples.en: A: He looks a bit off today — is he okay? / B: He had a fever at dawn but it's better now. Still not his best though.
examples.note: Teacher noticing → parent explaining; shows 컨디션 as follow-up to fever

examples.ko: 컨디션 안 좋으면 억지로 안 먹여도 돼요. 그냥 재워 주세요.
examples.romanization: keondisyeon an joeumyeon eokjiro an meogyeodo dwaeyo. geunyang jaewo juseyo.
examples.en: If he's not feeling well, you don't have to force-feed him — just let him sleep.
examples.note: 억지로 ('forcibly') + 재우다, giving the teacher leeway

entries.nuance: 오늘 컨디션이 안 좋아요 means '(he's) not in good condition/shape today' — 컨디션 (English loanword 'condition', but in Korean strictly means physical state/energy level, NOT a disease or a requirement) + 이 + 안 좋아요 ('is not good'). This is the everyday soft phrase for telling a daycare teacher that a child is fragile, run-down, or coming down with something — without committing to a specific diagnosis. Register: 존댓말 to staff; 반말 컨디션 안 좋아 to family. The false-friend trap is the biggest pitfall: English 'condition' means (1) a medical condition/disease, or (2) a requirement/term. Korean 컨디션 means neither — it only means how one feels physically (컨디션 좋아요 = 'I feel great'). A disease is 질환/병; a term is 조건. A near-synonym is 몸이 안 좋아요 ('the body's not good') — both work, but 컨디션 emphasizes energy/vitality and 몸 emphasizes the physical body. For a real fever add 열이 나요; for mood use 기분이 안 좋아요 (= 'in a bad mood', not physically unwell).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Thinking 컨디션 means a medical 'condition' (disease).
Korean 컨디션 = how you feel / your energy state. A disease is 질환/병. 컨디션이 안 좋아요 = 'feeling unwell', not 'has a condition'.
Using 컨디션 to mean a 'condition' (requirement/term).
That sense is 조건 (e.g. 계약 조건 'contract terms'). 컨디션 is only physical state. Don't say 컨디션 for stipulations.
Saying 기분이 안 좋아요 to mean physically unwell.
기분 = mood/emotion. 기분이 안 좋아요 = 'in a bad mood (upset)'. For physically unwell, use 컨디션이 / 몸이 안 좋아요.

structuredNuance.t: 컨디션이 안 좋아요 = 'condition is not good'. In Korean 컨디션 (from English 'condition') strictly means physical state/energy, not a medical diagnosis or a legal requirement. 'His condition is bad' in Korean = 'he's not feeling his best' — it's a soft, non-alarmist phrase.

존댓말 to daycare teachers, babysitters, or the pediatrician. 반말 (컨디션 안 좋아) to your partner. Use this at drop-off as a pre-emptive heads-up — it signals the child may be quieter, eat less, or need more patience. For a real fever you'd add 열도 있어요.

컨디션이 안 좋아요 vs 몸이 안 좋아요 — both mean physically unwell; 컨디션 leans toward energy/vitality, 몸 toward the physical body. Both are correct for a daycare heads-up. Neither = 기분이 안 좋아요 ('in a bad mood') — that's emotional, not physical.
오늘 컨디션이 안 좋아요 → 어제부터 컨디션이 안 좋았어요 (onset) → 컨디션이 좀 안 좋은 것 같아요 (uncertain) → 컨디션이 완전히 안 좋아요 (worse). Add cause: 잠을 못 자서 컨디션이 안 좋아요.

The false-friend trap: Korean 컨디션 ≠ 'a medical condition' (that's 질환/병) and ≠ 'a condition/term' (that's 조건). Korean 컨디션 = 'how one feels / energy state' only. Also: 기분이 안 좋아요 = bad mood (emotional); 컨디션이 안 좋아요 = physically off — don't mix these.

entries.english: Did you give him the medicine?
entries.shortExplanation: 약 먹였어요? is a practical expression meaning "Did you give him the medicine?".
entries.explanation: 약 먹였어요? (yang meogyeosseoyo?) means "Did you give him the medicine?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 약 먹였어요? ("Did you give him the medicine?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Did you give him the medicine?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking partner/caregiver/teacher

usagePhrases.en: Did you give him his meds?
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to your partner
Asking the teacher to administer it; -아 주세요
About the schedule, using 먹다 for the child's side

examples.ko: 애 약 먹였어요?
examples.romanization: ae yang meogyeosseoyo?
examples.en: Did you give the kid his medicine?
examples.note: Quick check with your partner

examples.ko: A: 점심 먹고 나서 이 약 한 봉지 먹여 주세요. / B: 네, 알겠어요. 약은 가방 안에 있죠?
examples.romanization: A: jeomsim meokgo naseo i ya kan bongji meogyeo juseyo. / B: ne, algesseoyo. yageun gabang ane itjyo?
examples.en: A: Please give him this one packet after lunch. / B: Sure, got it. The medicine is in his bag, right?
examples.note: Teacher confirms location of medicine; 봉지 = 'sachet' (how Korean kids' medicine is packaged)

examples.ko: 해열제 먹인 지 4시간 됐는데 열이 또 올라요. 한 번 더 먹여도 될까요?
examples.romanization: haeyeolje meogin ji 4sigan dwaenneunde yeori tto ollayo. han beon deo meogyeodo doelkkayo?
examples.en: It's been 4 hours since the fever reducer and it's rising again — can I give another dose?
examples.note: -(으)ㄴ 지 ... 됐다 ('it's been since'); asking dosing timing

entries.nuance: 약 먹였어요? means 'did (you) give (him) the medicine?' — 약 ('medicine') + 먹였어요 (past causative of 먹다: 먹이다 = 'to make eat/feed'). The foundational insight: Korean treats medicine as something you 먹다 ('eat'), not 'take' or 'give'. The child 약을 먹다 ('eats the medicine'); the parent 약을 먹이다 ('feeds the medicine' = gives/administers it). So asking whether the child took it = 약 먹었어요? (plain past); asking whether you administered it = 약 먹였어요? (causative past). Mixing these flips who did what. For a teacher: 약 좀 먹여 주세요 (polite request to administer). Don't say 약 줬어요? — 주다 means 'hand over/give', not 'administer'; 약 줬어요? only means 'did you hand the medicine over?', not 'did you give him his dose?'. Cultural detail: Korean pediatric medicine often comes in 봉지 (sachets) or as 가루약 (powder mixed with water) and 물약 (liquid) — so 한 봉지 먹이다 ('give one sachet') is the natural phrase.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 약 줬어요? to mean 'did you give the medicine'.
주다 ('hand over') only means you passed the medicine to someone. To administer it, use 먹이다: 약 먹였어요?. The child 'eats' medicine in Korean.
Saying 약 먹었어요? when you mean the caregiver gave it.
먹다 (plain) = the child took it himself. For 'did YOU give/administer it', use the causative 먹이다: 약 먹였어요?.
Using 복용하다 in casual speech.
복용하다 ('to take medication') is clinical/written. With family and teachers, say 약 먹이다/먹다. 약 먹였어요? is the natural spoken form.

structuredNuance.t: 약 먹였어요? = 'did you make-him-eat the medicine?' In Korean, medicine is eaten (먹다), not taken. The causative 먹이다 ('make someone eat') is the verb for 'administer'. This is not just grammar — it reflects how Koreans conceptualize medicine intake.

존댓말 (약 먹였어요?) to a daycare teacher or babysitter. 반말 (약 먹였어?) to your partner. To request administration: 약 좀 먹여 주세요. For timing: 점심 먹고 나서 먹여 주세요 ('give it after lunch'). Always specify the dose unit: 한 봉지 / 한 스푼.
약 먹였어요? (causative — YOU administered it) vs 약 먹었어요? (plain — the child took it). 약 줬어요? means only 'did you hand the medicine over?' — not 'did you give the dose'. 주다 ≠ 먹이다 in the medical context.
약 먹였어요? → 약 먹여 주세요 (request) → 약 먹을 시간이에요 (stating it's time). Dosing: 하루 세 번 먹여요 ('give 3x daily'), 식후에 먹여요 ('give after meals'). Types: 가루약 (powder), 물약 (liquid syrup), 알약 (pill).

Two traps: (1) 약 줬어요? — 주다 means 'hand over', not 'administer'. The correct verb is 먹이다: 약 먹였어요?. (2) 복용하다 ('to take medication') is clinical/written — fine for a prescription note but stiff in casual speech with family or teachers. Use 먹이다/먹다 in daily talk.

Korean pediatric medicine is usually dispensed at the pharmacy as 봉지 (individual sachets, often labelled 아침/점심/저녁). Parents hand these sachets to daycare teachers. So 약 한 봉지 먹여 주세요 ('give him one sachet') is the most natural request form.

entries.english: He's got a diaper rash
entries.shortExplanation: 기저귀 발진이 났어요 is a practical expression meaning "He's got a diaper rash".
entries.explanation: "He's got a diaper rash" — that is 기저귀 발진이 났어요 (gijeogwi baljini nasseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 기저귀 발진이 났어요 ("He's got a diaper rash"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; reporting to teacher or pharmacist
반말, to your partner
Plainer description; 빨개지다 = 'to turn red'
Asking staff to put on ointment; 바르다 = 'to apply'

examples.ko: 애기 엉덩이에 기저귀 발진이 났어요.
examples.romanization: aegi eongdeongie gijeogwi baljini nasseoyo.
examples.en: The baby's got a diaper rash on his bottom.
examples.note: 엉덩이에 ('on the bottom') + 발진이 나다 ('a rash breaks out')

examples.ko: A: 발진이 언제부터 났어요? / B: 어제부터 빨개지더니 오늘은 좀 더 심해졌어요.
examples.romanization: A: baljini eonjebuteo nasseoyo? / B: eojebuteo ppalgaejideoni oneureun jom deo simhaejyeosseoyo.
examples.en: A: When did the rash appear? / B: It started turning red yesterday and got worse today.
examples.note: Pharmacist or doctor asking for timeline; shows 빨개지다 → 심해지다 progression

examples.ko: 땀띠인지 기저귀 발진인지 모르겠어서 소아과 가 보려고요.
examples.romanization: ttamttiinji gijeogwi baljininji moreugesseoseo soagwa ga boryeogoyo.
examples.en: I can't tell if it's heat rash or diaper rash, so I'll try the pediatrician.
examples.note: 땀띠 ('heat rash') vs 기저귀 발진 — distinguishing skin issues; 소아과 ('pediatrics')

entries.nuance: 기저귀 발진이 났어요 means '(he's) got a diaper rash' — 기저귀 ('diaper') + 발진 (發疹, 'rash/eruption') + 이 + 났어요 (past of 나다 'to break out/occur'). As with 열이 나다 (fever), skin eruptions use 나다: 발진이 나다, 두드러기가 나다 ('hives break out'), 여드름이 나다 ('pimple breaks out'). Report this in 존댓말 to a daycare teacher, pharmacist, or doctor. For a milder everyday description, 엉덩이가 빨개졌어요 ('his bottom turned red') is perfectly natural. For the treatment, the verb is 바르다 ('to spread on/apply'): 연고 발라 주세요 ('please apply the cream') — NOT 붙이다 ('to stick on', which is for patches and band-aids). The rash under a diaper is specifically 기저귀 발진; other common baby skin issues are 땀띠 (heat/sweat rash), 습진 (eczema), and 아토피 (atopic dermatitis). Keep the subject particle 발진'이' 났어요 and don't use 가지다 ('have') for skin symptoms.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 발진을 가지고 있어요.
Calque of 'have a rash'. Korean: the rash breaks out — 발진이 났어요. 가지다 never fits symptoms.
Saying 연고 붙여 주세요 for applying cream.
붙이다 = 'to stick on' (patches, band-aids). Cream/ointment is spread: 바르다. 'Please apply the cream' is 연고 발라 주세요.
Calling any red skin 기저귀 발진.
기저귀 발진 is specifically the diaper-area rash. Sweat bumps are 땀띠, eczema is 습진. Use the term that matches what you see.

structuredNuance.t: 발진이 났어요 = 'a rash broke out'. The verb 나다 ('to occur/break out') is the idiomatic choice for bodily eruptions: rashes, hives, pimples all 나다. It's the same pattern as 열이 나다 ('fever breaks out'). Never say 발진을 가지고 있어요.
존댓말 to daycare teacher, pharmacist, or pediatrician. 반말 to your partner. At the pharmacy: 기저귀 발진이 났어요, 연고 추천해 주세요 ('please recommend an ointment'). At the daycare: 기저귀 갈 때마다 연고 좀 발라 주세요.

기저귀 발진 (diaper rash, friction/moisture) vs 땀띠 (heat rash/prickly heat, from sweat) vs 습진 (eczema) vs 아토피 (atopic dermatitis). These are distinct conditions requiring different responses — don't blur them. 엉덩이가 빨개졌어요 is a plain visual description that works when you're unsure of the diagnosis.
발진이 났어요 (rash appeared) → 발진이 심해졌어요 (got worse) → 발진이 좀 나아졌어요 (improved) → 발진이 나았어요 (healed). Treatment chain: 연고 발라 주세요 → 기저귀 자주 갈아 주세요 → 공기 중에 좀 노출시켜 주세요.
Two traps: (1) 발진을 가지고 있어요 — calque of 'have a rash'; use 발진이 났어요. (2) 연고 붙여 주세요 — 붙이다 means 'stick on' (patches, band-aids); cream/ointment is spread with 바르다: 연고 발라 주세요.
발진 = 發疹 — 發 'break out/emit', 疹 'rash/skin eruption'. The same 疹 character appears in 수두진 (chicken pox rash), 홍진 (measles rash), etc.

entries.english: He fusses a lot when he's sleepy
entries.shortExplanation: 잠투정이 심해요 is a practical expression meaning "He fusses a lot when he's sleepy".
entries.explanation: 잠투정이 심해요 (jamtujeongi simhaeyo) = "He fusses a lot when he's sleepy". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 잠투정이 심해요 ("He fusses badly when sleepy"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; explaining the child's sleep behavior
반말, to your partner or a friend

examples.note: Teacher explaining 잠투정 to a new parent; 토닥이다 = 'to pat gently'

examples.ko: 낮잠 잘 때 잠투정이 심해서 한참 울다가 잠들어요.
examples.romanization: natjam jal ttae jamtujeongi simhaeseo hancham uldaga jamdeureoyo.
examples.en: He fusses hard at naptime and cries a while before falling asleep.
examples.note: Ties to naptime; 한참 ('for a while') + 잠들다 ('to fall asleep')

entries.nuance: 잠투정이 심해요 means '(his) sleep-fussing is severe' — 잠투정 (잠 'sleep' + 투정 'fussing/grumbling') + 이 + 심해요 (from 심하다 'to be severe'). 잠투정 is a wonderfully specific Korean word with no clean English single-word equivalent — it names exactly the phenomenon of an overtired child becoming fussy and crying instead of sleeping (fighting sleep). You'd explain this to a daycare teacher in 존댓말 so they know what to expect at naptime. The natural verb pairing is 잠투정(을) 부리다 ('to throw a sleep-fuss'), where 부리다 = 'to act out/display a behavior' — it also collocates with 떼 부리다/떼쓰다 ('tantrum'), 고집 부리다 ('stubbornness'), 애교 부리다 ('cuteness'). Distinguish from 떼쓰다 ('tantrum', not sleep-specific, driven by wanting something) and plain 울다 ('cry'). The intensity verb is 심하다 ('severe') — not 크다 ('big') or 강하다 ('strong'), which don't collocate here. For the soothing action: 재우다 ('put to sleep'), with the comforting gesture 토닥이다 ('pat gently').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Overbuilding it as 졸려서 우는 거 since you don't know 잠투정.
Korean has the exact word: 잠투정 (fussing when sleepy). 'He's a fussy sleeper' is 잠투정이 심해요 — far more natural than a long paraphrase.
Saying 잠투정이 커요 / 강해요.
The intensity verb for 잠투정 is 심하다 ('severe'). 크다 ('big') and 강하다 ('strong') don't collocate. Say 잠투정이 심해요.
Confusing 잠투정 with 떼쓰기.
잠투정 = fussing specifically because he's tired/fighting sleep. 떼쓰다 = throwing a tantrum to get his way (anytime). Use 잠투정 for the sleepy-cranky kind.

structuredNuance.t: 잠투정 = 잠 ('sleep') + 투정 ('peevish fussing/complaining'). Literally 'sleep-grumbling'. The real meaning: the cranky, crying-but-won't-sleep fussing an overtired baby does when fighting sleep. There is no clean single-word English equivalent — 'sleep-fighting fussiness' is the closest description.

존댓말 to daycare teachers before naptime: 잠투정이 심해요, 안아서 토닥여 주시면 좋아요 ('sleep-fussing is bad, holding and patting helps'). 반말 to your partner. This is proactive information-sharing — teachers appreciate it because it explains pre-nap crying without alarm.

잠투정 (sleep-specific fussing when tired) vs 떼쓰다 (tantrum to get one's way, not sleep-specific) vs 징징대다 (general whining). Use 잠투정 only for the sleepy-cranky state. A child throwing a fit in a toy store is 떼쓰다, not 잠투정.
잠투정이 심해요 (intense) → 잠투정이 있어요 (milder: 'he has some sleep-fussing') → 잠투정 부려요 (verb form) → 잠투정 없이 잘 자요 ('sleeps without fussing'). After success: 겨우 재웠어요 / 드디어 잠들었어요.
Two traps: (1) Not knowing the word and overbuilding: 졸려서 짜증 내면서 우는 거 — natives just say 잠투정. (2) Using 잠투정이 강해요 / 커요 — the collocate is 심하다 ('severe'), not 강하다 or 크다.

entries.english: He's shy around strangers
entries.shortExplanation: 낯을 가려요 is a practical expression meaning "He's shy around strangers".
entries.explanation: 낯을 가려요 (nacheul garyeoyo) means "He's shy around strangers". Say it as one set phrase — for example 낯을 가려요 ("He's wary of strangers"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; explaining the child's temperament to the teacher
반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: He's a bit selective about people
usagePhrases.note: Variant; 사람을 가리다

usagePhrases.en: He needs some time to adjust
usagePhrases.note: Follow-up; 적응하다 = 'to adapt'

examples.ko: 우리 애가 낯을 좀 가려요.
examples.romanization: uri aega nacheul jom garyeoyo.
examples.en: Our child is a bit shy with strangers.
examples.note: Telling a new teacher to expect initial wariness

examples.ko: A: 처음에 많이 울었는데 이제 좀 나아졌어요. / B: 원래 낯을 가리는 편이에요. 한 달은 봐야 해요.
examples.romanization: A: cheoeume mani ureonneunde ije jom naajyeosseoyo. / B: wollae nacheul garineun pyeonieyo. han dareun bwaya haeyo.
examples.en: A: He cried a lot at first but it's gotten better. / B: He's naturally shy with strangers. Give it a month.
examples.note: Parent and teacher checking in; -는 편이에요 = 'tends to be'

examples.ko: 6개월쯤부터 낯을 가리기 시작해서 할머니한테도 안 가려고 해요.
examples.romanization: 6gaewoljjeumbuteo nacheul garigi sijakaeseo halmeonihantedo an garyeogo haeyo.
examples.en: He started getting stranger-shy around 6 months and won't even go to grandma.
examples.note: Developmental timing; 안 가려고 하다 ('refuses to go (to someone)')

entries.nuance: 낯을 가려요 means '(he) is shy/wary around strangers' — an idiom: 낯 ('face/unfamiliar faces', colloquially 'stranger's face') + 을 + 가리다 ('to distinguish/be selective about'). Literally 'to discriminate among faces', it's the standard term for a baby's stranger anxiety or shyness with unfamiliar people. Use it in 존댓말 to prepare a new teacher for clinginess or crying; 반말 to a friend: 낯 가려. The verb 가리다 runs through a whole family of 'being selective' idioms: 낯(을) 가리다 (shy with strangers), 음식을 가리다 ('picky eater'), 가리지 않다 ('not picky at all'). The first English-speaker pitfall is bypassing the idiom and saying 모르는 사람을 무서워해요 ('afraid of strangers') — understandable but 무서워하다 ('to fear') overstates it; the warm idiomatic phrase is 낯을 가리다. The second pitfall is misreading 가리다, which also means 'to cover/block' (해를 가리다 'block the sun') — with 낯 it always means stranger-shyness, not covering one's face. The object particle 낯'을' is often elided in speech: 낯 가려요 is equally natural.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 모르는 사람 무서워해요 instead of the idiom.
무서워하다 = 'to be afraid of', which overstates it. The set phrase for a baby's shyness with strangers is 낯을 가려요.
Reading 가리다 as 'to cover'.
가리다 has two senses; with 낯 it means 'be selective about faces' (stranger-shy), not 'cover'. 낯을 가리다 ≠ covering one's face.
Confusing 낯 with 낮.
낯 = 'face'; 낮 = 'daytime' (as in 낮잠 'nap'). 낯을 가리다 is about faces/strangers, not the time of day. Watch the final consonant.

structuredNuance.t: 낯 = face / unfamiliar face; 가리다 = to be selective/discriminating. Literally 'to distinguish among faces'. Real meaning: the developmental stage where a baby recognizes familiar vs unfamiliar faces and becomes upset with strangers. A precise, single-phrase name for what developmental psychology calls 'stranger anxiety'.

존댓말 to daycare teachers, babysitters, or any caregiver meeting the child for the first time. 반말 to friends and family. Often followed by an explanation: 조금 지나면 괜찮아질 거예요 ('he'll warm up after a bit') or 적응할 시간이 필요해요. Don't say this to a stranger in the room — say it privately to the caregiver.

낯을 가리다 (shy with strangers — the idiomatic, warm phrasing) vs 모르는 사람을 무서워하다 (afraid of strangers — stronger, less idiomatic) vs 사람을 가리다 (selective about people generally, slightly broader). For picky eating: 음식을 가리다 (same verb, swap noun).
낯을 가려요 → 낯을 좀 가리는 편이에요 ('tends to be shy with strangers') → 낯을 심하게 가려요 ('very shy') → 요즘은 낯을 안 가려요 ('not shy anymore'). Picky eater variant: 음식을 많이 가려요.

Two traps: (1) Saying 모르는 사람 무서워해요 — 무섭다 overstates it; use 낯을 가리다 for the mild developmental shyness. (2) Confusing 가리다 'to discriminate' with 가리다 'to cover/block' — with 낯, it always means stranger-shyness, not physically covering a face.

entries.english: Is there anything I need to pack/bring?
entries.shortExplanation: 준비물 챙겨야 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Is there anything I need to pack/bring?".
entries.explanation: "Is there anything I need to pack/bring?" — that is 준비물 챙겨야 돼요? (junbimul chaenggyeoya dwaeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 준비물 챙겨야 돼요? ("Do I need to bring any supplies?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Do I need to bring any supplies?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking the daycare what to pack
반말, to your partner

usagePhrases.en: What should I send with him?
usagePhrases.note: Variant; 챙겨 보내다 ('pack and send')

usagePhrases.en: I packed everything in the bag
usagePhrases.note: Reporting it's done; 챙기다 = 'to pack/gather'

examples.ko: 내일 소풍인데 준비물 챙겨야 돼요?
examples.romanization: naeil sopunginde junbimul chaenggyeoya dwaeyo?
examples.en: There's a field trip tomorrow — do I need to pack anything?
examples.note: 준비물 ('items to prepare') around a 소풍 ('outing')

examples.ko: A: 여벌 옷이랑 기저귀는 항상 챙겨 보내 주세요. / B: 네, 매일 두 벌씩 넣어 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: yeobeol osirang gijeogwineun hangsang chaenggyeo bonae juseyo. / B: ne, maeil du beolssing neoeo deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: Please always send a change of clothes and diapers. / B: Sure, I'll put in two outfits every day.
examples.note: Teacher instructing parent at enrollment; 여벌 옷 ('spare clothes'), 두 벌씩 ('two sets each time')

examples.ko: 물티슈 다 떨어졌다고 알림장에 적혀 있던데 챙겨 보낼게요.
examples.romanization: multisyu da tteoreojyeotdago allimjange jeokyeo itdeonde chaenggyeo bonaelgeyo.
examples.en: The notebook said the wet wipes ran out, so I'll pack some.
examples.note: 알림장 ('daycare notebook') is real; 물티슈 ('wet wipes')

entries.nuance: 준비물 챙겨야 돼요? means 'do I need to pack/bring any supplies?' — 준비물 (準備物, 'things to prepare/bring', the standard term for required items for school/daycare events) + 챙기다 ('to gather up and take, to pack, to conscientiously ensure') + -야 돼요 ('must/need to'). The star verb is 챙기다, which has no single English equivalent but captures the idea of making sure you don't forget the needed things: 가방 챙기다 ('pack the bag'), 밥 챙겨 먹다 ('make sure to eat'), 애 챙기다 ('look after the kid'). For sending items with a child, 챙겨 보내다 ('pack-and-send') is the natural pairing. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 가지고 가다 ('take along', fine but less precise) or 준비하다 ('prepare broadly') instead of the lived-in 챙기다. 준비물 specifically names required items (think 'school supply list'); don't vaguely say 필요한 것들 when 준비물 is the precise word. Note 챙기다's nuance of conscientiousness and responsibility — it implies not forgetting.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 준비물 가지고 가야 돼요? only.
가지고 가다 ('take along') works but misses the nuance. The lived-in verb for packing the needed items is 챙기다: 준비물 챙겨야 돼요?.
Using 준비하다 for the act of packing a bag.
준비하다 = 'prepare' broadly. For gathering and packing the actual items to bring, use 챙기다. 'I'll pack it' is 챙겨 보낼게요, not 준비해 갈게요.
Saying 필요한 거 instead of 준비물.
준비물 is the precise term for required items to bring (supplies). Vague 필요한 거 ('needed things') misses it. Ask 준비물 뭐예요? for the list.

structuredNuance.t: 준비물 = 準備物 'things prepared/to bring'; 챙기다 = conscientiously gather and take (without forgetting); -야 돼요 = need to. Literally 'do I need to conscientiously gather the required items?' The word 챙기다 carries a sense of responsibility and thoroughness — it implies not forgetting anything.

존댓말 to daycare or kindergarten teachers before events (소풍, 발표회, 생일잔치, etc.). 반말 to your partner. Also used daily: 오늘 준비물 뭐예요? ('what do I need to send today?'). The question implies trust in the teacher's list — you're asking what they require.

챙기다 (conscientiously pack/gather — implies responsibility) vs 가지고 가다 (simply bring/take along) vs 준비하다 (prepare broadly). For sending with the child: 챙겨 보내다 ('pack and send'). 준비물 (required supplies list) vs 필요한 것들 (vaguely 'needed things' — less precise).
준비물 챙겨야 돼요? → 준비물 뭐예요? ('what are the supplies?') → 준비물 다 챙겼어요 ('packed everything') → 준비물 빠진 거 없어요? ('nothing missing?'). For an event: 소풍 준비물 뭐 챙겨야 해요?

Two traps: (1) Using 준비하다 for packing — 준비하다 = 'prepare broadly'; 챙기다 = 'pack with care/not forgetting'. The daily childcare verb is 챙기다. (2) Saying 필요한 거 instead of 준비물 — 준비물 is precise and what teachers actually use on their list.
준비물 = 準備物 — 準備 'preparation' + 物 'things/items'. The same 준비 appears in 준비하다 ('to prepare') and 준비 운동 ('warm-up exercise').

entries.english: It's the adjustment period, so he leaves daycare early
entries.shortExplanation: 적응 기간이라 일찍 하원해요 is a practical expression meaning "It's the adjustment period, so he leaves daycare early".
entries.explanation: 적응 기간이라 일찍 하원해요 (jeogeung giganira iljji kawonhaeyo) = "It's the adjustment period, so he leaves daycare early". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 적응 기간이라 일찍 하원해요 ("It's the adjustment period so he leaves early"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: It's the adjustment period so he leaves early
usagePhrases.note: Polite; explaining the short early days

usagePhrases.en: It's the settling-in period so bring him early
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to your partner

usagePhrases.en: I'll pick him up early today
usagePhrases.note: Causative 하원시키다 — the parent takes him home early
Asking the teacher how adjustment is going

examples.ko: 이번 주는 적응 기간이라 11시에 하원해요.
examples.romanization: ibeon juneun jeogeung giganira 11sie hawonhaeyo.
examples.en: This week is the adjustment period, so he leaves at 11.
examples.note: 적응 기간 ('settling-in period') is standard for new daycare kids

examples.ko: A: 이번 주는 두 시간씩만 있다가 하원해요. 다음 주부터 늘려 볼게요. / B: 네, 적응 기간엔 천천히 하는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: A: ibeon juneun du siganssingman itdaga hawonhaeyo. daeum jubuteo neullyeo bolgeyo. / B: ne, jeogeung giganen cheoncheonhi haneun ge joayo.
examples.en: A: This week he'll stay just two hours before leaving. We'll increase it from next week. / B: Yes, taking it slow during the adjustment period is good.
examples.note: Parent and teacher discussing the gradual schedule; 천천히 ('slowly')

examples.ko: 적응 기간 끝나면 종일반으로 바꿀 거예요. 그때부턴 5시에 데리러 갈게요.
examples.romanization: jeogeung gigan kkeunnamyeon jongilbaneuro bakkul geoyeyo. geuttaebuteon 5sie derireo galgeyo.
examples.en: After the adjustment period we'll switch to full-day; then I'll pick him up at 5.
examples.note: 종일반 ('full-day class') vs the short adjustment schedule; ties to pickup

entries.nuance: 적응 기간이라 일찍 하원해요 means 'because it's the adjustment period, (he) goes home from daycare early' — 적응 기간 (適應期間, 'adaptation period', the settling-in weeks when a new daycare child attends briefly) + -이라(서) ('because it is') + 일찍 ('early') + 하원하다 (下園, 'to leave daycare for home', opposite of 등원). Korean daycares almost universally run a 적응 기간 where new kids build up from 1–2 hours/day to full-day over 1–2 weeks, and parents explain their odd short schedule constantly. 하원 is the must-learn counterpart to 등원: 등원 = arriving at daycare, 하원 = leaving for home. For real school it's 등교/하교. The crucial verb distinction: 하원하다 is intransitive (the child goes home), while 하원시키다 is causative (the parent takes him home) — 'I'll pick him up early' is 일찍 하원시킬게요. Saying 집에 일찍 가요 is understandable but imprecise; the daycare-specific term is 하원하다. -이라(서) is the spoken 'because' contraction of 이다, very common in explanation sentences.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 집에 일찍 가요 instead of 일찍 하원해요.
집에 가요 ('goes home') is generic. The daycare-specific term for going home from 어린이집 is 하원하다. Its partner is 등원하다 (arriving).
Confusing 하원하다 (child leaves) with 하원시키다 (you take him home).
하원하다 is intransitive — the CHILD goes home. For 'I'll pick him up early', use the causative 하원시키다: 일찍 하원시킬게요.
Using 적응 as a standalone verb.
적응 is a noun; the verb is 적응하다 ('to adapt'). 'He's adjusting well' is 적응 잘해요. The settling-in period is the noun phrase 적응 기간.

structuredNuance.t: 적응 기간이라 = 'because it's the adaptation period'; 일찍 = early; 하원해요 = leaves daycare (하원 = 下園, 'descend from the garden'). The phrase explains why a child's schedule is shorter than usual. The institution-specific word 하원 is what makes this precise and native-sounding.

존댓말 to teachers, other daycare parents, or family who wonder why pickup is so early. 반말 to your partner. Common in the first 1–2 weeks of any new daycare or kindergarten enrollment. -이라(서) is casual enough for conversation; in a formal letter use 이기 때문에.

하원하다 (child leaves) vs 하원시키다 (parent picks up). For school-age kids: 하교하다 / 하교시키다. 집에 일찍 가요 is understandable but generic — 일찍 하원해요 is the daycare-specific form. 적응 기간 vs 수습 기간 — 수습 is for adult probation/trial periods; for daycare use 적응 기간.
일찍 하원해요 → 일찍 하원시킬게요 (causative: I'll take him) → 하원 시간을 늘릴게요 ('we'll extend the time') → 이제 종일 하원해요 ('now leaves at full-day time'). Schedule stages: 한 시간 → 두 시간 → 반일 → 종일.

Three traps: (1) Not knowing 하원 and saying 집에 일찍 가요 — correct but missing the precise term. (2) Confusing 하원하다 (intransitive: child leaves) with 하원시키다 (causative: I take him home). (3) Saying 적응하다 as a standalone when you need the noun phrase 적응 기간 to name the period.
하원 = 下園 (下 'descend/leave', 園 'garden/daycare'). Mirrors 등원 = 登園 (登 'ascend/go to'). 적응 = 適應 ('fitting-response', adaptation).

entries.english: Stop fussing, would you
entries.shortExplanation: 투정 좀 그만 부려 is a practical expression meaning "Stop fussing, would you".
entries.explanation: 투정 좀 그만 부려 (tujeong jom geuman buryeo) means "Stop fussing, would you". Say it as one set phrase — for example 투정 좀 그만 부려 ("Stop fussing now"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 반말, scolding your own child gently
반말; 떼쓰다 for willful demanding
Softer, including yourself with -자 ('let's')

usagePhrases.en: Why are you fussing like this?
usagePhrases.note: Asking, half-exasperated; 떼를 쓰다

examples.ko: 아이고, 투정 좀 그만 부려.
examples.romanization: aigo, tujeong jom geuman buryeo.
examples.en: Oh come on, stop fussing.
examples.note: 아이고 ('oh dear') + a tired-parent plea to the child

examples.ko: A: (child crying) 엄마, 저거 사 줘! / B: 투정 좀 그만 부려. 집에 비슷한 거 있잖아.
examples.romanization: A: (child crying) eomma, jeogeo sa jwo! / B: tujeong jom geuman buryeo. jibe biseutan geo itjana.
examples.en: A: (child crying) Mom, buy me that! / B: Stop fussing. You already have something like it at home.
examples.note: Real parent-child store tantrum exchange; shows 투정 as a response to demanding

examples.ko: 배고파서 그런가? 투정 부리지 말고 밥 먼저 먹자.
examples.romanization: baegopaseo geureonga? tujeong buriji malgo bam meonjeo meokja.
examples.en: Is it because he's hungry? Don't fuss — let's eat first.
examples.note: Self-talk + to child; 투정 부리지 말고 ('don't fuss, and instead…')

entries.nuance: 투정 좀 그만 부려 means 'stop fussing/complaining, would you' — 투정 ('peevish complaining/fussing', especially about food or not getting one's way) + 좀 (softener-cum-impatience marker, 'a bit / please / would you') + 그만 ('stop') + 부려 (반말 imperative of 부리다 'to act out/display a behavior'). This is 반말 you say to your OWN small child — not to someone else's kid and not to anyone in 존댓말. The verb 부리다 is a critical collocate for behavioral idioms: 투정 부리다 ('fuss'), 떼 부리다/떼쓰다 ('tantrum'), 고집 부리다 ('be stubborn'), 애교 부리다 ('act cute'). The key distinction: 투정 = peevish grumbling about not getting something/food, often with whining, while 떼(를) 쓰다 = a fuller willful tantrum, actively demanding and not giving up. For 'stop doing X', the frame is 그만 + verb or verb + 지 마 — never 멈추다, which halts motion or machines. 'Stop crying' = 울지 마; 'stop fussing' = 투정 부리지 마 or 투정 좀 그만 부려.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 투정 멈춰 for 'stop fussing'.
멈추다 = halt motion/a machine. To tell someone to stop a behavior, use 그만(하다) or 그만 + verb / -지 마: 투정 좀 그만 부려 / 투정 부리지 마.
Mixing up 투정, 떼쓰다, 징징대다.
투정 = peevish complaining (esp. food/wants); 떼쓰다 = willfully demanding (tantrum); 징징대다 = whining. Pick by the behavior. They aren't interchangeable.
Using this 반말 line to someone else's child.
투정 좀 그만 부려 is 반말 for your OWN kid. To another's child or politely, you wouldn't command this way; soften or don't say it. Register matters.

structuredNuance.t: 투정 = peevish fussing/complaining (especially about food or not getting one's way); 좀 = adds impatience here, not 'a little'; 그만 = stop; 부려 = imperative of 부리다 ('display a behavior'). Literally 'display the fussing — stop it'. The phrase is mildly exasperated, not harsh — a tired parent's plea, not a scolding.

반말 exclusively — said to your OWN young child (3–8 year range typically). Never to someone else's child or in 존댓말. This is private family speech. In public you might soften: 그만 하자, or 왜 이러니? for a slightly gentler touch.

투정 부리다 (peevish fussing, grumbling — about food or minor wants) vs 떼쓰다 (full tantrum, willful demanding) vs 징징대다 (whining without a specific demand). 투정 좀 그만 부려 < 떼 좀 그만 써 in intensity. For stopping crying: 울지 마 ('don't cry').
투정 좀 그만 부려 (standard 반말 imperative) → 투정 부리지 마 ('don't fuss') → 투정 좀 그만 부릴래? (softer request form) → 이제 그만 투정 부려도 돼. For 떼: 떼 좀 그만 써 / 떼쓰지 마.

Two traps: (1) Using 멈추다 ('to stop/halt') for a behavior — 멈추다 is for motion/machines. To stop a behavior use 그만 + verb or -지 마: 투정 좀 그만 부려 / 투정 부리지 마. (2) Flattening 투정/떼쓰다/징징대다 all into 'fussing' — each has a distinct intensity and trigger.

entries.english: Did he have a good day at daycare?
entries.shortExplanation: 오늘 어린이집에서 잘 지냈어요? is a practical expression meaning "Did he have a good day at daycare?".
entries.explanation: "Did he have a good day at daycare?" — that is 오늘 어린이집에서 잘 지냈어요? (oneul eorinijibeseo jal jinaesseoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 오늘 어린이집에서 잘 지냈어요? ("Did he have a good day at daycare?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Did he have a good day at daycare?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; the standard pickup question to the teacher

usagePhrases.en: Did you have a good day at daycare?
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to the child

usagePhrases.en: Anything happen today? / Was everything okay?
usagePhrases.note: Checking for incidents; 별일 ('anything unusual')
Shorter open question to the teacher

examples.ko: 오늘 우리 애 어린이집에서 잘 지냈어요?
examples.romanization: oneul uri ae eorinijibeseo jal jinaesseoyo?
examples.en: Did our child have a good day at daycare today?
examples.note: The everyday pickup check-in with the teacher

examples.ko: A: 오늘 잘 지냈어요? 밥은 잘 먹었고요? / B: 네, 오늘은 밥도 잘 먹고 낮잠도 잘 잤어요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul jal jinaesseoyo? babeun jal meogeotgoyo? / B: ne, oneureun bapdo jal meokgo natjamdo jal jasseoyo.
examples.en: A: Did he do well today? And did he eat okay? / B: Yes, he ate well and napped well today.
examples.note: Stacking a second question with -고요; teacher gives positive rundown — the ideal pickup

examples.ko: 오늘 친구랑 안 싸우고 잘 지냈어요? 어제 좀 다퉜다고 해서요.
examples.romanization: oneul chingurang an ssaugo jal jinaesseoyo? eoje jom datwotdago haeseoyo.
examples.en: Did he get along with friends without fighting today? You said they squabbled yesterday.
examples.note: 잘 지내다 = 'get along/do well'; 다투다 ('to squabble')

entries.nuance: 오늘 어린이집에서 잘 지냈어요? means 'did (he) have a good day / spend the time well at daycare today?' — 오늘 ('today') + 어린이집에서 (에서 = location-of-action, 'at daycare') + 잘 ('well') + 지냈어요 (past of 지내다 'to spend time / fare / get along').
