This is THE daily pickup question to a daycare teacher in 존댓말; in 반말 to your child: 잘 지냈어? (or 어린이집 어땠어?). The verb 지내다 is the key — it's not just 'have a good time' but 'how did you fare, get on, get along?' (잘 지내다 = do well/get along, 어떻게 지내요 = how are you doing). For the particle: actions done AT a place take 에서. Saying 어린이집에 잘 지냈어요? with 에 (destination particle) is the classic learner error. Use 에 for direction/existence (가다/있다), 에서 for activities at a place (지내다, 놀다, 먹다). Translating 'have a good day' literally as 좋은 하루 보냈어요? is understandable but 잘 지냈어요? is more idiomatic and sounds warmer. Also don't confuse 지내다 ('to fare/spend time') with 지나다 ('to pass by/elapse').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 어린이집에 잘 지냈어요? with 에.
An action done AT a place takes 에서: 어린이집'에서' 잘 지냈어요?. 에 marks a destination ('to daycare'), which is wrong for 'spent the day there'.
Translating literally as 좋은 하루 보냈어요?
Understandable, but the natural pickup phrase is 잘 지냈어요? ('did he fare well / have a good time'). 지내다 is the lived-in verb for how someone got on.
Confusing 지내다 with 지나다.
지내다 = 'to fare/spend time/get along'; 지나다 = 'to pass by / elapse'. 잘 지냈어요? asks how he did, not whether time passed. Keep the verbs distinct.

structuredNuance.t: 오늘 어린이집에서 = at daycare today; 잘 지냈어요? = spent the time well / fared well. 지내다 covers both 'have a good time' and 'get along with people' — it's a warm, general wellbeing check. More idiomatic than 좋은 하루 보냈어요? ('had a good day?' — a direct calque).

존댓말 to daycare teacher at pickup — the first question after signing out. 반말 to your child on the way home: 어린이집 어땠어? / 잘 지냈어?. To probe for incidents: 별일 없었어요? ('nothing unusual?'). Stacking a follow-up: 밥은 잘 먹었어요? ('did he eat well?').

잘 지냈어요? (general wellbeing) vs 별일 없었어요? (checking for incidents) vs 오늘 어땠어요? (open-ended). 잘 지냈어요 invites a positive summary; 별일 없었어요 prompts the teacher to flag anything unusual. Both are needed in a parent's vocabulary.
오늘 잘 지냈어요? → 오늘 어떻게 지냈어요? ('how did he do today?') → 친구랑 잘 지냈어요? ('did he get along with friends?') → 요즘 잘 지내고 있어요? (ongoing check: 'is he doing well lately?'). To the child: 오늘 재미있었어?

Two traps: (1) Wrong particle: 어린이집'에서' (에서 for activity-at-a-place), not 어린이집'에' (에 for destination). This is the single most common particle error. (2) Translating literally as 좋은 하루 보냈어요? — understandable but 잘 지냈어요? is the natural, warmer phrasing used by Korean parents.

entries.english: I have a meeting
entries.shortExplanation: 회의가 있어요 is a practical expression meaning "I have a meeting".
entries.explanation: 회의가 있어요 (hoeuiga isseoyo) = "I have a meeting". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 회의가 있어요. ("I have a meeting."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Neutral-polite (해요체), telling a coworker why you're stepping away
반말, to a same-age colleague or close junior — particle 가 is often dropped in casual speech
격식체 (합쇼체), reporting your schedule to a boss or in a formal setting such as a briefing

usagePhrases.en: I have a meeting at 3 later.
usagePhrases.note: Extension: adding a time signals exactly when you'll be unavailable, so colleagues can plan around you

examples.ko: 지금 회의가 있어요.
examples.romanization: jigeum hoeuiga isseoyo.
examples.en: I have a meeting right now.
examples.note: The bare, single-sentence reason given when you can't talk this second — short and natural

examples.ko: A: 잠깐 얘기할 수 있어요? / B: 죄송한데 지금 회의가 있어서요. 끝나고 연락드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: jamkkan yaegihal su isseoyo? / B: joesonghande jigeum hoeuiga isseoseoyo. kkeunnago yeollakdeurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: Can we talk for a second? / B: Sorry, I have a meeting right now. I'll reach out after it's done.
examples.note: Real two-person exchange: B uses the polite reason clause -아/어서요 to soften the refusal without full explanation

examples.ko: 오후에 팀 회의가 있어서 보고서는 그 전에 끝낼게요.
examples.romanization: ohue tim hoeuiga isseoseo bogoseoneun geu jeone kkeunnaelgeyo.
examples.en: There's a team meeting this afternoon, so I'll finish the report before then.
examples.note: Shows 있다 used inside a causal clause (-아서), linking the meeting's existence to a plan — common in real work scheduling

entries.nuance: 회의가 있어요 is the everyday office phrase for 'a meeting is on my schedule.' Korean uses 있다 ('to exist/have') with the subject particle 가, treating the meeting as a thing that exists on your calendar — crucially, this is NOT 회의를 있어요 (있다 never takes the object particle 를). Drop to 회의 있어 with same-rank friends or juniors; rise to 회의가 있습니다 when briefing management or making a formal declaration. The closest alternative, 회의에 들어가요, means you are physically going into the meeting right now, whereas 있어요 is simply the schedule fact. A second comparison: 회의를 해요 ('I'm having / conducting a meeting') frames you as an active participant hosting it, not merely as an attendee — use 있어요 to announce your schedule, 해요 when you're running the meeting itself. English speakers almost always say 회의를 있어요 by copying the direct-object structure of 'have a meeting,' but 있다 in Korean always needs 이/가.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 회의를 있어요 by translating 'have a meeting' literally — 있다 takes the subject particle, so it must be 회의가 있어요.
Using 회의를 해요 to mean 'I have a meeting' — 회의하다 means to actively hold/conduct a meeting, not that one is on your schedule; for the schedule fact use 있어요.
Saying 회의 있어 to a manager — that's 반말; with a boss say 회의가 있어요 or the formal 회의가 있습니다.

structuredNuance.t: 'A meeting exists (on my schedule).' Korean uses 있다 ('to exist') with subject particle 가, not the object-verb structure English uses. The meeting is a thing that exists, not something you 'have' as a possession.
회의가 있어요 is polite-neutral (해요체) — safe for coworkers at the same or higher level. Use 있습니다 when reporting to senior management or in any formal announcement. Use 있어 only with close peers or juniors.

회의에 들어가요 = physically going into the meeting right now (in-progress action). 회의를 해요 = actively conducting/hosting the meeting. 회의가 있어요 = the calendar fact: a meeting is scheduled. Pick 있어요 for the 'I'm busy / I have one booked' message.
Add time: 3시에 회의가 있어요. Add a causal clause: 회의가 있어서 못 가요 ('I can't go because I have a meeting'). Pair with 이따 ('later today') for advance notice.
회의를 있어요 — copying English 'have a meeting' as object + 있다 is the #1 mistake. 있다 takes 이/가, never 을/를. Also: don't say 회의를 해요 when you simply mean 'I have one booked'; 해요 implies you're running it.

entries.english: They're not at their desk
entries.shortExplanation: 자리에 안 계세요 is a practical expression meaning "They're not at their desk".
entries.explanation: 자리에 안 계세요 (jarie an gyeseyo) means "They're not at their desk". Say it as one set phrase — for example 자리에 안 계세요. ("He's/She's not at their desk."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Honorific 계시다, said ABOUT a senior to a caller or visitor — never about yourself
반말/plain, talking about a peer to another peer — 없다 because no honorific is needed

usagePhrases.en: He/She is not at their desk at the moment.
usagePhrases.note: 격식체, answering an outside business call or speaking to a high superior
Softer extension implying a brief, temporary absence — suggests they'll be back soon

examples.ko: 김 과장님은 자리에 안 계세요.
examples.romanization: gim gwajangnimeun jarie an gyeseyo.
examples.en: Manager Kim isn't at her desk.
examples.note: Bare third-person report when someone asks for a colleague — note honorific 계시다 for the absent senior

examples.ko: A: 이 팀장님 좀 바꿔 주시겠어요? / B: 지금 자리에 안 계신데, 메모 남겨 드릴까요?
examples.romanization: A: i timjangnim jom bakkwo jusigesseoyo? / B: jigeum jarie an gyesinde, memo namgyeo deurilkkayo?
examples.en: A: Could I speak to Team Leader Lee? / B: He's not at his desk right now — shall I take a message?
examples.note: Classic phone-handling exchange: 계신데 ('not in, but…') naturally leads to an offer to help

examples.ko: 부장님은 외근 중이라 자리에 안 계세요. 들어오시면 전화드리라고 할게요.
examples.romanization: bujangnimeun oegeun jungira jarie an gyeseyo. deureoosimyeon jeonhwadeurirago halgeyo.
examples.en: The director is out on business, so he's not in. I'll have him call you when he's back.
examples.note: Fuller answer explaining the absence and offering a callback — 외근 (outside-work errand) adds context

entries.nuance: 자리에 안 계세요 is what you say ABOUT a senior colleague who isn't at their desk, to a caller, visitor, or anyone asking for them. 계시다 is the honorific equivalent of 있다, and its entire job here is to raise the absent person — you never use 계세요 about yourself. Location is marked with 에 (자리에, 'at the desk'), not 를. When the absent person is a peer, drop to 없어요 or 없어; save 계세요 for someone you owe deference. The close neighbor 잠시 자리 비웠어요 ('stepped away for a moment') promises a quick return and is said ABOUT a peer by a third party or about yourself when you come back; 안 계세요 is the neutral 'not here right now' with no return-time implied. The trap for English speakers: saying 자리에 안 있어요 about a boss uses plain 있다, which strips the honorific and comes across as rude or at least careless in a Korean office context.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 자리에 안 있어요 about a senior — plain 있다 fails to honor them; use the honorific 안 계세요.
Using 계세요 about yourself ('저는 자리에 안 계세요') — you never honorific-raise yourself; say 저는 자리에 없었어요.
Marking the spot with 를 (자리를 안 계세요) — location takes 에, so it's 자리에 안 계세요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'At the desk, [they] do not honorably-exist.' 실제: '[They are] not at their desk right now' — a standard third-party message relayed to a caller or visitor on behalf of the absent senior.

Used only about a third person (a senior), never yourself. 계시다 is always for someone you're honoring. For a peer, use 없어요/없어. For a formal phone call, upgrade to 안 계십니다. Never say 저는 자리에 안 계세요 — you cannot honorific-raise yourself.
잠시 자리 비우셨어요 = stepped away briefly, implies they'll be right back. 자리에 안 계세요 = neutral 'not here right now,' no return promise. 외출하셨어요 = went out (outside the building), a longer absence.
자리에 안 계신데 ('not in, but…') is the natural lead-in to an offer: 메모 남겨 드릴까요? ('Shall I take a message?'). Add 잠시 for a softer tone: 잠시 자리에 안 계세요.
자리에 안 있어요 about a boss — plain 있다 fails to honor them; 안 계세요 is required. Also: 자리를 안 계세요 is wrong — location takes 에, not 를.

entries.english: I stepped away for a moment
entries.shortExplanation: 잠시 자리 비웠어요 is a practical expression meaning "I stepped away for a moment".
entries.explanation: "I stepped away for a moment" — that is 잠시 자리 비웠어요 (jamsi jari biwosseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 잠시 자리 비웠어요. ("I stepped away for a bit."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: I stepped away for a bit.
usagePhrases.note: Polite (해요체), explaining your own brief absence when you return and find you missed someone

usagePhrases.en: I stepped out for a sec.
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a peer who was looking for you

usagePhrases.en: I stepped away for a moment.
usagePhrases.note: 격식체, in a formal reply or email apology for a missed call or message
Honorific past, said ABOUT a senior by a third party — note 비우셨어요, not 비웠어요, for the raised subject

examples.ko: 죄송해요, 잠시 자리 비웠어요.
examples.romanization: joesonghaeyo, jamsi jari biwosseoyo.
examples.en: Sorry, I stepped away for a moment.
examples.note: The bare apology when you missed someone at your desk — -었어요 past tense marks it as completed

examples.ko: A: 아까 전화했는데 못 받으셨어요? / B: 네, 잠시 자리 비웠었어요. 무슨 일이세요?
examples.romanization: A: akka jeonhwahaenneunde mot badeusyeosseoyo? / B: ne, jamsi jari biwosseosseoyo. museun iriseyo?
examples.en: A: I called earlier — did you miss it? / B: Yes, I'd stepped away for a bit. What's up?
examples.note: Two-person exchange: 비웠었어요 (past-perfect) signals the absence is fully over before the conversation

examples.ko: 아까 찾으셨다면서요? 잠시 자리 비웠어요. 지금 바로 도와드릴게요.
examples.romanization: akka chajeusyeotdamyeonseoyo? jamsi jari biwosseoyo. jigeum baro dowadeurilgeyo.
examples.en: I heard you were looking for me? I had stepped out — I can help you right now.
examples.note: Fuller exchange: returning, acknowledging the visit, and immediately offering to help

entries.nuance: 잠시 자리 비웠어요 explains YOUR OWN brief absence from your desk, said when you return and find you missed a call, visitor, or message. 비우다 literally means 'to empty / vacate,' so you 'emptied your seat' for a short time. 잠시 and 잠깐 are both 'briefly/momentarily' and interchangeable here. Use past 비웠어요 for 'I was away'; past-perfect 비웠었어요 emphasizes it's fully over before this moment. The key distinction from 자리에 안 계세요: that phrase is said by a THIRD PARTY about a senior, while 자리 비웠어요 is first-person about yourself — swapping them accidentally applies honorific speech to yourself, which sounds strange. A second neighbor, 나갔어요 ('I went out'), implies leaving the building entirely, whereas 자리 비웠어요 covers any brief step away from the desk — a bathroom break, a hallway chat, a short errand — without suggesting you left. English speakers consistently reach for 나갔어요 as a translation of 'I was out,' which overextends the absence.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 자리를 떠났어요 ('I departed my seat') — too heavy and final, like quitting; for a brief step away use 자리 비웠어요.
Using 나갔어요 to mean a quick desk break — that implies leaving the building; 자리 비웠어요 keeps it to a short absence.
Honorific-raising yourself with 자리 비우셨어요 about your own absence — 비우셨어요 is for a senior; say 자리 비웠어요 for yourself.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I briefly emptied my seat (비우다 = empty/vacate).' 실제: 'I stepped away from my desk for a moment' — a natural explanation given when returning to find a missed caller or visitor.

First-person only: said by YOU about your own absence. 비웠어요 (해요체) for coworkers; 비웠습니다 (격식) in email or formal settings; 비웠어 (반말) to peers. The honorific form 비우셨어요 belongs ONLY when talking about a senior third party, never yourself.
자리에 안 계세요 = third-person, about a senior (someone else). 나갔어요 = left the building/premises. 잠시 자리 비웠어요 = you personally stepped away from the desk briefly — doesn't imply leaving the office.
비웠어요 (past, simple) vs 비웠었어요 (past-perfect, fully over). Combine with reason: 잠깐 화장실 갔다 왔어요 ('I went to the bathroom quickly') is more specific but 자리 비웠어요 is the polite, neutral default.
'I was out' → 나갔어요 sounds like you left the building entirely. For a quick desk break, 자리 비웠어요 is correct. Also: never use 비우셨어요 to describe your own absence — that honorific form is for others.

entries.english: I'll check on it
entries.shortExplanation: 확인해 보겠습니다 is a practical expression meaning "I'll check on it".
entries.explanation: 확인해 보겠습니다 (hwaginhae bogetseumnida) = "I'll check on it". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 확인해 보겠습니다. ("I'll look into it."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 격식체 (합쇼체), to a client or boss — the standard business 'let me check'
Polite-casual (해요체), to a coworker — slightly warmer and less stiff than 보겠습니다
반말, to a peer or junior

usagePhrases.en: I'll check and get back to you.
usagePhrases.note: Extension pairing verification with a follow-up promise — common in customer service and formal calls

examples.ko: 네, 확인해 보겠습니다.
examples.romanization: ne, hwaginhae bogetseumnida.
examples.en: Yes, I'll check on it.
examples.note: The bare professional reply to a request — 네 at the front signals you've received and accepted the task

examples.ko: 재고가 있는지 확인해 보겠습니다. 잠시만 기다려 주세요.
examples.romanization: jaegoga inneunji hwaginhae bogetseumnida. jamsiman gidaryeo juseyo.
examples.en: I'll check whether we have it in stock. Please wait a moment.
examples.note: Everyday customer-service use: stating what you'll verify, then asking them to hold

examples.ko: A: 이 내용이 맞는지 확인해 주실 수 있어요? / B: 네, 확인해 보고 오늘 안으로 답변드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: A: i naeyongi manneunji hwaginhae jusil su isseoyo? / B: ne, hwaginhae bogo oneul aneuro dapbyeondeurigetseumnida.
examples.en: A: Can you check whether this is correct? / B: Yes, I'll check and get back to you by end of day.
examples.note: Two-person exchange showing -아/어 보다 softening the action and -겠습니다 committing to a follow-up

entries.nuance: 확인해 보겠습니다 is the workhorse business phrase for 'let me check/verify that.' 확인하다 means to confirm or check a known, specific thing — a fact, a status, a number — so this phrase is for verification, not research. The -아/어 보다 construction adds a 'give it a try / I'll go and see' nuance that softens the commitment: you're not declaring certainty, you're promising the attempt. -겠습니다 marks a polite statement of intention, essential in formal speech. The nearest phrase is 알아보겠습니다 ('I'll find out / investigate'), used when the information is unknown and needs to be discovered rather than confirmed — saying 알아보겠습니다 when the fact already exists but just needs checking can suggest you're less capable than expected. Dropping 보다 (saying just 확인하겠습니다) is grammatical but sounds blunter and more like a certainty claim; the softer 확인해 보겠습니다 is the professional default, especially in service interactions.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 알아보겠습니다 when you mean to verify a known item — that's for finding out unknown info; to confirm a specific fact say 확인해 보겠습니다.
Saying 확인해 볼게요 to an important client — it's a touch casual; in formal business use 확인해 보겠습니다.
Dropping 보다 and saying only 확인하겠습니다 in service contexts — it sounds curt; the softer 확인해 보겠습니다 is the norm.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I will try checking/verifying.' 실제: 'I'll look into it / let me confirm that' — a polite commitment to verify a specific thing, with -아/어 보다 softening from certainty to a promise to try.
확인해 보겠습니다 (합쇼체) for clients and bosses. 확인해 볼게요 (해요체) for coworkers. 확인해 볼게 (반말) for peers. Use this phrase whenever someone asks you to verify a specific fact, figure, or status.

확인해 보겠습니다 = verify something specific that exists (a document, a figure, an order status). 알아보겠습니다 = investigate or find out something unknown. Choosing wrong signals you don't know whether the info exists — use 확인 when you just need to check.
Chain into a follow-up: 확인하고 다시 말씀드리겠습니다 / 확인 후 연락드리겠습니다. For a question: 확인해 드릴까요? ('Shall I check for you?'). For casual team chat: 확인해 볼게요.

Dropping 보다: 확인하겠습니다 sounds curt and overconfident ('I will confirm it') rather than the softer service-minded 'let me check.' Also: using 알아보겠습니다 when the info exists — that phrase implies it's unknown and you must hunt for it.

entries.english: I've sent you the email
entries.shortExplanation: 메일 보내 드렸어요 is a practical expression meaning "I've sent you the email".
entries.explanation: 메일 보내 드렸어요 (meil bonae deuryeosseoyo) means "I've sent you the email". Say it as one set phrase — for example 메일 보내 드렸어요. ("I sent you the email."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite with humble 드리다 — appropriate when the recipient outranks or is a client
반말, to a peer or junior — plain 보내다 with no humility
격식체, to a client, external partner, or in formal reporting

usagePhrases.ko: 방금 메일 보내 드렸어요. 확인 부탁드려요.
usagePhrases.romanization: banggeum meil bonae deuryeosseoyo. hwagin butakdeuryeoyo.
usagePhrases.en: I just emailed you — please check.
usagePhrases.note: Extension: '방금 (just now)' makes the notification timely and nudges the reader to look

examples.ko: 요청하신 자료 메일로 보내 드렸어요.
examples.romanization: yocheonghasin jaryo meillo bonae deuryeosseoyo.
examples.en: I've emailed you the materials you requested.
examples.note: Bare delivery notice for a specific request — 로 ('by email') specifies the channel

examples.ko: A: 파일 아직 못 받았어요. / B: 방금 다시 보내 드렸습니다. 혹시 스팸함 확인해 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: A: pail ajing mot badasseoyo. / B: banggeum dasi bonae deuryeotseumnida. hoksi seupaemham hwaginhae jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: A: I haven't received the file yet. / B: I just resent it. Could you check your spam folder?
examples.note: Two-person exchange: 드렸습니다 is the formal delivery notice; suggesting spam-check is practical follow-through

examples.ko: 회의록은 참석자분들께 메일 보내 드렸으니, 못 받으신 분은 말씀해 주세요.
examples.romanization: hoeuirogeun chamseokjabundeulkke meil bonae deuryeosseuni, mot badeusin buneun malsseumhae juseyo.
examples.en: I've emailed the minutes to all attendees — please let me know if you didn't receive them.
examples.note: Broader announcement to a group: 분들께 ('to all of you') and 보내 드렸으니 (causal, 'since I've sent') are natural in post-meeting messages

entries.nuance: 메일 보내 드렸어요 means 'I've sent you the email,' and the key is 드리다 — the humble form of 주다 meaning 'to give to someone above you.' When you send something to a boss, client, or senior, 보내 드리다 frames the act as 'doing it FOR them,' which is the expected register in Korean work culture. Using plain 보냈어요 to the same person sounds abrupt and slightly disrespectful. Koreans use the loanword 메일 in everyday speech far more than formal 이메일 or Sino-Korean 전자우편 — the latter appears mainly in legal or government documents. The nearest neighbor 전달해 드렸어요 means 'I forwarded/passed on' (from someone else), not 'I personally composed and sent'; use 보내 드렸어요 for original sends. The English-speaker trap is applying 드리다 with peers or friends, which sounds oddly servile — reserve it for someone you actually owe deference.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 드리다 for a peer ('친구한테 보내 드렸어요') — humble 드리다 is for someone above you; with friends say 보냈어요.
Saying 메일 보내 받았어요 by mixing send/receive — 받다 is 'receive'; to say you SENT it, it's 보내 드렸어요.
Overformalizing with 전자우편 in casual office talk — Koreans say 메일; save 전자우편 for very formal documents.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I sent [it] giving it to you (보내 + 드리다).' 실제: 'I've sent you the email' with built-in deference — 드리다 marks the recipient as outranking you, signaling 'I did this for your benefit.'

보내 드렸어요 (해요체 + humble) for coworkers above you and clients. 보내 드렸습니다 (격식체 + humble) in formal emails or when reporting to senior management. 보냈어요 (no humble) for a same-rank colleague. 보냈어 (반말) for a peer or junior. Never use 드리다 for a friend or equal.
전달해 드렸어요 = forwarded from a third party. 보내 드렸어요 = you personally composed/sent it. 공유해 드렸어요 = shared to a group channel or shared drive (not a direct send).
방금 보내 드렸어요 (just sent). 다시 보내 드릴게요 (I'll resend). 첨부해서 보내 드렸어요 (sent with attachments). 확인 부탁드려요 or 확인해 주시겠어요? follows naturally to prompt the reader.

Overusing 드리다 with peers or friends ('친구한테 보내 드렸어요') — sounds oddly formal and obsequious. 드리다 is for genuine upward deference. Conversely, forgetting 드리다 with a boss ('메일 보냈어요') comes across as flat or rude.

entries.english: I'll get back to you
entries.shortExplanation: 다시 연락드리겠습니다 is a practical expression meaning "I'll get back to you".
entries.explanation: "I'll get back to you" — that is 다시 연락드리겠습니다 (dasi yeollakdeurigetseumnida). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 다시 연락드리겠습니다. ("I'll contact you again."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 격식체, the standard business 'I'll get back to you' — obligatory when speaking to a client or senior
Polite-casual (해요체), to a coworker — same meaning, warmer and less stiff
반말, to a peer or junior

usagePhrases.en: I'll check and get back to you.
usagePhrases.note: Extension pairing the promise with a clear reason for the wait — the most common full-sentence form in Korean business

examples.ko: 확인 후 다시 연락드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: hwagin hu dasi yeollakdeurigetseumnida.
examples.en: I'll get back to you after I check.
examples.note: The standard close to a business call when you can't answer immediately — brief and complete

examples.ko: A: 일정 조정이 가능한가요? / B: 지금 바로 말씀드리기 어려워서요, 내부 확인 후 다시 연락드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: A: iljeong jojeongi ganeunghangayo? / B: jigeum baro malsseumdeurigi eoryeowoseoyo, naebu hwagin hu dasi yeollakdeurigetseumnida.
examples.en: A: Is it possible to adjust the schedule? / B: I can't say right now — I'll check internally and get back to you.
examples.note: Real business exchange: B gracefully buys time and commits to a follow-up without overpromising

examples.ko: 담당 부서와 논의한 뒤 늦어도 내일 오전까지는 다시 연락드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: damdang buseowa nonuihan dwi neujeodo naeil ojeonkkajineun dasi yeollakdeurigetseumnida.
examples.en: After discussing with the relevant department, I'll get back to you by tomorrow morning at the latest.
examples.note: Fuller professional commitment with a deadline — 늦어도 ('at the latest') sets a firm upper bound

entries.nuance: 다시 연락드리겠습니다 is the polished business phrase for 'I'll get back to you,' said to a client, customer, or senior. 연락드리다 fuses 연락하다 ('to contact') with humble 드리다, lowering yourself to honor the recipient, and -겠- signals a firm stated intention. The result is the single most expected phrase to close a Korean business call when you can't answer immediately. Drop the humility for peers (연락할게, 연락할게요) but never drop 드리다 toward a customer-facing situation. 다시 전화드리겠습니다 ('I'll call you back') is the nearest neighbor but pins you to a phone call; 연락 covers any contact channel — phone, text, email — so 연락드리겠습니다 is safer when you haven't decided the method. The name particle for the recipient is 께 when mentioned (부장님께 연락드리겠습니다), not 한테/에게 — that distinction is a register marker native speakers notice immediately.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 다시 연락하겠습니다 to a customer — it omits the humble 드리다; client-facing, use 다시 연락드리겠습니다.
Adding 당신에게 ('to you') — 당신 sounds cold or confrontational; Korean omits the obvious listener.
Using 다시 전화드리겠습니다 when you might email instead — that pins you to a phone call; 연락 keeps the channel open.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I will humbly contact [you] again (다시 + 연락드리다 + -겠-).' 실제: 'I'll get back to you' — a polite commitment to follow up, with 드리다 built in to honor the listener.

연락드리겠습니다 (격식 + humble) for clients and senior managers — this is the expected professional closure. 연락드릴게요 (해요체 + humble) with familiar coworkers. 연락할게 (반말) with peers. For the senior's name, always use 께: 부장님께 연락드리겠습니다, not 부장님한테.
다시 전화드리겠습니다 = I will call you back (phone only). 다시 연락드리겠습니다 = I will contact you again (any channel). 말씀드리겠습니다 = I will tell/inform you (one-directional message, not a return contact).
확인 후 연락드리겠습니다 (after checking). 오늘 안으로 연락드리겠습니다 (by end of day). 메일로 연락드리겠습니다 (will contact by email). Adding the channel or deadline makes the commitment concrete.

Saying 다시 연락하겠습니다 to a customer skips the deference — 드리다 is not optional here in client-facing Korean. Also: 당신에게 다시 연락하겠습니다 — using 당신 ('you') sounds confrontational; the listener is already implied, so omit it.

entries.english: Thanks for your hard work / Good work
entries.shortExplanation: 고생하셨습니다 is a practical expression meaning "Thanks for your hard work / Good work".
entries.explanation: 고생하셨습니다 (gosaenghasyeotseumnida) = "Thanks for your hard work / Good work". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 고생하셨습니다. ("Thank you for your hard work."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Thank you for your hard work.
usagePhrases.note: 격식체 honorific — said at the end of a task, project, or meeting to acknowledge effort
반말, said DOWN to a junior or to a close peer at the same level
Warmer polite version — 많다 ('much/a lot') amplifies the acknowledgment; natural in conversation

usagePhrases.en: Thanks for your hard work today too.
usagePhrases.note: Extension: 오늘도 ('today too') marks it as a recurring daily appreciation, standard at close of day

examples.ko: 오늘 정말 고생 많으셨습니다. 덕분에 잘 마무리됐어요.
examples.romanization: oneul jeongmal gosaeng maneusyeotseumnida. deokbune jal mamuridwaesseoyo.
examples.en: You really worked hard today. Thanks to you it wrapped up well.
examples.note: Standard end-of-project send-off with a follow-up: 덕분에 ('thanks to you') adds warm credit and is a natural companion to the acknowledgment

examples.ko: 다들 고생 많으셨어요. 오늘은 여기서 마무리하죠.
examples.romanization: dadeul gosaeng maneusyeosseoyo. oneureun yeogiseo mamurihajyo.
examples.en: Everyone worked really hard today — let's wrap it up here.
examples.note: Everyday team close at end of day: 다들 ('everyone') + 고생 많으셨어요 + wrap-up suggestion

examples.ko: A: 발표 잘 하셨어요. / B: 감사합니다. 팀원들이 도와줘서 잘됐어요. / A: 다들 고생하셨습니다.
examples.romanization: A: balpyo jal hasyeosseoyo. / B: gamsahamnida. timwondeuri dowajwoseo jaldwaesseoyo. / A: dadeul gosaenghasyeotseumnida.
examples.en: A: You presented well. / B: Thank you — the team helped a lot. / A: Great work everyone.
examples.note: A/B exchange after a presentation: shows how 고생하셨습니다 wraps the thread naturally, crediting all participants

entries.nuance: 고생하셨습니다 recognizes someone's effort and toil, and is the standard Korean sign-off after a workday, meeting, or completed project. 고생 (苦生) literally means 'bitter/hard life' or 'hardship,' so you're acknowledging the cost the effort had for them — it's more empathetic than simple 'well done.' The honorific -셨- with formal -습니다 makes it appropriate for peers and juniors; importantly, the direction of politeness in Korean means this phrase is most natural from peer-to-peer or senior-to-junior. Said to a company president or very senior executive, it can carry an unintended 'I'm evaluating your labor' tone, so upward to the very top, 감사합니다 is safer. The near-twin 수고하셨습니다 is slightly lighter — 수고 shares the hanja 受苦 but has shifted in modern usage to the lighter sense of 'effort / trouble taken,' without 고생's connotation of real hardship — and is arguably more common as a universal clock-out phrase. Don't use 고생하셨습니다 as a substitute for 감사합니다 ('thank you') after receiving a gift or kindness — it credits labor, not generosity.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 고생하셨습니다 to a much higher superior (e.g., the CEO) — it can sound like you're grading their work; use 수고하셨습니다 or 감사합니다 upward.
Using it to thank someone for a gift or favor — that calls for 감사합니다; 고생하셨습니다 credits hard work, not kindness.
Saying 고생하셨어 to a senior — that mixes 반말 stem with the situation; for a senior use the full honorific 고생하셨습니다 or 고생 많으셨어요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'You (honorably) underwent hardship (고생 + -셨-).' 실제: 'Thank you for your hard work' — an empathetic acknowledgment of the effort something cost the other person, not just a cheerleader's 'well done.'

고생하셨습니다 (격식, honorific) for peers and juniors in formal/professional settings. 고생 많으셨어요 (해요체 + warmer) in conversation. 고생했어 (반말) downward to juniors or close friends. With a very high superior, skip it and say 감사합니다.

수고하셨습니다 = near-identical but lighter in feel; 수고 implies 'effort' without the 'hardship' weight. 고생하셨습니다 has more emotional acknowledgment. Both should not be directed upward to a CEO or top executive — use 감사합니다 in those cases.
오늘도 고생하셨습니다 (daily close). 정말 고생 많으셨습니다 (stronger: 'you really worked hard'). 고생하셨어요 (spoken/casual polite). Combine with a reason: 이번 프로젝트 마무리하시느라 고생 많으셨습니다.
Using it as 'thank you' for a gift or favor — 고생하셨습니다 credits labor, not kindness; for a gift say 감사합니다. Also: 고생하셨어 to a senior mixes 반말 with the wrong direction — honorific form required.

entries.english: I'll head out first (leaving before others)
entries.shortExplanation: 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다 is a practical expression meaning "I'll head out first (leaving before others)".
entries.explanation: 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다 (meonjeo deureoga bogetseumnida) means "I'll head out first (leaving before others)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다. ("I'll head out first."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 격식체, the correct phrase to leave before seniors — 들어가다 ('go in/home') + 먼저 ('ahead of you') + humble softener

usagePhrases.en: I'm going to head out first.
usagePhrases.note: Polite-casual (해요체), to coworkers you're close with — still deferential but warmer
반말, to peers — 갈게 instead of 들어갈게 is common in casual use

usagePhrases.ko: 오늘 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다. 내일 뵙겠습니다.
usagePhrases.romanization: oneul meonjeo deureoga bogetseumnida. naeil boepgetseumnida.
usagePhrases.en: I'll head out first today. See you tomorrow.
usagePhrases.note: Extension pairing the exit with a formal farewell — the complete, culturally correct office departure

examples.ko: 그럼 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다. 수고하세요.
examples.romanization: geureom meonjeo deureoga bogetseumnida. sugohaseyo.
examples.en: Well then, I'll head out first. Keep up the good work.
examples.note: Standard departure formula: the exit phrase + 수고하세요 to those still working — both parts together are the expected pair

examples.ko: A: 일 끝났어요? / B: 네, 오늘 약속이 있어서요. 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다. 고생하셨습니다.
examples.romanization: A: il kkeunnasseoyo? / B: ne, oneul yaksogi isseoseoyo. meonjeo deureoga bogetseumnida. gosaenghasyeotseumnida.
examples.en: A: Done for the day? / B: Yes, I have plans. I'll head out first — thanks for your hard work.
examples.note: A/B exchange: B gives a brief reason and closes with 고생하셨습니다 — the natural, complete Korean office-exit sequence

examples.ko: 부장님, 오늘 집안일이 있어서 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다. 남은 업무는 내일 처리하겠습니다.
examples.romanization: bujangnim, oneul jibaniri isseoseo meonjeo deureoga bogetseumnida. nameun eommuneun naeil cheorihagetseumnida.
examples.en: Director, I have a family matter today so I'll head out first. I'll take care of the remaining work tomorrow.
examples.note: Fuller, deferential request when leaving early while the boss is still working — brief reason + reassurance

entries.nuance: 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다 is how you formally announce leaving the office before colleagues — especially seniors — who are still at their desks. 들어가다 literally means 'to go in/inside,' and in the context of commuting, it idiomatically means going home (returning inside one's own space). 먼저 ('first / before others') is the politeness signal: you're acknowledging that you're breaking ranks from the group, and the -아/어 보다 + -겠습니다 frame softens it to 'I'll be going ahead.' This phrase is essential in Korean office culture where leaving before the boss is socially sensitive. Without 먼저, you lose the deference that signals you know others are still working. The near-equivalent 먼저 가 보겠습니다 uses 가다 ('go away'); 들어가다 is warmer because it implies 'heading home,' whereas 가다 is more directionally neutral. The English-speaker error is 지금 떠나요 ('I'm leaving now'), which uses 떠나다, a verb for permanent or emotional departures — it's dramatic and sounds odd as a daily work exit.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 지금 떠나요 for clocking out — 떠나다 sounds like a permanent departure; for going home say 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다.
Omitting 먼저 when leaving before seniors — 먼저 marks the polite 'ahead of you' courtesy; without it you lose the deference.
Using 먼저 갈게 to a boss — that's 반말; with a senior say 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I will first try going in/home.' 실제: 'I'm heading out before everyone else' — 들어가다 is the idiomatic 'go home (go back inside),' and 먼저 marks the politeness of departing before others.

Use this whenever you leave before colleagues, especially seniors. 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다 (격식) is mandatory with a boss. 먼저 들어가 볼게요 (해요체) with close coworkers. 먼저 갈게 (반말) with peers. Always pair with 수고하세요 (to those still working) or 고생하셨습니다 (if they're done).

먼저 가 보겠습니다 = same meaning with 가다 ('go') instead of 들어가다 ('go in/home'). 들어가다 is the preferred choice because it idiomatically evokes going home, making it warmer and more specific. 지금 떠나요 sounds dramatic, like a permanent farewell.
Pair it with a reason: 약속이 있어서 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다. Close with 내일 뵙겠습니다 ('See you tomorrow'). For email/chat: 먼저 퇴근하겠습니다 ('I'll clock out first') is more formal.

지금 떠나요 — 떠나다 means leaving permanently or dramatically, not going home from work. The natural exit is 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다. Also: omitting 먼저 removes the courtesy signal — without it, it sounds like an abrupt announcement, not a respectful heads-up.

entries.english: Do you have a moment?
entries.shortExplanation: 잠깐 시간 괜찮으세요? is a practical expression meaning "Do you have a moment?".
entries.explanation: "Do you have a moment?" — that is 잠깐 시간 괜찮으세요? (jamkkan sigan gwaenchaneuseyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 잠깐 시간 괜찮으세요? ("Do you have a moment?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Honorific 괜찮으세요, approaching a senior or anyone you want to address politely
반말, to a peer or junior
격식체, very formal — appropriate to a high superior or an important external meeting

usagePhrases.en: Do you happen to have a moment?
usagePhrases.note: 혹시 ('by any chance') softens the request and makes it easy for the other person to decline without awkwardness

examples.ko: 과장님, 잠깐 시간 괜찮으세요? 여쭤볼 게 있어서요.
examples.romanization: gwajangnim, jamkkan sigan gwaenchaneuseyo? yeojjwobol ge isseoseoyo.
examples.en: Manager, do you have a moment? I have something to ask.
examples.note: Everyday approach to a senior before a question — 여쭤보다 (humble form of 묻다) is the correct verb when asking a senior

examples.ko: A: 지금 바쁘세요? / B: 왜요? / A: 혹시 잠깐 시간 괜찮으세요? 회의 일정 관련해서 여쭤볼 게 있어서요.
examples.romanization: A: jigeum bappeuseyo? / B: waeyo? / A: hoksi jamkkan sigan gwaenchaneuseyo? hoeui iljeong gwallyeonhaeseo yeojjwobol ge isseoseoyo.
examples.en: A: Are you busy right now? / B: What is it? / A: Do you happen to have a moment? I wanted to ask about the meeting schedule.
examples.note: Two-person exchange: 혹시 softens the ask, and giving a topic upfront is the polite Korean way to 'prepare' the listener

examples.ko: 지금 바쁘시면 이따 다시 올게요. 혹시 잠깐 시간 괜찮으세요?
examples.romanization: jigeum bappeusimyeon itta dasi olgeyo. hoksi jamkkan sigan gwaenchaneuseyo?
examples.en: If you're busy now I'll come back later — do you by any chance have a moment?
examples.note: Shows the considerate add-on: offering to return later makes the question easier to answer, reducing pressure

entries.nuance: 잠깐 시간 괜찮으세요? is the standard polite opener for pulling someone aside for a conversation; 괜찮다 ('to be okay/fine') with honorific -으세요 asks whether now is convenient, and 잠깐 ('briefly') reassures them it won't take much time. The question checks timing and willingness — much gentler than 얘기 좀 해요 ('let's talk'), which assumes they're free. Adding 혹시 at the front makes it even more deferential by framing the approach as a tentative 'by any chance,' which is natural and expected in Korean workplaces. To a very high superior or external client, 잠시 시간 괜찮으십니까? with the formal -십니까 ending is the safest register. The closest neighbor 시간 있으세요? ('do you have time?') is more blunt, asking whether time EXISTS rather than whether NOW is convenient — 괜찮으세요? is the softer, more face-saving choice. English speakers often translate 'Can I talk to you?' as 얘기할 수 있어요?, which in Korean sounds like asking permission to literally be capable of speech, rather than checking availability.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'Can I talk to you?' as 말할 수 있어요? — that asks about ability to speak; the natural opener is 잠깐 시간 괜찮으세요?
Saying 잠깐 시간 괜찮아? to a manager — that's 반말; with a senior use 괜찮으세요? or formal 괜찮으십니까?
Dropping 잠깐/잠시 — without it the request sounds open-ended; 잠깐 reassures the person it'll be quick.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'Is [your] time briefly okay?' 실제: 'Do you have a moment?' — 괜찮다 checks whether NOW is convenient rather than directly demanding attention; it's a face-saving opener, not an interrogation.

괜찮으세요? (honorific, 해요체) for any senior or equal colleague. 괜찮으십니까? (격식) for very high superiors or formal external meetings. 괜찮아? (반말) for peers/juniors. Add 혹시 at the front to make declining even easier — this is expected and natural in Korean workplaces.

시간 있으세요? = 'Do you have time?' — more direct, asks about the existence of free time. 잠깐 시간 괜찮으세요? = 'Is now convenient for a moment?' — softer, checks willingness and timing. 얘기 좀 해요 = 'Let's talk' — assumes they're free and sounds more assertive.
혹시 지금 잠깐 시간 괜찮으세요? (now specifically). 잠깐 시간 내 주실 수 있어요? (slightly more deferential: 'could you spare a moment?'). Add a topic: 잠깐 시간 괜찮으세요? ___에 대해 여쭤볼 게 있어서요.
얘기할 수 있어요? — sounds like asking permission to physically speak. 시간 있어요? to a senior — skips the softening 괜찮다 and sounds blunt. Always use 잠깐 to reassure the person it'll be brief.

entries.english: When's the deadline?
entries.shortExplanation: 마감이 언제예요? is a practical expression meaning "When's the deadline?".
entries.explanation: 마감이 언제예요? (magami eonjeyeyo?) = "When's the deadline?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 마감이 언제예요? ("When's the deadline?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite (해요체), to a coworker, manager, or whoever owns the schedule — subject particle 이 marks the deadline as the topic
반말, to a peer or junior — particle often dropped in casual speech
격식체, in a formal meeting, email, or when addressing a client
Extension with 까지 ('by/until') — emphasizes the hard cutoff point rather than the named date

examples.ko: 이거 마감이 언제예요?
examples.romanization: igeo magami eonjeyeyo?
examples.en: When's the deadline for this?
examples.note: The direct question about a specific task — 이거 ('this') pinpoints which task without extra context

examples.ko: A: 기획서 마감이 언제예요? / B: 이번 주 금요일 오후 5시까지예요.
examples.romanization: A: gihoekseo magami eonjeyeyo? / B: ibeon ju geumyoil ohu 5sikkajiyeyo.
examples.en: A: When's the deadline for the proposal? / B: By 5 PM this Friday.
examples.note: Two-person exchange: B's answer uses 까지예요 ('by …') — the natural complete answer to a 마감 question

examples.ko: 이 건은 마감이 언제예요? 일정이 빠듯하면 미리 말씀해 주시면 조정해 볼게요.
examples.romanization: i geoneun magami eonjeyeyo? iljeongi ppadeutamyeon miri malsseumhae jusimyeon jojeonghae bolgeyo.
examples.en: When's the deadline on this? If the schedule's tight, let me know in advance and I'll try to adjust.
examples.note: Fuller exchange proactively offering flexibility — shows 마감이 언제예요? naturally opens a scheduling negotiation

entries.nuance: 마감이 언제예요? asks when a task or submission is due. 마감 is a native Korean word derived from the verb 막다 ('to close / block') and literally means 'closing / cutoff' — it is the natural everyday Korean word for deadline in both work and academic contexts. The subject particle 이 marks 마감 as the topic of the copula 언제예요 ('when is it') — this is why the particle must be 이/가, not 을/를, and the question is 마감이 언제예요? not 마감을 언제예요?. Drop to 마감 언제야? with peers. The close neighbor 언제까지예요? ('by when?') shifts focus to the final allowed moment rather than the named date; blending them as 마감이 언제까지예요? is very natural. The English loanword 데드라인 (deadline) exists in Korean but sounds imported and less natural in everyday office talk — Koreans say 마감. Adding 까지 after the answer (금요일까지예요 — 'by Friday') is the standard form for the reply, so learning both question and answer together helps.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 마감을 언제예요? — 언제예요 is 'when is it' with the copula, so use the subject particle: 마감이 언제예요?
Defaulting to the loanword 데드라인 — Koreans say 마감 in everyday office speech; 데드라인 sounds borrowed.
Writing 언제에요 — the copula after a vowel is 예요, so it's 언제예요, not 언제에요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'The closing/cutoff (마감) — when is it?' 실제: 'When's the deadline?' — 마감 is the precise Korean word for a closing or cutoff point, used for work tasks, applications, and publications alike.
마감이 언제예요? (해요체) for coworkers and managers. 마감이 언제입니까? (격식) in formal meetings or with clients. 마감 언제야? (반말) with peers. Use to clarify your own deadlines or negotiate when taking on a new task.

마감이 언제예요? = names the deadline date ('when is the cutoff?'). 언제까지예요? = 'by when?' — focuses on the latest acceptable moment. 제출 기한이 언제예요? = 'When is the submission period?' — more formal, used for official submissions.
마감이 언제까지예요? (adds 까지 for emphasis on the cutoff). 마감일이 언제예요? (마감일 = deadline date, more noun-explicit). The standard reply: [day/time] + 까지예요 ('by [day/time]').
마감을 언제예요? — 언제예요 is a copula ('when is it'), so the subject needs 이/가, never 을/를. Also: 데드라인이 언제예요? is understood but sounds borrowed; 마감 is the natural Korean word.

entries.english: I'll book the meeting room
entries.shortExplanation: 회의실 잡을게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll book the meeting room".
entries.explanation: 회의실 잡을게요 (hoeuisil jabeulgeyo) means "I'll book the meeting room". Say it as one set phrase — for example 회의실 잡을게요. ("I'll book the meeting room."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite (해요체), volunteering to a team or coworker — the casual-professional way to offer
반말, to peers or juniors
격식체, using the official verb 예약하다 — more formal, suitable for written communication

usagePhrases.en: I'll have the meeting room reserved in advance.
usagePhrases.note: Extension with -아 두다 ('do it and keep it ready') — stresses that you'll hold it ahead of time

examples.ko: 제가 회의실 잡을게요. 몇 시로 할까요?
examples.romanization: jega hoeuisil jabeulgeyo. myeot siro halkkayo?
examples.en: I'll book the room — what time shall I put it down for?
examples.note: Natural volunteer offer followed by a practical follow-up question — the combo is common in team coordination

examples.ko: A: 내일 3시에 회의 어때요? / B: 좋아요. 제가 회의실 잡을게요. / A: 감사합니다, 큰 방으로 부탁해요.
examples.romanization: A: naeil 3sie hoeui eottaeyo? / B: joayo. jega hoeuisil jabeulgeyo. / A: gamsahamnida, keun bangeuro butakaeyo.
examples.en: A: How about a meeting at 3 tomorrow? / B: Sounds good. I'll book the room. / A: Thanks — please get a big one.
examples.note: A/B exchange showing how the phrase naturally fits in meeting-setup coordination

examples.ko: 참석 인원이 많으니 큰 회의실로 잡을게요. 프로젝터도 미리 확인해 두겠습니다.
examples.romanization: chamseok inwoni maneuni keun hoeuisillo jabeulgeyo. peurojekteodo miri hwaginhae dugetseumnida.
examples.en: Since there are a lot of attendees, I'll book the big room — I'll check the projector in advance too.
examples.note: Fuller logistics message: room booking + equipment prep, showing how 잡을게요 anchors a practical action chain

entries.nuance: 회의실 잡을게요 means 'I'll book/grab the meeting room' and uses 잡다, which literally means 'to grab/catch' but has become the natural conversational verb for securing a room, time slot, or table. -ㄹ게요 expresses your own voluntary commitment — it's 'I'll do it' as a promise to the listener, not an instruction to someone else. To direct another person to book it, say 회의실 잡아 주세요. In formal writing or email, 예약하다 ('to reserve') is the correct official verb: 회의실 예약하겠습니다. In speech, 잡다 is overwhelmingly preferred in Korean offices — saying 회의실을 예약할게요 in a casual team chat is grammatically fine but sounds stiff. The variant 잡아 두다 (-아 두다 = 'do and keep') adds the sense of holding it in advance, useful when you're booking ahead of time to secure it. Object particle 을 (회의실을) can be added but is often dropped in natural speech.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 예약하다 in casual speech — it's correct but stiff; coworkers say 회의실 잡을게요 with 잡다.
Using -ㄹ게요 to direct someone else ('네가 회의실 잡을게요') — -ㄹ게요 states YOUR intention; to ask another person say 잡아 주세요.
Forcing the literal 'catch' sense elsewhere — 잡다 works for rooms, slots, and appointments, but for 'catch a bus' it's a different meaning; keep it to securing/reserving here.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I'll grab/catch the meeting room.' 실제: 'I'll book/reserve the meeting room.' 잡다 ('grab') has become the idiomatic conversational verb for securing any bookable slot or space — room, table, seat, or appointment.

잡을게요 (해요체) for spoken team coordination and chat messages. 잡을게 (반말) with close peers. 예약하겠습니다 (격식) in formal written communication. The -ㄹ게요 ending marks this as YOUR own promise; to ask someone else, use 잡아 주세요.

회의실 잡을게요 = conversational 'I'll grab a room' (spoken). 회의실 예약하겠습니다 = official 'I will make a reservation' (written/formal). 회의실 잡아 두겠습니다 = 'I'll reserve it in advance and hold it' (-아 두다 = proactive, advance preparation).
잡아 둘게요 (hold in advance). 잡아 놓을게요 (reserve ahead and leave it). 잡았어요 (I booked it — done). Time/size: 2시로 / 큰 방으로 잡을게요.

Using 예약하다 in casual spoken chat — it's correct but sounds stiff; 잡다 is what coworkers say. Also: 회의실 잡을게요 to someone you want to ask (not volunteer) — -ㄹ게요 means YOU will do it; to request someone else say 잡아 주세요.

entries.english: Please share the materials
entries.shortExplanation: 자료 공유해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please share the materials".
entries.explanation: "Please share the materials" — that is 자료 공유해 주세요 (jaryo gongyuhae juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 자료 공유해 주세요. ("Please share the materials."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite (해요체) request, to a coworker — standard for casual internal requests
반말, to a peer or junior

usagePhrases.en: I would appreciate you sharing the materials.
usagePhrases.note: 격식체, the standard polite-formal email phrasing — noun 공유 + 부탁드립니다 ('I request') is the email default
-주시겠어요? is even softer and more deferential than -주세요 — use when making a favor-like request of a senior

examples.ko: 회의 자료 공유해 주세요. 메일로 주시면 돼요.
examples.romanization: hoeui jaryo gongyuhae juseyo. meillo jusimyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: Please share the meeting materials — email is fine.
examples.note: Practical request specifying the channel so the recipient knows exactly how to fulfill it

examples.ko: A: 오늘 발표 자료 있어요? / B: 네, 지금 공유해 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul balpyo jaryo isseoyo? / B: ne, jigeum gongyuhae deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: Do you have today's presentation materials? / B: Yes, I'll share them with you now.
examples.note: A/B exchange: B uses 공유해 드릴게요 (humble 드리다) to honor A, showing how register shifts when offering to share upward

examples.ko: 다음 회의 전에 관련 자료 미리 공유해 주시면 검토하고 가겠습니다.
examples.romanization: daeum hoeui jeone gwallyeon jaryo miri gongyuhae jusimyeon geomtohago gagetseumnida.
examples.en: If you could share the relevant materials before the next meeting, I'll review them beforehand.
examples.note: Fuller professional request with a clear purpose — the conditional -면 ('if you…') is a polite non-demanding frame

entries.nuance: 자료 공유해 주세요 means 'please share the materials/data' and is the go-to office request for documents, files, or reference information. 자료 covers materials, data, and reference documents of any kind. 공유하다 ('to share') is the standard verb, carrying the sense of making something accessible to others — implying a shared channel, drive, or group chat rather than a one-on-one file transfer. -아/어 주세요 makes it a polite 'please do this for me' request. The nearest alternative 보내 주세요 ('please send it') is person-to-person sending; 공유하다 implies broader, group-wide access — pick 공유 for team distributions or shared-drive uploads, and 보내다 for one-to-one delivery. In email, the noun form 자료 공유 부탁드립니다 is more common and natural than the verb form. The critical English-speaker trap: 나누다 ('divide/split') is the Korean word for the action of physically splitting something into portions; translating 'share information' as 자료를 나눠 주세요 suggests you want the documents cut in half, not distributed.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'share' as 나누다 ('자료 나눠 주세요') — 나누다 means split/divide; for sharing information use 공유하다.
Using 보내 주세요 when you mean group access — 보내다 is one-to-one sending; for team-wide sharing say 공유해 주세요.
Dropping the verb politeness ('자료 공유') as a standalone command — add -해 주세요 or, in email, 공유 부탁드립니다 to stay polite.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'Please share (make common/공유하다) the materials for me.' 실제: 'Please share the files/data' — 공유하다 (共有, 'co-possess') implies making something available to a group, not just handing one copy to one person.
공유해 주세요 (해요체) for spoken or chat requests. 공유 부탁드립니다 (격식 noun form) for email — this is the most common email phrasing. 공유해 줘 (반말) for peers. 공유해 주시겠어요? for a more deferential ask of a senior.

공유해 주세요 = share to a group or make accessible broadly. 보내 주세요 = send directly to one person. 전달해 주세요 = pass on/forward (from a third party to others). Choose by distribution scope: one-to-one → 보내다; one-to-many → 공유하다.
공유해 드릴게요 (I will share it with/for you — humble). 공유받았어요 (I received the shared file). 미리 공유해 주세요 (please share in advance). In email sign-offs: 확인 부탁드립니다 naturally follows 공유해 드렸습니다.
나눠 주세요 — 나누다 means 'divide/split into portions,' not share information. 자료를 나눠 주세요 sounds like you want the files cut up. For sharing information, always 공유해 주세요.

entries.english: Want to grab lunch together?
entries.shortExplanation: 점심 같이 드실래요? is a practical expression meaning "Want to grab lunch together?".
entries.explanation: 점심 같이 드실래요? (jeomsim gachi deusillaeyo?) = "Want to grab lunch together?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 점심 같이 드실래요? ("Would you like to have lunch together?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Would you like to have lunch together?
usagePhrases.note: Honorific 드시다, to a senior or coworker you want to address politely — the standard workplace invite
반말, to a peer or junior — 먹다 with plain -ㄹ래?

usagePhrases.en: Would you care to have lunch together?
usagePhrases.note: 격식체, more formal invitation — 하다 is less direct about eating and sounds slightly elevated

usagePhrases.en: Want to have lunch together later?
usagePhrases.note: Extension with 이따 ('later') to set it up in advance — natural when planning mid-morning

examples.ko: 점심 드셨어요? 아직이면 같이 드실래요?
examples.romanization: jeomsim deusyeosseoyo? ajigimyeon gachi deusillaeyo?
examples.en: Have you had lunch? If not, want to eat together?
examples.note: Shows the difference between 드셨어요? (care question: 'have you eaten?') and 드실래요? (invitation: 'want to eat together?') in the same breath

examples.ko: A: 오늘 점심 계획 있어요? / B: 아직 없는데요. / A: 그럼 같이 드실래요? 근처에 새로 생긴 데 가 보려고요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul jeomsim gyehoek isseoyo? / B: ajik eopsneundeyo. / A: geureom gachi deusillaeyo? geuncheoe saero saenggin de ga boryeogoyo.
examples.en: A: Any lunch plans today? / B: Not yet. / A: Want to join then? I was going to try that new place nearby.
examples.note: Natural two-person exchange: checking availability first before the actual invite is the polite Korean sequence

examples.ko: 새로 생긴 식당 가 보려고 하는데, 점심 같이 드실래요? 좋은 분들이랑 가면 더 좋을 것 같아서요.
examples.romanization: saero saenggin sikdang ga boryeogo haneunde, jeomsim gachi deusillaeyo? joeun bundeurirang gamyeon deo joeul geot gataseoyo.
examples.en: I'm thinking of trying the new restaurant — want to come for lunch? It'd be nicer to go with good company.
examples.note: Fuller invitation giving a reason and a social reason — 분들이랑 ('with [honorific] people') is a warm, natural add-on

entries.nuance: 점심 같이 드실래요? invites a colleague or senior to eat lunch together. The key grammar: 드시다 is the honorific form of 먹다 ('eat'), and -ㄹ래요? is the friendly 'would you like to?' — the combination shows both deference and warmth. The most important distinction to know: 점심 드셨어요? ('have you eaten?') is a Korean greeting expression, NOT an invitation to eat together — it means 'I care about whether you've had lunch' and does not mean 'let's eat.' Confusing them is very common among English speakers. Use 드실래요? when you actually want to share a meal. With a peer, drop to 먹을래? For extra formality, 같이 하시겠어요? (using 하다 instead of the eating verb) is slightly elevated. English speakers wrongly use plain 먹다 with an honorific listener ('점심 같이 먹을래요?' to a boss) — the verb needs to honor them, so 드실래요? is required. Textbook Korean 먹기 원해요? ('do you want to eat?') sounds unnatural; no Korean adult uses it for a lunch invite.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using plain 먹다 to a senior ('점심 같이 먹을래요?') — honor the listener with 드시다: 점심 같이 드실래요?
Confusing it with 점심 드셨어요? — that asks IF they ate (a greeting), not an invitation; to invite, use 드실래요?
Saying 점심 먹기 원해요? — literal 'want to eat' is unnatural; the everyday invite is 같이 드실래요? or 먹을래?

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'Would [you] honorably eat lunch together?' 실제: 'Want to grab lunch together?' — 드시다 (honorific 먹다) + -ㄹ래요? makes this a warm, respectful invitation, not a command.

드실래요? (honorific + 해요체) for any senior or colleague you address politely. 같이 하시겠어요? (more formal) for a business associate or high superior. 먹을래? (반말) for peers or friends. Adding the person's name/title upfront (과장님, 같이 드실래요?) sounds more natural and inviting.

점심 드셨어요? = 'Have you eaten?' — a care/greeting question, NOT an invitation. 점심 같이 드실래요? = an actual invitation to eat together. Never use 드셨어요? when you mean to invite; use 드실래요? Mixing these is the #1 mistake.
오늘 점심 약속 없으시면 같이 드실래요? ('If you don't have plans…'). 이따 점심 같이 드실래요? (advance invite). After acceptance: 어디 가실래요? ('Where would you like to go?').
점심 같이 먹을래요? to a boss — plain 먹다 fails to honor the senior; use 드시다. Saying 점심을 같이 먹기 원해요? — textbook but unnatural; no Korean says this as a lunch invite.

entries.english: Could you help me out a bit?
entries.shortExplanation: 좀 도와주실 수 있을까요? is a practical expression meaning "Could you help me out a bit?".
entries.explanation: 좀 도와주실 수 있을까요? (jom dowajusil su isseulkkayo?) means "Could you help me out a bit?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 좀 도와주실 수 있을까요? ("Could you help me out a bit?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Could you help me out a bit?
usagePhrases.note: Honorific + tentative (-을까요?), the most polite and face-saving way to ask for a favor at work
반말, to a peer or junior — plain -ㄹ 수 있어?

usagePhrases.en: Might you be able to help?
usagePhrases.note: 격식체, very formal/deferential — double honorific -시- + -신가요? for high superiors or clients

usagePhrases.ko: 혹시 이것 좀 도와주실 수 있을까요?
usagePhrases.romanization: hoksi igeot jom dowajusil su isseulkkayo?
usagePhrases.en: Could you perhaps help me with this?
usagePhrases.note: 혹시 ('by any chance') + 이것 pinpoints the specific task and gives the person an easy out

examples.ko: 바쁘실 텐데, 혹시 이것 좀 도와주실 수 있을까요?
examples.romanization: bappeusil tende, hoksi igeot jom dowajusil su isseulkkayo?
examples.en: You must be busy, but could you perhaps help me with this?
examples.note: The most natural considerate form: acknowledging their busyness upfront softens the ask considerably

examples.ko: A: 엑셀 수식이 잘 안 되는데, 좀 도와주실 수 있을까요? / B: 네, 잠깐 볼게요. 어디서 막히셨어요?
examples.romanization: A: eksel susigi jal an doeneunde, jom dowajusil su isseulkkayo? / B: ne, jamkkan bolgeyo. eodiseo makisyeosseoyo?
examples.en: A: I'm having trouble with an Excel formula — could you help me out? / B: Sure, let me take a look. Where are you stuck?
examples.note: Real exchange: B accepts with 볼게요 and immediately asks a clarifying question — the natural helpful response pattern

examples.ko: 바쁘신데 죄송하지만, 자료 정리 좀 도와주실 수 있을까요? 혼자 하기엔 양이 많아서요.
examples.romanization: bappeusinde joesonghajiman, jaryo jeongni jom dowajusil su isseulkkayo? honja hagien yangi manaseoyo.
examples.en: Sorry to bother you when you're busy, but could you help me organize the materials? There's too much for me alone.
examples.note: Fuller considerate request: apology up front, request, reason — the complete polite Korean help-request formula

entries.nuance: 좀 도와주실 수 있을까요? is the most polite way to ask a coworker or senior for help, and every element is load-bearing: 좀 (shortened 조금, 'a bit') downgrades the imposition; 도와주다 ('help, do it for the listener'); -시- honorific raises the subject; -ㄹ 수 있다 frames it as ability rather than demand; and -을까요? is the gentlest possible sentence-end ('I wonder if…'). Remove any one of these and the request immediately sounds blunter. The nearest alternative 도와주세요 ('help me') is a direct imperative — fine in urgent or simple cases, but for a favor that costs effort or time, the -ㄹ 수 있을까요? frame is far more considerate. A slightly softer variant is 도와주실 수 있으실까요? (double -시-), but that can sound over-formal. The English pitfall: saying 도와줄 수 있어요? to a senior uses plain stem rather than the honorific -시- and sounds too direct. Dropping 좀 also makes the request feel abrupt, as if you're owed the help.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Omitting 좀 — without this softener the request sounds blunt; 좀 도와주실 수 있을까요? is the polite norm.
Using plain 도와줄 수 있어요? to a senior — add the honorific -시-: 도와주실 수 있을까요?
Defaulting to the bare imperative 도와주세요 for a big favor — it's direct; the tentative 도와주실 수 있을까요? is more courteous.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'A bit (좀), help-give me (도와주다), would [you] honorably be able to (수 있을까요)?' 실제: 'Could you help me out a bit?' — every softening layer is intentional; together they make the request easy to decline without embarrassment.

도와주실 수 있을까요? (honorific + tentative) for seniors and anyone you need to address politely. 도와줄 수 있어? (반말) for peers. 도와주실 수 있으신가요? (격식, double honorific) for very formal situations or high superiors. Never omit 좀 — it's the main politeness softener.

도와주세요 = direct imperative 'help me' — fine for quick, easy requests. 좀 도와주실 수 있을까요? = face-saving tentative request — better for larger favors that take the other person's time. 혹시 도움이 필요하시면 말씀해 주세요 = 'Let me know if you need help' — offering help rather than requesting it.
혹시 [task] 좀 도와주실 수 있을까요? adds 혹시 for extra tentativeness. Add context: [reason] + 도와주실 수 있을까요? — a reason acknowledges the imposition. After: 감사합니다 / 덕분에 잘 됐어요 ('Thanks to you it worked out well').

도와줄 수 있어요? to a senior — plain stem instead of honorific -시- sounds flat. Dropping 좀 — the request immediately sounds blunt and entitled. 도와주세요 for a big favor — that's the imperative; use the tentative -을까요? frame instead.

entries.english: I hit 'like'
entries.shortExplanation: 좋아요 눌렀어요 is a practical expression meaning "I hit 'like'".
entries.explanation: 좋아요 눌렀어요 (joayo nulleosseoyo) means "I hit 'like'". Say it as one set phrase — for example 좋아요 눌렀어요 ("I hit 'like'"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; reporting you liked someone's post
반말, telling a friend
Asking viewers/followers to like (e.g. a creator's request)
Very casual slang; 박다 ('to ram') = liked enthusiastically

examples.ko: 방금 좋아요 눌렀어요.
examples.romanization: banggeum joayo nulleosseoyo.
examples.en: I just hit like.
examples.note: Reporting a simple completed action with 방금 ('just now')

examples.ko: A: 제 사진 봤어요? / B: 네, 좋아요 눌렀어요!
examples.romanization: A: je sajin bwasseoyo? / B: ne, joayo nulleosseoyo!
examples.en: A: Did you see my photo? / B: Yes, I liked it!
examples.note: Classic two-person exchange; 눌렀어요 confirms the tap was done

examples.ko: 구독하고 좋아요 눌러 주세요!
examples.romanization: gudokago joayo nulleo juseyo!
examples.en: Please subscribe and hit like!
examples.note: The set creator-request phrase; 구독 ('subscribe') pairs with 좋아요

entries.nuance: 직역하면 '좋아요'는 '(it) is good' 또는 '(I) like it'이라는 완성된 문장이지만, 모든 한국 플랫폼(인스타그램, 유튜브, 카카오스토리, 네이버)에서 하트나 엄지 버튼을 가리키는 고정 명사로도 쓰여요. 따라서 좋아요 눌렀어요 = '(나는) 좋아요(버튼)를 눌렀다'는 뜻이에요. 버튼을 누르는 것이라 동사는 반드시 누르다를 써야 하고, 하다나 치다는 틀려요. 친한 친구한테는 좋아요 박았어요처럼 박다(세게 꽂다)를 써서 '엄청 좋아요를 눌렀다'는 뉘앙스를 줄 수 있어요. 가장 중요한 함정: 좋아요(버튼 누르기) vs 좋아해요(감정, 좋아하다의 현재형) — 당신 게시물에 좋아요 눌렀어요는 버튼 클릭이고, 당신을 좋아해요는 낭만적 감정 표현이라 완전히 달라요. 비공개 계정에는 좋아요를 누를 수 없으니 상황도 체크해야 해요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 좋아요 했어요 ('I did a like').
Korean treats the like as a button you PRESS, so the verb is 누르다, not 하다. Correct: 좋아요 눌렀어요.
Saying 좋아했어요 to mean 'I liked your post'.
좋아했어요 is past-tense of the FEELING 좋아하다 ('I used to like it'). For the button action say 좋아요 눌렀어요.
Saying 좋아요 쳤어요 by analogy with 'hit like'.
치다 ('to hit/strike') is wrong for a button. Koreans 누르다 (press) a button: 좋아요 눌렀어요, or casually 좋아요 박았어요.

structuredNuance.t: '좋아요' literally means 'it is good / I like it' (좋다 + polite 요), a complete polite sentence. But on every Korean platform it doubles as the FIXED NOUN for the like button itself — the heart or thumb. So 좋아요 눌렀어요 = 'I pressed [the] 좋아요 [button]'. The action verb is 누르다 ('to press a button'), never 하다 or 치다.

Used in any SNS context: telling a friend you liked their post, asking followers to tap the button, or reacting to content. With strangers or content creators, keep the polite -았어요 form (좋아요 눌렀어요). Among close friends drop to 반말: 좋아요 눌렀어. Young people use the slang 좋아요 박았어요 (박다 = 'to ram in') for enthusiastic likes — fine with peers, odd with a brand account.

좋아요 눌렀어요 (button action) vs 좋아해요 (the FEELING, 좋아하다 present tense). '당신을 좋아해요' means 'I have feelings for you' — romantic — while '좋아요 눌렀어요' is just the tap. 좋아했어요 (past of 좋아하다) means 'I used to have that feeling', nothing to do with the button.

English speakers directly translate 'I liked it' as 좋아했어요, which is past tense of the FEELING 좋아하다 and has no connection to the like button. For the button action the only natural phrase is 좋아요 눌렀어요. Also, 좋아요 했어요 ('I did a like') is wrong — the verb is 누르다, not 하다.

entries.english: I'll follow you
entries.shortExplanation: 팔로우할게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll follow you".
entries.explanation: "I'll follow you" — that is 팔로우할게요 (pallouhalgeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 팔로우할게요 ("I'll follow you"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; announcing you'll follow their account
반말, to a friend
맞팔 = mutual follow; common request between users
Asking someone to follow your account

examples.ko: 계정 알려 주세요, 팔로우할게요.
examples.romanization: gyejeong allyeo juseyo, pallouhalgeyo.
examples.en: Tell me your account, I'll follow you.
examples.note: Chain 계정 알려 주세요 ('tell me your account') then the action

examples.ko: A: 저 팔로우했어요. / B: 아, 맞팔 가능해요?
examples.romanization: A: jeo pallouhaesseoyo. / B: a, matpal ganeunghaeyo?
examples.en: A: I followed you. / B: Oh, can we follow each other?
examples.note: Typical exchange after discovering someone; 맞팔 가능해요 = follow-back request

examples.ko: 팔로워 천 명 넘었어요!
examples.romanization: pallowo cheon myeong neomeosseoyo!
examples.en: I passed a thousand followers!
examples.note: 팔로워 ('follower') is the person; note it differs from the act 팔로우

entries.nuance: 팔로우는 영어 'follow'의 한국어 표기로, SNS에서 '팔로우(하다)'는 팔로우 행위 자체, '팔로워'는 나를 팔로우하는 사람을 뜻해요. 즉 직역하면 '나 팔로우할게요'는 '나 너를 팔로우(follow) 할(will do) 게요(polite volition)'예요. 핵심 구분: 팔로우 ≠ 팔로워 — 팔로우할게요(동사), 팔로워가 많아요(명사). 맞팔(맞+팔로우)은 서로 팔로우하는 것으로 한국 SNS의 인사 문화예요. 반대어는 언팔(언팔하다 = unfollow)이고, 더 강한 조치는 차단이에요. -ㄹ게요는 '내가 그렇게 할게'라는 의지·예고를 뜻해요. 친구한테는 팔로우할게라고 해도 돼요. 따라가다('물리적으로 뒤따르다')를 SNS에 쓰면 스토킹처럼 들리니 절대 쓰지 마세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 팔로워할게요 to mean 'I'll follow you'.
팔로워 is the NOUN for the person (a follower). The verb is 팔로우하다: 팔로우할게요.
Using 따라가다 for following on SNS.
따라가다 means physically tailing a person and sounds stalkerish. The platform sense is 팔로우하다: 팔로우할게요.
Saying 팔로우가 많아요 to mean 'I have many followers'.
The people are 팔로워. 'I have many followers' = 팔로워가 많아요. 팔로우 is the act, not the people.

structuredNuance.t: 팔로우할게요 = '팔로우(follow) + 할게요(I will do it, polite volition)' — a straightforward loan-verb. The critical split: 팔로우(하다) is the ACT of following, while 팔로워 is the PERSON who follows you. 팔로우할게요 = 'I'll follow you (the act)'; 팔로워가 많아요 = 'I have many followers (the people)'.

Said when you discover someone's account online and want to connect, or after a mutual introduction. -ㄹ게요 is polite first-person volition ('I'll do it, heads-up'). With friends use 팔로우할게. For a mutual follow-back, the fixed request is 맞팔해요 or 맞팔 가능해요?. The opposite of following is 언팔 (unfollow, 언팔했어요) and the harsher 차단 (block).

팔로우할게요 (I will follow = one-directional) vs 맞팔해요 (let's follow EACH OTHER = bilateral). The loanword 팔로워 is the noun for the person; never say 팔로워할게요 — that treats the noun as a verb. Don't use 따라가다 ('physically follow/tail') for SNS — it sounds like stalking.

The two big traps: (1) Using 팔로워 as a verb ('I'll 팔로워 you') — 팔로워 is only the noun for the follower-person, the verb is 팔로우하다. (2) Using 따라가다 ('to physically walk behind someone') for SNS following — it sounds like stalking; the platform sense is 팔로우하다 only.

entries.english: I'll send you a DM
entries.shortExplanation: 디엠 보낼게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll send you a DM".
entries.explanation: 디엠 보낼게요 (diem bonaelgeyo) = "I'll send you a DM". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 디엠 보낼게요 ("I'll send you a DM"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; you'll message them privately
반말, to a friend
Asking them to message you privately
Specifying the channel with -으로 ('via')

examples.ko: 자세한 건 디엠 보낼게요.
examples.romanization: jasehan geon diem bonaelgeyo.
examples.en: I'll DM you the details.
examples.note: 자세한 건 ('as for the details') routes private info to DM

examples.ko: A: 문의 있는데요. / B: 디엠 주세요, 바로 답해 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: munui inneundeyo. / B: diem juseyo, baro dapae deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: I have an inquiry. / B: DM me — I'll reply right away.
examples.note: Typical seller-to-buyer exchange routing contact to private channel

examples.ko: 공구 문의는 디엠 주세요.
examples.romanization: gonggu munuineun diem juseyo.
examples.en: For group-buy inquiries, DM me.
examples.note: Sellers route questions to DM; 디엠 주세요 = 'DM me'

entries.nuance: 디엠은 'DM(Direct Message)'의 한국어 음차로 '디-엠'이라 읽어요. 직역하면 '다이렉트 메시지를 보내겠습니다'이지만 실제로는 인스타그램·X 등에서 1:1 비공개 채팅을 시작하는 행동을 가리켜요. 보내다('전달하다')와 주다('주세요 형태로 상대에게 요청')가 자연스러운 동사예요. 채널을 표시할 때는 수단 조사 -으로(디엠으로)를 써야 해요. 디엠은 1:1 비공개인 반면, 댓글은 공개 댓글이에요. 카카오톡을 쓸 때는 카톡 보낼게요라고 해야 자연스러워요. 디엠 하다(디엠했어요)처럼 하다를 붙일 수도 있지만, 보내다/주다가 더 표준적이에요. 보내다(send) vs 받다(receive)를 혼동하면 방향이 반대가 되니 주의하세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 디엠 말할게요 ('I'll say a DM').
A message is sent, not 'said'. Use 보내다: 디엠 보낼게요, or 디엠 주세요 to ask them.
Confusing 디엠 (private) with 댓글 (public comment).
디엠 is a private direct message; 댓글 is a public comment under a post. For something private, say 디엠으로 보내 주세요, not 댓글로.
Saying 디엠 보냈어요 when you mean you received one.
보내다 is to send; 받다 is to receive. 'I got a DM' = 디엠 받았어요, not 보냈어요.

structuredNuance.t: 디엠 is the phonetic Korean spelling of the initials 'DM' (Direct Message), read 'dee-em'. 디엠 보낼게요 literally means 'I will send a DM' — the DM is the noun object and 보내다 ('to send') is the verb. The key point: it signals a PRIVATE one-to-one message on Instagram or X, as opposed to a public 댓글 (comment).

Used when someone needs private info (price, address, personal detail) that shouldn't be public. On sales posts you'll see 디엠 주세요 or 디엠으로 문의 주세요. -ㄹ게요 is polite ('I'll do it, heads-up'); with friends use 디엠 보낼게. When using KakaoTalk, say 카톡 보낼게요 instead — using 디엠 for KakaoTalk sounds off.

디엠 (private, one-to-one on SNS) vs 댓글 (public comment under a post) vs 문자/메시지 (SMS text). For KakaoTalk specifically, 카톡 보낼게요 is the natural phrase; 디엠 is reserved for Instagram/X. Also: 보내다 (send, you give it out) vs 받다 (receive, it comes to you) — 디엠 받았어요 = 'I GOT a DM', the opposite direction from 디엠 보냈어요.

The main pitfalls: (1) Writing 'DM' in Latin letters in Korean speech/text — always romanize as 디엠. (2) Saying 디엠 말할게요 ('I'll say a DM') — a message is sent (보내다), not 'said'. (3) Confusing 보내다 (send) with 받다 (receive) and saying 디엠 보냈어요 when you mean you got one — that should be 디엠 받았어요.

entries.english: Please leave a comment
entries.shortExplanation: 댓글 달아 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please leave a comment".
entries.explanation: 댓글 달아 주세요 (daetgeul dara juseyo) means "Please leave a comment". Say it as one set phrase — for example 댓글 달아 주세요 ("Please leave a comment"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; inviting people to comment
반말, to a friend
남기다 ('to leave behind') variant, slightly more formal

usagePhrases.en: Let me know in the comments
usagePhrases.note: Routing replies to the comment section with -로

examples.ko: 궁금한 거 있으면 댓글 달아 주세요.
examples.romanization: gunggeumhan geo isseumyeon daetgeul dara juseyo.
examples.en: If you have questions, leave a comment.
examples.note: -으면 ('if') invites comments conditionally

examples.ko: A: 여기 맛있어요? / B: 네! 댓글로 후기 남겨 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: yeogi masisseoyo? / B: ne! daetgeullo hugi namgyeo deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: Is it tasty there? / B: Yes! I'll leave a review in the comments.
examples.note: 댓글로 routes the reply to the comment section; 후기 = review

examples.ko: 악플 말고 선플 달아 주세요.
examples.romanization: akpeul malgo seonpeul dara juseyo.
examples.en: Please post kind comments, not hateful ones.
examples.note: Contrast 악플 ('hate comment') with 선플 ('kind comment')

entries.nuance: 댓글은 게시물이나 영상 아래 달리는 공개 댓글이에요. 핵심 동사는 달다로, '걸다/붙이다'처럼 무언가를 게시물에 '매달다'는 뉘앙스예요(직역: 'to hang/attach'). 댓글 달아 주세요는 '댓글을 달아주세요'의 압축형이에요. 남기다('두고 가다')도 비슷하지만 약간 더 격식 있어요. 대댓글이나 답글은 댓글에 달리는 답변이에요. 문화적으로 중요한 단어: 악플(악성 댓글, hate comment) vs 선플(선한 댓글, kind comment). 댓글 쓰다('쓰다'로 글을 쓰다)는 어색하진 않지만 원어민은 달다/남기다를 훨씬 많이 써요. 디엠은 비공개이고 댓글은 공개라는 점이 핵심 차이예요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 댓글 써 주세요 by translating 'write a comment'.
Korean ATTACHES a comment: 댓글 달다. Say 댓글 달아 주세요 or 댓글 남겨 주세요; 쓰다 fits a full post, not a comment.
Using 코멘트 instead of 댓글.
The everyday word is the native-style 댓글. 코멘트 sounds like jargon. Say 댓글 달아 주세요.
Confusing 댓글 (comment) with 답글 (reply).
A 댓글 is a top-level comment; a 답글 (or 대댓글) is the reply to one. 'I replied to your comment' = 답글 달았어요.

structuredNuance.t: 댓글 달아 주세요 = '댓글 (a comment) + 달아 주세요 (please hang/attach it for me)'. 달다 literally means 'to hang/attach something' — a comment is conceptualized as something you ATTACH to a post, not just write. This is why natives say 달다 or 남기다 ('leave behind'), not 쓰다 ('write'), for comments specifically.

Used by creators inviting interaction, sellers soliciting feedback, or anyone wanting a reply. 달아 주세요 is the standard polite request; friends get 달아 줘. 댓글로 알려 주세요 ('let me know in the comments') routes the answer publicly. Note: -로 here is the channel particle ('through/via comments'), so you could say 디엠으로 알려 주세요 for a private reply instead.

댓글 달아 주세요 (public comment under a post) vs 디엠 주세요 (private message to you) vs 후기 남겨 주세요 (leave a review/rating). Also: 댓글 (top-level comment) vs 답글/대댓글 (reply to a comment). Don't say 코멘트 — the native word 댓글 is standard. 악플 (hate comment) vs 선플 (kind comment) are culture-specific terms you'll see constantly.

The main English-speaker mistake is using 쓰다 ('to write'): 댓글 써 주세요 is understandable but not idiomatic. Natives strongly prefer 달다/남기다 for comments. Also, don't say 코멘트 — that sounds like borrowed jargon; the everyday word is 댓글. And confusing 댓글 (comment) with 답글 (reply to a comment) will make your sentence mean the wrong thing.

entries.english: Please send me the link
entries.shortExplanation: 링크 보내 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please send me the link".
entries.explanation: "Please send me the link" — that is 링크 보내 주세요 (ringkeu bonae juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 링크 보내 주세요 ("Please send me the link"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; asking for a URL
반말, to a friend
걸다 ('to hang') = paste a clickable link somewhere
Telling someone to click through; 타고 들어가다 ('enter via')

examples.ko: 그 영상 링크 보내 주세요.
examples.romanization: geu yeongsang ningkeu bonae juseyo.
examples.en: Send me the link to that video.
examples.note: Name the thing (그 영상) then ask for its 링크

examples.ko: A: 어디서 살 수 있어요? / B: 프로필에 링크 걸어 놨어요, 타고 들어가세요.
examples.romanization: A: eodiseo sal su isseoyo? / B: peuropire ringkeu georeo nwasseoyo, tago deureogaseyo.
examples.en: A: Where can I buy it? / B: I've posted the link in my profile — click through it.
examples.note: Seller's typical answer; 링크 걸어 놨어요 = a standing link is already posted there

examples.ko: 링크 클릭하면 바로 신청돼요.
examples.romanization: ringkeu keullikamyeon baro sincheongdwaeyo.
examples.en: If you click the link, you can sign up right away.
examples.note: 클릭하다 ('to click') + 신청되다 ('gets applied')

entries.nuance: 링크는 'link'의 음차로 클릭 가능한 URL을 뜻해요. 상황에 따라 동사가 달라지는 게 핵심이에요: 누군가에게 보낼 때는 보내다(링크 보내 주세요), 공개 장소(프로필, 댓글)에 올릴 때는 걸다(링크 걸다 — 직역: 걸어두다/매달다), 클릭해서 들어갈 때는 클릭하다 또는 링크 타고 들어가다('링크를 타고 이동하다')예요. 보내다 vs 걸다의 차이: 보내다는 상대방에게 전달, 걸다는 공개 장소에 게시해 두는 것이에요. 링크 vs 주소: 주소는 URL 텍스트 그 자체, 링크는 클릭 가능한 연결이지만 일상 대화에서는 혼용돼요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 링크 줘 보내 (wrong word order).
Korean puts the verb last: 링크 보내 줘 (casual) / 링크 보내 주세요 (polite). The object comes before the verb.
Using 보내다 when you mean post a clickable link publicly.
보내다 sends it to a person. To embed a live link in a bio/comment, use 걸다: 링크 걸어 주세요.
