structuredNuance.t: 동물등록 (動物登錄) = 'animal registration' — the government-mandated registration of your dog. 해야 돼요 = 'I have to do it', expressing legal obligation. Registering links the pet's microchip/tag to your identity in the national database.

Polite-neutral 존댓말, exactly what you'd say to a vet, another owner, or at the 동사무소 (district office, one registration venue). In 반말 with a friend: 동물등록 해야 돼. It's a practical obligation topic, not sensitive.

내장칩 (internal microchip, permanent) vs. 인식표 (external ID tag on collar, can be lost). 과태료 (administrative fine for civil violations) vs. 벌금 (criminal/court fine) — pet registration non-compliance is 과태료. 등록하다 (register with a government body) vs. 가입하다 (join/subscribe to a service).
동물등록 is 動物登錄: 동물 (動物) = animal, 등록 (登錄) = registration/recording. The -하다 verb 등록하다 is the standard registration verb across many domains (학교 등록, 회원 등록, etc.).

Trap 1: 가입하다 for pet registration — 가입 is joining/subscribing to services; official government registration is 등록하다. Trap 2: thinking registration is optional for dogs — it is legally required in Korea. Trap 3: 벌금 for the fine — it's 과태료 (administrative), not a criminal 벌금.

entries.english: How much was the vet bill?
entries.shortExplanation: 진료비 얼마 나왔어요? is a practical expression meaning "How much was the vet bill?".
entries.explanation: "How much was the vet bill?" — that is 진료비 얼마 나왔어요? (jillyobi eolma nawasseoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 진료비 얼마 나왔어요? ("How much was the vet bill?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: How much was the vet bill?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; 진료비 = consultation/treatment fee

usagePhrases.en: How much is the exam fee?
usagePhrases.note: Asking the price up front
펫보험 = pet insurance; 들다 = to take out (insurance)
나오다 used for a bill 'coming out' to an amount

examples.ko: A: 동물병원 갔다 왔어요? / B: 네, 진료비 얼마 나왔어요? / A: 검사까지 해서 십오만 원 나왔어요.
examples.romanization: A: dongmulbyeongwon gatda wasseoyo? / B: ne, jillyobi eolma nawasseoyo? / A: geomsakkaji haeseo siboman won nawasseoyo.
examples.en: A: Did you go to the vet? / B: Yes — how much was the bill? / A: With the tests, it came to 150,000 won.
examples.note: A/B exchange showing 나오다 as the natural verb for a calculated bill amount

examples.ko: 검사까지 해서 십만 원 나왔어요.
examples.romanization: geomsakkaji haeseo simman won nawasseoyo.
examples.en: With the tests, it came to 100,000 won.
examples.note: 검사 = (medical) test; -까지 해서 = 'including ...'; 십만 원 = 100,000 won (count in 만-units)

examples.ko: 동물병원은 보험이 안 돼서 좀 비싸요.
examples.romanization: dongmulbyeongwoneun boheomi an dwaeseo jom bissayo.
examples.en: Vets are pricey since insurance doesn't apply.
examples.note: 보험이 안 되다 = insurance doesn't cover it — national health insurance is humans-only

entries.nuance: 진료비 = 'consultation / treatment fee' (診療費), the vet bill; the suffix -비 (費) is the Sino-Korean morpheme for 'fee/cost' seen in 교통비 (transport cost), 식비 (food cost), 병원비 (hospital bill). The natural, idiomatic verb for a bill is 나오다 ('to come out / be issued') — 얼마 나왔어요? = 'how much did it come out to?', the phrasing Koreans instinctively use for any calculated total. The nearest near-synonym question is 얼마였어요? ('how much was it?'), which is understandable but less specific for a tabulated bill — 나오다 is the verb that belongs here. Korean vet care is NOT covered by national health insurance (reserved for humans), so bills can surprise people; 펫보험 ('pet insurance') exists but you must 들다 / 가입하다 ('take it out / sign up') well in advance. The English-speaker trap is 가격 ('price tag of a product') for a service fee — for service bills/fees, use 비(용) or 진료비. Don't confuse 진료비 (exam/treatment fee) with 약값 ('medicine cost') — they may appear as separate line items. Currency: Korean amounts use Sino-Korean numbers + 원, counted in 만 (ten-thousands): 십만 원 = 100,000 won.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 가격 얼마예요? for a vet bill.
가격 is the price of goods. A service fee/bill is 진료비 or 비용: 진료비 얼마 나왔어요?
Saying 얼마였어요? for the total bill.
Understandable, but for a calculated bill Koreans say 얼마 나왔어요? ('how much did it come out to'). Use 나오다 for bills.
Assuming national insurance covers the vet.
건강보험 covers humans only; vet care isn't covered, so it's pricey. For coverage you need private 펫보험, taken out in advance.

structuredNuance.t: 진료비 (診療費) = consultation/treatment fee — the vet bill. 얼마 나왔어요? = 'how much did it come out to?' using 나오다 ('come out/be issued'), the standard verb for calculated bills. The phrase is asking about the final total after seeing the vet.
Polite-neutral 존댓말, perfect at the checkout desk, with another owner, or discussing vet costs. In 반말: 진료비 얼마 나왔어? It's a common, empathetic topic among pet owners as vet costs are high in Korea.

진료비 (exam/treatment fee) vs. 약값 (medicine cost) — may be separate items on the bill. 나오다 for a calculated bill total vs. 얼마예요? which asks the listed price upfront. 가격 is for the price tag on goods, not service fees. 건강보험 covers humans; for pets you need private 펫보험.
진료비 is 診療費: 진료 (診療) = examination and treatment, 비 (費) = cost/fee. The -비 morpheme appears in 교통비, 식비, 생활비, 병원비 — all meaning 'cost of X'.

Trap 1: 가격 얼마예요? for a vet bill — 가격 is the price of a product; service fees are 비(용) or 진료비. Trap 2: 얼마였어요? for a bill total — natural but less idiomatic; prefer 얼마 나왔어요? Trap 3: assuming national health insurance covers the vet — it covers humans only; vet care requires private 펫보험.

entries.english: Are pets allowed in here?
entries.shortExplanation: 여기 반려동물 출입 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Are pets allowed in here?".
entries.explanation: 여기 반려동물 출입 돼요? (yeogi ballyeodongmul churip dwaeyo?) = "Are pets allowed in here?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 반려동물 출입 돼요? ("Are pets allowed in?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; 출입 = entry/access

usagePhrases.en: Can I bring my dog in?
usagePhrases.note: 데리고 들어가다 = enter with (a pet)
애견 동반 = accompanied by a dog
동반 = accompanying; common signage

examples.ko: A: 저기요, 여기 반려동물 출입 돼요? / B: 네, 이동장에 넣으시면 돼요.
examples.romanization: A: jeogiyo, yeogi ballyeodongmul churip dwaeyo? / B: ne, idongjange neoeusimyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: A: Excuse me, are pets allowed here? / B: Yes, if it's in a carrier it's fine.
examples.note: A/B exchange showing the common condition (케이지/이동장); 이동장 = pet carrier

examples.ko: 반려동물 동반 가능한 카페 찾고 있어요.
examples.romanization: ballyeodongmul dongban ganeunghan kape chatgo isseoyo.
examples.en: I'm looking for a pet-friendly café.
examples.note: 동반 가능 = accompaniment possible (pet-friendly); common on app searches and signs

examples.ko: 여기는 케이지에 넣으면 출입 돼요.
examples.romanization: yeogineun keijie neoeumyeon churip dwaeyo.
examples.en: Here it's allowed if it's in a carrier.
examples.note: 케이지/이동장 = carrier; 넣다 = put (the pet) in; conditional permission is common indoors

entries.nuance: 반려동물 = 'companion animal' (반려 '伴侶' companion + 동물 animal), the modern respectful umbrella term for pets, now standard on signs, in apps, and in media — much warmer than the older 애완동물 ('plaything animal'). 출입 = 'entry / coming and going' (出入), so 출입 돼요? = 'is entry allowed?'; 동반 = 'accompanying', so 반려동물 동반 가능 = 'pets may accompany you' = pet-friendly, the exact wording on café and store signage. To say you bring your pet in, use 데리고 들어가다 ('go in WITH a living being') — the verb 데리다 marks the companion as living; 가지고 들어가다 ('bring an object in') for a dog sounds dehumanizing and odd. The nearest near-synonym question is 강아지 데리고 들어가도 돼요? ('may I go in with my dog?'), which is slightly more conversational; 출입 돼요? is more sign/formal in register. The English-speaker trap is 허락돼요? ('is it permitted?' from 허락 'personal permission/consent') — 허락 is for person-to-person permission, not public access rules; use 출입 돼요? or 들어가도 돼요?. 동반 sounds formal/sign-like; in speech, 강아지 데리고 가도 돼요? is the casual spoken version.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 허락돼요? for whether pets are allowed.
허락 is personal permission/consent. For public entry, ask 출입 돼요? or 들어가도 돼요?: 반려동물 출입 돼요?
Saying 강아지 가지고 들어가도 돼요?
가지고 (가지다) is for objects. For a living animal use 데리고: 강아지 데리고 들어가도 돼요?
Using 애완동물 on/about modern pet-friendly places.
Signs and polite speech use 반려동물 (companion animal). 애완동물 sounds dated; prefer 반려동물 동반.

structuredNuance.t: 반려동물 출입 돼요? literally means 'is pet entry/access permitted?' — 출입 (出入) = in-and-out access, 돼요? = is it okay/permitted? It's a polite public-space question. The phrase reflects real-world Korean access culture where many venues are 반려동물 동반 가능 (pet-friendly) or 금지 (prohibited).

Polite-neutral 존댓말, correct for asking staff at any venue. More casual spoken version: 강아지 데리고 들어가도 돼요? 동반 is the formal/sign register; 데리고 가다 is the everyday spoken register. With a friend: 강아지 데리고 가도 돼? (반말).

반려동물 출입 돼요? (formal/sign-style) vs. 강아지 데리고 들어가도 돼요? (everyday spoken). 반려동물 (modern, respectful) vs. 애완동물 (older, slightly dated). 데리고 (with a living being) vs. 가지고 (with an object) — the choice shows whether you're treating the animal as a companion or a thing.
출입 is 出入, 'going out and coming in' — used for access/entry to places. 반려 is 伴侶, 'companion/partner'. 동반 is 同伴, 'accompanying together'.

Trap 1: 허락돼요? for public access — 허락 is personal permission between people; for institutional access use 출입 돼요? or 들어가도 돼요? Trap 2: 강아지 가지고 들어가도 돼요? — 가지고 is for objects; use 데리고 for living companions. Trap 3: 애완동물 on formal inquiries — use 반려동물.

entries.english: It passed away (crossed the rainbow bridge)
entries.shortExplanation: 무지개다리 건넜어요 is a practical expression meaning "It passed away (crossed the rainbow bridge)".
entries.explanation: 무지개다리 건넜어요 (mujigaedari geonneosseoyo) means "It passed away (crossed the rainbow bridge)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 무지개다리 건넜어요 ("It crossed the rainbow bridge"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Gentle euphemism for a pet's death
Soft way to say a pet died
What you say to a grieving owner
펫로스 = pet loss (the grief)

examples.ko: A: 요즘 좀 힘들어 보여요. 무슨 일 있어요? / B: 우리 강아지가 지난주에 무지개다리 건넜어요.
examples.romanization: A: yojeum jom himdeureo boyeoyo. museun il isseoyo? / B: uri gangajiga jinanjue mujigaedari geonneosseoyo.
examples.en: A: You look a bit down lately. Is everything okay? / B: My dog crossed the rainbow bridge last week.
examples.note: A/B exchange showing how 무지개다리 건넜어요 is delivered as difficult news, gently

examples.ko: 많이 힘드시겠어요, 위로의 말 전해요.
examples.romanization: mani himdeusigesseoyo, wiroui mal jeonhaeyo.
examples.en: You must be hurting — my condolences.
examples.note: 위로의 말 = words of comfort; the appropriate response when you hear this news

examples.ko: 반려동물 장례식장도 있어요.
examples.romanization: ballyeodongmul jangnyesikjangdo isseoyo.
examples.en: There are pet funeral homes too.
examples.note: 장례식장 = funeral hall; pet funerals and cremation are now a real service in Korea

entries.nuance: 무지개다리(를) 건너다 = 'to cross the rainbow bridge', the same tender euphemism English uses, and the most common gentle way Koreans speak of a pet's death; 하늘나라(에) 가다 ('go to heaven/sky-country') is another soft option. You generally avoid the blunt 죽었어요 ('it died') when comforting a grieving owner — factually correct but cold; the euphemisms show respect for how deeply Koreans grieve pets. The nearest near-synonym expression is 하늘나라 갔어요, but 무지개다리 건넜어요 is the most recognized pet-specific phrase online and in communities. To express condolences: 많이 힘드시겠어요 ('you must be having a hard time') or 위로의 말 전해요 ('I offer words of comfort') are warm and appropriate. The formal funeral phrase 삼가 고인의 명복을 빌어요 (traditionally for people) is increasingly used for pets too — Koreans take pet grief seriously. The English-speaker trap is 잃어버렸어요 ('I lost it') to mean the pet died — 잃어버리다 means you misplaced or lost track of it (it ran away), a very different meaning that creates confusion. Another trap: 안락사 (euthanasia) is a heavy clinical word; don't blurt it as casual sympathy. This register is gentle 존댓말. Korea now has 반려동물 장례식장 ('pet funeral homes') and cremation services.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 죽었어요 bluntly to a grieving owner.
It's correct but cold. Use the gentle 무지개다리 건넜어요 or 하늘나라 갔어요 when comforting someone.
Saying 잃어버렸어요 to mean the pet died.
잃어버리다 = lost track of / misplaced (it ran away). For death, say 무지개다리 건넜어요, not 잃어버렸어요.
Blurting 안락사 as casual sympathy.
안락사 (euthanasia) is a heavy clinical term. Don't introduce it lightly; offer comfort: 많이 힘드시겠어요.

structuredNuance.t: 무지개다리(를) 건너다 literally means 'to cross the rainbow bridge' — 무지개 = rainbow, 다리 = bridge, 건너다 = to cross. This is the standard tender euphemism for a pet's death, shared across Korean and English pet culture. It softens the directness of 죽다 ('to die').

Gentle 존댓말, used when sharing or receiving news of a pet's death. Used in online communities (카카오톡, 인스타그램) and in person. If someone shares this, respond with 위로의 말 전해요 or 많이 힘드시겠어요 — never just change the subject. Pet grief (펫로스) is taken seriously in Korea.

무지개다리 건넜어요 (pet-specific, warmest) vs. 하늘나라 갔어요 (gentle, also used for people) vs. 세상을 떠났어요 (passed away, more formal, usually for people) vs. 죽었어요 (blunt, factual — avoid with grieving owners). 잃어버렸어요 ≠ died; it means you lost track of/misplaced the pet.
무지개다리 건너간 지 1년 됐어요 ('it's been a year since it crossed'), 사진 보면 아직도 보고 싶어요 ('I still miss it when I see photos'), 무지개다리 너머에서 잘 지내고 있을 거예요 ('it's probably doing well beyond the rainbow bridge').

Trap 1: 잃어버렸어요 to mean 'it passed away' — 잃어버리다 = lost/misplaced (it ran away); for death say 무지개다리 건넜어요. Trap 2: 죽었어요 to a grieving owner — correct but cold; use the euphemism. Trap 3: 안락사 as casual sympathy — it's a heavy clinical word; offer comfort instead: 많이 힘드시겠어요.

entries.english: Hello? (on the phone)
entries.shortExplanation: 여보세요? is a practical expression meaning "Hello? (on the phone)".
entries.explanation: "Hello? (on the phone)" — that is 여보세요? (yeoboseyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 여보세요? ("Hello?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말, neutral-polite; the default opening the moment anyone answers a call — stranger, elder, or customer-service line
Flat, non-rising intonation to a close friend whose unsaved number you just spotted on the screen; same word, same register, different tone
More formal/businesslike; leading with 네 before 여보세요 is common at work or with strangers to sound composed and attentive
Natural extension mid-call to test a silent or dropping line; the two-word combo makes the check explicit without sounding rude

examples.ko: A: (전화 받으며) 여보세요? / B: 아, 저 준혁인데요. 지금 통화 괜찮아요?
examples.romanization: A: (jeonhwa badeumyeo) yeoboseyo? / B: a, jeo junhyeogindeyo. jigeum tonghwa gwaenchanayo?
examples.en: A: (picks up) Hello? / B: Oh, it's Junhyeok. Is now a good time?
examples.note: A/B exchange showing the canonical opening pair: 여보세요? triggers the caller's self-introduction

examples.ko: 여보세요, 김민수 씨 휴대폰 맞으세요?
examples.romanization: yeoboseyo, gimminsu ssi hyudaepon majeuseyo?
examples.en: Hello, is this Kim Minsu's phone?
examples.note: Everyday use: verifying you reached the right person right after they pick up

examples.ko: 여보세요? 여보세요? 소리가 자꾸 끊겨요.
examples.romanization: yeoboseyo? yeoboseyo? soriga jakku kkeunkyeoyo.
examples.en: Hello? Hello? You keep cutting out.
examples.note: Fuller situation: repeating it as a line-check when a bad connection keeps dropping — shows how 여보세요 doubles as an attention-getter mid-call

entries.nuance: 여보세요 is the phone-only 'hello' — it derives from 여기 보세요 ('look here'), a call for attention, which is why it works as a mid-call line-check as well as an opener. Said to someone standing in front of you, it sounds like a sarcastic 'hello? anyone home?' or a joke, because in-person the greeting is 안녕하세요. The two are not swappable: 안녕하세요 asks after wellbeing; 여보세요 just opens the voice channel. Register sits at neutral-polite (the 세요 ending) — correct for strangers, elders, customer service, and bosses alike. Never clip it to 여보: between spouses 여보 means 'honey/darling', so it is bizarre and intimate to a stranger. The classic English-speaker error is using 여보세요 like 'hi' when meeting people in person; keep it strictly for phones.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 여보세요 to greet someone in person — it is phone-only; for meeting people say 안녕하세요.
Shortening it to 여보 to sound casual — 여보 alone means 'dear/honey' between a married couple, so it is bizarre to a stranger; keep the full 여보세요.
Translating 'hello, this is John' as 여보세요, 존이에요 and stopping — after 여보세요 Koreans usually add 안녕하세요 or 저 ...인데요 to introduce themselves.

structuredNuance.t: 여보세요 literally traces to '여기 보세요' — 'please look here' — a call for attention. On the phone that attention-getting function survives perfectly, which is why you can also use it mid-call as a line check ('hello? hello?'). It does NOT mean 'how are you' or 'hi'; it simply opens the audio channel.

Phone-only, neutral-polite (the -세요 ending). Correct for strangers, elders, customer service, and bosses. In person it sounds like a joke or a sarcastic snap — for face-to-face greetings the word is 안녕하세요.

안녕하세요 vs 여보세요: 안녕하세요 asks after wellbeing and is used in person; 여보세요 opens a voice channel on the phone. The two are not interchangeable. Also 네, 여보세요 (leading with 네) sounds more composed and businesslike.
여보세요 (standard) → 네, 여보세요 (formal/businesslike opener) → 여보세요, 들리세요? (mid-call line-check). Never clip to 여보 alone, which is the spousal term of address ('honey').
Using 여보세요 to greet someone in person — it is strictly phone-only; in person say 안녕하세요. Also: shortening to 여보 to sound casual sounds bizarre to a stranger because 여보 = 'honey' between spouses.

entries.english: Is now a good time to talk?
entries.shortExplanation: 지금 통화 괜찮으세요? is a practical expression meaning "Is now a good time to talk?".
entries.explanation: 지금 통화 괜찮으세요? (jigeum tonghwa gwaenchaneuseyo?) = "Is now a good time to talk?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 지금 통화 괜찮으세요? ("Is now okay to talk?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; polite check to an elder, boss, or anyone you respect — opening a call without asking first is considered slightly rude in Korean phone etiquette
반말 to a close friend or younger person — perfectly natural but only with someone you address as 반말

usagePhrases.en: Would it be possible to talk now?
usagePhrases.note: More formal/격식; 가능하실까요 adds extra deference — best for a first call to a stranger or an important client

usagePhrases.en: Do you have a minute to talk?
usagePhrases.note: Extension with 잠깐 signalling you will be brief — useful when you know the other person is busy

examples.ko: A: 여보세요, 지금 통화 괜찮으세요? / B: 네, 잠깐은 돼요.
examples.romanization: A: yeoboseyo, jigeum tonghwa gwaenchaneuseyo? / B: ne, jamkkaneun dwaeyo.
examples.en: A: Hello, is now a good time? / B: Yes, briefly I can.
examples.note: The classic A/B opener right after the other person picks up — B's 잠깐은 돼요 signals they're available but pressed

examples.ko: 팀장님, 지금 통화 괜찮으세요? 잠깐 보고드릴 게 있어서요.
examples.romanization: timjangnim, jigeum tonghwa gwaenchaneuseyo? jamkkan bogodeuril ge isseoseoyo.
examples.en: Sir, is now okay to talk? I have something brief to report.
examples.note: Work use: always check before launching into business with a senior; 보고드릴 게 있어서요 gives a gentle heads-up about purpose

examples.ko: 지금 통화 괜찮으세요? 혹시 운전 중이시면 이따 다시 걸게요.
examples.romanization: jigeum tonghwa gwaenchaneuseyo? hoksi unjeon jungisimyeon itta dasi geolgeyo.
examples.en: Is now a good time? If you're driving, I'll call back later.
examples.note: Fuller situation: offering a call-back shows consideration for the other person's circumstances — a mark of good phone manners

entries.nuance: 지금 통화 괜찮으세요? is the courteous gate-check that Korean phone etiquette expects before you launch into business — launching straight in without asking is considered mildly rude, especially toward elders, clients, or a boss. 통화 means specifically 'a phone call/conversation', so this phrase is not interchangeable with the face-to-face 지금 시간 괜찮으세요? ('do you have time now?'); the word 통화 names the medium. To go casual, drop to 통화 괜찮아? with a friend; to go formal, use 통화 가능하실까요?, which sounds more deferential and businesslike. The closest alternative 지금 전화해도 돼요? ('is it okay if I call now?') works but sounds like you already called while asking — 통화 괜찮으세요? is the cleaner, more natural idiom. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'can you talk?' as 말할 수 있어요?, which asks whether the person is physically capable of speech — wrong and bizarre; the idiom is built on 통화, not 말하다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 말할 수 있어요? for 'can you talk?' — that asks about the ability to speak; use 통화 괜찮으세요? for 'is it a good time to talk.'
Dropping 지금 in a context that needs it — without 지금 it can sound like a general request; add 지금 to mean 'right now.'
Using flat 통화 괜찮아? with a boss or client — that is 반말; raise it to 괜찮으세요? or 가능하실까요?.

structuredNuance.t: Literally '지금(now) 통화(phone call) 괜찮으세요?(is it okay)?' — the real function is a gate-check that says 'I respect your time, may I have it?' Korean phone etiquette treats skipping this as slightly rude, especially with superiors.

존댓말; the standard opener when YOU are the caller and want to be polite. 통화 괜찮아? is 반말 for friends. 통화 가능하실까요? is extra-deferential for first calls to strangers or important clients. Do not skip this opener when calling a boss.
지금 시간 괜찮으세요? is the face-to-face 'do you have time?' — 통화 names the phone medium, so it is NOT a synonym. 통화 괜찮으세요? vs 통화 가능하실까요?: same meaning, the latter is more deferential and businesslike.
지금 통화 괜찮으세요? → 잠깐 통화 괜찮으세요? (adding 잠깐 signals brevity) → 지금 통화 가능하실까요? (formal) → 지금 통화 괜찮아? (반말).

Calquing 'can you talk?' as 말할 수 있어요? — that asks about physical ability to speak, not availability. The phone-specific idiom is 통화 괜찮으세요?. Also, using 반말 통화 괜찮아? with a boss or client is a register error.

entries.english: Just a moment.
entries.shortExplanation: 잠시만요. is a practical expression meaning "Just a moment.".
entries.explanation: "Just a moment." — that is 잠시만요. (jamsimanyo.). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 잠시만요. ("One moment, please."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; asking anyone to hold the line briefly — phone, counter, or crowded space
반말; to a close friend or younger person — the full 잠깐만요 is also widely used as a less formal polite form

usagePhrases.en: Could you hold for a moment?
usagePhrases.note: More formal/격식; the expanded form for reception or customer service — explicitly requests patience

usagePhrases.en: One moment, I'll put them right on.
usagePhrases.note: Extension; holding to transfer the call — 바로 ('right away') signals minimum wait time

examples.ko: A: 거기 예약 담당자 좀 부탁드려요. / B: 잠시만요, 바로 연결해 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: geogi yeyak damdangja jom butakdeuryeoyo. / B: jamsimanyo, baro yeongyeolhae deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: Could I speak to the reservations person? / B: One moment, I'll connect you right away.
examples.note: Natural A/B transfer exchange — B uses 잠시만요 as a smooth hold signal before transferring

examples.ko: 잠시만요, 펜 좀 가져올게요.
examples.romanization: jamsimanyo, pen jom gajyeoolgeyo.
examples.en: Hold on, let me grab a pen.
examples.note: Everyday use: pausing to write down what they're saying — the reason after 잠시만요 makes the hold feel considerate

examples.ko: 잠시만요, 담당자 연결해 드리겠습니다. 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요.
examples.romanization: jamsimanyo, damdangja yeongyeolhae deurigetseumnida. kkeunchi malgo gidaryeo juseyo.
examples.en: One moment, I'll connect you to the right person. Please don't hang up.
examples.note: Fuller situation: a call-center transfer script — 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요 ('don't hang up') is the canonical follow-up

entries.nuance: 잠시만요 means 'just a moment' and is the all-purpose 'hold on' on the phone, at a counter, or even to slip past someone in a crowd. On a call it signals you are stepping away briefly without ending the conversation. 잠시 is slightly more formal than everyday 잠깐, but 잠시만요 and 잠깐만요 are interchangeable in practice; the 반말 form is 잠깐만 (or 잠시만), dropping the polite 요. The dividing line with 기다려 주세요 ('please wait') is register and weight: 잠시만요 is a quick, reflexive 'one sec', while 기다려 주세요 is a fuller, explicit request that implies a longer wait. For a formal phone hold, Koreans extend it: 잠시만 기다려 주시겠어요? The English-speaker error is reaching for 기다리세요 ('wait') — that is a bare command and sounds abrupt; the softening idiom is 잠시만요 plus the -아/어 주세요 request form.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Commanding 기다리세요 to mean 'hold on' — that is an order; soften to 잠시만요 or 잠시만 기다려 주시겠어요?.
Saying 잠깐만 to a customer or elder — it is 반말; use 잠시만요 or the fuller 잠시만 기다려 주세요.
Spelling/spacing it as 잠시 만요 — it is one chunk, 잠시만요, with 만요 attached.

structuredNuance.t: 잠시(a short while) + 만(only) + 요(polite) — literally 'just a short while, please.' In practice it functions as a smooth, automatic hold signal on the phone, meaning 'don't hang up, I'll be back in a second.'

Neutral-polite (존댓말) thanks to 요; fine for strangers, elders, and customer service. In 반말 context drop the 요: 잠깐만 or 잠시만. For formal phone holds, extend to 잠시만 기다려 주시겠어요?. Avoid the bare 잠깐만요 with a very senior person — prefer the fuller form.

잠시만요 vs 기다려 주세요: 잠시만요 is a quick, reflexive hold; 기다려 주세요 is a fuller, more explicit wait-request implying a longer pause. vs 잠깐만요: nearly identical meaning; 잠시 is slightly more formal. Neither can be replaced by 기다리세요, which sounds like a command.

잠시만요 (neutral-polite, the core form) → 잠깐만요 (equally common; 잠깐 is slightly less formal than 잠시 but both are used with 요) → 잠시만 기다려 주시겠어요? (full formal hold request; -겠어요? is appropriate for customer service) → 잠깐만 (반말, to a close friend; never to a stranger). Adding a reason after 잠시만요 — 잠시만요, 펜 가져올게요 — makes the hold feel considerate rather than abrupt.
Using 기다리세요 to mean 'hold on' — that is an order ('you, wait!'); the natural idiom is 잠시만요, and the polite request form adds 주시겠어요?. Also: 잠시 만요 (with a space) is wrong — it is one chunk, 잠시만요.

entries.english: You've got the wrong number.
entries.shortExplanation: 전화 잘못 거셨어요. is a practical expression meaning "You've got the wrong number.".
entries.explanation: 전화 잘못 거셨어요. (jeonhwa jalmot geosyeosseoyo.) = "You've got the wrong number.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 전화 잘못 거셨어요. ("You've dialed the wrong number."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; politely telling a stranger they misdialed — the honorific 거셨어요 still respects the caller while delivering the news
반말; to a friend who called you by mistake — informal and direct

usagePhrases.en: I believe you have the wrong number.
usagePhrases.note: More formal/격식; the hedging 것 같습니다 softens the correction — preferred at work or when speaking to an elder

usagePhrases.ko: 여기 그런 사람 없는데요. 전화 잘못 거셨어요.
usagePhrases.romanization: yeogi geureon saram eopsneundeyo. jeonhwa jalmot geosyeosseoyo.
usagePhrases.en: There's no one here by that name. Wrong number.
usagePhrases.note: Extension; explaining first ('no such person') then labeling it a misdial — the natural Korean sequence

examples.ko: A: 이민준 씨 계세요? / B: 아, 저희 회사에 그런 분 안 계세요. 전화 잘못 거신 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: A: iminjun ssi gyeseyo? / B: a, jeohui hoesae geureon bun an gyeseyo. jeonhwa jalmot geosin geot gatayo.
examples.en: A: Is Lee Minjun there? / B: We don't have anyone by that name. I think you have the wrong number.
examples.note: Natural A/B exchange: B explains first, then delivers the misdial conclusion with a softening hedge

examples.ko: 죄송한데 전화 잘못 거신 것 같아요. 몇 번에 거셨어요?
examples.romanization: joesonghande jeonhwa jalmot geosin geot gatayo. myeot beone geosyeosseoyo?
examples.en: Sorry, I think you have the wrong number. What number did you dial?
examples.note: Everyday use: gently checking which number they meant — the follow-up question helps the caller correct themselves

examples.ko: 여보세요? 김 과장님이요? 여기 그런 분 안 계세요. 전화 잘못 거신 것 같은데요.
examples.romanization: yeoboseyo? gim gwajangnimiyo? yeogi geureon bun an gyeseyo. jeonhwa jalmot geosin geot gateundeyo.
examples.en: Hello? Manager Kim? There's no one here by that name. I think you misdialed.
examples.note: Fuller situation: a misdirected call at an office — shows the full sequence: repeat the name → deny → label the error

entries.nuance: 전화 잘못 거셨어요 tells a caller they reached the wrong number — 잘못 is the adverb 'wrongly' and 걸다 is the verb 'to place/hang a call', conjugated as the honorific past 거셨어요 to maintain respect toward the stranger. The dialing verb in Korean is 걸다 (전화를 걸다 = 'to make a call'); do not substitute 하다 here. Softening is important: bare 전화 잘못 거셨어요 can sound curt, so Koreans cushion it with 죄송한데 ('sorry but') or hedge with ...것 같아요 ('seems like'). The 반말 form is 잘못 걸었어 to a friend. A common extra-polite form: 전화 잘못 거신 것 같습니다. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'wrong number' as 틀린 번호 — 틀리다 means 'to be incorrect/mistaken (as a fact)', so 틀린 번호 sounds like the phone number itself is defective; the Korean idiom describes the ACTION of dialing wrongly with the adverb 잘못 and the verb 걸다, not the number.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 틀린 번호예요 for 'wrong number' — 틀리다 is for factual errors; the natural form is 전화 잘못 거셨어요 (misdialed action).
Using 전화 잘못 했어요 — dialing uses 걸다, not 하다; say 잘못 거셨어요/잘못 걸었어요.
Delivering it flatly to a stranger — add 죄송한데 or ...것 같아요 so it doesn't sound annoyed.

structuredNuance.t: 전화(phone) 잘못(wrongly) 거셨어요(you placed-honorific-past) — 'you wrongly placed a call.' The literal meaning IS the real meaning here: it's about the action of dialing wrong, not about the number being wrong. This is key for the 틀린 번호 trap.
존댓말; always use with a stranger caller. Bare 전화 잘못 거셨어요 can sound abrupt — cushion with 죄송한데 ('sorry but') or hedge with 것 같아요. The 반말 form for a friend who misdialed is 잘못 걸었어.
전화 잘못 거셨어요 vs 전화 잘못 거신 것 같아요: same meaning, the latter is hedged and gentler. vs 틀린 번호예요: 틀리다 describes a factual error — the number is defective — which sounds wrong; the idiom always uses 잘못 + 걸다.
The verb for dialing is 걸다 (전화를 걸다). 잘못 거셨어요 (honorific past) → 잘못 거신 것 같습니다 (formal/hedged) → 잘못 걸었어 (반말). Never use 전화 잘못 했어요 — dialing uses 걸다, not 하다.

Translating 'wrong number' as 틀린 번호예요 — 틀리다 is for factual errors, so it makes the number sound defective. The Korean idiom describes the dialing action: 잘못 + 걸다. Also: delivering it flatly to a stranger sounds annoyed — add 죄송한데 or hedge with 것 같아요.

entries.english: I can't hear you well.
entries.shortExplanation: 잘 안 들려요. is a practical expression meaning "I can't hear you well.".
entries.explanation: 잘 안 들려요. (jal an deullyeoyo.) means "I can't hear you well.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 잘 안 들려요. ("I can't hear you well."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; telling anyone the line is bad — the intransitive 들리다 puts the fault on the audio, not on you or the other person
반말; to a close friend or younger person — same grammar, just no 요
More formal/격식; -는데요 is softer and more polished — slightly more appropriate in a business context

usagePhrases.ko: 소리가 잘 안 들려요. 좀 크게 말씀해 주시겠어요?
usagePhrases.romanization: soriga jal an deullyeoyo. jom keuge malsseumhae jusigesseoyo?
usagePhrases.en: I can't hear well. Could you speak up a bit?
usagePhrases.note: Extension; pairing the bad-line report with an actionable request — the natural follow-up pair

examples.ko: A: ...그래서 서류는 내일까지... / B: 여보세요? 잘 안 들려요. 다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: A: ...geuraeseo seoryuneun naeilkkaji... / B: yeoboseyo? jal an deullyeoyo. dasi han beon malsseumhae jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: A: ...so the documents by tomorrow... / B: Hello? I can't hear you. Could you say that again?
examples.note: A/B mid-conversation example: B interrupts a bad line with 잘 안 들려요 and immediately asks for a repeat

examples.ko: 죄송한데 잘 안 들려요. 다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: joesonghande jal an deullyeoyo. dasi han beon malsseumhae jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Sorry, I can't hear well. Could you say that again?
examples.note: Everyday use: combining an apology with the bad-line report and a repeat request — polite and complete

examples.ko: 여기 지하라서 그런지 잘 안 들려요. 밖으로 나가서 다시 걸게요.
examples.romanization: yeogi jiharaseo geureonji jal an deullyeoyo. bakkeuro nagaseo dasi geolgeyo.
examples.en: Maybe because I'm underground, I can't hear you. Let me step out and call back.
examples.note: Fuller situation: naming the cause (underground) and offering a practical fix — models how Koreans explain dropped-signal situations

entries.nuance: 잘 안 들려요 says the other person's voice is not coming through clearly — 들리다 is the intransitive/passive-feeling verb 'to be heard/audible', so the subject is the sound itself, not you. This is the crucial verb choice: 듣다 ('to listen') is a deliberate action the listener controls, so 못 들어요 could imply you are choosing not to listen — wrong and potentially rude. 들리다 means the audio physically isn't reaching your ear. Keep the adverb order fixed: 잘 안 들려요 ('well-not-audible') — the ungrammatical 안 잘 들려요 inverts it. For business, 잘 안 들리는데요 is softer. The nearest alternative 소리가 작아요 ('the volume is low') blames the volume specifically; 잘 안 들려요 covers any reason — static, dropout, noise. The English-speaker trap is 당신을 못 들어요, which uses 듣다 with the person as a direct object — this sounds like 'I'm refusing to listen to you'; native phrasing makes the sound or signal the subject.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 못 들어요 with the person as object — use 들리다 (안 들려요), because the sound is what isn't getting through.
Word order 안 잘 들려요 — the adverb order is fixed as 잘 안 들려요.
Confusing it with 못 알아들어요 ('I can't understand') — that is about comprehension; for a bad line use 잘 안 들려요.

structuredNuance.t: 잘(well) 안(not) 들려요(is audible) — 'it's not being heard well.' The subject is the SOUND, not you; 들리다 is intransitive/passive-feeling, so the phrase describes a technical audio problem, not your listening effort. This is why it's polite.
존댓말; usable with anyone on a bad line. For business, 잘 안 들리는데요 (-는데요 ending) sounds smoother. 반말 is simply 잘 안 들려 (drop 요). Word order is fixed: 잘 안 들려요, not 안 잘 들려요.

잘 안 들려요 vs 소리가 작아요: 잘 안 들려요 is the general bad-line report (any cause); 소리가 작아요 specifically says the volume is low. vs 못 알아들어요: that reports comprehension failure (didn't understand the words), not a signal problem.
잘 안 들려요 (standard) → 잘 안 들리는데요 (softer/formal) → 잘 안 들려 (반말). Add 소리가 잘 안 들려요 (making 소리 the explicit subject) for extra clarity.

당신을 못 들어요 — this uses 듣다 (active listening verb) with a person as object, sounding like 'I refuse to listen to you.' Always use 들리다 (안 들려요) to put the fault on the audio signal, not on your willingness to listen.

entries.english: The call dropped.
entries.shortExplanation: 전화가 끊겼어요. is a practical expression meaning "The call dropped.".
entries.explanation: "The call dropped." — that is 전화가 끊겼어요. (jeonhwaga kkeunkyeosseoyo.). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 전화가 끊겼어요. ("The call got cut off."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; reporting a dropped call to anyone — the subject particle 가 marks the call as the thing that dropped, not you
반말; to a close friend when redialing — the natural casual version
More formal/격식; 통화 and the observational -네요 ending sound a touch more composed — appropriate at work

usagePhrases.en: The call suddenly dropped a moment ago.
usagePhrases.note: Extension; explaining a prior drop when you reconnect — 갑자기 ('suddenly') emphasizes the unintentional nature

examples.ko: A: (재연결 후) 여보세요? / B: 아, 아까 전화가 끊겼네요. 괜찮으세요?
examples.romanization: A: (jaeyeongyeol hu) yeoboseyo? / B: a, akka jeonhwaga kkeunkyeonneyo. gwaenchaneuseyo?
examples.en: A: (after reconnecting) Hello? / B: Oh, the call dropped earlier. Are you okay?
examples.note: A/B reconnection exchange — the 네요 ending signals B is observing what just happened rather than blaming anyone

examples.ko: 미안해요, 전화가 끊겼어요. 터널을 지나가서 그랬나 봐요.
examples.romanization: mianhaeyo, jeonhwaga kkeunkyeosseoyo. teoneoreul jinagaseo geuraenna bwayo.
examples.en: Sorry, the call dropped. Must've been the tunnel.
examples.note: Everyday use: apologizing and guessing the cause — 그랬나 봐요 ('seems that was it') is a natural way to speculate about a reason

examples.ko: 방금 통화하다가 전화가 끊겨서 다시 걸었어요. 어디까지 얘기했죠?
examples.romanization: banggeum tonghwahadaga jeonhwaga kkeunkyeoseo dasi georeosseoyo. eodikkaji yaegihaetjyo?
examples.en: The call cut out mid-conversation so I called back. Where were we?
examples.note: Fuller situation: resuming after redialing — 어디까지 얘기했죠? is the natural pick-up line after a dropped call

entries.nuance: 전화가 끊겼어요 reports an unintentional call drop — 끊기다 is the passive form of 끊다 ('to cut'), so 'the call got cut on its own.' This voice distinction is the most critical thing to get right: 전화를 끊었어요 uses the active verb 끊다 with the object particle 를 and means 'I hung up on purpose' — saying this instead of the passive can flip an accident into an accusation of deliberately hanging up, which is rude. 전화가 끊겼어요 uses the passive 끊기다 with the subject particle 가, making the call the intransitive subject. A nearby trap phrase: 전화 끊을게요 ('I'll hang up now') announces an intentional end to the call — entirely different meaning. For a more formal tone, 통화가 끊어졌네요. The English-speaker error is using the active 끊었어요 for an accidental drop — understand which voice matches the intent.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 전화를 끊었어요 for an accidental drop — that is the active 'I hung up'; use the passive 전화가 끊겼어요.
Mixing particles: 전화를 끊겼어요 — the passive 끊기다 takes the subject marker 가 (전화가 끊겼어요).
Confusing it with 끊을게요 ('I'll hang up') — that announces ending the call on purpose, not a dropout.

structuredNuance.t: 전화(the call) 가(subject: it) 끊겼어요(got-cut-passive) — 'the call got itself cut.' The passive form 끊기다 makes the drop seem accidental, like the call acted on its own. This is not a coincidence — it's the correct grammatical choice for an unintentional drop.

존댓말; use when redialing after any dropped call. 반말 is 전화 끊겼어. For formal contexts: 통화가 끊어졌네요 (-네요 sounds observational, not accusatory). Always include an apology (미안해요/죄송해요) when YOU are the one redialing.

전화가 끊겼어요 (passive, accidental drop, subject particle 가) vs 전화를 끊었어요 (active, intentional hang-up, object particle 를) — particle choice flips the meaning entirely. vs 전화 끊을게요: 'I'll hang up now' — a deliberate, announced end to the call.
전화가 끊겼어요 (standard) → 통화가 끊어졌네요 (formal/composed) → 전화 끊겼어 (반말) → 아까 전화가 갑자기 끊겼어요 (explaining a prior drop).

Using 전화를 끊었어요 for an accidental drop — the active voice means 'I hung up intentionally,' which sounds rude. Use the passive 전화가 끊겼어요. Also: 전화를 끊겼어요 (passive verb + object particle 를) mixes the forms and is wrong — the passive takes subject particle 가.

entries.english: I'll call you back.
entries.shortExplanation: 다시 전화할게요. is a practical expression meaning "I'll call you back.".
entries.explanation: 다시 전화할게요. (dasi jeonhwahalgeyo.) = "I'll call you back.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 다시 전화할게요. ("I'll call again."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; promising to call back, neutral-polite — the -ㄹ게요 marks YOUR own intention
반말; to a close friend or younger person — drop 요 only
More formal/격식; humble 드리다 + -겠습니다 for a client, boss, or formal business context

usagePhrases.en: I'll call you back in a bit.
usagePhrases.note: Extension; 이따가 pins the callback to later today — more specific and more committed-sounding than 나중에

examples.ko: A: 지금 잠깐 통화 돼요? / B: 지금 좀 바빠서요, 이따 다시 전화할게요.
examples.romanization: A: jigeum jamkkan tonghwa dwaeyo? / B: jigeum jom bappaseoyo, itta dasi jeonhwahalgeyo.
examples.en: A: Can you talk for a sec? / B: I'm a bit busy right now — I'll call you back later.
examples.note: Classic A/B exchange: B declines with a polite reason and commits to a callback — shows the natural flow of a deferred call

examples.ko: 회의 끝나고 다시 전화할게요. 한 시간쯤 뒤에요.
examples.romanization: hoeui kkeunnago dasi jeonhwahalgeyo. han siganjjeum dwieyo.
examples.en: I'll call back after my meeting, in about an hour.
examples.note: Everyday use: giving a rough time makes the promise feel concrete and reliable

examples.ko: 지금 운전 중이라 다시 전화할게요. 도착하면 바로 연락드릴게요.
examples.romanization: jigeum unjeon jungira dasi jeonhwahalgeyo. dochakamyeon baro yeollakdeurilgeyo.
examples.en: I'm driving, so I'll call you back. I'll reach out as soon as I arrive.
examples.note: Fuller situation: explaining why AND giving a trigger (도착하면 = 'when I arrive') makes this a specific, credible commitment

entries.nuance: 다시 전화할게요 is a personal promise that YOU will phone again — 다시 means 'again', and the -ㄹ게요 ending specifically marks the SPEAKER's own intention or commitment toward the listener; it would be grammatically wrong to use it about someone else's future action. To raise politeness toward a boss or client, swap 전화하다 for the humble 전화드리다: 다시 전화드릴게요 or the more formal 다시 전화드리겠습니다. The nearest natural alternative 다시 걸게요 uses 걸다 (the dialing verb) and is equally common; the difference in nuance is negligible. The English-speaker trap is trying to render 'call you back' with 부르다 — 부르다 means 'to call out to someone / summon them', which is physical and not telephonic; the phone verb is 전화하다 or 전화 걸다. Another trap is inserting 당신을 — Korean simply omits the second-person pronoun; the sentence stands without it.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 다시 불러요 for 'call back' — 부르다 means summon/call out; the telephone verb is 전화하다 (다시 전화할게요).
Using -ㄹ게요 for someone else's action — it marks YOUR own intention; to ask them to call, say 전화 주세요.
Adding 당신을 — 전화하다 doesn't take a person as object that way; just say 다시 전화할게요.

structuredNuance.t: 다시(again) 전화(phone) 할게요(I will-commitment) — 'I will phone again.' The -ㄹ게요 ending is key: it marks the SPEAKER's own commitment and cannot be used to describe someone else's future action. It also implies the listener's preference is being considered.

존댓말; fine for any peer or neutral relationship. For seniors, bosses, and clients use the humble form: 다시 전화드릴게요 (전화드리다 = humble 'give a call'). 반말 is 다시 전화할게. The most formal business form is 다시 전화드리겠습니다.

다시 전화할게요 vs 다시 걸게요: nearly identical; 걸다 is the dialing verb, 전화하다 names the action — both are natural. vs 다시 전화드릴게요: same meaning, humble level — for seniors. vs 이따 전화할게요: the version with 이따 specifies later TODAY, making it more concrete.

다시 전화할게요 (standard polite; peer-level) → 다시 걸게요 (same meaning; 걸다 is the dialing verb, equally natural) → 다시 전화드릴게요 (humble; adds 드리다 to elevate the listener — use with bosses and clients) → 다시 전화드리겠습니다 (most formal; -겠습니다 for job interviews, first business calls) → 다시 전화할게 (반말; close friends only). Adding 이따 or a specific time (회의 끝나고, 한 시간 뒤에) makes any variant feel like a firm commitment.
Saying 다시 불러요 for 'call back' — 부르다 means to summon/call out physically, not to telephone. The phone verb is 전화하다/전화 걸다. Also: inserting 당신을 is unnatural — Korean omits the second-person pronoun.

entries.english: Please leave a message.
entries.shortExplanation: 메시지 남겨 주세요. is a practical expression meaning "Please leave a message.".
entries.explanation: 메시지 남겨 주세요. (mesiji namgyeo juseyo.) means "Please leave a message.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 메시지 남겨 주세요. ("Please leave a message."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; voicemail prompt or asking a caller to leave word — 남기다 ('to leave behind') is the correct verb for any message or note
반말; to a close friend — direct and casual

usagePhrases.en: If you leave a message, I'll pass it on.
usagePhrases.note: More formal/격식; reception or a colleague relaying to an absent person — the conditional 주시면 + promise makes it sound professional

usagePhrases.ko: 삐 소리 후에 메시지 남겨 주세요.
usagePhrases.romanization: ppi sori hue mesiji namgyeo juseyo.
usagePhrases.en: Please leave a message after the beep.
usagePhrases.note: Extension; the standard Korean voicemail recording line — 삐 소리 is 'the beep sound'

examples.ko: A: 이 대리님 계세요? / B: 지금 자리를 비우셨는데요. 메시지 남겨 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: A: i daerinim gyeseyo? / B: jigeum jarireul biusyeonneundeyo. mesiji namgyeo jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: A: Is Deputy Lee there? / B: He's stepped away right now. Would you like to leave a message?
examples.note: Natural A/B desk exchange — B uses 남겨 주시겠어요? (question form) rather than an imperative, which sounds more professional

examples.ko: 담당자가 자리를 비웠는데, 메시지 남겨 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: damdangjaga jarireul biwonneunde, mesiji namgyeo jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: The person in charge has stepped out — would you like to leave a message?
examples.note: Everyday use at an office desk — 주시겠어요? softens it into an offer rather than a command

examples.ko: 연결이 안 되네요. 메시지 남겨 주시면 확인하고 바로 연락드릴게요.
examples.romanization: yeongyeori an doeneyo. mesiji namgyeo jusimyeon hwaginhago baro yeollakdeurilgeyo.
examples.en: I can't reach them. If you leave a message, I'll check it and get back to you right away.
examples.note: Fuller situation: the conditional form 남겨 주시면 + a specific callback promise — models how to turn a dead-end call into a productive outcome

entries.nuance: 메시지 남겨 주세요 asks a caller to leave word — 남기다 ('to leave something behind') plus the polite-request 주세요, softened with the implicit 좀. The verb is specifically 남기다 for leaving a message behind; do not use 두다 ('to put/place'), 놓다, or especially 떠나다 ('to depart a place'). A useful register distinction: 메모 남겨 주세요 uses 메모 ('a written memo/note') and is common at a reception desk when you will physically write it down on paper; 메시지 leans toward a voicemail recording or a relayed verbal message. The -주시겠어요? form ('would you...?') converts the instruction into a polite offer, which is preferred in business. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'leave a message' with the verb 떠나다: 메시지를 떠나세요 means 'depart from the message (place)', which is nonsensical — for leaving an object or information behind, Korean uses 남기다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 떠나다 for 'leave a message' — 떠나다 is to depart a place; leaving a note/message takes 남기다 (메시지 남겨 주세요).
Saying 메시지를 두세요/놓으세요 — 두다/놓다 are 'put/place' objects; the idiom is 남기다.
Dropping 주세요 and barking 남겨 — without 주세요 it sounds like an order; keep 남겨 주세요 or 남겨 주시겠어요?.

structuredNuance.t: 메시지(message) 남겨(leaving-behind) 주세요(please-do-for-me) — 'please leave a message behind for me.' 남기다 specifically describes leaving something behind for another person to find, which is exactly what a voicemail or relayed message is.

존댓말; used at reception desks, on voicemail, or by a colleague taking a message. The imperative 주세요 is fine; upgrade to 주시겠어요? for extra politeness. 반말 is 메시지 남겨. Business: 메시지 남겨 주시면 전달해 드리겠습니다 sounds professional.
메시지 남겨 주세요 vs 메모 남겨 주세요: 메모 is a written note (paper); 메시지 is a voicemail or relayed verbal message. Both use 남기다. Neither uses 두다/놓다/떠나다.
메시지 남겨 주세요 → 메시지 남겨 주시겠어요? (polite offer) → 메시지 남겨 주시면 전달해 드리겠습니다 (formal with callback promise) → 삐 소리 후에 메시지 남겨 주세요 (voicemail recording).

Calquing 'leave a message' as 메시지를 떠나세요 — 떠나다 means to depart a place, not to leave an object. Leaving something behind for someone to find uses 남기다. Also: barking 남겨 without 주세요 sounds like an order; always keep the 주세요 or 주시겠어요?.

entries.english: Shall we set up a time to meet?
entries.shortExplanation: 약속 잡을까요? is a practical expression meaning "Shall we set up a time to meet?".
entries.explanation: "Shall we set up a time to meet?" — that is 약속 잡을까요? (yaksok jabeulkkayo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 약속 잡을까요? ("Shall we make plans to meet?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Shall we make plans to meet?
usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; proposing to schedule a meeting with a colleague, client, or acquaintance — -ㄹ까요? invites the other's agreement
반말; to a close friend — drop 요 only

usagePhrases.en: Let's go ahead and set a meeting.
usagePhrases.note: More formal/격식; 잡으시죠 (hortative + honorific) is a gentle push — appropriate when suggesting a meeting to a client or senior

usagePhrases.en: Then shall we set it for next week?
usagePhrases.note: Extension; proposing a specific window after agreeing in principle — the natural next step

examples.ko: A: 그 내용은 전화로 설명하기 어렵네요. / B: 그럼 직접 만나는 게 좋겠어요. 약속 잡을까요?
examples.romanization: A: geu naeyongeun jeonhwaro seolmyeonghagi eoryeomneyo. / B: geureom jikjeom mannaneun ge jokesseoyo. yaksok jabeulkkayo?
examples.en: A: That's hard to explain over the phone. / B: Then meeting in person would be best. Shall we set a time?
examples.note: Natural A/B transition from a call to proposing a face-to-face meeting — shows when and why 약속 잡을까요? gets used

examples.ko: 그 건은 직접 만나서 얘기하는 게 좋겠어요. 약속 잡을까요?
examples.romanization: geu geoneun jikjeom mannaseo yaegihaneun ge jokesseoyo. yaksok jabeulkkayo?
examples.en: That matter is better discussed in person. Shall we set a time?
examples.note: Everyday use: moving from a call to an in-person meeting — the -ㄹ까요? ending invites the other person's input, not a one-sided decision

examples.ko: 이번 주는 제가 좀 바빠서요, 다음 주 초로 약속 잡을까요? 화요일이나 수요일 어떠세요?
examples.romanization: ibeon juneun jega jom bappaseoyo, daeum ju choro yaksok jabeulkkayo? hwayoirina suyoil eotteoseyo?
examples.en: I'm busy this week, so shall we set it for early next week? How about Tuesday or Wednesday?
examples.note: Fuller situation: proposing and offering candidate days immediately — the most cooperative form of scheduling

entries.nuance: 약속 잡을까요? proposes pinning down a meeting — the verb 잡다 literally means 'to grab/catch' and is the standard verb for fixing an appointment or time slot; 약속을 잡다 is an unchangeable set phrase. The -ㄹ까요? ending makes it a soft collaborative proposal ('shall we?') rather than a decision or command. 약속 has a dual meaning: (a) a promise or commitment, and (b) a scheduled plan to meet — the verb 잡다 is what marks it specifically as scheduling. For more formal business, 미팅을 잡다 or 일정을 잡다 work too. The 반말 form is 약속 잡을까?; formal is 약속을 잡으시죠. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'make an appointment' as 약속을 만들까요? — 만들다 ('to make/create') is wrong here; appointments in Korean are 'grabbed/caught' with 잡다, not manufactured.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 약속을 만들까요? — 'making' an appointment uses 잡다, not 만들다; say 약속 잡을까요?.
Confusing 약속 with only 'promise' — with 잡다 it means scheduling a meet-up; the verb signals the meaning.
Using a flat statement 약속 잡아요 when proposing — the inviting form is the -ㄹ까요? question, 약속 잡을까요?.

structuredNuance.t: 약속(plan/appointment) 잡을까요(shall we grab/catch it?) — 잡다 means 'to grab or catch'; in Korean, appointments are 'caught' or 'pinned down', not 'made'. This mental image helps avoid the 만들다 trap.
존댓말; soft proposal tone thanks to -ㄹ까요?. Use when moving from a phone discussion to an in-person meeting. 반말: 약속 잡을까?. Formal push to a senior: 약속을 잡으시죠 or 한번 뵙겠습니다 followed by date-setting.
약속 잡을까요? vs 미팅 잡을까요? vs 일정 잡을까요?: all use 잡다; 약속 implies a personal meet-up; 미팅 sounds more business-formal (from English 'meeting'); 일정 ('schedule/itinerary') is used for more formal planned events.
약속 잡을까요? → 약속 잡을까? (반말) → 약속을 잡으시죠 (formal push) → 그럼 날짜를 정할까요? (more explicit: shall we settle on a date?)

약속을 만들까요? — 만들다 means 'to create/manufacture'; appointments are 'caught/pinned down' with 잡다, not manufactured. Also: stating 약속 잡아요 (flat declarative) reads as a unilateral announcement rather than a proposal — the -ㄹ까요? question is what makes it collaborative.

entries.english: I think I'll be a little late.
entries.shortExplanation: 좀 늦을 것 같아요. is a practical expression meaning "I think I'll be a little late.".
entries.explanation: 좀 늦을 것 같아요. (jom neujeul geot gatayo.) means "I think I'll be a little late.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 좀 늦을 것 같아요. ("I think I'll be a bit late."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: I think I'll be a bit late.
usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; hedged warning to anyone you're meeting — the -ㄹ 것 같아요 frame softens bad news into an apologetic prediction
반말; to a close friend — same hedge, drop 요

usagePhrases.en: I'm afraid I'll be slightly late.
usagePhrases.note: More formal/격식; -습니다 for work meetings or a senior — 조금 (Sino-Korean nuance) sounds slightly more formal than 좀

usagePhrases.ko: 차가 막혀서 10분 정도 늦을 것 같아요.
usagePhrases.romanization: chaga makyeoseo 10bun jeongdo neujeul geot gatayo.
usagePhrases.en: Traffic's bad, so I'll be about 10 minutes late.
usagePhrases.note: Extension; giving the reason (traffic) and the approximate delay — the complete heads-up message you send when running late

examples.ko: A: 지금 어디예요? / B: 미안, 지하철이 좀 밀려서 10분 정도 늦을 것 같아.
examples.romanization: A: jigeum eodiyeyo? / B: mian, jihacheori jom millyeoseo 10bun jeongdo neujeul geot gata.
examples.en: A: Where are you now? / B: Sorry, the subway is packed so I think I'll be about 10 minutes late.
examples.note: Natural A/B lateness notification — B gives reason + specific estimate, which is the considerate Korean way

examples.ko: 죄송한데 좀 늦을 것 같아요. 5분만 기다려 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: joesonghande jom neujeul geot gatayo. 5bunman gidaryeo jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Sorry, I'll be a little late. Could you wait five minutes?
examples.note: Everyday use: combining an apology, a hedged prediction, and a specific wait request — the polished three-part formula

examples.ko: 팀장님, 지하철이 연착돼서 조금 늦을 것 같습니다. 먼저 시작하고 계세요.
examples.romanization: timjangnim, jihacheori yeonchakdwaeseo jogeum neujeul geot gatseumnida. meonjeo sijakago gyeseyo.
examples.en: Sir, the subway is delayed so I'll be a bit late. Please start without me.
examples.note: Fuller situation: notifying a boss, using -습니다 for formality, and the considerate 먼저 시작하고 계세요 ('please start without me')

entries.nuance: 좀 늦을 것 같아요 hedges a lateness warning with the -ㄹ 것 같다 ('it seems I will') frame — this is precisely the softening Korean expects when delivering inconvenient news like tardiness; bare 늦어요 sounds like a blunt, unapologetic fact. 좀 ('a bit') further cushions the degree. The verb is 늦다 ('to be late as a person'); for a transit vehicle use 연착되다/지연되다. The degree scale: 좀 늦을 것 같아요 (mild hedge) → 조금 늦겠어요 (more assertive/formal prediction) → 많이 늦을 것 같아요 (significantly late). The dividing line between 늦을 것 같아요 and 늦겠어요 is hedged-apologetic vs more confident/abrupt; -ㄹ 것 같아요 suits the apologetic social context better. The English-speaker trap is the flat 늦어요 ('I'm late') — that announces a present fact without any apology or mitigation; native speakers always wrap the lateness prediction in 죄송한데/미안한데 ... -ㄹ 것 같아요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying flat 늦어요 to warn of lateness — it sounds blunt; hedge with 좀 늦을 것 같아요 and add 죄송한데.
Using 늦었어요 (past) when you haven't arrived yet — that means 'I was/am already late'; for a prediction use 늦을 것 같아요.
Confusing 늦다 with 느리다 — 느리다 is 'slow (speed)'; being late to an appointment is 늦다.

structuredNuance.t: 좀(a bit) 늦을(late-future) 것 같아요(it seems) — 'it seems I'll be a bit late.' The -ㄹ 것 같다 frame is not mere uncertainty — it's the polite Korean way to deliver bad news as a softened prediction rather than an abrupt statement. The hedge IS the apology.

존댓말; the standard way to warn anyone you're running late. ALWAYS lead with 죄송한데/미안한데 before it. 반말: 좀 늦을 것 같아. Formal (to boss): 조금 늦을 것 같습니다. Never deliver the bare 늦어요 as a lateness warning — it sounds unapologetic.

좀 늦을 것 같아요 vs 늦겠어요: -ㄹ 것 같아요 is hedged and apologetic; -겠어요 is a more assertive (and slightly abrupt) prediction. vs 늦어요: that's a present-tense fact ('I'm late now'), not a heads-up warning. vs 못 갈 것 같아요: 'I might not make it' — stronger and often triggers a reschedule.
좀 늦을 것 같아요 → 10분 정도 늦을 것 같아요 (give the specific delay) → 차가 막혀서 좀 늦을 것 같아요 (add reason) → 조금 늦을 것 같습니다 (formal).
Flat 늦어요 as a warning — that's a blunt present-tense statement with no apology; wrap it in 죄송한데/미안한데 + 늦을 것 같아요. Also: 늦었어요 (past) is 'I was/am already late' — don't use it as a future warning.

entries.english: Could we push the appointment back?
entries.shortExplanation: 약속을 미뤄도 될까요? is a practical expression meaning "Could we push the appointment back?".
entries.explanation: "Could we push the appointment back?" — that is 약속을 미뤄도 될까요? (yaksogeul mirwodo doelkkayo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 약속을 미뤄도 될까요? ("Could we postpone our plans?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; the polite permission frame -아도 될까요? asks for the other person's consent rather than announcing unilaterally
반말; to a close friend — 좀 softens slightly even in 반말

usagePhrases.en: Would it be alright to postpone?
usagePhrases.note: More formal/격식; 괜찮으실까요 is extra-deferential — appropriate for a client or senior you are inconveniencing

usagePhrases.ko: 혹시 약속을 다음 주로 미뤄도 될까요?
usagePhrases.romanization: hoksi yaksogeul daeum juro mirwodo doelkkayo?
usagePhrases.en: Could we possibly move it to next week?
usagePhrases.note: Extension; proposing the new timing alongside the request — the considerate way to reschedule

examples.ko: A: 내일 약속 말이에요. / B: 죄송한데 약속을 미뤄도 될까요? 급한 일이 생겨서요.
examples.romanization: A: naeil yaksong marieyo. / B: joesonghande yaksogeul mirwodo doelkkayo? geupan iri saenggyeoseoyo.
examples.en: A: About tomorrow's plans. / B: Sorry, could we postpone? Something urgent came up.
examples.note: Natural A/B rescheduling exchange — B leads with 죄송한데 before the permission request, and gives a brief reason without over-explaining

examples.ko: 갑자기 일이 생겨서요, 오늘 약속을 미뤄도 될까요?
examples.romanization: gapjagi iri saenggyeoseoyo, oneul yaksogeul mirwodo doelkkayo?
examples.en: Something came up suddenly — could we postpone today's plans?
examples.note: Everyday use: 갑자기 일이 생겼다 is the most common reason for rescheduling and is socially accepted without further detail

examples.ko: 정말 죄송한데 제가 몸이 좀 안 좋아서, 약속을 다음 주로 미뤄도 될까요? 날짜는 편하신 때로 맞출게요.
examples.romanization: jeongmal joesonghande jega momi jom an joaseo, yaksogeul daeum juro mirwodo doelkkayo? naljjaneun pyeonhasin ttaero matchulgeyo.
examples.en: I'm so sorry, I'm not feeling well — could we move it to next week? I'll fit whatever date suits you.
examples.note: Fuller situation: full apology + reason + proposed new timing + offer of flexibility — the gold standard for a reschedule request

entries.nuance: 약속을 미뤄도 될까요? asks permission to postpone a plan — 미루다 ('to put off / push back') plus the permission frame -아도 될까요? ('would it be okay if...?'). The -아도 될까요? structure explicitly makes it a request for the other's consent, not a unilateral decision — this is the socially correct frame when YOU are the one inconveniencing them. 미루다 means push to a later time within the same general intent to meet; cancelling outright is 취소하다. This distinction matters: saying 약속을 취소해도 될까요? when you mean to reschedule can alarm the other person because 취소 means the plan is off entirely. The formal versions: 미뤄도 괜찮으실까요? (extra deferential). The English-speaker trap is the assertive 약속을 미뤄요 or the bare 약속을 미룰게요 — these sound like unilateral announcements; the permission question is what makes it polite.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 약속을 취소해도 될까요? when you mean to reschedule — 취소 is to cancel entirely; to push it later use 미루다.
Commanding 약속을 미뤄요 — that orders them; ask permission with 미뤄도 될까요?.
Confusing 미루다 with 늦추다 alone — both can mean delay, but for rescheduling plans 약속을 미루다 is the set collocation.

structuredNuance.t: 약속을(the appointment) 미뤄도(even if postponed) 될까요?(would it be okay?) — 'would it be okay if I postponed our appointment?' The -아도 될까요? frame is a genuine request for the other person's permission, not a rhetorical question — you're giving them the power to say no.
존댓말; ALWAYS precede with 죄송한데/죄송하지만 when calling to reschedule — Korean social norms expect you to acknowledge the inconvenience explicitly. 반말: 약속 좀 미뤄도 돼?. Formal: 약속을 좀 미뤄도 괜찮으실까요?.

약속을 미루다 vs 약속을 취소하다: 미루다 = postpone (intent to meet stays intact); 취소하다 = cancel (meeting is off). Using 취소 when you mean 미루다 can worry or offend. vs 약속을 바꾸다: 'change the appointment' — also acceptable but less common for time-shifting.
약속을 미뤄도 될까요? → 약속을 미뤄도 괜찮으실까요? (extra deferential) → 약속을 다음 주로 미뤄도 될까요? (with proposed new time) → 약속 좀 미뤄도 돼? (반말).

Announcing 약속을 미룰게요 ('I'll postpone our appointment') — that's a unilateral statement, not a request for permission, which sounds presumptuous. Use the question form -아도 될까요?. Also: 약속을 미뤄요 is a command/statement — equally problematic.

entries.english: I'll be in touch.
entries.shortExplanation: 연락드릴게요. is a practical expression meaning "I'll be in touch.".
entries.explanation: 연락드릴게요. (yeollakdeurilgeyo.) = "I'll be in touch.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 연락드릴게요. ("I'll get in touch."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 (humble); the courteous promise to a boss, client, or elder — 드리다 lowers the speaker to honor the listener
반말; to a close friend — drops the humble 드리다 entirely
More formal/격식; -겠습니다 used in formal business contexts — standard at the end of a job interview or client meeting

usagePhrases.en: I'll check and get back to you.
usagePhrases.note: Extension; promising to follow up after looking into something — the -고 나서/확인하고 lead-in is the natural connector

examples.ko: A: 그 부분은 확인이 필요해서요. / B: 네, 제가 확인하고 오늘 중으로 연락드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: geu bubuneun hwagini piryohaeseoyo. / B: ne, jega hwaginhago oneul jungeuro yeollakdeurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: That part needs checking. / B: Understood — I'll verify and get back to you today.
examples.note: Classic A/B business follow-up exchange — B commits to a specific timeframe (오늘 중으로 = by today), which makes the promise credible

examples.ko: 자리 나는 대로 바로 연락드릴게요.
examples.romanization: jari naneun daero baro yeollakdeurilgeyo.
examples.en: I'll contact you as soon as a spot opens up.
examples.note: Everyday use: a service promising to reach out the moment availability changes — 나는 대로 ('as soon as it comes') is the natural trigger

examples.ko: 지원해 주셔서 감사합니다. 결과는 다음 주 중으로 연락드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: jiwonhae jusyeoseo gamsahamnida. gyeolgwaneun daeum ju jungeuro yeollakdeurigetseumnida.
examples.en: Thank you for applying. We'll contact you with the result sometime next week.
examples.note: Fuller situation: formal post-interview close — the -겠습니다 ending and 다음 주 중으로 set a professional, specific promise

entries.nuance: 연락드릴게요 promises future contact — 연락하다 ('to contact') in the humble form 연락드리다, where 드리다 ('to give, humbly') lowers the speaker to elevate the listener. The -ㄹ게요 ending marks YOUR own intention. 연락 is medium-neutral: it covers a phone call, text, email, or any channel, making it broader and more flexible than 전화할게요 (phone only). The dividing line is channel-specific (전화 = phone call) vs open-channel (연락 = any contact method). To go plain-polite (peers): 연락할게요; to go casual (friends): 연락할게; to go formal: 연락드리겠습니다. The English-speaker trap is inserting 당신에게 — 당신 to a real second person sounds confrontational or awkwardly intimate in Korean; simply omit it. Another grammar trap is 연락이 될게요, which incorrectly mixes the passive 되다 with the intentional -ㄹ게요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Inserting 당신에게 — 당신 sounds confrontational/odd to a real listener; just say 연락드릴게요 and omit the pronoun.
Using plain 연락할게요 to a client or boss — prefer the humble 연락드릴게요 to show respect.
Saying 연락이 될게요 — the speaker's intention uses active 연락하다/연락드리다 + -ㄹ게요, not 되다.

structuredNuance.t: 연락(contact) 드릴게요(I will give humbly-commitment) — the 드리다 ('give humbly') is the humble form, meaning you are 'giving the act of contacting' to the listener as a service. This is a structural humility marker, not just politeness vocabulary.
The humble 연락드릴게요 is for bosses, clients, and elders. With a peer use 연락할게요; with a close friend 반말 is 연락할게. The formal version is 연락드리겠습니다 (-겠습니다 for job-interview / business letter level).
연락드릴게요 vs 전화드릴게요: 연락 is medium-neutral (any channel); 전화 is phone-only. If you are not sure how you'll contact them, 연락드릴게요 is safer. vs 이따 연락드릴게요: adds 이따 (later today) to make it more concrete.
연락드릴게요 → 연락드리겠습니다 (formal) → 연락할게요 (plain polite) → 연락할게 (반말) → 확인하고 연락드릴게요 (with follow-up trigger).

Inserting 당신에게 — 당신 to a real addressee sounds confrontational or oddly intimate; Korean simply omits the second-person pronoun. Also: 연락이 될게요 is wrong — the speaker's promise uses active 연락드리다 + -ㄹ게요, not 되다.

entries.english: I'll call you later.
entries.shortExplanation: 이따 전화드릴게요. is a practical expression meaning "I'll call you later.".
entries.explanation: 이따 전화드릴게요. (itta jeonhwadeurilgeyo.) means "I'll call you later.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 이따 전화드릴게요. ("I'll call you later."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 (humble); promising to phone a boss, client, or elder later the same day — 드리다 elevates the listener
반말; to a close friend — drop the humble 드리다 and use plain 하다
More formal/격식; -겠습니다 in a business context — sounds measured and professional
Extension; 저녁에 narrows the later-today window to the evening — turns a vague promise into a concrete commitment

examples.ko: A: 지금 잠깐 얘기할 수 있어요? / B: 지금 회의 중이라서요. 이따 전화드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: jigeum jamkkan yaegihal su isseoyo? / B: jigeum hoeui jungiraseoyo. itta jeonhwadeurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: Can we talk briefly now? / B: I'm in a meeting. I'll call you later.
examples.note: Classic A/B polite deferral — B gives a brief reason and the specific this-day promise makes it more than a brush-off

examples.ko: 회의 중이라서요, 이따 전화드릴게요. 한 시쯤 괜찮으세요?
examples.romanization: hoeui jungiraseoyo, itta jeonhwadeurilgeyo. han sijjeum gwaenchaneuseyo?
examples.en: I'm in a meeting, so I'll call you later. Is around one okay?
examples.note: Everyday use: giving a rough time (한 시쯤 = around 1 o'clock) alongside the promise makes it concrete and considerate

examples.ko: 지금 손님이 계셔서 통화가 어려워요. 이따 일 끝나고 전화드릴게요.
examples.romanization: jigeum sonnimi gyesyeoseo tonghwaga eoryeowoyo. itta il kkeunnago jeonhwadeurilgeyo.
examples.en: I have a customer right now so I can't talk. I'll call you after work.
examples.note: Fuller situation: stating the obstacle and the trigger event (일 끝나고 = after work) — the complete, credible callback formula

entries.nuance: 이따 전화드릴게요 promises to call later today — 이따(가) is the adverb 'in a while / later (same day)', so it is near-term and specific to today, unlike 나중에 ('sometime later', open-ended). This distinction is socially meaningful: 이따 전화드릴게요 feels like a genuine commitment; 나중에 전화할게요 can read as a brush-off, especially if said to a person who needs a prompt answer. 전화드리다 (humble form) + -ㄹ게요 (speaker's intention) make this the correct formula for addressing seniors. The 반말 is 이따 전화할게. For business, 이따 전화드리겠습니다. Spelling trap: 이따 is the 'later' adverb — do NOT write 있다가, which is the verb 있다 + -다가 ('after being/staying somewhere'), a completely different grammar structure. The English-speaker trap is reaching for 나중에 when 이따 is the right precision.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 있다가 for 'later' — that is the verb 있다 + -다가 ('after being'); the time adverb is 이따(가).
Saying 나중에 전화할게요 when you mean later the same day — 나중에 is open-ended and can sound like a brush-off; use 이따.
Using plain 전화할게요 to an elder or boss — prefer the humble 전화드릴게요.

structuredNuance.t: 이따(later today) 전화(call) 드릴게요(I will give humbly-commitment) — 이따 is key: it pins the callback to the same day, making this a concrete near-term promise, not a vague 'someday.' This is the word that separates a genuine commitment from a polite brush-off.

존댓말 (humble); for bosses, clients, elders. 반말: 이따 전화할게. Formal: 이따 전화드리겠습니다. Add a time if possible (이따 두 시쯤 = around 2) to make the promise more credible. Do NOT use 이따 for something that might be tomorrow — 내일 전화드릴게요 is more honest.

이따 vs 나중에: 이따 = later today (specific, committed); 나중에 = sometime later (vague, can sound like a brush-off). vs 곧 전화드릴게요 ('I'll call soon'): even more immediate than 이따 — implies minutes rather than hours.
이따 전화드릴게요 → 이따 저녁에 전화드릴게요 (with time of day) → 이따 전화드리겠습니다 (formal) → 이따 전화할게 (반말) → 이따 두 시쯤 전화드릴게요 (with specific time).

Writing 있다가 for 이따 — 있다가 is 있다 + -다가 ('after being/staying somewhere'), a different grammar word entirely. The 'later today' time adverb is 이따(가). Also: using 나중에 when you mean later today weakens the commitment and can sound like avoidance.

entries.english: Could you give me your number?
entries.shortExplanation: 전화번호 좀 알려 주세요. is a practical expression meaning "Could you give me your number?".
entries.explanation: "Could you give me your number?" — that is 전화번호 좀 알려 주세요. (jeonhwabeonho jom allyeo juseyo.). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 전화번호 좀 알려 주세요. ("Please give me your phone number."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Please give me your phone number.
usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; the standard polite request — 좀 softens it from a demand into 'if you would'
반말; to a close friend or younger person — equally natural in a casual context

usagePhrases.en: Could you give me your contact info?
usagePhrases.note: More formal/격식; 연락처 covers phone number and/or email; -주시겠어요? makes it an offer question, appropriate in business

usagePhrases.ko: 혹시 전화번호 좀 알 수 있을까요?
usagePhrases.romanization: hoksi jeonhwabeonho jom al su isseulkkayo?
usagePhrases.en: Could I possibly get your number?
usagePhrases.note: Extension; extra-tentative phrasing with 혹시 ('perhaps') + 알 수 있을까요? — ideal when asking a stranger or someone senior you don't know well

examples.ko: A: 다음에 연락드릴게요. / B: 네, 전화번호 좀 알려 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: A: daeume yeollakdeurilgeyo. / B: ne, jeonhwabeonho jom allyeo jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: A: I'll get in touch next time. / B: Sure, could you give me your number?
examples.note: Natural A/B exchange at the end of a call or meeting — B transitions the conversation into a number exchange

examples.ko: 나중에 연락드릴게요. 전화번호 좀 알려 주세요.
examples.romanization: najunge yeollakdeurilgeyo. jeonhwabeonho jom allyeo juseyo.
examples.en: I'll get in touch later — could you give me your number?
examples.note: Everyday use: asking so you can follow up — the sequential phrasing (연락드릴게요 → 번호 주세요) models natural Korean flow

examples.ko: 예약 확인 문자를 보내 드릴게요. 연락처 좀 알려 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: yeya kwagin munjareul bonae deurilgeyo. yeollakcheo jom allyeo jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: I'll text you a booking confirmation. Could you give me your contact number?
examples.note: Fuller situation: a staffer taking a number for a reservation — the reason given first (문자를 보내 드릴게요) makes the request feel purposeful and trustworthy

entries.nuance: 전화번호 좀 알려 주세요 politely asks for a phone number — 알리다 ('to let someone know / inform') plus the request 주세요, with 좀 ('just a little') softening the whole thing into a gentle ask. The verb must be 알려 주다: do NOT use 가르치다 ('to teach'), which is for teaching a skill or subject; 번호를 가르쳐 주세요 sounds like you want a lesson in phone numbers. For business, 연락처 ('contact details', can include email or phone) is more professional than 전화번호. A very natural and honorific alternative: 전화번호가 어떻게 되세요? — this uses 어떻게 되세요?, the Korean honorific formula for asking for personal information ('how does it go?'), which is far more polite than 전화번호가 뭐예요?. The English-speaker trap is dropping 좀 and 주세요 to get the bare 전화번호 알려 — without these softeners it is abrupt and slightly pushy.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 가르쳐 주세요 for a number — 가르치다 is to teach a subject; to share info say 알려 주세요.
Asking 전화번호가 뭐예요? to an elder/stranger — prefer the honorific 어떻게 되세요? or 알려 주세요.
Dropping 좀/주세요 (전화번호 알려) — it sounds abrupt; keep 좀 알려 주세요 to stay polite.

structuredNuance.t: 전화번호(phone number) 좀(just a little) 알려(let-know) 주세요(please-do-for-me) — literally 'please let me know your phone number a little bit.' The '좀' + '주세요' combination is what makes this a polite request rather than a demand; both softeners are required.
존댓말; standard for anyone. For business or seniors, upgrade to 연락처 좀 알려 주시겠어요? or the honorific 전화번호가 어떻게 되세요?. 반말: 전화번호 좀 알려 줘. Never ask 전화번호가 뭐예요? to an elder — 뭐예요 is too blunt for personal info.

전화번호 좀 알려 주세요 vs 전화번호가 어떻게 되세요?: both polite; the former is a direct request, the latter is the honorific inquiry form ('how does the number go?') — 어떻게 되세요? is the standard Korean way to ask for personal details honorifically. vs 연락처 알려 주세요: 연락처 is broader (phone + email).
전화번호 좀 알려 주세요 → 전화번호가 어떻게 되세요? (honorific inquiry) → 연락처 좀 알려 주시겠어요? (formal, business) → 혹시 전화번호 좀 알 수 있을까요? (extra-tentative) → 전화번호 좀 알려 줘 (반말).

가르쳐 주세요 for 'tell me your number' — 가르치다 is to teach a skill or subject; for sharing a piece of information use 알려 주다. Also: stripping away 좀 and 주세요 to get 전화번호 알려 sounds rude and demanding — the softeners are not optional politeness additions.

entries.english: I came to buy a SIM card
entries.shortExplanation: 유심 사러 왔어요 is a practical expression meaning "I came to buy a SIM card".
entries.explanation: 유심 사러 왔어요 (yusim sareo wasseoyo) = "I came to buy a SIM card". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 유심 사러 왔어요 ("I came to buy a SIM card"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: I came to buy a SIM card
usagePhrases.note: Polite; said as you walk into a phone shop or convenience store

usagePhrases.en: I'm here to get a SIM
usagePhrases.note: 반말, only with a friend tagging along, not to staff
Straight request once you know they have it
선불 ('prepaid') vs. 후불 ('postpaid') — ask which they sell

examples.ko: 유심 사러 왔어요.
examples.romanization: yusim sareo wasseoyo.
examples.en: I came to buy a SIM card.
examples.note: Opening line as you reach the counter; 사러 왔다 = came in order to buy

examples.ko: 외국인인데 유심 사러 왔어요. 여권 보여 드릴까요?
examples.romanization: oegugininde yusim sareo wasseoyo. yeogwon boyeo deurilkkayo?
examples.en: I'm a foreigner, I came for a SIM — should I show my passport?
examples.note: Offering your 여권 up front speeds things up; ID is required for 유심 registration

examples.ko: A: 어서 오세요. 뭐 찾으세요? / B: 선불 유심 사러 왔어요. 여행용으로요.
examples.romanization: A: eoseo oseyo. mwo chajeuseyo? / B: seonbul yusim sareo wasseoyo. yeohaengyongeuroyo.
examples.en: A: Welcome! What can I help you with? / B: I came to buy a prepaid SIM — for travel.
examples.note: A/B exchange: give 선불 ('prepaid') and your purpose so staff can pull the right product immediately

entries.nuance: 유심 is the Korean pronunciation of 'USIM', the subscriber identity chip — Koreans almost never say 'SIM 카드' with both English words; the single word 유심 is standard everywhere from street kiosks to carrier shops. The grammar pattern is verb-stem + -(으)러 ('in order to') + 왔어요 ('came'), literally 'I came in order to buy', which is the natural way to state your purpose on entering any shop. This purpose-statement form 사러 왔어요 is distinct from 유심 하나 주세요 (the direct purchase request): use 사러 왔어요 first as your opening, then switch to 주세요 once stock is confirmed. Crucially, 유심 (the physical chip) and 개통 (activating the line) are two separate steps — buying a 유심 does not automatically mean your number is live. Default 존댓말 with staff in all situations; 반말 사러 왔어 is only possible between peers.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 유심 카드 (sim-card) as two English words.
Koreans say just 유심. Adding '카드' is redundant and sounds learner-ish. Use 유심 하나 주세요 or 유심 사러 왔어요.
Asking 유심 살 수 있어요? to open.
That literally checks your ability/permission to buy. To state your purpose on entering, say 유심 사러 왔어요; to order, 유심 하나 주세요.
Confusing 유심 with 개통.
유심 is the physical chip; 개통 is activating the phone line. Buying a 유심 doesn't automatically mean 개통 — you may still need to ask them to 개통해 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I came in order to buy a USIM.' 실제: a natural shop-entry purpose statement, not a description of movement. The -(으)러 왔어요 frame is how you announce WHY you walked in; it does NOT imply you searched for a store — it simply declares intent.
