examples.ko: 일반우편이랑 등기랑 가격 차이 얼마나 나요? 그럼 등기로 보내 주세요.
examples.romanization: ilbanupyeonirang deunggirang gagyeok chai eolmana nayo? geureom deunggiro bonae juseyo.
examples.en: How much is the difference between regular and registered? Then please send it registered.
examples.note: Price-compare before committing; 그럼 ('then') signals the decision

entries.nuance: 이거 등기로 보내 주세요 is 이거 ('this') + 등기 ('registered mail', Sino-Korean 登記, lit. 'registration') + -로 ('by/via', the method particle) + 보내 주세요 ('please send for me'). 등기(우편) is mail that is logged, tracked, and requires the recipient's signature on delivery — you use it for contracts, official documents, anything you must prove arrived. The crucial particle is -로, which marks the METHOD ('by registered'); leaving it out (등기 보내 주세요) sounds off, and using the wrong particle (등기를) makes 등기 the object rather than the manner. For extra formality, 등기로 보내 주시겠어요? adds -주시겠어요; once the item is already on the counter you can shorten to 등기로 해 주세요. The sharp contrast is 등기 vs 일반우편 ('ordinary mail'): 일반우편 is cheap and untracked — fine for a postcard but risky for documents; 등기 costs more but is provable. Don't confuse 등기 (registered MAIL) with 등기부등본 (a property-registration certificate) — same 등기 root, totally different errand. The English-speaker pitfall is calling it 'certified mail' and trying to coin 인증우편, which isn't the term; the real word is 등기. Also, learners often forget the favor verb and say 등기로 보내요, which describes rather than requests — keep 보내 주세요 to actually ask the clerk.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Dropping -로 and saying 등기 보내 주세요 / 등기를 보내 주세요.
등기 is the method here, so it needs -로: 등기로 보내 주세요. 등기를 wrongly makes 'registered' the object being sent.
Confusing 등기 (registered mail) with 등기부등본.
등기 here is a postal service; 등기부등본 is a property registry document. Asking for 등기부등본 at the parcel counter is a different errand entirely.
Inventing 인증우편 for 'certified mail'.
The Korean term for tracked, signed-for mail is 등기(우편), not a literal 인증우편. Say 등기로 보내 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 이거 ('this') + 등기 ('registered mail') + -로 (method particle, 'by/via') + 보내 주세요 ('please send for me'). 등기(우편) is mail that is logged, tracked, and requires the recipient's signature on delivery — use it for contracts, official documents, anything you must prove arrived.

등기 literally means 'registration' (登記) — the mail service is named for the act of officially recording the package in the postal log. Calling it 'certified mail' or coining 인증우편 misses this; the correct term is 등기(우편).

등기 vs 일반우편: 일반우편 is cheap and untracked — fine for a postcard, risky for documents; 등기 costs more but is provable. Don't confuse 등기 (registered MAIL) with 등기부등본 (a property-registration certificate) — same root, different errand.
Shorter once item is on the counter: 등기로 해 주세요. More formal: 등기로 보내 주시겠어요? Full explicit version: 이거 등기우편으로 보내 주세요. To add speed: 빠른우편으로 해 주세요.

Calling it 'certified mail' and inventing 인증우편 doesn't work — the Korean term is 등기(우편). Dropping -로 and saying 등기 보내 주세요 or using 등기를 makes the method the object instead. Learners also say 등기로 보내요 (just describes) instead of 보내 주세요 (the actual request).

entries.english: Could you tell me the tracking number?
entries.shortExplanation: 송장 번호 좀 알려 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Could you tell me the tracking number?".
entries.explanation: "Could you tell me the tracking number?" — that is 송장 번호 좀 알려 주세요 (songjang beonho jom allyeo juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 송장 번호 좀 알려 주세요 ("Could you tell me the tracking number?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Could you tell me the tracking number?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking the clerk for the number to track the parcel
반말, asking a friend who sent it
운송장 = the fuller word; 어떻게 돼요 is the natural 'what is it'

usagePhrases.en: Please text me the tracking number
usagePhrases.note: 문자로 ('by text') to get it sent to your phone

examples.ko: A: 다 됐어요. / B: 감사해요! 송장 번호 좀 알려 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: da dwaesseoyo. / B: gamsahaeyo! songjang beonho jom allyeo juseyo.
examples.en: A: All done. / B: Thank you! Could you tell me the tracking number?
examples.note: Said right after paying and handing over the parcel — the natural moment to ask

examples.ko: 택배 보냈는데 송장 번호로 조회하면 돼요?
examples.romanization: taekbae bonaenneunde songjang beonhoro johoehamyeon dwaeyo?
examples.en: I sent a parcel — can I track it with the tracking number?
examples.note: 조회하다 ('to look up/check') is the verb for checking parcel status online

examples.ko: 송장 번호 받았는데 아직 조회가 안 돼요. 언제부터 떠요?
examples.romanization: songjang beonho badanneunde ajik johoega an dwaeyo. eonjebuteo tteoyo?
examples.en: I got the tracking number but it's not showing yet. When does it appear?
examples.note: 뜨다 ('to come up/appear on screen') is how Koreans say tracking info 'appears'

entries.nuance: 송장 번호 좀 알려 주세요 is 송장 ('waybill/invoice slip', Sino-Korean 送狀, the shipping label on a parcel) + 번호 ('number') + 좀 (softener) + 알려 주세요 ('please let me know / tell me'). The 송장 is the slip stuck on the box; its 번호 (also called 운송장 번호 or 택배 번호) is what you punch into a carrier's website or app to follow the parcel. The verb you then pair with that number is 조회하다 ('to look up/track'), and on screen Koreans say the status 뜨다 ('appears/shows up'). A key distinction: 송장 번호 (shipping waybill number for tracking) is NOT 영수증 (the payment receipt) — the 송장 number tracks the parcel, the 영수증 proves you paid; asking for the wrong one gets you the wrong slip. Note 송장 also means a commercial 'invoice' in trade contexts, but at a parcel counter it's always the shipping label. Common variants: 운송장 번호 (slightly more formal), 택배 번호 (casual shortening). The English-speaker pitfall is translating 'tracking number' literally as 추적 번호 — understandable, and 추적 ('tracking/chasing') exists, but the everyday counter term is 송장 번호 / 운송장 번호. Another classic slip is using 가르치다 ('to teach') instead of 알려 주다 ('to inform'): 번호 가르쳐 주세요 sounds like asking for a lesson; 알려 주세요 means 'let me know.'
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 추적 번호 for the tracking number.
추적 ('tracking/chasing') is understandable but not the counter term. Koreans say 송장 번호 or 운송장 번호 for a parcel's tracking number.
Confusing 송장 번호 with 영수증.
송장 번호 is the shipping waybill number used to track the parcel; 영수증 is the payment receipt. Ask for 송장 번호 to track, 영수증 to prove you paid.
Using 가르쳐 주세요 instead of 알려 주세요.
가르치다 means 'to teach (a skill)'. To ask someone to tell you a number, use 알려 주다: 송장 번호 좀 알려 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 송장 ('waybill/invoice slip', 送狀 — the shipping label stuck on the parcel) + 번호 ('number') + 좀 (softener) + 알려 주세요 ('please let me know'). This number lets you track the parcel; the verb for looking it up is 조회하다, and the status 뜨다 ('appears') on screen.

송장 literally means 'dispatch document' (送狀). At a parcel counter it is the waybill label glued to the box, and its 번호 is the unique tracking ID — not 'invoice number' in the financial sense, and definitely not 영수증 (the payment receipt).

송장 번호 = 운송장 번호 = 택배 번호 — all refer to the same tracking ID, in decreasing formality. 영수증 is the payment receipt — a completely different slip. Don't confuse them: 송장 번호 tracks the parcel, 영수증 proves you paid.
Slightly more formal: 운송장 번호 좀 알려 주세요. Casual shortening: 택배 번호 좀요. To ask it be texted to you: 송장 번호 문자로 보내 주세요. To ask if tracking works yet: 지금 조회 돼요?

Translating 'tracking number' as 추적 번호 is understandable but not the counter term — say 송장 번호 or 운송장 번호. Using 가르치다 ('to teach') instead of 알려 주다 ('to inform') is a classic error: 번호 가르쳐 주세요 sounds like asking for a lesson.

entries.english: Please send it cash-on-delivery (recipient pays)
entries.shortExplanation: 착불로 보내 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please send it cash-on-delivery (recipient pays)".
entries.explanation: 착불로 보내 주세요 (chakbullo bonae juseyo) = "Please send it cash-on-delivery (recipient pays)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 착불로 보내 주세요 ("Please send it C.O.D. (recipient pays)"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the receiver pays the shipping fee on delivery
반말, to a friend
Short form once the parcel is already on the counter

usagePhrases.en: Please send it prepaid (I pay now)
usagePhrases.note: The opposite: 선불, sender pays up front — useful to contrast

examples.ko: A: 선불이에요, 착불이에요? / B: 착불로 보내 주세요. 상대방이 내기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: A: seonburieyo, chakburieyo? / B: chakbullo bonae juseyo. sangdaebangi naegiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: A: Prepaid or C.O.D.? / B: C.O.D., please — the other person agreed to pay.
examples.note: The clerk's 선불/착불 question and your answer; 상대방 = 'the other party'

examples.ko: 받는 분이 낼 거예요. 착불로 보내 주세요.
examples.romanization: banneun buni nael geoyeyo. chakbullo bonae juseyo.
examples.en: The recipient will pay — send it C.O.D.
examples.note: 받는 분 ('the recipient') makes clear who covers the shipping fee

examples.ko: 중고거래라서 착불로 하기로 했어요. 그렇게 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: junggogeoraeraseo chakbullo hagiro haesseoyo. geureoke hae juseyo.
examples.en: It's a secondhand sale so we agreed to 착불. Please do it that way.
examples.note: 중고거래 (secondhand deals) routinely use 착불; 그렇게 해 주세요 confirms the arrangement

entries.nuance: 착불로 보내 주세요 is 착불 ('payment on arrival', Sino-Korean 着拂, lit. 'pay-on-arrival') + -로 ('by', method particle) + 보내 주세요 ('please send'). 착불 means the RECIPIENT pays the shipping fee when the parcel is handed to them — extremely common in Korea for online resale (중고거래), returns, and favors between acquaintances. Its exact opposite is 선불 ('prepay', 先拂), where the SENDER pays at the counter now. The clerk will often ask 선불이에요, 착불이에요? and this is your answer, so getting the pair straight is essential: 착불 = receiver pays later, 선불 = sender pays now. The method particle -로 is required (착불로); 착불을 would wrongly make 착불 the object. For a shorter on-counter version once you've handed the parcel, 착불로 해 주세요 is perfectly natural. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 착불 to 'C.O.D.' and assuming it covers the price of the GOODS — in Korean parcels 착불 almost always refers only to the SHIPPING FEE, not the product price. Another social trap: deciding 착불 for someone without telling them — they'll be charged at their door. Don't confuse 착불 with 반품 ('return of goods'); they often co-occur but mean different things.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Mixing up 착불 and 선불.
착불 = the recipient pays on delivery; 선불 = the sender pays now at the counter. If YOU want to pay up front, say 선불로 보내 주세요, not 착불로.
Thinking 착불 means the receiver pays for the product.
In parcels, 착불 refers to the SHIPPING FEE, not the item's price. The goods are settled separately; 착불 only decides who pays delivery.
Dropping -로: 착불 보내 주세요 / 착불을 보내 주세요.
착불 is a method, so it takes -로: 착불로 보내 주세요. 착불을 wrongly treats 'C.O.D.' as the thing being sent.

structuredNuance.t: 착불 ('payment on arrival', 着拂) + -로 ('by', method particle) + 보내 주세요. 착불 means the RECIPIENT pays the shipping fee at their door. Extremely common in 중고거래 (secondhand transactions) and returns. The method particle -로 is required; 착불을 wrongly makes it the object.

착불 literally means 'pay upon arrival' (着拂). In practice it covers ONLY the shipping fee, not the product price. This differs from English 'C.O.D.' where the goods cost is also collected at delivery — in Korean 착불 parcels, the item's price is settled separately.

착불 (receiver pays on delivery) vs 선불 (sender pays now at the counter). The clerk asks 선불이에요, 착불이에요? — know both sides. Don't confuse 착불 with 반품 ('product return'); they often co-occur (returns are usually sent 착불) but are different concepts.
Shorter on-counter form: 착불로 해 주세요. Confirming agreement: 착불로 하기로 했어요. The full opposite: 선불로 보내 주세요 (I pay now). Checking which: 선불이에요 착불이에요?

Thinking 착불 = C.O.D. including the goods price is wrong — it covers only the shipping fee. Dropping -로 (착불 보내 주세요) or using 착불을 makes 착불 the object instead of the method. Also, socially you must tell the recipient in advance — they'll be charged at the door without warning.

entries.english: It's fragile, so please handle it carefully
entries.shortExplanation: 깨지는 거라서 조심히 다뤄 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "It's fragile, so please handle it carefully".
entries.explanation: 깨지는 거라서 조심히 다뤄 주세요 (kkaejineun georaseo josimhi darwo juseyo) means "It's fragile, so please handle it carefully". Say it as one set phrase — for example 깨지는 거라서 조심히 다뤄 주세요 ("It's fragile, so please handle it carefully"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: It's fragile, so please handle it carefully
usagePhrases.note: Polite; warning staff the contents can break

usagePhrases.en: It's breakable, so handle it carefully
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend or mover

usagePhrases.ko: 파손 주의 스티커 좀 붙여 주세요
usagePhrases.romanization: pason juui seutikeo jom butyeo juseyo
usagePhrases.en: Please put a 'Fragile' sticker on it
usagePhrases.note: 파손 주의 = the printed 'handle with care' label

usagePhrases.en: There's glass inside. It breaks easily
usagePhrases.note: Stating the risk plainly; 깨지기 쉽다 = 'easy to break'

examples.ko: A: 안에 뭐 있어요? / B: 유리 그릇이에요. 깨지는 거라서 조심히 다뤄 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: ane mwo isseoyo? / B: yuri geureusieyo. kkaejineun georaseo josimhi darwo juseyo.
examples.en: A: What's inside? / B: Glass dishes. It's fragile so please handle it carefully.
examples.note: The staff's content question leads naturally into the fragile warning

examples.ko: 안에 그릇이 있어서요, 파손 주의로 보내 주세요.
examples.romanization: ane geureusi isseoseoyo, pason juuiro bonae juseyo.
examples.en: There are dishes inside, so please send it as 'fragile'.
examples.note: 파손 주의로 marks the official fragile-handling service option

examples.ko: 이거 깨지기 쉬운 거예요. 위에 뭐 올리지 말아 주세요.
examples.romanization: igeo kkaejigi swiun geoyeyo. wie mwo olliji mara juseyo.
examples.en: This breaks easily. Please don't stack anything on top.
examples.note: 위에 ('on top') + 올리다 ('to place on') for a specific stacking warning

entries.nuance: 깨지는 거라서 조심히 다뤄 주세요 is 깨지는 거 (깨지다 'to break/shatter' + 거 'thing' = 'a breakable thing') + -라서 ('because it is') + 조심히 ('carefully') + 다뤄 주세요 (다루다 'to handle' + 주세요 = 'please handle for me'). It warns staff or a mover that the contents are fragile. The verb pairing is key: 깨지다 is INTRANSITIVE ('it shatters on its own') — which is why you describe the contents as 깨지는 거, not 깨는 거 (that would imply you're smashing it deliberately). The post-office set term is 파손 주의 ('caution: breakage', the printed Fragile label), so a very practical request is 파손 주의로 보내 주세요 or asking for the 파손 주의 스티커. Contrast 조심히 다뤄 주세요 ('handle carefully', a general plea) with 파손 주의로 해 주세요 (asking for the official fragile-handling service/label). The softer variant 깨지기 쉬워요 ('breaks easily') explains the risk without issuing a direct request. Also avoid 부서지다 confusion: 부서지다 is for things crumbling/falling apart (furniture, equipment), while glass and ceramics 깨지다. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 'be careful' → 조심하세요, which tells the PERSON to watch themselves rather than asking them to handle the BOX gently; 조심히 다뤄 주세요 keeps the focus on the parcel.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 깨다 instead of 깨지다.
깨다 means 'to break something on purpose'; the contents break by themselves, so use intransitive 깨지다: 깨지는 거라서…. 깨는 거 would imply you smash it.
Saying just 조심하세요 to mean 'handle it carefully'.
조심하세요 tells the person 'be careful (for yourself)'. To ask them to handle the parcel gently, say 조심히 다뤄 주세요 or 파손 주의로 보내 주세요.
Mixing up 깨지다 and 부서지다.
깨지다 is for glass/ceramics shattering; 부서지다 is for things crumbling apart (like furniture). For dishes or bottles, 깨지는 거예요 is the right word.

structuredNuance.t: 깨지는 거 ('a breakable thing', from intransitive 깨지다 'to shatter') + -라서 ('because it is') + 조심히 ('carefully') + 다뤄 주세요 (다루다 'to handle'). Warns staff the contents are fragile; the post-office label equivalent is 파손 주의 ('caution: breakage').

깨지는 거 literally = 'a thing that breaks'. -라서 gives the reason. The phrase functions as a warning + polite request to the handler, not just a description. At the counter, following it immediately with 파손 주의 스티커 좀 붙여 주세요 gets a concrete result.

조심히 다뤄 주세요 (general careful-handling plea) vs 파손 주의로 해 주세요 (requesting the official fragile service/label). 깨지다 is for glass/ceramics shattering; 부서지다 is for things crumbling apart (furniture). Don't swap them.
Softer risk statement: 깨지기 쉬워요. Official label request: 파손 주의 스티커 좀 붙여 주세요. Stacking prevention: 위에 뭐 올리지 말아 주세요. 반말 variant: 깨지는 거니까 조심히 다뤄 줘.

Saying 조심하세요 tells the person to watch out for themselves, not to handle the parcel gently — use 조심히 다뤄 주세요. Using transitive 깨는 거 instead of intransitive 깨지는 거 implies you're smashing it on purpose. Also 부서지는 거 is for crumbling items, not glass.

entries.english: Can I buy a box here?
entries.shortExplanation: 박스 하나 살 수 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I buy a box here?".
entries.explanation: "Can I buy a box here?" — that is 박스 하나 살 수 있어요? (bakseu hana sal su isseoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 박스 하나 살 수 있어요? ("Can I buy a box here?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Can I buy a box here?
usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; asking if packing boxes are for sale
반말, casual spot
파나요 ('do you sell') is the most natural shop phrasing
포장 박스 = a packing/shipping box; 있어요 asks if they have it

examples.ko: A: 어떻게 오셨어요? / B: 박스 하나 살 수 있어요? 포장을 못 해 왔어요.
examples.romanization: A: eotteoke osyeosseoyo? / B: bakseu hana sal su isseoyo? pojangeul mo tae wasseoyo.
examples.en: A: What brings you in? / B: Can I buy a box? I didn't bring packaging.
examples.note: 포장을 못 해 왔어요 ('I didn't manage to pack it') naturally explains the request

examples.ko: 여기 박스도 팔아요? 제일 작은 거로 하나 주세요.
examples.romanization: yeogi bakseudo parayo? jeil jageun georo hana juseyo.
examples.en: Do you sell boxes too? Give me one of the smallest.
examples.note: 제일 작은 거로 ('the smallest one') picks a size; 우체국 sells numbered sizes 1호~5호

examples.ko: 짐이 좀 큰데, 큰 박스 있어요? 테이프도 같이 주세요.
examples.romanization: jimi jom keunde, keun bakseu isseoyo? teipeudo gachi juseyo.
examples.en: My stuff's a bit big — do you have a large box? Give me tape too.
examples.note: Add 테이프 ('tape') so you can seal it on the spot

entries.nuance: 박스 하나 살 수 있어요? is 박스 (loanword 'box') + 하나 ('one') + 살 수 있어요? (사다 'to buy' + -ㄹ 수 있다 'can' = 'can I buy?'). Post offices and convenience stores sell 우체국 택배 박스 in numbered sizes (1호, 2호, 3호…), so this is a practical first question when you show up with loose items. In real speech, Koreans very naturally ask availability instead: 박스 파나요? ('do you sell boxes?') or 박스 있어요? ('do you have boxes?') — these are often more natural than the literal 'can I buy.' A subtle vocab note: 박스 (loanword) is the colloquial word everyone uses for a shipping carton; 상자 is the native Korean word — both are understood, but 박스 is the default at counters. Sizes are counted with 호 (號): 1호 is the smallest, larger numbers are bigger; ask for 제일 작은 거 or 3호 박스. The English-speaker pitfall is the heavy formal phrasing 제가 박스를 구매할 수 있습니까? — grammatically fine but stiff for a counter; the light, natural ask is 박스 하나 살 수 있어요? or simply 박스 있어요?. Another trap is asking for 종이 ('paper') when you mean a 'cardboard box' — say 박스 or 종이 박스 specifically. Don't forget 테이프 (tape) to seal the box if you're packing on the spot.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 종이 있어요? when you want a box.
종이 is 'paper'. A shipping box is 박스 (or 상자/종이 박스). Say 박스 있어요? or 박스 하나 살 수 있어요?
Over-heavy 제가 박스를 구매할 수 있습니까?
구매하다 ('to purchase') is stiff/formal for a counter. The natural everyday ask is 박스 하나 살 수 있어요? or 박스 있어요?
Assuming there's one box size.
Post-office boxes come in numbered sizes (1호, 2호…); bigger number = bigger box. Ask 제일 작은 거 / 제일 큰 거 to specify which size.

structuredNuance.t: 박스 ('box', loanword) + 하나 ('one') + 살 수 있어요? (사다 'to buy' + -ㄹ 수 있다 'can' = 'can I buy?'). Post offices sell 우체국 택배 박스 in numbered sizes (1호~5호). The everyday alternative 박스 있어요? or 박스 파나요? is often more natural than the ability-question frame.

-ㄹ 수 있어요? asks 'is it possible to…' but in a retail context it functions as a polite purchase inquiry, not a literal capability question. 박스 있어요? ('do you have a box?') is even lighter and equally natural — Koreans often check availability first rather than stating intent to buy.

박스 (loanword, everyday) vs 상자 (native Korean, more formal/written). Both mean a box/carton, but 박스 is what you say at a counter. 여기 박스 파나요? (do you sell?) vs 박스 있어요? (do you have?) — pairing both covers your bases.
More direct: 박스 파나요? / 박스 있어요? Pick a size: 제일 작은 거로 주세요 / 3호 박스 주세요. Add-on: 테이프도 주세요. 반말: 박스 하나 살 수 있어? / 박스 있어?

Heavy 제가 박스를 구매할 수 있습니까? is grammatical but stiff — say 박스 하나 살 수 있어요? or just 박스 있어요?. Asking for 종이 when you want a box doesn't work — say 박스 or 종이 박스. Don't forget sizes come in 호 numbers, not S/M/L.

entries.english: Do I write the recipient's address here?
entries.shortExplanation: 받는 사람 주소는 여기 적으면 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Do I write the recipient's address here?".
entries.explanation: 받는 사람 주소는 여기 적으면 돼요? (banneun saram jusoneun yeogi jeogeumyeon dwaeyo?) = "Do I write the recipient's address here?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 받는 사람 주소는 여기 적으면 돼요? ("Do I write the recipient's address here?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.ko: 받는 사람 주소는 여기 적으면 돼요?

examples.ko: 받는 사람이랑 보내는 사람 둘 다 적어야 돼요? 전화번호도요?
examples.romanization: banneun saramirang bonaeneun saram dul da jeogeoya dwaeyo? jeonhwabeonhodoyo?
examples.en: Do I write both recipient and sender? Phone numbers too?
examples.note: 둘 다 ('both') confirms both sides; 전화번호도요 tacks on the extra question

examples.ko: 글씨 좀 못 써서요, 받는 사람 주소 좀 대신 적어 주실 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: geulssi jom mot sseoseoyo, banneun saram juso jom daesin jeogeo jusil su isseoyo?
examples.en: My handwriting's bad — could you write the recipient's address for me?
examples.note: 대신 적어 주다 ('write on my behalf') is a natural request when you're unsure of the format

entries.nuance: 받는 사람 주소는 여기 적으면 돼요? is 받는 사람 (받다 'to receive' + -는 + 사람 'person' = 'the receiving person/recipient') + 주소 ('address') + 는 (topic) + 여기 ('here') + 적으면 (적다 'to write down' + -(으)면 'if') + 돼요? (되다 'to be okay' = 'is it okay if…?'). The frame -(으)면 돼요? ('is it okay if I…?') is the polite, natural way to confirm a procedure before doing it — perfect for checking where to write on an unfamiliar form. The two parties on every Korean parcel form are 받는 사람 ('recipient') and 보내는 사람 ('sender') — these participial labels are printed on the slip itself, so recognizing them is essential. The verb 적다 ('to write down/note') is the right choice for filling in a form; both 적다 and 쓰다 ('to write') work, but 적다 specifically connotes jotting into a field. Note 적다 the verb ('write') is a homograph of 적다 the adjective ('to be few') — context disambiguates. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for formal terms 수신자/발신자 ('addressee/sender', telecom/mail-header language), when everyday parcel language is 받는 사람/보내는 사람. Another trap is spelling: 돼요 (되 + 어요 → 돼요) is the correct form; 되요 is a frequent native-speaker error too, so watch for it.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 수신자/발신자 at the parcel counter.
수신자/발신자 ('addressee/sender') are formal telecom/mail-header terms. On a parcel slip the everyday words are 받는 사람 (recipient) and 보내는 사람 (sender).
Writing 되요 instead of 돼요.
되 + 어요 contracts to 돼요. 되요 is a spelling error. The question 'is it okay if I write here?' is 여기 적으면 돼요?
Reaching only for 쓰다 to mean 'fill in'.
쓰다 works but is broad (also 'use', 'bitter'). For noting something into a form field, 적다 is the precise verb: 주소 적으면 돼요?

structuredNuance.t: 받는 사람 ('recipient', participial label on the parcel slip) + 주소 ('address') + 는 (topic) + 여기 ('here') + 적으면 돼요? (-(으)면 돼요? = 'is it okay if I…?'). The -(으)면 돼요? frame is the natural way to confirm a procedure before acting — correct for pointing at a form field and checking.

Literally: 'As for the recipient's address, if I write it here, is it okay?' In practice it's a humble clarifying question as you hold the pen — not expressing doubt, just politely checking the layout. It invites the clerk to guide or simply confirm.

받는 사람 (everyday parcel label) vs 수신자 (formal mail/telecom term) — say 받는 사람 at the counter. 적다 ('jot into a field') vs 쓰다 ('write', broader) — both work but 적다 is the more precise form-filling verb. Note 적다 the adjective ('few') is a homograph — context resolves it.
Other field questions: 보내는 사람은 어디에 적어요? / 전화번호도 적어야 돼요? / 우편번호도요? To ask the clerk to fill it in: 대신 적어 주실 수 있어요? 반말: 받는 사람 주소는 여기 적으면 돼?

Using 수신자/발신자 (formal telecom terms) at a parcel counter sounds bureaucratic — say 받는 사람/보내는 사람. Writing 되요 instead of 돼요 is a spelling error; the contraction is 되 + 어요 → 돼요. Reaching only for 쓰다 and ignoring 적다 — for form fields, 적다 is more precise.

entries.english: About when will it arrive?
entries.shortExplanation: 언제쯤 도착해요? is a practical expression meaning "About when will it arrive?".
entries.explanation: 언제쯤 도착해요? (eonjejjeum dochakaeyo?) means "About when will it arrive?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 언제쯤 도착해요? ("About when will it arrive?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking the expected delivery time
반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: How many days does it take?
usagePhrases.note: Asking duration instead of a date
Checking specifically for next-day delivery

examples.ko: A: 오늘 발송 처리 됩니다. / B: 그럼 언제쯤 도착해요?
examples.romanization: A: oneul balsong cheori doemnida. / B: geureom eonjejjeum dochakaeyo?
examples.en: A: It'll be dispatched today. / B: So about when will it arrive?
examples.note: 그럼 ('then/so') links the staff's confirmation to your timing question naturally

examples.ko: 오늘 보내면 언제쯤 도착해요? 제주도까지요.
examples.romanization: oneul bonaemyeon eonjejjeum dochakaeyo? jejudokkajiyo.
examples.en: If I send today, about when does it arrive? All the way to Jeju.
examples.note: Name the destination (제주도) since islands take longer than the mainland

examples.ko: 급한 건데 내일까지 도착할 수 있어요? 안 되면 더 빠른 서비스 있어요?
examples.romanization: geupan geonde naeilkkaji dochakal su isseoyo? an doemyeon deo ppareun seobiseu isseoyo?
examples.en: It's urgent — can it arrive by tomorrow? If not, is there a faster service?
examples.note: 급하다 ('urgent') + 안 되면 ('if not') pushes for a faster option

entries.nuance: 언제쯤 도착해요? is 언제 ('when') + -쯤 ('approximately/around') + 도착하다 ('to arrive', Sino-Korean 到着) in polite present/future form. The -쯤 is the politeness and realism softener — it signals you want an estimate, not a guarantee, exactly right for asking delivery staff about timing. The verb 도착하다 takes the PARCEL as its subject; don't say 제가 도착해요 (that means YOU arrive). A natural alternative framing is duration: 며칠 걸려요? ('how many days does it take?'), using 걸리다 ('to take time'). Contrast the two: 언제쯤 도착해요? asks for a calendar date or time ('Wednesday?', '3 days from now?'), while 며칠 걸려요? asks for a number of days — choose based on whether you need a specific day or just a count. For island destinations add 제주도까지 ('to Jeju') because sea shipping adds days. The English-speaker pitfall is omitting -쯤 and asking the blunt 언제 도착해요?, which demands a precise time staff often can't commit to. Another trap is the 직역 'when does it come?' → 언제 와요?, which is fine for something coming TO YOU but sounds odd when you've just SENT something away; for outbound parcels, 도착하다 is the cleaner verb.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 제가 도착해요 to mean 'when will it arrive'.
도착하다's subject is the parcel, not you. 제가 도착해요 means 'I arrive'. For the package, say (택배가) 언제쯤 도착해요?
Dropping -쯤 and demanding 언제 도착해요?
Without -쯤 it asks for an exact time, which staff can't always promise. 언제쯤 도착해요? politely signals you want an estimate.
Using 걸리다 for a date: 언제 걸려요?
걸리다 measures duration, so it pairs with 며칠/얼마나: 며칠 걸려요? For a specific date, use 도착하다: 언제쯤 도착해요?

structuredNuance.t: 언제 ('when') + -쯤 ('approximately') + 도착하다 ('to arrive', 到着). The -쯤 marks this as a request for an estimate — polite and realistic. The parcel is the subject of 도착하다; 제가 도착해요 means 'I arrive', not the package.

Literally 'approximately when does it arrive?' In use it's the standard post-office timeline question. Without -쯤 it demands an exact time; without 도착해요 and using 와요 instead, it sounds like something coming to you personally, not a dispatched parcel.

언제쯤 도착해요? (asks for a specific arrival date/time) vs 며칠 걸려요? (asks for number of days). Use the first when you need a day, the second when you just need a count. Both are natural — the staff answers either way.
Duration version: 며칠 걸려요? / 보통 이틀 정도 걸려요? Deadline check: 내일까지 도착 가능해요? Naming destination: 제주도까지 언제쯤 도착해요? 반말: 언제쯤 도착해?

Dropping -쯤 (언제 도착해요?) demands an exact time staff can't always promise. Using 언제 와요? sounds like you're waiting for something to come to you, not asking about a dispatched parcel — say 도착해요. Saying 제가 도착해요 means you yourself arrive.

entries.english: I'm here to pick up a parcel
entries.shortExplanation: 택배 받으러 왔어요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm here to pick up a parcel".
entries.explanation: "I'm here to pick up a parcel" — that is 택배 받으러 왔어요 (taekbae badeureo wasseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 택배 받으러 왔어요 ("I'm here to pick up a parcel"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: I'm here to pick up a parcel
usagePhrases.note: Polite; said at a counter or pickup point to collect a package

usagePhrases.en: I came to get a parcel
usagePhrases.note: 반말, casual

usagePhrases.en: I came to collect a parcel
usagePhrases.note: 찾다 ('to retrieve/claim') is also very natural for pickup
수령 = the formal word for 'receipt/collection'; stiffer, official tone

examples.ko: A: 어떻게 오셨어요? / B: 택배 받으러 왔어요. 어제 부재중이라서요.
examples.romanization: A: eotteoke osyeosseoyo? / B: taekbae badeureo wasseoyo. eoje bujaejungiraseoyo.
examples.en: A: What brings you in? / B: I'm here to pick up a parcel — I was out yesterday.
examples.note: 어제 부재중이라서요 ('I was absent yesterday') explains why you're collecting in person

examples.ko: 부재중이라 못 받아서 택배 찾으러 왔는데요.
examples.romanization: bujaejungira mot badaseo taekbae chajeureo wanneundeyo.
examples.en: I missed it while I was out, so I came to collect the parcel.
examples.note: 부재중 ('absent/not in') is the official status word used on missed-delivery notices

examples.ko: 여기 우체국이죠? 택배 수령하러 왔어요. 신분증 필요해요?
examples.romanization: yeogi uchegugijyo? taekbae suryeonghareo wasseoyo. sinbunjeung piryohaeyo?
examples.en: This is the post office, right? I'm here to receive a parcel. Do I need ID?
examples.note: 수령 in an official setting; ask about 신분증 (ID) proactively

entries.nuance: 택배 받으러 왔어요 is 택배 ('parcel') + 받으러 (받다 'to receive' + -(으)러 'in order to') + 왔어요 ('I came'). The -(으)러 왔어요 frame literally means 'I came in order to receive' and is the standard way to state your PURPOSE on arriving somewhere. There are three near-synonyms with different registers: 받다 ('to receive', everyday and warm), 찾다 ('to claim/retrieve', also very common for picking up something held for you — 택배 찾으러 왔는데요), and 수령하다 ('to take receipt', Sino-Korean 受領, formal/official — what signs and staff use). For a friendly pickup, 받으러/찾으러 왔어요 is the natural choice; 수령하러 왔어요 matches official language on forms and signs. The crucial grammar point is the connective -(으)러, which marks purpose-of-motion: it must attach to a movement verb (오다/가다). Don't confuse it with -(으)려고 ('intending to'): 받으러 왔어요 (purpose: I came to receive) vs 받으려고 왔어요 (intent: I came because I intend to receive) — both are used, but 받으러 is the lighter, more natural counter line. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 'I came for my parcel' → 택배를 위해 왔어요 (위해 = 'for the sake of'), which sounds abstract; use -(으)러 for concrete-purpose arrivals.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 택배를 위해 왔어요.
위해 ('for the sake of') is abstract and unnatural for an errand. Use purpose-of-motion -(으)러: 택배 받으러 왔어요 / 찾으러 왔어요.
Attaching -(으)러 to a non-motion verb.
-(으)러 needs 오다/가다. 받으러 왔어요 (came to receive) is correct; you can't say 받으러 했어요. With 하다, use a different frame.
Using 수령하러 왔어요 with a casual clerk.
수령 is formal/bureaucratic. For an ordinary pickup, 받으러 왔어요 or 찾으러 왔어요 sounds friendlier and more natural.

structuredNuance.t: 택배 ('parcel') + 받으러 (받다 'to receive' + -(으)러 'in order to') + 왔어요 ('I came'). The -(으)러 왔어요 frame is the standard purpose-of-motion construction; it tells the clerk exactly why you're there in the fewest syllables.

Literally 'I came in order to receive a parcel.' It functions as a one-line counter opener that replaces a whole explanation. The -(으)러 specifically signals you've arrived at a destination to perform an action — not just wandering in.
받다 (everyday, warm) vs 찾다 (claim/retrieve — 택배 찾으러 왔는데요, also very common) vs 수령하다 (formal/official — matches signs and forms). For casual pickup: 받으러/찾으러. For matching official language: 수령하러.
Softer version: 택배 찾으러 왔는데요 (trailing -는데요 invites the clerk's guidance). Official: 수령하러 왔어요. 반말: 택배 받으러 왔어. Adding explanation: 부재중이라서 못 받았어요.

택배를 위해 왔어요 ('came for the sake of the parcel') is abstract — use -(으)러 for concrete-purpose arrivals. -(으)러 must pair with a movement verb; you can't say 받으러 했어요. Don't confuse -(으)러 (purpose of motion) with -(으)려고 (general intent).

entries.english: I'd like to return this to the sender
entries.shortExplanation: 이거 반송하고 싶은데요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to return this to the sender".
entries.explanation: 이거 반송하고 싶은데요 (igeo bansonghago sipeundeyo) = "I'd like to return this to the sender". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 이거 반송하고 싶은데요 ("I'd like to return this to the sender"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to return this to the sender
usagePhrases.note: Polite; sending an item back where it came from
반말, to a friend
처리하다 ('to process') for the official handling
수취 거부 = refusing the parcel at the door so it goes back

examples.ko: A: 어떻게 오셨어요? / B: 이거 반송하고 싶은데요. 주소가 잘못 왔어요.
examples.romanization: A: eotteoke osyeosseoyo? / B: igeo bansonghago sipeundeyo. jusoga jalmot wasseoyo.
examples.en: A: What brings you in? / B: I'd like to return this — it came to the wrong address.
examples.note: 주소가 잘못 왔어요 ('it came to the wrong address') is a natural explanation for 반송

examples.ko: 주소가 틀려서 왔어요. 반송 처리해 주세요.
examples.romanization: jusoga teullyeoseo wasseoyo. bansong cheorihae juseyo.
examples.en: It came because the address was wrong. Please process a return.
examples.note: 주소가 틀리다 ('the address is wrong') is the most common reason for 반송

examples.ko: 아직 안 뜯었어요. 그냥 반송하면 되죠? 수취 거부도 돼요?
examples.romanization: ajik an tteudeosseoyo. geunyang bansonghamyeon doejyo? suchwi geobudo dwaeyo?
examples.en: I haven't opened it yet. I can just return it, right? Can I also refuse receipt?
examples.note: 안 뜯다 ('not opened yet') matters for clean returns; 수취 거부 as an alternative option

entries.nuance: 이거 반송하고 싶은데요 is 이거 ('this') + 반송하다 ('to return/send back', Sino-Korean 返送, lit. 'return-dispatch') + -고 싶다 ('want to') + -은데요 (soft, conversation-opening sentence ender). 반송 specifically means redirecting a parcel BACK to its origin or sender — triggered by a wrong address, a refused delivery, or a return. The trailing -은데요 is the politeness engine: it softens the request and leaves room for the clerk to guide you, rather than issuing a flat command. Distinguish 반송 ('return to SENDER', physical redirection) from 반품 ('product return/refund', the consumer transaction with the seller) — they often co-occur (a 반품 is usually shipped as a 반송) but are not synonyms: 반품 is about the refund/exchange, 반송 is about the physical rerouting. A third related term is 수취 거부 ('refusal of receipt'), where you decline the parcel at your door before ever accepting it, so it returns automatically — useful when you want to reject it entirely. For the official short request once at the counter: 반송 처리 좀 해 주세요. The English-speaker pitfall is using 돌려주다 ('to give back to a person') for mailing something back — 돌려주다 fits handing an item back face-to-face; for posting a parcel back to its origin, 반송하다 is the term. Also, -고 싶은데요 ('I'd like to, and…') is softer and more natural to staff than the blunt 반송할래요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 반송 with 반품.
반송 = sending a parcel back to its sender/origin; 반품 = returning purchased goods for a refund. For a refund request to a shop, you'd talk about 반품; to physically send the box back, 반송.
Using 돌려주다 to mean 'return by mail'.
돌려주다 is handing something back to a person directly. To post a parcel back to where it came from, use 반송하다: 이거 반송하고 싶은데요.
Saying flat 반송할래요 to staff.
-(으)ㄹ래요 can sound a bit willful. Softer and more natural is 반송하고 싶은데요 or 반송 처리 좀 해 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 이거 ('this') + 반송하다 ('to return/send back', 返送) + -고 싶다 ('want to') + -은데요 (soft opener). 반송 = physically redirecting a parcel back to its sender/origin. The -은데요 ender invites the clerk's guidance rather than issuing a command.

반송 literally means 'return dispatch' (返送). At the counter it always means sending the physical package back — not requesting a refund. The refund/exchange conversation is 반품; the shipping-it-back action is 반송.

반송 (return to sender, about the physical rerouting) vs 반품 (product return for refund, about the transaction) — they overlap but aren't the same. 수취 거부 is refusing a parcel at your door before accepting it, triggering automatic return. Use 반송 once you've already received the package.
Official short form: 반송 처리 좀 해 주세요. Before delivery: 수취 거부할게요. Explaining reason: 주소가 잘못 왔어요 / 잘못 배송된 것 같아요. 반말: 반송하고 싶어.

돌려주다 ('give back face-to-face') doesn't work for mailing a parcel back — use 반송하다. Confusing 반송 with 반품 means you may ask for a refund when you just want to redirect the box. -고 싶은데요 is softer than 반송할래요 — stick with the -은데요 form at counters.

entries.english: What are the contents? — It's clothes
entries.shortExplanation: 내용물이 뭐예요? — 옷이에요 is a practical expression meaning "What are the contents? — It's clothes".
entries.explanation: 내용물이 뭐예요? — 옷이에요 (naeyongmuri mwoyeyo? — osieyo) means "What are the contents? — It's clothes". Say it as one set phrase — for example 내용물이 뭐예요? ("What are the contents?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: What staff ask you; you answer with the item
More casual phrasing of the same question, often asked by staff
Your reply: name the item + 이에요/예요
Reassuring there are no fragile contents

examples.ko: A: 내용물이 뭐예요? / B: 옷이에요. 깨지는 건 없어요.
examples.romanization: A: naeyongmuri mwoyeyo? / B: osieyo. kkaejineun geon eopseoyo.
examples.en: A: What are the contents? / B: Clothes. Nothing breakable.
examples.note: The natural counter exchange — answer the item, then volunteer that nothing is fragile

examples.ko: 안에 뭐 들어 있어요? — 책이랑 옷이요. 깨지는 건 없어요.
examples.romanization: ane mwo deureo isseoyo? — chaegirang osiyo. kkaejineun geon eopseoyo.
examples.en: What's inside? — Books and clothes. Nothing breakable.
examples.note: List with -이랑; note no fragile items to preempt the follow-up question

examples.ko: 내용물 적어 주셔야 돼요. — 화장품이에요. 액체도 좀 있어요.
examples.romanization: naeyongmul jeogeo jusyeoya dwaeyo. — hwajangpumieyo. aekchedo jom isseoyo.
examples.en: You need to write the contents. — Cosmetics. There's some liquid too.
examples.note: For shipping you may need to declare 액체 (liquid); the staff's instruction triggers your answer

entries.nuance: 내용물이 뭐예요? — 옷이에요 pairs the clerk's question 내용물 ('contents', Sino-Korean 內容物) + 이 (subject particle, attaches because 내용물 ends in a consonant) + 뭐예요? ('what is it?') with your answer 옷 ('clothes') + 이에요. Staff ask what's inside before accepting a parcel — for safety and to flag prohibited or fragile items — so you'll almost always be ANSWERING this question rather than asking it. The copula agreement rule is the core learner point: consonant-final nouns take 이에요 (옷이에요, 책이에요, 신발이에요), vowel-final nouns take 예요 (우유예요, 커피예요, 의류예요) — getting this right signals solid Korean. The casual staff version is 안에 뭐 들어 있어요? ('what's inside?'), using 들어 있다 ('to be contained in'). Once you've named the item, proactively adding 깨지는 건 없어요 ('nothing breakable') saves a follow-up question. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 'what is it?' → 이게 뭐예요? — fine when pointing at an unknown object, but when staff mean 'what's IN the box,' the precise term is 내용물. Another slip is over-formal 이것은 의류입니다; a plain 옷이에요 is exactly right at a counter.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 이에요 and 예요 in the answer.
Consonant-final nouns take 이에요 (옷이에요, 책이에요); vowel-final nouns take 예요 (우유예요, 커피예요). Match the noun's last sound — 신발 ends in ㄹ, so it's 신발이에요, not 신발예요.
Hearing 내용물 as the object itself.
내용물 means 'the contents (inside)'. The question asks what's IN the parcel, so answer with the item (옷이에요), not 'it's a box'.
Over-formal answer 의류입니다.
At a counter a plain 옷이에요 is natural. The bookish 의류입니다 ('it is apparel') sounds like a customs form, not speech.

structuredNuance.t: 내용물 ('contents', 內容物) + 이 (subject, consonant-final) + 뭐예요? ('what is it?'). Staff ask this for safety and prohibited-item checks. You answer: item + 이에요 (consonant-final) or 예요 (vowel-final). A natural add-on: 깨지는 건 없어요 ('nothing breakable').

내용물 literally means 'contents-substance' (內容物). The question asks what is physically inside the parcel, not what the parcel itself is. 이게 뭐예요? ('what is this?') describes the object; 내용물이 뭐예요? asks what's packed inside it.

내용물이 뭐예요? (formal, exactly what's printed on some declaration forms) vs 안에 뭐 들어 있어요? (casual, same meaning). Your answer: 옷이에요 (natural, casual) vs 의류입니다 (stiff, like a customs form). Plain 옷이에요 is correct at a counter.
Copula agreement: 옷이에요 / 책이에요 / 신발이에요 (consonant-final) vs 우유예요 / 의류예요 / 커피예요 (vowel-final). Add-ons: 깨지는 건 없어요 / 액체도 있어요 / 식품이에요. Declaring multiple items: 책이랑 옷이요.

이게 뭐예요? asks about the object itself, not its contents — use 내용물이 뭐예요? for 'what's inside'. Confusing 이에요 vs 예요: consonant-final → 이에요, vowel-final → 예요. Over-formal 의류입니다 sounds like a customs declaration form, not counter speech.

entries.english: Please send it the cheapest way
entries.shortExplanation: 제일 싼 걸로 보내 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please send it the cheapest way".
entries.explanation: "Please send it the cheapest way" — that is 제일 싼 걸로 보내 주세요 (jeil ssan geollo bonae juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 제일 싼 걸로 보내 주세요 ("Please send it the cheapest way"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Please send it the cheapest way
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking for the lowest-cost shipping option
반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: Please send it the fastest way
usagePhrases.note: The opposite priority: speed over price

usagePhrases.en: Slow is fine, so the cheap one
usagePhrases.note: 느려도 되다 ('it's okay if it's slow') justifies choosing cheap

examples.ko: A: 빠른 거랑 일반 중에 어떤 걸로 해 드릴까요? / B: 급한 거 아니에요. 제일 싼 걸로 보내 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: ppareun georang ilban junge eotteon geollo hae deurilkkayo? / B: geupan geo anieyo. jeil ssan geollo bonae juseyo.
examples.en: A: Fast or regular — which would you like? / B: It's not urgent. Please send it the cheapest way.
examples.note: 급한 거 아니에요 ('not urgent') sets up the choice; the clerk offers the options

examples.ko: 제일 싼 거랑 제일 빠른 거 가격 차이 얼마예요? 그럼 싼 걸로 할게요.
examples.romanization: jeil ssan georang jeil ppareun geo gagyeok chai eolmayeyo? geureom ssan geollo halgeyo.
examples.en: What's the price gap between cheapest and fastest? Then I'll go with the cheap one.
examples.note: Compare options before deciding; 그럼 ('then') + 할게요 confirms the choice

examples.ko: 멀리 보내는 거라서 느려도 괜찮아요. 제일 싼 걸로 부탁드려요.
examples.romanization: meolli bonaeneun georaseo neuryeodo gwaenchanayo. jeil ssan geollo butakdeuryeoyo.
examples.en: It's going far but I don't mind if it's slow. The cheapest option, please.
examples.note: 느려도 괜찮아요 ('slow is fine') + 부탁드려요 (polite request) for a longer-distance send

entries.nuance: 제일 싼 걸로 보내 주세요 is 제일 ('most', the everyday superlative adverb) + 싼 (싸다 'to be cheap', adnominal form) + 걸로 (것 'thing' + -로 'with/by' = 'with the ___ one') + 보내 주세요 ('please send'). The whole frame '제일 [adjective]ㄴ 걸로 (해/보내) 주세요' is the all-purpose counter phrase for selecting the most-X option, swapping the adjective: 싼 (cheapest), 빠른 (fastest), 안전한 (safest). The 걸로 (것+로) signals 'go with / choose' a specific option from a menu the staff implicitly knows — don't overthink it. A refined alternative is 제일 저렴한 걸로, where 저렴하다 ('inexpensive/economical') is a softer, more polite word than 싸다 — both mean cheap, but 저렴하다 carries less of the 'bargain-hunting' feel. The key pitfall is confusing 싸다 ('cheap') with 비싸다 ('expensive') — they differ by one syllable and are exact opposites; 제일 비싼 걸로 would get you the premium option instead. Another trap is the heavy 직역 'the cheapest one' → 가장 값싼 것을 보내 주세요, which is grammatical but stiff; colloquial Korean prefers 제일 싼 걸로. Note: 가장 and 제일 both mean 'most', but 제일 is more spoken and everyday at counters.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Mixing up 싸다 and 비싸다.
싸다 = cheap, 비싸다 = expensive. They sound similar but are opposites; 제일 싼 걸로 = the cheapest, 제일 비싼 걸로 = the most expensive.
Saying 제일 싼 방법으로 every time.
Understandable but heavy. The natural counter phrase uses 걸로 (것+로): 제일 싼 걸로 (보내) 주세요 = 'go with the cheapest one'.
Over-literal 가장 값싼 것을 보내 주세요.
값싸다 / 가장 ... 것을 is bookish. In speech use 제일 싼 걸로 보내 주세요, or politely 제일 저렴한 걸로.

structuredNuance.t: 제일 ('most', everyday superlative) + 싼 (싸다 'cheap', adnominal) + 걸로 (것+로 = 'with/by the ___ one') + 보내 주세요. The frame '제일 ___ㄴ 걸로 해 주세요' picks the most-X option at any counter — swap 싼 for 빠른, 안전한, etc.

걸로 (것+로) literally means 'with the thing'. In practice it functions as 'go with / choose the ___-one option from what's available'. It's lighter than 방법으로 ('by the method of') and is the natural spoken form at service counters.
싸다 ('cheap', direct) vs 저렴하다 ('inexpensive/economical', softer/politer). Both work here, but 제일 저렴한 걸로 sounds slightly more refined. 가장 and 제일 both mean 'most', but 제일 is the more casual spoken form.
More refined: 제일 저렴한 걸로 보내 주세요. Speed-first: 제일 빠른 걸로 보내 주세요. Justifying slowness: 느려도 되니까 싼 걸로요. Checking gap: 제일 싼 거랑 빠른 거 가격 차이가 얼마나 나요?

Confusing 싸다 ('cheap') with 비싸다 ('expensive') — one syllable apart but opposite meanings. 가장 값싼 것을 보내 주세요 is stiff — use 제일 싼 걸로. Saying 제일 싼 방법으로 is understandable but heavy; 걸로 is the natural spoken shorthand.

entries.english: Do you do international shipping too?
entries.shortExplanation: 국제 배송도 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Do you do international shipping too?".
entries.explanation: 국제 배송도 돼요? (gukje baesongdo dwaeyo?) = "Do you do international shipping too?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 국제 배송도 돼요? ("Do you do international shipping too?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Do you do international shipping too?
usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; asking if overseas sending is possible
반말, casual

usagePhrases.en: Can you send abroad as well?
usagePhrases.note: 해외로 ('to overseas') + 보낼 수 있어요 as a fuller variant

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to send it by EMS
usagePhrases.note: EMS = the express international postal service Koreans name directly

examples.ko: A: 어떻게 오셨어요? / B: 국제 배송도 돼요? 미국으로 보내고 싶어서요.
examples.romanization: A: eotteoke osyeosseoyo? / B: gukje baesongdo dwaeyo? migugeuro bonaego sipeoseoyo.
examples.en: A: What brings you in? / B: Do you do international shipping? I want to send to the US.
examples.note: 미국으로 보내고 싶어서요 ('I want to send to the US') explains the reason naturally

examples.ko: 미국으로 보내려고 하는데 국제 배송도 돼요? 얼마나 걸려요?
examples.romanization: migugeuro bonaeryeogo haneunde gukje baesongdo dwaeyo? eolmana geollyeoyo?
examples.en: I want to send it to the US — do you ship internationally? How long does it take?
examples.note: 미국으로 ('to the US') names the destination; 얼마나 걸려요 asks timeline

examples.ko: EMS랑 일반 국제우편 중에 뭐가 더 빨라요? 국제 배송으로 보내 주세요.
examples.romanization: EMSrang ilban gukjeupyeon junge mwoga deo ppallayo? gukje baesongeuro bonae juseyo.
examples.en: Between EMS and regular international mail, which is faster? Send it international.
examples.note: Compare EMS vs 국제우편 directly; then commit to whichever the staff recommends

entries.nuance: 국제 배송도 돼요? is 국제 ('international', Sino-Korean 國際) + 배송 ('delivery/shipping', 配送) + 도 ('also/too') + 돼요? (되다 'to be possible' → 'is it possible?'). 되다 frames this as a feasibility/availability question — 'is international shipping (also) doable here?' — the natural way to check a service before committing. The particle 도 ('too/also') subtly implies 'in addition to domestic,' a smooth way to ask whether they ALSO handle overseas. For sending abroad, Koreans name concrete services: EMS (빠르고 추적 가능한 국제특송), 국제우편/국제소포 (regular international post), and 항공/선편 ('air/sea' options for cost vs speed). Distinguish 배송 ('the shipping/delivery process') from 배달 ('delivery to a door', strongly associated with local food delivery) — for cross-border parcels use 배송 or 국제우편, never 배달. Also watch 국제 vs 국내 (國內, 'domestic') — one syllable apart, exact opposites; 국내 배송 is local Korean shipping. The English-speaker pitfall is framing the question as an ability question about the staff (당신이 보낼 수 있어요?), which sounds like doubting their competence; the impersonal 국제 배송 돼요? is much more natural.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 국제 (international) with 국내 (domestic).
국제 배송 = overseas shipping; 국내 배송 = domestic. They differ by one syllable but mean opposite directions.
Using 배달 for cross-border shipping.
배달 is door delivery (often food/local). For sending a parcel abroad, the word is 배송 / 국제우편: 국제 배송도 돼요?
Framing it as 당신이 보낼 수 있어요?
That questions the staff's ability and sounds rude. Use the impersonal feasibility frame: 국제 배송 돼요? / 해외로 보낼 수 있어요?

structuredNuance.t: 국제 ('international', 國際) + 배송 ('shipping', 配送) + 도 ('also/too') + 돼요? (되다 = 'is it possible?'). Checks service availability before committing. 도 implies 'in addition to domestic' and softens the question. Named services: EMS (fast, trackable), 국제우편/국제소포 (regular), 항공/선편 (air/sea).

Literally 'Is international shipping also possible?' In practice it's a service-availability check at the counter — not a challenge, just confirming the branch handles overseas. 돼요? (from 되다) is the go-to impersonal feasibility question.

국제 배송 돼요? (impersonal, natural) vs 해외로도 보낼 수 있어요? (more explicit, same meaning). 배송 ('shipping process') vs 배달 ('door delivery', food-associated) — for international parcels always say 배송. 국제 ('international') vs 국내 ('domestic') — one syllable, opposite meanings.
Fuller alternative: 해외로도 보낼 수 있어요? Naming destination: 미국으로 보내려고 하는데 돼요? Specific service: EMS로 보내고 싶은데요. Asking cost: 국제 배송 요금은 어떻게 돼요?

당신이 보낼 수 있어요? questions the staff's ability — rude. Use impersonal 국제 배송 돼요?. Confusing 국제 (international) with 국내 (domestic) gets you the wrong service. Using 배달 for cross-border parcels is wrong — say 배송.

entries.english: Could you weigh it, please?
entries.shortExplanation: 무게 좀 달아 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Could you weigh it, please?".
entries.explanation: 무게 좀 달아 주세요 (muge jom dara juseyo) means "Could you weigh it, please?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 무게 좀 달아 주세요 ("Could you weigh it, please?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking the clerk to put it on the scale
반말, to a friend
Asking the resulting weight directly
재다 ('to measure') is interchangeable with 달다 for weighing

examples.ko: A: 여기 올려 주세요. / B: 무게에 따라 요금이 달라지죠? 무게 좀 달아 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: yeogi ollyeo juseyo. / B: mugee ttara yogeumi dallajijyo? muge jom dara juseyo.
examples.en: A: Please set it here. / B: The fee changes by weight, right? Could you weigh it?
examples.note: 무게에 따라 ('according to weight') sets up the reason for asking; natural follow-up to placing the parcel

examples.ko: 박스가 좀 무거워 보이는데요. 무게 재 주시면 요금 알 수 있을까요?
examples.romanization: bakseuga jom mugeowo boineundeyo. muge jae jusimyeon yogeum al su isseulkkayo?
examples.en: The box looks a bit heavy. If you weigh it, can I find out the fee?
examples.note: 재다 variant with a conditional -(으)면; prompts the clerk to weigh and quote simultaneously

examples.ko: 이거 몇 킬로예요? 5kg 넘으면 요금 많이 올라가요?
examples.romanization: igeo myeot killoyeyo? 5kg neomeumyeon yogeum mani ollagayo?
examples.en: How many kilos is this? If it's over 5kg, does the fee jump a lot?
examples.note: Ask the actual weight first, then check the pricing threshold

entries.nuance: 무게 좀 달아 주세요 is 무게 ('weight') + 좀 (softener) + 달아 주세요 (달다 'to weigh/hang on a scale' + 주세요 = 'please weigh for me'). Parcel pricing depends on 무게 (weight) and sometimes 부피 ('volume/size'), so weighing is the first step before confirming the rate. Two verbs cover 'weigh': 달다 ('to weigh out, place on a scale') and 재다 ('to measure') — 무게를 달다 and 무게를 재다 are both natural, with 달다 evoking the physical act of hanging/placing on a scale. A simpler alternative is the outcome-focused 이거 몇 킬로예요? ('how many kilos is this?'), which asks the RESULT rather than requesting the action. The homophone trap: 달다 also means 'to be sweet' (맛이 달다) and 'to attach/hang' (간판을 달다) — pairing it with 무게 makes the 'weigh' sense unambiguous. Weight is counted with Sino-Korean numbers plus 킬로(그램): 오 킬로 (5kg), 십 킬로 (10kg) — not native-Korean 다섯 킬로. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 무겁다 ('to be heavy', an adjective) and producing 무거워 주세요 — adjectives can't take 주세요 that way; the verb you need is 달다 or 재다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 무거워 주세요.
무겁다 ('to be heavy') is an adjective and can't take 주세요. To weigh it, use the verb 달다 or 재다: 무게 좀 달아 주세요 / 재 주세요.
Confusing 달다 'weigh' with 달다 'sweet'.
달다 has several meanings; pair it with 무게 so it clearly means 'weigh': 무게 달아 주세요, not just 달아 주세요 out of context.
Counting kilos with native numbers.
Weight uses Sino-Korean numbers with 킬로: 오 킬로 (5kg), 십 킬로 (10kg) — not 다섯 킬로. So '5kg' is 오 킬로(그램).

structuredNuance.t: 무게 ('weight') + 좀 (softener) + 달아 주세요 (달다 'to weigh on a scale' + 주세요). Parcel rates depend on weight, so this is a routine first step. Alternative: 이거 몇 킬로예요? asks the result instead of requesting the action.

달다 literally means 'to hang/suspend', from the idea of hanging something on a balance scale. In context it means 'to weigh by placing on a scale.' Without 무게, 달아 주세요 is ambiguous (could mean 'please attach/hang'); pair with 무게 for clarity.

달다 ('weigh on a scale') vs 재다 ('measure') — both work with 무게 and are interchangeable here. 무게 좀 달아 주세요 (request the action) vs 이거 몇 킬로예요? (ask the result directly) — choose the second when you just want to know the number quickly.
Result question: 이거 몇 킬로예요? Threshold check: 5킬로 넘어요? Rate question: 무게에 따라 요금이 달라지나요? 반말: 무게 좀 달아 줘. Alternative verb: 무게 재 주세요.

무거워 주세요 doesn't work — 무겁다 is an adjective; you need the verb 달다 or 재다. Forgetting that 달다 also means 'sweet' and 'attach' — always pair with 무게 to be unambiguous. Weight uses Sino-Korean numbers: 오 킬로 (5kg), not 다섯 킬로.

entries.english: If I send it today, will it arrive the day after tomorrow?
entries.shortExplanation: 오늘 보내면 모레 도착해요? is a practical expression meaning "If I send it today, will it arrive the day after tomorrow?".
entries.explanation: "If I send it today, will it arrive the day after tomorrow?" — that is 오늘 보내면 모레 도착해요? (oneul bonaemyeon more dochakaeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 오늘 보내면 모레 도착해요? ("If I send today, will it arrive the day after tomorrow?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: If I send today, will it arrive the day after tomorrow?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; confirming a specific send-to-arrive timeline

usagePhrases.en: If I send today, arrives day after tomorrow?
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.ko: 오늘 보내면 내일 받을 수 있어요?
usagePhrases.romanization: oneul bonaemyeon naeil badeul su isseoyo?
usagePhrases.en: If I send today, can they get it tomorrow?
usagePhrases.note: 내일 ('tomorrow') for next-day; 받다 from the recipient's side

usagePhrases.en: Does it take longer if a weekend's in there?
usagePhrases.note: 주말 끼다 ('a weekend falls in between') affects timing

examples.ko: A: 오늘 보내면 보통 이틀 걸립니다. / B: 그럼 모레 도착해요?
examples.romanization: A: oneul bonaemyeon botong iteul geollimnida. / B: geureom more dochakaeyo?
examples.en: A: If you send today it normally takes two days. / B: So it arrives the day after tomorrow?
examples.note: Staff gives the days; you convert 이틀 ('two days') → 모레 to confirm the specific date

examples.ko: 생일 선물이라 날짜 맞춰야 돼요. 오늘 보내면 모레까지 확실히 도착해요?
examples.romanization: saengil seonmurira naljja matchwoya dwaeyo. oneul bonaemyeon morekkaji hwaksilhi dochakaeyo?
examples.en: It's a birthday gift so the date matters. If I send today, will it surely arrive by then?
examples.note: 날짜 맞추다 ('hit the date') + 확실히 ('for sure') presses for a firm answer

examples.ko: 금요일에 보내면 월요일에 도착해요? 주말엔 배송 안 하죠?
examples.romanization: geumyoire bonaemyeon woryoire dochakaeyo? jumaren baesong an hajyo?
examples.en: If I send Friday, does it arrive Monday? No delivery on weekends, right?
examples.note: Check weekend gaps explicitly — many carriers don't deliver Saturday/Sunday

entries.nuance: 오늘 보내면 모레 도착해요? is 오늘 ('today') + 보내면 (보내다 + -(으)면 'if/when I send') + 모레 ('the day after tomorrow') + 도착해요? ('does it arrive?'). The conditional -(으)면 sets up a hypothetical send-day and asks the resulting arrival — the precise way to pin down a delivery deadline. The key vocabulary set to memorize: 어제 (yesterday), 오늘 (today), 내일 (tomorrow), 모레 (the day after tomorrow), 글피 (three days from now) — learners consistently confuse 모레 with 내일. 도착하다's subject is the parcel (it arrives at the destination); contrast with the recipient's side: 받을 수 있어요? ('can they receive it?') — same timeline, different viewpoint. Adding 확실히 ('for sure') or 모레까지 ('by the day after tomorrow') sharpens the deadline question. The English-speaker pitfall is adding a redundant 만약 in front: 만약에 오늘 보내면 모레 도착해요? is grammatical but heavy — Korean folds 'if' into the verb with -(으)면 (보내면) and needs no separate 'if' word. Another trap is rendering 'the day after tomorrow' as 다음다음 날 instead of the single word 모레.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Mixing up 모레 and 내일.
내일 = tomorrow; 모레 = the day after tomorrow. They're different days; confirm which you mean: 모레 도착해요? vs 내일 도착해요?
Adding a separate 'if' word like 만약 보내다면.
Korean expresses 'if' with the verb ending -(으)면: 오늘 보내면…. You don't need 만약/만일, and 보내다면 is the wrong form (use 보내면).
Saying 다음다음 날 for 'day after tomorrow'.
The natural single word is 모레. 다음다음 날 is clunky; for two days after tomorrow there's even 글피.

structuredNuance.t: 오늘 ('today') + 보내면 (보내다 + -(으)면 'if') + 모레 ('day after tomorrow') + 도착해요? The -(으)면 conditional sets up the hypothetical send-day and asks the resulting arrival — the standard deadline-confirmation question at a post office or carrier.

Literally 'If I send today, does it arrive the day after tomorrow?' It functions as a deadline-feasibility check, not a general curiosity. The urgency lives in the specific day word (모레, 내일, 오후) — swap it to match your actual deadline.

Sender-side: 보내면 ... 도착해요? ('if I send, does it arrive?') vs recipient-side: 받을 수 있어요? ('can they receive it?') — same timeline, different focus. 모레 vs 내일: 모레 = day after tomorrow (2 days); 내일 = tomorrow (1 day). Getting these reversed is a common error.
Next-day check: 오늘 보내면 내일 도착해요? Weekend gap: 주말 껴 있으면 더 걸려요? Firm deadline: 모레까지 확실히 도착해요? 반말: 오늘 보내면 모레 도착해?

Adding 만약에 before 보내면 is redundant — Korean embeds 'if' in -(으)면 itself (보내면). Saying 다음다음 날 for 'day after tomorrow' is clunky; use 모레. Confusing 모레 (2 days away) with 내일 (1 day away) changes your deadline by a full day.

entries.english: The address changed — can I update it?
entries.shortExplanation: 주소가 바뀌었는데 변경할 수 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "The address changed — can I update it?".
entries.explanation: 주소가 바뀌었는데 변경할 수 있어요? (jusoga bakkwieonneunde byeongyeonghal su isseoyo?) = "The address changed — can I update it?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 주소가 바뀌었는데 변경할 수 있어요? ("The address changed — can I update it?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: The address changed — can I update it?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking to change the delivery address after sending

usagePhrases.en: Address changed — can I change it?
usagePhrases.note: 반말, casual

usagePhrases.en: I wrote the address wrong — can it be corrected?
usagePhrases.note: 잘못 적다 ('wrote wrong') + 수정 ('correction') for a typo fix
배송지 = the official 'delivery address' field

examples.ko: A: 이미 발송됐어요. / B: 그래도 주소가 바뀌었는데 변경할 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: A: imi balsongdwaesseoyo. / B: geuraedo jusoga bakkwieonneunde byeongyeonghal su isseoyo?
examples.en: A: It's already been dispatched. / B: Even so, the address changed — can I update it?
examples.note: 그래도 ('even so') shows persistence after the bad news; the question stays polite

examples.ko: 받는 사람 주소를 잘못 적었어요. 아직 출발 안 했으면 변경 가능해요?
examples.romanization: banneun saram jusoreul jalmot jeogeosseoyo. ajik chulbal an haesseumyeon byeongyeong ganeunghaeyo?
examples.en: I wrote the recipient's address wrong. If it hasn't shipped yet, can I change it?
examples.note: 받는 사람 ('recipient') + 출발 안 했으면 ('if not yet departed') — timing is critical for changes

examples.ko: 이미 보냈는데 배송지 변경 좀 해 주세요. 송장 번호 알려 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: imi bonaenneunde baesongji byeongyeong jom hae juseyo. songjang beonho allyeo deurilgeyo.
examples.en: I already sent it — please change the delivery address. I'll give you the tracking number.
examples.note: Offer the 송장 번호 proactively so they can locate the parcel in the system

entries.nuance: 주소가 바뀌었는데 변경할 수 있어요? is 주소 ('address', Sino-Korean 住所) + 가 (subject) + 바뀌었는데 (바뀌다 'to change/be changed' + -었- past + -는데 soft connective) + 변경하다 ('to change/modify', 變更) + -ㄹ 수 있어요? ('can I?'). The -는데 links your situation ('the address has changed, so…') to the request, softening what would otherwise be an abrupt demand. The verb pair 바뀌다/바꾸다 is a classic Korean distinction: 바뀌다 is INTRANSITIVE ('it changed on its own' — right for describing the address situation), while 바꾸다 is TRANSITIVE ('to actively change something'). So: 주소가 바뀌었어요 ('the address has changed') uses 바뀌다 + subject particle 가; but 주소를 변경하고 싶어요 ('I want to change the address') uses 변경하다 + object particle 를. The near-synonym 수정 ('correction') is best for typos — writing the wrong number or zip code; 변경 is for a genuinely different address. Timing matters: once a parcel is 출발/배송 중 ('departed/in transit'), changes become harder or impossible; mention if it hasn't left yet. The English-speaker pitfall is the wrong-particle error 주소를 바뀌었어요 (object marker on an intransitive verb) instead of the correct 주소가 바뀌었어요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 주소를 바뀌었어요.
바뀌다 is intransitive, so the address takes 가, not 를: 주소가 바뀌었어요. To actively change it, use the transitive 바꾸다/변경하다: 주소를 변경하다.
Confusing 바뀌다 and 바꾸다.
바뀌다 = 'it changed (on its own)'; 바꾸다 = 'to change something'. State the situation with 바뀌었다, request the action with 바꾸다/변경하다.
Using 변경 when you mean fixing a typo.
변경 = updating to a new value; 수정 = correcting a mistake. For a wrong-written address, 수정 가능해요? is more precise.

structuredNuance.t: 주소 ('address', 住所) + 가 (subject, NOT 를) + 바뀌었는데 (바뀌다 intransitive 'changed on its own' + -었- past + -는데 soft connective) + 변경할 수 있어요? ('can I change it?'). The -는데 softs the transition from situation to request.

Literally 'The address has changed, and can I modify it?' In use it's a customer-service request — polite because of -는데, specific because of 변경. Adding context (출발 전이에요? / 아직 안 보냈어요) helps the clerk act quickly.

변경 ('modification', updating to new correct info) vs 수정 ('correction', fixing an error). Use 변경 when the recipient genuinely moved; use 수정 when you made a typo. 배송지 변경 is the official form-field label for delivery-address changes.
Typo fix: 주소 잘못 적었는데 수정 가능해요? Official field: 배송지 변경 좀 해 주세요. Pre-departure: 아직 출발 안 했으면 바꿀 수 있어요? 반말: 주소 바뀌었는데 변경할 수 있어?
주소를 바뀌었어요 is wrong — 바뀌다 is intransitive, so the address takes 가: 주소가 바뀌었어요. Confusing 바뀌다 (it changed) with 바꾸다 (I change it). Using 변경 for a typo fix — that's 수정; 변경 is for a genuinely new address.

entries.hangul: 박스 안 터지게 단단히 포장해 주세요
entries.romanization: bakseu an teojige dandanhi pojanghae juseyo
entries.english: Please pack it tightly so the box doesn't burst
entries.shortExplanation: 박스 안 터지게 단단히 포장해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please pack it tightly so the box doesn't burst".
entries.explanation: 박스 안 터지게 단단히 포장해 주세요 (bakseu an teojige dandanhi pojanghae juseyo) means "Please pack it tightly so the box doesn't burst". Say it as one set phrase — for example 박스 안 터지게 단단히 포장해 주세요 ("Please pack it tightly so the box doesn't burst"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.ko: 박스 안 터지게 단단히 포장해 주세요
usagePhrases.romanization: bakseu an teojige dandanhi pojanghae juseyo
usagePhrases.en: Please pack it tightly so the box doesn't burst
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking for secure, sturdy packing

usagePhrases.ko: 박스 안 터지게 단단히 포장해 줘
usagePhrases.romanization: bakseu an teojige dandanhi pojanghae jwo
usagePhrases.en: Pack it tight so it doesn't burst
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: Please put on plenty of tape
usagePhrases.note: Concrete sub-request: more tape (테이프) for security
완충재 ('cushioning material') / 뽁뽁이 (bubble wrap) inside

examples.ko: A: 포장 다 됐어요? / B: 테이프 좀 더 붙여 주세요. 박스 안 터지게 단단히 포장해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: pojang da dwaesseoyo? / B: teipeu jom deo butyeo juseyo. bakseu an teojige dandanhi pojanghae juseyo.
examples.en: A: Is the packing done? / B: Please add more tape. Pack it firmly so the box won't burst.
examples.note: Stacking two requests: more tape + the overall secure-packing result

examples.ko: 안에 무거운 게 있어서요, 터지지 않게 단단히 포장해 주세요.
examples.romanization: ane mugeoun ge isseoseoyo, teojiji anke dandanhi pojanghae juseyo.
examples.en: There's something heavy inside, so pack it firmly so it won't burst.
examples.note: 무거운 거 ('something heavy') is the concrete reason for requesting sturdy packing

examples.ko: 멀리 가는 거라 완충재 넣고 테이프 단단히 붙여 주세요. 안 터지게요.
examples.romanization: meolli ganeun geora wanchungjae neoko teipeu dandanhi butyeo juseyo. an teojigeyo.
examples.en: It's going far, so add cushioning and tape it firmly. So it won't burst.
examples.note: Layer concrete steps (완충재 + 테이프) then restate the goal: 안 터지게요

entries.nuance: 박스 안 터지게 단단히 포장해 주세요 is 박스 ('box') + 안 ('not') + 터지게 (터지다 'to burst/split open' + -게 'so that') + 단단히 ('firmly/sturdily') + 포장해 주세요 (포장하다 'to pack/wrap', Sino-Korean 包裝 + 주세요). The -게 of 터지게 means 'in such a way / so that', and combined with 안 it expresses a negative purpose: 'pack it so it does NOT burst.' This 안 ...-게 해 주세요 frame is the natural way to request any outcome you want to prevent. 단단히 ('firmly, solidly', from 단단하다 'to be hard/firm') is the adverb for secure, tight packing; its near-synonym 꼼꼼히 ('thoroughly/meticulously') stresses careful attention to detail rather than physical strength — use 단단히 for structural strength, 꼼꼼히 for thoroughness. The verb 터지다 is intransitive ('the box gives way on its own'), correct for a packed box splitting under pressure; don't use 깨지다 (for fragile contents shattering) — the BOX 터지다, the GLASS inside 깨지다. Concrete co-requests: 완충재/뽁뽁이 (bubble wrap) + 테이프 (tape). The English-speaker pitfall is the vague 직역 '잘 포장해 주세요' ('pack it well'), which is understood but less effective; 단단히/안 터지게 tells the packer exactly what 'well' means. Another slip is misplacing 안: 박스 터지게 안 포장해 주세요 negates 'pack', not 'burst' — keep 안 on 터지다: 안 터지게.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 깨지게 instead of 터지게 for the box.
깨지다 is for fragile things shattering (glass); a box gives way with 터지다. So 'so the box won't burst' is 박스 안 터지게.
Misplacing the negative: 박스 터지게 안 포장해 주세요.
Put 안 on 터지다: 안 터지게 포장해 주세요 ('pack it so it won't burst'). The other order negates 'pack', which is confusing.
Saying only 잘 포장해 주세요.
잘 ('well') is vague. Specify the outcome: 단단히 (firmly) and 안 터지게 (so it won't burst), optionally 완충재 넣어 주세요 for cushioning.

structuredNuance.t: 박스 ('box') + 안 ('not') + 터지게 (터지다 'to burst' + -게 'so that') + 단단히 ('firmly') + 포장해 주세요 (포장하다 'to pack', 包裝). The 안 ...-게 frame = 'so that it does NOT burst.' 단단히 specifies the degree of tightness required.

Literally 'Pack it firmly so the box doesn't burst.' In practice it's a specific, actionable request to a counter clerk or mover — more effective than 잘 포장해 주세요 ('pack it well') because it names the failure mode (터지다) and the method (단단히).
단단히 ('firmly', structural strength) vs 꼼꼼히 ('meticulously', careful attention). 터지다 (box splits/bursts) vs 깨지다 (glass/ceramics shatter) — the BOX 터지다, the fragile contents 깨지다. Don't swap these.
Add cushioning: 완충재 좀 넣어 주세요 / 뽁뽁이 넣어 주세요. More tape: 테이프 좀 많이 붙여 주세요. Stacking prevention: 위에 뭐 올리지 말아 주세요. 반말: 안 터지게 단단히 포장해 줘.

잘 포장해 주세요 is vague — specify 단단히 and 안 터지게 for a concrete instruction. Misplacing 안: 터지게 안 포장해 주세요 negates 'pack', not 'burst' — keep 안 before 터지게. Using 깨지게 instead of 터지게 for the box: 깨지다 is for fragile contents, not the outer box.

entries.hangul: 택배가 안 왔는데 어떻게 된 거예요?
entries.romanization: taekbaega an wanneunde eotteoke doen geoyeyo?
entries.english: My parcel hasn't come — what's going on?
entries.shortExplanation: 택배가 안 왔는데 어떻게 된 거예요? is a practical expression meaning "My parcel hasn't come — what's going on?".
entries.explanation: "My parcel hasn't come — what's going on?" — that is 택배가 안 왔는데 어떻게 된 거예요? (taekbaega an wanneunde eotteoke doen geoyeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 택배가 안 왔는데 어떻게 된 거예요? ("My parcel hasn't come — what's going on?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.ko: 택배가 안 왔는데 어떻게 된 거예요?
usagePhrases.romanization: taekbaega an wanneunde eotteoke doen geoyeyo?
usagePhrases.en: My parcel hasn't come — what's going on?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; querying a missing or delayed delivery

usagePhrases.ko: 택배가 안 왔는데 어떻게 된 거야?
usagePhrases.romanization: taekbaega an wanneunde eotteoke doen geoya?
usagePhrases.en: My parcel hasn't come — what's up?
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend or familiar courier

usagePhrases.en: Tracking says delivered but I didn't get it
usagePhrases.note: Reporting a mismatch between tracking status and reality

usagePhrases.ko: 분실된 것 같은데 확인 좀 해 주세요
usagePhrases.romanization: bunsildoen geot gateunde hwagin jom hae juseyo
usagePhrases.en: I think it's lost — could you check?
usagePhrases.note: 분실되다 ('to be lost') for a missing or unaccounted parcel

examples.ko: A: 고객센터입니다. / B: 택배가 안 왔는데 어떻게 된 거예요? 3일 전에 보냈다고 했는데요.
examples.romanization: A: gogaeksenteoimnida. / B: taekbaega an wanneunde eotteoke doen geoyeyo? 3il jeone bonaetdago haenneundeyo.
examples.en: A: Customer service. / B: My parcel hasn't come — what's going on? They said it was sent three days ago.
examples.note: 3일 전에 보냈다고 했는데요 ('they said it was sent 3 days ago') gives specific context to the agent

examples.ko: 3일 전에 보냈다는데 아직도 안 왔어요. 어떻게 된 거예요?
examples.romanization: 3il jeone bonaetdaneunde ajikdo an wasseoyo. eotteoke doen geoyeyo?
examples.en: They say it was sent 3 days ago but it still hasn't come. What's going on?
examples.note: Give the timeline (3일 전) to push for a concrete answer

examples.ko: 송장에는 배송 완료라는데 저는 못 받았어요. 분실된 거 아니에요? 확인 좀 부탁드려요.
examples.romanization: songjangeneun baesong wallyoraneunde jeoneun mot badasseoyo. bunsildoen geo anieyo? hwagin jom butakdeuryeoyo.
examples.en: The waybill says delivered but I didn't get it. Isn't it lost? Please check.
examples.note: 배송 완료 ('delivery complete') vs reality; 부탁드려요 escalates the request politely

entries.nuance: 택배가 안 왔는데 어떻게 된 거예요? is 택배 ('parcel') + 가 (subject) + 안 왔는데 (안 'not' + 오다 'come' past 왔다 + -는데 soft connective) + 어떻게 ('how') + 된 거예요? (되다 'to become/turn out' + -ㄴ 거예요 = 'what has it become?'). The set phrase 어떻게 된 거예요? literally 'how did it turn out?' is the standard way to ask 'what's going on / what happened?' about a problem — firm but civil, because it uses impersonal 되다 rather than blaming a specific person. The -는데 connective ties your situation ('it hasn't come, so…') to the question, softening the complaint. Key companion vocabulary: 배송 조회 ('tracking lookup'), 배송 완료 ('delivery complete' status), 분실 ('loss', 紛失), 지연 ('delay', 遲延). A sharp contrast to note: 어떻게 된 거예요? asks for an explanation of the situation ('what happened?'), while 어떡해요? (어떻게 해요?) means 'what should I do / what now?' — the first seeks information, the second seeks a remedy; use the first when querying a missing parcel. The English-speaker pitfall is the blunt 직역 '왜 안 왔어요?' ('why didn't it come?'), which can sound accusatory toward the listener; 어떻게 된 거예요? or adding 혹시 ('by any chance') keeps it civil while still pressing for answers.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 어떻게 된 거예요? with 어떡해요?
어떻게 된 거예요? = 'what's the situation/what happened?' (asks for info); 어떡해요? = 'what should I do?' (asks for a remedy). Use the first to query a missing parcel.
Blunt 왜 안 왔어요? as the opener.
왜 ('why') can sound accusatory toward the listener. The neutral, civil query is 택배가 안 왔는데 어떻게 된 거예요?, optionally softened with 혹시.
Saying 제가 안 왔어요.
오다's subject here is the parcel: 택배가 안 왔어요 ('the parcel didn't come'). 제가 안 왔어요 would mean 'I didn't come'.

structuredNuance.t: 택배 ('parcel') + 가 (subject) + 안 왔는데 ('hasn't come' + -는데 soft connective) + 어떻게 된 거예요? ('what's going on?', lit. 'how did it turn out?'). 어떻게 된 거예요? is the standard civil complaint opener — firm without blaming, impersonal because of 되다.

Literally 'The parcel hasn't come — how has it turned out?' In use it's a polite service complaint: you're asking the carrier/clerk to investigate and explain. The impersonal 된 거예요 ('it has become') avoids placing blame on the listener directly.

어떻게 된 거예요? ('what's the situation/what happened?' — asks for info) vs 어떡해요? ('what should I do?' — asks for a remedy). For a missing parcel use the first. Adding 혹시 ('by any chance') before the question softens it further: 혹시 어떻게 된 거예요?
Tracking mismatch: 배송 완료라는데 못 받았어요. Loss report: 분실된 것 같은데 확인해 주세요. With timeline: 3일 전에 보냈다는데 아직도요. Softer opener: 혹시 어떻게 된 거예요?

왜 안 왔어요? ('why didn't it come?') can sound accusatory — use the neutral 어떻게 된 거예요?. Confusing 어떻게 된 거예요? (seeks explanation) with 어떡해요? (seeks remedy). 제가 안 왔어요 means 'I didn't come' — 오다's subject is the parcel: 택배가 안 왔어요.

entries.english: Really? — a polite check that you heard right, mild surprise or interest.
entries.shortExplanation: 정말요? is a practical expression meaning "Really? — a polite check that you heard right, mild surprise or interest.".
entries.explanation: 정말요? (jeongmaryo?) = "Really? — a polite check that you heard right, mild surprise or interest.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 정말요? ("really?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: polite -요, to anyone you'd use 존댓말 with
casual banmal, to a friend or younger person
fuller polite form, slightly stronger doubt
natural extension asking about a situation
