entries.nuance: 정말요? (polite) / 정말? (casual) is the everyday 'really?' you say to confirm you heard correctly — it signals mild surprise or interest, not strong disbelief. Literally 정말 'truly' + polite particle -요, so dropping -요 flips it to banmal immediately: use plain 정말? only with friends or those younger than you, and keep 정말요? with bosses, elders, or any stranger. The nearest alternative is 진짜요?, but the dividing line is register feel: 정말요? is the neutral, safe choice that even works in formal contexts, while 진짜요? is warmer and more colloquial. As a variation, 정말이에요? pushes a bit harder, implying you want to verify the claim — not just a reflex. The classic English-speaker trap is intonation: 정말요 MUST rise sharply to read as a question; said flat it becomes the adverb 'truly' (정말 감사합니다 'I'm truly grateful') and the listener waits for you to finish. Also, don't stack 정말 진짜요? — that's redundant; pick one.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying plain 정말? to a boss or elder — the bare form is banmal and too casual; keep the polite 정말요? with anyone you use 존댓말 with.
Saying it flat without rising intonation — 정말 with no upward pitch reads as the adverb 'truly,' not the question 'really?'; the pitch must rise.
Stacking 정말 진짜요? to sound more surprised — these are two words for the same thing; native speakers use one, not both together.

structuredNuance.t: 정말요? is the everyday 'really?' you say to confirm you heard right — mild surprise or interest, NOT strong disbelief. It works at any politeness level by toggling the -요 suffix.

Plain 정말? is banmal — to friends or younger people. With a boss, elder, or any stranger you must keep the -요: 정말요?. Even in formal or semi-formal settings 정말요? holds up; 진짜요? can feel a touch too casual there.

진짜요? and 정말요? overlap as 'really?' but 진짜요? is warmer and more spontaneous — the default among friends. 정말요? is more neutral and registers as safer in formal or unfamiliar settings. 정말이에요? is a fuller form that implies you want to double-check a claim, not just react.
Core forms: 정말? (banmal) → 정말요? (polite) → 정말이에요? (fuller doubt) → 정말 그래요? (asking about a situation). Stronger disbelief uses 말도 안 돼요 instead.
Intonation: 정말요 said FLAT sounds like the adverb 'truly,' not a question — the pitch must rise at the end. Also, never stack 정말 진짜요? ('really really?'); Koreans use one, not both.

entries.english: Really?! / for real? — surprised, more colloquial and emotional than 정말요.
entries.shortExplanation: 진짜요? is a practical expression meaning "Really?! / for real? — surprised, more colloquial and emotional than 정말요.".
entries.explanation: 진짜요? (jinjjayo?) means "Really?! / for real? — surprised, more colloquial and emotional than 정말요.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 진짜요? ("for real?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: polite -요, casual-friendly tone with strangers your age
casual banmal, very common among friends
fuller polite form, stronger surprise
doubled for playful, excited disbelief

examples.romanization: A: na rotto dwaesseo / B: jinjja?!
examples.en: A: I won the lottery / B: For real?!
examples.note: the bare banmal reaction — excited, can't-believe-it surprise between friends

entries.nuance: 진짜요? (polite) / 진짜? (casual) is the more emotional, colloquial cousin of 정말요? — it leaks genuine excitement and surprise in a way 정말요? doesn't. Literally 진짜 'real/genuine' (the 진 is the Sino-Korean 眞 'true') + polite -요; 진짜? alone is banmal. The dividing line against 정말요? is tone and setting: 진짜? is the default 'really?' among friends because it's warm and spontaneous, while 정말요? is more neutral and holds up in stiffer formal contexts where 진짜요? can feel a touch too relaxed. The key variant ladder is 진짜? (bare casual) → 진짜요? (polite-ish) → 진짜예요? (fuller, doubting) → 진짜 진짜? (doubling for playful disbelief). The English-speaker pitfall is register over-confidence: 진짜요? has -요 but still carries an informal flavor — with a CEO or in ceremony, the cleaner choice is 정말요?. Also, like 정말요?, intonation must rise; said flat 진짜 becomes the emphasis adverb 'genuinely' (진짜 좋아 'I genuinely like it') rather than a question.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 진짜요? in a very formal or ceremonial setting — it stays casual in flavor; with a CEO or in a formal context use 정말요? or 그래요?.
Saying flat 진짜 expecting it to mean 'really?' — without rising pitch it's the emphasis adverb 'for real / genuinely,' a statement, not a question.
Confusing 진짜 (real, the opposite of fake) with 정말 in writing — as a reaction they overlap, but 진짜 is more colloquial and 정말 more neutral; don't assume they're interchangeable in every sentence.

structuredNuance.t: 진짜요? is the more emotional, colloquial 'really?!' — it leaks genuine surprise and excitement. 진짜? alone is banmal; add -요 for a polite-ish but still informal version.
진짜 comes from Sino-Korean 眞짜 — 眞 (진) meaning 'true/genuine.' So 진짜 is literally 'the real thing,' and 진짜? means 'is this the real thing?' i.e., 'for real?'

진짜? is the default casual 'really?' among friends because it's warmer and more spontaneous. 정말요? is safer in formal or unfamiliar settings. In stiff contexts (a CEO, a ceremony), 정말요? is cleaner. 정말요? and 진짜요? are not always interchangeable in feel.
진짜? (banmal) → 진짜요? (polite-casual) → 진짜예요? (fuller doubt) → 진짜 진짜? (playful disbelief doubling).

Register over-confidence: 진짜요? has -요 but its flavor is still casual — with a CEO or in ceremony, use 정말요? instead. Intonation must rise; said flat, 진짜 becomes the emphasis adverb 'genuinely,' not the question 'for real?'

entries.english: Awesome! / wow / no way — a big reaction to something amazing, shocking, or extreme.
entries.shortExplanation: 대박 is a practical expression meaning "Awesome! / wow / no way — a big reaction to something amazing, shocking, or extreme.".
entries.explanation: "Awesome! / wow / no way — a big reaction to something amazing, shocking, or extreme." — that is 대박 (daebak). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 대박 ("awesome / wow"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: casual banmal, to friends, very common
polite -이에요 form, softens the slang
full casual sentence form, exclaiming
with 완전 to intensify

examples.ko: A: 나 승진했어 / B: 대박!
examples.romanization: A: na seungjinhaesseo / B: daebak!
examples.en: A: I got promoted / B: Awesome!
examples.note: the bare slang reaction between friends — pure excited celebration

examples.ko: A: 이 카페 디저트 봐 / B: 와, 대박이다.
examples.romanization: A: i kape dijeoteu bwa / B: wa, daebagida.
examples.en: A: Look at this cafe's dessert / B: Wow, that's amazing.

examples.ko: A: 옆집에 불났대 / B: 헐, 대박. 다친 사람은 없대?
examples.romanization: A: yeopjibe bulnatdae / B: heol, daebak. dachin sarameun eopsdae?
examples.en: A: They say the next building caught fire / B: Whoa, no way. Anyone hurt?

entries.nuance: 대박 literally means 'a big hit / jackpot' (대 大 'big' + 박 = jackpot), and as a reaction it explodes out for anything extreme — amazingly good, but also shocking or unbelievably bad. It is youth slang and firmly casual: 대박 alone is banmal among friends; for even a little politeness say 대박이에요, though that still reads as informal in flavor. The variant ladder is 대박 → 대박이다 → 대박이에요 → 완전 대박 (intensified). The dividing line against 헐 is emotional direction: 헐 leans toward shock/dismay ('oh no, whoa'), while 대박 leans toward 'wow, that's enormous' — though both can appear together as 헐 대박. Because it's casual slang, the English-speaker pitfall is using it in formal or hierarchical settings — to a boss or elder, 대박 sounds flippant and disrespectful; use 대단하네요 or 굉장하네요 instead. A second pitfall is assuming it's always positive: Koreans say 대박 at a car crash too, meaning 'unbelievable/shocking.'
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 대박 with a boss, professor, or elder — it's casual slang and sounds disrespectful in formal settings; use 대단하네요 or 굉장하네요.
Assuming 대박 is only for good news — it reacts to anything extreme, including shocking bad events; tone and context decide the meaning.
Adding -요 as 대박요 — that's not natural; the polite form is 대박이에요, since 대박 is a noun that needs the 이에요 copula.

structuredNuance.t: 대박 literally means 'big jackpot/hit.' As a reaction it explodes out for anything extreme: something amazingly good, surprising, or even shockingly bad. The literal origin is the lucky strike in a bet or harvest — now stretched into a general 'wow' for anything over-the-top.

대박 is casual youth slang — banmal by default. Use with friends and peers. With a boss or elder it sounds flippant and disrespectful; switch to 대단하네요 or 굉장하네요. Even 대박이에요 (polite form) retains an informal, youthful flavor.

대박 is 'wow, this is huge!' — the emphasis is scale and amazement. 헐 leans toward shock/dismay ('oh no, what?!'). They often appear together as 헐 대박 when something is both shocking and enormous. 대박 can be positive or negative; 헐 skews negative.
대박 (banmal bare) → 대박이다 (casual exclamatory) → 대박이에요 (polite) → 완전 대박 (intensified). Note: 대박요 is unnatural — the noun needs 이에요, not raw -요.

Using 대박 with a boss or in formal settings — it's youth slang and sounds rude there. Also, assuming it's only positive: 대박 reacts to anything extreme, including shocking bad news. Adding 대박요 is unnatural; the polite form is 대박이에요.

entries.english: Whoa / OMG / no way — a gut reaction of shock, disbelief, or mild dismay.
entries.shortExplanation: 헐 is a practical expression meaning "Whoa / OMG / no way — a gut reaction of shock, disbelief, or mild dismay.".
entries.explanation: 헐 (heol) = "Whoa / OMG / no way — a gut reaction of shock, disbelief, or mild dismay.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 헐 ("whoa / OMG"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: casual banmal, friends and texting, very common
paired with 대박 for double shock
shock plus asking if it's true

usagePhrases.en: oh no, what do we do
usagePhrases.note: shock shading into worry

examples.note: the bare interjection — instant shock between friends; one syllable, immediate

examples.note: real situation: 헐 is the gut reaction; 진짜? asks for confirmation; 왜? asks for detail — a classic three-step gossip chain

entries.nuance: 헐 is a pure interjection of shock — the involuntary sound that comes out when something startling, dismaying, or unbelievable hits you. It's hugely common in texting and casual conversation among friends and younger people. Because it's a raw exclamation there is no polite form: there is no 헐요 or 헐이에요; it lives entirely in banmal territory. The dividing line against 대박 is emotional direction: 헐 carries surprise often tinged with 'oh no' or dismay, while 대박 leans toward 'wow, that's enormous' — that's why 헐 어떡해 (shock + worry) is a natural pair but 대박 어떡해 is odd. Also don't confuse 헐 with 헉: 헐 is drawn-out disbelief ('whoa, no way'), while 헉 is a sharp one-syllable gasp of fright or physical surprise. The English-speaker pitfall is using 헐 in a professional or respectful setting — to an elder or boss it sounds childish and rude; in those moments use 어머 for neutral surprise or a full 정말요? 그런 일이. A second pitfall is trying to write 헐요 to be polite — simply switch words.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 헐 with a boss, elder, or in a formal email — it's casual youth slang and sounds immature/rude; use 어머 or 정말요? instead.
Trying to make a polite version like 헐요 — it doesn't exist; 헐 is a raw interjection that stays casual, so switch words for politeness.
Mixing up 헐 and 헉 — 헐 is disbelief/dismay ('whoa, no way'), while 헉 is a startled gasp of fright; they aren't interchangeable.

structuredNuance.t: 헐 is a pure interjection of shock — the involuntary sound you make when something startling, dismaying, or unbelievable hits you. It is hugely common in texting and casual speech. It lives entirely in banmal/casual territory; there is no polite version of 헐 itself.

Strictly casual — among friends and peers, in texts and informal chat. To an elder or boss it sounds childish and rude. In formal or respectful situations, react with 어머 (neutral gasp) or 정말요? 그런 일이 (full polite expression of shock). There is no 헐요 — just switch words.

헐 skews toward shock and dismay ('oh no, whoa'). 대박 skews toward 'wow, enormous.' They often pair as 헐 대박 for maximum shock. 헉 is a short gasp of fright or physical surprise — more sudden and bodily, while 헐 is drawn-out disbelief.
헐 alone is most common. Common expansions: 헐 대박, 헐 진짜?, 헐 어떡해 (shock + worry). You can write multiple 헐헐헐 in texts to show escalating disbelief.

Using 헐 with a boss, elder, or in a formal context — it sounds immature and rude there. Trying to add -요 as 헐요 — that form doesn't exist; switch to 어머 or 정말요? instead. Mixing up 헐 (drawn-out disbelief) with 헉 (sharp fright gasp).

entries.english: Wow, that's cool / awesome — admiring something or someone impressive.
entries.shortExplanation: 와 멋있다 is a practical expression meaning "Wow, that's cool / awesome — admiring something or someone impressive.".
entries.explanation: 와 멋있다 (wa meositda) means "Wow, that's cool / awesome — admiring something or someone impressive.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 와 멋있다 ("wow, that's cool"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

polite -어요, to someone you respect
with 진짜 to intensify the praise
honorific -으시- praising an elder/senior

examples.romanization: A: na maraton wanjuhaesseo / B: wa meositda!
examples.en: A: I finished the marathon / B: Wow, that's awesome!
examples.note: the bare admiring reaction — praising a friend's achievement

examples.ko: A: 이 야경 좀 봐 / B: 와, 멋있다.
examples.romanization: A: i yagyeong jom bwa / B: wa, meositda.
examples.en: A: Look at this night view / B: Wow, that's gorgeous.

examples.ko: A: 부장님이 영어로 발표하셨어 / B: 와, 멋있으시다. 정말 대단하세요.

entries.nuance: 와 멋있다 is the spontaneous 'wow, that's cool/awesome/impressive' you exclaim at something or someone admirable. 와 is the gasp 'wow' and 멋있다 means 'is cool/stylish/admirable.' The plain 멋있다 is the casual exclamatory form used even to oneself, 멋있어요 is polite, and when praising a senior you insert honorific -으시-: 멋있으시다 or 멋있으세요. The variant ladder is 멋있다 → 멋있어요 → 멋있으시다 → 진짜 멋있다 (intensified). The dividing line against 예쁘다 and 대단하다 is the type of admiration: 멋있다 is cool/stylish/admirable (a skill, a view, an attitude), 예쁘다 is cute/pretty (appearance, small charming things), 대단하다 is remarkable/impressive in terms of effort or achievement. A hiker who summited alone → 멋있다 AND 대단하다 both work, but 멋있다 adds a cooler, more stylish tone. The English-speaker pitfall is avoiding the exclamatory -다 ending because it looks like a dictionary base form — but 멋있다! as a live reaction is completely natural spoken Korean. Another pitfall is praising a senior with plain 멋있어 and omitting the honorific -으시-.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Praising a boss or elder with plain 멋있어 / 멋있다 — for a senior add honorific -으시-: 멋있으세요 / 멋있으시다, or you sound too familiar.
Using 멋있다 for something cute or pretty — that's 예쁘다; 멋있다 is for cool/stylish/admirable things, a different flavor of praise.
Avoiding 멋있다! as a reaction because -다 looks like dictionary form — the bare -다 exclamation is natural spoken Korean for live admiration.

structuredNuance.t: 와 멋있다 is the spontaneous 'wow, that's cool/awesome' you exclaim at something or someone impressive. 와 is the gasp 'wow'; 멋있다 means 'is cool/stylish/admirable.'

Plain 멋있다 is casual and used to oneself or friends. Polite: 멋있어요. Honorific for elders/seniors: 멋있으시다 / 멋있으세요. Add 진짜/완전 before 멋있다 to intensify. Never use plain 멋있어 with a senior — it sounds over-familiar.

멋있다 = cool/stylish/admirable (a skill, a scene, an attitude). 예쁘다 = cute/pretty (looks, small charming things). 대단하다 = remarkable/impressive for effort or achievement. A drone pilot's skill → 멋있다; their hard years of practice → 대단하다; a flower arrangement → 예쁘다.

Avoiding 멋있다! as a live reaction because -다 looks like dictionary form — but bare -다 exclamations are completely natural spoken Korean. Praising a senior with plain 멋있어 / 멋있다 instead of honorific 멋있으세요 / 멋있으시다 — that sounds too familiar.

entries.explanation: "That's great / good for you / it worked out — happy something turned out well." — that is 잘됐다 (jaldwaetda). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 잘됐다 ("that's great / glad it worked out"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

polite -어요, to anyone you respect
casual with -네 reacting to news
with 정말 to warm up the congratulation

examples.note: the bare reaction — sharing a friend's good news; 잘됐다 expresses happiness for them, not yourself

examples.ko: A: 엄마 수술 잘 끝났어 / B: 아, 정말 잘됐다. 걱정했잖아.
examples.romanization: A: eomma susul jal kkeunnasseo / B: a, jeongmal jaldwaetda. geokjeonghaetjana.
examples.en: A: Mom's surgery went well / B: Oh, I'm so glad. I was worried.
examples.note: everyday: 잘됐다 + acknowledgment of prior worry — shows you genuinely cared; 정말 warms it further

examples.ko: A: 비자 드디어 나왔어요 / B: 잘됐어요! 고생 많으셨어요.
examples.romanization: A: bija deudieo nawasseoyo / B: jaldwaesseoyo! gosaeng maneusyeosseoyo.
examples.en: A: My visa finally came through / B: That's wonderful! You worked so hard for it.
examples.note: real situation: polite 잘됐어요 plus 고생 많으셨어요 acknowledges the effort behind the result — a natural pairing

entries.nuance: 잘됐다 means 'it turned out well / that's great' — the warm, celebratory reaction when a good outcome arrives. Built from 잘 'well' + 되다 'to turn out, to happen,' frozen as an exclamation: 잘됐다/잘됐어 (casual), 잘됐어요 (polite), 잘됐네(요) (softly reacting to news). The key dividing line versus 다행이다 is the emotional starting point: 잘됐다 is happy at good news with no prior dread attached — 'yay, it worked out!'; 다행이다 implies you were worried and disaster was dodged — 'thank goodness, what a relief.' A job offer you hoped for → 잘됐다; a health scare that turned out fine → 다행이다. A second near-synonym is 다행히 잘됐다, which blends both feelings. The English-speaker pitfall is the spelling/spacing: it must be written as one word 잘됐다 (not 잘 됐다 with a space, not 잘 됬다 — 됬다 is always wrong; the past of 되다 is 됐다). Another critical pitfall is tone: if you say 잘됐다 flat or with a sarcastic lilt it flips to 'serves you right,' so keep your voice clearly warm.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 잘됬다 — this spelling is always wrong; the past of 되다 is 됐다 (되+었), so it's 잘됐다.
Using 잘됐다 when you mean 'what a relief' — for a feared outcome that didn't happen use 다행이다; 잘됐다 is for genuinely good news.
Saying 잘됐다 flatly or with a sour tone — it can flip to sarcastic 'serves you right'; keep your voice warm so it reads as sincere congratulations.

structuredNuance.t: 잘됐다 literally means 'it went well / turned out well.' As a reaction it means 'that's great / I'm so happy for you.' It's not just an observation — it carries emotional warmth and shared happiness.
잘됐다/잘됐어 are casual banmal. 잘됐어요 is polite and safe with coworkers, seniors, or clients. 잘됐네요 softly reacts to news heard in the moment. To warm it up further, prepend 정말 or 너무.

잘됐다 = happy at good news, no prior worry needed. 다행이다 = relieved because a feared bad outcome didn't happen — the worry is the key component. A passed exam where you studied confidently → 잘됐다. A passed exam you feared failing → 다행이다.

Spelling: write 잘됐다 as one word (not 잘 됐다 or 잘 됬다). 됬다 is always wrong — the past of 되다 is 됐다 (되+었=됐). Tone trap: said flatly or with a sarcastic edge, 잘됐다 means 'serves you right.' Keep your voice warm to show it's sincere.

entries.english: Thank goodness / what a relief — relieved that something bad was avoided.
entries.shortExplanation: 다행이다 is a practical expression meaning "Thank goodness / what a relief — relieved that something bad was avoided.".
entries.explanation: 다행이다 (dahaengida) = "Thank goodness / what a relief — relieved that something bad was avoided.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 다행이다 ("thank goodness"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: casual banmal, exhaling relief
polite -이에요, to anyone you respect
casual with -네 on hearing reassuring news
stronger, for a serious near-miss

examples.ko: A: 검사 결과 괜찮대 / B: 다행이다.
examples.romanization: A: geomsa gyeolgwa gwaenchantae / B: dahaengida.
examples.en: A: The test results are fine / B: Thank goodness.
examples.note: the bare reaction — pure relief exhaled; the context of earlier worry makes 다행이다 feel right here

examples.ko: A: 지갑 택시에서 찾았어 / B: 아, 다행이다. 걱정했잖아.
examples.romanization: A: jigap taeksieseo chajasseo / B: a, dahaengida. geokjeonghaetjana.
examples.en: A: I found my wallet in the taxi / B: Oh, what a relief. I was so worried.
examples.note: everyday: 다행이다 + 걱정했잖아 ('I was worried') — this pairing is very natural and shows the worry-then-relief arc

examples.ko: A: 사고 났는데 다친 데는 없어요 / B: 다행이에요, 정말. 몸조심하세요.
examples.romanization: A: sago nanneunde dachin deneun eopseoyo / B: dahaengieyo, jeongmal. momjosimhaseyo.
examples.en: A: There was an accident but no one's hurt / B: That's such a relief, truly. Please take care.
examples.note: real situation: polite 다행이에요 reacting to a serious near-miss with a senior; 정말 intensifies; 몸조심하세요 is the natural follow-up

entries.nuance: 다행이다 is the 'thank goodness, what a relief' you breathe out when a feared bad outcome was avoided — built from the noun 다행 'good fortune (that it wasn't worse)' + the copula 이다. The variant ladder is 다행이다/다행이야 (casual) → 다행이에요 (polite) → 다행이네(요) (softly on hearing news) → 천만다행이다 (for a grave near-miss, '천만 = ten million' times lucky). The critical dividing line versus 잘됐다 is the emotional starting point: 다행이다 implies you were worried and disaster was dodged; 잘됐다 is happiness at good news with no prior dread. Surgery that ended safely → 다행이다; a job offer you hoped for → 잘됐다. The English-speaker pitfall is translating 'lucky' as 운이 좋다 — that means fortunate in a winning-the-raffle sense, while 'what a relief it wasn't bad' is specifically 다행이다. Another pitfall is dropping the copula and saying just 다행 — that's a noun left incomplete; native speakers always say 다행이다 or 다행이에요 to close the sentence.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 다행 by itself — it's a noun and needs the copula: 다행이다 (casual) or 다행이에요 (polite) to be a complete sentence.
Using 운이 좋다 ('lucky') for relief — 운이 좋다 means fortunate/got a break, but 'phew, it wasn't bad' is 다행이다, a different feeling.
Swapping in 잘됐다 — 잘됐다 is happiness at good news, while 다행이다 specifically means a feared bad outcome was avoided; the worry is the key difference.

structuredNuance.t: 다행이다 is the exhaled 'thank goodness / what a relief' when a feared bad outcome was avoided. The emotional arc is: worry → something could have gone wrong → it didn't → relief. Without that prior worry, the natural word is 잘됐다, not 다행이다.

다행 is a Sino-Korean noun (多幸 — 多 'many/much' + 幸 'good fortune/blessing') meaning 'good fortune, fortunate outcome.' Adding copula 이다 makes it a complete reaction. 천만다행 (千萬多幸) means '10 million blessings' — hyperbole for an enormous relief.

다행이다 = you were worried and it turned out okay (relief from fear). 잘됐다 = it turned out well, happy news (no fear required). 운이 좋다 = you were lucky/fortunate in a positive-outcome sense (winning a raffle). A near-miss accident with no injuries → 다행이다, NOT 잘됐다 or 운이 좋다.
다행이다/다행이야 (casual) → 다행이에요 (polite) → 다행이네요 (reacting to news) → 천만다행이다 (serious near-miss). Never drop the copula: 다행 alone is an incomplete sentence.

Translating 'lucky' as 운이 좋다 when you mean relief — 운이 좋다 is fortuitous luck, not relief from fear. Saying 다행 alone without the copula — it's a noun and needs 이다/이에요. Using 다행이다 for joyful good news when no worry was involved — that's 잘됐다.

entries.english: That's a shame / too bad / I wish it were different — mild regret or disappointment.
entries.shortExplanation: 아쉽다 is a practical expression meaning "That's a shame / too bad / I wish it were different — mild regret or disappointment.".
entries.explanation: "That's a shame / too bad / I wish it were different — mild regret or disappointment." — that is 아쉽다 (aswipda). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 아쉽다 ("that's a shame"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: casual banmal, mild regret
polite -어요, to anyone you respect
casual with -네 reacting in the moment

usagePhrases.en: it's a bit of a letdown
usagePhrases.note: with 좀 to soften it further

examples.ko: A: 표 다 팔렸대 / B: 아쉽다.
examples.romanization: A: pyo da pallyeotdae / B: aswipda.
examples.en: A: The tickets are all sold out / B: That's a shame.
examples.note: the bare reaction — light disappointment; 아쉽다 is exactly right for a small letdown, not 슬프다

examples.ko: A: 저 다음 주에 이사 가요 / B: 아, 아쉬워요. 자주 봤는데.
examples.romanization: A: jeo daeum jue isa gayo / B: a, aswiwoyo. jaju bwanneunde.
examples.en: A: I'm moving next week / B: Oh, that's too bad. We saw each other so often.
examples.note: everyday: polite 아쉬워요 expressing regret at parting; the follow-up 자주 봤는데 explains WHY it's a shame

examples.ko: A: 비 와서 소풍 취소됐어 / B: 아쉽다. 날씨만 좋았어도.
examples.romanization: A: bi waseo sopung chwisodwaesseo / B: aswipda. nalssiman joasseodo.
examples.en: A: The picnic got canceled because of rain / B: What a shame. If only the weather had held.
examples.note: real situation: 아쉽다 paired with a wistful -았/었어도 conditional ('if only X') — this is a very natural 아쉽다 follow-up pattern

entries.nuance: 아쉽다 is mild, wistful regret — 'that's a shame / I wish it were otherwise' — the feeling when something nice didn't happen, ended too soon, or fell just short. It's soft; it's NOT deep sadness. The variant ladder: 아쉽다/아쉬워 (casual) → 아쉬워요 (polite) → 아쉽네(요) (in-the-moment reaction to news) → 좀 아쉽다 (softened, noting a small lack). Note the conjugation: 아쉽다 is a -ㅂ irregular adjective, so the polite stem is 아쉬워요 (아쉽+어요 → 아쉬워요), never 아쉽어요. The dividing line against 슬프다 and 속상하다: 아쉽다 is a gentle 'aw, too bad' about a missed chance or something pleasant ending; 슬프다 is real sadness (loss, grief); 속상하다 is being genuinely hurt or upset inside (frustration, heartache). Sold-out tickets → 아쉽다; a pet dying → 슬프다; your work criticized unfairly → 속상하다. 아쉽다 also covers the sense of 'feeling a lack / something's missing' (뭔가 아쉽다 'something feels lacking'), so context decides. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 슬프다 for everyday letdowns — to a Korean ear that's melodramatic.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 슬프다 ('sad') for small letdowns like a canceled plan — that sounds melodramatic; the natural word for mild regret is 아쉽다.
Confusing 아쉽다 with 아깝다 — 아깝다 is 'what a waste / too good to waste' (about value/resources), while 아쉽다 is 'a shame, wish it were otherwise' (about a missed chance).
Conjugating the -ㅂ irregular adjective wrong: the polite form is 아쉬워요 (아쉽+어요 → 아쉬워요), not 아쉽어요.

structuredNuance.t: 아쉽다 is mild, wistful regret — 'that's a shame / I wish it were otherwise.' It covers both 'disappointed a nice thing didn't happen' and 'feeling a small lack.' It is NOT deep sadness; it's a gentle sigh.
아쉽다/아쉬워 (casual) → 아쉬워요 (polite) → 아쉽네(요) (in-the-moment reaction). 좀 아쉽다 softens it further. Conjugation note: -ㅂ irregular, so polite = 아쉬워요, NOT 아쉽어요.

아쉽다 = mild regret / missed chance (gentle). 슬프다 = real sadness/grief (deep emotion). 속상하다 = hurt/upset inside (frustrated or heartbroken). 아깝다 = 'what a waste' (something valuable was wasted or lost). Sold-out tickets → 아쉽다; a pet dying → 슬프다; unfair criticism → 속상하다; spilling expensive wine → 아깝다.

Using 슬프다 for small everyday disappointments — to a Korean ear that's melodramatic; 아쉽다 is the right word. Conjugating as 아쉽어요 (wrong; -ㅂ irregular makes it 아쉬워요). Confusing 아쉽다 with 아깝다 — 아깝다 is about wasted value, 아쉽다 is about a missed wish.

entries.english: Ugh, so annoying / this is irritating — frustration at something getting on your nerves.
entries.shortExplanation: 짜증 나 is a practical expression meaning "Ugh, so annoying / this is irritating — frustration at something getting on your nerves.".
entries.explanation: 짜증 나 (jjajeung na) means "Ugh, so annoying / this is irritating — frustration at something getting on your nerves.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 짜증 나 ("ugh, so annoying"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: casual banmal, venting to a friend
polite -요, but still informal in flavor
casual exclamatory -ㄴ다 form
with 완전 to intensify

examples.ko: A: 또 에러야 / B: 아, 짜증 나.
examples.romanization: A: tto ereoya / B: a, jjajeung na.
examples.en: A: It's an error again / B: Ugh, so annoying.
examples.note: the bare vent between friends — low-grade prickly frustration, not deep anger

examples.ko: A: 버스 또 놓쳤어. 진짜 짜증 나.
examples.romanization: A: beoseu tto notchyeosseo. jinjja jjajeung na.
examples.en: A: Missed the bus again. So annoying.
examples.note: everyday: venting a small daily frustration to yourself or a friend; 진짜 before 짜증 나 intensifies it naturally

examples.ko: A: 옆에서 계속 시끄럽게 해서 짜증 났어 / B: 아, 그럴 만하다.
examples.romanization: A: yeopeseo gyesok sikkeureopge haeseo jjajeung nasseo / B: a, geureol manhada.
examples.en: A: They kept being loud next to me, it got on my nerves / B: Yeah, that's understandable.
examples.note: real situation: 짜증 나다 in past tense (짜증 났어) describing something that irritated you over time; 그럴 만하다 is a natural empathic reply

entries.nuance: 짜증 나 means 'it's irritating / getting on my nerves' — the low-grade, prickly frustration of small annoyances piling up (repeated errors, delays, noise). 짜증 is the noun 'irritation/peevishness' and 나다 means 'arises,' so literally 'irritation arises.' The particle structure is 짜증(이) 나다 — 짜증 is the subject that 'comes up,' which means 짜증해 (treating it as a 하다 verb) is not a real form. Casual 짜증 나; exclamatory 짜증 난다; polite 짜증 나요 exists but still sounds blunt. Related: 짜증 내다 means 'to show/express irritation' (you actively let it out). The dividing line against 화나다 is degree and direction: 짜증 나다 is low-grade, diffuse annoyance ('ugh, this again'), while 화나다 is real anger directed at someone. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb form: don't say 짜증해 or 짜증을 해 — the correct forms are 짜증(이) 나다 (it arises) or 짜증 내다 (you express it). Another pitfall is register: even 짜증 나요 carries a raw, blunt edge, so to an elder or boss soften to 좀 힘드네요 or 불편하네요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 짜증해 or 짜증을 해 — there's no verb 짜증하다; it's 짜증(이) 나다 (irritation arises) or 짜증 내다 (to show irritation).
Using 짜증 나요 with a boss or elder — even the -요 form is raw/blunt; soften to 좀 힘드네요 / 불편하네요 in respectful settings.
Confusing 짜증 나다 with 화나다 — 짜증 나다 is low-grade peevish annoyance, while 화나다 is genuine anger at someone; they differ in intensity.

structuredNuance.t: 짜증 나 is literally 'irritation arises' — 짜증 (noun: irritation/peevishness) + 나다 (to arise). The real meaning is the prickly, low-grade frustration of small things getting on your nerves. It's NOT deep anger — it's the 'ugh, again?!' feeling.

짜증 나 is casual banmal — for venting to friends or peers. 짜증 나요 is polite but still blunt in flavor — fine with coworkers your age but avoid with elders or bosses. With seniors, soften to 좀 힘드네요 (a bit tough), 불편하네요 (a bit uncomfortable), or 어렵네요 (it's difficult).

짜증 나다 = irritation arises (passive; something is getting on your nerves). 화나다 = anger arises at someone (stronger, directed outward). 짜증 내다 = you actively EXPRESS or show your irritation (can annoy others around you). 짜증 나다 + 화가 나다 can co-occur when something both annoys and angers.

Saying 짜증해 or 짜증을 해 — there's no verb 짜증하다; it's 짜증(이) 나다 (irritation arises) or 짜증 내다 (to show irritation). Using 짜증 나요 with a boss or elder — even with -요 it's too raw; use 좀 힘드네요 or 불편하네요. Confusing 짜증 나다 with 화나다 — the first is low-grade diffuse annoyance, the second is real anger at someone.

entries.english: I'm so excited / this is fun / yay — bubbling, happy excitement.
entries.shortExplanation: 신난다 is a practical expression meaning "I'm so excited / this is fun / yay — bubbling, happy excitement.".
entries.explanation: "I'm so excited / this is fun / yay — bubbling, happy excitement." — that is 신난다 (sinnanda). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 신난다 ("yay, I'm so excited"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: casual exclamatory, to oneself or friends
casual banmal, plain form
polite -요, cheerful but informal
with 완전 to amp up the excitement

examples.ko: A: 내일 여행 가! / B: 신난다!
examples.romanization: A: naeil yeohaeng ga! / B: sinnanda!
examples.en: A: We go on the trip tomorrow! / B: Yay!
examples.note: the bare reaction — bubbling joy at something coming; exclamatory -다 form is natural here

examples.ko: A: 오늘 일찍 끝나서 신나.
examples.romanization: A: oneul iljjik kkeunnaseo sinna.
examples.en: A: We finish early today, so I'm excited.
examples.note: everyday: casual self-expression of happy excitement; 신나 as a plain statement to a friend

examples.ko: A: 콘서트 티켓 구했어! / B: 진짜? 신난다! 빨리 가고 싶다.
examples.romanization: A: konseoteu tiket guhaesseo! / B: jinjja? sinnanda! ppalli gago sipda.
examples.en: A: I got the concert tickets! / B: Really? Yay! I can't wait to go.
examples.note: real situation: 신난다 + 빨리 가고 싶다 is a very natural chain — the excitement immediately becomes eager anticipation

entries.nuance: 신난다 is bright, bubbling excitement — 'yay, this is so fun / I can't wait!' — the happy energy buzz before or during something enjoyable. Built from 신(이) 나다 'spirit/mood arises': plain 신나 (casual), exclamatory 신난다, polite 신나요. Because it's cheerful and casual, it's perfect among friends but too breezy for formal settings. The variant ladder: 신나 → 신난다 → 완전 신난다 (hyped). The dividing line against 기대돼요 and 재미있다: 신나다 is active, energetic excitement right now (you're bouncing); 기대되다 is calm, forward-looking anticipation ('I'm looking forward to it'); 재미있다 describes how fun an activity actually IS or WAS (not about anticipation). Road-trip vibe the night before → 신난다; quietly looking forward to seeing an old friend → 기대돼요; describing how the trip turned out → 재미있었어. The English-speaker pitfall is using 흥분되다 for 'excited' — 흥분되다 means agitated/worked-up (can imply arousal or anger) and sounds very off for innocent fun; the right word for happy excitement is 신나다. A second pitfall is expressing enthusiasm to a superior with 신난다 — it's too casual; use 기대돼요 or 정말 기쁩니다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'excited' as 흥분되다 — that means agitated/worked-up (can imply arousal or anger); cheerful excitement is 신나다.
Saying 신난다 to a boss to show enthusiasm — it's breezy and casual; in respectful settings use 기대돼요 or 정말 기쁩니다.
Forming it as 신하다 or 신해 — there's no such verb; it's 신(이) 나다, so the forms are 신나 / 신난다 / 신나요.

structuredNuance.t: 신난다 comes from 신(이) 나다 — 신 (spirit/energy/mood) + 나다 (to arise). Literally 'the spirit arises.' As a reaction it means 'I'm buzzing with excitement / yay!' — active, energetic, happy anticipation.
신나 (casual plain) → 신난다 (casual exclamatory) → 신나요 (polite but informal-flavored). 완전 신난다 intensifies. With a superior or in a formal setting, switch to 기대돼요 or 정말 기쁩니다 — 신난다 sounds too breezy.

신나다 = active, energetic excitement right now (you're bouncing with enthusiasm). 기대되다 = calm forward-looking anticipation ('I'm looking forward to it'). 재미있다 = describes how fun an activity IS or WAS (assessment). Trip-eve energy → 신난다; quietly anticipating → 기대돼요; recounting how fun it was → 재미있었어.

Using 흥분되다 for 'excited' — 흥분되다 means agitated/worked-up (can imply arousal or even anger) and sounds jarring for innocent fun. The right word for happy excitement is 신나다. Using 신난다 with a boss or superior — it's casual; switch to 기대돼요 or 정말 기쁩니다.

entries.english: Whoa, you scared me! / yikes — startled when something jumps out or surprises you suddenly.
entries.shortExplanation: 깜짝이야 is a practical expression meaning "Whoa, you scared me! / yikes — startled when something jumps out or surprises you suddenly.".
entries.explanation: 깜짝이야 (kkamjjagiya) = "Whoa, you scared me! / yikes — startled when something jumps out or surprises you suddenly.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 깜짝이야 ("you scared me!"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: casual banmal, instant startle reaction
with 아 as the natural gasp lead-in
fuller form, mild complaint
polite -어요, to someone you respect

examples.ko: (친구가 갑자기 등장) A: 야! / B: 아, 깜짝이야!
examples.romanization: (chinguga gapjagi deungjang) A: ya! / B: a, kkamjjagiya!
examples.en: (friend pops up suddenly) A: Hey! / B: Oh, you scared me!
examples.note: the bare startle — instant reflex; 아 leads in naturally before 깜짝이야

examples.ko: A: 뒤에서 갑자기 부르지 마, 깜짝이야.
examples.romanization: A: dwieseo gapjagi bureuji ma, kkamjjagiya.
examples.en: A: Don't call me from behind suddenly, you scared me.
examples.note: everyday: mild complaint after being startled — 깜짝이야 at the end explains WHY the request is being made

examples.ko: A: (문 열다 마주침) 어머! / B: 아, 깜짝 놀랐어요. 안에 계신 줄 몰랐어요.
examples.romanization: A: (mun yeolda majuchim) eomeo! / B: a, kkamjjang nollasseoyo. ane gyesin jul mollasseoyo.
examples.en: A: (opens door, bumps into someone) Oh! / B: Oh, you startled me. I didn't know you were inside.
examples.note: real situation: polite 깜짝 놀랐어요 to a senior after a mutual startle — you can't use 깜짝이야 politely, so you switch to 깜짝 놀랐어요

entries.nuance: 깜짝이야 is the reflex 'whoa, you scared me!' that bursts out the instant something startles you — a friend appearing suddenly, a loud noise, a jump-scare. It comes from 깜짝 (the mimetic/sound-symbolic word for a sudden flinch) + 이야 (casual 이다 declaration). Because it's a raw reflex exclamation it's inherently casual; there's no polite 깜짝이에요 that sounds natural. In a respectful situation you switch to 깜짝 놀랐어요 ('I was startled') which carries the same meaning with -어요 politeness. The dividing line against 무섭다 ('I'm scared/afraid') is duration: 깜짝이야 / 깜짝 놀라다 is a momentary jolt that's over in a second, while 무섭다 is sustained fear or dread (a horror movie, a threatening person). A friend jumping out → 깜짝이야; a dark alley at night → 무서워. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 너 나를 무섭게 했어 ('you scared me' — literal translation) — that's unnatural; Koreans say 깜짝 놀랐잖아 or 깜짝이야. Another pitfall is treating 놀라다 as transitive: you can't 'scare someone' directly with 놀라다 — the person 놀라다 (gets startled); to say you startled them use 놀라게 하다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 너 나 무섭게 했어 for 'you scared me' — that's a literal, unnatural calque; natives say 깜짝 놀랐잖아 or 아, 깜짝이야.
Using 무섭다 for a momentary startle — 무섭다 is sustained fear/dread; a sudden jolt of surprise is 깜짝 놀라다 / 깜짝이야.
Treating 놀라다 as 'to scare (someone)' — the person 놀라다 (is startled); to startle them you say 놀라게 하다, since 놀라다 itself is intransitive.

structuredNuance.t: 깜짝이야 is built from 깜짝 — a mimetic (sound-symbolic) word for a sudden flinch or start — + 이야 (casual copula). Literally 'it's a 깜짝!' meaning 'what a shock!' As a reaction it means 'you startled me / you scared me!' — an instant, involuntary exclamation.

깜짝이야 is casual/banmal — a raw reflex that you can't really dress up. With a senior or in a formal situation, switch to 깜짝 놀랐어요 ('I was startled') to convey the same meaning politely. 아, 깜짝이야 with the lead-in 아 is the most natural everyday form.

깜짝이야 / 깜짝 놀라다 = momentary jolt of surprise (over in a second). 무섭다 = sustained fear/dread (horror movie, threatening situation). 헉 = a sharp gasp of fright, slightly more physical than 깜짝이야. Friend jumping out → 깜짝이야; dark alley → 무서워; sudden loud bang → 헉.

Saying 너 나 무섭게 했어 for 'you scared me' — that's a literal but unnatural calque; Koreans say 깜짝 놀랐잖아 or 깜짝이야. Treating 놀라다 as transitive: 놀라다 is intransitive (the person gets startled); to say you caused it use 놀라게 하다. Using 무섭다 for a momentary startle — 무섭다 is sustained fear, not a flinch.

entries.english: No way / that's ridiculous / unbelievable — strong disbelief at something absurd or shocking.
entries.shortExplanation: 말도 안 돼 is a practical expression meaning "No way / that's ridiculous / unbelievable — strong disbelief at something absurd or shocking.".
entries.explanation: 말도 안 돼 (maldo an dwae) means "No way / that's ridiculous / unbelievable — strong disbelief at something absurd or shocking.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 말도 안 돼 ("no way / that's ridiculous"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: casual banmal, strong disbelief
polite -요, to someone you respect
slight variant stressing 'doesn't make sense'
with 진짜 to intensify

examples.ko: A: 그 사람이 1등이래 / B: 말도 안 돼.
examples.romanization: A: geu sarami 1deungirae / B: maldo an dwae.
examples.en: A: They say that person came first / B: No way.
examples.note: the bare reaction — flat, strong disbelief; 말도 안 돼 rejects the claim as impossible, not just 'really?'

examples.ko: A: 집값이 두 배 올랐대 / B: 말도 안 돼. 어떻게 그래?
examples.romanization: A: jipgapsi du bae ollatdae / B: maldo an dwae. eotteoke geurae?
examples.en: A: They say housing prices doubled / B: That's ridiculous. How is that even possible?
examples.note: everyday: disbelief at outrageous news; 어떻게 그래? is a natural follow-up to extend the protest

examples.ko: A: 환불이 안 된다고 하시네요 / B: 네? 말도 안 돼요. 영수증도 있는데요.
examples.romanization: A: hwanburi an doendago hasineyo / B: ne? maldo an dwaeyo. yeongsujeungdo inneundeyo.
examples.en: A: They're saying no refunds / B: What? That's outrageous. I even have the receipt.
examples.note: real situation: polite 말도 안 돼요 protesting something unfair — with -요 it's still firm but directed appropriately at a service situation

entries.nuance: 말도 안 돼 literally means 'it doesn't even become words' → 'that makes no sense / no way / this is ridiculous' — a strong reaction of disbelief or protest at something absurd, shocking, or unfair. Built from 말+도 안 되다 — 말 'words/speech,' 도 'even (additive particle),' 안 되다 'doesn't work out.' (Note: the subject particle 이 is dropped when 도 follows: 말이+도 → 말도.) Casual 말도 안 돼, polite 말도 안 돼요. The dividing line against 진짜? / 정말요? is strength: 진짜? is a light 'really?' that is open to it being true; 말도 안 돼 flatly rejects the claim as impossible or outrageous — much stronger. It also differs from 대박 ('wow, huge'): 대박 can be amazed positive or shocked; 말도 안 돼 specifically protests/rejects. The English-speaker pitfall is the spelling: 돼 is 되+어, never just 되; writing 말도 안 되 (without the final ㅓ vowel) is a very common error. Another pitfall is register/strength — 말도 안 돼요 to a superior can sound confrontational; to push back politely use 그럴 리가요 ('surely not') or 이해가 안 되네요 ('I don't quite understand').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 말도 안 되 — the form is 말도 안 돼 (되+어 = 돼); as a sentence-final reaction it must end in 돼, not 되.
Using 말도 안 돼(요) for mild surprise — it's strong rejection ('impossible/ridiculous'); for open-minded 'really?' use 진짜? / 정말요?.
Dropping 말도 안 돼요 on a superior in a dispute — it can sound confrontational; to push back politely use 그럴 리가요 or 이해가 안 되네요.

structuredNuance.t: 말도 안 돼 literally means 'it doesn't even become words' — the idea is so absurd or wrong that language itself can't accommodate it. In use: strong disbelief, rejection, or protest at something ridiculous or unfair. It is NOT just 'really?' — it actively denies the claim.

말도 안 돼 is casual banmal. 말도 안 돼요 is polite. Both are strong in tone, so with a superior or in a polite dispute you may need to soften further: 그럴 리가요 ('surely not'), 이해가 안 되네요 ('that doesn't quite make sense to me'). 말도 안 돼요 to a boss in anger can sound confrontational.

진짜? = light 'really?' — open-minded, you might believe it. 말도 안 돼 = strong rejection — you flatly disbelieve or protest it. 그럴 리가(요) = polite/softer disbelief ('it can't be / surely not') — same rejection, but gentler register, safer with seniors.

Spelling: 돼 = 되+어, NOT just 되; writing 말도 안 되 as a sentence-final reaction is a common error. Treating it like mild surprise — it's strong; for a light 'really?' use 진짜? or 정말요?. Using it confrontationally with a superior — soften to 그럴 리가요 or 이해가 안 되네요.

entries.english: Oh my / oh! — a quick gasp of surprise, more neutral and usable than 헐.
entries.shortExplanation: 어머 is a practical expression meaning "Oh my / oh! — a quick gasp of surprise, more neutral and usable than 헐.".
entries.explanation: 어머 (eomeo) = "Oh my / oh! — a quick gasp of surprise, more neutral and usable than 헐.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 어머 ("oh my / oh!"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: neutral surprise, common (esp. women, all ages)
stronger, more emphatic gasp

usagePhrases.en: oh my, what do we do
usagePhrases.note: surprise sliding into worry
startled-apologetic, e.g. a small bump

examples.ko: A: (컵을 떨어뜨림) / B: 어머!
examples.romanization: A: (keobeul tteoreotteurim) / B: eomeo!
examples.en: A: (drops a cup) / B: Oh!
examples.note: the bare gasp — instant surprise at a sudden event; pure reflex

examples.ko: A: 이거 선물이에요 / B: 어머, 뭘 이런 걸 다. 감사해요.
examples.romanization: A: igeo seonmurieyo / B: eomeo, mwol ireon geol da. gamsahaeyo.
examples.en: A: This is a gift for you / B: Oh my, you shouldn't have. Thank you.
examples.note: everyday: pleased-surprised reaction to a gift; 뭘 이런 걸 다 ('you didn't have to') is the perfect polite follow-up after 어머

examples.ko: A: 비 갑자기 쏟아진다 / B: 어머, 우산도 없는데 어떡해.
examples.romanization: A: bi gapjagi ssodajinda / B: eomeo, usando eopsneunde eotteokae.
examples.en: A: It's suddenly pouring / B: Oh my, and I don't have an umbrella, what do I do.
examples.note: real situation: 어머 triggers 어떡해 as surprise flows naturally into worry — this two-step chain is very common in women's speech

entries.nuance: 어머 is a quick, soft gasp of surprise — 'oh!' / 'oh my' — far more neutral and polite-safe than slangy 헐 or 대박. It is a pure interjection so it doesn't take -요; to be polite you follow it with a full polite sentence. The register difference: 어머 is gentle, refined surprise that anyone can use across ages and contexts, including in front of elders and in semi-formal moments where 헐 would sound rude. Stronger and more emphatic is 어머나; surprise that turns to worry naturally extends as 어머 어떡해. A social note: 어머 / 어머나 is used by everyone but has a stronger association with women's speech; men tend to reach for 어 / 어이쿠 / 헐 instead. The dividing line against 헐: 헐 is casual youth slang with a shock/dismay tilt, while 어머 is softer and registers as more composed and socially graceful. The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to 헐 in every surprised moment — with an older Korean or in a slightly formal context, 헐 can sound rude, so 어머 is the safe default. Another pitfall is treating 어머 as filler and saying it flatly; it carries genuine emotional color and should sound like a real gasp.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Defaulting to 헐 in every surprised moment, including with elders — 헐 is slang and can sound rude; 어머 is the neutral, polite-safe gasp.
Adding -요 as 어머요 — it's a reflexive interjection and doesn't take -요; for politeness, follow it with a full polite sentence.
Treating 어머 as meaningless filler — it carries genuine surprise/emotion, so saying it flatly with no feeling sounds odd; it should sound like a real gasp.

structuredNuance.t: 어머 is a soft gasp of surprise — 'oh!' / 'oh my' — neutral and polite-safe across ages and contexts. It's a reflexive interjection (no -요 attached); politeness comes from the full sentence that follows.

어머 works in casual AND semi-formal settings — safe with elders, colleagues, or strangers where 헐 would sound rude. It doesn't take -요 directly. Social note: commonly used by women of all ages; men often prefer 어 / 어이쿠. 어머나 is stronger; 어머 어떡해 adds worry.

헐 = casual youth slang, shock/dismay tilt — only among friends and peers; sounds rude with elders. 어머 = softer, more refined surprise, cross-generational, polite-safe. 어이쿠 = similar neutral gasp, slightly more physical surprise (oops/ow/yikes), skewing male speech. All three are interjections that don't take -요.
어머 (base gasp) → 어머나 (stronger emphasis) → 어머 어떡해 (surprise + worry). In texts you might write 어머나 세상에 for dramatic emphasis. None of these take a -요 suffix directly.

Defaulting to 헐 in every surprised moment — with elders or in formal contexts 헐 is rude; 어머 is the neutral, graceful default. Adding -요 as 어머요 — interjections don't take -요; follow 어머 with a full polite sentence instead. Saying 어머 flatly without genuine surprise energy — it carries real emotional color and should sound like a true gasp.

entries.english: I see / so that's how it is — calmly taking in information you've just been told.
entries.shortExplanation: 그렇군요 is a practical expression meaning "I see / so that's how it is — calmly taking in information you've just been told.".
entries.explanation: 그렇군요 (geureokunyo) means "I see / so that's how it is — calmly taking in information you've just been told.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 그렇군요 ("I see / ah, so that's how it is"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: I see / ah, so that's how it is
usagePhrases.note: polite -요, composed acknowledgment of new info; slightly formal in feel
casual banmal, to a friend or someone younger; warmer and more natural in chat
the 아 marks the moment it lands — sounds more engaged than a bare 그렇군요
honorific -시- inserted when the new information is about the listener themselves

examples.ko: A: 이 건물은 주말엔 문을 닫아요 / B: 아, 그렇군요. 몰랐어요.
examples.romanization: A: i geonmureun jumaren muneul dadayo / B: a, geureokunyo. mollasseoyo.
examples.en: A: This building closes on weekends / B: Ah, I see. I didn't know.
examples.note: the core use — a fact you learned this second; 몰랐어요 makes explicit that it's new to you

examples.ko: A: 제가 원래 부산 사람이에요 / B: 그러시군요. 어쩐지 사투리가 살짝 들리더라고요.
examples.romanization: A: jega wollae busan saramieyo / B: geureosigunyo. eojjeonji saturiga saljjak deullideoragoyo.
examples.en: A: I'm originally from Busan / B: Oh, I see. That's why I could hear a bit of the dialect.
examples.note: info about the listener → honorific 그러시군요; the follow-up shows you actually did something with what you heard

examples.ko: A: 그래서 예약을 다시 잡아야 해요 / B: 그렇군요. 그럼 언제가 괜찮으세요?
examples.romanization: A: geuraeseo yeyageul dasi jabaya haeyo / B: geureokunyo. geureom eonjega gwaenchaneuseyo?
examples.en: A: So we have to rebook the appointment / B: I see. Then when works for you?
examples.note: workplace/service: 그렇군요 accepts the explanation without emotion and hands the turn back — neutral and composed

entries.nuance: 그렇군요 means 'I see / ah, so that's how it is' — you are registering information you did not have a moment ago. It's 그렇다 'to be so' + -군요, the ending whose whole job is to mark a fact as newly learned; drop the -요 for casual 그렇구나/그렇군, add -시- for 그러시군요 when the news is about the listener. The dividing line against 그러게요 is the direction of the knowledge: 그러게요 says 'I know, right' about a feeling you ALREADY shared, while 그렇군요 says 'oh, I didn't know that' about something NEW — swap them and you either sound like you already knew (dismissive) or like you're learning your own opinion. Against 아 그래요?: 그렇군요 closes the loop calmly with no question attached; 아 그래요? is surprised and asks for more. Against 그렇네요: -네요 is for what you notice with your own eyes and ears (비가 오네요, looking out the window), -군요 for what you were told. The English-speaker pitfall is volume of use: textbook learners answer everything with 그렇군요 until it sounds like a distant, robotic nod. With friends 그렇구나 or 아 진짜요? sound like a person listening. Also 그렇군요 is not 알겠습니다 — that's 'understood, I'll do it,' a receipt for an instruction.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 그렇군요 to respond to a shared feeling or opinion ('오늘 덥네요') — 그렇군요 frames it as news you just learned; agreeing with a feeling you also have is 그러게요 or 그러네요.
Answering every single turn with 그렇군요 — it's grammatically fine but reads as a distant, robotic nod, especially with friends; 그렇구나 or 아 그래요? sound like an actual listener.
Using 그렇군요 where 알겠습니다 is needed — a boss gives you an instruction and 그렇군요 only says 'oh, interesting,' not 'understood, I'll do it.'

structuredNuance.t: 그렇군요 = 'I see, so that's how it is.' You are taking in information that is NEW to you, calmly and without pushing back. The -군요 ending exists precisely to flag a fact as newly learned. It is acknowledgment, not agreement and not surprise.

그렇군요 is polite and a touch composed — it fits coworkers, service situations, and anyone you use 존댓말 with. With friends it can sound stiff and distant, so use 그렇구나. When the new fact is about the listener personally (their hometown, their job, their family), add -시-: 그러시군요.

그렇군요 = NEW info, accepted calmly, no question. 그러게요 = a feeling you ALREADY shared ('I know, right') — using it on new info implies you knew all along. 아 그래요? = mild surprise that asks for more, opening the topic instead of closing it. 그렇네요 = you noticed it yourself (-네요 is for direct perception: 비가 오네요), while -군요 is for what you were told.
그렇구나 (casual) → 그렇군요 (polite) → 그러시군요 (honorific, about the listener). Prefixing 아 (아, 그렇군요) makes it sound like the fact is landing in real time rather than being ticked off a list.

Overusing it — 그렇군요 as your default reply to everything reads as flat and disengaged, a classic textbook-learner tell; vary with 그렇구나, 아 그래요?, 정말요?. Using 그렇군요 for something you already knew (that's 그러게요 or 아 맞다). Treating it as 'understood, will do' — that's 알겠습니다.

entries.english: Oh really? / is that so? — light surprise plus a nudge for the other person to tell you more.
entries.shortExplanation: 아 그래요? is a practical expression meaning "Oh really? / is that so? — light surprise plus a nudge for the other person to tell you more.".
entries.explanation: "Oh really? / is that so? — light surprise plus a nudge for the other person to tell you more." — that is 아 그래요? (a geuraeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 아 그래요? ("oh really? / is that so?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: polite -요, mild surprise that invites more; requires clearly rising intonation
casual banmal, to a friend or someone younger
without the 아 it lands flatter and, with an edge, can sound like a challenge
past tense, reacting to something that already happened

examples.ko: A: 저 그 영화 벌써 봤어요 / B: 아 그래요? 어땠어요?
examples.romanization: A: jeo geu yeonghwa beolsseo bwasseoyo / B: a geuraeyo? eottaesseoyo?
examples.en: A: I already saw that movie / B: Oh really? How was it?
examples.note: the model pattern — light surprise, then a follow-up question; 아 그래요? alone would stall the conversation

examples.ko: A: 사장님 오늘 휴가세요 / B: 아 그래요? 몰랐네요.
examples.romanization: A: sajangnim oneul hyugaseyo / B: a geuraeyo? mollanneyo.
examples.en: A: The boss is on vacation today / B: Oh, is that so? I had no idea.
examples.note: workplace: mild surprise at news; polite and completely safe with a coworker

examples.ko: A: 나 어제 너 봤는데 / B: 아 그랬어? 어디서?
examples.romanization: A: na eoje neo bwanneunde / B: a geuraesseo? eodiseo?
examples.en: A: I saw you yesterday / B: Oh yeah? Where?
examples.note: casual banmal in the past tense; the reaction opens the topic rather than closing it

entries.nuance: 아 그래요? is the everyday 'oh really? / is that so?' — you accept that what they said is true and react to it with mild surprise, then usually ask for more. The 아 is doing real work: it marks the information as landing right now, which is what makes the line sound interested rather than skeptical. Intonation is not optional here. Said with a clear rise, 아 그래요? means 'oh! tell me more.' Said flat, low, and slow, the exact same syllables become the bored 'oh, is that right' that tells your friend you'd like them to stop talking — and 그래요? without the 아, delivered with a sharp edge, tips into 'oh yeah?', a challenge. That's why beginners should keep all three parts: 아 + rise + a follow-up question. The line against 정말요?/진짜요? is what you're questioning: those ask whether the claim is TRUE (verification, mild doubt); 아 그래요? takes it as true and reacts to the news itself. Against 그렇군요: 그렇군요 absorbs the fact and closes the loop; 아 그래요? hands the turn back. And watch the punctuation — 그래요 without the rise isn't a reaction at all but agreement or consent: 그래요, 그럼 그렇게 해요 'okay, let's do that.'
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 아 그래요? flat and low, the way English 'oh really' can be said neutrally — in Korean the falling version reads as bored or sneering; it must rise clearly to mean 'tell me more.'
Using 아 그래요? when you actually doubt the claim — for 'wait, is that TRUE?' the natural choice is 정말요? or 진짜요?; 아 그래요? already accepts what they said.
Dropping 그래요? as a standalone with nothing after it — with no follow-up question the conversation dies and you sound unmoved; pair it with 어땠어요? / 언제부터요? / 왜요?

structuredNuance.t: 아 그래요? = 'oh really? / is that so?' You believe what they said; you're mildly surprised by it and you want more. Its function is to keep the other person talking, which is why it almost always comes with a follow-up question (어땠어요? / 언제요? / 왜요?).

그래요? is polite and safe with coworkers, neighbors, and strangers. 그래? is the banmal partner for friends. When the news is about the listener personally and they're clearly senior to you, 아, 그러세요? / 그러시군요 sounds more deferential than a bare 그래요?.

정말요? / 진짜요? question whether it's TRUE — verification with a touch of doubt. 아 그래요? accepts it's true and reacts to the news, then asks for more. 그렇군요 also accepts it but closes the loop calmly with no question. 그러게요 agrees with a feeling you already shared — a completely different move; using it on someone's news implies you already knew.

아 그래? (casual) → 아 그래요? (polite) → 아, 그러세요? (honorific, about a senior). Past tense 아 그랬어요? / 아 그랬어? for things already finished. The 아 can be dropped, but keeping it is what makes the line sound freshly interested.

Intonation decides everything. Rising = genuine interest. Flat, low, and slow = the sarcastic-sounding 'oh, is that right,' i.e. 'I don't care' — the single most common way learners accidentally offend with this phrase. A sharp 그래요? with no 아 can read as 'oh yeah?', a challenge. And 그래요 with NO rise isn't a reaction at all — it's 'okay / sure' (그래요, 그렇게 해요).

entries.english: Exactly / that's what I'm saying — emphatic agreement with someone's opinion or complaint.
entries.shortExplanation: 그러니까요 is a practical expression meaning "Exactly / that's what I'm saying — emphatic agreement with someone's opinion or complaint.".
entries.explanation: 그러니까요 (geureonikkayo) = "Exactly / that's what I'm saying — emphatic agreement with someone's opinion or complaint.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 그러니까요 ("exactly / right? that's what I'm saying"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: exactly / right? that's what I'm saying
usagePhrases.note: polite -요, forceful agreement with an opinion
casual banmal, to a friend
fuller polite form, stronger and more heartfelt
near-equivalent; leans even harder on 'I've been saying this'

examples.ko: A: 요즘 배달비가 너무 비싸요 / B: 그러니까요. 음식값보다 더 나올 때도 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: yojeum baedalbiga neomu bissayo / B: geureonikkayo. eumsikgapsboda deo naol ttaedo isseoyo.
examples.en: A: Delivery fees are so expensive these days / B: Exactly. Sometimes it comes out higher than the food.
examples.note: the natural shape: you already felt this way and you pile on your own evidence

examples.ko: A: 회의를 굳이 금요일 6시에 잡네 / B: 그러니까. 누가 정한 거야?
examples.romanization: A: hoeuireul guji geumyoil 6sie jamne / B: geureonikka. nuga jeonghan geoya?
examples.en: A: They really scheduled the meeting for 6pm Friday / B: Right?? Who decided that?
examples.note: casual banmal complaint; 그러니까 says 'you're preaching to the choir'

examples.ko: A: 그 길로 가면 항상 막혀요 / B: 그러니까요. 제가 진작 말씀드렸잖아요.
examples.romanization: A: geu gillo gamyeon hangsang makyeoyo / B: geureonikkayo. jega jinjang malsseumdeuryeotjanayo.
examples.en: A: That road is always jammed / B: Exactly. I told you so ages ago, remember?
examples.note: notice the edge — 그러니까요 can carry a faint 'I've been saying this all along,' fine with peers but pointed if aimed upward

entries.nuance: 그러니까요 is emphatic agreement: 'exactly / that's what I'm saying.' It's 그러다 'to be like that' + -니까 'because,' and that etymology is why it carries a whiff of 'that's exactly WHY' — you're not just nodding along, you're endorsing their point as one you already held. The ladder runs 그러니까 (casual) → 그러니까요 (polite) → 그러니까 말이에요 (emphatic). The line against 그러게요 is intensity and posture: 그러게요 is soft and often faintly resigned, 'I know, right, what can you do'; 그러니까요 is louder and leans forward, closer to 'see? this is my point.' Against 맞아요 it's a hard grammatical line: 맞아요 confirms a FACT is correct — 서울이 수도예요 → 맞아요 — while 그러니까요 only works on an opinion, complaint, or observation. Answer a factual question with 그러니까요 and you've said nothing. It also cannot absorb new information; that's 그렇군요. The English-speaker pitfall is that 그러니까 mid-sentence is a totally different word: the connective 'so, therefore' (비가 와요, 그러니까 우산 챙기세요) and the rephrasing filler 'I mean...'. Only a standalone 그러니까(요) as a whole response is the agreement reaction. Second, aimed at a boss, that 'I've been saying this' undertone can read as pushy — 맞습니다 or 저도 그렇게 생각합니다 is safer.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 그러니까요 to agree that a fact is correct — for '서울이 한국 수도예요' the answer is 맞아요; 그러니까요 only works on an opinion, complaint, or shared observation.
Mixing up the standalone reaction with the connective 그러니까 'so/therefore' mid-sentence — 그러니까 우산 챙기세요 means 'so bring an umbrella,' not 'exactly, bring an umbrella.'
Firing 그러니까요 at a boss's remark — it carries an 'I've been saying this all along' edge that can sound like you're correcting them; use 맞습니다 or 저도 그렇게 생각합니다.

structuredNuance.t: 그러니까요 = 'exactly / that's what I'm saying.' Strong agreement with an opinion, complaint, or observation the other person just made — and an implicit claim that you already thought so yourself. It leans forward; it's not a polite nod.

그러니까요 is polite and completely normal with coworkers and friends' parents. But the built-in 'as I've been saying' assertiveness means that with a boss or a much older person it can read as pushing your view. Upward, 맞습니다 / 그렇습니다 / 저도 그렇게 생각합니다 does the same job without the edge.

그러게요 = soft, often resigned 'I know, right' — sharing a feeling. 그러니까요 = emphatic 'exactly, that's my point' — endorsing a view you already held, more forceful. 맞아요 = 'that's correct' — it can confirm FACTS, which 그러니까요 cannot (a quiz answer gets 맞아요, never 그러니까요). 그렇군요 = new info you just learned, the opposite situation entirely.
그러니까 (casual) → 그러니까요 (polite) → 그러니까 말이에요 (emphatic full agreement) → 제 말이 그 말이에요 / 내 말이 (that's my point exactly). Colloquial 그니까 / 그니까요 is the same word contracted in speech and texting.

Confusing the standalone reaction with the connective: mid-sentence 그러니까 means 'so, therefore' (비가 와요, 그러니까 우산 챙기세요) or the filler 'I mean...' when you rephrase. Only 그러니까(요) as a complete response is 'exactly.' Also, using it on facts instead of opinions, and firing it at a superior, where the 'I told you so' undertone shows.

entries.english: Oh good, that worked out — reacting on the spot to a situation turning out well.
entries.shortExplanation: 잘됐네요 is a practical expression meaning "Oh good, that worked out — reacting on the spot to a situation turning out well.".
entries.explanation: 잘됐네요 (jaldwaenneyo) means "Oh good, that worked out — reacting on the spot to a situation turning out well.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 잘됐네요 ("oh good, that worked out"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: polite; -네요 = you're reacting the moment you hear it
casual banmal, to a friend
polite, but a flat statement rather than an in-the-moment reaction
about a situation that suits everyone — not about anyone's achievement

examples.ko: A: 다음 주에 재택근무 해도 된대요 / B: 잘됐네요! 출퇴근 시간 아끼겠어요.
examples.romanization: A: daeum jue jaetaekgeunmu haedo doendaeyo / B: jaldwaenneyo! chultoegeun sigan akkigesseoyo.
examples.en: A: They said I can work from home next week / B: Oh, that's great! You'll save the commute.
examples.note: a situation landing well, not an achievement — 잘됐네요 fits; 축하해요 would be strange here

examples.ko: A: 저 3시 이후에 시간 돼요 / B: 아, 잘됐네요. 저도 그때가 편해요.
examples.romanization: A: jeo 3si ihue sigan dwaeyo / B: a, jaldwaenneyo. jeodo geuttaega pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: A: I'm free after 3 / B: Oh, that works out nicely. That time suits me too.
examples.note: the scheduling sense — it's convenient for BOTH of you; 축하해요 is impossible in this situation

examples.ko: A: 아버지 검사 결과 괜찮대요 / B: 잘됐네요, 정말 다행이에요.
examples.romanization: A: abeoji geomsa gyeolgwa gwaenchantaeyo / B: jaldwaenneyo, jeongmal dahaengieyo.
examples.en: A: My father's test results came back fine / B: Oh good — what a relief.
examples.note: paired with 다행이에요 when there was real worry: 잘됐네요 reacts to the outcome, 다행이에요 names the relief

entries.nuance: 잘됐네요 is 잘 'well' + 되다 'to turn out' + -네요, and that -네요 is the whole point: it marks the words as a reaction forming right now, in response to news you are hearing this second, which is why 잘됐네요 sounds alive where the flatter 잘됐어요 sounds like a statement. The dividing line against 축하해요 is what produced the good outcome. 축하해요 congratulates a PERSON for something they achieved or a milestone they reached — 합격, 승진, 결혼, 졸업 — so it needs an accomplishment to attach to. 잘됐네요 only says the situation landed well, which lets it cover things nobody earned: a meeting getting canceled, two schedules matching, test results coming back clean, the rain stopping. It also works for your own convenience — 그럼 잘됐네요 'then that suits me' — something 축하해요 can never do. Flip side: for a genuine achievement, 잘됐네요 alone can land a little thin, like 'well, that worked out,' so stack them: 합격했다고요? 잘됐네요, 축하해요! Against 다행이에요, the difference is prior dread — 다행 requires that you were worried. Pitfalls: the tone trap that also haunts 잘됐다 (say it flat or clipped and it flips to a sour 'well, isn't that nice for you'), and the spelling — 됐 comes from 되+었, so 잘됬네요 is always wrong.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Reaching for 축하해요 when nobody achieved anything — for a canceled meeting or two schedules lining up, 축하해요 is nonsense; 잘됐네요 is the word for a situation that simply worked out.
Answering someone's 합격 or 승진 with only 잘됐네요 — it reads as thin, closer to 'well, that worked out'; add 축하해요 because a personal achievement needs to be credited to them.
Writing 잘됬네요 — the past of 되다 is 됐다 (되+었), so it's 잘됐네요, written as one word.

structuredNuance.t: 잘됐네요 = 'oh good, that worked out.' You're reacting on the spot, warmly, to a situation that turned out well. The -네요 ending is what marks it as a live reaction to news you're hearing right now, rather than a considered statement.

잘됐네요 is polite and safe with coworkers, seniors, and clients; 잘됐네 is the banmal partner for friends. For a big achievement, don't stop at 잘됐네요 — it can read as thin praise; add 축하해요 (or, if effort was involved, 고생 많으셨어요) to make it warm.

축하해요 congratulates a person for an ACHIEVEMENT or milestone (합격, 승진, 결혼) — it needs someone to credit. 잘됐네요 just says the SITUATION worked out, so it covers things nobody earned (a canceled meeting, matching schedules) and even your own convenience (그럼 잘됐네요 'then that suits me'), which 축하해요 cannot. 다행이에요 requires prior dread — relief that a feared outcome didn't happen. 잘됐어요 is the same word without the live-reaction feel of -네요.
잘됐네 (casual) → 잘됐네요 (polite, reacting to news) → 잘됐어요 (polite statement) → 그럼 잘됐네요 ('then that works out'). Prepend 정말 / 너무 to warm it up: 정말 잘됐네요.

Tone: said flat or clipped, 잘됐네요 flips to a sour 'well, isn't that nice for you' — keep your voice clearly warm. Spelling: 됐 = 되+었, so 잘됬네요 is always wrong and 잘 됐네요 with a space is off too. And using 잘됐네요 alone for someone's big win undersells it; 축하해요 belongs there.

entries.english: Me too / same here — saying that what they just said about themselves is true of you as well.
entries.shortExplanation: 저도요 is a practical expression meaning "Me too / same here — saying that what they just said about themselves is true of you as well.".
entries.explanation: "Me too / same here — saying that what they just said about themselves is true of you as well." — that is 저도요 (jeodoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 저도요 ("me too / same here"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: polite; the ellipsis of 저도 그래요, safe with anyone you use 존댓말 with
casual banmal, to a friend
fuller polite form — warmer and less clipped, good for feelings
a shade more formal; natural in a workplace

examples.ko: A: 만나서 반가워요 / B: 저도요.
examples.romanization: A: mannaseo bangawoyo / B: jeodoyo.
examples.en: A: Nice to meet you / B: You too.
examples.note: the classic — 저도요 stands in for 저도 반가워요; English says 'you too,' Korean says 'me too'

examples.ko: A: 저는 커피 안 마셔요 / B: 저도요. 카페인이 안 받아서요.
examples.romanization: A: jeoneun keopi an masyeoyo / B: jeodoyo. kapeini an badaseoyo.
examples.en: A: I don't drink coffee / B: Me neither. Caffeine doesn't agree with me.
examples.note: note the negative: Korean uses the same 저도요 where English is forced to switch to 'me neither'

examples.ko: A: 요즘 너무 피곤해요 / B: 저도요. 잠을 제대로 못 자서요.
examples.romanization: A: yojeum neomu pigonhaeyo / B: jeodoyo. jameul jedaero mot jaseoyo.
examples.en: A: I'm so tired lately / B: Same here. I haven't been sleeping properly.
examples.note: everyday empathy; adding one clause of your own keeps 저도요 from sounding like you're brushing them off

entries.nuance: 저도요 is 저 (humble 'I') + 도 ('also') + 요 (polite tag) — an elliptical 저도 그래요 where the other person's verb is understood and dropped. That ellipsis is exactly what limits it: it only works when their sentence was about THEMSELVES and the same predicate can carry over to you. If they said something about you (칭찬해 주셔서 감사해요), 저도요 misfires and you need the verb spelled out — 저도 감사해요 or 저야말로 감사해요. One place Korean is kinder than English: 도 rides over negatives, so where English must swap 'me too' for 'me neither,' 저도요 handles both. Against 저도 그래요, the split is what kind of predicate you're echoing: 그래요 restates 'I'm like that too,' which fits states and feelings (피곤해요 → 저도 그래요 ✓) but goes vague on a specific action — A: 어제 그 카페 갔어요 → 저도요 ✓ (I went too) but 저도 그래요 ✗. 저도요 borrows their verb whatever it was; 저도 그래요 substitutes 그렇다. And 나도 is the plain banmal partner. The half-and-half 나도요 (casual 나 + polite 요) is genuinely common in speech between people on a fuzzy footing, but it's an inconsistent mix — with a boss or a stranger, say 저도요. Pitfall: it's very short, and a bare 저도요 to someone's bad news can read as making it about you.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Hunting for a 'me neither' equivalent after a negative sentence — Korean 도 works over negatives, so 저는 커피 안 마셔요 → 저도요 is correct; there is no separate negative form.
Replying 저도요 to something said about you, like 감사합니다 or 도와주셔서 고마워요 — the ellipsis has no verb to borrow; use 저도 감사해요 or 저야말로 감사합니다.
Saying 나도요 to a boss or a stranger because it 'has 요 in it' — 나 is casual and 요 is polite, so it's a mismatched half-form; the polite version is 저도요.

structuredNuance.t: 저도요 = 'me too / same here.' It's an ellipsis of 저도 그래요 — the other person's verb is understood and left out. That means it only works when they said something about THEMSELVES and the same predicate can transfer to you.

저도요 is polite twice over — humble 저 plus the -요 tag — so it's safe with bosses, strangers, and elders; 나도 is the banmal partner for friends. In a formal meeting, 저도 마찬가지입니다 / 저 역시 그렇습니다 sounds more substantial than the clipped 저도요.

저도요 borrows whatever verb they used, so it covers actions too: A: 어제 그 카페 갔어요 → 저도요 ✓ ('I went too'). 저도 그래요 substitutes 그렇다 'be like that,' so it fits states and feelings (피곤해요 → 저도 그래요) but goes vague on a specific action (갔어요 → 저도 그래요 ✗). 나도 is the plain banmal version. 나도요 mixes casual 나 with polite 요 — very common in real speech between people on a fuzzy footing, but inconsistent; use 저도요 upward.
나도 (casual) → 저도요 (polite, clipped) → 저도 그래요 (polite, warmer) → 저도 마찬가지예요 / 저 역시 그렇습니다 (more formal). When you want to sound sincere rather than reflexive, spell the verb out: 저도 반가워요, 저도 피곤해요.

Using 저도요 when they said something about YOU rather than themselves — 감사해요 → 저도요 doesn't parse; say 저도 감사해요 or 저야말로 감사해요. Assuming you need a 'me neither' form for negatives — you don't, 저도요 covers both. And a bare 저도요 after someone's bad news can sound like you're redirecting to yourself; add a clause.

entries.english: Oh right! — the sound of a forgotten thing suddenly surfacing in your own memory.
entries.shortExplanation: 아 맞다 is a practical expression meaning "Oh right! — the sound of a forgotten thing suddenly surfacing in your own memory.".
entries.explanation: 아 맞다 (a matda) = "Oh right! — the sound of a forgotten thing suddenly surfacing in your own memory.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 아 맞다 ("oh right! / oh yeah, I just remembered"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: oh right! / oh yeah, I just remembered
usagePhrases.note: casual interjection; keep it as-is and continue the sentence in 해요체
the 참 stresses that it nearly slipped away
same recall function without 맞다

usagePhrases.en: oh, now that you mention it
usagePhrases.note: more composed — the safer choice in front of a boss or client

examples.ko: A: 내일 몇 시에 만나요? / B: 아 맞다, 저 내일 병원 가야 돼요.
examples.romanization: A: naeil myeot sie mannayo? / B: a matda, jeo naeil byeongwon gaya dwaeyo.
examples.en: A: What time should we meet tomorrow? / B: Oh right — I have to go to the hospital tomorrow.
examples.note: the core use: their question yanks a forgotten fact out of your own head; note 아 맞다 stays in plain form while the rest of the sentence goes polite

examples.ko: A: 우산 챙겼어? / B: 아 맞다! 깜빡했다.
examples.romanization: A: usan chaenggyeosseo? / B: a matda! kkamppakaetda.
examples.en: A: Did you grab your umbrella? / B: Oh right! It totally slipped my mind.
examples.note: casual banmal; 깜빡했다 'I blanked on it' is the natural partner phrase

examples.ko: A: 오늘 은행 문 닫아요 / B: 아 맞다, 공휴일이었죠.
examples.romanization: A: oneul eunhaeng mun dadayo / B: a matda, gonghyuirieotjyo.
examples.en: A: The bank is closed today / B: Oh right, it's a holiday, isn't it.
examples.note: you already knew it was a holiday and had forgotten — that's why 아 맞다 works and 그렇군요 would be wrong

entries.nuance: 아 맞다 is the noise a memory makes when it resurfaces: 'oh right! — I forgot.' The 맞다 in it is frozen. It looks like the plain form of 맞다 'to be correct,' but as a recall interjection it never conjugates: 맞다요 doesn't exist, and 맞아요 has a different job. The dividing line is where the fact came from. 아 맞다 fires from YOUR OWN memory — you already knew this and had lost track of it; 아 그렇군요 / 아 그렇구나 fires from SOMEONE ELSE's information — the fact is new to you. Tell a Korean your birthday for the first time and get 아 맞다 back and they've just claimed they knew all along. 맞아요 / 맞네요 is a third thing again: 'you're right, that's correct,' an evaluation of their statement rather than a memory of yours. 아 그렇지 sits nearby — also self-recall, but for something logical clicking into place ('oh right, of course') rather than a forgotten errand. Register: 아 맞다 leans casual, but it's a reflex, so it passes in polite conversation as long as the sentence after it is polite (아 맞다, 저 그거 아직 안 냈어요). In front of a boss or a client, the composed 아, 그러고 보니 or 제가 깜빡했네요 reads better.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

Using 아 맞다 when someone tells you something for the first time — it means 'I knew that and forgot,' so it sounds like a false claim of prior knowledge; the right reaction to new info is 아 그렇군요 / 아 그렇구나.
Inventing a polite form 맞다요 — it doesn't exist; 아 맞다 is a frozen interjection, and you get politeness from the sentence that follows (아 맞다, 저 내일 못 가요).
Substituting 아 맞아요 for 아 맞다 with a superior, thinking it's just the polite version — 맞아요 tells them their statement is correct, which is grading them; for recall say 아, 그러고 보니 or 제가 깜빡했네요.
