usagePhrases.note: natural extension; 시간을 내다 (carve out / make time) is a touch more explicit about asking them to set aside time for you

examples.ko: A: 혹시 시간 좀 괜찮으세요? 여쭤볼 게 있어서요. / B: 네, 말씀하세요.
examples.romanization: A: hoksi sigan jom gwaenchaneuseyo? yeojjwobol ge isseoseoyo. / B: ne, malsseumhaseyo.
examples.en: A: Do you have a moment? I have something to ask. / B: Yes, go ahead.
examples.note: the natural two-turn opener — 혹시 시간 좀 괜찮으세요? + reason; the response 말씀하세요 signals they're open

examples.ko: 바쁘시면 나중에 괜찮은데, 혹시 지금 시간 좀 괜찮으세요?
examples.romanization: bappeusimyeon najunge gwaenchaneunde, hoksi jigeum sigan jom gwaenchaneuseyo?
examples.en: If you're busy, later is fine — but do you have a moment now?
examples.note: offering the out first ('나중에 괜찮아요') frames you as considerate, not pushy — a classic Korean politeness move

examples.ko: 팀장님, 혹시 시간 좀 괜찮으실까요? 프로젝트 관련해서 여쭤볼 게 있어서요.
examples.romanization: timjangnim, hoksi sigan jom gwaenchaneusilkkayo? peurojekteu gwallyeonhaeseo yeojjwobol ge isseoseoyo.
examples.en: Manager, might you have a moment? I have something to ask about the project.
examples.note: 격식 -실까요? for a boss; naming the topic ('프로젝트 관련') lets them prepare mentally before you start

entries.nuance: This is the courteous availability check before imposing on someone — the Korean equivalent of 'do you have a minute?'. 혹시 ('by any chance') and 좀 ('a little') are both softeners; 괜찮다 ('be okay/alright') frames the question around their comfort rather than just asking '시간 있어요?'. The double-softener structure (혹시 + 좀) and the 괜찮다 framing (around their well-being, not just time) is what makes it more considerate than 시간 있으세요?. Casual: 시간 좀 괜찮아? (반말) with friends. More tentative: 괜찮으실까요? upward. The nearest alternative 시간 있으세요? ('do you have time?') is fine but feels more transactional; 시간 괜찮으세요? centers their ease. For asking them to carve out a chunk of time, 시간 내주실 수 있어요? (시간을 내다 = make/set aside time) is more explicit. English speakers often translate 'are you free?' as '자유로워요?' — 자유롭다 means free as in liberated, never 'available'.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying '자유로워요?' to mean 'are you free?'.
자유롭다 = free as in unconstrained/liberated, not available. For availability use '시간 괜찮으세요?' or '시간 있으세요?'
Dropping 혹시 and 좀.
Without them the question feels abrupt. '혹시 시간 좀 괜찮으세요?' is the soft, considerate version.
Using 너 시간 있어? to an elder or boss.
That's 반말 and too direct upward. Polite is '혹시 시간 좀 괜찮으세요?' or '시간 좀 내주실 수 있어요?'

structuredNuance.t: 혹시 시간 좀 괜찮으세요? = 'by any chance + time + a little + is it okay (for you)?'. 괜찮다 literally means 'okay/alright' — you're asking if it's okay for THEM, centering their comfort. This is more gracious than '시간 있어요?' (just asking if they have time).

Before any favor, question, or conversation that takes their time. The phrase signals you're aware you might be imposing. Use it with coworkers, acquaintances, teachers, bosses (괜찮으실까요? upward), and anyone you want to show respect to. With close friends: 시간 좀 괜찮아? Never open a favor with the full request cold — this opener first.

시간 있으세요?: slightly more transactional — asks if they simply have time. 괜찮으세요?: asks if it's comfortable/okay for them — warmer framing. 시간 내주실 수 있어요?: explicitly asks them to carve out time — use for longer requests. 잠깐 얘기 좀 할 수 있을까요?: signals a conversation is coming, not just a quick question.
시간 좀 괜찮아? (반말) → 혹시 시간 좀 괜찮으세요? (존댓말) → 혹시 시간 좀 괜찮으실까요? (격식/조심스러운). Pair with a topic hint ('프로젝트 건으로요' / '여쭤볼 게 있어서요') and the gracious out ('나중에 괜찮아요') for maximum politeness.

'자유로워요?' means 'are you free/liberated?' (from constraints) — never 'are you available?'. For availability: 시간 괜찮으세요? or 시간 있으세요?. Also: dropping 혹시 and 좀 makes the question feel abrupt ('시간 괜찮아요?' without softeners sounds blunter than intended). Both softeners are load-bearing.

entries.hangul: 이것 좀 봐 주실 수 있어요?
entries.romanization: igeot jom bwa jusil su isseoyo?
entries.english: Could you take a look at this for me?
entries.shortExplanation: 이것 좀 봐 주실 수 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Could you take a look at this for me?".
entries.explanation: 이것 좀 봐 주실 수 있어요? (igeot jom bwa jusil su isseoyo?) means "Could you take a look at this for me?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 이것 좀 봐 주실 수 있어요? ("Could you take a look at this?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.ko: 이것 좀 봐 주실 수 있어요?
usagePhrases.romanization: igeot jom bwa jusil su isseoyo?
usagePhrases.en: Could you take a look at this?
usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; ask someone to check/look over something for you

usagePhrases.en: Can you take a look at this?
usagePhrases.note: 반말; to a friend

usagePhrases.en: Would you take a look at this, please?
usagePhrases.note: more formal; to a stranger, staff member, or superior

usagePhrases.ko: 이것 좀 확인해 주실 수 있어요?
usagePhrases.romanization: igeot jom hwaginhae jusil su isseoyo?
usagePhrases.en: Could you check this for me?
usagePhrases.note: natural variant; 확인하다 (verify/confirm) when you want them to check accuracy or correctness, not just glance

examples.ko: A: 이것 좀 봐 주실 수 있어요? 제가 쓴 게 맞는지요. / B: 아, 잠깐 볼게요.
examples.romanization: A: igeot jom bwa jusil su isseoyo? jega sseun ge manneunjiyo. / B: a, jamkkan bolgeyo.
examples.en: A: Could you take a look at this? Just to see if what I wrote is correct. / B: Oh, let me have a quick look.
examples.note: the natural two-turn: stating what to check ('맞는지') guides their attention and makes the favor precise and easy to do

examples.ko: 주소가 맞는지 모르겠어서요, 이것 좀 확인해 주실 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: jusoga manneunji moreugesseoseoyo, igeot jom hwaginhae jusil su isseoyo?
examples.en: I'm not sure the address is right — could you check this for me?
examples.note: 확인하다 (verify) fits better here than 보다 (look) — you need confirmation, not just a glance

examples.ko: 제가 한국어로 썼는데요, 이것 좀 봐 주실 수 있어요? 어색한 부분이 있으면 알려 주세요.
examples.romanization: jega hangugeoro sseonneundeyo, igeot jom bwa jusil su isseoyo? eosaekan bubuni isseumyeon allyeo juseyo.
examples.en: I wrote it in Korean — could you take a look? Please let me know if anything sounds awkward.
examples.note: adding '어색한 부분이 있으면 알려 주세요' tells them exactly what kind of feedback you want, making the ask easier to fulfill

entries.nuance: 보다 = to see/look; with the benefactive 주다 it becomes 봐 주다 = 'look at it for me (as a favor)'. This is the casual check — a quick glance over a form, a piece of writing, or a screen. The -ㄹ 수 있어요? frame (polite ability/permission) makes it gentle and easy to decline. Casual: 봐 줄래? Formal: 봐 주시겠어요?. The dividing line with 확인해 주실 수 있어요?: 봐 주다 = take a look (informal, quick, no specific correctness check required), 확인하다 = verify/confirm (you want to know if something is accurate — a fact, a number, a date). English speakers most commonly make two errors: (1) saying '이것 좀 보세요' — that's a command/announcement ('look at this!'), not a request for help; the benefactive 봐 주다 is what makes it 'check this for me'; (2) using Konglish 체크하다 instead of the natural Korean 확인하다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying '이것 좀 보세요' to mean 'please check this for me'.
Bare 보세요 = 'look at this!' (pointing it out). For a favor use the benefactive: '이것 좀 봐 주실 수 있어요?'
Using 체크하다 instead of 확인하다.
체크하다 is Konglish. The natural verb for verifying is 확인하다: '이것 좀 확인해 주실 수 있어요?'
Dropping 주다: '이것 좀 봐 줄 수 있어요?' vs '봐요'.
The benefactive 봐 주다 ('look for me') is what makes it a request done on your behalf. Keep 주다 so it's clearly help, not a command.

structuredNuance.t: 이것 좀 봐 주실 수 있어요? = 'this + softener + see/look + give-to-me + is it possible?'. The benefactive 주다 is essential — it changes 'look at this (command)' into 'look at this FOR me (favor)'. Without 주다 you are pointing something out, not asking for help.

Checking a form, a document, an address, a piece of writing, or a phone screen. Fine for coworkers, staff, friends, or strangers nearby. Use -ㄹ 수 있어요? (존댓말) for most contexts; -주시겠어요? (격식) for a superior or formal setting. Always hint at WHAT to check ('맞는지', '어색한지', '주소가 맞는지') to make the favor easy.

봐 주다 (look over, informal): a quick glance to see if something looks okay. 확인해 주다 (verify): confirming something is accurate or correct — more precise. Both are used frequently; choose based on whether you need casual reassurance (봐 주다) or actual fact-checking (확인해 주다).

봐 줄래? (반말) → 봐 주실 수 있어요? (존댓말) → 봐 주시겠어요? (격식). Add specifics: 맞는지 봐 주세요 (check if it's right), 어색한 부분 봐 주세요 (check for awkward parts), 확인해 주세요 (verify). The more specific you are, the easier the favor is to do.

'이것 좀 보세요' = 'look at this!' — it announces something to look at, not a request for help. The benefactive 봐 주다 is the structural key to making this a favor. Also: 체크하다 is Konglish; the natural Korean for verifying something is 확인하다. Don't drop 주다 or you lose the 'for me' meaning entirely.

entries.english: I don't think I can make it today
entries.shortExplanation: 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요 is a practical expression meaning "I don't think I can make it today".
entries.explanation: "I don't think I can make it today" — that is 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요 (oneul mot gal geot gatayo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요 ("I don't think I can make it today"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: I don't think I can make it today
usagePhrases.note: Polite; the soft, standard way to back out of plans

usagePhrases.en: I don't think I can come today
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a close friend

usagePhrases.en: I'm afraid I won't be able to attend today
usagePhrases.note: Formal 합쇼체, to a boss or in a work message

usagePhrases.ko: 오늘 참석 못 할 것 같아요
usagePhrases.romanization: oneul chamseong mo tal geot gatayo
usagePhrases.en: I don't think I can attend today
usagePhrases.note: 참석하다 ('attend') for a meeting/event rather than a casual hangout

examples.ko: 미안한데 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: mianhande oneul mot gal geot gatayo.
examples.en: Sorry, but I don't think I can make it today.
examples.note: Open with 미안한데 ('sorry, but') to cushion the bad news — bare 못 갈 것 같아요 without it can feel abrupt

examples.ko: 저 오늘 좀 아파서 못 갈 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: jeo oneul jom apaseo mot gal geot gatayo.
examples.en: I'm a bit sick today, so I don't think I can come.
examples.note: 좀 아파서 ('a bit sick, so') gives a brief, face-saving reason before the cancellation

examples.ko: A: 오늘 회식 오시죠? / B: 죄송한데 오늘 못 갈 것 같습니다. 갑자기 일이 생겨서요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul hoesik osijyo? / B: joesonghande oneul mot gal geot gatseumnida. gapjagi iri saenggyeoseoyo.
examples.en: A: You're coming to the team dinner tonight, right? / B: Sorry, I don't think I can make it — something came up.
examples.note: Formal 같습니다 fits the work setting; 갑자기 일이 생겨서요 as a vague, face-saving reason

entries.nuance: 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요 is 못 ('cannot') + 가다 ('to go') + -ㄹ 것 같다 ('it seems / I think'), so literally 'it seems I can't go today.' The whole trick is the -ㄹ 것 같다 hedge: Korean almost never uses a flat 못 가요 to cancel, because that sounds blunt and final, almost like a refusal. Wrapping it in 같아요 softens it into a gentle 'I don't think I can make it' — even when you are 100% certain you can't go, you still say 같아요. The nearest near-synonym 안 갈 것 같아요 uses 안 ('won't, by choice') instead of 못 ('can't, prevented'), and that difference matters: 못 implies an external barrier (work, illness), which reads as a valid excuse, while 안 implies you simply choose not to come — so for canceling, default to 못. Common collocations: 미안한데/죄송한데 + 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요 (opener + cancellation), and a trailing reason like 일이 생겨서요. Register: 같아요 for everyday polite, 같습니다 for work/superiors, 같아 for close friends only. The classic English-speaker pitfall is translating 'I can't make it' word-for-word and dropping the hedge, producing a cold 오늘 못 가요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying a flat 오늘 못 가요 to cancel.
Without the hedge it sounds blunt and final, almost like a refusal. Soften it to 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요 — the -ㄹ 것 같다 makes it polite and apologetic even when you're certain.
Using 안 갈 것 같아요 when something is preventing you.
안 = 'won't (by choice)', which can sound like you just don't feel like coming. If circumstances stop you, use 못 ('can't'): 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요.
Mistranslating 'make it' literally with 만들다.
'Make it' here is idiomatic English for 'attend'. 만들다 means 'to build/create' — never 오늘 못 만들어요. Use 못 가요/못 갈 것 같아요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'it seems I cannot go today' — the -ㄹ 것 같다 hedge is the key: even when you are certain you can't come, Korean social norms call for this softened prediction form. A flat 못 가요 would sound like a sharp refusal, not an apologetic cancellation.

Use this when canceling any plan — casual meetup, work dinner, appointment — at any point from hours before to the day of. 같아요 is standard polite (친구의 친구, 직장 동료); 같습니다 for a boss or formal work chat; 같아 only among close friends. Always open with 미안한데/죄송한데 before the cancellation line.

안 갈 것 같아요 ('I don't think I'll go') uses 안 (volitional 'won't') not 못 (inability 'can't'). 못 sounds like circumstances stopped you; 안 sounds like you just don't feel like it — so for a polite cancellation, 못 갈 것 같아요 is always safer.

Add a reason before: 일이 생겨서 못 갈 것 같아요. Substitute the destination: 오늘 못 올 것 같아요 ('I don't think I can come', if the other person is the host). For leaving early: 먼저 나가야 할 것 같아요 ('I think I have to head out first').
Dropping the hedge and saying 오늘 못 가요 reads as blunt and cold in Korean. Always wrap it: 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요. Also, never render 'make it' as 만들다 — 만들다 means 'create/build'; use the motion verb 가다/오다.

entries.english: Because something suddenly came up
entries.shortExplanation: 갑자기 일이 생겨서요 is a practical expression meaning "Because something suddenly came up".
entries.explanation: 갑자기 일이 생겨서요 (gapjagi iri saenggyeoseoyo) = "Because something suddenly came up". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 갑자기 일이 생겨서요 ("Something suddenly came up, so…"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the all-purpose vague reason for canceling
반말 / trailing reason, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: An urgent matter suddenly came up
usagePhrases.note: Add 급한 ('urgent') to stress it's serious and unavoidable
집에 ('at home') hints at a family matter without details

examples.ko: 갑자기 일이 생겨서요. 다음에 봬요.
examples.romanization: gapjagi iri saenggyeoseoyo. daeume bwaeyo.
examples.en: Something came up, so… Let's meet next time.
examples.note: Trailing -서요 lets the excuse stand alone; the unsaid conclusion is 'so I can't come' — Korean listeners fill it in politely

examples.ko: 미안, 갑자기 일이 생겨서 오늘 못 갈 것 같아.
examples.romanization: mian, gapjagi iri saenggyeoseo oneul mot gal geot gata.
examples.en: Sorry, something came up so I don't think I can come today.
examples.note: 반말 to a friend, chaining the reason into the full cancellation line

examples.ko: A: 오늘 왜 못 와요? / B: 죄송합니다, 갑자기 급한 일이 생겨서 오늘 미팅 참석이 어려울 것 같습니다.
examples.romanization: A: oneul wae mot wayo? / B: joesonghamnida, gapjagi geupan iri saenggyeoseo oneul miting chamseogi eoryeoul geot gatseumnida.
examples.en: A: Why can't you come today? / B: I'm sorry — an urgent matter suddenly came up, so I don't think I can attend today's meeting.
examples.note: Formal work register: 급한 일 + 참석이 어렵다, responding directly to a 'why' question

entries.nuance: 갑자기 일이 생겨서요 is 갑자기 ('suddenly') + 일 ('a matter/thing/work') + 생기다 ('to arise/come up') + -어서 ('because') + 요 (polite ender). This is the socially perfect vague excuse: 일 is deliberately broad — it can mean work, an errand, a family thing, anything — so you can bow out without disclosing private details, and Koreans accept it without prying. The trailing -서요 (reason + 요, with the main clause left unsaid) is extremely natural; it implies '…so I can't make it' without you having to spell out the blunt part. The nearest near-synonym 바빠서요 ('because I'm busy') is fine but can sound like a weaker brush-off since busyness feels self-inflicted; 일이 생겨서요 implies a concrete unforeseen event and lands as stronger, more legitimate. The 갑자기 ('suddenly') is what signals this wasn't your fault — it's the difference between a genuine emergency and a vague excuse, so keep it. Watch the verb: it must be 생기다 ('to arise', intransitive) with subject particle 이/가; learners wrongly use 만들다 or the wrong particle 을/를.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 일을 만들었어요 to mean 'something came up'.
만들다 ('make') + 일을 means 'I created work/trouble'. The event-arising verb is 생기다, used with 이: 일이 생겼어요 / 일이 생겨서요.
Wrong particle: 일을 생겨서요.
생기다 is intransitive and takes the subject particle: 일이 생겨서요, not 일을. The thing 'arises' on its own; you don't act on it.
Over-explaining the private reason.
The point of 일이 생겨서요 is its vagueness — Koreans won't pry. Volunteering every detail can sound like over-justifying; the trailing -서요 is enough.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'because a thing suddenly arose'. The power is in what it does NOT say: 일 is kept vague on purpose, and the trailing -서요 leaves the consequence ('so I can't come') unsaid. Koreans read the full meaning without it being spoken — this is intentional, face-saving indirectness.

Works in almost any cancellation context: casual hangout, work meeting, family dinner. The trailing -서요 is the polite everyday register; for work/superiors use 갑자기 급한 일이 생겨서 참석이 어렵게 되었습니다. In 반말 the 요 drops: 갑자기 일이 생겨서.

바빠서요 ('because I'm busy') feels weaker — busyness can look like poor planning. 갑자기 일이 생겨서요 signals an unforeseeable event, so it carries more social legitimacy. 급한 일이 생겨서요 is even stronger, implying genuine urgency.

Specifying the domain: 집에 일이 생겨서요 (family matter), 회사에 갑자기 일이 생겨서요 (work issue). Stacking with the cancel: 갑자기 일이 생겨서 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요. More formal: 갑작스럽게 일이 생겨서요 (갑작스럽다 = 'abrupt/sudden', more written register).

Two particle/verb traps in one phrase: (1) 생기다 is intransitive — the subject is 일이, never 일을. (2) Never use 만들다 ('make/create') here: 일을 만들었어요 means 'I caused trouble', not 'something came up'. The event arises on its own; you don't make it.

entries.english: Would it be okay to cancel our plans?
entries.shortExplanation: 약속 취소해도 될까요? is a practical expression meaning "Would it be okay to cancel our plans?".
entries.explanation: 약속 취소해도 될까요? (yaksok chwisohaedo doelkkayo?) means "Would it be okay to cancel our plans?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 약속 취소해도 될까요? ("Would it be okay to cancel our plans?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Would it be okay to cancel our plans?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asks permission/forgiveness to cancel

usagePhrases.en: Is it okay if I cancel?
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a close friend

usagePhrases.en: Would it be alright to cancel?
usagePhrases.note: 괜찮을까요 ('would it be alright') is a touch gentler

usagePhrases.en: Would it be a problem if I canceled today?
usagePhrases.note: Negative-question form, sounds extra apologetic/pleading

examples.ko: 미안한데 오늘 약속 취소해도 될까요?
examples.romanization: mianhande oneul yaksok chwisohaedo doelkkayo?
examples.en: Sorry, but would it be okay to cancel today's plans?
examples.note: 미안한데 softens the request before asking permission — opening with the apology first is the Korean norm

examples.ko: 나 컨디션이 너무 안 좋은데 약속 취소해도 돼?
examples.romanization: na keondisyeoni neomu an joeunde yaksok chwisohaedo dwae?
examples.en: I'm really not feeling well — is it okay if I cancel?
examples.note: 반말 with 컨디션이 안 좋다 ('feeling off') as the reason; 취소해도 돼? stays light and direct between friends

examples.ko: A: 내일 만나기로 했잖아요. / B: 정말 죄송한데 갑자기 일이 생겨서 오늘 약속 취소하면 안 될까요?
examples.romanization: A: naeil mannagiro haetjanayo. / B: jeongmal joesonghande gapjagi iri saenggyeoseo oneul yaksok chwisohamyeon an doelkkayo?
examples.en: A: We were supposed to meet tomorrow. / B: I'm really sorry, but something came up — would it be a problem if I canceled today?
examples.note: The 안 될까요 negative form is the most apologetic variant; use it when you feel especially bad

entries.nuance: 약속 취소해도 될까요? is 약속 ('plans/appointment/promise') + 취소하다 ('to cancel', Sino-Korean 取消) + -아도 되다 ('is it okay to…') + -ㄹ까요 ('I wonder, may I?'). Framing the cancellation as a permission question is the polite, face-saving move: instead of announcing you ARE canceling, you ask whether you may, handing the other person dignity. Note 약속 carries real weight — it covers plans to meet, an appointment, AND a promise, so canceling 약속 carries a slight sense of breaking your word, which is exactly why you ask so gently. The near-synonym 약속 취소할게요 ('I'll cancel our plans', -ㄹ게요) just DECLARES the cancellation and can feel one-sided/abrupt for personal plans; reserve 취소할게요 for impersonal bookings (a restaurant reservation, a delivery). The negative-question variant 취소하면 안 될까요? ('would it be a problem if I canceled?') sounds even more apologetic — handy when you feel genuinely bad. The direct English-speaker trap is saying 약속을 깨다 ('break the appointment') — 깨다 literally 'shatters' a promise and sounds like a betrayal; use 취소하다 for an ordinary cancel.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 약속을 깨도 될까요? to cancel plans.
깨다 ('break/shatter') sounds like betraying a serious promise. For ordinary plans use 취소하다: 약속 취소해도 될까요?
Declaring 약속 취소할게요 to a person.
-ㄹ게요 announces your decision and can feel abrupt for plans involving someone else. Ask permission instead: 취소해도 될까요? Save 취소할게요 for bookings/reservations.
Confusing 약속 with only 'a promise'.
약속 also means 'plans/an appointment to meet'. 'Cancel our plans' is 약속 취소하다 — it's the correct everyday word, not just for breaking a vow.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'even if I cancel the plans, would it be okay?'. The -아도 되다 framing is crucial: you are ASKING permission to cancel, not announcing it. This turns a potentially hurtful action into a considerate request, preserving the other person's face.

Use with anyone you have made personal plans with — a friend, a colleague, a date. 될까요 is standard polite; 괜찮을까요 is slightly warmer and more apologetic (better when you feel extra bad); 돼? is the 반말 version for close friends only. Never use 깨도 될까요 (깨다= shatter) for a normal cancel.

약속 취소할게요 (-ㄹ게요) declares YOUR decision unilaterally — appropriate for impersonal bookings (식당 예약 취소할게요 'I'll cancel the restaurant reservation'). For plans with a person, asking with 될까요? is more considerate. 약속을 깨다 ('break a promise') is too harsh for an ordinary cancellation.

약속 전체를 취소할게요 (direct declaration, for impersonal bookings); 오늘 약속 취소해도 될까요? (asking for today); 이번 약속은 취소하고 다음에 다시 잡을까요? ('shall we cancel this one and reschedule?'). For escalating apology: 정말 죄송한데 약속 취소해도 괜찮을까요? Switching cancel to reschedule: 취소 말고 다른 날로 미뤄도 될까요? ('instead of canceling, could we move it to another day?'). 취소하다 also pairs with 예약 (reservation): 식당 예약 취소할게요 — but for personal plans always use the permission-question form.

(1) Saying 약속을 깨도 될까요? — 깨다 ('shatter/break') sounds like betraying a serious vow; use 취소하다 for a normal cancel. (2) Treating 약속 as only 'a promise' and reaching for 계획 ('plan') instead — 약속 is exactly the right word for 'our plans to meet'.

entries.english: Could we change the time of our plans?
entries.shortExplanation: 약속 시간 좀 바꿔도 될까요? is a practical expression meaning "Could we change the time of our plans?".
entries.explanation: "Could we change the time of our plans?" — that is 약속 시간 좀 바꿔도 될까요? (yaksok sigan jom bakkwodo doelkkayo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 약속 시간 좀 바꿔도 될까요? ("Could we change our meeting time?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Could we change our meeting time?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking to move the time, not cancel
반말, to a friend
변경하다 (Sino-Korean) sounds more formal/official than 바꾸다

usagePhrases.en: Could we push the time back just a little?
usagePhrases.note: 미루다 ('postpone') when you want it slightly later, not a different slot

examples.ko: 혹시 약속 시간 좀 바꿔도 될까요?
examples.romanization: hoksi yaksok sigan jom bakkwodo doelkkayo?
examples.en: Could we possibly change our meeting time?
examples.note: 혹시 ('by any chance') softens the request — a key politeness opener before any favor

examples.ko: 나 길이 막혀서 그런데 약속 시간 30분만 늦춰도 돼?
examples.romanization: na giri makyeoseo geureonde yaksok sigan 30bunman neutchwodo dwae?
examples.en: I'm stuck in traffic — can we push it 30 minutes later?
examples.note: 30분만 늦추다 ('push back just 30 min') is more precise than 바꾸다 when you know the direction and amount

examples.ko: A: 오늘 3시에 만나기로 했는데요. / B: 죄송한데 회의 시간 좀 변경해도 될까요? 오전은 일정이 꽉 차서요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul 3sie mannagiro haenneundeyo. / B: joesonghande hoeui sigan jom byeongyeonghaedo doelkkayo? ojeoneun iljeongi kkwak chaseoyo.
examples.en: A: We agreed on 3 o'clock today. / B: Sorry, could we change the meeting time? My morning is fully booked.
examples.note: 변경하다 + reason 일정이 꽉 차다 ('schedule is packed') fits a professional exchange

entries.nuance: 약속 시간 좀 바꿔도 될까요? is 약속 시간 ('meeting time') + 좀 (softener) + 바꾸다 ('to change/swap') + -아도 될까요 ('may I…?'). The crucial distinction from the cancel card: this CHANGES the time but KEEPS the plan, whereas 취소 kills it — and Koreans much prefer rescheduling to canceling, so this is the friendlier ask. 바꾸다 is the everyday verb for changing/swapping; the Sino-Korean 변경하다 means the same but is more formal (business emails, official bookings). If you specifically want it LATER, the precise verb is 미루다 or 늦추다 ('postpone/push back'); if EARLIER, 당기다 ('move up, pull forward'). To swap one specific time for another, the pattern is A를 B로 바꾸다 — the 를 on the original slot and 로 on the new one are both required. The 좀 here is a politeness softener, not 'a little'; add 조금만 for a small shift. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) dropping the -로 on the new time: say 3시를 5시로 바꿔도 될까요?, not 3시를 5시 바꿔도 될까요?. (2) Using formal 변경하다 with a close friend — sounds overly stiff; stick with 바꾸다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Forgetting -로 when swapping times: 3시를 5시 바꿔도 돼요?
To replace A with B you mark the new value with -로: 3시를 5시로 바꿔도 될까요? ('change 3 to 5'). Without -로 it's incomplete.
Using formal 변경하다 with a close friend.
변경하다 is Sino-Korean and sounds official/business-like. With friends use the everyday 바꾸다: 시간 좀 바꿔도 돼?
Saying 시간을 옮기다 for the clock time.
옮기다 ('move/relocate') fits dates or venues (날짜를 옮기다) better than the time of day. For the time, prefer 바꾸다 or, for 'later', 미루다/늦추다.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'even if I change the meeting time a bit, would it be okay?' — the -아도 될까요 again frames the change as a permission request, not a declaration. This is the socially preferred move: rescheduling rather than canceling, and asking rather than announcing.

Use when you need to adjust the clock time while keeping the same day and same meeting. 될까요? is standard polite; 변경해도 될까요? is more formal (work context); 바꿔도 돼? is 반말 between friends. For a superior, upgrade to 변경해도 괜찮으실까요?.

바꾸다 = everyday 'change/swap' (casual to semi-formal). 변경하다 = Sino-Korean 'modify/revise' (formal, documents, official contexts). 미루다/늦추다 = specifically 'push LATER'. 당기다/앞당기다 = specifically 'move EARLIER'. If you know the direction, the directional verb is more natural than the neutral 바꾸다.
Slot-swap pattern: 3시를 5시로 바꾸다 ('change 3 to 5'). Directional variants: 시간을 좀 미루다 (later) / 시간을 좀 당기다 (earlier). Honorific escalation: 시간 변경해도 괜찮으실까요? for a senior.

(1) Dropping -로 when swapping slots: 3시를 5시로 바꿔도 될까요? — both particles (를 on old, 로 on new) are required. (2) Reaching for 변경하다 with friends — it sounds too formal; use 바꾸다 in casual conversation. (3) 시간을 옮기다 ('move/relocate') works for dates and venues but is less idiomatic for a clock time; prefer 바꾸다 or 늦추다/당기다.

entries.english: Could we push it to another day?
entries.shortExplanation: 다른 날로 미뤄도 될까요? is a practical expression meaning "Could we push it to another day?".
entries.explanation: 다른 날로 미뤄도 될까요? (dareun nallo mirwodo doelkkayo?) = "Could we push it to another day?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 다른 날로 미뤄도 될까요? ("Could we move it to another day?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Could we move it to another day?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asks to postpone to a different day

usagePhrases.en: Can we do it another day?
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: Would it be possible to push it to another day?
usagePhrases.note: -ㄹ 수 있을까요 ('would it be possible') is a touch softer/formal

usagePhrases.en: Could we move it to next week?
usagePhrases.note: Swap in a concrete time (다음 주 'next week') instead of vague 다른 날

examples.ko: 오늘은 좀 힘들 것 같은데, 다른 날로 미뤄도 될까요?
examples.romanization: oneureun jom himdeul geot gateunde, dareun nallo mirwodo doelkkayo?
examples.en: Today's a bit hard — could we move it to another day?
examples.note: 오늘은 힘들 것 같다 is a gentle 'today doesn't work' that sets up the postpone request without blaming anyone

examples.ko: 미안, 나 이번 주 너무 바빠서 다른 날로 미뤄도 돼?
examples.romanization: mian, na ibeon ju neomu bappaseo dareun nallo mirwodo dwae?
examples.en: Sorry, I'm so busy this week — can we do it another day?
examples.note: 반말 with a busy-week reason; 이번 주 ('this week') makes the constraint concrete

examples.ko: A: 이번 주 금요일은 어때요? / B: 죄송한데 다음 주로 미룰 수 있을까요? 그때는 꼭 시간 낼게요.
examples.romanization: A: ibeon ju geumyoireun eottaeyo? / B: joesonghande daeum juro mirul su isseulkkayo? geuttaeneun kkok sigan naelgeyo.
examples.en: A: How about this Friday? / B: Sorry, could we push it to next week? I'll definitely make time then.
examples.note: 꼭 시간 낼게요 ('I'll be sure to make time') shows good faith and keeps the door open

entries.nuance: 다른 날로 미뤄도 될까요? is 다른 날 ('another day') + -로 (direction particle 'to') + 미루다 ('to postpone/put off') + -아도 될까요 ('may I…?'). 미루다 is THE everyday verb for postponing — pushing an event to a later point — and the -로 on 다른 날 is essential: you move it TO another day (다른 날로, 다음 주로, 주말로); dropping -로 sounds off. Two key contrasts: (1) 미루다 vs. 취소하다 — 미루다 keeps the plan alive for later (much preferred socially), 취소하다 kills it; reach for 미루다 whenever you can still meet, just not now. (2) 미루다 vs. 연기하다 (Sino-Korean 延期) — both mean 'postpone', but 연기하다 is formal/official (postponing an event, a wedding, a match: 경기가 연기됐다); for casual plans use 미루다. Be aware 미루다 also means 'to procrastinate' (일을 자꾸 미루다), but paired with 다른 날로 it unambiguously means 'reschedule to another day'. The English-speaker trap is confusing 미루다 ('postpone in time') with 밀다 ('push physically').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Dropping -로: 다른 날 미뤄도 될까요?
You postpone something TO a day, so the target takes -로: 다른 날로 미뤄도 될까요? Without -로 the destination is unmarked and sounds incomplete.
Using 연기하다 for casual plans with a friend.
연기하다 is formal/official ('postpone an event'). For everyday plans say 미루다: 다른 날로 미뤄도 돼? Save 연기되다 for matches/ceremonies.
Confusing 미루다 with 밀다.
밀다 is 'to push (physically)' or 'to shove'. 'Postpone' is 미루다. 약속을 밀다 isn't the idiom — say 약속을 미루다 / 다른 날로 미루다.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'even if I push it to another day, would it be okay?' The verb 미루다 carries the core idea of deferring to a later time. It is a more cooperative, relationship-preserving move than 취소하다 — you're not dropping the plan, you're keeping it alive.

Use when you can't make a specific day but genuinely want to meet another time. 될까요? is standard polite. 돼? is 반말. For extra deference: 다른 날로 미룰 수 있을까요? (-ㄹ 수 있을까요 is more tentative). In formal work contexts: 일정을 연기해도 괜찮겠습니까?.

미루다 (casual/everyday) vs. 연기하다 (Sino-Korean 延期, formal/official): 약속을 미루다 for personal plans; 행사/경기를 연기하다 for public events. 취소하다 ends the plan; 미루다 saves it. These three verbs form a natural set for any learner studying rescheduling.
Replace 다른 날 with a specific target: 다음 주로 미루다, 주말로 미루다, 다음 달로 미루다. Softer: 조금 미뤄도 될까요? ('could we push it back a bit?'). Formal: 일정을 연기해도 될까요?

(1) Dropping -로: 다른 날 미뤄도 될까요? — the destination requires -로 because you are moving the event TO that day. (2) Confusing 미루다 ('postpone in time') with 밀다 ('push physically'): 약속을 밀다 is not idiomatic — say 약속을 미루다. (3) Over-using 연기하다 in casual conversation — it sounds stiff and bureaucratic between friends; 미루다 is the natural word.

entries.english: Let's meet another time
entries.shortExplanation: 다음에 봬요 is a practical expression meaning "Let's meet another time".
entries.explanation: 다음에 봬요 (daeume bwaeyo) means "Let's meet another time". Say it as one set phrase — for example 다음에 봬요 ("See you another time"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; soft closer after canceling/parting
반말, to a friend
뵙다 (humble 'see') to an elder/superior; very respectful

usagePhrases.en: Let's see each other again sometime
usagePhrases.note: 또 ('again') warms it up, keeps the door open

examples.ko: 오늘은 아쉽지만 다음에 봬요.
examples.romanization: oneureun aswipjiman daeume bwaeyo.
examples.en: It's a shame about today, but let's meet another time.
examples.note: 아쉽지만 ('it's a pity, but') keeps the tone warm rather than dismissive — the combination signals genuine regret

examples.ko: 알겠어, 그럼 다음에 봐!
examples.romanization: algesseo, geureom daeume bwa!
examples.en: Got it, see you next time then!
examples.note: 반말 reply accepting a reschedule; 그럼 ('well then') bridges the acceptance naturally

examples.ko: A: 오늘 정말 죄송했습니다. / B: 괜찮아요. 다음에 꼭 뵐게요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul jeongmal joesonghaetseumnida. / B: gwaenchanayo. daeume kkok boelgeyo.
examples.en: A: I'm really sorry about today. / B: It's okay. I'll be sure to see you next time.
examples.note: The humble 뵐게요 (from 뵙다) is appropriate when speaking to or about a senior; 꼭 ('definitely') makes the promise feel sincere

entries.nuance: 다음에 봬요 is 다음에 ('next time / another time') + 봬요, the contracted polite form of 뵈어요 (from 뵙다, the humble verb 'to see/meet someone'). This is the gentle closer that softens a cancellation — by promising a future meeting, it signals 'no hard feelings, we'll still get together.' Spelling is a notorious trap: 봬요 (= 뵈어요) is correct, NOT 뵈요; in speech both sound like 'bwae-yo', but 뵈요 is a misspelling even many native speakers make. Register matters here: 뵙다 is the humble/honorific verb for 'see/meet', so 봬요 and 뵐게요 carry extra warmth and respect — more polite than plain 봐요/볼게요 (from 보다, the neutral 'see'). To an elder, boss, or someone you respect, 다음에 뵐게요 is gracious; among peers 다음에 봬요 is fine; for close friends 다음에 봐 is natural. The near-synonym 다음에 만나요 (from 만나다 'to meet') is also correct and slightly more direct, but 봬요 carries that built-in humble warmth. English-speaker pitfall: treating 다음에 as a firm commitment — it's an intentionally vague 'sometime', not a scheduled meeting. To actually pin down a next date, add 다음에 언제 볼까요?.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing or saying 뵈요 instead of 봬요.
봬요 is the contraction of 뵈어요; 뵈요 is a misspelling. When in doubt, expand it: 뵈어요 → 봬요. (Same logic as 돼요 from 되어요.)
Using plain 봐요 to an elder/superior.
보다's plain 봐요 is fine among peers, but for respect use the humble 뵙다: 다음에 뵐게요/봬요 lowers yourself politely before them.
Reading 다음에 as a firm commitment.
다음에 봬요 is a warm, vague 'sometime'. It doesn't fix a date. To actually schedule, follow up with 언제 볼까요? or 날짜 정해요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'next time, (let me) see you (humbly)'. The humble verb 뵙다 makes even a parting phrase carry a nuance of respect — you are positioning yourself below the other person. It turns a simple 'see you later' into something genuinely warm and considerate.

Said at the end of a cancellation, as a text sign-off, or when parting after a meeting cut short. 봬요 is standard polite (적당한 격식); 뵐게요 adds your own volition and is more forward-looking ('I will see you'); 봐 is 반말. With superiors: 꼭 다음에 뵐게요 is the ideal close after any cancellation.

다음에 만나요 (from 만나다) is natural and slightly more neutral — it doesn't carry the humble register of 뵙다 and works well among equals. 다음에 봬요 is slightly warmer because of the humble verb. Both can follow a cancellation; choose by your relationship.

다음에 또 봬요 ('see you again sometime') — 또 warms it up. 다음에 꼭 봬요 ('let's definitely meet next time') — 꼭 makes it a mild promise. 그때 봬요 ('see you then') — when a next date has already been set. To fix a real meeting: 다음에 언제 볼까요?

(1) Misspelling/saying 뵈요 instead of 봬요 — 봬요 is the contraction of 뵈어요; 뵈요 is simply wrong. Think of it like 돼요 (= 되어요): the ㅓ from 어 contracts in. (2) Pinning a date to 다음에 — it's a warm but vague 'sometime'; if you mean a real next meeting, say 다음에 언제 볼까요?.

entries.english: I think I'll be a little late
entries.shortExplanation: 조금 늦을 것 같아요 is a practical expression meaning "I think I'll be a little late".
entries.explanation: "I think I'll be a little late" — that is 조금 늦을 것 같아요 (jogeum neujeul geot gatayo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 조금 늦을 것 같아요 ("I think I'll be a little late"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: I think I'll be a little late
usagePhrases.note: Polite; heads-up that you're running behind
반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: I'm afraid I'll be a little late
usagePhrases.note: Formal 합쇼체, to a boss / in a work chat
Give a number (10분 정도) so they can plan

examples.ko: 미안, 나 조금 늦을 것 같아. 5분만 기다려 줘.
examples.romanization: mian, na jogeum neujeul geot gata. 5bunman gidaryeo jwo.
examples.en: Sorry, I think I'll be a bit late. Give me 5 minutes.
examples.note: 반말 + 기다려 줘 ('please wait for me') — text this the moment you know, not after you've already arrived late

examples.ko: 길이 막혀서 한 10분 늦을 것 같아요. 먼저 들어가 계세요.
examples.romanization: giri makyeoseo han 10bun neujeul geot gatayo. meonjeo deureoga gyeseyo.
examples.en: Traffic's bad, so I'll be about 10 minutes late. Please go on in first.
examples.note: 먼저 들어가 계세요 ('go in ahead') is the considerate add-on that shows you respect the other person's time

examples.ko: A: 지금 어디예요? / B: 죄송합니다, 차가 너무 막혀서 15분 정도 늦을 것 같습니다.
examples.romanization: A: jigeum eodiyeyo? / B: joesonghamnida, chaga neomu makyeoseo 15bun jeongdo neujeul geot gatseumnida.
examples.en: A: Where are you now? / B: I'm sorry, traffic is terrible, so I'll be about 15 minutes late.
examples.note: Formal register with a concrete delay; responding directly to 'where are you?' with an ETA is natural

entries.nuance: 조금 늦을 것 같아요 is 조금 ('a little') + 늦다 ('to be late') + -ㄹ 것 같다 ('I think / it seems'). This isn't a cancel — it's the polite running-late heads-up, and in Korea sending it the moment you know you'll be late is basic courtesy; silently arriving late is read as inconsiderate. The -ㄹ 것 같다 functions as a genuine prediction here, not just politeness softening, so 같아요 is doubly natural. The verb 늦다 is an adjective-verb ('to be late') and must not be confused with 늦추다 ('to delay/push back something', transitive): you 늦추다 a schedule, but you yourself 늦다. Pair with a specific number (10분/15분 정도) and a reason (길이 막혀서 'because of traffic') to show consideration. The near-synonym 늦어요 (flat 'I'm late') sounds after-the-fact and less apologetic; 늦을 것 같아요 is a proactive forward-looking warning. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) confusing 늦다 ('late in time') with 느리다 ('slow in speed') — 'I'll be late' is 늦다, not 느려요. (2) Translating 'I'll be late' as 저는 늦을 것입니다 — accurate but stilted; 늦을 것 같아요 is the natural spoken form.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 늦출 것 같아요 to mean 'I'll be late'.
늦추다 is transitive ('delay something', e.g. a meeting). For your own lateness use the adjective 늦다: 조금 늦을 것 같아요.
Confusing 늦다 with 느리다.
느리다 = 'slow (in speed)'; 늦다 = 'late (in time)'. 'I'll be late' is 늦을 것 같아요, not 느릴 것 같아요.
Just showing up late with no message.
In Korea a proactive heads-up is expected courtesy. Text 조금 늦을 것 같아요 (ideally with minutes + reason) as soon as you know, rather than arriving silently late.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'it seems I will be a little late'. Unlike the cancellation cards where -ㄹ 것 같다 is mainly a politeness hedge, here it is also a genuine prediction — you're informing someone of an expected delay. Both uses coexist, making 같아요 the only natural choice for this sentence.

Send this as a text the moment you realize you'll be late — not after you arrive. 같아요 is standard polite; 같습니다 for work; 같아 for close friends. Adding a specific delay (10분 정도) and a reason (길이 막혀서) is courteous and reduces the other person's anxiety. Follow with 먼저 들어가 계세요 ('go on in') or 기다려 줘 ('wait for me') depending on the situation.

늦어요 ('I'm late') is a flat present-tense statement — better for when you're already on-site and apologizing. 늦을 것 같아요 is proactive: you're warning before it happens. The proactive form is always more considerate.

Add amount: 10분 늦을 것 같아요. Add reason: 길이 막혀서 / 버스가 늦어서 ('the bus is running late'). Add ETA follow-through: 늦을 것 같은데, 5시쯤 도착할 것 같아요 ('I'll be late — I think I'll arrive around 5'). For leaving early from an ongoing event: 먼저 일어나야 할 것 같아요.

(1) Confusing 늦다 ('late in time') with 느리다 ('slow in speed'): 'I'll be late' = 늦을 것 같아요, never 느릴 것 같아요. (2) Confusing 늦다 (be late, intransitive) with 늦추다 ('to delay/push back something', transitive): 'I will be late' = 늦을 것 같아요; 'let's push the meeting back' = 회의를 늦추다. Do not say 저를 늦출 것 같아요.

entries.english: Excuse me! (to get attention) / Over here!
entries.shortExplanation: 저기요 is a practical expression meaning "Excuse me! (to get attention) / Over here!".
entries.explanation: 저기요 (jeogiyo) means "Excuse me! (to get attention) / Over here!". Say it as one set phrase — for example 저기요 ("excuse me (hailing someone)"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: the everyday polite way to flag a stranger or call a server
calling staff to YOUR table; signaling your spot
반말-ish, soft opener to a friend or to trail into a question

usagePhrases.en: we'd like to order over here
usagePhrases.note: natural extension; flagging staff to take an order

examples.ko: 저기요, 이거 얼마예요?
examples.romanization: jeogiyo, igeo eolmayeyo?
examples.en: Excuse me, how much is this?
examples.note: flagging a shop clerk to ask a question; 저기요 comes first, then the question

examples.ko: A: 여기요, 물 좀 주세요. / B: 네, 잠시만요.
examples.romanization: A: yeogiyo, mul jom juseyo. / B: ne, jamsimanyo.
examples.en: A: Excuse me (over here), some water please. / B: Yes, one moment.
examples.note: calling a server to your table; 여기요 signals YOUR location, not theirs

examples.ko: 저기요, 이거 떨어뜨리셨어요.
examples.romanization: jeogiyo, igeo tteoreotteurisyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Excuse me, you dropped this.
examples.note: getting a passing stranger's attention to help them; natural and polite

entries.nuance: 저기요 is the workhorse 'excuse me' for HAILING someone — a server, a shop clerk, or a stranger you need to flag down — and it is far more common in daily life than the textbook 실례합니다. The word breaks down as 저기 ('over there', a distal deictic pointing to the listener's space) + 요 (the polite sentence-final particle), so it literally means 'hey, over there'. 여기요 ('over here') flips the direction: it calls staff to YOUR location. Both are polite-but-casual: perfectly normal in shops, cafés, and restaurants, but a touch direct toward a clear senior or in a very formal setting, where 실례합니다 / 실례지만 is more polished. Register: bare 저기 is the soft 반말-ish opener to someone you know ('저기, 있잖아…'); 저기요/여기요 add 요 for strangers and staff. The dividing line versus 실례합니다: 저기요/여기요 get attention quickly and are the real-life default in eateries; 실례합니다 is more formal and covers not just hailing but also passing by or interrupting. English speakers err in two ways: over-using the formal 실례합니다 everywhere (sounds stiff in a café), or trying to hail a server with 미안해요 ('I'm sorry for a fault') or by snapping fingers — both are culturally off.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 실례합니다 to call a waiter every time — in casual eateries Koreans say 저기요 or 여기요; 실례합니다 sounds overly formal there.
Saying 미안해요 to get a stranger's or server's attention — that's 'I'm sorry (for a fault)', not a hail; use 저기요.
Confusing 저기요 (hailing) with 거기요 — to flag someone it's 저기요/여기요; 거기 ('there, by you') isn't the attention-getter.

structuredNuance.t: 저기 is a distal deictic — 'over there (where you are)' — and 요 makes it politely sentence-final. Literally: 'hey, over there!' The real use is hailing someone: a server, a clerk, a stranger. 여기요 ('here!') is the same structure pointing to the SPEAKER'S location instead.

저기 (반말-ish, friends) → 저기요/여기요 (polite everyday, strangers/staff) → 실례합니다 (more formal, or when passing/interrupting). 저기요/여기요 are the default in cafés, restaurants, and shops — comfortable and direct, not rude.

The dividing line versus 실례합니다: 저기요/여기요 quickly get attention and are the daily default in eateries; 실례합니다 is more polished and formal, and also covers passing by or interrupting a conversation. Both are correct; the choice is about register.

여기요 + request: 여기요, 물 한 잔만요 / 여기요, 주문할게요. 저기요 + question: 저기요, 여기 주차 가능한가요? Soften: 저기요, 잠깐만요. Do NOT use 저기요 alone as a farewell or general filler — it strictly serves to hail someone present. Also, 저기요? with a questioning rise can politely mean 'yes?' when someone calls your name.

Two common errors: over-using 실례합니다 in casual eateries (sounds stiff); and using 미안해요 to hail a waiter (it means 'I'm sorry for a fault', not a hail). In Korea, calling out 저기요 clearly is natural and expected — do not be timid about it.

entries.english: Could I have the menu, please?
entries.shortExplanation: 메뉴 좀 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Could I have the menu, please?".
entries.explanation: "Could I have the menu, please?" — that is 메뉴 좀 주세요 (menyu jom juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 메뉴 좀 주세요 ("Could I have the menu, please?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Could I have the menu, please?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; the everyday customer line the moment you sit down

usagePhrases.en: Could you bring the menu, please?
usagePhrases.note: More polite/formal with -주시겠어요; names the physical 메뉴판 (board/booklet)

usagePhrases.en: Let me see the menu again
usagePhrases.note: When you want it back mid-meal to add an order

usagePhrases.en: Could you recommend something off the menu?
usagePhrases.note: Natural follow-on once you have it but can't decide

examples.ko: 메뉴 좀 주세요.
examples.romanization: menyu jom juseyo.
examples.en: The menu, please.
examples.note: Said as you sit or the moment the server comes by — the plainest version

examples.ko: 여기요, 메뉴판 좀 주세요.
examples.romanization: yeogiyo, menyupan jom juseyo.
examples.en: Excuse me, could we get a menu?
examples.note: 여기요 to call, then ask for 메뉴판 (the physical booklet/board) you want placed in hand

examples.ko: A: 메뉴 좀 다시 주시겠어요? 더 시킬게요. / B: 네, 여기 있습니다.
examples.romanization: A: menyu jom dasi jusigesseoyo? deo sikilgeyo. / B: ne, yeogi itseumnida.
examples.en: A: Could we see the menu again? We'll order more. / B: Sure, here you go.
examples.note: Asking it back to add dishes; staff hand it over with 여기 있습니다 ('here you are')

entries.nuance: 메뉴 좀 주세요 is 메뉴 ('menu') + 좀 (softener) + 주세요 (the honorific 'please give'), the bread-and-butter way a customer asks for the menu. The 좀 here is NOT 'a little' — it is a politeness lubricant that turns a bare command into a gentle request, so dropping it (메뉴 주세요) is grammatical but noticeably blunter, closer to 'give me the menu.' Note the split between 메뉴 (the menu as concept/list, also the dishes themselves) and 메뉴판 (specifically the physical board or booklet); both fit here, with 메뉴판 clearer when you want the object placed in your hands. To go more deferential, swap 주세요 for 주시겠어요? ('would you give…?'), which reframes it as a question and reads as extra courteous to an older owner or in an upscale room. The English-speaker trap is over-translating 'can I get the menu' into 제가 받을 수 있어요? — Korean expresses 'can I have X' simply as 'please give X' with 주세요, since the 'can I' is already baked into the polite request. With family at the table you'd just drop to 메뉴 좀 줘; note too that many places now have QR-code menus, so you might instead ask QR로 보는 거예요? ('is it the QR-code one?').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'Can I get the menu?' as 메뉴를 받을 수 있어요?

Korean doesn't phrase customer requests with 'can I get/receive'; it uses 'please give me' — 메뉴 좀 주세요. The literal 받을 수 있어요 asks whether you're physically able to receive the menu, which sounds odd and overly cautious to a server.
Dropping 좀 and saying only 메뉴 주세요 to staff.

It's understandable but blunt, closer to 'give me the menu' than 'could I have the menu.' The softener 좀 is what makes it polite and natural, so keep it: 메뉴 좀 주세요. The 좀 costs you nothing and instantly warms the request.
Using 메뉴판 when you mean the food choices.
메뉴판 is the physical menu board/booklet; the dishes/options are 메뉴. To ask 'what's good on the menu' say 메뉴 추천, not 메뉴판 추천 — the latter sounds like you want the booklet itself recommended to you.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'menu / a bit / please give' — but the 좀 is not 'a bit/a little'. It's a softener that lubricates the request, so the real meaning is a polite 'could I have the menu?'. Without 좀 (메뉴 주세요) it's correct but reads as a flatter 'give me the menu.' If you truly meant a small amount of something, that's 조금만, a different word entirely.

Polite (해요체) and exactly right for a customer to staff in any normal eatery. Upgrade to 메뉴판 좀 주시겠어요? for an older owner or an upscale place; drop to 메뉴 좀 줘 only with family or friends at the table. You wouldn't say this to a peer about ordering — it's a server-facing request, always aimed at the person who can hand you the menu.

메뉴 vs 메뉴판: 메뉴 is the menu as a list / the dishes; 메뉴판 is the physical booklet or board. Both work to ask for it, but use 메뉴판 when you want the object in hand, and 메뉴 (not 메뉴판) when you mean the food choices, e.g. 메뉴 추천 ('a dish recommendation'). Saying 메뉴판 추천 sounds like you want the booklet itself recommended.

Politeness ladder: 메뉴 좀 줘 (반말) → 메뉴 좀 주세요 → 메뉴판 좀 주시겠어요? (most courteous). Situational spin-offs: 메뉴 좀 다시 주세요 (to reorder), 메뉴 추천 좀 해 주세요 (can't decide), 메뉴 다른 거 없어요? (asking for other options), 영어 메뉴 있어요? (asking for an English menu).

Don't render 'can I get the menu' as 메뉴를 받을 수 있어요? — that literally asks about your ability to receive and sounds strange. Korean wraps 'can I have' inside the polite 주세요, so 메뉴 좀 주세요 already means 'may I have the menu, please.' Likewise don't tack on 제가 ('I') — it's not needed and makes the request oddly self-focused.

entries.english: I'd like to order
entries.shortExplanation: 주문할게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to order".
entries.explanation: 주문할게요 (jumunhalgeyo) = "I'd like to order". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 주문할게요 ("I'd like to order"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; announces you're ready, to a server who's already there
Flags the server to COME and take it (a summons, not a declaration)
Formal 합쇼체 for stiffer, upscale, or business settings
What STAFF say to you; you reply with 주문할게요

examples.ko: 주문할게요.
examples.romanization: jumunhalgeyo.
examples.en: We're ready to order.
examples.note: Said the moment the server arrives at your table — a simple heads-up that you've decided

examples.ko: 여기요, 이제 주문할게요.
examples.romanization: yeogiyo, ije jumunhalgeyo.
examples.en: Excuse me, we'll order now.
examples.note: 이제 ('now') signals you've finished deciding and are ready to go

examples.ko: A: 주문 도와드릴까요? / B: 네, 주문할게요. 김치찌개 둘이요.
examples.romanization: A: jumun dowadeurilkkayo? / B: ne, jumunhalgeyo. gimchijjigae duriyo.
examples.en: A: May I take your order? / B: Yes, we'll order — two kimchi stews, please.
examples.note: Staff open with 도와드릴까요?; you answer 주문할게요, then list with the count + 이요

entries.nuance: 주문할게요 is 주문하다 ('to order', from Sino-Korean 注文) in the -ㄹ게요 form, which announces YOUR OWN intention as a courteous heads-up: 'I'm going to order (now).' That -ㄹ게요 is the natural customer register — polite but unstuffy, and it quietly signals the action to the listener rather than ordering them around. The line against 주문 좀 받아 주세요 ('please take our order') is DIRECTION: 주문할게요 declares what you will do, while 받아 주세요 asks the server to do something (come and take it); use 주문할게요 when staff are already at your table, and 받아 주세요 to summon them over. For upscale or business meals you can elevate to 주문하겠습니다. The English-speaker error is reaching for 'I would like to order' and producing 주문하고 싶어요 — literally 'I want to order', which sounds like voicing a private desire rather than actually doing it; Koreans just say 주문할게요. Among friends the casual verb is 시키다 (뭐 시킬까? / 나 이거 시킬게), but to the server's face 주문하다 is cleaner and more respectful. Don't confuse 주문 ('an order of food/goods') with 명령 ('a command') — only 주문 belongs in a restaurant.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 주문하고 싶어요 to order.

That literally means 'I want to order' and stalls at expressing a wish rather than doing the deed; a server may wait for you to actually start listing dishes. To place the order, announce it with the action form 주문할게요.
Using 시키다 as 시킬게요 to the server's face.

시키다 ('to order food / make someone do something') is fine among friends (뭐 시킬까?) but feels casual aimed at staff. To the server the cleaner, more respectful verb is 주문하다: 주문할게요. Save 시키다 for the table chat about what to get.
Over-formalizing every time with 주문하겠습니다.

합쇼체 can sound stiff or even stand-offish in a casual eatery, as if you're at a formal ceremony or a business meeting. Default to 주문할게요; reserve 주문하겠습니다 for upscale or business settings where that heightened register actually fits the room.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'I will do an order' (주문하다 + the -ㄹ게요 'I'll' ending). The real force is a courteous heads-up: 'we're ready, I'm about to order.' -ㄹ게요 commits the speaker to an action while signaling it to the listener, which is why it sounds considerate rather than demanding — it's a promise about your own move, not an instruction to them.

Polite (해요체) and the everyday customer default in any normal restaurant. Drop to 주문할게 with friends deciding for the table; rise to 주문하겠습니다 (합쇼체) only in upscale or business settings, where 주문할게요 might feel a touch casual. Say it to staff who are present, not as an announcement to your own group across the table.

주문할게요 (you declare your action) vs 주문 좀 받아 주세요 (you ask staff to come take it) vs 주문 도와드릴까요? (what staff say to you). Direction is the dividing line: declare when they're present, summon when they're not, and recognize 도와드릴까요? as their cue to you. Against 시키다, that's the friend-to-friend verb, not the server-facing one.

Register ladder: 주문할게 (반말) → 주문할게요 → 주문하겠습니다 (formal). Among friends 시키다 is the casual verb (뭐 시킬까?, 시킬게), but to the server's face the cleaner choice is 주문하다. Extend it as 주문할게요, 잠깐만요 (need a second more), 추가 주문할게요 (ordering more), or 따로 주문할게요 (ordering separately).

Don't say 주문하고 싶어요 ('I want to order') to actually place an order — it states a wish instead of acting on it, and a server may keep waiting for you to start. Use 주문할게요. Also keep 주문 (a food/goods order) apart from 명령 (a command); only 주문 fits a restaurant, and 시키다 stays among friends.

entries.english: Could I get some water, please?
entries.shortExplanation: 물 좀 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Could I get some water, please?".
entries.explanation: "Could I get some water, please?" — that is 물 좀 주세요 (mul jom juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 물 좀 주세요 ("Some water, please"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the standard request in any eatery
Insert 더 ('more') for a refill of what you already had
More polite/formal with -주시겠어요, e.g. to an older owner
Many Korean places have 셀프 (self-serve) water; worth checking first

examples.ko: 물 좀 주세요.
examples.romanization: mul jom juseyo.
examples.en: Some water, please.
examples.note: Said to a passing server; the 좀 keeps it polite, not curt

examples.ko: 여기요, 물 좀 주세요. 그리고 컵도요.
examples.romanization: yeogiyo, mul jom juseyo. geurigo keopdoyo.
examples.en: Excuse me, some water please. And cups too.
examples.note: Chain a second request with 그리고 …도요 ('and … too')

examples.ko: A: 물 좀 더 주시겠어요? 다 마셨어요. / B: 네, 셀프바에 있어요. / A: 아, 감사합니다.
examples.romanization: A: mul jom deo jusigesseoyo? da masyeosseoyo. / B: ne, selpeubae isseoyo. / A: a, gamsahamnida.
examples.en: A: Could we get more water? We've run out. / B: Sure, it's at the self-serve bar. / A: Oh, thank you.
examples.note: 더 for a refill; staff may point you to the 셀프바 (self-serve station) instead of bringing it

entries.nuance: 물 좀 주세요 is 물 ('water') + 좀 (politeness softener) + 주세요 ('please give'). In Korea drinking water is normally free and either self-serve or brought on request, so this is one of the most-used lines in any eatery — you'll say it constantly. Again 좀 is NOT 'a little' — it cushions the request; 물 주세요 without it is correct but curt. For a refill you slot in 더 ('more'): 물 좀 더 주세요, and without that 더 the server may think you've had none yet. To sound extra polite, especially to an older owner, phrase it as the question 물 좀 주시겠어요?. The English-speaker trap is asking 'can I have water' as a literal ability question — 물 마실 수 있어요? means 'am I able to drink water?', which probes permission or capacity rather than making a request; Koreans simply say 'please give water'. And since restaurant water is just 물, you rarely need to specify — don't over-explain with 수돗물 ('tap water') unless that's genuinely what you mean. Many places are 셀프, so be ready to be pointed to a water station (정수기) rather than served.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 물 마실 수 있어요? to request water.
That means 'am I able to drink water?' — a question about permission or ability, not an order. A server might just say yes and walk off without bringing anything. To actually get water, say 물 좀 주세요.
Saying 물 좀 주세요 expecting it to mean 'a little water'.

좀 is a softener, not a quantity word; it doesn't limit the amount, it just makes the request polite. If you truly want only a small amount, say 물 조금만 주세요 — that 조금만 is the word that actually caps the quantity.
Forgetting 더 when you want a refill.

물 좀 주세요 asks for water in general; for more of what you already had, add 더: 물 좀 더 주세요. Without 더 the server may think you haven't been given any yet and bring a fresh first glass instead of topping you up.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'water / a bit / please give', but the 좀 is a politeness softener, not the quantity 'a little'. The real meaning is 'could I have some water, please.' If you actually want a SMALL amount, you'd say 물 조금만 주세요, not rely on 좀 — the two are easy to mix up but do different jobs.

Polite (해요체), aimed at staff, and totally routine since drinking water is free almost everywhere in Korea. Upgrade to 물 좀 주시겠어요? for an older owner; drop to 물 좀 줘 with a friend at the table. Note many places are 셀프 — you may be pointed to a 정수기 (water dispenser) or 셀프바 rather than waited on.

물 좀 주세요 (first water) vs 물 좀 더 주세요 (a refill — the 더 is what marks 'more'). Without 더, staff may assume you have none yet and bring a first glass. Don't reach for 수돗물 ('tap water') as the default — restaurant drinking water is just 물; 수돗물 specifically flags the faucet, which sounds odd to request to drink.

Politeness ladder: 물 좀 줘 (반말) → 물 좀 주세요 → 물 좀 주시겠어요? (most courteous). Refill: 물 좀 더 주세요. Self-serve check: 물은 셀프예요? / 물 어디 있어요? / 정수기 어디 있어요?. Chain other requests: 물 좀 주세요, 컵도요 / 물 좀 주세요, 얼음은 빼고요 (no ice).

Don't ask 물 마실 수 있어요? to request water — that means 'am I able to drink water?' (permission/capacity), not 'please bring water.' The request frame in Korean is 'please give', so 물 좀 주세요, not a 'can I' ability question. Expecting bottled or paid water by default is also off — tap-quality drinking water is the free norm.

entries.english: Could you recommend something?
entries.shortExplanation: 추천 좀 해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Could you recommend something?".
entries.explanation: 추천 좀 해 주세요 (chucheon jom hae juseyo) = "Could you recommend something?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 추천 좀 해 주세요 ("Could you recommend something?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; hands the choice to staff when you can't decide
Asks for the popular pick — concrete info rather than their personal judgment
More polite/formal with -주시겠어요
Asks for the house specialty specifically

examples.ko: 추천 좀 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: chucheon jom hae juseyo.
examples.en: Could you recommend something?
examples.note: Hand the choice to the server when you're genuinely unsure

examples.ko: 여기 뭐가 맛있어요? 추천 좀 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: yeogi mwoga masisseoyo? chucheon jom hae juseyo.
examples.en: What's good here? Could you recommend something?
examples.note: Pair with 뭐가 맛있어요 to warmly invite their pick

examples.ko: A: 처음 왔는데 추천 좀 해 주시겠어요? / B: 그럼 제육볶음 어떠세요? 제일 인기 많아요.
examples.romanization: A: cheoeum wanneunde chucheon jom hae jusigesseoyo? / B: geureom jeyukbokkeum eotteoseyo? jeil ingi manayo.
examples.en: A: It's our first time — could you recommend something? / B: How about the spicy pork stir-fry? It's our most popular.
examples.note: 처음 왔다 makes the ask natural; staff suggest with 어떠세요? + 인기 많다

entries.nuance: 추천 좀 해 주세요 is 추천 ('recommendation', Sino-Korean 推薦) + 좀 (softener) + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'). The 해 주세요 (해 주다 = 'do as a favor') is what makes it a request for the server's help rather than a bare statement; the 좀 softens it further, so the whole thing reads as warm and trusting. It's the polite go-to when you can't decide and want the staff to pick for you — and asking it actually flatters their expertise. The nearest rivals are content questions — 뭐가 맛있어요? ('what's tasty?'), 뭐가 제일 잘 나가요? ('what sells best?') — which ask for specific info, whereas 추천 좀 해 주세요 invites them to choose for you; the dividing line is that the recommendation request leans on their judgment, while the questions fish for facts. The English-speaker error is using 추천하다 without 주다 and saying 추천하세요 — that commands the server TO recommend, like ordering them around, which is too blunt; the favor verb 해 주세요 keeps it courteous. Also note 추천 is a 하다-noun, so it needs the verb 하다: with the softener it's 추천 좀 해 주세요, joined it's 추천해 주세요 — but never 추천 주세요, since you can't 'give' a recommendation as if it were an object.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 추천하세요 to the server.

Bare 추천하세요 is an imperative ('you, recommend!') and lands as bossy, as if you're issuing an instruction to an employee. The polite favor form is 추천 좀 해 주세요, which asks them to do it for you as a kindness.
Saying 추천 주세요 without 하다.

추천 is a 하다-noun, so it can't be 'given' like an object — 추천 주세요 is ungrammatical. It needs the verb 하다 plus the favor 주다: 추천 좀 해 주세요 (or joined, 추천해 주세요). You do the recommending, you don't hand it over.
Over-literal 'recommend me' as 저를 추천해 주세요.

저를 추천해 주세요 means 'please recommend ME (to a third party)', as if for a job or an introduction. To get a food suggestion, drop the personal object: 추천 좀 해 주세요, or specify the domain with 메뉴 추천 좀 해 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'recommendation / a bit / please do-for-me'. The meaning is 'please recommend something for me.' The key piece is 해 주다 ('do as a favor'): it converts the noun 추천 into an action done ON YOUR BEHALF, which is why it reads as a polite request rather than an order. Strip the 주다 and you'd be barking a command instead.

Polite (해요체) and a normal, even flattering, thing to ask staff — it trusts their expertise. Drop to 추천 좀 해 줘 with a friend; rise to 추천 좀 해 주시겠어요? for extra courtesy with an older owner. Pairs naturally with 처음 왔는데… ('it's our first time') as a lead-in that makes the ask feel earned.

추천 좀 해 주세요 (leans on their judgment) vs 뭐가 맛있어요? / 뭐가 제일 잘 나가요? (asks for facts — tasty / best-selling) vs 시그니처 메뉴가 뭐예요? (the house specialty). Use the recommendation form when you genuinely want them to decide for you; use the questions when you'd rather have concrete data and choose yourself.

With softener: 추천 좀 해 주세요; joined without it: 추천해 주세요. Politeness ladder: 추천 좀 해 줘 (반말) → 추천 좀 해 주세요 → 추천 좀 해 주시겠어요?. Narrow the scope: 메뉴 추천 좀 해 주세요, 안 매운 거로 추천 좀 해 주세요, 둘이 먹을 거 추천 좀 해 주세요, 여기 처음인데 뭐가 괜찮아요?.

Two traps: 추천하세요 commands the server to recommend (bossy, like an order) — use 추천 좀 해 주세요. And 추천 주세요 is broken because 추천 is a 하다-noun you can't 'give'; you must keep the verb 하다 plus the favor 주다. A third: 저를 추천해 주세요 means recommend ME to someone, like for a job — drop the personal object.

entries.english: Could you make it not spicy?
entries.shortExplanation: 안 맵게 해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Could you make it not spicy?".
entries.explanation: 안 맵게 해 주세요 (an maepge hae juseyo) means "Could you make it not spicy?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 안 맵게 해 주세요 ("Please make it not spicy"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asks the kitchen to remove the heat entirely
덜 ('less') when you want some heat, just not as much

usagePhrases.en: Can it be made not spicy?
usagePhrases.note: Checks first whether the kitchen can even do it

usagePhrases.ko: 아이도 먹을 수 있게 해 주세요
usagePhrases.romanization: aido meogeul su itge hae juseyo
usagePhrases.en: Make it so a child can eat it too
usagePhrases.note: Frames mild-ness around who's eating, a natural real-life cue

examples.ko: 안 맵게 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: an maepge hae juseyo.
examples.en: Make it not spicy, please.
examples.note: Said right after ordering a spicy dish — the plain request

examples.ko: 저 매운 거 잘 못 먹어서 안 맵게 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: jeo maeun geo jal mon meogeoseo an maepge hae juseyo.
examples.en: I can't handle spicy well, so please make it not spicy.
examples.note: Give a reason with 잘 못 먹다 ('not good at eating') so the ask lands softly

examples.ko: A: 떡볶이 덜 맵게 돼요? / B: 네, 가능해요. 어느 정도로 해 드릴까요? / A: 아이도 먹을 정도로요.
examples.romanization: A: tteokbokki deol maepge dwaeyo? / B: ne, ganeunghaeyo. eoneu jeongdoro hae deurilkkayo? / A: aido meogeul jeongdoroyo.
examples.en: A: Can the tteokbokki be made less spicy? / B: Yes, we can. How mild would you like it? / A: Mild enough for a kid.
examples.note: Check first with 돼요?; staff ask the degree with 어느 정도로?, you scope it by who's eating

entries.nuance: 안 맵게 해 주세요 is 안 ('not') + 맵게 (the adverbial form of 맵다 'to be spicy', so 'spicily') + 해 주세요 ('please make it for me'). The -게 turns the adjective into a manner ('in a not-spicy way'), and 해 주다 asks the cook to make it that way as a favor — so literally 'please make it in a not-spicy manner.' You're describing HOW you want it cooked, not naming a separate mild dish. The key distinction is 안 맵게 ('not spicy at all') vs. 덜 맵게 ('less spicy'): use 덜 when you still want some heat, because many English speakers overshoot with 안 and end up with a flat, bland dish. 맵다 conjugates irregularly (맵다 → 매워요, but 맵게 for the adverb), and a frequent slip is 맵지 않게 — which is actually fine and natural, just longer; 안 맵게 is the crisp spoken default. Another trap is treating 맵다 like a verb and saying 안 매워 주세요 — you need the adverb 맵게 before 해 주세요, not the conjugated 매워. To check feasibility first, ask 안 맵게 돼요?, since some dishes are pre-made and can't be de-spiced.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 안 매워 주세요.

맵다 is an adjective, and before 해 주세요 you need its manner-adverb form 맵게, not the sentence-final 매워. 안 매워 주세요 doesn't parse as 'make it not spicy' — it's a broken stitch of two patterns. Correct: 안 맵게 해 주세요.
Using 안 맵게 when you actually want mild, not bland.

안 맵게 strips out the spice entirely, which can leave a dish flat and lifeless. If you just want the heat dialed down while keeping the flavor, say 덜 맵게 해 주세요 ('less spicy') — that's the difference between toning it down and gutting it.
Putting the negative on the wrong word: 맵게 안 해 주세요.

맵게 안 해 주세요 negates the whole 'make' action and sounds like 'don't make it spicily (at all)', which is odd and ambiguous. The natural placement negates the adjective directly: 안 맵게 해 주세요 — the 안 hugs 맵게, not 해.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'not / spicily / please make-for-me' = 'please make it in a not-spicy way.' The -게 builds a manner adverb ('not-spicily'), and 해 주다 is the favor 'do/make for me.' So you're describing HOW you want it cooked, not naming a separate mild dish on the menu — the heat is a setting, not a different item.

Polite (해요체) and a normal special request to kitchen staff right after ordering. Drop to 안 맵게 해 줘 with a friend cooking or at a casual stall. A reason makes it land better: 매운 거 잘 못 먹어서… ('since I can't handle spicy…'). Some dishes can't be de-spiced once prepped, so 안 맵게 돼요? first is courteous and saves disappointment.

안 맵게 (zero heat — can come out bland) vs 덜 맵게 (less heat, keeps flavor) vs 맵지 않게 (also natural, just wordier). For a child you might frame it as 아이도 먹을 수 있게. Pick 덜 맵게 if you actually want mild rather than plain — the difference between 'tone it down' and 'strip it out' matters a lot in Korean food.

맵다 → 매워요 (sentence) but 맵게 (adverb before 해 주세요). Degree ladder: 안 맵게 / 덜 맵게 / 조금만 맵게 / 보통 맛으로. Check-first form: 안 맵게 돼요? / 덜 맵게 돼요?. Politeness floor: 안 맵게 해 줘 (반말) → 안 맵게 해 주세요 → 안 맵게 해 주실 수 있어요?. Same frame for other tweaks: 안 짜게, 덜 달게, 양파 빼고.

Don't conjugate 맵다 as a verb: 안 매워 주세요 is wrong because 매워 isn't a manner adverb. You need 맵게 before 해 주세요. Also don't reflexively pick 안 (none) when you mean 'mild' — that over-corrects into bland; 덜 맵게 keeps some heat. And misplacing the 안 (맵게 안 해 주세요) negates the wrong verb.

entries.english: Can I get this to go?
entries.shortExplanation: 포장돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I get this to go?".
entries.explanation: "Can I get this to go?" — that is 포장돼요? (pojangdwaeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 포장돼요? ("Can I get it to go?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Can I get it to go?
usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; checks whether takeout is even possible
Once it's confirmed, this asks them to actually wrap it
싸 주다 for taking home what's left on the table
A one-word answer when staff ask 드시고 가세요, 포장이세요?

examples.ko: 포장돼요?
examples.romanization: pojangdwaeyo?
examples.en: Can I get this to go?
examples.note: Asked before ordering, to confirm takeout is even possible here

examples.ko: 여기서 먹을 거예요, 아니면 포장돼요?
examples.romanization: yeogiseo meogeul geoyeyo, animyeon pojangdwaeyo?
examples.en: Will you eat here, or — can I get it to go?
examples.note: Contrast 먹다 (dine in) with 포장 (take out) in one question

examples.ko: A: 드시고 가세요, 포장이세요? / B: 포장이요. 이거 포장해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: deusigo gaseyo, pojangiseyo? / B: pojangiyo. igeo pojanghae juseyo.
examples.en: A: For here or to go? / B: To go. Please pack this.
examples.note: Staff ask with 드시고 가세요?; you answer 포장이요 then request 포장해 주세요

entries.nuance: 포장돼요? is 포장 ('packaging/wrapping', Sino-Korean 包裝) + 되다 ('to be done/possible') in polite question form, literally 'is packing possible?' — i.e. 'can I get this to go?'. The 되다 means 'is it doable', which is why it probes feasibility; once the answer is yes, you switch to the request 포장해 주세요 ('please pack it'). Korean increasingly also uses the loanword 테이크아웃, especially in cafés, but 포장 is the all-purpose, native-feeling term for any food. The dividing line: 포장돼요? asks IF takeout is available, while 포장해 주세요 ASKS them to do it — don't merge them, or staff may just say 'yes' and wait. The English-speaker error is rendering 'to go' literally with 가지고 가다 in the wrong frame, e.g. 가지고 갈 수 있어요? ('can I take it and go?'), which sounds like asking permission to carry it off; the idiomatic ask is 포장돼요?. For leftovers specifically, Koreans say 싸 주세요 ('please wrap it up'), and watch that 포장 (you carry it out) isn't 배달 (delivery to your door) — asking 배달돼요? orders a completely different service.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 포장돼요? when you've already decided and just want it packed.
포장돼요? only asks WHETHER takeout is possible, so staff may just answer 'yes' and stand there waiting. To actually request it once you know it's offered, say 포장해 주세요 ('please pack it').
Translating 'to go' as 가지고 갈 수 있어요?

That means 'am I allowed to carry it away?' and frames it as a permission question, which sounds unsure and slightly anxious. The natural takeout phrases are 포장돼요? (to check) and 포장해 주세요 (to request).
Confusing 포장 with 배달.

포장 is takeout you carry yourself; 배달 is delivery brought to your door by a rider. Asking 배달돼요? requests a different service entirely and many sit-down places don't offer it. Use 포장 for to-go that you pick up and carry out.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'does packing get done?' (포장 'packaging' + 되다 'be possible/get done'). The real meaning is 'can I get this to go?' The -돼요 probes feasibility, which is why it's a yes/no FEASIBILITY question, not yet a request to actually wrap anything. The -되다 ('get done') frame is what flags it as 'is this offered?' rather than 'do it now.'

Polite-neutral and aimed at staff, fine at any counter, stall, or restaurant. Drop to 포장돼? with a friendly stall owner; soften to 포장 되나요? for a gentler tone. Often it's the answer to the staff's own 드시고 가세요, 포장이세요? — at a counter you can just reply 포장이요 and skip the question entirely.

포장돼요? (is takeout possible) vs 포장해 주세요 (do it) — feasibility vs request. 포장 (native-feeling, any food) vs 테이크아웃 (loanword, café-leaning, mostly drinks). And crucially 포장 (you carry it out yourself) vs 배달 (delivered to your door) — 배달돼요? orders a totally different service that may not even be offered in-store.

Feasibility: 포장돼요? / 포장 되나요? / 포장 가능해요?. Request: 이거 포장해 주세요 / 포장으로 주세요. Leftovers: 남은 거 싸 주세요 / 이거 포장돼요?. One-word reply to staff: 포장이요 (vs 여기서 먹을게요 for dine-in). Politeness floor: 포장돼? (반말) → 포장돼요?.

Don't translate 'to go' as 가지고 갈 수 있어요? — that asks permission to carry it off and sounds like you're worried it's not allowed. The idiomatic line is 포장돼요? (to check) or 포장해 주세요 (to request). Keep 포장 distinct from 배달 (delivery), and don't stop at 포장돼요? if you've already decided — follow with the request.

entries.english: Separate checks, please
entries.shortExplanation: 따로 계산해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Separate checks, please".
entries.explanation: 따로 계산해 주세요 (ttaro gyesanhae juseyo) means "Separate checks, please". Say it as one set phrase — for example 따로 계산해 주세요 ("Please ring us up separately"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; each person pays for their own
1/n(분의 일) for an even per-head split of one total
The opposite — one combined bill (often one person treating)

usagePhrases.en: I'll pay just for mine first
usagePhrases.note: 제 것만 to settle only your own portion ahead of the group

examples.ko: 따로 계산해 주세요.
examples.romanization: ttaro gyesanhae juseyo.
examples.en: Separate checks, please.
examples.note: Said at the counter when each person pays their own share

examples.ko: 저희 따로 계산해 주세요. 제 것만 먼저요.
examples.romanization: jeohui ttaro gyesanhae juseyo. je geonman meonjeoyo.
examples.en: Please ring us up separately — just mine first.
examples.note: 제 것만 ('just mine') to pay only your portion ahead of the others

examples.ko: A: 같이 계산하세요, 따로 하세요? / B: 따로 계산해 주세요. / A: 네, 그럼 한 분씩 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: gachi gyesanhaseyo, ttaro haseyo? / B: ttaro gyesanhae juseyo. / A: ne, geureom han bunssi kae juseyo.
examples.en: A: Together or separate? / B: Separately, please. / A: Okay, one at a time then.
examples.note: Answering the cashier's 같이/따로 question; staff line you up 한 분씩 ('one person at a time')

entries.nuance: 따로 계산해 주세요 is 따로 ('separately, apart') + 계산해 주세요 ('please ring up'), used when each person in a group pays their own. The cashier will often ask 같이 계산하세요, 따로 하세요? ('together or separate?'), and this is your answer. Culturally Korea has long leaned toward one person treating (한턱 내다) or paying together (같이 계산), so splitting per item is less automatic than in the West — but 따로 계산 (separate) and 더치페이 (Dutch-pay) are now common among younger people, so it's a normal, unremarkable thing to ask for. The dividing line: 따로 계산 means each pays for what they had / their own check, while 같이 계산 (or 1/n, 'split into N') means one combined bill. The English-speaker error is saying 'split the bill' as 나눠 주세요 ('please divide it'), which is vague and can be mistaken for dividing the FOOD; the clear requests are 따로 계산해 주세요 (separate) or 1/n로 해 주세요 (even split). Keep the word order — 따로 modifies 계산, so lead with 따로 계산, since 계산 따로 sounds reshuffled. And don't assume separate is the default; if you want it, state it outright before the cashier rings up one total.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 나눠 주세요 to mean 'split the bill'.
