The biggest practical fact unique to Korea's transit system: if you tap your same 교통카드 when switching within roughly 30 minutes, you receive a 환승 할인 (transfer discount) and often pay little or nothing extra for the connection — but ONLY if you tap both in and out with the same card; paying cash or changing cards forfeits the discount entirely. The colloquial native-Korean equivalent is 갈아타다 ('change and board'); both 환승하다 and 갈아타다 are correct, with 환승 sounding slightly more official or system-level and 갈아타다 more conversational. Polite -요 for agents and strangers.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Not tapping the card on transfer and losing the discount.
The 환승 할인 only applies if you tap OUT and tap IN with the same 교통카드, within the time limit (roughly 30 minutes). Paying cash or switching to a different card forfeits the free or discounted transfer.
Using 에 instead of 로 for direction: 어디에 가요?
'Where do I go (toward)?' uses the direction particle 로/으로: 어디로 가요? 어디에 가요 marks a static destination and sounds odd when you are asking which way to head inside a busy station.
Thinking only 환승하다 is correct and avoiding 갈아타다.
Both are correct. 갈아타다 ('to change and board') is very natural in colloquial speech: 2호선으로 갈아타요. Do not over-rely on the Sino-Korean 환승 everywhere; 갈아타다 is just as common in conversation.

structuredNuance.t: 환승(換乘) literally 'change-ride'. In practice it means switching subway lines at an interchange station, or moving from bus to subway (or vice versa). The -려면 structure means 'in order to / if you intend to'.

Ask a station agent or look for 환승 signs inside the station. Polite -요 with anyone you ask. 환승 is also used at bus hubs (환승 센터) where you switch between bus routes — the discount rule applies there too.

환승하다 (Sino-Korean, slightly formal/official) and 갈아타다 (native Korean, colloquial) both mean 'to transfer/change'. In everyday speech 갈아타다 is heard more: 2호선으로 갈아타세요. 환승 appears more in signage, apps, and system announcements. Both are always correct.
환승하다 → 환승해요 (transfer), 환승했어요 (I transferred), 환승 통로 (connecting corridor), 환승 할인 (transfer discount), 환승역 (interchange station). 환승 센터 = bus transfer hub.

The direction particle must be 로/으로: 어디로 가요? (which way do I go?). 어디에 가요? marks a static endpoint, not a direction — it sounds slightly off. Also, many English speakers forget to tap out on the bus before tapping in on the subway, losing the 환승 할인 automatically.

entries.english: Do I change trains here?
entries.shortExplanation: 여기서 갈아타면 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Do I change trains here?".
entries.explanation: 여기서 갈아타면 돼요? (yeogiseo garatamyeon dwaeyo?) means "Do I change trains here?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 여기서 갈아타면 돼요? ("Do I change trains here?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; confirming this is the correct station to transfer at
반말 — only use this with a close friend you are traveling with
Honorific -셔야 — how station staff or an elder addresses you

usagePhrases.en: Which line do I change to?
usagePhrases.note: Asking which specific line to switch onto — 로/으로 marks the target line

examples.ko: 여기서 갈아타면 돼요?
examples.romanization: yeogiseo garatamyeon dwaeyo?
examples.en: Do I change here?
examples.note: Confirming with a passenger at the station before you step off — the -면 돼요? ending asks permission or confirmation of a correct action.

examples.ko: 사당역에서 4호선으로 갈아타면 돼요.
examples.romanization: sadangyeogeseo 4hoseoneuro garatamyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: You change to Line 4 at Sadang Station.
examples.note: Giving someone else directions: location + line-with-로 + 갈아타면 돼요 is the full informative sentence.

examples.ko: A: 잠실에서 갈아타야 해요? / B: 네, 거기서 2호선으로 갈아타세요.
examples.romanization: A: jamsireseo garataya haeyo? / B: ne, geogiseo 2hoseoneuro garataseyo.
examples.en: A: Do I transfer at Jamsil? / B: Yes, change to Line 2 there.
examples.note: 갈아타야 해요 (question) — 갈아타세요 (polite instruction back) — a real exchange with a helpful local.

entries.nuance: 갈아타다 is a native Korean compound: 갈아 (from 갈다 'to change/replace') + 타다 ('to ride/board'), literally 'change what you ride'. It is the most commonly spoken word for transferring — more colloquial than the Sino-Korean 환승하다, and exactly what you'll hear from locals and helpful strangers. 여기서 갈아타면 돼요? uses the confirmation grammar -면 돼요? ('is it okay if…?'), the standard way to check whether an action is correct. Two particles to get right: the PLACE of transfer takes 에서/서 (여기서, 사당역에서) because the action happens AT that station, and the TARGET LINE takes 로/으로 (4호선으로 갈아타요) because 로 marks the direction or destination you are switching toward. Register: 갈아타면 돼요? (polite -요) for strangers; 갈아타세요 (polite command/suggestion) is what staff give back to you; 갈아타 (반말) only with a friend. An English speaker's typical wrong turn is reaching for 바꾸다 ('to exchange an object') — 기차를 바꿔요 sounds like you want to literally exchange the physical train, which is nonsensical; the correct verb for switching which vehicle you ride is 갈아타다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 바꾸다 to mean 'change trains'.
바꾸다 is 'to exchange/replace an object'. Switching which vehicle you ride is 갈아타다: 여기서 갈아타요. 기차를 바꿔요 wrongly sounds like you are trying to swap the physical train for a different one.
Marking the place with 에 instead of 서: 여기에 갈아타요.
Transferring happens AT a station, so use the action-location particle 에서/서: 여기서 갈아타요, 사당역에서 갈아타요. Static 에 is wrong for the place of an action.
Using the wrong particle for the target line: 4호선에 갈아타요.
The line you switch TO takes the direction/target particle 로/으로: 4호선으로 갈아타요 ('change to Line 4'). 4호선에 갈아타요 misuses 에 as though it were a destination marker rather than a direction marker.

structuredNuance.t: 갈아타다 = 갈아 (change) + 타다 (ride) = 'to change what you ride'. 여기서 갈아타면 돼요? = 'is it okay to change (vehicles) here?' — a polite request for confirmation that this station is the right transfer point.
Ask to any fellow passenger before stepping off. Polite -요 is right with strangers. Staff tell you 갈아타세요 (polite command) or 갈아타셔야 해요 (you must transfer — honorific). With a friend: 여기서 갈아타 (반말).

갈아타다 = colloquial, native Korean ('change and board'). 환승하다 = formal, Sino-Korean (official signage, apps). Both mean the same thing; 갈아타다 is heard more in everyday speech, 환승 more on signs. Neither is wrong in conversation.
갈아타다 → 갈아타요 (changes), 갈아타세요 (please change — polite request), 갈아타야 해요 (must change), 갈아탔어요 (I changed). The target line always takes 로/으로: 4호선으로 갈아타세요.

Do not use 바꾸다 ('to exchange an object') for changing vehicles — 기차를 바꿔요 sounds like swapping the physical train. The verb is 갈아타다. Also, the place of transfer takes 에서/서 (action at a location), not 에: 여기서 갈아타요, not 여기에 갈아타요.

entries.english: Did you tap your bus card?
entries.shortExplanation: 버스 카드 찍으셨어요? is a practical expression meaning "Did you tap your bus card?".
entries.explanation: "Did you tap your bus card?" — that is 버스 카드 찍으셨어요? (beoseu kadeu jjigeusyeosseoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 버스 카드 찍으셨어요? ("Did you tap your card?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Honorific question (with 시) — how a driver or older passenger addresses you
Polite request — reminding someone to tap at the front

usagePhrases.en: Do I tap when getting off too?
usagePhrases.note: Asking about the tap-out requirement, critical for transfer discounts
Plain statement confirming you have already tapped

examples.ko: A: 카드 찍었어요? / B: 네, 찍었어요.
examples.romanization: A: kadeu jjigeosseoyo? / B: ne, jjigeosseoyo.
examples.en: A: Did you tap? / B: Yes, I tapped.
examples.note: 찍다 is the standard verb; the exchange is quick and natural between any two bus riders.

examples.ko: 저기요, 내릴 때도 카드 찍어야 돼요?
examples.romanization: jeogiyo, naeril ttaedo kadeu jjigeoya dwaeyo?
examples.en: Excuse me, do I tap when getting off too?
examples.note: Tap-out is required on Korean city buses to preserve your 환승 할인 and to be charged the correct distance-based fare.

examples.ko: 뒷문으로 내릴 때 단말기에 카드 찍으세요.
examples.romanization: dwinmuneuro naeril ttae danmalgie kadeu jjigeuseyo.
examples.en: Tap your card on the reader at the back door when you get off.
examples.note: 단말기 = card reader/terminal; 뒷문 = back door; this sentence describes exactly what to do.

entries.nuance: The everyday verb for tapping a transit card on a reader is 찍다 — literally 'to stamp, press, or dot'. So 'tap your card' is 카드(를) 찍다 and the reader itself is the 단말기. A slightly different but also acceptable alternative is 대다 ('to touch/put against': 카드를 대다), but 찍다 is what most people say and what drivers use in announcements. Korean city buses require TWO taps: once boarding at the front door and again alighting at the back door — this is the 하차 태그 ('alighting tag'). Skipping the tap-out risks voiding the 환승 할인 (transfer discount) on your next connection and may trigger a penalty fare. The honorific 찍으셨어요? (with 시) is how a driver or an older person politely addresses you; your plain answer is 찍었어요. The verb 찍다 has multiple meanings — 사진을 찍다 is 'take a photo', 찍어 먹다 is 'dip and eat' — but in the bus/subway context it unambiguously means tapping the card. One convenience: the same 교통카드 (T-money or Cashbee) works on both buses and subways; there is no separate 'bus-only card'.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Forgetting to tap out (하차 태그) when getting off the bus.
Korean buses require tapping AGAIN at the back-door reader when you exit. Skipping the tap-out voids your 환승 할인 and can trigger a penalty fare on the next ride. Always 내릴 때 카드 찍으세요.
Using a verb other than 찍다/대다 for tapping.
The idiomatic verb is 찍다 (or 대다): 카드 찍으세요. Do not say 누르다 ('press a button') or 터치하다 ('touch') — 찍다 is what Koreans say for tapping the card reader.
Thinking you need a separate 'bus card'.
The same 교통카드 (T-money/Cashbee) works on buses, subways, and most intercity trains. There is no special bus-only card to buy; tap the same card you use on the subway.

structuredNuance.t: 찍다 literally means 'to stamp/press'. For a transit card it means tapping the card on the reader (단말기). Korean buses require tapping TWICE: at boarding (front door) and at alighting (back door — 하차 태그). Missing the tap-out forfeits your 환승 할인 and may charge a penalty.
찍으셨어요? (with honorific 시) is how a driver or elder asks you. You answer 네, 찍었어요. To ask a fellow passenger: 카드 찍었어요? (plain polite). A reminder to someone else: 카드 찍어 주세요.

대다 ('to touch/place against') is also heard — 카드를 대세요 — and is acceptable but less idiomatic. 누르다 ('to press') is for buttons (the bell 벨), not for card tapping. Don't confuse 찍다 (transit card tap) with 찍다 in other contexts: 사진을 찍다 (take a photo), 도장을 찍다 (stamp a seal).

찍다 → 찍어요 (taps), 찍으세요 (please tap — polite instruction), 찍으셨어요? (did you tap? — honorific), 찍었어요 (I tapped — past). 안 찍으면 ('if you don't tap') + consequence is a common warning structure: 안 찍으면 환승 할인이 안 돼요.

Two traps: (1) forgetting to tap OUT at the back door — the tap-out is not optional on Korean buses, unlike some other transit systems; and (2) reaching for 터치하다 or 누르다 for tapping the card reader — the correct verb is 찍다 (or 대다).

entries.english: Can I pay with cash too?
entries.shortExplanation: 현금도 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I pay with cash too?".
entries.explanation: 현금도 돼요? (hyeongeumdo dwaeyo?) = "Can I pay with cash too?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 현금도 돼요? ("Can I pay with cash too?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Can I pay with cash too?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking the bus driver if cash is accepted alongside card

usagePhrases.en: I don't have a card — does cash work?
usagePhrases.note: Explaining the reason first, then asking — a natural softening sequence
현금으로 ('by cash') + 낼게요 ('I'll pay') — stating your payment method
Critical follow-up: city buses often give no change at all

examples.ko: 현금도 돼요?
examples.romanization: hyeongeumdo dwaeyo?
examples.en: Can I pay cash too?
examples.note: Asked to the driver as you board without a card — a single question that tells the driver everything.

examples.ko: 카드가 안 돼서 그러는데, 현금 내도 돼요?
examples.romanization: kadeuga an dwaeseo geureoneunde, hyeongeum naedo dwaeyo?
examples.en: My card isn't working, so — can I pay cash?
examples.note: 안 돼서 그러는데 ('because it's not working, so…') politely explains your situation before asking for an exception.

examples.ko: A: 버스 현금 내면 거스름돈 안 줘요? / B: 네, 거스름돈은 없어요. 딱 맞게 내야 돼요.
examples.romanization: A: beoseu hyeongeum naemyeon geoseureumdon an jwoyo? / B: ne, geoseureumdoneun eopseoyo. ttang matge naeya dwaeyo.
examples.en: A: If I pay cash on the bus, no change is given? / B: That's right, no change. You need to have exact change.
examples.note: 딱 맞게 ('exactly fitting') = exact change; this confirms the practical reality of cash payment on Korean city buses.

entries.nuance: 현금 is Sino-Korean 現金 ('current money' = cash), and 현금도 돼요? = 'does cash work too?' — the particle 도 ('also/too') implies 'in addition to the default payment method (card)', the most natural framing when card is the norm and you are checking the alternative. A major practical trap: on most Korean city buses, paying cash means you drop the exact fare into a cash box and walk on — NO change (거스름돈) is given. Overpaying is lost money. Subway station ticket machines DO give change, but buses generally do not. So 거스름돈 줘요? ('do I get change?') is a smart follow-up before handing in a large bill. The payment-method particle is -으로: 현금으로 낼게요 ('I'll pay by cash'), 카드로 낼게요 ('by card'). English speakers' most common mistake is using 돈 ('money' in general) where they mean 현금 — 돈으로 돼요? is grammatically understandable but vague, because 돈 includes card, bank transfer, and cash; say 현금으로 when you mean physical banknotes and coins. Polite -요 with the driver is always correct.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Expecting change when paying cash on a city bus.
Korean buses usually give NO 거스름돈 (change) for cash — you pay the exact fare or lose the difference. Prepare exact coins, or better, use a 교통카드. Subway ticket machines do give change.
Using 돈 instead of 현금 for 'cash'.
돈 means money in general (including cards and bank balances). Physical cash specifically is 현금: 현금도 돼요? Say 현금으로 낼게요 ('pay by cash'), not 돈으로.
Mixing up the particle: 현금에 낼게요.
'Pay BY cash' uses the means particle 으로: 현금으로 낼게요, 카드로 낼게요. 현금에 is wrong; 으로 marks the method or instrument of payment.

structuredNuance.t: 현금(現金) = physical cash (banknotes and coins). 현금도 돼요? = 'does cash also work?' The particle 도 ('also') signals that card is the assumed default and you are asking whether cash is accepted as an alternative.

Ask the bus driver (기사님) as you approach the front. Polite -요 is right. On a subway, cash goes into the ticket machine (which gives change), not to a person. On buses, prepare exact change because most drivers and cash boxes give none back.
돈 = money in general (includes card balance, bank transfer, cash). 현금 = physical cash only. When you mean physical banknotes/coins, say 현금, not 돈. 현금으로 낼게요 (pay by cash) vs 카드로 낼게요 (pay by card).
현금도 돼요? → 현금 내도 돼요? (same meaning), 현금으로 낼게요 (I'll pay cash), 거스름돈 있어요? (do you have change? — alternate way to ask). On a bus: 교통카드 없어요, 현금으로 해도 돼요? (I don't have a transit card, can I pay cash?).

Two traps: (1) using 돈 when you mean physical cash — say 현금 for clarity; (2) expecting change on a bus — most Korean city buses give NO 거스름돈 for cash, so prepare exact coins or use a 교통카드 to avoid the problem.

entries.english: Where's the (bus) stop?
entries.shortExplanation: 정류장이 어디예요? is a practical expression meaning "Where's the (bus) stop?".
entries.explanation: 정류장이 어디예요? (jeongnyujangi eodiyeyo?) means "Where's the (bus) stop?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 정류장이 어디예요? ("Where's the bus stop?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking a passerby for the location of a bus stop
Adding 버스 makes it unambiguous — useful on a busy street

usagePhrases.en: Which numbered bus should I take?
usagePhrases.note: Asking which bus by route number before finding the stop

usagePhrases.en: Do I board at this stop?
usagePhrases.note: Confirming this specific stop is the right one to wait at

examples.ko: 저기요, 버스 정류장이 어디예요?
examples.romanization: jeogiyo, beoseu jeongnyujangi eodiyeyo?
examples.en: Excuse me, where's the bus stop?
examples.note: Asked to a passerby on the street; 저기요 draws attention politely without startling them.

examples.ko: 강남역 가는 버스 정류장이 어디예요?
examples.romanization: gangnamyeok ganeun beoseu jeongnyujangi eodiyeyo?
examples.en: Where's the stop for a bus going to Gangnam Station?
examples.note: 가는 ('that goes') is a relative clause narrowing the stop to buses heading toward Gangnam.

examples.ko: A: 146번은 어느 정류장에서 타요? / B: 저 골목 건너편이에요.
examples.romanization: A: 146beoneun eoneu jeongnyujangeseo tayo? / B: jeo golmok geonneopyeonieyo.
examples.en: A: Which stop do I catch the 146 at? / B: It's just across that alley over there.
examples.note: 어느 정류장에서 타요 = 'at which stop do I board?'; 건너편 = 'the other side / across'.

entries.nuance: 정류장 is Sino-Korean 停留場 ('stopping-staying place'), the word for a bus stop. This is distinct from 역 (驛), which is a subway or rail station — beginners consistently confuse the two, but using 역 for a bus stop sounds wrong to Koreans. Full form: 버스 정류장 (or 버스 정류소, same meaning). Korean buses are identified by route NUMBER (번호), and you ask which one with 몇 번 버스 — route numbers are read as Sino-Korean figures (146번 = 백사십육 번), not counted items. To say where you board, use the action-location particle 에서: 이 정류장에서 타요 ('I board at this stop'), because boarding is an action happening at a place. A subtle but common English-speaker error is asking 버스 어디예요? ('where is the bus?') when they mean the stop — that question asks for the vehicle's current location, not the designated waiting area; ask 정류장 어디예요? instead. 종점 = the final terminus or last stop on a route, not a regular stop. Polite -요 with any stranger on the street.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Calling a bus stop a 역.
역 is a subway or train station. A bus stop is a 정류장 (or 버스 정류장). Ask 정류장이 어디예요? for a bus stop; using 역 here confuses locals.
Asking 버스 어디예요? when you mean the stop.
That question asks where the bus VEHICLE currently is. To find the designated waiting area, ask 정류장이 어디예요? or 버스 정류장 어디예요?
Using native numbers for bus route numbers.
Bus route numbers are Sino-Korean: 146번 = 백사십육 번, 7016번 = 칠천십육 번. Do not say 일곱 번 for route 7 — route numbers are read as written figures, not counted items with native numbers.

structuredNuance.t: 정류장(停留場) = 'stopping-staying place' = bus stop. You find the stop and wait there; the bus number tells you which route. 버스 정류장 is the full form; 정류소 is a synonym used interchangeably.

Ask any passerby on the street. Polite -요 is right with strangers. If you already know the route number, add it: 146번 버스 정류장이 어디예요? — giving the route number helps locals point you to the exact stop, since multiple stops for different routes can be near each other.

역 = subway/train station (never use for a bus stop). 정류장 = bus stop. 종점 = the final terminus of a bus route — on a bus near the end of the line, 종점 is the last stop where everyone must get off. These three words mark distinct concepts.
정류장이 어디예요? → 정류장 어디예요? (particle dropped in casual speech), 이 정류장에서 타면 돼요? (do I board here?), 다음 정류장이 어디예요? (what's the next stop?). The same 정류장 root works across all these questions.
Do not ask 버스 어디예요? — that asks where the physical bus vehicle is, not where the stop is. To find the waiting area say 버스 정류장 어디예요? Also, do not use 역 for a bus stop; 역 is subway/rail only.

entries.english: Does this bus come often?
entries.shortExplanation: 이 버스 자주 와요? is a practical expression meaning "Does this bus come often?".
entries.explanation: "Does this bus come often?" — that is 이 버스 자주 와요? (i beoseu jaju wayo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 이 버스 자주 와요? ("Does this bus come often?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking frequency/wait time to someone at the stop
More precise: 배차 간격 ('dispatch interval') — the official term used on apps and signs

usagePhrases.en: How long do I have to wait?
usagePhrases.note: Asking the wait time directly in minutes
Asking the exact next arrival — often answered with 몇 분 있어요 ('it's in X minutes')

examples.ko: 이 버스 자주 와요?
examples.romanization: i beoseu jaju wayo?
examples.en: Does this bus come often?
examples.note: Ask to someone already waiting at the stop — they usually know the route well and will give a realistic answer.

examples.ko: 146번 배차 간격이 어떻게 돼요?
examples.romanization: 146beon baecha gangyeogi eotteoke dwaeyo?
examples.en: What's the interval for the 146?
examples.note: 배차 간격 (配車間隔) = the time gap between consecutive buses on the same route; the term used on electronic signs and transit apps.

examples.ko: A: 다음 버스 언제 와요? 앱에는 10분이라는데. / B: 맞아요, 한 10분 돼요.
examples.romanization: A: daeum beoseu eonje wayo? aebeneun 10buniraneunde. / B: majayo, han 10bun dwaeyo.
examples.en: A: When's the next bus? The app says 10 minutes. / B: That's right, about 10 minutes.
examples.note: Cross-checking the real-time arrival app with a local; 한 10분 ('about 10 minutes') is the natural approximate answer.

entries.nuance: 이 버스 자주 와요? is 이 버스 ('this bus') + 자주 ('often/frequently') + 와요? ('does it come?') — a warm, casual way to gauge how long your wait might be. The more official register uses 배차 간격 (配車間隔): the set interval between buses on a route, the term found on digital signs and apps. In practice most people check a real-time app (카카오맵, 네이버 지도, 서울 버스 앱) or the electronic display at the stop, but knowing 자주 와요? and 언제 와요? lets you ask a human nearby. An important vocabulary distinction: 자주 is an adverb of FREQUENCY ('often'), whereas 빨리 is an adverb of SPEED ('quickly') — 이 버스 빨리 와요? oddly asks 'does it come fast?' (speed), not 'often'. Equally, 많이 ('a lot, in quantity') answers a different question — 버스 많이 와요? sounds like 'do many buses come?' (count), not 'does it come frequently?'. The natural answer from a local is a minute count: 한 10분마다 와요 ('it comes about every 10 minutes'). Polite -요 with fellow passengers at the stop.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 빨리 (fast) when you mean 자주 (often).
자주 asks how FREQUENTLY the bus runs; 빨리 asks how FAST it travels. 이 버스 자주 와요? = 'does it come often?'. 이 버스 빨리 와요? = 'does it come quickly?' — a very different and less useful question.
Using 많이 for frequency: 버스 많이 와요?
많이 = 'a lot (in quantity)'. 버스 많이 와요? sounds like 'are many buses coming?' (quantity), not 'does this one come frequently?'. Use 자주 for frequency: 이 버스 자주 와요?
Saying 배차 alone without 간격: 배차가 어때요?
배차 간격 together means 'the gap between buses'. 배차 alone means 'vehicle dispatch' and is incomplete for asking about wait time. Say 배차 간격이 어떻게 돼요? or keep it simple with 이 버스 자주 와요?

structuredNuance.t: 자주 = 'often/frequently' (adverb of frequency). 이 버스 자주 와요? = 'does this bus come often?'. The answer tells you the approximate wait time. The official term for bus frequency is 배차 간격 — the time gap between buses on a route.

Ask a fellow passenger at the stop. Polite -요 is right. For exact arrival times, the real-time apps (카카오맵, 네이버 지도) and the stop's electronic display are more reliable than asking a person, but knowing the question is useful when your phone battery is dead or signal is poor.

자주 = frequently (how often). 빨리 = quickly (how fast). 많이 = a lot/in quantity (how many). Only 자주 correctly asks frequency: 이 버스 자주 와요?. 빨리 와요? asks if it arrives fast; 많이 와요? asks if many buses come at once.
이 버스 자주 와요? → 배차 간격이 어떻게 돼요? (more formal), 얼마나 기다려야 돼요? (how long do I wait?), 다음 버스 언제 와요? (when is the next one?). All probe the same 'wait time' question from different angles.
Do not use 빨리 (speed) or 많이 (quantity) when you mean 자주 (frequency): 이 버스 자주 와요? is 'does it come often?'. 이 버스 많이 와요? sounds like 'are there lots of buses?' — a different and odd question.

entries.english: What time's the last train/bus?
entries.shortExplanation: 막차 몇 시예요? is a practical expression meaning "What time's the last train/bus?".
entries.explanation: 막차 몇 시예요? (makcha myeot siyeyo?) = "What time's the last train/bus?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 막차 몇 시예요? ("What time's the last one?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking the last departure time of the night
언제 ('when') variant — slightly more casual than 몇 시
첫차 ('first vehicle of the day') — the exact opposite of 막차

usagePhrases.en: Has the last one already gone?
usagePhrases.note: Asking if service has ended for the night — 끊기다 = 'to be cut off'

examples.ko: 막차 몇 시예요?
examples.romanization: makcha myeot siyeyo?
examples.en: What time's the last train?
examples.note: Ask a station agent late at night — the simplest, most direct form.

examples.ko: 지하철 막차 몇 시예요? 자정 전에 끊겨요?
examples.romanization: jihacheol makcha myeot siyeyo? jajeong jeone kkeunkyeoyo?
examples.en: What time's the last subway? Does it stop before midnight?
examples.note: 끊기다 ('to be cut off') is the idiomatic verb for transit service ending for the night; 자정 = midnight.

examples.ko: A: 막차 놓쳤어요. / B: 그럼 심야버스 타거나 택시 타야 돼요.
examples.romanization: A: makcha notchyeosseoyo. / B: geureom simyabeoseu tageona taeksi taya dwaeyo.
examples.en: A: I missed the last train. / B: Then you'll need to take a night bus or a taxi.
examples.note: 놓치다 = 'to miss/let slip'; 심야버스 = late-night bus route that partially replaces the subway after it stops.

entries.nuance: 막차 is 막 ('last/final', a native Korean prefix marking the end) + 차 ('vehicle/train/bus'), compactly meaning 'the last transit vehicle of the day'. This is a critical survival word in Korea because the Seoul subway typically stops running between 11 PM and 1 AM depending on the line and station — missing the 막차 means an expensive taxi or waiting for the 심야버스 (night bus). Its opposite is 첫차 ('first vehicle of the morning'). The verb for service ending is 끊기다 ('to be cut off/severed'): 막차 끊겼어요? = 'has the last one already gone?'. Note that 끊기다 here is not about a phone call dropping; it is the idiom for transit service stopping for the night. To say you missed it: 막차 놓쳤어요 ('I missed the last train'), using 놓치다 ('to miss/let something slip away'). Why not 마지막 기차? Both are understood, but 막차 is the native compound that everyone uses — it is more compact, more natural, and sounds like a local. Time: hours use NATIVE Korean numbers with 시 (열두 시 = 12 o'clock), while minutes use Sino-Korean with 분 (삼십 분 = 30 minutes) — confusing these is a very common learner error.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 마지막 차/기차 instead of 막차.
마지막 차 is understandable but the compact, idiomatic word is 막차 (and 첫차 for the first). Ask 막차 몇 시예요?, not 마지막 기차 몇 시예요?
Using 끝나다 instead of 끊기다 for service ending.
막차 끊겼어요? is the idiomatic question for 'has service ended for the night?'. 끝나다 ('to finish') sounds odd in this context; 끊기다 ('to be cut off') is the natural word for transit shutting down.
Mixing number systems for time.
Hours with 시 use native Korean numbers (열두 시 = 12:00), but minutes use Sino-Korean (삼십 분 = 30 min). So '12:30' is 열두 시 삼십 분 — do not say 십이 시 for the hour.

structuredNuance.t: 막차 = 막 ('last/final') + 차 ('vehicle') = the last subway or bus of the day. 막차 몇 시예요? = 'what time is the last one?'. It is one of the most practically important words a newcomer can learn.

Ask a station agent, fellow passenger, or the driver late at night. Polite -요 is right. Alternatively, check the transit app or the station schedule board — but knowing the phrase is essential when you can't read the sign.

structuredNuance.e: VS 마지막 기차 / 끊기다 vs 끝나다
structuredNuance.t: 마지막 기차 ('the final train') is understandable but unnatural — locals always say 막차. 끊기다 ('be cut off') is the idiomatic verb for service ending, preferred over 끝나다 ('to finish') in transit contexts: 지하철 끊겼어요? is what Koreans say, not 지하철 끝났어요?
막차 몇 시예요? → 막차 언제예요? (when?), 막차 끊겼어요? (has it ended?), 막차 놓쳤어요 (I missed it). 첫차 몇 시예요? = 'what time is the first one?'. 막차 시간표 = last-train timetable.

Two traps: (1) saying 마지막 기차 instead of 막차 — understandable but unnatural; and (2) mixing up number systems for times: hours with 시 use native numbers (열두 시 = 12:00), but minutes use Sino-Korean (삼십 분 = 30 min). Getting this backwards is very common.

entries.english: Is this seat free?
entries.shortExplanation: 이 자리 비었어요? is a practical expression meaning "Is this seat free?".
entries.explanation: 이 자리 비었어요? (i jari bieosseoyo?) means "Is this seat free?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 이 자리 비었어요? ("Is this seat free?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the direct way to ask before sitting down
Asking permission to sit — slightly softer/more deferential

usagePhrases.en: Is there a seat / any space?
usagePhrases.note: Asking whether any open seat is available in the car or area
Checking if the spot is occupied — asks about a person rather than vacancy

examples.ko: 이 자리 비었어요?
examples.romanization: i jari bieosseoyo?
examples.en: Is this seat free?
examples.note: Ask to the person sitting next to the empty seat before you sit — waiting for their nod or verbal 아니요, 없어요 ('no, no one's there').

examples.ko: A: 여기 사람 있어요? / B: 아니요, 앉으세요.
examples.romanization: A: yeogi saram isseoyo? / B: aniyo, anjeuseyo.
examples.en: A: Is anyone here? / B: No, please sit down.
examples.note: The standard exchange: 앉으세요 ('please sit') is the polite invitation to take the seat.

examples.ko: 죄송한데, 여기 노약자석이에요.
examples.romanization: joesonghande, yeogi noyakjaseogieyo.
examples.en: Sorry, but this is a priority seat.
examples.note: 노약자석 = priority seating reserved for the elderly, disabled, or pregnant — even an empty one should not be taken by a healthy young person.

entries.nuance: 이 자리 비었어요? is 이 자리 ('this seat') + 비었어요? (past/resultant state of 비다 'to be empty'), literally 'is this seat empty/vacant?'. The related options cover slightly different angles: 여기 사람 있어요? checks whether a PERSON is occupying the spot (often the quickest social probe), while 여기 앉아도 돼요? directly asks PERMISSION (more deferential). All are polite -요; 반말 with a stranger on the subway would be rude. A major cultural point: Korean subway cars have clearly marked 노약자석 (priority seats for the elderly, pregnant, or disabled) at the ends of cars, and 임산부 배려석 (pink seats for pregnant passengers) in the middle — even when these are empty, a young healthy person sitting there will draw disapproval from other passengers. 이 자리 비었어요? does not override that etiquette. Vocabulary note: 비었어요 ('it's empty') and 자리 없어요 ('there are no seats') are nearly OPPOSITE: 이 자리 비었어요 = this specific seat is open; 자리 없어요 = all seats are taken. English speakers often use 자유 ('freedom') to translate 'free/vacant' — 이 자리 자유예요? — but 자유 means 'liberty', not 'available'; the correct word for an empty seat is 비다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'free' literally with 자유: 이 자리 자유예요?
자유 means 'freedom/liberty', not 'vacant'. An empty/available seat uses 비다: 이 자리 비었어요? or check the occupant: 여기 사람 있어요?
Sitting in 노약자석 or 임산부 배려석 when able-bodied.

Priority seats (노약자석) and pink pregnant-passenger seats (임산부 배려석) should be left empty for those who need them, even on an otherwise empty train. Sitting there as a healthy young rider draws real and immediate social disapproval.
Confusing 이 자리 비었어요 (this seat is empty) with 자리 없어요 (no seats at all).
비었어요 ('it's empty/free') says THIS SPECIFIC SEAT is open; 자리 없어요 ('there aren't seats') means all seats are full. They describe opposite situations — keep them distinct.

structuredNuance.t: 이 자리 비었어요? = 'is this seat empty?' 비다 = to be empty/vacant (intransitive). The past/resultant form 비었어요 describes the current state of emptiness. A nod or 아니요, 없어요 from the neighbor means 'go ahead'.

Always use polite -요 form with strangers on transit. Never drop to 반말 with someone you don't know. On a quiet car, making eye contact and asking quietly is the norm. If the neighbor is wearing headphones, tap your own ear or point to the seat — they understand.

structuredNuance.e: VS 여기 사람 있어요 / 자리 없어요
structuredNuance.t: 이 자리 비었어요? focuses on the seat's vacancy. 여기 사람 있어요? focuses on whether a person is using it — slightly more natural and direct. 자리 없어요 ('there are no seats') = ALL seats are taken, the opposite situation.
이 자리 비었어요? → 여기 앉아도 돼요? (may I sit?), 여기 사람 있어요? (is anyone here?), 자리 있어요? (any seat available?). All are interchangeable for checking a seat; choose the one that feels most natural.

Do not use 자유 ('freedom') for 'free/vacant' — 이 자리 자유예요? means nothing in Korean. A vacant seat is 비었어요 (empty). Also, 비었어요 (this seat is empty) and 자리 없어요 (all seats are taken) are nearly opposites — do not confuse them.

entries.english: Let me through, please
entries.shortExplanation: 좀 지나갈게요 is a practical expression meaning "Let me through, please".
entries.explanation: "Let me through, please" — that is 좀 지나갈게요 (jom jinagalgeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 좀 지나갈게요 ("Let me through / coming through"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; said when squeezing past people toward the door on a crowded train
The most natural and gentle way to make people step aside briefly
Announcing you need to exit at this stop — triggers people near the door to clear the way
More direct request to clear the way — polite but slightly stronger than 잠깐만요

examples.ko: 저기요, 좀 지나갈게요.
examples.romanization: jeogiyo, jom jinagalgeyo.
examples.en: Excuse me, let me through.
examples.note: Said while moving toward the door on a packed subway — 저기요 gets attention first, then the announcement of your intent.

examples.ko: 잠깐만요, 내릴게요!
examples.romanization: jamkkanmanyo, naerilgeyo!
examples.en: One sec — I'm getting off!
examples.note: 잠깐만요 + 내릴게요 together part a packed crowd right at your stop; locals respond to 내릴게요 very reliably.

examples.ko: A: 죄송합니다, 좀 지나갈게요. 다음에 내려요. / B: 아, 네. 잠깐만요.
examples.romanization: A: joesonghamnida, jom jinagalgeyo. daeume naeryeoyo. / B: a, ne. jamkkanmanyo.
examples.en: A: Sorry, coming through — I'm getting off next. / B: Oh sure, just a second.
examples.note: A complete real exchange: apologize, announce your intent, state the reason; the response is immediate.

entries.nuance: 좀 지나갈게요 breaks down as 좀 (softener/politeness particle) + 지나가다 ('to pass by/through') + -ㄹ게요 (first-person polite announcement of an intended action). The -ㄹ게요 ending signals 'I'm going to do X, just so you know' — it is courteous by nature, not a command. On a packed Seoul subway this phrase gets you to the door before your stop. The key verb hierarchy from gentlest to most direct: 잠깐만요 ('just a moment', barely a request) → 좀 지나갈게요 ('I'm going to pass through') → 내릴게요 ('I'm getting off' — most effective near your stop) → 좀 비켜 주세요 ('please move aside' — direct but polite). English speakers commonly reach for 실례합니다 ('pardon the intrusion') — correct in formal settings but stiff and overly ceremonial for a quick train-car squeeze; 잠깐만요 or 내릴게요 is what real people say. Also note: 미안해요 alone is an apology for doing something wrong; it does not signal you need to pass. Pair an apology with the action announcement: 죄송합니다, 좀 지나갈게요. The softener 좀 and the -요 ending are load-bearing — dropping them makes the phrase sound blunter and potentially rude.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 실례합니다 to squeeze past on a crowded train.
실례합니다 is formal and suited for interrupting someone to ask a question, not for navigating a packed subway car. Say 잠깐만요 ('one moment') or 좀 지나갈게요 ('coming through') to part the crowd naturally.
Staying silent and physically pushing to the door.
Without a word, pushing past feels rude and you may miss your stop in the commotion. Announcing 잠깐만요! or 내릴게요! signals your need clearly — people will reliably step aside when they hear 내릴게요.
Saying 미안해요 alone when you mean 'excuse me, let me by'.
미안해요 apologizes for a wrong you have done but does not signal you need to pass. To move through a crowd, pair any apology with the action: 죄송합니다, 좀 지나갈게요 — or simply say 잠깐만요 to get people to move.

structuredNuance.t: 좀 지나갈게요 = 'I'm going to pass through (just so you know)'. 지나가다 = to pass by/through; -ㄹ게요 = polite announcement of intended action; 좀 = softener. The whole phrase is a polite way of saying 'coming through, make way please' without issuing a direct command.

Use on crowded subway cars or buses when you need to reach the door before your stop. Polite -요 is essential; dropping 좀 or -요 makes it sound impolite. 내릴게요 (just 'I'm getting off') is the single most effective phrase to use — people at the door will step aside immediately.

실례합니다 = 'pardon the intrusion' — formal and ceremonial, used when interrupting someone's attention (e.g., asking a question at a counter), not for quickly squeezing past on a subway. 좀 비켜 주세요 ('please move aside') is more direct and appropriate for physical crowd navigation.

좀 지나갈게요 → 죄송합니다, 지나갈게요 (sorry, coming through), 잠깐만요 (just a moment), 내릴게요 (I'm getting off), 죄송합니다, 좀 비켜 주세요 (sorry, please move). The shortest version that works every time: 내릴게요 (said twice if needed).
실례합니다 is the wrong choice for a crowd-squeeze — it is too formal and sounds odd in this context. Also, 미안해요 alone apologizes but does NOT tell people you need to pass; add the action: 죄송합니다, 좀 지나갈게요.

entries.english: Is this the express train?
entries.shortExplanation: 이거 급행이에요? is a practical expression meaning "Is this the express train?".
entries.explanation: 이거 급행이에요? (igeo geupaengieyo?) = "Is this the express train?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 이거 급행이에요? ("Is this the express?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; checking if a train skips stops before you board

usagePhrases.en: Is this train express or all-stop?
usagePhrases.note: Asking which type it is directly — useful when signs are unclear

usagePhrases.en: Does the express stop at City Hall?
usagePhrases.note: The critical follow-up: express trains skip many stations

usagePhrases.en: I should take the regular train
usagePhrases.note: Deciding to take the all-stop train instead — 일반/완행 = the non-express

examples.ko: 이거 급행이에요?
examples.romanization: igeo geupaengieyo?
examples.en: Is this the express?
examples.note: Ask on the platform before boarding a 1호선 or 9호선 train — yes/no answer tells you whether to wait for the next one.

examples.ko: 급행 타면 우리 역 안 서요?
examples.romanization: geupaeng tamyeon uri yeok an seoyo?
examples.en: If I take the express, won't it stop at our station?
examples.note: 안 서요 ('doesn't stop') is the danger — the express passes certain stations without stopping.

examples.ko: A: 급행 놓쳤는데 다음 일반 열차 언제 와요? / B: 한 3분이요.
examples.romanization: A: geupaeng notchyeonneunde daeum ilban yeolcha eonje wayo? / B: han 3buniyo.
examples.en: A: I missed the express — when's the next regular train? / B: About 3 minutes.
examples.note: 일반/완행 = all-stop train; the fallback if you miss the express or your station is not an express stop.

entries.nuance: 급행 is Sino-Korean 急行 ('urgent-go' = express), a train or bus service that skips intermediate stations to reach major stops faster. In the Seoul subway, Lines 1, 9, the Gyeongui-Jungang Line, and the Suin-Bundang Line run 급행 trains alongside regular trains on the same tracks. The all-stop alternative is 완행 (緩行, 'slow-go') or, more commonly in everyday speech, 일반 (열차) ('ordinary/regular train'). The must-know verb for stopping is 서다 — '(급행이) 서요?' means 'does the express STOP there?', distinct from '가요?' which asks the destination. You can be on the right line heading the right direction and still overshoot your station if you board the 급행 and your station is not an express stop — this is how 9호선 catches tourists and newcomers. Checking 급행 서요? before boarding is therefore crucial. Signs and platform announcements mark each train as 급행 or 일반; learning to spot the 급행 character on a display board is a worthwhile five-second investment. English speakers who say 빠른 기차 ('fast train') are understood but sound un-natural — the system term is 급행; use it.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Boarding a 급행 without checking it stops at your station.
An express skips many stops. Always confirm 급행 (우리) 역 서요? before boarding, or you will sail past your station. If unsure, take the 일반/완행 (all-stop) train.
Using 가다 instead of 서다 to ask about stopping.
급행 시청역 가요? asks the destination/direction; to ask whether it STOPS there, use 서다: 급행 시청역 서요? The express may 'go' that direction without 'stopping' at your station.
Calling it 빠른 기차 instead of 급행.
빠른 기차 ('fast train') is understandable but not the system term. The correct label is 급행 (express) vs 일반/완행 (all-stop). Use 이거 급행이에요? to ask.

structuredNuance.t: 급행(急行) literally 'urgent-go' = an express service that skips intermediate stations. It is faster between major stops but useless if your station is not on the express route. The all-stop alternative is 완행/일반 열차.

Ask on the platform before boarding. Polite -요 with any fellow passenger or station agent. Signs and the digital display above the platform edge show 급행 vs 일반 — watch for this every time you board on 9호선, 1호선, or 경의중앙선.

가요? = does it go (toward) that destination? 서요? = does it stop at that station? On an express, 시청역으로 가요 ('it goes toward City Hall') but 시청역에 안 서요 ('it doesn't stop at City Hall') are both possible if your station is skipped. Always check 서요?, not just 가요?.
급행이에요? → 이거 급행이에요, 일반이에요? (express or regular?), 급행 서요? (does the express stop here?), 급행 안 서요? (doesn't it stop?), 다음 급행 언제 와요? (when's the next express?).

Using 빠른 기차 ('fast train') instead of 급행 sounds unnatural — the system term is 급행. Also, the most common practical mistake is not checking 서요? — an express goes in the right direction but may not stop at your station.

entries.english: Please press the stop bell
entries.shortExplanation: 벨 눌러 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please press the stop bell".
entries.explanation: 벨 눌러 주세요 (bel nulleo juseyo) means "Please press the stop bell". Say it as one set phrase — for example 벨 눌러 주세요 ("Please press the stop bell"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking a passenger near the button to press it for you
Checking that the stop has been requested before the bus passes

usagePhrases.en: You press the (alighting) bell to get off
usagePhrases.note: 하차벨 = the formal compound; explaining the system to someone who doesn't know

usagePhrases.en: I'll get off next, I'll press the bell
usagePhrases.note: Announcing your intention — 누를게요 (-ㄹ게요) = I'll press it

examples.ko: 벨 눌러 주세요!
examples.romanization: bel nulleo juseyo!
examples.en: Please press the bell!
examples.note: Said to a passenger standing near the button when you cannot reach it — instinctive, understood immediately.

examples.ko: 내릴 거면 미리 벨 눌러요.
examples.romanization: naeril geomyeon miri bel nulleoyo.
examples.en: If you're getting off, press the bell ahead of time.
examples.note: 미리 ('in advance') is the key word — press the bell before the stop, not exactly at it, so the driver has time to pull over.

examples.ko: A: 벨 안 누르면 그냥 지나가요? / B: 네, 아무도 기다리지 않으면 그냥 가요.
examples.romanization: A: bel an nureumyeon geunyang jinagayo? / B: ne, amudo gidariji aneumyeon geunyang gayo.
examples.en: A: If no one presses the bell, does it just drive past? / B: Yes, if no one is waiting there it just goes.
examples.note: Confirming the most important practical rule: Korean buses skip stops with neither a bell nor a waiting rider.

entries.nuance: 벨 is the loanword 'bell' — in the bus context it always refers to the stop-request button (하차벨, 하차 'alighting' + 벨), and 벨 눌러 주세요 = 'please press the bell', using 누르다 ('to press a button/switch') + the favor form 주세요. The single most important practical fact: Korean city buses do NOT stop at every stop automatically. If no one has pressed the 하차벨 AND no one is standing waiting at the stop, the driver drives right past. So you must press the bell in advance (미리) when your stop is approaching — ideally as the previous stop is passing. The verb is 누르다 (르-irregular: 눌러요/눌러 주세요/눌렀어요); do NOT use 찍다 (that's for tapping the transit card) or 치다 ('to hit/strike') — those are wrong for pressing a button. The formal compound term is 하차벨, but in speech simply 벨 눌러 주세요 or 벨 누르세요 is understood by everyone. If you cannot reach the button on a crowded bus, ask the nearest passenger 벨 좀 눌러 주세요. Subways stop at every station automatically — there is no 벨 underground. Between friends: 벨 눌러 (반말). With the driver or strangers: 벨 눌러 주세요 or 벨 누르세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Assuming the bus stops at every stop without pressing the bell.
Korean buses skip a stop if no one pressed the 하차벨 and no one is waiting outside. To exit, press the bell in advance (미리) before your stop arrives, or the bus drives straight past.
Using 찍다 or 치다 for pressing the bell.
찍다 is for tapping the transit card; 치다 means 'to hit/strike'. Pressing a button is 누르다: 벨 눌러 주세요. These verbs are not interchangeable.
Pressing the bell too late, right as the stop arrives.
Press 미리 ('ahead of time') as the previous stop passes — the driver needs enough warning to pull over safely. Pressing at the last second may result in overshooting your stop.

structuredNuance.t: 하차벨 ('alighting bell') = the stop-request button on a Korean city bus. Pressing it signals the driver you want to exit at the next stop. Without a press (and no one waiting outside), the bus drives past.

Bus-only — subways stop at every station automatically. On a bus, press 미리 ('in advance') as the previous stop passes. If you cannot reach the button, ask a neighbor: 벨 좀 눌러 주세요. With strangers: polite -요; with a friend: 벨 눌러 (반말).

누르다 = to press a button/switch — the correct verb for the 벨. 찍다 = to tap/stamp — the correct verb for tapping the transit card on the reader. 치다 = to hit/strike — wrong for either. Do not mix these three verbs.
벨 눌러 주세요 → 하차벨 눌러 주세요 (more formal), 벨 누르세요 (polite imperative without 주세요), 벨 눌렀어요? (did you press?), 벨 누를게요 (I'll press it). The 르-irregular of 누르다: 눌러요, 눌러 주세요, 눌렀어요.

Two traps: (1) assuming the bus stops automatically at every stop — it does NOT; and (2) saying 버튼 ('button') instead of 벨 — 버튼 is understood but 벨 is the idiomatic word for the bus stop-request in Korean.

entries.english: Please take me to this address.
entries.shortExplanation: 이 주소로 가 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please take me to this address.".
entries.explanation: "Please take me to this address." — that is 이 주소로 가 주세요 (i jusoro ga juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 이 주소로 가 주세요. ("Please go to this address."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 — what you say to a taxi driver while showing your phone screen
반말 — only to a friend driving, never to a real taxi driver

usagePhrases.en: Could you take me to this address, please?
usagePhrases.note: More formal/softer — adds politeness when handing over a written address
Natural extension — checking the driver can find it before setting off

examples.ko: 기사님, 이 주소로 가 주세요.
examples.romanization: gisanim, i jusoro ga juseyo.
examples.en: Driver, please take me to this address.
examples.note: 기사님 is the standard respectful way to address a taxi driver — never 아저씨

examples.ko: A: 이 주소로 가 주세요. 내비에 찍어 주시면 돼요. / B: 네, 알겠습니다.
examples.romanization: A: i jusoro ga juseyo. naebie jjigeo jusimyeon dwaeyo. / B: ne, algetseumnida.
examples.en: A: Please take me to this address — you can just put it in the GPS. / B: Got it.
examples.note: 내비 is the everyday word for car navigation/GPS; offering to let the driver input it is a thoughtful move

examples.ko: 이 주소로 가 주세요. 영어로 되어 있는데 제가 읽어 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: i jusoro ga juseyo. yeongeoro doeeo inneunde jega ilgeo deurilgeyo.
examples.en: Please take me to this address. It's in English, but I'll read it for you.
examples.note: Real situation when your booking confirmation shows only a romanized or English address

entries.nuance: This is the opening line you say to a taxi driver the moment you get in, showing or reading a written destination — customer-to-driver, always 존댓말, never 반말 to a stranger. The structure is [destination] + 로/으로 + 가 주세요: the particle 로 marks the direction, and 가 주세요 (가다 + 주세요) is the polite request form meaning 'please do the going for me'. To sound warmer or more formal, prefix with 기사님 and upgrade to 가 주시겠어요? The 반말 form 가 줘 is exclusively for a friend at the wheel. The dividing line with 여기로 가 주세요 is what you're handing over: 이 주소 names a typed or written address, while 여기 points at a map spot — if you're reading out numbers use 이 주소로; if you're tapping a pin use 여기로. An English speaker's first instinct is to drop the helper verb and say 이 주소 가요, which sounds like you're narrating your own movement ('I'm going to this address') rather than asking the driver to take you; the 주세요 is the crucial request morpheme.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Defaulting to 이 주소까지 가 주세요 — that's fine, but for handing a driver a destination the idiomatic, taught form marks it with 로/으로: 이 주소로 가 주세요 (이 주소에 가 주세요 is grammatical but sounds flatter).
Dropping 주세요 and saying 이 주소 가요 — that's you stating your own plan, not asking the driver; you need 가 주세요 to make it a request to him.
Calling the driver 아저씨 ('mister') to get his attention — it's not rude but sounds rough; 기사님 is the respectful, standard term.

structuredNuance.t: 이 주소로 가 주세요 breaks down as: 이 주소 'this address' + 로 (direction particle) + 가다 'go' + 주세요 'please do it for me'. The literal sense and the real sense match — it IS a polite direction command — but the 주세요 is not optional courtesy fluff; it's what grammatically converts the statement into a request.

Customer-to-driver, the moment you board. Plain 존댓말 (가 주세요) is exactly right; upgrade to 가 주시겠어요? if you want extra warmth. Prefix with 기사님 to address the driver respectfully. The 반말 가 줘 is only for a friend driving you — never to a professional driver.

여기로 가 주세요 is the nearest alternative. The dividing line: 이 주소 refers to a typed or written street address you read aloud, whereas 여기 points at a visual map location. If you're showing a pinned map use 여기로; if you're reading out numbers or showing text use 이 주소로.
기사님, 이 주소로 가 주세요 (warmest); 이 주소로 가 주시겠어요? (softest/most formal); 이 주소로 가 줘 (반말, friend only); 이 주소 아세요? (checking before departure).

Dropping 주세요 and saying 이 주소 가요 — that reads as 'I'm going to this address', a self-report, not a request. The entire politeness and the grammatical direction of the action hinge on 가 주세요. Another trap: using the topic particle 는 (이 주소는 가 주세요) which breaks the syntax — keep 이 주소로 as a directional phrase.

entries.english: Please take me here.
entries.shortExplanation: 여기로 가 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please take me here.".
entries.explanation: 여기로 가 주세요 (yeogiro ga juseyo) = "Please take me here.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 여기로 가 주세요. ("Please go here."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 — said while pointing at a map pin or address on your phone
반말 — only to a friend who's driving

usagePhrases.en: Could you take me here, please?
usagePhrases.note: Softer/more formal — when you want to sound extra polite
Natural extension — asking the route to a pin you're showing

examples.ko: 여기로 가 주세요.
examples.romanization: yeogiro ga juseyo.
examples.en: Please take me here.
examples.note: The bare request while tapping a location on the screen — the visual gesture replaces the need for an address

examples.ko: A: 여기로 가 주세요. 지도에 표시해 놨어요. / B: 아, 이쪽이요? 알겠습니다.
examples.romanization: A: yeogiro ga juseyo. jidoe pyosihae nwasseoyo. / B: a, ijjogiyo? algetseumnida.
examples.en: A: Please take me here — I've marked it on the map. / B: Ah, this direction? Got it.
examples.note: 표시하다 = to mark; confirming the spot before driving prevents ending up at the wrong entrance

examples.ko: 여기로 가 주세요. 큰길 말고 골목 안쪽이에요.
examples.romanization: yeogiro ga juseyo. keungil malgo golmok anjjogieyo.
examples.en: Please take me here. It's not on the main road — it's inside the alley.
examples.note: Real situation: the destination is set back from the road; without this note the driver stops short

entries.nuance: You say this when you physically show the driver a point — a dropped pin, a screenshot, a paper map — rather than reading out a street address. The 로 particle marks the direction ('toward here'), and 가 주세요 is the polite 존댓말 request form. Upgrade to 가 주시겠어요? for extra courtesy; drop to 반말 가 줘 only with a friend behind the wheel. The key dividing line with 이 주소로 가 주세요 is what you're presenting: 여기 is a deictic pointer ('this spot right here'), while 이 주소 names a written address. In practice: map pin → 여기로, written text → 이 주소로. Be careful not to drop the 로 particle; while Koreans do omit it in very casual speech, the clean learner form is 여기로 가 주세요, and the particle makes the destination role unambiguous. Also avoid substituting 이리 ('this way'), which is stiff and literary — 여기 is the everyday word. An English speaker's trap is inverting the word order to sound like English ('가 주세요 여기로') — Korean keeps the destination phrase before the verb.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 에서 instead of 로 — 여기에서 means 'from here' (starting point), but you want the destination, so it's 여기로 가 주세요.
Saying 여기 와 주세요 ('please come here') — 오다 (come) is wrong because you're already in the cab going somewhere; the verb is 가다 (go).
Pointing and only saying 여기 — to a driver that's abrupt; add 로 가 주세요 so it's a complete polite request.

structuredNuance.t: 여기로 가 주세요 = 'toward here, please go (for me)'. The literal and real meanings align — it is a direction command — but the deictic 여기 does real work: it means 'this exact spot I am pointing at', not just 'here' in the abstract. Without a physical gesture (phone screen, map, pointed finger) the sentence is incomplete.

Customer-to-driver while showing a location — 존댓말 throughout; add 기사님 to open respectfully. Soften with 가 주시겠어요?. 반말 가 줘 is only for a friend. This is more visual/gestural than 이 주소로 가 주세요, so it works best when you can show the screen.

이 주소로 가 주세요 vs 여기로 가 주세요: the first is for a written address you read; the second is for a visual pin you show. Also avoid 이리 가 주세요 ('please go this way') — 이리 sounds formal/literary; 여기로 is everyday Korean.
여기로 가 주시겠어요? (softest); 여기로 가 줘 (반말); 여기 어떻게 가요? (asking the route). If the pin is far ahead and you want to note it's inside an area: 여기 안쪽으로 가 주세요.

Dropping the 로 particle: saying 여기 가 주세요 is commonly heard but the standard taught form includes 로. A bigger trap is using 이리 instead of 여기 — 이리 is literary and sounds stiff. Also note 여기에서 가 주세요 is wrong: 에서 marks the origin ('from here'), not the destination — for a destination use 여기로.

entries.english: Please stop here.
entries.shortExplanation: 여기서 세워 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please stop here.".
entries.explanation: 여기서 세워 주세요 (yeogiseo sewo juseyo) means "Please stop here.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 여기서 세워 주세요. ("Please stop here."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 — the standard way to tell a driver to pull over
반말 — to a friend driving you

usagePhrases.en: Could you pull over here, please?
usagePhrases.note: Softer — 좀 + 시겠어요 cushions the request

usagePhrases.en: Please stop here for a sec.
usagePhrases.note: Natural extension — 잠깐 implies a brief stop, e.g. to let someone off

examples.ko: 여기서 세워 주세요.
examples.romanization: yeogiseo sewo juseyo.
examples.en: Please stop here.
examples.note: The bare instruction as you recognize your destination — 세워 주세요 is all you need; no extra words required

examples.ko: A: 아, 여기서 세워 주세요. 다 왔어요. / B: 네, 잠깐만요.
examples.romanization: A: a, yeogiseo sewo juseyo. da wasseoyo. / B: ne, jamkkanmanyo.
examples.en: A: Oh, stop here please — we're here. / B: Sure, just a moment.
examples.note: 아 signals the moment you spot your stop; pairing 다 왔어요 confirms it for the driver

examples.ko: 저기 신호등 지나서 바로 여기서 세워 주세요.
examples.romanization: jeogi sinhodeung jinaseo baro yeogiseo sewo juseyo.
examples.en: Right after that traffic light, please stop here.
examples.note: Real situation: giving the driver a landmark so he starts slowing in time — critical on fast roads

entries.nuance: This tells a taxi driver to pull over right where you are, customer-to-driver, in plain 존댓말. The key verb is the causative 세우다 — not the intransitive 서다. 서다 means 'the car/person stops on its own', but you are asking the driver to bring the vehicle to a stop, so you need the causative: 세우다 ('to make [it] stand still'). 세워 주세요 = 'please make it stop for me'. For extra softness add 좀 or switch to 세워 주시겠어요?; 반말 is 세워 줘. The nearest alternative is 저 앞에서 내릴게요 ('I'll get off up ahead'), which announces your own exit rather than commanding a stop — the dividing line is agency: 세워 주세요 orders the driver's action; 내릴게요 describes your own. Koreans also say 여기 세워 주세요 (without 서), which is the contracted form of 여기에서 — both are natural. The English-speaker's error is reaching for 서다 and saying 여기서 서 주세요; that sounds like you're telling the driver to stand up personally. Another mistake is 멈춰 주세요, which fits stopping any action or machine in general but is not the idiomatic taxi phrase.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 여기서 서 주세요 — 서다 is 'to stand/stop oneself'; the driver stopping the car needs the causative 세우다, so 세워 주세요.
Using 멈춰 주세요 — 멈추다 means 'halt/cease' (an action or machine) and sounds odd for pulling a car over; 세워 주세요 is the idiomatic taxi phrase.
Saying 여기에 세워 주세요 with 에 — for the spot where the stopping happens Koreans use 에서, so 여기서 (=여기에서) 세워 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 여기서 세워 주세요 = 'at/from here, please make (it) stand still for me'. The literal causative sense is transparent: you are directing the driver to halt the vehicle. The verb choice — 세우다 (causative) not 서다 (intransitive) — is not optional; it is grammatically required because you are causing the car to stop, not waiting for it to stop itself.

Customer-to-driver as you approach or reach your stop — 존댓말 throughout. Add 좀 or upgrade to 세워 주시겠어요? to soften; 반말 세워 줘 is for a friend only. If you want to signal ahead of time, tack on a landmark: 저기 신호등 지나서 세워 주세요.

저 앞에서 내릴게요 ('I'll get off up ahead') announces your own exit — softer and less commanding. 세워 주세요 commands the driver directly. 멈춰 주세요 is technically correct but feels like stopping a machine mid-action; 세워 주세요 is the fixed taxi phrase. 여기서 = 여기에서 (contracted); both are heard.
여기서 좀 세워 주시겠어요? (politest); 여기서 잠깐 세워 주세요 (brief stop); 저기서 세워 주세요 (stop over there); 여기서 세워 줘 (반말).

Saying 여기서 서 주세요 (using intransitive 서다) — 서다 means the subject stops itself; to make the car stop you need the causative 세우다. Also, 멈춰 주세요 is not the idiomatic phrase for pulling over a taxi — 세워 주세요 is.

entries.english: I'll get off just up ahead.
entries.shortExplanation: 저 앞에서 내릴게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll get off just up ahead.".
entries.explanation: "I'll get off just up ahead." — that is 저 앞에서 내릴게요 (jeo apeseo naerilgeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 저 앞에서 내릴게요. ("I'll get off up ahead."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 — politely announcing where you want to be let out
반말 — to a friend driving

usagePhrases.en: I will get off just ahead.
usagePhrases.note: More formal (격식) — 겠습니다 is crisp and deferential

usagePhrases.en: I'll get off at the crosswalk ahead.
usagePhrases.note: Natural extension — naming the exact landmark

examples.ko: 저 앞에서 내릴게요.
examples.romanization: jeo apeseo naerilgeyo.
examples.en: I'll get off up ahead.
examples.note: The bare announcement pointing forward — the -ㄹ게요 ending signals your own intention, which is softer than a command

examples.ko: 저 앞에서 내릴게요. 거기 편의점 앞이에요.
examples.romanization: jeo apeseo naerilgeyo. geogi pyeonuijeom apieyo.
examples.en: I'll get off up ahead, in front of that convenience store.
examples.note: Pinpointing with a visible landmark so the driver doesn't overshoot

examples.ko: A: 지금 세우긴 좀 그렇고, 저 앞에서 내릴게요. / B: 네, 저기 편의점 앞에요?
examples.romanization: A: jigeum seugin jom geureoko, jeo apeseo naerilgeyo. / B: ne, jeogi pyeonuijeom apeyo?
examples.en: A: It's a bit awkward to stop now, so I'll get off just ahead. / B: Sure, in front of that convenience store?
examples.note: Real situation when the current spot is a no-stopping zone — the driver confirms the landmark

entries.nuance: You use this to tell the driver you'll be getting out at a spot a short distance ahead, rather than commanding a stop with 세워 주세요. The verb is 내리다 ('to get off/alight'), and the -ㄹ게요 ending (volitional intention) signals your own decision — 'I'll go ahead and get off there' — which is naturally polite and non-confrontational. Formal/격식 is 내리겠습니다; 반말 is 내릴게. The critical distance word is 저 앞 ('that spot ahead, away from us') — 저 points to something visible but not immediately beside you, like a crosswalk or a shop sign you can see from the cab. Use 이 앞 only if the spot is right in front of your current position. The dividing line with 여기서 세워 주세요 is agency: 세워 주세요 commands the driver to stop the car; 내릴게요 declares your own action of exiting, leaving the driver to choose how and where to slow. An English speaker's instinct is to say 내리고 싶어요 ('I want to get off'), but this sounds tentative like a child expressing a preference; the adult, situation-natural form is the volitional -ㄹ게요. Another trap is using 타다 ('to board') or 내려가다 ('to go down') — exiting a vehicle is simply 내리다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 내려요 (plain present) — that states a general fact ('I get off'); for a here-and-now intention you need 내릴게요.
Using 타다 or 떨어지다 — 타다 is 'to get ON', 떨어지다 is 'to fall'; getting OUT of a vehicle is 내리다.
Saying 이 앞에서 when the spot is some meters ahead — 이 앞 is right at your position; for a point further forward use 저 앞.

structuredNuance.t: 저 앞에서 내릴게요 = 'at that spot up ahead, I will get off'. 저 앞 means a visible but not-immediate point in the near distance. The -ㄹ게요 ending marks a personal intention/decision ('I will go ahead and ~'), not a command — this is what makes it feel cooperative and gentle rather than demanding.

Customer-to-driver as you're nearing your stop — 존댓말 throughout. Upgrade to 내리겠습니다 for very formal situations (business car). 반말 내릴게 only with a friend. Pair with a landmark (편의점, 횡단보도) so the driver can plan the stop safely.

여기서 세워 주세요 commands the driver to stop; 저 앞에서 내릴게요 announces your own exit — the latter is softer and often used when you're still moving and just signaling intent. 저 앞에서 세워 주세요 (stop command) vs 저 앞에서 내릴게요 (exit announcement) — both are natural but carry different perspectives.
저 앞 횡단보도에서 내릴게요 (named landmark); 저기 편의점 앞에서 내릴게요 (shop reference); 거의 다 왔어요, 저 앞에서 내릴게요 (paired with arrival signal); 내리겠습니다 (격식).

Saying 내리고 싶어요 ('I want to get off') — this sounds like expressing a wish rather than stating a plan; use -ㄹ게요 for a here-and-now intention. Also, confusing 저 앞 (visible ahead) with 이 앞 (right in front of you now) — pick based on actual distance.

entries.english: Please go a bit faster / Please hurry.
entries.shortExplanation: 좀 빨리 가 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please go a bit faster / Please hurry.".
entries.explanation: 좀 빨리 가 주세요 (jom ppalli ga juseyo) means "Please go a bit faster / Please hurry.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 좀 빨리 가 주세요. ("Please hurry a bit."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 — 좀 softens the push so it isn't bossy
반말 — to a friend driving

usagePhrases.en: Could you hurry just a little?
usagePhrases.note: More formal/polite — 서둘러 주시겠어요 is gentler and refined

usagePhrases.en: Please go as fast as possible.
usagePhrases.note: Natural extension — 최대한 = 'as much as possible', for real urgency

examples.ko: 죄송한데 좀 빨리 가 주세요. 시간이 없어서요.
examples.romanization: joesonghande jom ppalli ga juseyo. sigani eopseoseoyo.
examples.en: Sorry, but please hurry. I'm short on time.
examples.note: 죄송한데 apologizes before the imposition; always adding a reason makes this polite rather than rude

examples.ko: A: 기차 시간이 다 돼서요, 좀 빨리 가 주실 수 있을까요? / B: 최대한 해 볼게요.
examples.romanization: A: gicha sigani da dwaeseoyo, jom ppalli ga jusil su isseulkkayo? / B: choedaehan hae bolgeyo.
examples.en: A: My train's about to leave, could you possibly go a bit faster? / B: I'll do my best.
examples.note: 수 있을까요? is the softest possible form; the driver's reply 최대한 해 볼게요 is the natural response

examples.ko: 좀 빨리 가 주세요. 지금 막히면 비행기 놓칠 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: jom ppalli ga juseyo. jigeum makimyeon bihaenggi notchil geot gatayo.
examples.en: Please hurry a bit. If we hit traffic now I might miss my flight.
examples.note: Real situation: giving a concrete consequence (missing a flight) frames it as urgency, not rudeness

entries.nuance: You say this to ask the driver to increase speed, customer-to-driver, in 존댓말, and the word 좀 ('a little / please') is essential — it converts what would otherwise be a curt order (빨리 가 주세요) into a polite request. Without 좀 the phrase can feel demanding to Korean ears. For maximum courtesy, use 서둘러 주시겠어요? or attach a reason (시간이 없어서요, 비행기가 있어서요); 반말 is 빨리 가 줘. The dividing line with 서둘러 주세요 is nuance: 빨리 가 주세요 specifically targets driving speed, while 서둘러 주세요 ('please hurry') covers haste more generally — Koreans often soften both with 좀. An English-speaker's first move is the bare imperative 빨리! or 빨리 가요, both of which land abruptly to a stranger; 좀 ... 주세요 is the politeness wrapper you cannot skip. Prefacing with 죄송한데 ('sorry, but') is a cultural nicety — acknowledging that pressing someone is slightly burdensome — and makes the request feel considerate. Note: Korean drivers are constrained by traffic and law, so Koreans always frame urgency as a polite request, never a demand.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying just 빨리! or 빨리 가요 — to a stranger that's an abrupt order; add 좀 and 주세요: 좀 빨리 가 주세요.
Using 빠르게 instead of 빨리 — 빠르게 is more written/technical; the everyday spoken adverb for 'quickly' is 빨리.
Dropping the reason — Koreans usually justify a hurry ('시간이 없어서요'); without it the push feels demanding even with 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 좀 빨리 가 주세요 = 'please go a little quickly (for me)'. The literal meaning is close to the real one, but 좀 does double duty: it means 'a little' (softening the degree) AND functions as a politeness marker similar to 'please'. Remove 좀 and the same request becomes noticeably more blunt.

Customer-to-driver mid-ride when you're running late — 존댓말 always, with 좀 mandatory. Add 죄송한데 (sorry, but) as a cultural opening. Give a reason (시간이 없어서요) to make it feel like information rather than a demand. 반말 빨리 가 줘 only with a friend.

서둘러 주세요 = 'please hurry' (general haste); 빨리 가 주세요 = specifically drive faster. Both are fine but need 좀. 최대한 빨리 가 주세요 escalates the urgency for real emergencies (hospital, flight). 천천히 가 주세요 ('please go slowly') is the opposite.
죄송한데 좀 빨리 가 주시겠어요? (politest); 최대한 빨리 가 주세요 (most urgent); 조금만 서둘러 주세요 (gentle alternative); 빨리 가 줘 (반말).

Saying just 빨리! or 빨리 가요 to a stranger — these read as blunt commands. The full polite form 좀 빨리 가 주세요 is required. Using 빠르게 instead of 빨리 is also off — 빠르게 is formal/written; the everyday spoken adverb is 빨리.

entries.english: Keep the change.
entries.shortExplanation: 잔돈은 괜찮아요 is a practical expression meaning "Keep the change.".
entries.explanation: 잔돈은 괜찮아요 (jandoneun gwaenchanayo) = "Keep the change.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 잔돈은 괜찮아요. ("The change is fine (keep it)."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 — politely telling the driver to keep small change
반말 — to a friend or very casual
More formal (격식) — 습니다 is crisp and courteous
Natural extension — explicitly telling him to take it

examples.ko: 잔돈은 괜찮아요.
examples.romanization: jandoneun gwaenchanayo.
examples.en: Keep the change.
examples.note: The bare phrase as you hand over a bill — the topic particle 은 ('as for the change') frames the decision neatly

examples.ko: A: 9,500원이에요. / B: 여기 만 원이요. 잔돈은 괜찮아요.
examples.romanization: A: 9,500wonieyo. / B: yeogi man woniyo. jandoneun gwaenchanayo.
examples.en: A: It's 9,500 won. / B: Here's 10,000 won — keep the change.
examples.note: Real scenario: 500원 (one coin) is a common amount people wave off; not a tip, just sparing the coin-return

examples.ko: 감사합니다. 잔돈은 괜찮으니까 그냥 받으세요.
examples.romanization: gamsahamnida. jandoneun gwaenchaneunikka geunyang badeuseyo.
examples.en: Thank you. The change is fine — just take it, please.
examples.note: 괜찮으니까 ('since it's fine') + 받으세요 ('please take it') is used when the driver hesitates to keep the coins

entries.nuance: You say this when handing over a bill and telling the driver not to bother returning the small change, customer-to-driver, in 존댓말. 잔돈 (殘돈) = 'remaining money / change', and 괜찮아요 here means 'it's fine / no need to return it' — the same 괜찮아요 used for 'no thank you' or 'it's okay'. The topic particle 은 on 잔돈 works like 'as for the change — (don't worry)'. Formal version: 괜찮습니다; 반말: 잔돈은 됐어. The more direct alternative is 그냥 가지세요 ('just keep it'), which is a clear directive; 잔돈은 괜찮아요 is softer and more indirect, the way Koreans usually wave off a tip. A cultural note: tipping in Korean taxis is NOT customary — this phrase is used only for small rounding (a few hundred won of coins), not a percentage-based tip. Saying it for a large amount would feel strange. The English-speaker's most spectacular error is a literal translation of 'keep the change': mapping 'change' to 변화 (transformation) and 'keep' to 지키다 (guard), producing 변화를 지켜요 — this is completely nonsensical. The money sense of 'change' is 잔돈 (or 거스름돈), and you wave it off with 괜찮아요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 변화를 지켜요 — that's 'keep (guard) the transformation'; money-change is 잔돈, and you wave it off with 괜찮아요.
Marking 잔돈 with 를 (잔돈을 괜찮아요) — 괜찮다 is descriptive and takes 은/는 or no particle here; say 잔돈은 괜찮아요.
Expecting to tip a percentage — Korean taxis don't use tipping; this phrase just rounds the fare up, so don't over-explain a 'tip'.

structuredNuance.t: 잔돈은 괜찮아요 = 'as for the change, it is fine'. 괜찮아요 in this context means 'no need / don't bother', not 'I'm okay'. The topic particle 은 does real work: it isolates 잔돈 as the subject of your reassurance — 'the change specifically is what I'm saying is fine'.

Customer-to-driver as you pay — 존댓말 throughout. Use 괜찮습니다 for extra formality. 반말 잔돈은 됐어 is very casual. Only use this for small coin amounts (hundreds of won); for a large amount it would feel odd in the Korean context where taxi tipping is not expected.

잔돈은 그냥 가지세요 ('just keep it') is more direct and explicit — used when the driver starts looking for change to return. 잔돈은 괜찮아요 is softer and more common as a casual wave-off. 거스름돈 and 잔돈 are both correct; 잔돈 is the everyday word.
잔돈은 괜찮으니까 받으세요 (when the driver hesitates); 잔돈은 그냥 가지세요 (explicit command to keep); 잔돈은 괜찮습니다 (격식); 잔돈은 됐어 (반말).

Literal-translating 'keep the change' as 변화를 지켜요 — 변화 is 'transformation/change (abstract)' and 지키다 is 'to guard/protect'. Money change is 잔돈; the verb is not 'keep (hold)' but 괜찮아요 (it's fine, no need to return). An entirely different sentence is needed.

entries.english: Could you please open the trunk?
entries.shortExplanation: 트렁크 좀 열어 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Could you please open the trunk?".
entries.explanation: 트렁크 좀 열어 주세요 (teureongkeu jom yeoreo juseyo) means "Could you please open the trunk?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 트렁크 좀 열어 주세요. ("Please open the trunk."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 — 좀 makes the request polite, to load luggage
반말 — to a friend

usagePhrases.en: Could you open the trunk, please?
usagePhrases.note: Softer/more formal — for heavier courtesy

usagePhrases.ko: 짐 좀 실을게요, 트렁크 열어 주세요.
usagePhrases.romanization: jim jom sireulgeyo, teureongkeu yeoreo juseyo.
usagePhrases.en: I've got luggage to load, please open the trunk.
usagePhrases.note: Natural extension — explaining you have bags

examples.ko: 트렁크 좀 열어 주세요.
examples.romanization: teureongkeu jom yeoreo juseyo.
examples.en: Please open the trunk.
examples.note: The complete bare request as you approach with a suitcase — 좀 is doing the politeness work

examples.ko: A: 캐리어가 있어서요, 트렁크 좀 열어 주세요. / B: 네, 잠깐요.
examples.romanization: A: kaerieoga isseoseoyo, teureongkeu jom yeoreo juseyo. / B: ne, jamkkanyo.
examples.en: A: I have a suitcase, so please open the trunk. / B: Sure, just a moment.
examples.note: 캐리어 = rolling suitcase (loanword); leading with the reason (있어서요) is the natural Korean way to frame a request

examples.ko: 기사님, 짐이 좀 많은데 트렁크 좀 열어 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: gisanim, jimi jom maneunde teureongkeu jom yeoreo jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Driver, I have quite a bit of luggage — could you open the trunk?
examples.note: Real situation at an airport with multiple bags; 기사님 + 주시겠어요? gives the politest version

entries.nuance: You say this so the driver pops the boot for your luggage, customer-to-driver, in 존댓말 with 좀 softening the imperative. 트렁크 is the universally understood Korean loanword for a car's storage compartment (British 'boot', American 'trunk' — both are expressed as 트렁크). The verb is 열다 ('to open [something]'), and 열어 주세요 = 'please open it for me'. Upgrade to 열어 주시겠어요? for the fullest courtesy; 반말 is 열어 줘. There is no real competing phrase — this is the only natural way to make this request — but leading with context (캐리어가 있어서요, 짐이 있어서요) before the request sounds more conversational than the bare 열어 주세요. The English-speaker's most common grammatical error is the intransitive/transitive confusion: 열리다 is the intransitive 'to be opened (on its own)', while 열다 is the transitive 'to open (something)'. You need the driver to actively open it, so use 열다 → 열어 주세요. Using 열려 주세요 sounds like you're asking the trunk to open itself. Another error is reaching for 문 ('door') and asking 문 열어 주세요, which would be the door to the passenger compartment — specify 트렁크 clearly.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 트렁크 열려 주세요 — 열리다 is 'to be opened (by itself)'; you want the driver to open it, so use the transitive 열다: 열어 주세요.
Dropping 좀 and 주세요 (트렁크 열어) — to a stranger that's a blunt command; add 좀 ... 열어 주세요.
Calling it 부트 (boot) or other English — in Korean the universally understood word is 트렁크.

structuredNuance.t: 트렁크 좀 열어 주세요 = 'please open the trunk a little for me'. 좀 here is not actually about degree ('a little') — it's a softener that makes the command courteous. 열어 주세요 combines 열다 (to open) + 주다 (to do for me) + 세요 (polite ending).

Customer-to-driver before you get in or when you've arrived and need luggage out — 존댓말 always. Soften further with 주시겠어요?. Give a reason (캐리어가 있어서요) to make the request feel natural. 반말 열어 줘 only with a friend.

짐 좀 실을게요, 트렁크 열어 주세요 — the extended version leading with your intention to load. This is actually more natural in conversation. There is no competing phrase for this specific request; 트렁크 열어 주세요 is the fixed form.
트렁크 좀 열어 주시겠어요? (politest); 트렁크 닫아 주세요 (close the trunk); 캐리어 트렁크에 넣어 주시겠어요? (asking the driver to load it too); 트렁크 좀 열어 줘 (반말).
Saying 트렁크 열려 주세요 — 열리다 is intransitive ('to be opened'); you need 열다 (transitive) → 열어 주세요. Also, dropping 좀 and 주세요 leaves 트렁크 열어, which is a blunt command to a stranger.

entries.english: Please put on your seatbelt.
entries.shortExplanation: 안전벨트 매 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please put on your seatbelt.".
entries.explanation: "Please put on your seatbelt." — that is 안전벨트 매 주세요 (anjeonbelteu mae juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 안전벨트 매 주세요. ("Please buckle your seatbelt."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 — what a driver says to YOU; you may also hear it
반말 — to a friend/child in the car
More formal (격식) — 착용하다 is the official 'to wear/fasten'
Natural extension — shortened to 벨트 in casual speech

examples.ko: 안전벨트 매 주세요.
examples.romanization: anjeonbelteu mae juseyo.
examples.en: Please put on your seatbelt.
