examples.note: The bare reminder as the cab pulls out — 매 주세요 is the complete, natural form; nothing else is needed

examples.ko: 손님, 뒷자리도 안전벨트 매 주세요.
examples.romanization: sonnim, dwitjarido anjeonbelteu mae juseyo.
examples.en: Sir/ma'am, please buckle up in the back seat too.
examples.note: 손님 = 'customer/passenger'; Korean law requires drivers to remind back-seat passengers — this is a genuine, frequent phrase

examples.ko: A: 출발하겠습니다. 안전벨트 매 주세요. / B: 네, 맸어요.
examples.romanization: A: chulbalhagetseumnida. anjeonbelteu mae juseyo. / B: ne, maesseoyo.
examples.en: A: I'll get going now. Please fasten your seatbelt. / B: Yes, I've buckled up.
examples.note: Real situation: the driver announces departure and reminds you; 맸어요 (past tense of 매다) confirms it's done

entries.nuance: In a taxi this is most often spoken by the driver to the passenger ('please buckle up'), but you could say it to any passenger in your own car. The register is plain 존댓말. The key verb choice is 매다 ('to tie/fasten') — Korean has a specific and non-obvious verb for putting on a seatbelt: you 매다 (fasten/tie) a belt, not 입다 (wear clothes) or 하다 (do). 안전벨트 매 주세요 = 'please fasten the seatbelt for me'. The formal/격식 equivalent heard on public transport announcements is 착용해 주세요 (착용하다 = 'to wear/don'); in everyday spoken Korean 매다 is the natural choice. 반말 is just 안전벨트 매. The English speaker's deepest trap is reaching for 입다 ('to put on clothing') — a seatbelt is not a garment you step into; you fasten (매다) it. Another common error is 묶다 ('to tie up/bundle'), which is used for tying shoelaces or ropes, not belts; the fixed collocation is 벨트를 매다. Note also 안전벨트 and 좌석벨트 are both used; 안전벨트 is more common in daily speech.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 안전벨트 입어 주세요 — 입다 is only for clothing; a seatbelt is fastened with 매다, so 안전벨트 매 주세요.
Using 묶다 — that's tying a rope/bundle; the fixed collocation is 벨트를 매다, so 매 주세요.
Confusing the formal verb: 착용하다 is for signs/announcements; in casual speech use 매다, not a mix like 착용해.

structuredNuance.t: 안전벨트 매 주세요 = 'please tie/fasten the safety belt for me'. 안전벨트 (安全belt) is a Sino-Korean + English hybrid noun. 매다 originally means 'to tie' (as in tying a knot), and from that it extended to fastening anything with a strap — seatbelt, tie, bow. The literal sense is transparent once you know 매다.

Driver-to-passenger as the car starts — 존댓말 매 주세요. In formal public-transport announcements: 착용해 주세요. To a child or friend: 반말 안전벨트 매. Note this is also a legal requirement in Korea (all seats), so drivers say it routinely.

안전벨트 착용해 주세요 vs 안전벨트 매 주세요 — both mean the same thing, but 착용하다 is the formal/official/written verb, while 매다 is everyday spoken Korean. On a bus announcement you'll hear 착용; in a taxi you'll hear 매다.
안전벨트 착용해 주세요 (formal); 안전벨트 매 주셨어요? (checking if they've buckled); 벨트 매 (반말); 안전벨트 풀어도 돼요? (may I unbuckle?).
Saying 안전벨트 입어 주세요 — 입다 is only for clothing you put your body through; a seatbelt is fastened with 매다. Saying 묶어 주세요 is also wrong — 묶다 ties a bundle or parcel, not a belt.

entries.english: Please turn on the meter.
entries.shortExplanation: 미터기 켜 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please turn on the meter.".
entries.explanation: 미터기 켜 주세요 (miteogi kyeo juseyo) = "Please turn on the meter.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 미터기 켜 주세요. ("Please turn on the meter."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 — politely insisting on the metered fare
반말 — only with a friend (you wouldn't really say this to a driver in 반말)
More pointed — 켜고 가다 = turn it on and drive

usagePhrases.en: We're going by the meter, right?
usagePhrases.note: Natural extension — confirming it's metered before haggling starts

examples.ko: 미터기 켜 주세요.
examples.romanization: miteogi kyeo juseyo.
examples.en: Please turn on the meter.
examples.note: The bare request — firm but polite; this alone is enough; no elaborate sentence needed

examples.ko: A: 미터기 켜 주세요. 미터기로 가는 게 맞죠? / B: 아, 네, 켤게요.
examples.romanization: A: miteogi kyeo juseyo. miteogiro ganeun ge matjyo? / B: a, ne, kyeolgeyo.
examples.en: A: Please turn on the meter. We go by the meter, right? / B: Oh, yes, I'll turn it on.
examples.note: Following up with a confirmation question is a polite way to insist without being confrontational

examples.ko: 저, 미터기 켜 주세요. 정찰제 아니고 미터기로요.
examples.romanization: jeo, miteogi kyeo juseyo. jeongchalje anigo miteogiroyo.
examples.en: Um, please turn on the meter. Not a flat rate — by the meter.
examples.note: Real situation at an airport taxi stand where drivers sometimes quote flat fares; 정찰제 = fixed-rate pricing

entries.nuance: You say this to insist the driver activate the fare meter rather than accept a quoted flat price, customer-to-driver, in firm but plain 존댓말. 미터기 is the Korean loanword for a taxi meter (from English 'meter' + 기器), and the verb for switching any device on is 켜다 — not 열다 ('open'), not 시작하다 ('start'), but 켜다 (its opposite is 끄다, 'turn off'). 켜 주세요 = 'please turn it on for me'. The nearby expression 미터기로 가 주세요 ('please go by the meter') asserts the payment method overall, while 켜 주세요 specifically activates the device — in practice both push back against off-meter deals. In Korea, all licensed taxis are metered and the driver is legally required to run it; this phrase is most useful at airports, tourist zones, and late-night stands where unregistered or unmetered flat-price offers sometimes occur. An English speaker's first verb instinct is 열다 ('open'), producing 미터기 열어 주세요, which sounds like opening a lid; a second mistake is 틀어 주세요, which is correct for turning on audio/video equipment (radio, TV) but not for a fare meter — 켜다 is the right verb here.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 미터기 열어 주세요 — 열다 is 'open (a door/lid)'; a meter is switched on with 켜다, so 켜 주세요.
Using 시작해 주세요 ('please start') — devices take 켜다/끄다 for on/off; 켜 주세요 is correct.
Marking method with 에 (미터기에 가 주세요) — the means/method particle is 로/으로, so 미터기로 가 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 미터기 켜 주세요 = 'please turn on the meter (for me)'. 켜다 means 'to turn on (a device/light)'. The semantics are fully transparent — this is a literal instruction — but the verb choice (켜다 not 열다, not 시작하다) is the key learnable fact.

Customer-to-driver at the start of a ride — 존댓말, no 반말 to a professional driver. Most useful at airports, tourist taxi stands, and late nights when flat-fare offers appear. Pair with 미터기로 가는 거죠? to make it a question rather than a pure command.

미터기 켜 주세요 (turn on the device) vs 미터기로 가 주세요 (go by metered method). The first is about activating hardware; the second is about insisting on the pricing system. Use 켜 주세요 when the meter is visibly off; use 미터기로 가 주세요 when the driver is proposing a flat price before moving.
미터기 켜고 가 주세요 (turn on and go); 미터기로 가는 거죠? (confirming the method); 미터기로 가 주세요 (asserting metered travel); 미터기 켰어요? (checking if it's running).
Saying 미터기 열어 주세요 — 열다 is for opening doors or lids, not activating a device. Saying 틀어 주세요 is also wrong here — 틀다 is specifically for audio/video devices. Devices with on/off switches use 켜다/끄다.

entries.english: What's the base fare?
entries.shortExplanation: 기본요금이 얼마예요? is a practical expression meaning "What's the base fare?".
entries.explanation: 기본요금이 얼마예요? (gibonyogeumi eolmayeyo?) means "What's the base fare?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 기본요금이 얼마예요? ("How much is the base fare?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: How much is the base fare?
usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 — asking the starting/flag-fall fare
반말 — to a friend

usagePhrases.en: May I ask the base fare?
usagePhrases.note: Softer/more formal — 인가요 is gentle and polite

usagePhrases.en: How much more on top of the base fare?
usagePhrases.note: Natural extension — asking the extra beyond the base

examples.ko: 기본요금이 얼마예요?
examples.romanization: gibonyogeumi eolmayeyo?
examples.en: How much is the base fare?
examples.note: The bare question — 이 (subject particle) marks 기본요금 as the thing being asked about; do not drop it

examples.ko: 여기 택시 기본요금이 얼마예요? 서울이랑 다를 것 같아서요.
examples.romanization: yeogi taeksi gibonyogeumi eolmayeyo? seourirang dareul geot gataseoyo.
examples.en: What's the taxi base fare here? I think it might differ from Seoul.
examples.note: Base fares vary by city (서울 / 부산 / 경기도 등); asking is always valid

examples.ko: A: 심야에는 기본요금이 얼마예요? 할증 붙죠? / B: 야간 할증 20% 붙어서 4,800원이에요.
examples.romanization: A: simyaeneun gibonyogeumi eolmayeyo? haljeung butjyo? / B: yagan haljeung 20% buteoseo 4,800wonieyo.
examples.en: A: What's the base fare late at night? There's a surcharge, right? / B: There's a 20% nighttime surcharge, so it's 4,800 won.
examples.note: Real situation: 야간 할증 (nighttime surcharge) is a key taxi vocabulary item; knowing this question will save you surprises

entries.nuance: This asks the flag-fall (starting/minimum) fare — the amount the meter begins at before any distance is covered — customer-to-driver or anyone, in plain 존댓말. The compound 기본요금 is built from 기본 (基本, 'basic/base') + 요금 (料金, 'fee/fare'), both Sino-Korean. You pair it with 얼마예요? ('how much is it?'). The subject particle 이 after 기본요금 is correct and should not be dropped — it marks the fare as what is being assessed. Softer form: 얼마인가요?; 반말: 얼마야?. Korean taxis post the base fare on the door or window, so in practice this question often confirms what you see. The critical dividing line: 얼마예요? (and 얼마) = MONEY; 얼마나 걸려요? = TIME. English speakers with both patterns fresh in memory often cross them and ask 기본요금이 얼마나 걸려요?, accidentally asking how long the fare 'takes' — the 걸리다 verb is time-only, never money. Another trap is 얼마에요 (with 에요) — after 얼마 the correct copula question form is 예요, giving 얼마예요?, not 얼마에요?
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 기본요금이 얼마나 걸려요? — 걸리다 is for time; price is 얼마예요, so 기본요금이 얼마예요?.
Writing 얼마에요 — the correct copula form after a vowel-final noun-question is 얼마예요 (예요), not 에요.
Confusing 기본요금 with 요금 alone — 요금 is just 'fare'; the specific starting fare is 기본요금.

structuredNuance.t: 기본요금이 얼마예요? = 'as for the base fare, how much is it?'. 기본요금 (基本料金) is fully transparent Sino-Korean: 기본 'basic/base' + 요금 'fee/charge'. The meaning is literal with no idiom layer.

Customer-to-driver before boarding or while checking the meter at ride-start — 존댓말. Softer version: 기본요금이 얼마인가요?. Often asked when moving between cities (base fares vary by region). Korean taxis display the base fare on the vehicle door.

얼마예요? (MONEY) vs 얼마나 걸려요? (TIME) — both use 얼마 but the structure is different: money uses the copula 예요, time uses the verb 걸리다. Also, 요금이 얼마예요? is slightly broader ('what's the fare?') while 기본요금이 얼마예요? specifically asks the starting flag-fall.

기본 (基本) = base, foundation; 요금 (料金) = fee, charge. Both are Sino-Korean. Knowing the 한자 meaning helps distinguish 기본요금 (base fare) from 추가요금 (追加料金, additional/extra charge) and 할증요금 (割增料金, surcharge).

기본요금이 얼마인가요? (softest, slightly more formal); 기본요금 얼마야? (반말); 야간 기본요금이 얼마예요? (asking the nighttime base fare, which includes the 할증 surcharge); 기본요금에서 얼마나 더 나와요? (asking how much beyond the base — useful when estimating total cost). Note: Seoul taxis post the base fare on the door, so this question often confirms a posted amount.
Saying 기본요금이 얼마나 걸려요? — 걸리다 is for time duration, never for prices. Price questions use 얼마예요?. Also, writing 얼마에요 instead of 얼마예요 — after 얼마, the question copula must be 예요 (contracted from 이에요).

entries.english: Please don't take a detour (the long way).
entries.shortExplanation: 돌아가지 말아 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please don't take a detour (the long way).".
entries.explanation: "Please don't take a detour (the long way)." — that is 돌아가지 말아 주세요 (doragaji mara juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 돌아가지 말아 주세요. ("Please don't go the long way."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Please don't go the long way.
usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 — politely asking not to detour for a higher fare
반말 — to a friend driving

usagePhrases.en: Could you please not take a detour?
usagePhrases.note: Softer/more formal — extra cushioned
Natural positive extension — asking for the direct route instead

examples.ko: 돌아가지 말아 주세요.
examples.romanization: doragaji mara juseyo.
examples.en: Please don't take the long way.
examples.note: The bare polite prohibition — -지 말아 주세요 is the correct negative-request structure, not 안 돌아가 주세요

examples.ko: 여기 길 잘 아니까 돌아가지 말아 주세요.
examples.romanization: yeogi gil jal anikka doragaji mara juseyo.
examples.en: I know this area well, so please don't go the long way.
examples.note: Signaling you will notice a detour — said gently but the implication is clear; this framing is culturally normal

examples.ko: A: 내비대로만 가 주세요. 돌아가지 말고요. / B: 네, 당연하죠.
examples.romanization: A: naebidaeroman ga juseyo. doragaji malgoyo. / B: ne, dangyeonhajyo.
examples.en: A: Please just follow the GPS, and no detours. / B: Of course.
examples.note: Real situation: telling him to follow the navigation removes ambiguity; 당연하죠 ('of course') is the driver's polite reassurance

entries.nuance: You say this to tell the driver not to take a longer route than necessary — either because you want to save money or because you know the area and will notice. Customer-to-driver, in careful 존댓말. The verb 돌아가다 means 'to go around/take a roundabout path', and the negative polite request structure is -지 말아 주세요 ('please don't ~'). Softer: -지 말아 주시겠어요?; 반말: 돌아가지 마. Note that 돌아가다 is polysemous: it can mean (1) to take a detour/go around, (2) to return/go back, and (3) in a poetic register, to pass away — context (inside a moving taxi) unambiguously picks meaning (1). A tactful alternative is to make the same request positively: 지름길로 가 주세요 ('take the shortcut') or 내비대로 가 주세요 ('follow the GPS'). The dividing line in tone: 돌아가지 말아 주세요 implies suspicion (I know you might try), while 내비대로 가 주세요 is neutral instruction. The English-speaker's grammar error is using the 안 negation: 안 돌아가 주세요 is ungrammatical as a prohibition request — Korean prohibitions use -지 말다, so 돌아가지 말아 주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 안 돌아가 주세요 — negative requests use -지 말다, not 안 + verb; the correct form is 돌아가지 말아 주세요.
Using 돌아오다 instead of 돌아가다 — 돌아오다 is 'to come back (here)'; taking a roundabout route away from you is 돌아가다, so 돌아가지 말아 주세요.
Over-bluntly saying 돌아가지 마! to a driver — that sounds accusatory; soften with 주세요 or flip to the positive 지름길로 가 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 돌아가지 말아 주세요 = 'please don't go around (for me)'. 돌아가다 literally means 'to go around/circle', extended to 'take a roundabout route'. The -지 말아 주세요 structure is the fixed Korean form for 'please don't [verb]'.

Customer-to-driver, especially at airports, tourist areas, and at night when detour risks are higher. 존댓말 throughout. The phrase implies mild suspicion, so Koreans often soften it with 여기 좀 아니까 ('I know the area a bit') or flip to the positive 내비대로 가 주세요.

지름길로 가 주세요 ('take the shortcut') makes the same request positively and sounds less accusatory. 내비대로 가 주세요 ('follow the GPS') is the most neutral option — it delegates the route decision to a third party (the app). Use 돌아가지 말아 주세요 only when you have reason to be firm.
돌아가지 말아 주시겠어요? (softest); 지름길로 가 주세요 (positive alternative); 내비대로만 가 주세요 (neutral GPS-based); 돌아가지 마 (반말).

Forming the negative request as 안 돌아가 주세요 — 안 negation cannot combine with -아/어 주세요 to make a prohibition. Prohibitions use -지 말다: 돌아가지 말아 주세요. This is one of the most common grammatical errors English speakers make with Korean requests.

entries.english: We're (almost) here.
entries.shortExplanation: 다 왔어요 is a practical expression meaning "We're (almost) here.".
entries.explanation: 다 왔어요 (da wasseoyo) = "We're (almost) here.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 다 왔어요. ("We're here / We've nearly arrived."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 — said by you or the driver as you reach the spot
반말 — to a friend
More formal (격식) — a driver may announce it this way
Natural extension — 거의 = 'almost', when not quite there yet

examples.ko: 다 왔어요. 여기서 세워 주세요.
examples.romanization: da wasseoyo. yeogiseo sewo juseyo.
examples.en: We're here. Please stop here.
examples.note: The natural pair — 다 왔어요 signals arrival, then 세워 주세요 gives the action; in practice these two are said together

examples.ko: 손님, 다 왔습니다. 14,200원입니다.
examples.romanization: sonnim, da watseumnida. 14,200wonimnida.
examples.en: Sir/ma'am, we've arrived. That'll be 14,200 won.
examples.note: How a driver announces arrival and transitions to payment — 손님 is the polite customer address

examples.ko: A: 거의 다 왔어요. 저기 건물 앞에 잠깐 세워 주시면 돼요. / B: 네, 알겠습니다.
examples.romanization: A: geoui da wasseoyo. jeogi geonmul ape jamkkan sewo jusimyeon dwaeyo. / B: ne, algetseumnida.
examples.en: A: We're nearly here. You can pull up in front of that building. / B: Got it.
examples.note: Real situation: 거의 다 왔어요 (almost there) used while still moving, then directing the exact stopping spot

entries.nuance: This announces that the taxi ride has reached (or nearly reached) its destination — said by either driver or passenger, in plain 존댓말. The phrase is grammatically past tense: 다 + 왔어요 (past of 오다, 'to come'). 다 ('all/completely') + 왔어요 = 'have come all the way' → 'we've arrived'. Note the counterintuitive verb: although you have been going somewhere (가다), the idiom uses 오다 (come), treating the destination as the reference point now that you are there. This is a fixed expression — do not swap 오다 for 가다. Formal is 다 왔습니다; 반말 is 다 왔어; not-quite-there is 거의 다 왔어요. The nearest neutral-formal alternative is 도착했어요 ('have arrived'), which is more written/impersonal; 다 왔어요 is warmer and is the everyday spoken choice. English-speaker errors fall into two categories: (1) using the wrong tense — 다 와요 (present) sounds odd, because arrival is a completed action; use past 왔어요. (2) using the wrong verb — 다 갔어요 means 'we've gone (away/all gone)', not 'we've arrived'. The deictic shift that makes 오다 correct here is a genuine Korean/English difference.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 다 가요 — arrival idiom uses 오다 in the past: 다 왔어요, not 가다.
Using present 다 와요 — the arriving is complete, so it's past tense 왔어요.
Reading it literally as 'everyone came' — 다 왔어요 is a set phrase meaning 'we've arrived / we're here'.

structuredNuance.t: 다 왔어요 = 'all came (arrived)'. 다 acts as 'completely/all the way', and 왔어요 is past tense of 오다 ('to come'). The idiom treats the destination as the viewpoint — you have 'come' to the place that is now 'here'. This is idiomatic: English says 'we're here' (present), Korean says 'we've come' (past-completed).

Driver-to-passenger or passenger-to-driver as the cab arrives — 존댓말 throughout. 다 왔습니다 is the driver's more formal announcement. 거의 다 왔어요 is used while still moving (not quite there). 반말 다 왔어 to a friend.

도착했어요 ('we have arrived') is the more neutral/formal alternative — suitable for announcements or writing. 다 왔어요 is the warm, everyday spoken version. 거의 다 왔어요 specifically means 'almost there (not yet)' — use this while still moving.
거의 다 왔어요 (almost there); 다 왔습니다 (driver's formal); 도착했어요 (neutral formal); 다 왔어 (반말); 이제 다 왔네요 (expressing a mild sense of relief or note on arrival).

Saying 다 갔어요 — 갔어요 is past tense of 가다 ('to go away') and means 'we have gone (away)' or 'it's all gone', not 'we've arrived'. Saying 다 와요 (present) is also wrong — arrival is treated as a completed past action in Korean: 왔어요.

entries.english: Thank you, take care / keep up the good work.
entries.shortExplanation: 감사합니다 수고하세요 is a practical expression meaning "Thank you, take care / keep up the good work.".
entries.explanation: 감사합니다 수고하세요 (gamsahamnida sugohaseyo) means "Thank you, take care / keep up the good work.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 감사합니다, 수고하세요. ("Thank you, take care."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 — the standard goodbye to a driver as you leave
반말 — to a friend (rarely to a driver)
More formal (격식) — 수고하셨습니다 acknowledges the completed effort
Natural extension — a warm alternative sign-off

examples.ko: 감사합니다, 수고하세요.
examples.romanization: gamsahamnida, sugohaseyo.
examples.en: Thank you, take care.
examples.note: The complete set farewell as you step out — these two phrases are said together as one breath; neither alone is wrong but the pair is warmer

examples.ko: 잘 왔습니다. 감사합니다, 수고하세요.
examples.romanization: jal watseumnida. gamsahamnida, sugohaseyo.
examples.en: Got here safely. Thank you, keep it up.
examples.note: 잘 왔습니다 ('came well / arrived safely') is an optional warm opener before the goodbye

examples.ko: A: 카드 결제됐어요? / B: 네, 됐습니다. / A: 감사합니다, 수고하세요!
examples.romanization: A: kadeu gyeoljedwaesseoyo? / B: ne, dwaetseumnida. / A: gamsahamnida, sugohaseyo!
examples.en: A: Did the card go through? / B: Yes, it did. / A: Thank you, take care!
examples.note: Real situation: closing out the payment, then leaving — the natural sequence shows how this phrase bookends the ride

entries.nuance: This is the set farewell phrase you give a taxi driver — and broadly any service worker — as you finish and leave, customer-to-worker, in 존댓말. 감사합니다 = 'thank you', and 수고하세요 literally means 'please continue your effort/labor' — it is a uniquely Korean acknowledgment of someone's ongoing work, without a clean English equivalent. The tense distinction matters: 수고하세요 (present-habitual, 'keep at it') is correct when the driver is still on shift; 수고하셨습니다 (past-respectful, 'you have labored') is correct when a task is fully completed for you — at the end of a service you received, e.g. a long delivery is done. In a taxi you leave mid-shift, so 수고하세요 is the right pick. A warm variant is 안전 운전하세요 ('drive safely'), which works perfectly here. The central cultural trap for English speakers is hierarchical register: 수고하세요 is said downward or laterally — to someone doing work on your behalf, a peer, or a service worker. Saying it to a superior (boss, professor, much older elder) implies you are evaluating their effort from above, which is patronizing in Korean culture. Never say 수고하세요 to your senior; use 감사합니다 or 안녕히 계세요 instead.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 수고하세요 to a boss or much-older superior — it implies you're evaluating their work; to superiors use 감사합니다 alone or 안녕히 계세요.
Mixing up the tense: 수고하셨습니다 is for when they've finished; as you leave a driver still on shift, use 수고하세요.
Translating 'take care' as 조심하세요 — that warns of danger; the effort-acknowledging farewell is 수고하세요.

structuredNuance.t: 수고하세요 literally = 'please undergo labor/effort (honorific)'. The real meaning is a warm send-off acknowledging the other person's work — closest to 'take care' or 'keep it up', but richer. It cannot be translated word-for-word; it must be understood as a culturally embedded expression of appreciation for effort.

Customer leaving a taxi, delivery person finishing a drop-off, shop assistant after a transaction — always customer/peer TO service worker, in 존댓말. Never say this upward in hierarchy (to a boss or professor). 반말 version: 수고해 (to a friend doing a favor).

수고하세요 (still working → keep going) vs 수고하셨습니다 (done for you → you've worked hard). 안전 운전하세요 is a warm driver-specific alternative. 조심하세요 ('be careful') warns of danger — it does NOT convey thanks for effort, and substituting it loses the warmth entirely.
감사합니다, 수고하셨습니다 (격식, when the task is done); 감사합니다, 안전 운전하세요 (driver-specific warmth); 수고해요 (slightly informal but still polite); 고생하셨어요 (acknowledged a harder job).

Translating English 'take care' as 조심하세요 — 조심하세요 warns of an imminent danger or asks for caution; it does not acknowledge effort or say goodbye warmly. Also, using 수고하세요 with a superior is the most serious cultural mistake — it is condescending in Korean hierarchy.

entries.english: Driver, how do I get there?
entries.shortExplanation: 기사님, 여기 어떻게 가요? is a practical expression meaning "Driver, how do I get there?".
entries.explanation: 기사님, 여기 어떻게 가요? (gisanim, yeogi eotteoke gayo?) = "Driver, how do I get there?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 기사님, 여기 어떻게 가요? ("Driver, how do we get there?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Driver, how do we get there?
usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 — asking the route while showing a destination
반말 — to a friend

usagePhrases.en: Do you know how to get here?
usagePhrases.note: Softer/indirect — 가는지 아세요 checks his knowledge politely

usagePhrases.ko: 여기 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요.
usagePhrases.romanization: yeogi ganeun gil jom allyeo juseyo.
usagePhrases.en: Please tell me the way to get here.
usagePhrases.note: Natural extension — directly asking for directions

examples.ko: 기사님, 여기 어떻게 가요?
examples.romanization: gisanim, yeogi eotteoke gayo?
examples.en: Driver, how do we get here?
examples.note: The bare route question while tapping the location on your phone — 기사님 upfront is courteous and signals you want his expertise

examples.ko: 여기 어떻게 가요? 골목이 복잡해서 잘 모르겠어요.
examples.romanization: yeogi eotteoke gayo? golmogi bokjapaeseo jal moreugesseoyo.
examples.en: How do we get here? The alleys are confusing and I'm not sure.
examples.note: Admitting uncertainty (잘 모르겠어요) naturally invites the driver's help rather than sounding like a test

examples.ko: A: 기사님, 여기 어떻게 가요? 빠른 길로 가면 좋겠는데요. / B: 낮에는 강변 타는 게 제일 빨라요.
examples.romanization: A: gisanim, yeogi eotteoke gayo? ppareun gillo gamyeon jokenneundeyo. / B: najeneun gangbyeon taneun ge jeil ppallayo.
examples.en: A: Driver, how do we get here? The quickest way would be great. / B: During the day the riverside road is fastest.
examples.note: Real situation: adding 빠른 길로 ('the fast way') shapes the answer you want; the driver's local knowledge response is the pay-off

entries.nuance: You ask this to a driver when you know the destination but not the route — especially useful when the GPS is unavailable, the address is confusing, or you want the driver's local knowledge. Customer-to-driver, plain 존댓말, typically opening with 기사님 to address him respectfully. 어떻게 = 'how', 가요 = '(do we/you) go', and 여기 points at the visible destination on your screen: 여기 어떻게 가요? = 'how do we go here?'. A softer, face-saving indirect version is 여기 어떻게 가는지 아세요? ('do you know how to get here?'), which lets the driver say 'I'll look it up' without losing face. 반말 is 여기 어떻게 가?. The nearest alternative with a different framing is 여기 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요 ('please tell me the way'), which directly requests directions, while 어떻게 가요? asks how more openly. The English-speaker's grammatical error is using the ability construction: 어떻게 갈 수 있어요? ('how am I able to go?') over-formalizes the question with an unneeded 수 있다 — Koreans simply say 어떻게 가요?. Another trap is 어디 가요? ('where are we going?'), which asks for the destination, not the route, and confuses the driver if you already have a pin showing.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 어떻게 갈 수 있어요? — the ability form is unneeded; the natural route question is just 어떻게 가요?.
Confusing 어떻게 (how) with 어디 (where) — 어디 가요? asks the destination; for the route use 어떻게 가요?.
Using 오다 (여기 어떻게 와요) when you mean traveling there — for going to the spot use 가다: 여기 어떻게 가요?.

structuredNuance.t: 여기 어떻게 가요? = 'here, how does one go?' The literal and real meanings are the same — a route question. 여기 in this context means 'this place I'm showing you' (the destination on the screen), not 'here where we currently are'. The deictic shift is important: 여기 = the destination, not the current location.

Customer-to-driver while showing a location — 존댓말, with 기사님 as a respectful opener. Soften with 가는지 아세요? when you want to give the driver room to look it up. 반말 어떻게 가? to a friend. Add context (빠른 길, 경치 좋은 길) to shape the answer.

어떻게 가요? (how to get there — route) vs 어디 가요? (where are we going — destination). Very different meanings; mixing them is a common beginner slip. 여기 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요 is more direct ('please tell me the way') and is used when you want step-by-step directions rather than an open route question.
여기 어떻게 가는지 아세요? (softest, indirect); 여기 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요 (direct directions request); 빠른 길로 가면 어떻게 가요? (fastest route); 이 근처 어떻게 가요? (asking about an area, not a pin).

Saying 어떻게 갈 수 있어요? — the ability form is unneeded and sounds stilted; the natural everyday form is just 어떻게 가요?. Also, using 오다 (여기 어떻게 와요?) when you mean traveling to the destination — use 가다 for going to a place.

entries.english: Thank you.
entries.shortExplanation: 고맙습니다 is a practical expression meaning "Thank you.".
entries.explanation: "Thank you." — that is 고맙습니다 (gomapseumnida). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 고맙습니다 ("thank you (polite, warm)"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 to anyone; native-Korean feel
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
softer polite, to a peer or familiar adult
natural extension adding sincerity

examples.ko: 고맙습니다.
examples.romanization: gomapseumnida.
examples.en: Thank you.
examples.note: the warm native-Korean polite thanks; safe with anyone

examples.ko: 챙겨 줘서 고마워.
examples.romanization: chaenggyeo jwoseo gomawo.
examples.en: Thanks for looking out for me.
examples.note: 반말 with ~아/어 줘서 between close friends; the ㅂ-irregular is 고마워, never 고맙어

examples.ko: A: 걱정 많이 했는데 잘 됐다니 다행이에요. / B: 이렇게까지 신경 써 주시고, 정말 고맙습니다.
examples.romanization: A: geokjeong mani haenneunde jal dwaetdani dahaengieyo. / B: ireokekkaji singyeong sseo jusigo, jeongmal gomapseumnida.
examples.en: A: I was worried, but I'm glad it worked out. / B: Thank you so much for caring this much about me.
examples.note: A/B exchange showing 고맙습니다 in heartfelt context, not just a ritual reply

entries.nuance: 고맙습니다 is the native-Korean twin of 감사합니다 and is equally polite — many Koreans feel it sounds warmer and more personal, while 감사합니다 has a slightly formal, Sino-Korean edge. You say it to anyone in 존댓말; drop to 고마워요 (gently polite) or 고마워 (반말) as closeness rises and age or rank falls. The dividing line versus 감사합니다 is feel and origin (native vs Sino-Korean), NOT politeness level — 고맙습니다 is never 'less polite'. The verb 고맙다 is a ㅂ-irregular: polite ending → 고맙습니다 (formal polite with ㅂ kept before consonant), casual polite → 고마워요, 반말 → 고마워 (ㅂ softens to 워 before vowel). Never say 고맙어 — that is the most common conjugation error for English speakers. A second pitfall is defaulting to 감사합니다 in every context; sprinkling 고맙습니다 with people you know sounds more human and emotionally genuine.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Conjugating 반말 as 고맙어 — 고맙다 is a ㅂ-irregular, so it becomes 고마워, never 고맙어.
Assuming 고맙습니다 is less polite than 감사합니다 and avoiding it with seniors — both are fully polite; the difference is warmth, not rank.
Saying 고마워요 to your boss in a formal setting — prefer 고맙습니다 or 감사합니다; 고마워요 can feel a touch too casual upward.

structuredNuance.t: 고맙습니다 is the native-Korean twin of 감사합니다 and is equally polite — many Koreans feel it sounds warmer and more personal, while 감사합니다 has a slightly formal, Sino-Korean edge. Use it to anyone in 존댓말; drop register as closeness rises.
고마워 (반말, friends/juniors) → 고마워요 (gently polite) → 고맙습니다 (standard polite) → 참 고맙습니다 (more heartfelt). The 반말 form 고마워 is only for people you are already close with.
The dividing line versus 감사합니다 is feel and origin (native vs Sino-Korean), NOT politeness level. 고맙습니다 sounds more personal and heartfelt; 감사합니다 sounds more standard and composed.
ㅂ-irregular conjugation: 고맙다 → 고맙습니다 (formal polite, ㅂ before consonant) / 고마워요 (casual polite, ㅂ→워 before vowel) / 고마워 (반말). Never 고맙어 — that ignores the ㅂ-irregular rule.
English speakers conjugate 반말 as 고맙어 — but 고맙다 is ㅂ-irregular, so it must be 고마워. A second trap is always reaching for 감사합니다; Koreans find 고맙습니다 warmer and more heartfelt in personal contexts.

entries.english: I'm sorry.
entries.shortExplanation: 미안해요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm sorry.".
entries.explanation: 미안해요 (mianhaeyo) = "I'm sorry.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 미안해요 ("I'm sorry (gently polite)"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 to a peer or familiar adult; warm, personal
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
격식-leaning polite, neutral and a bit firmer
natural extension adding sincerity in 반말

examples.ko: 미안해요.
examples.romanization: mianhaeyo.
examples.en: I'm sorry.
examples.note: a soft, personal polite apology to someone familiar or at peer level

examples.ko: 연락 늦어서 미안해.
examples.romanization: yeollang neujeoseo mianhae.
examples.en: Sorry for the late reply.
examples.note: everyday 반말 apology with ~아/어서 to a friend; note 연락 (contact) + 늦어서

examples.ko: A: 약속을 못 지켰네. 정말 미안해. / B: 아니야, 괜찮아. 다음에 보면 되지.
examples.romanization: A: yaksogeul mot jikyeonne. jeongmal mianhae. / B: aniya, gwaenchana. daeume bomyeon doeji.
examples.en: A: I couldn't keep my promise. I'm really sorry. / B: No, it's fine. We'll see each other next time.
examples.note: 반말 exchange showing authentic apology and warm reassurance between friends

entries.nuance: 미안해요/미안하다 is the warmer, more horizontal 'sorry' — used downward or sideways: to friends, peers, your kids, or people close in age and rank. From Sino-Korean 미안(未安), literally 'not at ease (in my heart)', it expresses personal guilt rather than formal deference. The register ladder: 미안해 (반말) → 미안해요 (gently polite) → 미안합니다 (firmer polite) → 죄송합니다 (deferential, upward/격식). The key dividing line versus 죄송하다 is deference: 미안하다 does NOT lower you toward the listener, so it can feel too casual or even presumptuous with a boss or customer — for those situations always choose 죄송합니다. English speakers wrongly treat 미안해요 and 죄송합니다 as interchangeable 'sorry'; using 미안해요 to your boss sounds insufficiently deferential, while using 죄송합니다 to a close friend sounds coldly distant. Also: the small 'sorry, excuse me' to squeeze past a stranger on the street is NOT 미안해요 but 실례합니다 / 잠시만요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 미안해요 to a boss, customer, or elder for a real fault — it isn't deferential enough; say 죄송합니다.
Using 미안하다 to brush past someone in a crowd — Koreans say 실례합니다 or 잠시만요, not 미안해요, for that.
Saying 미안해 to someone you've just met — too familiar; with strangers use 미안합니다/죄송합니다.

structuredNuance.t: From 미안(未安), literally 'not at ease in my heart'. The real meaning is personal guilt or regret — not the formal deference of 죄송합니다. This makes it warmer but less deferential.

Register ladder: 미안해 (반말) → 미안해요 (gently polite, peer level) → 미안합니다 (firmer polite) → 죄송합니다 (deferential, upward). Use 미안해요 with peers and familiar adults; switch up to 죄송합니다 with bosses, strangers, and customers.

The key dividing line versus 죄송하다: 미안하다 does NOT lower you toward the listener; it expresses personal guilt at peer level. Using 미안해요 to a boss sounds under-deferential; using 죄송합니다 to a close friend sounds stiff.
Attach reason with ~아/어서: 연락 늦어서 미안해, 잊어버려서 미안해요. Intensify: 정말 미안해 / 너무 미안해. To apologize repeatedly or dramatically: 미안하고 미안해.

English speakers treat 미안해요 and 죄송합니다 as interchangeable — they are not. Also, don't use 미안해요 to squeeze past someone in a crowd; that's 실례합니다 or 잠시만요. And never say 미안해 to someone you just met — too intimate.

entries.english: Thanks to you.
entries.shortExplanation: 덕분에요 is a practical expression meaning "Thanks to you.".
entries.explanation: "Thanks to you." — that is 덕분에요 (deokbuneyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 덕분에요 ("(it's) thanks to you"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: polite; crediting someone for a good outcome
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
격식-leaning polite, firmer and more neutral
natural extension emphasizing full credit

examples.ko: 덕분이에요.
examples.romanization: deokbunieyo.
examples.en: It's thanks to you.
examples.note: crediting the other person graciously for a good result

examples.ko: A: 잘 지내셨어요? / B: 네, 덕분에 잘 지냈어요.
examples.romanization: A: jal jinaesyeosseoyo? / B: ne, deokbune jal jinaesseoyo.
examples.en: A: Have you been well? / B: Yes, thanks to you I've been well.
examples.note: the set polite exchange; 덕분에 잘 지냈어요 is the warm standard reply to 'how have you been?'

examples.ko: 이번 일 잘 끝났어요. 다 부장님 덕분입니다.
examples.romanization: ibeon il jal kkeunnasseoyo. da bujangnim deokbunimnida.
examples.en: This project wrapped up well. It's all thanks to you, sir.
examples.note: 격식 form giving a senior full credit; 부장님 덕분 = 'thanks to the department head'

entries.nuance: 덕분에/덕분이에요 credits another person for a POSITIVE result — 'because of you, things went well'. From Sino-Korean 덕분(德分), meaning 'thanks to your virtue/grace/help'. It shines as a gracious, humble gesture toward someone who helped, especially a senior, and is particularly warm in the set exchange 덕분에 잘 지냈어요 in response to 잘 지내셨어요? The register ladder: 덕분이야 (반말) → 덕분이에요/덕분에요 (polite) → 덕분입니다 (격식). The critical contrast English speakers miss is 덕분 vs 때문: 덕분 is for POSITIVE outcomes only ('thanks to'), while 때문 is neutral-to-negative cause ('because of', often implying blame). Saying '너 때문에 잘 됐어' actually sounds sarcastic or odd — credit good things with 덕분에, not 때문에. Also, 덕분에 needs either a result clause following it (덕분에 잘 지냈어요) or the copula 이에요/입니다 to stand as a sentence (덕분이에요/덕분입니다) — you cannot drop these endings and use 덕분에 as a bare English-style shout.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 너 때문에 for 'thanks to you' — 때문에 sounds like blame; for positive credit use 덕분에.
Replying to '잘 지냈어요?' with bare 덕분 — say the set 덕분에 잘 지냈어요 / 덕분이에요.
Using 덕분 for a bad result ('덕분에 망했어') — that's sarcastic; neutral/negative cause is 때문에.

structuredNuance.t: From 덕분(德分), literally 'thanks to your virtue/grace/share'. The real meaning is crediting someone for a POSITIVE outcome — 'because of you, things went well'. It always points to something good happening.

덕분이야 (반말, to friends/juniors) → 덕분이에요/덕분에요 (standard polite) → 덕분입니다 (격식, to seniors or in formal speech). The set phrase 덕분에 잘 지냈어요 is the warm standard polite reply to 잘 지내셨어요?, used across all adult relationships.

Critical contrast: 덕분 is for positive outcomes ('thanks to'); 때문 is neutral-to-negative cause ('because of', often blame). Never say '너 때문에' to credit someone — it implies fault. Use 덕분에 to credit, 때문에 to explain a negative cause.
덕분에 + result clause: 덕분에 잘 됐어요 / 덕분에 합격했어요. Standalone: 덕분이에요 / 다 선생님 덕분입니다. You cannot say bare 덕분에 without a clause or copula following.

Saying '너 때문에' to mean 'thanks to you' sounds like blame or sarcasm — always use 덕분에 for positive credit. Also, 덕분에 cannot stand alone as an exclamation; it needs a result clause (덕분에 잘 됐어요) or the copula (덕분이에요).

entries.english: Thank you for your thoughtfulness / for caring.
entries.shortExplanation: 신경 써 주셔서 감사합니다 is a practical expression meaning "Thank you for your thoughtfulness / for caring.".
entries.explanation: 신경 써 주셔서 감사합니다 (singyeong sseo jusyeoseo gamsahamnida) = "Thank you for your thoughtfulness / for caring.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 신경 써 주셔서 감사합니다 ("thank you for your thoughtfulness"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: polite; thanking someone for taking trouble/care

usagePhrases.en: thanks for caring / for the trouble
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
격식, to a customer/senior, written or spoken

usagePhrases.en: thank you for going to such trouble
usagePhrases.note: natural extension stressing the effort

examples.ko: 신경 써 주셔서 감사합니다.
examples.romanization: singyeong sseo jusyeoseo gamsahamnida.
examples.en: Thank you for your thoughtfulness.
examples.note: thanking someone who took extra care or attention for you

examples.ko: A: 몸은 좀 어떠세요? / B: 신경 써 주셔서 감사합니다, 많이 좋아졌어요.
examples.romanization: A: momeun jom eotteoseyo? / B: singyeong sseo jusyeoseo gamsahamnida, mani joajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: A: How are you feeling? / B: Thank you for asking — I'm much better.
examples.note: responding warmly to concern about your health; 신경 써 주셔서 thanks the ACT of caring, not just the words

examples.ko: 선물까지 챙겨 주시고, 이렇게 신경 써 주셔서 정말 감사합니다.
examples.romanization: seonmulkkaji chaenggyeo jusigo, ireoke singyeong sseo jusyeoseo jeongmal gamsahamnida.
examples.en: You even prepared a gift — thank you so much for all your thoughtfulness.
examples.note: thanking someone who went out of their way; 챙겨 주시다 = 'take care to prepare / look after'

entries.nuance: 신경 써 주셔서 감사합니다 thanks someone for the care, attention, and effort they took on your behalf — for worrying about you, asking after you, or quietly handling something you didn't ask for. 신경(을) 쓰다 literally means 'to put nerves/attention into (something)' — it describes the internal effort of paying attention or worrying, not just a concrete action. The structural engine is the favor pattern ~아/어 주셔서 ('because you kindly did…') + 감사합니다, which frames the care as a gift to you. Register: 신경 써 줘서 고마워 (반말) → 신경 써 주셔서 감사합니다 (polite) → 신경 써 주셔서 감사드립니다 (격식). The nearest alternative is 도와주셔서 감사합니다 ('thanks for helping'), which thanks a concrete action; the dividing line is that 신경 써 주셔서 specifically thanks the emotional care and ongoing attention, not just a one-time deed. The two English-speaker mistakes: (1) writing 신경써 without a space — the verb is 신경(을) 쓰다, so the gerund is 신경 써; (2) dropping 주다 and saying plain 신경 써서 감사합니다, which removes the 'kindly did for me' nuance and sounds like you are just narrating that they worried.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Dropping 주다 → '신경 써서 감사합니다' — without ~아/어 주셔서 it loses the 'kindly did me a favor' nuance; keep 신경 써 주셔서.
Writing 신경써 with no space — the verb is 신경(을) 쓰다, so it is 신경 써 (주셔서).
Using it to a close friend in full 존댓말 — too stiff; say 신경 써 줘서 고마워.

structuredNuance.t: 신경(을) 쓰다 literally means 'to put one's nerves/attention into (something)' — i.e. 'to worry, to take pains over, to fret'. The full phrase thanks someone for that internal effort and ongoing care they showed toward you.

신경 써 줘서 고마워 (반말) → 신경 써 주셔서 감사합니다 (polite) → 신경 써 주셔서 감사드립니다 (격식). Use this when someone showed sustained concern — asking after your health, remembering something important to you, or quietly managing something.

Nearest alternative: 도와주셔서 감사합니다 ('thanks for helping'), which thanks a concrete action. The dividing line: 신경 써 주셔서 thanks emotional care and ongoing attention; 도와주셔서 thanks a specific deed. Use 신경 써 주셔서 when the effort was internal/sustained.
Add 이렇게 or 이렇게까지 to stress the extent: 이렇게 신경 써 주셔서 감사합니다. Swap 감사합니다 for 감사드립니다 upward: 신경 써 주셔서 감사드립니다.

Two errors: (1) Writing 신경써 without a space — the verb is 신경(을) 쓰다, so the spacing is 신경 써. (2) Dropping 주다 and saying '신경 써서 감사합니다' — without ~아/어 주셔서 you lose the 'kindly did me a favor' nuance and it sounds like you're just describing their worry.

entries.english: Excuse me for a second. / Let me just slip in for a moment.
entries.shortExplanation: 잠깐 실례할게요 is a practical expression meaning "Excuse me for a second. / Let me just slip in for a moment.".
entries.explanation: 잠깐 실례할게요 (jamkkan sillyehalgeyo) = "Excuse me for a second. / Let me just slip in for a moment.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 잠깐 실례할게요 ("excuse me for a sec"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: polite; before passing, reaching past, or briefly intruding
반말-ish/clipped, among close people or muttered

usagePhrases.en: please excuse me for a moment (formal)
usagePhrases.note: 격식, before stepping away or entering

usagePhrases.en: just one quick second, excuse me
usagePhrases.note: natural extension; 잠깐만 stresses brevity

examples.ko: 잠깐 실례할게요, 여기 좀 지나갈게요.
examples.romanization: jamkkan sillyehalgeyo, yeogi jom jinagalgeyo.
examples.en: Excuse me a sec, let me get through here.
examples.note: squeezing past in a tight aisle; both the excuse and the intent are stated

examples.ko: A: 잠깐 실례할게요, 이 자리 잠깐 비켜 주실 수 있을까요? / B: 아, 네 물론이죠.
examples.romanization: A: jamkkan sillyehalgeyo, i jari jamkkan bikyeo jusil su isseulkkayo? / B: a, ne mullonijyo.
examples.en: A: Excuse me for a moment, could you step aside briefly? / B: Oh, sure, of course.
examples.note: politely asking someone to move, with their consent — both the excuse and the request

examples.ko: 통화 좀 하고 올게요. 잠시 실례하겠습니다.
examples.romanization: tonghwa jom hago olgeyo. jamsi sillyehagetseumnida.
examples.en: I need to take a call. Please excuse me for a moment.
examples.note: 격식 form 실례하겠습니다 when stepping away from a formal meeting or group

entries.nuance: 잠깐 실례할게요 is a brief, courteous heads-up before you reach past someone, slip by, step away, or briefly intrude on a space or group. 잠깐/잠시 means 'for a short while', 실례하다 means 'commit a small breach of etiquette', and ~ㄹ게요 is the 'I'm going to…' announcement form that flags YOUR own imminent action rather than ordering anyone else. The formality ladder: clipped 잠깐 실례 (casual) → 잠깐 실례할게요 (polite) → 잠시 실례하겠습니다 (격식). The ~ㄹ게요 vs ~겠습니다 split mirrors formality: use ~겠습니다 in formal/professional settings. The nearest alternatives are 잠시만요 / 잠깐만요 ('one moment / let me through'), which are shorter and very common in daily life, and bare 실례합니다 (a touch more formal). The dividing line: 잠깐 실례할게요 explicitly announces a brief, self-initiated intrusion; 잠시만요 is more versatile but can also mean 'hold on / wait'. Two English-speaker mistakes: (1) using ~ㄹ게요 toward a senior in formal settings where ~겠습니다 is safer; (2) saying 잠깐 실례하세요 — the 하세요 form commands the OTHER person to excuse themselves, but you mean YOURSELF, so it must be 실례할게요/실례하겠습니다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 잠깐 실례하세요 — 하세요 tells the other person to excuse themselves; for your own action say 실례할게요/실례하겠습니다.
Using ~ㄹ게요 to a clear superior in a formal setting — prefer 잠시 실례하겠습니다.
Forgetting Koreans more often just say 잠시만요/잠깐만요 to pass or pause — it's the most natural everyday form.

structuredNuance.t: 잠깐 = 'for a short while'; 실례하다 = 'commit a small breach of etiquette'; ~ㄹ게요 = 'I'm going to (announcing own action)'. Together: 'I'm going to commit a small intrusion for just a moment.' The ~ㄹ게요 ending is key — it announces YOUR action, not a command to them.
Clipped 잠깐 실례 (casual/muttered) → 잠깐 실례할게요 (polite) → 잠시 실례하겠습니다 (격식). The ~ㄹ게요 vs ~겠습니다 split tracks formality directly: use ~겠습니다 in professional or senior-present contexts.

Alternatives: 잠시만요 / 잠깐만요 ('one moment / let me through') — shorter and very common, but also means 'hold on / wait'. 잠깐 실례할게요 more explicitly flags a brief self-initiated intrusion. In tight spaces, either works.

Add 잠깐만 to stress brevity: 잠깐만 실례할게요. Formal step-away: 잠시 실례하겠습니다. Add reason after: 잠깐 실례할게요, 전화 받고 올게요. The clipped 잠깐 실례 is muttered while passing and socially acceptable in casual settings, but use the full form with anyone you don't know well.

Two mistakes: (1) Saying 잠깐 실례하세요 — 하세요 commands THE OTHER PERSON to excuse themselves; you want to excuse YOURSELF, so say 실례할게요/실례하겠습니다. (2) Using ~ㄹ게요 to a clear superior in a formal setting — prefer the more deferential 잠시 실례하겠습니다.

entries.english: Are you okay? / Is everything all right?
entries.shortExplanation: 괜찮으세요? is a practical expression meaning "Are you okay? / Is everything all right?".
entries.explanation: 괜찮으세요? (gwaenchaneuseyo?) means "Are you okay? / Is everything all right?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 괜찮으세요? ("are you okay? (polite)"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; checking on someone who stumbled, looks unwell, etc.
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
격식, e.g. staff to a customer or a senior
natural extension; 혹시 softens the check-in

examples.ko: A: 어, 괜찮으세요? 많이 놀라셨죠. / B: 네, 괜찮아요. 감사합니다.
examples.romanization: A: eo, gwaenchaneuseyo? mani nollasyeotjyo. / B: ne, gwaenchanayo. gamsahamnida.
examples.en: A: Oh, are you okay? That must have startled you. / B: Yes, I'm all right. Thank you.
examples.note: the natural A/B exchange right after someone gets a shock or stumbles — notice the natural pair of 죄송합니다 + 괜찮으세요?

examples.ko: 안색이 안 좋아 보이는데, 괜찮으세요? 좀 쉬실래요?
examples.romanization: ansaegi an joa boineunde, gwaenchaneuseyo? jom swisillaeyo?
examples.en: You look pale — are you all right? Want to rest a bit?
examples.note: a caring full check-in on someone unwell; 안색이 안 좋다 = 'your color looks off'

examples.ko: 넘어지셨는데, 괜찮으세요? 다치신 데 없으세요?
examples.romanization: neomeojisyeonneunde, gwaenchaneuseyo? dachisin de eopseuseyo?
examples.en: You fell — are you okay? Are you hurt anywhere?
examples.note: checking for injury after a fall; 다치신 데 없으세요? = 'are you hurt anywhere?' is the natural follow-up

entries.nuance: 괜찮으세요? is the polite 'are you okay?' used to check on someone who tripped, got startled, looks unwell, or had a hard time. The 으시 honorific infix raises the LISTENER, making it respectful to anyone you'd use 존댓말 with. Register: 괜찮아? (반말) → 괜찮으세요? (polite) → 괜찮으십니까? (격식/서비스). When you bump into someone or they stumble, Koreans immediately pair 죄송합니다 + 괜찮으세요? — this pairing is a cultural reflex worth memorizing. The nearest alternative is 어디 안 좋으세요? ('is something wrong / are you unwell?'), which specifically targets physical illness; 괜찮으세요? is broader, covering shock, distress, injury, and wellness. Critical distinction English speakers miss: 괜찮아요 (statement, falling tone) means 'I'm fine / no thanks'; 괜찮으세요? (question, rising tone + 으세요 ending) asks about the OTHER person — the form and intonation are different. A second error is saying 괜찮아? to a stranger or elder — that is 반말 and sounds rude.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 괜찮아? to a stranger or senior — that's 반말; use 괜찮으세요?/괜찮으십니까?.
Confusing the offer-decline 괜찮아요 with the check-in 괜찮으세요? — the 으세요 + rising tone makes it a question about THEM.
Saying 괜찮해요/괜찮하세요 — there's no ㅎ; the stem is 괜찮다 → 괜찮아요, 괜찮으세요.

structuredNuance.t: 괜찮으세요? is the polite question form of 괜찮다, used to check on someone who tripped, was shocked, or looks unwell. When you bump into someone, the culturally expected reflex is 죄송합니다 + 괜찮으세요? together.
괜찮아? (반말, friends/juniors) → 괜찮으세요? (polite) → 괜찮으십니까? (격식, staff to customer). The 으시 honorific infix raises the listener. Always use 괜찮으세요? with strangers and seniors.

Nearest alternative: 어디 안 좋으세요? ('is something wrong / are you unwell?') — targets physical illness specifically. 괜찮으세요? is broader (shock, distress, injury, wellness all covered). Use 어디 안 좋으세요? when someone looks persistently ill.
Follow up naturally: 괜찮으세요? + 다치신 데 없으세요? (any injuries?), 괜찮으세요? + 좀 쉬실래요? (want to rest?). Soften with 혹시: 혹시 괜찮으세요?

English speakers confuse 괜찮아요 (statement: 'I'm fine / no thanks') with 괜찮으세요? (question about them) — the 으세요 ending and rising tone make it a question about the OTHER person. Also, saying 괜찮아? to a stranger is 반말 and rude; always use 괜찮으세요? with people you are not close with.

entries.english: I'd like to ask a favor. / Please (I'm counting on you).
entries.shortExplanation: 부탁드립니다 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to ask a favor. / Please (I'm counting on you).".
entries.explanation: "I'd like to ask a favor. / Please (I'm counting on you)." — that is 부탁드립니다 (butakdeurimnida). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 부탁드립니다 ("I (humbly) ask this of you"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: humble polite; making a request of a senior/customer
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer

usagePhrases.en: I look forward to working with you / please take care of this
usagePhrases.note: 격식, first meetings, handing off a task

usagePhrases.en: may I ask you a small favor
usagePhrases.note: natural extension softening the request

examples.ko: 이 자료 검토 좀 부탁드립니다.
examples.romanization: i jaryo geomto jom butakdeurimnida.
examples.en: Could I ask you to review this document, please?
examples.note: asking a colleague or senior for a task; 부탁드립니다 frames it as a humble request, not a command

examples.ko: 처음 뵙겠습니다. 앞으로 잘 부탁드립니다.
examples.romanization: cheoeum boepgetseumnida. apeuro jal butakdeurimnida.
examples.en: Nice to meet you. I look forward to working with you.
examples.note: the indispensable first-meeting set line; 잘 부탁드립니다 is a goodwill formula, NOT a comment on quality

examples.ko: A: 이번 건 제가 담당하게 됐습니다. 잘 부탁드립니다. / B: 저야말로요, 잘 부탁드립니다.
examples.romanization: A: ibeon geon jega damdanghage dwaetseumnida. jal butakdeurimnida. / B: jeoyamalloyo, jal butakdeurimnida.
examples.en: A: I'll be in charge of this matter. I'm counting on your support. / B: Likewise, looking forward to working together.
examples.note: reciprocal 잘 부탁드립니다 exchange — this back-and-forth is extremely common in Korean professional and social contexts

entries.nuance: 부탁드립니다 is the humble, polite way to ask a favor or entrust a task — literally 'I respectfully offer this request upward to you'. The base is 부탁(을) 하다 ('to make a request'), raised to the humble 부탁(을) 드리다 by replacing 하다 with 드리다 (the humble auxiliary 'give upward'). The set phrase 잘 부탁드립니다 is indispensable in Korean life: it greases first meetings ('please be good to me / I look forward to working with you') and task hand-offs ('please handle this well') and is said reciprocally. Register: 부탁해 (반말) → 부탁해요 (polite) → 부탁드립니다 (humble/격식). The dividing line versus a bare imperative like ~해 주세요 ('please do it') is deference and softness: 부탁드립니다 frames the whole thing as a humble plea, which is the expected tone when asking upward. Two English-speaker mistakes: (1) using plain 부탁합니다 or 부탁해 toward a senior — use the humble 부탁드립니다; (2) interpreting 잘 부탁드립니다 literally as 'please do a good job' — it is a fixed social formula of goodwill and mutual reliance, not performance feedback.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 부탁해 or 부탁한다 to a senior/customer — use the humble 부탁드립니다.
Reading 잘 부탁드립니다 literally as 'do a good job' — it's a set goodwill phrase for first meetings/hand-offs.
Issuing a bare command (해 주세요) where deference is needed — soften with 부탁드립니다 to sound properly polite upward.

structuredNuance.t: 부탁(을) 드리다 = 'I respectfully offer/give this request upward'. The 드리다 (humble 'give upward') is what makes it deferential. The real meaning is a humble, polite plea — much softer than a direct command ~해 주세요.
부탁해 (반말) → 부탁해요 (polite) → 부탁드립니다 (humble/격식). Use 부탁드립니다 with seniors, customers, and anyone you need to address deferentially. 잘 부탁드립니다 is obligatory at first meetings and task hand-offs.
The dividing line versus ~해 주세요 ('please do it') is deference: ~해 주세요 is a polite request; 부탁드립니다 is a humble plea. When asking upward, 부탁드립니다 is far more deferential and expected.
부탁 좀 드릴게요 (softer, 'may I ask a small favor'). 잘 부탁드립니다 (set first-meeting/hand-off formula). ~를 부탁드립니다 (task-specific: 이 자료 검토를 부탁드립니다). Adding 다시 한번: 다시 한번 잘 부탁드립니다.

Two traps: (1) Using 부탁합니다 or 부탁해 toward a senior — the humble 드리다 (부탁드립니다) is required. (2) Reading 잘 부탁드립니다 literally as 'do a good job' — it is a fixed social formula of goodwill and mutual reliance at a new relationship's start, never performance feedback.

entries.english: I'd like to check in.
entries.shortExplanation: 체크인할게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to check in.".
entries.explanation: 체크인할게요 (chekeuinhalgeyo) = "I'd like to check in.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 체크인할게요. ("I'd like to check in."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Guest to hotel front desk, polite and natural
반말 — only muttered to a friend you're traveling with, never to staff
More formal 격식 — at a nicer hotel or business trip
Softer opener that invites the clerk to take over

examples.ko: 안녕하세요, 체크인할게요.
examples.romanization: annyeonghaseyo, chekeuinhalgeyo.
examples.en: Hi, I'd like to check in.
examples.note: The standard one-line opener at any front desk; the -ㄹ게요 ending makes your intention clear without sounding demanding

examples.ko: A: 어서 오세요. / B: 안녕하세요, 체크인할게요. 이름은 김민수예요.
examples.romanization: A: eoseo oseyo. / B: annyeonghaseyo, chekeuinhalgeyo. ireumeun gimminsuyeyo.
examples.en: A: Welcome. / B: Hi, I'd like to check in. The name is Kim Minsu.
examples.note: Typical A/B exchange at arrival — give your name right after so the clerk can pull up the booking

examples.ko: 지금 체크인할 수 있어요? 시간이 좀 이른데요.
examples.romanization: jigeum chekeuinhal su isseoyo? sigani jom ireundeyo.
examples.en: Can I check in now? It's a bit early.
examples.note: Real early-arrival situation — 체크인할게요 upgrades to a question only here because you're unsure the room is ready

entries.nuance: 체크인할게요 is the guest's opener to hotel staff to start the check-in process. The -ㄹ게요 ending communicates your own confident intention ('I'll go ahead and check in') and is warm, polite, and perfectly calibrated for service situations — not a question, not a command. To go more formal use 체크인 부탁드립니다 or the crisper 체크인하겠습니다. The softer 체크인하려고 하는데요 trails off so the clerk takes the lead — choose -ㄹ게요 when you're ready and direct, -려고 하는데요 when you want them to guide you. With a travel companion you might say 체크인하자 ('let's check in'), but you would never drop 반말 with the desk clerk. English speakers often open with 체크인할 수 있어요? ('am I able to check in?'), which sounds as if you doubt it's possible; just state 체크인할게요. Also remember 체크인 is a noun and needs -하다, so the clipped 체크인요 sounds unfinished.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 체크인 있어요? thinking it means 'do you have check-in?' — 있다 asks about existence/availability, which is nonsensical here. Say 체크인할게요 to perform the action.
체크인할게요.
Using 반말 체크인할게 to the front-desk clerk because it's shorter. Staff are strangers, so the -요 is required. Drop the 요 only with a friend.
체크인할게요.
Pronouncing it 'chek-in-hal-ge-yo' but writing 체크인 할게요 with a space — 체크인하다 is one verb, so keep 체크인할게요 together.
체크인할게요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'I will check in (as my intention)'. The -ㄹ게요 ending signals your own willful intention, not a permission-seeking question. It is the natural, polite opener a guest directs at front-desk staff to kick off the process — confident but not blunt.

Standard-polite (존댓말). Use this at any hotel, hostel, or guesthouse counter with staff you don't know. Upgrade to 체크인 부탁드립니다 or 체크인하겠습니다 at upscale or business hotels. Use 체크인하려고 하는데요 when you'd rather the staff lead the conversation.

체크인하려고 하는데요 ('I'm here to check in...') invites the clerk to take charge of the process; use it when you want to be guided. 체크인할게요 is you announcing what you are about to do, so it is the more assertive, direct opener. Neither is rude — they differ in who drives the interaction.

Formality scale: 체크인하겠습니다 (격식, formal—business hotels, written requests) → 체크인할게요 (standard polite) → 체크인하려고 하는데요 (deferential trailing form) → 체크인하자 (반말 proposal to a companion). Compound request: 체크인 좀 부탁드릴게요 layers the formal 부탁드리다 on top, common at luxury properties where deference matters. 체크인해요? as a rising-intonation question to a companion ('shall we check in?') is the polite-suggestion form without any command.

Opening with 체크인할 수 있어요? ('am I able to check in?') sounds like you doubt the hotel can serve you; just declare 체크인할게요. Also, 체크인 is a noun loan-word and must be joined with -하다 to make a verb — writing it as standalone 체크인요 sounds cut short and unnatural.

entries.english: Do you have a room available?
entries.shortExplanation: 빈방 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Do you have a room available?".
entries.explanation: "Do you have a room available?" — that is 빈방 있어요? (binbang isseoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 빈방 있어요? ("Do you have a vacant room?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Do you have a vacant room?
usagePhrases.note: Polite — walk-in guest asking a motel/hotel desk
반말 — asking a friend who works there, or a very casual guesthouse
격식 — formal, businesslike tone

usagePhrases.en: Do you have a room for tonight?
usagePhrases.note: Natural extension specifying you need it tonight

examples.ko: A: 어서 오세요! / B: 예약은 안 했는데요, 빈방 있어요?
examples.romanization: A: eoseo oseyo! / B: yeyageun an haenneundeyo, binbang isseoyo?
examples.en: A: Welcome! / B: I didn't book, but do you have a room free?
examples.note: Prototypical walk-in A/B — admit you have no reservation, then ask; this phrasing is natural and non-abrupt

examples.ko: 오늘 하룻밤만 묵으려고 하는데, 빈방 있어요?
examples.romanization: oneul harutbamman mugeuryeogo haneunde, binbang isseoyo?
examples.en: I just want to stay one night — do you have a vacancy?
examples.note: Everyday: late arrival asking for a single-night spot

examples.ko: 두 명인데 빈방 있어요? 더블 아니면 트윈 상관없어요.
examples.romanization: du myeonginde binbang isseoyo? deobeul animyeon teuwin sanggwaneopseoyo.
examples.en: It's two people — any rooms free? Double or twin is fine.
examples.note: Real situation: walk-in couple stating headcount and flexibility about bed type

entries.nuance: 빈방 있어요? is literally 'is there an empty room?' — 빈 (empty/vacant) + 방 (room), written as one compound noun. It is the walk-in traveler's first question when no booking was made. Register is standard-polite; 빈방 있습니까? is formal, 빈방 있어? is casual 반말. The key contrast is with 방 있어요? ('do you have a room?'), which omits the vacancy element — add 빈 specifically when you want to signal 'right now, free to give me tonight'. Another everyday phrase, 자리 있어요?, fits restaurants and transport ('is there a seat/spot?') but not lodging rooms; for a place to sleep, 빈방 is the right compound. The English-speaker pitfall is translating 'available' with a possibility verb (방 가능해요?) — Korean expresses availability through 있다 (existence), not 가능하다 (possibility). Also keep the rising question intonation: spoken with a falling tone, 빈방 있어요 sounds like a statement.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 방 가능해요? as a literal 'is a room available' — 가능하다 means 'is it possible' and clashes with 방. Use 있다: 빈방 있어요?
빈방 있어요?
Writing 빈 방 with a space and treating 빈 as a separate word every time — the fixed compound 빈방 is most natural here. 빈방 있어요?
빈방 있어요?
Using 자리 있어요? for a hotel room because it worked at a restaurant. 자리 is a seat/spot; a room to sleep in is 방. 빈방 있어요?
빈방 있어요?

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'Is there an empty room?' — 빈 (empty/vacant) modifies 방 (room) as one compound 빈방. The 있다 structure expresses availability through existence ('there is / there isn't'), not through possibility. That is why 방 가능해요? sounds wrong to Korean ears.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Use as a walk-in at any hotel, motel, guesthouse, or 펜션. 빈방 있습니까? is the formal upgrade; 빈방 있어? is 반말 for a friend working the desk. Pair with 오늘 밤 (tonight) or 이틀 (two nights) to narrow the request.

방 있어요? drops 빈 and is slightly vaguer — fine once they see you're a walk-in, but 빈방 있어요? is clearer. 자리 있어요? asks about a seat or spot (restaurants, trains) and is wrong for lodging. Do not substitute 빈자리 here.

Time: 오늘 밤 빈방 있어요? / 이번 주말에 빈방 있어요? — 에 attaches to the time expression. Range: 5일부터 7일까지 빈방 있어요? — 부터...까지 spans a date range. Situation: 혼자인데 싱글룸 빈방 있어요? — stating your situation first (혼자인데 / 두 명인데) lets the clerk know which room type to look for. Type upgrade: 비어 있는 방 있어요? is a slightly fuller alternative using the verb phrase 비어 있다 instead of the compound adjective 빈.

Translating 'available' with 가능해요 — 방 가능해요? — is the most common error; Koreans use 있다 for availability. Also, the question only works with rising intonation; 빈방 있어요 said flat sounds like you're stating a fact (there is an empty room), not asking.

entries.english: What's the Wi-Fi password?
entries.shortExplanation: 와이파이 비밀번호가 뭐예요? is a practical expression meaning "What's the Wi-Fi password?".
entries.explanation: 와이파이 비밀번호가 뭐예요? (waipai bimilbeonhoga mwoyeyo?) = "What's the Wi-Fi password?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 와이파이 비밀번호가 뭐예요? ("What's the Wi-Fi password?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite — guest to staff or host
반말 + slang 비번 — to a friend or younger host

usagePhrases.en: May I have the Wi-Fi password?
usagePhrases.note: 격식 / extra-polite — softer, very common at front desks
Natural extension — first check it exists before asking the password

examples.ko: 와이파이 비밀번호가 뭐예요?
examples.romanization: waipai bimilbeonhoga mwoyeyo?
examples.en: What's the Wi-Fi password?
examples.note: The bare question once you know there's Wi-Fi — subject particle 가 is required for a natural question

examples.ko: A: 와이파이 돼요? / B: 네, 돼요. / A: 비밀번호가 뭐예요?
examples.romanization: A: waipai dwaeyo? / B: ne, dwaeyo. / A: bimilbeonhoga mwoyeyo?
examples.en: A: Is there Wi-Fi? / B: Yes, there is. / A: What's the password?
examples.note: Natural A/B exchange — first confirm it works, then ask the password; this two-step is how Koreans do it in real life

examples.ko: 와이파이가 안 잡히는데, 비밀번호가 어떻게 되나요?
examples.romanization: waipaiga an japineunde, bimilbeonhoga eotteoke doenayo?
examples.en: I can't pick up the Wi-Fi — could you tell me the password?
examples.note: Real situation: the network isn't connecting; 어떻게 되나요 is gentler than 뭐예요 when something has already gone wrong

entries.nuance: 와이파이 비밀번호가 뭐예요? is the everyday polite question a guest asks staff or a host for the Wi-Fi password. The subject particle 가 on 비밀번호 marks it as what is being asked about — dropping it ('비밀번호 뭐예요?') is understood but sounds bare. 비밀번호 (비밀 'secret' + 번호 'number') is the standard polite form; speech shortens it to 비번, acceptable with friends but keep the full form with strangers. The courteous upgrade 어떻게 되나요? ('how does it go?') is what front-desk staff themselves say and sounds less blunt than 뭐예요?. The two questions are interchangeable in meaning but different in feel: 뭐예요 is direct and natural, 어떻게 되나요 is extra-courteous service-register. First ask 와이파이 돼요? to confirm the network works; jumping straight to 비밀번호가 뭐예요? when the signal is absent will get you the code but not solve the problem. Never say '비밀번호를 주세요' — 주다 is for physical objects you hand over, not strings of information.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Dropping the subject particle: 비밀번호 뭐예요? sounds bare. The natural form marks the subject — 비밀번호가 뭐예요?
와이파이 비밀번호가 뭐예요?
Using 비번 with formal staff because you learned it's shorter — 비번 is casual slang. With a clerk, say the full 비밀번호.
와이파이 비밀번호가 뭐예요?
Saying 와이파이 돼요? when you actually want the password — that only asks if Wi-Fi exists. To get the code, ask 비밀번호가 뭐예요?
와이파이 비밀번호가 뭐예요?

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'As for the Wi-Fi password, what is it?' The subject particle 가 on 비밀번호 is grammatically load-bearing — it marks the thing being asked about. Dropping the particle produces a correct but bare-sounding version; the particle is what makes it natural standard Korean.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Use with hotel staff, Airbnb hosts, café staff, or anyone you don't know well. Upgrade to 비밀번호가 어떻게 되나요? at formal or luxury settings — it sounds courteous rather than demanding. 비번 뭐야? is 반말 for friends only; never abbreviate 비밀번호 to 비번 with strangers.

비밀번호가 어떻게 되나요? and 비밀번호가 뭐예요? are essentially synonymous, but the '어떻게 되나요' form sounds gentler and is the version service workers prefer. Use 뭐예요 for directness, 어떻게 되나요 when you want extra courtesy or when following up a problem (Wi-Fi not connecting).

Direct request vs. question: 와이파이 비밀번호 알려 주세요 (tell me please) vs. 비밀번호가 뭐예요? (what is it?) — the request form is softer when someone looks busy. Network scope: 객실 와이파이 비밀번호 (in-room network) vs. 로비 / 공용 와이파이 비밀번호 (lobby/shared network) — at large hotels these are often different codes. Connectivity first: 와이파이가 안 되는데요 ('the Wi-Fi isn't working') + 비밀번호가 맞아요? ('is the password right?') is the natural sequence when the code doesn't work.

Two traps: (1) dropping the particle — 비밀번호 뭐예요? is understandable but unpolished; keep 가. (2) Saying 비밀번호를 주세요 — 주다 is for physical handover; for asking someone to tell you information, use 알려 주세요 or just ask with 뭐예요/어떻게 되나요.

entries.english: Is breakfast included?
entries.shortExplanation: 조식 포함이에요? is a practical expression meaning "Is breakfast included?".
entries.explanation: 조식 포함이에요? (josik pohamieyo?) means "Is breakfast included?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 조식 포함이에요? ("Is breakfast included?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite — guest checking what the rate covers
반말 — to a travel companion comparing options
격식 — fuller, very polite verb form for a front desk

usagePhrases.en: Do I have to pay separately for breakfast?
usagePhrases.note: Natural extension flipping the question to the cost

examples.ko: 이 가격에 조식 포함이에요?
examples.romanization: i gagyeoge josik pohamieyo?
examples.en: Is breakfast included in this price?
examples.note: The most common real form — tie the question to the rate you've just been quoted

examples.ko: A: 조식 포함이에요? / B: 네, 오전 7시부터 10시까지 뷔페로 운영돼요.
examples.romanization: A: josik pohamieyo? / B: ne, ojeon 7sibuteo 10sikkaji bwipero unyeongdwaeyo.
examples.en: A: Is breakfast included? / B: Yes, the buffet runs from 7 to 10 a.m.
examples.note: Natural A/B: guest asks, clerk confirms and gives the hours — the two questions most travelers want answered

examples.ko: 조식 포함이에요? 포함이면 몇 시부터예요?
examples.romanization: josik pohamieyo? pohamimyeon myeot sibuteoyeyo?
examples.en: Is breakfast included? If so, what time does it start?
examples.note: Real situation: confirming inclusion and checking the opening hour in one breath

entries.nuance: 조식 포함이에요? asks whether breakfast is bundled into the room rate; 포함이에요 is the copula '(it) is included', treating 포함 (包含, inclusion) as a noun and describing the rate with it. 조식 (朝食) is the hotel/formal Sino-Korean word for breakfast — everyday Korean says 아침, but at a hotel counter 조식 is the expected register. The fuller verb form 조식이 포함되어 있나요? uses the passive-progressive 포함되어 있다 ('is included / exists in included state') and sounds more formal and deliberate — staff often say it this way. The nearest alternative, 조식 따로 내야 돼요? ('do I pay extra for breakfast?'), asks the same question from the cost angle; use 포함이에요? to ask whether it's bundled, and 따로 내야 돼요? when you suspect it's extra and want to confirm. A common English-speaker error is 조식 있어요? which asks whether breakfast merely exists, not whether it's free with the room.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 조식 있어요? to mean 'is breakfast included' — that only asks whether breakfast exists. To ask if it's bundled with the rate, say 조식 포함이에요?
조식 포함이에요?
Using 아침 at a hotel desk — it's understood but 조식 is the expected hotel term. 조식 포함이에요?
조식 포함이에요?
Saying 조식 포함해요? (active 'do you include breakfast') — the natural form is the descriptive 포함이에요 or 포함되어 있나요. 조식 포함이에요?
조식 포함이에요?

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'As for breakfast, is it (a) inclusion?' — 포함 is a noun ('inclusion') and 이에요 is the copula. The more formal variant 포함되어 있나요? turns 포함 into a passive verb ('is it in a state of being included?'). Both ask exactly the same thing; the copula version is shorter and more conversational.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Use 조식 (Sino-Korean 朝食) at any hotel counter — this is the expected term in hospitality. Everyday speech uses 아침 (아침 식사), but 아침 포함이에요? is less hotel-natural. The 격식 upgrade is 조식이 포함되어 있나요?; 반말 포함이야? is for friends.

조식 따로 내야 돼요? ('do I pay extra for breakfast?') is the complementary question: 포함이에요? asks if it's bundled, 따로 내야 돼요? asks if you'll be charged separately. Use whichever angle fits — both are natural. 조식 있어요? only asks whether breakfast is served at all, not whether it's covered by the rate.

조식(朝食): 朝 (아침 조, morning) + 食 (밥 식, meal). The 朝 character recurs across the meal system: 朝食 breakfast / 中食·점심 lunch / 夕食·석식 dinner — hotel menus use all three. 포함(包含): 包 (쌀 포, to wrap) + 含 (머금을 함, to contain). The opposite 미포함(未包含) or 불포함(不包含) means 'not included'; hearing either on the phone tells you the breakfast is extra. 포함되다 / 포함시키다 are the verb forms: 조식이 포함되어 있다 = it is included (passive-progressive); 조식을 포함시키다 = to add breakfast to the booking.

조식 있어요? sounds like 'is there breakfast?' (does it exist?) rather than 'is it included in the price?' — a very different question. Always use 포함이에요? to ask if it's covered by the rate. A second pitfall: 조식 포함해요? (active 'do you include breakfast?') sounds like asking about the hotel's habit, not the specific rate; stick with the descriptive 포함이에요.

entries.english: What time is check-out?
entries.shortExplanation: 체크아웃 몇 시예요? is a practical expression meaning "What time is check-out?".
entries.explanation: "What time is check-out?" — that is 체크아웃 몇 시예요? (chekeuaun myeot siyeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 체크아웃 몇 시예요? ("What time is check-out?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite — guest asking the desk
반말 — to a friend in the same room
격식 — fuller, very polite phrasing

usagePhrases.en: Can I check out a little late?
usagePhrases.note: Natural extension asking for late check-out

examples.ko: 체크아웃 몇 시예요?
examples.romanization: chekeuaun myeot siyeyo?
examples.en: What time is check-out?
examples.note: The bare timing question at any hotel desk — 몇 시 + 예요 with no added particle is the correct natural form

examples.ko: A: 내일 체크아웃 몇 시예요? / B: 정오까지예요.
examples.romanization: A: naeil chekeuaun myeot siyeyo? / B: jeongokkajiyeyo.
examples.en: A: What time is check-out tomorrow? / B: It's until noon.
examples.note: Classic A/B — guest confirms the deadline the night before, staff gives the cut-off

examples.ko: 체크아웃이 몇 시예요? 11시 넘으면 추가 요금 있어요?
examples.romanization: chekeuausi myeot siyeyo? 11si neomeumyeon chuga yogeum isseoyo?
examples.en: What time is check-out? Is there a surcharge if I go past 11?
examples.note: Real situation: checking the time and the late-check-out penalty in one go

entries.nuance: 체크아웃 몇 시예요? asks for the posted check-out time; 몇 시 ('what time') is directly followed by the copula 예요 with no extra particle — that is how Korean asks 'what time IS it / is X'. The formal version 체크아웃이 몇 시까지인가요? adds 까지 ('until') to stress the hard deadline and -인가요 for extra courtesy. The meaningful contrast between the two: 몇 시예요 asks 'what is the official time', whereas 몇 시까지예요 asks 'what is the latest I can leave' — choose the 까지 form when you suspect you'll be cutting it close. With friends 몇 시야? is fine. The classic particle error is inserting the time-marker 에 and saying 몇 시에예요? — that mixes the action time-marker 에 with the copula 예요 in a way that is grammatically wrong; for 'what time IS X', you simply use 몇 시예요. Also, never use 뭐예요 ('what is it') for a clock time — Korean time questions use 몇 시, not 뭐.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 체크아웃 몇 시에예요? — you don't add the time-marker 에 before the copula. For 'what time is it', use 몇 시예요. 체크아웃 몇 시예요?
체크아웃 몇 시예요?
Asking 체크아웃 뭐예요? to mean 'what time' — 뭐 is 'what (thing)', not a clock time. Clock times use 몇 시. 체크아웃 몇 시예요?
체크아웃 몇 시예요?
Reading 몇 시 as written 'myeot si' but it sounds 'myeot ssi' — pronunciation aside, keep the spelling 몇 시 with a space. 체크아웃 몇 시예요?
체크아웃 몇 시예요?

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'Check-out, what-time is it?' — the copula structure [noun] 몇 시예요 is the standard Korean form for 'what time is [noun]'. No particle sits between 몇 시 and 예요. This contrasts with action sentences (몇 시에 열어요?) where the time-marker 에 IS required.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Ask at check-in or the evening before departure. 체크아웃이 몇 시까지인가요? is the 격식 upgrade that emphasizes the deadline; use it when asking at a business hotel or when you may be running late. 반말 몇 시야? is only between friends sharing a room.

몇 시예요 asks the official posted time. 몇 시까지예요 asks the latest moment you are allowed to leave — more useful if you're planning to sleep in. 늦게 체크아웃 할 수 있어요? is the follow-up question when you want to negotiate a late check-out.

Service register: 체크아웃 시간이 어떻게 돼요? — the polite 어떻게 되다 pattern ('how does it work?') is how staff and guests phrase procedural questions. Late checkout: 체크아웃 좀 늦춰 주실 수 있어요? uses 늦추다 (to delay/push back). 늦게 체크아웃 가능해요? and 레이트 체크아웃 가능해요? are the casual and loan-word variants respectively. Penalty: 늦게 나가면 추가 요금 있어요? — asking if a surcharge applies is the natural follow-up once you know there is a hard cut-off time.

Two distinct errors: (1) Inserting 에 — 몇 시에예요? sounds like you're asking 'at what time?' about an action, but check-out IS a scheduled time, so the copula 예요 alone is correct; no 에 needed. (2) Substituting 뭐예요 — 뭐 asks about the identity of a thing ('what IS it?'), not a clock value; clock questions require 몇 시 ('what number hour').
