A third trap: 체크아웃이 언제예요? asks 'when' broadly and could get a date in return — for the specific clock time, stick with 몇 시예요.

entries.english: Can I leave my bags here?
entries.shortExplanation: 짐 좀 맡길 수 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I leave my bags here?".
entries.explanation: 짐 좀 맡길 수 있어요? (jim jom matgil su isseoyo?) = "Can I leave my bags here?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 짐 좀 맡길 수 있어요? ("Can I leave my luggage?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite — guest to desk, 좀 softens the ask
반말 — to a friend at the counter, rare with staff

usagePhrases.en: Could I possibly leave my bags?
usagePhrases.note: 격식 / extra-polite — -ㄹ까요 makes the request gentler

usagePhrases.ko: 체크인 전까지 짐 좀 맡아 주세요.
usagePhrases.romanization: chekeuin jeonkkaji jim jom mata juseyo.
usagePhrases.en: Please hold my bags until check-in.
usagePhrases.note: Natural extension as a direct request to keep them

examples.ko: 방이 아직 준비 안 됐으면 짐 좀 맡길 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: bangi ajik junbi an dwaesseumyeon jim jom matgil su isseoyo?
examples.en: If the room isn't ready yet, can I leave my bags?
examples.note: Early-arrival ask — the conditional makes it sound considerate rather than demanding

examples.ko: A: 체크아웃했는데 비행기가 저녁이라서요. / B: 짐 맡아 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: chekeuautaenneunde bihaenggiga jeonyeogiraseoyo. / B: jim mata deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: I've checked out but my flight isn't until the evening. / B: We'll hold your bags for you.
examples.note: The classic late-flight exchange — guest implies the need, staff offers proactively with 맡아 드릴게요 (the staff's own 주다 form)

examples.ko: 짐이 좀 많은데, 몇 시간 맡길 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: jimi jom maneunde, myeot sigan matgil su isseoyo?
examples.en: I have quite a few bags — can I leave them for a few hours?
examples.note: Real situation: specifying duration so staff know how long to store them

entries.nuance: 짐 좀 맡길 수 있어요? asks hotel staff to store your luggage temporarily; 맡기다 is 'to entrust (something to someone for safekeeping)', and 좀 makes the request polite rather than demanding. Register is standard-polite; soften to 맡길 수 있을까요? for extra courtesy. The crucial verb pair: 맡기다 (you hand your bags over to them) vs 맡다 (they accept responsibility for them) — from the guest's side you always 맡기다. The direct-request alternative 짐 좀 맡아 주세요 ('please look after my bags') skips the ability question and asks outright; use the 맡길 수 있어요? form when you're not sure they offer this service, 맡아 주세요 when you know they do. English speakers often reach for 두다/놓다 ('to place/put down'), producing 짐 둘 수 있어요? — that only asks if you can set bags on the floor, not if someone will guard them. The 좀 must stay; removing it shifts the sentence from a polite request to a blunt demand.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 짐 둘 수 있어요? ('can I put my bags down') for storage — 두다 is just placing. To have them safely held, use 맡기다: 짐 좀 맡길 수 있어요?
짐 좀 맡길 수 있어요?
Mixing up 맡다 and 맡기다: 맡기다 = you hand it over, 맡다 = they take it on. As the guest entrusting bags, you 맡기다. 짐 좀 맡길 수 있어요?
짐 좀 맡길 수 있어요?
Dropping 좀 and saying 짐 맡길 수 있어요? — it's grammatical but blunt. 좀 turns it into a courteous request. 짐 좀 맡길 수 있어요?
짐 좀 맡길 수 있어요?

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'Can I entrust my bags?' — 맡기다 is the verb for handing something to someone for safekeeping, not merely placing it somewhere. This is why 짐 둘 수 있어요? ('can I put my bags down?') is the wrong verb: it describes physical placement, not entrusting.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Use at hotel check-in (room not ready yet) or after check-out (late flight). 맡길 수 있을까요? is the extra-polite version for higher-end hotels. Never use 반말 with staff; 맡길 수 있어? is only for a companion who works there.

짐 맡아 주세요 is the direct-request alternative ('please hold my bags') — use it when you already know they offer luggage storage. 짐 좀 맡길 수 있어요? is the permission-seeking version — use it when you are unsure. The meaning is the same; the framing differs.

Time frame: 체크인 전까지 맡길 수 있어요? (before check-in) / 체크아웃 후에 몇 시간만 맡길 수 있어요? (a few hours after check-out) — 까지 and 후에 anchor the storage window. Quantity: 가방 두 개 맡길 수 있어요? — counting bags with 개. Service enquiry: 짐 보관 서비스 있어요? or 코인 로커 있어요? (coin locker) are both real options to check first; coin lockers are common at Korean stations. Pickup: 짐 맡겨 놨는데, 찾으러 왔어요 — 맡겨 놓다 (to leave in storage) and 찾으러 오다 (to come to retrieve) are the natural pair for the collection.

짐 둘 수 있어요? uses 두다 (to place/put), which asks permission to set bags on the floor — not to have them guarded. The safekeeping verb is 맡기다. Also, omitting 좀 (짐 맡길 수 있어요?) is grammatically correct but sounds blunt; 좀 is the social lubricant that makes this a genuine request.

entries.english: Please show me your passport.
entries.shortExplanation: 여권 보여 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please show me your passport.".
entries.explanation: 여권 보여 주세요 (yeogwon boyeo juseyo) means "Please show me your passport.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 여권 보여 주세요. ("Please show me your passport."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite — staff/official to a traveler
반말 — a friend joking, or peer to peer; not used by officials

usagePhrases.en: Could you show me your passport?
usagePhrases.note: 격식 / extra-polite — softer official request

usagePhrases.en: Please show your passport and boarding pass.
usagePhrases.note: Natural extension asking for both documents

examples.ko: 여권 보여 주세요.
examples.romanization: yeogwon boyeo juseyo.
examples.en: Please show me your passport.
examples.note: The bare line an official says at a check-in counter or immigration booth

examples.ko: A: 체크인하시려면 여권 보여 주세요. / B: 여기 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: chekeuinhasiryeomyeon yeogwon boyeo juseyo. / B: yeogi isseoyo.
examples.en: A: To check in, please show me your passport. / B: Here you go.
examples.note: Typical A/B at an airline desk — the phrase you will hear most often as a traveler and should be ready to respond to

examples.ko: 여권 보여 주세요. 그리고 손가락 여기에 올려 주세요.
examples.romanization: yeogwon boyeo juseyo. geurigo songarak yeogie ollyeo juseyo.
examples.en: Please show your passport. And place your finger here.
examples.note: Real immigration encounter: two polite -아/어 주세요 requests in sequence — important to understand as a traveler

entries.nuance: 여권 보여 주세요 is what an airline clerk, hotel, or immigration officer says to request sight of a passport; as a traveler you mostly hear this, but you apply the same -아/어 주세요 pattern to make any polite request of your own. 보여 주다 is 'to show (someone something)', literally 'do the favor of causing (it) to be seen'. The critical verb distinction: 보여 주세요 asks only to display the passport, while 여권 주세요 asks the person to physically hand it over for the official to hold — if you only need to see it, use 보여 주세요. Another easily confused form is 봐 주세요: 봐 주다 means 'do me the favor of watching/looking after', so 여권 봐 주세요 would mean 'please look after my passport', not 'show it to me'. Upgrade to 보여 주시겠어요? for softer courtesy; use 보여 줘 only with friends.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 여권 봐 주세요 to mean 'show your passport' — 봐 주다 means 'look after / do me the favor of watching'. To display it, use 보여 주세요.
여권 보여 주세요.
Confusing 여권 주세요 (hand it over) with 여권 보여 주세요 (just show it). If you only need to see it, add 보여. 여권 보여 주세요.
여권 보여 주세요.
Writing 보여주세요 as one chunk or forcing 여권을 — natural spoken form drops 을 and spaces 보여 주세요. 여권 보여 주세요.
여권 보여 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'Please do the favor of making (it) seen' — 보이다 is the causative of 보다 ('to see'), so 보여 주다 = 'cause it to be visible for me'. This is why the spacing is 보여 주세요 (two words): 보여 is the causative stem, 주세요 is the favor verb.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Heard most at airports, hotels, and immigration desks — both spoken to you and by you when you need documents from someone. 보여 주시겠어요? is the extra-courteous upgrade typical of formal officials. 보여 줘 is 반말 reserved for friends.

여권 주세요 asks the person to physically hand the passport to the official (who then holds it). 여권 보여 주세요 only asks for a visual display — the traveler keeps the document. Choose 주세요 for hand-over, 보여 주세요 for show-only.

Documents combined: 여권이랑 탑승권 보여 주세요 — 이랑 links nouns casually (보다 formal: 여권과 탑승권). ID swap: 신분증 보여 주세요 — 신분증 (ID card) replaces 여권 at domestic counters; pattern is identical. Polite softening: 보여 주시겠어요? raises the courtesy a full level. Reciprocal situation: as a traveler, 비자 보여 주세요 and 예방접종 증명서 보여 주세요 apply the same 보이다 + 주다 pattern to other travel documents.

봐 주세요 and 보여 주세요 look similar but are completely different: 봐 주세요 = 'please take care of (watch over)'; 보여 주세요 = 'please show'. Using 봐 주세요 for passport display is a serious error. Remember: 보여 = causative, 봐 = plain past/stem.

entries.english: Where is the gate?
entries.shortExplanation: 게이트가 어디예요? is a practical expression meaning "Where is the gate?".
entries.explanation: "Where is the gate?" — that is 게이트가 어디예요? (geiteuga eodiyeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 게이트가 어디예요? ("Where is the gate?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite — passenger asking airport staff
반말 — to the friend you're flying with
격식 — native term 탑승구 + formal ending
Natural extension giving the gate number and asking direction

examples.ko: 죄송한데, 34번 게이트가 어디예요?
examples.romanization: joesonghande, 34beon geiteuga eodiyeyo?
examples.en: Excuse me — where is gate 34?
examples.note: The most natural real opener: apologize briefly to stop someone, then give the gate number

examples.ko: A: 탑승 시간이 다 됐는데, 게이트가 어디예요? / B: 저쪽 끝으로 쭉 가시면 돼요.
examples.romanization: A: tapseung sigani da dwaenneunde, geiteuga eodiyeyo? / B: jeojjok kkeuteuro jjuk gasimyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: A: It's almost boarding time — where's the gate? / B: Just keep going all the way to the far end.
examples.note: Rushing A/B exchange — the urgency shows in the -는데 clause, the reply gives a direction

examples.ko: 인천공항인데 탑승구가 어디인가요? 게이트 번호가 달라서요.
examples.romanization: incheongonghanginde tapseungguga eodiingayo? geiteu beonhoga dallaseoyo.
examples.en: I'm at Incheon Airport — where is the boarding gate? The gate number seems different.
examples.note: Real situation: a discrepancy on the boarding pass causes confusion; uses the formal 탑승구 because it matches signage

entries.nuance: 게이트가 어디예요? asks airport staff or a fellow traveler where the boarding gate is; the loanword 게이트 is universally understood in airports while the official signage term is 탑승구 (탑승 'boarding' + 구 'mouth/opening'). Both mean the same physical gate, but 게이트 is what you say, 탑승구 is what you read on boards. Register is standard-polite; the subject particle 가 marks 게이트 before the location copula 어디예요. 탑승구가 어디인가요? is the formal upgrade. The key contrast with the direction alternative 게이트 어느 쪽이에요? ('which way is the gate?'): use 어디예요 when you genuinely don't know where the gate is, 어느 쪽이에요 when you know the general area and just need left/right. A common English-speaker error is jumping to 게이트 어떻게 가요? ('how do I get to the gate?'), which presumes you know the destination — use 어디예요 to locate it first, then 어떻게 가요 if the route is complicated.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 게이트 어떻게 가요? before you know where it is — that asks the route, not the location. Find it first: 게이트가 어디예요?
게이트가 어디예요?
Dropping the particle: 게이트 어디예요? is OK casually, but the polished form marks the subject. 게이트가 어디예요?
게이트가 어디예요?
Reading signage 탑승구 and then not recognizing spoken 게이트 — they mean the same gate. Either works: 게이트가 어디예요?
게이트가 어디예요?

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'As for the gate, where is it?' — 어디예요 is the location copula ('where IS it'), not 어디 있어요 ('where does it exist'). Both work for a fixed place; 어디예요 is the more concise spoken form at an airport.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Use with airport staff, fellow travelers, or info desks. 탑승구가 어디인가요? is the 격식 version that matches signage language — useful when your boarding pass shows 탑승구 and you need to ask. 반말 어디야? is only for friends.

어디예요 = where is it (location unknown). 어느 쪽이에요 = which direction (rough area known). 어떻게 가요 = how do I get there (you know the destination but not the route). Sequence matters: find it (어디예요), then navigate (어느 쪽/어떻게).

Gate number: n번 게이트가 어디예요? — 번 attaches to the number (34번 게이트). Terminal: 제2터미널 게이트 어디예요? — critical at Incheon, which has two separate terminals; 제1/제2터미널 must be confirmed on the boarding pass. Signs: 탑승구 표지판이 어디예요? — when the gate zone is unknown, finding the sign first is the practical first step. Direction narrowing: 게이트 어느 쪽이에요? — use once you know the general concourse but need left vs. right; this is the natural follow-up to 어디예요?

게이트 어떻게 가요? ('how do I get to the gate?') is an error when you don't yet know WHERE the gate is — it presumes you know the destination. Establish location first with 어디예요, then ask the route if needed. A second trap: reading the sign 탑승구 but not recognizing spoken 게이트 — know both terms.

entries.english: Could you take a photo for me?
entries.shortExplanation: 사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요? is a practical expression meaning "Could you take a photo for me?".
entries.explanation: 사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요? (sajin jom jjigeo jusigesseoyo?) means "Could you take a photo for me?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요? ("Could you take a photo for me?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Could you take a photo for me?
usagePhrases.note: Polite/courteous — asking a stranger a favor
반말 — to a friend

usagePhrases.en: Sorry, but could you take a photo?
usagePhrases.note: 격식 — adding 죄송한데 to a stranger makes it gentler
Natural extension explaining how, after they agree

examples.ko: 죄송한데, 사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: joesonghande, sajin jom jjigeo jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Sorry to bother you, but could you take a photo for us?
examples.note: The most natural real-world opener — preface with 죄송한데 when stopping a stranger; this small apology makes the request far more natural

examples.ko: A: 저희 둘이 같이 사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요? / B: 네, 물론이죠!
examples.romanization: A: jeohui duri gachi sajin jom jjigeo jusigesseoyo? / B: ne, mullonijyo!
examples.en: A: Could you take a photo of the two of us together? / B: Of course!
examples.note: The complete exchange — couple asks a passerby, who agrees; 저희 둘이 makes it clear both people should be in frame

examples.ko: 저기 배경 나오게 사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요? 저기까지 다 나오면 좋겠어요.
examples.romanization: jeogi baegyeong naoge sajin jom jjigeo jusigesseoyo? jeogikkaji da naomyeon jokesseoyo.
examples.en: Could you take a photo with that background in it? It'd be great if you could get all the way over there in the shot.
examples.note: Real situation: giving framing instructions to your volunteer photographer

entries.nuance: 사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요? is how you ask a stranger to photograph you; -아/어 주시겠어요 is the highest-courtesy request form ('would you do the favor of...') and is exactly right for imposing on someone you don't know. 좀 softens it further. Dropping to 찍어 주세요 is still polite but slightly more direct; 찍어 줘 is 반말 for friends only. The critical verb distinction: 찍다 = active 'to take a photo' (what the person you ask does), whereas 찍히다 = passive 'to get photographed' (what happens to you) — so the favor form must use the active 찍어 주다. The near-synonym 사진 좀 찍어 주실 수 있어요? ('would you be able to...') is essentially the same courtesy level. The English-speaker trap is 사진 찍을 수 있어요? — that asks about physical ability ('are you capable of taking a photo?'), not for a favor; 주시겠어요/주세요 is what makes it a polite request. Forgetting 주다 produces 사진 찍으세요, which commands THEM to photograph something for themselves — the opposite of your intention.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 사진 찍을 수 있어요? to ask the favor — that questions their ability. Use the favor pattern: 사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요?
사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요?
Dropping 주다 and saying 사진 찍으세요 — that orders them to take a photo (for themselves). To have them shoot YOU, keep 찍어 주다: 사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요?
사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요?
Mixing 찍히다 (get photographed) with 찍다 (take a photo). The helper 찍다 the photo. 사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요?
사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요?

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'Would you do the favor of pressing the shutter?' — 주시겠어요 is the highest-courtesy 주다 ending, conveying 'would you do this for me?'. The 찍어 is the stem of 찍다 ('to take/shoot'), not the passive 찍히다 ('to get photographed'). The direction of the favor (you asking them to shoot you) requires the active form.

Courteous-polite — exactly calibrated for asking a stranger at a tourist spot. Add 죄송한데 at the start to soften the interruption further. Drop to 찍어 주세요 with someone you've been chatting with. Use 반말 찍어 줘 only with friends.

사진 좀 찍어 주실 수 있어요? ('would you be able to take a photo?') is essentially the same politeness level. 사진 찍어 주세요 is slightly more direct — still polite, but doesn't have the deferential 겠 ('would'). Neither is wrong; 주시겠어요 is the safest choice with a stranger.

Instructions after agreement: 여기 버튼만 누르시면 돼요 (just press this button) — the -시면 돼요 pattern ('you just need to -') is the polite way to explain a simple action to a helper. Framing: 저 배경이랑 같이 나오게 찍어 주세요 — 나오다 ('to come out/appear') is the standard verb for what appears in a photo. Repeat: 한 장 더 찍어 주시겠어요? — 한 장 더 adds 'one more shot'. Orientation: 세로로 / 가로로 찍어 주세요 — portrait vs. landscape, useful for tall landmarks.

사진 찍을 수 있어요? questions their physical capability — 'are you capable of taking a photo?' Strangers find this odd. To ask a favor, use 주시겠어요/주세요. Forgetting 주다 entirely (사진 찍으세요) is an even bigger error — it orders them to take a photo for themselves.

entries.english: Where do I buy tickets?
entries.shortExplanation: 표는 어디서 사요? is a practical expression meaning "Where do I buy tickets?".
entries.explanation: "Where do I buy tickets?" — that is 표는 어디서 사요? (pyoneun eodiseo sayo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 표는 어디서 사요? ("Where do I buy tickets?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite — asking staff or a passerby
반말 — to a friend
격식 — fuller 'should I' phrasing, very polite

usagePhrases.en: Where do I buy the admission ticket?
usagePhrases.note: Natural extension swapping in 입장권 for an attraction

examples.ko: 지하철 표는 어디서 사요?
examples.romanization: jihacheol pyoneun eodiseo sayo?
examples.en: Where do I buy subway tickets?
examples.note: The most common real use — add 지하철/KTX/영화관 before 표 to specify what kind of ticket

examples.ko: A: 표는 어디서 사요? / B: 저기 자동발매기에서 사시면 돼요.
examples.romanization: A: pyoneun eodiseo sayo? / B: jeogi jadongbalmaegieseo sasimyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: A: Where do I buy tickets? / B: You can buy them at that vending machine over there.
examples.note: Typical A/B at a station — asking a stranger who points to the machine; 자동발매기 (automatic ticket machine) is the word you need to understand in reply

examples.ko: 줄이 두 개인데, 표는 어디서 사요?
examples.romanization: juri du gaeinde, pyoneun eodiseo sayo?
examples.en: There are two lines — which one is for buying tickets?
examples.note: Real situation: confused by separate queues; 표 + 어디서 사요 elegantly collapses the question

entries.nuance: 표는 어디서 사요? asks where to purchase tickets; 에서 (contracted to 서 in speech) marks the PLACE where an action is performed, so 어디서 사요 = 'at which place do (I) buy'. The topic particle 는 on 표 sets 'tickets' as the subject we're discussing, which also implies a mild contrast ('as for tickets, specifically'). Register is standard-polite; 어디서 사야 하나요? adds the obligation nuance 'where SHOULD I buy' for extra courtesy. 표 covers tickets broadly; at an attraction or museum the specific word is 입장권 (admission ticket), at a train station it's 승차권 or just 표. The alternative phrasing 표 어디서 파는지 아세요? ('do you know where they sell tickets?') is gentler for stopping a random stranger — it asks about their knowledge rather than demanding information. The key grammar trap is 에 vs 에서: buying is an action and needs the action-location marker 에서, not the static-location 에 (어디에 사요? is wrong).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 표는 어디에 사요? — buying is an action, so it needs 에서/서, not the static location 에. 표는 어디서 사요?
표는 어디서 사요?
Dropping the particle: 표 어디 사요? sounds incomplete. Use 어디서 for the place of an action. 표는 어디서 사요?
표는 어디서 사요?
Saying 표 어디 있어요? to mean 'where do I buy' — that asks where tickets are located, not where to purchase. To buy, use 어디서 사요. 표는 어디서 사요?
표는 어디서 사요?

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'As for tickets, where does one buy them?' — 어디서 is 어디 + 에서 contracted; 에서 marks the place of an action ('at which place'). This is not the same as 에 (static location). The topic marker 는 on 표 frames 'tickets' as the subject under discussion, subtly implying you may already know other things but want to clarify this specifically.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Use at stations, airports, cinemas, tourist attractions. 표는 어디서 사야 하나요? is the polite-formal upgrade with 'should I' nuance. 반말 표 어디서 사? is for friends. Note 표 is the general word; say 입장권 for an attraction's entry ticket, 승차권 for transport.

표 어디서 파는지 아세요? ('do you know where tickets are sold?') is softer for a random stranger — it frames the question as asking about their knowledge, not commanding information. 표는 어디서 사요 is more direct and appropriate with staff. Both are correct; choose based on who you're asking.

Transport: KTX 표는 어디서 사요? uses the same 어디서+사다 skeleton. Machine: 자동발매기 어디에 있어요? — note 있어요 takes 에 (static location), not 에서, because you're asking where the machine exists, not where to perform an action. Attraction: 입장권은 어디서 사요? — 입장권 for entry tickets. Online: 온라인으로도 살 수 있어요? — 으로 marks the means; 도 adds 'also'. 어디서 파는지 아세요? — softer stranger form ('do you know where they sell them?') avoids sounding demanding.

어디에 사요? uses the static-location particle 에 — buying is an action, so 에서 (action location) is required. 어디 사요? with no particle sounds incomplete. These are two different but common errors; always use 어디서 with action verbs like 사다, 먹다, 만나다.

entries.english: How much is admission?
entries.shortExplanation: 입장료가 얼마예요? is a practical expression meaning "How much is admission?".
entries.explanation: 입장료가 얼마예요? (ipjangnyoga eolmayeyo?) = "How much is admission?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 입장료가 얼마예요? ("How much is admission?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite — visitor at a ticket window
반말 — to a friend

usagePhrases.en: How much is the entrance fee?
usagePhrases.note: 격식 — fuller, very polite ending

usagePhrases.en: How much is admission per adult?
usagePhrases.note: Natural extension asking the adult price

examples.ko: 어른 두 명인데 입장료가 얼마예요?
examples.romanization: eoreun du myeonginde ipjangnyoga eolmayeyo?
examples.en: It's two adults — how much is admission?
examples.note: Everyday: stating headcount first is natural and helps the ticket seller quote the right total

examples.ko: A: 아이는 무료예요? 어른 입장료가 얼마예요? / B: 아이는 무료고요, 어른은 한 명에 12,000원이에요.
examples.romanization: A: aineun muryoyeyo? eoreun ipjangnyoga eolmayeyo? / B: aineun muryogoyo, eoreuneun han myeonge 12,000wonieyo.
examples.en: A: Are kids free? How much is adult admission? / B: Kids are free, and adults are 12,000 won each.
examples.note: Family arrival A/B — two questions in one turn, staff answers both; listen for 무료 (free) and the number

examples.ko: 청소년 할인이 있어요? 어른 입장료랑 얼마 차이 나요?
examples.romanization: cheongsonyeon harini isseoyo? eoreun ipjangnyorang eolma chai nayo?
examples.en: Is there a student discount? How much difference is there from the adult admission?
examples.note: Real situation: asking about a discount tier and comparing it to the regular adult price

entries.nuance: 입장료가 얼마예요? asks the admission fee at a museum, palace, theme park, or any ticketed attraction; 입장료(入場料, 입장 'entry' + 료 'fee/charge') is the precise term for an entry fee and the subject particle 가 marks it before 얼마예요 ('how much is it'). The formal upgrade 입장료가 얼마인가요? sounds more deliberate; 입장료 얼마야? is 반말. The important vocabulary boundary: 입장료 is the fee/charge itself (the price), while 입장권 is the physical or digital ticket — ask 입장료가 얼마예요? for the cost, 입장권은 어디서 사요? for where to buy the ticket. Distinguish also 입장료 (entry fee) from 요금 (general service charge/fare, e.g. 버스 요금) and 가격/값 (price of goods bought, e.g. 커피 가격). The English-speaker error is dropping 료 and asking 입장 얼마예요?, which is incomplete, or asking 비싸요? ('is it expensive?') when what you need is the actual number.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 입장 얼마예요? without 료 — that's incomplete. The fee word is 입장료. 입장료가 얼마예요?
입장료가 얼마예요?
Confusing 입장권 (the ticket) with 입장료 (the fee). To ask the cost, use 입장료. 입장료가 얼마예요?
입장료가 얼마예요?
Asking 입장료 비싸요? when you want the number — that asks if it's expensive. For the amount, use 얼마예요. 입장료가 얼마예요?
입장료가 얼마예요?

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'As for the entry fee, how much is it?' — 입장료 is the fee itself (the number), not the ticket (입장권, the document). 료 (料) means 'charge/fee', so dropping it to 입장 얼마예요? leaves the noun incomplete. 가 is the subject particle: 입장료가 얼마예요 = 'what amount is the entry fee?'

Standard-polite 존댓말. Use at ticket booths, reception desks of attractions, or when calling ahead. 입장료가 얼마인가요? is the 격식 upgrade for formal or upscale venues. 반말 얼마야? is only for friends. Add 어른 / 아이 / 청소년 before 입장료 to ask about specific pricing tiers.

입장권이 얼마예요? is nearly identical but focuses on the ticket (the document/card), not the fee. In practice both are used for 'how much does it cost to get in', but if staff are asking you to pay first and get the ticket later, 입장료 is more precise. Also do not confuse with 요금 (fare/service charge for ongoing services like buses) or 가격 (price of a purchasable item).

입장료(入場料): 入 (들 입, to enter) + 場 (마당 장, venue/place) + 料 (헤아릴 료, measure/fee). The 料 character also appears in 요금 (料金), which is why both relate to charges — but 요금 is a recurring or service fee, 입장료 is a one-time entry charge.

Dropping 료 and saying 입장 얼마예요? sounds incomplete — the head noun needs 료. Asking 비싸요? ('is it expensive?') when you need the actual figure asks for a subjective judgment, not a number; 얼마예요? is what gets you the price.

entries.english: Is there a good restaurant nearby?
entries.shortExplanation: 근처에 맛집 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Is there a good restaurant nearby?".
entries.explanation: 근처에 맛집 있어요? (geuncheoe matjip isseoyo?) means "Is there a good restaurant nearby?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 근처에 맛집 있어요? ("Is there a good restaurant nearby?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Is there a good restaurant nearby?
usagePhrases.note: Polite — asking a local, host, or hotel staff
반말 — to a friend

usagePhrases.ko: 이 근처에 맛집 좀 추천해 주시겠어요?
usagePhrases.romanization: i geuncheoe matjip jom chucheonhae jusigesseoyo?
usagePhrases.en: Could you recommend a good restaurant nearby?
usagePhrases.note: 격식 / courteous — asking for a recommendation

usagePhrases.en: Is there a place locals go to nearby?
usagePhrases.note: Natural extension asking for a local favorite

examples.ko: 이 동네 처음인데, 근처에 맛집 있어요?
examples.romanization: i dongne cheoeuminde, geuncheoe matjip isseoyo?
examples.en: It's my first time in this neighborhood — any good places nearby?
examples.note: Admitting you're new lowers the social barrier and often gets warmer, more detailed advice

examples.ko: A: 근처에 맛집 있어요? 한식이면 좋겠어요. / B: 이 길 따라 5분 걷다 보면 삼겹살집이 하나 있는데 거기 진짜 맛있어요.
examples.romanization: A: geuncheoe matjip isseoyo? hansigimyeon jokesseoyo. / B: i gil ttara 5bun geotda bomyeon samgyeopsaljibi hana inneunde geogi jinjja masisseoyo.
examples.en: A: Is there a good restaurant nearby? Korean food would be great. / B: If you walk five minutes down this street there's a samgyeopsal place — it's really good.
examples.note: Natural A/B: stating a cuisine preference gets you a specific recommendation; the reply uses -다 보면 ('if you walk along') which is common in giving directions

examples.ko: 저녁 먹으려고 하는데, 현지인들이 자주 가는 맛집 있어요? 관광객 식당 말고요.
examples.romanization: jeonyeong meogeuryeogo haneunde, hyeonjiindeuri jaju ganeun matjip isseoyo? gwangwanggaek sikdang malgoyo.
examples.en: I'm looking for dinner — is there a place locals actually go? Not a touristy one.
examples.note: Real situation: the tourist explicitly asks for a local spot, not a tourist-trap restaurant; 관광객 식당 말고요 ('not a tourist restaurant') is a natural qualifier

entries.nuance: 근처에 맛집 있어요? asks a local, your hotel concierge, or a host whether there is a restaurant worth eating at nearby; 맛집 is the cherished everyday compound for 'a place famous for tasty food' (맛 'taste' + 집 'house/shop'), and 에 on 근처 marks where you want it to exist. Register is standard-polite. If you want a personal recommendation rather than a yes/no, pivot to 맛집 좀 추천해 주시겠어요? ('could you recommend...') — that makes the person name a specific place. English speakers instinctively say 좋은 식당 있어요? ('is there a good restaurant?') which is grammatically fine but feels flat — 맛집 implies specifically 'a place worth going to for the food', a cultural concept Koreans take seriously. Do not ask 맛집 어디 있어요? before confirming one exists; 있어요? ('is there one?') is the correct opener, then 어디예요? gets the location. Also, 맛집 맛있어요? ('is the tasty-place tasty?') is redundant since the 맛 is already in the word.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 좋은 식당 있어요? — grammatical but flat. The natural word for a tasty, recommended spot is 맛집. 근처에 맛집 있어요?
근처에 맛집 있어요?
Dropping 에: 근처 맛집 있어요? is understandable but 근처에 with the location particle is cleaner. 근처에 맛집 있어요?
근처에 맛집 있어요?
Asking 맛집 맛있어요? thinking it intensifies — 맛집 already means 'tasty place', so that's redundant. Just ask if one exists: 근처에 맛집 있어요?
근처에 맛집 있어요?

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'Near here, is there a tasty-place?' — 맛집 is not just 'a restaurant' but a place with a reputation for good food; locals use it for places they genuinely recommend. Saying 식당 있어요? ('is there a restaurant?') only asks if a dining establishment exists — 맛집 adds the qualitative 'worth eating at' meaning.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Best asked of hotel staff, Airbnb hosts, or a friendly-looking local. 맛집 좀 추천해 주시겠어요? is the more courteous request form that invites a specific recommendation instead of a yes/no. 반말 맛집 있어? is only for friends.

근처에 맛집 있어요? = 'Is there a good eatery nearby?' (existence question, yes/no). 이 근처 맛집 좀 추천해 주시겠어요? = 'Please name a good place nearby' (recommendation request, expects a specific answer). Use 있어요? to open, 추천해 주세요 when you want them to commit to a choice.

Cuisine: 근처에 한식/일식/횟집 맛집 있어요? — drop the cuisine type right before 맛집. Distance: 걸어갈 수 있는 거리에 맛집 있어요? — 걸어갈 수 있는 거리 ('walkable distance') is a set phrase; 걸어서 5분 거리에 맛집 있어요? is the tighter form. Type: 현지인들이 가는 맛집 ('a place locals go') vs. 줄 서는 맛집 ('a place people queue for') — the second implies it's worth waiting. Recommendation pivot: 맛집 좀 추천해 주시겠어요? shifts from asking whether one exists to asking them to name it.

좋은 식당 있어요? is grammatically correct but culturally flat — 맛집 is the word Koreans use when they want to eat somewhere good. Using 좋은 식당 makes you sound like you're asking from a phrasebook rather than talking like a local. Also, 맛집 맛있어요? is redundant (the 맛 is already in the word).

entries.english: What time do you open?
entries.shortExplanation: 몇 시에 문 열어요? is a practical expression meaning "What time do you open?".
entries.explanation: "What time do you open?" — that is 몇 시에 문 열어요? (myeot sie mun yeoreoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 몇 시에 문 열어요? ("What time do you open?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite — customer asking a shop/attraction
반말 — to a friend
격식 — fuller, slightly more formal ending
Natural extension — the closing-time counterpart

examples.ko: 내일 아침에 몇 시에 문 열어요?
examples.romanization: naeil achime myeot sie mun yeoreoyo?
examples.en: What time do you open tomorrow morning?
examples.note: The most common real form — add 내일 아침에 to confirm for the next day's plan

examples.ko: A: 몇 시에 문 열어요? / B: 오전 10시에 열어요.
examples.romanization: A: myeot sie mun yeoreoyo? / B: ojeon 10sie yeoreoyo.
examples.en: A: What time do you open? / B: We open at 10 a.m.
examples.note: Clean A/B exchange — note 에 in the reply too (열어요 = action, so 10시에 = 'at 10')

examples.ko: 주말에도 몇 시에 문 열어요? 평일이랑 시간이 같아요?
examples.romanization: jumaredo myeot sie mun yeoreoyo? pyeongirirang sigani gatayo?
examples.en: What time do you open on weekends too? Is it the same as weekdays?
examples.note: Real situation: checking whether weekend hours differ — very practical before making a trip

entries.nuance: 몇 시에 문 열어요? asks a shop, museum, or restaurant what time it opens; 에 here is the time-point marker ('at what time') attached to the action verb 열다 ('to open'). 문 열다 ('open the door') is the idiomatic phrase for a business opening for the day — you can drop 문 and just say 몇 시에 열어요?, but keeping 문 sounds natural and specific. The formal variant 문 여나요? replaces the plain -어요 ending with -나요, adding slight distance and courtesy. The all-important grammar contrast with check-out time: 체크아웃 몇 시예요 uses the COPULA (no 에 needed), while 몇 시에 문 열어요 uses an ACTION VERB (에 is required) — this is one of the most confusing pairs for learners. Passive 문이 열려요 describes a door physically swinging open; for regular business hours always use active 문 열어요. The closing counterpart is 몇 시에 문 닫아요? and the rest-day question is 무슨 요일에 쉬어요?
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 몇 시 문 열어요? without 에 — action verbs need the time-marker 에 ('at what time'). 몇 시에 문 열어요?
몇 시에 문 열어요?
Confusing this with the copula case (체크아웃 몇 시예요, no 에). With the verb 열다 you DO add 에. 몇 시에 문 열어요?
몇 시에 문 열어요?
Using passive 문이 열려요 for business hours — that describes a door physically opening. For opening time, use active 문 열어요. 몇 시에 문 열어요?
몇 시에 문 열어요?

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'At what time do (you) open the door?' — 문 열다 is the idiom for a business opening. The 에 after 몇 시 is the time-point marker required with action verbs ('AT' a time). Compare: 체크아웃 몇 시예요 (copula, no 에) vs 몇 시에 열어요 (action verb, 에 required) — this is the core contrast.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Use with any shop, cafe, museum, attraction, or government office. 문 여나요? is a touch more formal, appropriate for official venues. 반말 문 열어? is for friends. The natural pair: 몇 시에 문 열어요? / 몇 시에 문 닫아요? (opening and closing hours).

영업 몇 시에 시작해요? ('when does the business start?') is a formal alternative using the noun 영업 (business operation). 언제 열어요? asks 'when' more loosely and could get a day-of-week answer rather than a clock time. Use 몇 시에 when you want a specific clock-time answer.

Closing pair: 몇 시에 문 닫아요? mirrors the opening question exactly — 닫다 (to close) takes the same 에 + action-verb structure. Duration: 오늘 몇 시까지 해요? — 까지 ('until') asks for the deadline rather than the opening time; use this when you're already inside. Weekends: 주말에도 열어요? — 에도 = 'even on'; 주말 hours often differ. Days off: 무슨 요일에 쉬어요? — 쉬다 (to rest/be closed) is the natural word for a business's day off, not 닫다. All four form a family of hours-related questions with identical grammar.

The classic error: dropping 에 and saying 몇 시 문 열어요? Learners drop 에 because 체크아웃 몇 시예요 (copula) takes no particle. But 열다 is an action verb and MUST have 에. Active 열어요 vs passive 열려요 is a second trap: 문이 열려요 means a door physically opens (like a sliding door); for business hours, always say 문 열어요 (active).

entries.hangul: 공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요
entries.romanization: gonghang ganeun gil jom allyeo juseyo
entries.english: Please tell me how to get to the airport.
entries.shortExplanation: 공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please tell me how to get to the airport.".
entries.explanation: 공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요 (gonghang ganeun gil jom allyeo juseyo) = "Please tell me how to get to the airport.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요. ("Please tell me the way to the airport."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.ko: 공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요.
usagePhrases.romanization: gonghang ganeun gil jom allyeo juseyo.
usagePhrases.en: Please tell me the way to the airport.
usagePhrases.note: Polite — asking staff or a passerby

usagePhrases.ko: 공항 가는 길 좀 알려 줘.
usagePhrases.romanization: gonghang ganeun gil jom allyeo jwo.
usagePhrases.en: Tell me how to get to the airport.
usagePhrases.note: 반말 — to a friend

usagePhrases.ko: 공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주시겠어요?
usagePhrases.romanization: gonghang ganeun gil jom allyeo jusigesseoyo?
usagePhrases.en: Could you tell me how to get to the airport?
usagePhrases.note: 격식 / courteous — softer favor-ask to a stranger

usagePhrases.en: How do I get to the airport?
usagePhrases.note: Natural extension — the common 'how do I get to' phrasing

examples.ko: 죄송한데, 공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: joesonghande, gonghang ganeun gil jom allyeo jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Excuse me, could you tell me how to get to the airport?
examples.note: The most natural stranger-stop opener — 죄송한데 softens the interruption, -시겠어요 shows respect

examples.ko: A: 비행기 시간이 얼마 안 남았는데, 공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요. / B: 저기 버스 정류장에서 6001번 타시면 돼요.
examples.romanization: A: bihaenggi sigani eolma an namanneunde, gonghang ganeun gil jom allyeo juseyo. / B: jeogi beoseu jeongnyujangeseo 6001beon tasimyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: A: My flight's soon — please tell me how to get to the airport. / B: Take bus 6001 from that stop over there.
examples.note: Urgent A/B: -는데 clause signals the problem, the reply gives a concrete transport option

examples.ko: 여기서 인천공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요. 버스로 가면 얼마나 걸려요?
examples.romanization: yeogiseo incheongonghang ganeun gil jom allyeo juseyo. beoseuro gamyeon eolmana geollyeoyo?
examples.en: Please tell me how to get to Incheon Airport from here. How long does it take by bus?
examples.note: Real situation: specify the airport name and immediately ask for the travel time — both are practical follow-ups

entries.nuance: 공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요 asks someone to explain the route to the airport; 가는 길 is the nominalised phrase for 'the way (one) goes to / the route to', and 알려 주다 ('do the favor of informing me') with 좀 makes it a polite request. Register is standard-polite; the softest form for a stranger is 알려 주시겠어요?, a full -시겠어요 courtesy upgrade. The verb to use is 알려 주다 ('to inform'), NOT 가르쳐 주다 — 가르치다 means 'to teach a subject' (like a school class) and sounds odd for giving directions. The quick-and-casual alternative, 공항 어떻게 가요? ('how do I get to the airport?'), asks for the method in one short phrase — use 가는 길 알려 주세요 when you want them to walk you step-by-step through the route, 어떻게 가요 when a brief method ('take the subway') is enough. Do not drop 좀; it's the social lubricant that distinguishes a polite favor from a command.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 공항 가는 길 가르쳐 주세요 — 가르치다 means 'teach a subject', so it sounds like asking for a lesson. For directions use 알려 주다. 공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요.
공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요.
Dropping 좀 and the favor verb: 공항 길 어디예요? is vague. To ask the route politely, use 알려 주세요. 공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요.
공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요.
Saying 공항 어떻게 가요 is fine for 'how', but to have them spell out the route, use 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요.
공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'Please inform me of the going-route for the airport' — 가는 길 is a nominalized phrase: 가는 (present-tense modifier of 가다) + 길 (road/route) = 'the route one takes (to get somewhere)'. 알려 주다 means 'inform / let know', not 가르치다 ('teach'). These two verbs are the key distinction in this expression.

Standard-polite 존댓말. Use with hotel concierge, taxi drivers, locals, or info desks. Soften to 알려 주시겠어요? for a stranger you stop on the street. 반말 알려 줘 is for friends only. Do not omit 좀 — it turns the request from a polite favor into a blunt command.

공항 어떻게 가요? ('how do I get to the airport?') is shorter and asks for the method — appropriate when you have time and the answer might be 'take subway line 5'. 공항 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요 implies you want a step-by-step explanation. Use the former for a quick answer, the latter when genuinely lost and wanting guidance.

Airport specified: 인천공항 / 김포공항 가는 길 알려 주세요 — always clarify which airport; in Seoul both are options and the routes differ significantly. From-to frame: 여기서 공항까지 어떻게 가요? — 서 (from here) + 까지 (to/until) makes the departure point explicit. Transport: 공항 버스 어디서 타요? / 공항 철도 어디서 타요? — 어디서 + 타다 (action verb) correctly uses 에서. Duration: 여기서 공항까지 얼마나 걸려요? is the natural follow-up once the route is established.

가르쳐 주세요 is the most common substitution error — 가르치다 is 'teach a subject/skill' and sounds as if you want a lesson, not directions. For giving information or directions, the correct verb is 알려 주다. Also, 공항 길 어디예요? ('where is the airport road?') is too literal; say 가는 길 알려 주세요 for route guidance.

entries.english: Could you change my room, please?
entries.shortExplanation: 방 좀 바꿔 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Could you change my room, please?".
entries.explanation: 방 좀 바꿔 주세요 (bang jom bakkwo juseyo) means "Could you change my room, please?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 방 좀 바꿔 주세요. ("Please change my room."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite — guest to front desk with a room problem
반말 — to a friend, not staff

usagePhrases.ko: 방 좀 바꿔 주실 수 있어요?
usagePhrases.romanization: bang jom bakkwo jusil su isseoyo?
usagePhrases.en: Could you possibly change my room?
usagePhrases.note: 격식 / courteous — softer for a bigger request

usagePhrases.en: Please move me to a different room.
usagePhrases.note: Natural extension specifying 'a different room'

examples.ko: 옆방이 너무 시끄러워서요, 방 좀 바꿔 주세요.
examples.romanization: yeopbangi neomu sikkeureowoseoyo, bang jom bakkwo juseyo.
examples.en: The next room is too loud — could you change my room?
examples.note: -서요 ending gives the reason politely before the request; this phrasing sounds considerate, not aggressive

examples.ko: A: 에어컨이 전혀 안 되는데, 다른 방으로 바꿔 주실 수 있어요? / B: 죄송합니다, 바로 확인해 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: eeokeoni jeonhyeo an doeneunde, dareun bangeuro bakkwo jusil su isseoyo? / B: joesonghamnida, baro hwaginhae deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: The air-con doesn't work at all — could you move me to another room? / B: I'm sorry about that, let me check right away.
examples.note: Complete A/B: guest gives the problem, staff apologizes and acts — 다른 방으로 with 으로 (direction marker) is the correct particle

examples.ko: 방 뷰가 주차장이에요. 혹시 바다 보이는 방으로 바꿔 주실 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: bang byuga juchajangieyo. hoksi bada boineun bangeuro bakkwo jusil su isseoyo?
examples.en: My room overlooks a car park. Could you possibly switch me to a room with an ocean view?
examples.note: Real situation: upgrade request framed politely — 혹시 ('by any chance') softens the ask when you're requesting something better

entries.nuance: 방 좀 바꿔 주세요 asks hotel staff to move you to a different room; 바꾸다 is 'to swap/change', and -아/어 주세요 with 좀 frames it as a polite favor request rather than a complaint. Register is standard-polite; if the problem is significant (broken AC, loud neighbors), soften further to 바꿔 주실 수 있어요? or 바꿔 주시겠어요?. The nearby synonym 다른 방으로 옮겨 주세요 (옮기다 'to move/transfer') puts the emphasis on physically relocating you — both are correct, but 옮기다 sounds a touch more like a logistical move while 바꾸다 stresses the swap itself. Adding 으로 after the new room specification is essential: 다른 방으로 바꿔 주세요 (으로 = 'to/into'), not 다른 방을. The English-speaker error is using 변경하다 ('to formally modify/alter'), which fits changing a reservation date over the phone but sounds bureaucratically stiff when you're standing at the desk asking to be moved; in person, 바꾸다 is natural.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 방 변경해 주세요 — 변경하다 is formal 'modify' for bookings/schedules. To be moved rooms in person, use 바꾸다. 방 좀 바꿔 주세요.
방 좀 바꿔 주세요.
Using 을 when naming the new room: 다른 방을 바꿔 주세요 is off. The destination takes 으로. 다른 방으로 바꿔 주세요.
방 좀 바꿔 주세요.
Dropping 좀 and the favor verb, e.g. 방 바꿔! — that's blunt. Polite requests use 좀 ... 주세요. 방 좀 바꿔 주세요.
방 좀 바꿔 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'Please do the favor of swapping the room' — 바꾸다 is the everyday verb for swapping/changing something. The -아/어 주세요 favor pattern is what makes it a polite request. Specifying a destination requires 으로: 다른 방으로 바꿔 주세요 ('swap me to a different room').

Standard-polite 존댓말 with 좀. For a more serious problem (broken AC, safety issue) or a luxury hotel, upgrade to 바꿔 주실 수 있어요? or 바꿔 주시겠어요?. Adding the reason first (-서요 'because...') makes the request sound cooperative rather than demanding. 반말 바꿔 줘 is only for friends.

다른 방으로 옮겨 주세요 (옮기다 'to move/transfer') is nearly synonymous but emphasizes physical relocation — your bags move, not just the room number. 바꿔 주세요 emphasizes the swap of one room for another. In practice both are used; 옮기다 is slightly more common when you mention moving your belongings.

Reason-first pattern: 소음 때문에 방 좀 바꿔 주세요 / 에어컨이 고장 나서 방 좀 바꿔 주실 수 있어요? — stating the reason before the request with 때문에 or -서 makes you sound cooperative rather than demanding. Destination particle: 다른 방으로 바꿔 주세요 — 으로 is non-negotiable for the target room. Price: 같은 가격의 다른 방으로 바꿔 주실 수 있어요? — adding 같은 가격의 shows you're not asking for a free upgrade. Upgrade: 업그레이드 가능해요? or 더 좋은 방 있어요? are the natural ways to ask for a better room if you're willing to pay.

변경하다 ('to formally modify') sounds like filing a bureaucratic change request — too stiff for an in-person ask. Use 바꾸다 when speaking to staff at the desk. A second error is using 을 for the destination: 다른 방을 바꿔 주세요 is wrong; the destination always takes 으로 (다른 방으로 바꿔 주세요).

entries.english: Nice weather, isn't it?
entries.shortExplanation: 날씨 좋네요 is a practical expression meaning "Nice weather, isn't it?".
entries.explanation: "Nice weather, isn't it?" — that is 날씨 좋네요 (nalssi jonneyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 날씨 좋네요 ("the weather's nice, isn't it"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: polite; the classic small-talk opener to anyone
반말; muttered to a friend or to yourself
with 참 for a warmer, more heartfelt tone

usagePhrases.en: the weather's so nice it puts me in a good mood
usagePhrases.note: extension that adds why it matters

examples.ko: A: 오늘 날씨 좋네요. / B: 그렇네요, 산책하기 딱 좋은 날이에요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul nalssi jonneyo. / B: geureonneyo, sanchaekagi ttak joeun narieyo.
examples.en: A: Nice weather today, isn't it? / B: Indeed, it's a perfect day for a walk.
examples.note: the classic opener plus the natural comeback — shows -네요 inviting agreement

examples.ko: 날씨 참 좋네요. 나들이라도 가고 싶다.
examples.romanization: nalssi cham jonneyo. nadeurirado gago sipda.
examples.en: The weather's really lovely. I feel like going on an outing.
examples.note: adding 참 for warmth; shows how it opens a wish or follow-up desire

examples.ko: 오랜만에 날씨가 좋네요. 그동안 계속 흐렸잖아요.
examples.romanization: oraenmane nalssiga jonneyo. geudongan gyeso keuryeotjanayo.
examples.en: The weather's finally nice for once. It'd been cloudy the whole time, you know.
examples.note: small talk referencing the recent gloomy stretch; -잖아요 invites shared memory

entries.nuance: 날씨 좋네요 is the single most common Korean weather small-talk opener — the same social role as 'lovely day, isn't it?' in English. The ending -네요 is the crux: it expresses a fresh, shared, in-the-moment reaction ('oh, the weather IS nice, I just noticed'), which is warmer and more sociable than flat 날씨 좋아요 (mere statement of fact) or 날씨가 좋습니다 (sounds like a weather broadcast). The nearest near-synonym is 날씨가 화창하네요 ('it's sunny and clear'), which is more specific to blue-sky days; 날씨 좋네요 is broader and more casual. Add 참 for extra warmth (날씨 참 좋네요) or 진짜 for emphasis among friends. Dropping the subject particle 가 (날씨 좋네요 vs 날씨가 좋네요) is natural in quick speech. The English-speaker trap is reaching for 좋습니다 (formal/broadcast register) or asserting 좋아요 (fact) rather than using -네요 to share the moment.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 날씨가 좋습니다 to chat — it sounds like a forecast or formal statement; for small talk use 날씨 좋네요.
Using flat 날씨 좋아요 — it just states a fact; -네요 conveys the sociable 'oh, isn't it nice' that opens conversation.
Forcing the subject particle (날씨가 좋네요) in a quick remark — dropping it (날씨 좋네요) sounds more natural and casual.

structuredNuance.t: 날씨 ('weather') + 좋다 ('to be good') + -네요 ('I see / isn't it'). Literally 'the weather is good, isn't it' — but the real function is social bonding, not information transfer. -네요 signals a fresh, shared observation, converting a neutral fact into an invitation for connection.

Polite casual; safe with neighbors, coworkers, shopkeepers, anyone. Casual equivalent: 날씨 좋다 (to a friend or to yourself). Adding 참 (날씨 참 좋네요) adds warmth. Never use 날씨가 좋습니다 in small talk — it sounds like a formal announcement or weather report.

날씨가 화창하네요 is specific to bright sunny days; 날씨 좋네요 works on any pleasant day. 날씨 좋아요 states a fact neutrally; -네요 invites shared appreciation. 좋은 날씨네요 is also fine but a touch more descriptive-literary.
날씨 참 좋네요 (warmer), 날씨 진짜 좋네요 (more emphatic), 날씨가 너무 좋아서 기분이 좋네요 (adds the emotional effect), 정말 날씨 좋은 날이에요 (descriptive form).

Two traps: (1) reaching for 날씨가 좋습니다 — correct but formal/stiff, heard in broadcasts not conversations; (2) using flat 날씨 좋아요 — states a fact but doesn't invite shared reaction the way -네요 does. Also avoid forcing the particle: 날씨 좋네요 (no particle) sounds more natural in a quick remark than 날씨가 좋네요.

entries.english: How's the weather today?
entries.shortExplanation: 오늘 날씨 어때요? is a practical expression meaning "How's the weather today?".
entries.explanation: 오늘 날씨 어때요? (oneul nalssi eottaeyo?) = "How's the weather today?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 오늘 날씨 어때요? ("how's the weather today?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: polite; asking someone who's been outside
반말; to a friend or family
variant when you're indoors asking about outside
extension asking about another place, e.g. on the phone

examples.ko: A: 오늘 날씨 어때요? 우산 가져가야 해요? / B: 조금 흐린데 비는 안 와요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul nalssi eottaeyo? usan gajyeogaya haeyo? / B: jogeum heurinde bineun an wayo.
examples.en: A: How's the weather today? Should I take an umbrella? / B: It's a little cloudy but not raining.
examples.note: practical A/B exchange — shows the question leading to a real answer and decision

examples.ko: 밖에 날씨 어때요? 좀 쌀쌀해요?
examples.romanization: bakke nalssi eottaeyo? jom ssalssalhaeyo?
examples.en: How's it outside? Is it a bit chilly?
examples.note: asking someone who just came in; 밖에 variant for indoor-to-outdoor inquiry

examples.ko: 부산은 날씨 어때요? 여기는 비가 와요.
examples.romanization: busaneun nalssi eottaeyo? yeogineun biga wayo.
examples.en: How's the weather in Busan? It's raining here.
examples.note: weather small talk on a call between cities; shows how 거기/place name replaces 오늘

entries.nuance: 오늘 날씨 어때요? asks for someone's live read on the weather and doubles as a small-talk opener — genuinely useful before leaving home and also just friendly. 어때요? comes from 어떻다 ('how is something / what is it like'), the verb for assessing a state or quality; the full literary form 어떠해요 is never used in speech. Casual is 오늘 날씨 어때?. Swap 오늘 for 밖에 ('outside'), 거기 ('over there'), or a place name to ask about a different location — very common in phone calls between people in different cities. The nearest near-synonym question is 날씨 좀 어때요? (same but 좀 softens/adds 'so' flavor). The English-speaker traps: (1) 어떻게요? uses 어떻게 ('by what means/how'), which asks about method, not state — 날씨 어떻게요? is ungrammatical here; (2) calquing 'how is the weather' as 날씨가 어떻게 있어요 is not Korean at all. Keep it as the fixed chunk 날씨 어때요?.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 오늘 날씨 어떻게요? — 어떻게 is 'by what means'; for 'what's it like' use 어때요: 오늘 날씨 어때요?
Calquing as 날씨가 어떻게 있어요? — not Korean; the natural chunk is 날씨 어때요?
Using 어때요? to a senior who expects formality — in a stiff setting say 날씨가 어떻습니까? (formal); 어때요 is casual-polite.

structuredNuance.t: 오늘 ('today') + 날씨 ('weather') + 어때요? ('how is it / what's it like?'). Literally 'today, weather how is it?' — functions both as genuine pre-departure information gathering and as everyday small talk that shows you care about the other person's experience outside.

Polite casual (-어요 ending); appropriate to anyone. Swap to 어떻습니까? for high formal settings. Casual is 오늘 날씨 어때?. Can replace 오늘 with 밖에 (outside), 거기 (over there), or a city name to ask about another location — especially common on phone calls.

날씨 어때요? (without 오늘) is equally natural. 날씨 어떤가요? is slightly more formal/written. 날씨 좋아요? ('is the weather nice?') asks for a yes/no, while 어때요? invites a fuller description. Don't confuse with 날씨 좋네요 — that comments, this asks.
오늘 날씨 좀 어때요? (softer), 오늘 날씨 어때요, 우산 가져가야 해요? (practical follow-up chained on), 거기 날씨 어때요? 여기는 비 와요 (comparing locations).

Two critical traps: (1) 어떻게요? — 어떻게 means 'by what means' (method), NOT 'what is it like' (state); for 'how is the weather' you MUST use 어때요; (2) 날씨가 어떻게 있어요 is a direct calque of 'how is the weather' that doesn't exist in Korean. Keep it as the fixed chunk 날씨 어때요?. For a stiff formal setting say 날씨가 어떻습니까.

entries.english: It's so cold these days.
entries.shortExplanation: 요즘 날씨가 너무 춥네요 is a practical expression meaning "It's so cold these days.".
entries.explanation: 요즘 날씨가 너무 춥네요 (yojeum nalssiga neomu chumneyo) means "It's so cold these days.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 요즘 날씨가 너무 춥네요 ("it's so cold these days"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: polite; shared complaint about the cold
반말; grumbling to a friend
swap 요즘→오늘, 너무→진짜 for today specifically
extension noting a sudden drop with 추워지다

examples.ko: A: 요즘 날씨가 너무 춥네요. / B: 그러게요. 이번 겨울은 특히 추운 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: A: yojeum nalssiga neomu chumneyo. / B: geureogeyo. ibeon gyeoureun teuki chuun geot gatayo.
examples.en: A: It's so cold these days. / B: I know. This winter feels especially cold.
examples.note: bonding-through-complaint exchange; shows how -네요 invites agreement and builds rapport

examples.ko: 아침에 진짜 춥네요. 패딩 꺼냈어요.
examples.romanization: achime jinjja chumneyo. paeding kkeonaesseoyo.
examples.en: It's really cold in the mornings. I dug out my padded coat.
examples.note: relatable detail about daily cold; shows how the weather comment leads to a practical consequence

examples.ko: 갑자기 추워졌네요. 어제까지 따뜻했는데.
examples.romanization: gapjagi chuwojyeonneyo. eojekkaji ttatteutaenneunde.
examples.en: It's suddenly gotten cold. It was warm until yesterday.
examples.note: small talk about the abrupt change; 추워지다 vs 춥다 contrast

entries.nuance: 요즘 날씨가 너무 춥네요 is bonding-through-complaint small talk — Koreans commiserate about heat and cold to build rapport, and weather grumbling is universally safe. 요즘 = 'these days/lately', 너무 = 'so/very' (in conversation 너무 is freely used to intensify, even positively), and 춥다 is a ㅂ-irregular describing ambient cold — not a person or object. The sociable -네요 marks a shared in-the-moment reaction. For today specifically say 오늘 진짜 춥네요; for a sudden drop say 갑자기 추워졌네요. The nearest near-synonym phrase is 날씨가 쌀쌀하네요, which refers to a milder, brisk cool rather than deep cold. The English-speaker traps: (1) ㅂ-irregular conjugation — past is 추웠어요 and 'got cold' is 추워졌어요, never 춥었어요 or 춥어졌어요; (2) 춥다 describes the air/weather being cold, NOT objects — a cold drink or surface is 차갑다 (차가워요); (3) the subject can be omitted: 추워요 alone already means 'it's cold' without needing '저는'.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing the past as 춥었어요 — 춥다 is a ㅂ-irregular: it's 추웠어요, and 'got cold' is 추워졌어요.
Using 춥다 for a cold object/drink — ambient cold is 춥다, but a cold thing is 차갑다 (차가워요).
Over-formalizing with 춥습니다 in chit-chat — for small talk the warm form is 춥네요.

structuredNuance.t: 요즘 ('these days') + 날씨가 ('weather-SUBJ') + 너무 ('so/very') + 춥네요 ('cold, isn't it'). Literally 'these days the weather is so cold, I notice' — real function: social bonding through shared complaint, signaling mutual understanding of discomfort.
Polite casual (-네요); safe with anyone. Casual: 요즘 너무 춥다. Over-formal 날씨가 춥습니다 sounds stiff in small talk. The complaint almost always pairs with care: 감기 조심하세요 follows naturally.

날씨가 쌀쌀하네요 = brisk, mildly cool (autumn-jacket weather); 춥네요 = genuinely cold. 날씨가 제법 춥네요 adds 제법 ('quite, considerably') for a mid-level complaint. 얼어 죽겠네요 ('freezing to death') is the emphatic exaggeration form.
춥다 is a ㅂ-irregular: 춥네요 → 추워요 → 추웠어요 (past) → 추워졌어요 (got cold). 갑자기 추워졌네요 ('it suddenly got cold') and 더 추워질 것 같아요 ('it seems it'll get colder') are common extensions.

Three traps: (1) ㅂ-irregular: past is 추웠어요, 'got cold' is 추워졌어요 — never 춥었어요; (2) 춥다 is only for ambient cold — for cold objects/drinks use 차갑다 (차가워요); (3) '저는 춥다' is NOT how you express feeling cold — say 추워요 (no subject needed) or 저 추워요 informally.

entries.english: It's so hot I could die / It's unbearably hot.
entries.shortExplanation: 더워 죽겠어요 is a practical expression meaning "It's so hot I could die / It's unbearably hot.".
entries.explanation: "It's so hot I could die / It's unbearably hot." — that is 더워 죽겠어요 (deowo jukgesseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 더워 죽겠어요 ("it's unbearably hot"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: polite-casual; emphatic complaint, friendly register
반말; to a friend
with 진짜 + -네 for a vivid grumble

usagePhrases.en: it's even worse because it's humid
usagePhrases.note: extension blaming the humidity

examples.ko: A: 오늘 진짜 더워 죽겠어요. / B: 그러게요, 에어컨 없으면 못 버티겠어요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul jinjja deowo jukgesseoyo. / B: geureogeyo, eeokeon eopseumyeon mot beotigesseoyo.
examples.en: A: It's unbearably hot today. / B: I know, I don't think I could stand it without AC.
examples.note: mutual summer complaint; shows how the expression invites commiseration

examples.ko: 장마라 습해서 더 더워 죽겠어요. 그냥 집에 있고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: jangmara seupaeseo deo deowo jukgesseoyo. geunyang jibe itgo sipeoyo.
examples.en: It's the rainy season so the humidity makes it even more unbearable. I just want to stay home.
examples.note: humidity extension tying heat to the monsoon; practical consequence follow-up

examples.ko: 이 더위에 걸어서 왔어요? 더워 죽겠겠다.
examples.romanization: i deowie georeoseo wasseoyo? deowo jukgetgetda.
examples.en: You walked in this heat? You must be dying of heat.
examples.note: sympathetic/teasing third-person use; shows 더워 죽겠다 applied to another person

entries.nuance: 더워 죽겠어요 literally means 'it's hot, I'm going to die', but -아/어 죽겠어요 is an everyday exaggeration suffix meaning 'unbearably/to death' — totally normal, not alarming. The same pattern runs across states: 배고파 죽겠어요 (starving), 피곤해 죽겠어요 (exhausted), 추워 죽겠어요 (freezing). It sits in a casual-polite register: perfect among coworkers and friends, a touch too dramatic for a stiff formal meeting. The nearest near-synonym phrase is 너무 더워서 못 살겠어요 ('it's so hot I can barely survive'), which is similar in intensity but more speech-like. 덥다 is the base (ambient heat); it's a ㅂ-irregular so the conjugated form is 더워, never 덥어. Critically, 덥다 / 더워요 is ONLY for ambient air heat — a hot object or liquid is 뜨겁다 (뜨거워요). The English-speaker traps: (1) avoiding 죽겠어요 as morbid — Koreans hear it as light venting; (2) writing 덥어 죽겠어요 (wrong conjugation); (3) using 더워요 for a hot coffee or soup — that's 뜨거워요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 덥어 죽겠어요 — 덥다 is a ㅂ-irregular, so it's 더워 죽겠어요 (past 더웠어요).
Using 덥다 for a hot object/drink — ambient heat is 덥다, but a hot thing is 뜨겁다 (뜨거워요).
Avoiding 죽겠어요 as too literal/morbid — it's normal light venting ('I'm dying of heat'), not real distress.

structuredNuance.t: 더워 (it's hot) + 죽겠어요 (I'm going to die). Literal: 'I'm going to die because it's hot.' Real meaning: a totally ordinary, friendly exaggeration — 'it's unbearably hot.' The -아/어 죽겠어요 pattern is a productive suffix for expressing overwhelming sensation, not literal mortal danger.

Casual-polite; great among coworkers and friends as light venting. Casual: 더워 죽겠어. Avoid in strictly formal settings with a senior where complaint sounds undignified. Pairs well with 에어컨 틀어요 / 에어컨 없으면 못 살아요.

너무 더워서 못 살겠어요 ('so hot I can barely live') is equally expressive and similar. 날씨가 너무 덥네요 is more measured and less dramatic. 찜통 같아요 ('it's like a steamer') is a vivid metaphor for humid heat. 죽겠어요 is the most common dramatic intensifier.
덥다 is a ㅂ-irregular: 더워 (base) → 더워요 (present) → 더웠어요 (past) → 더워 죽겠어요 (unbearable). Other -아/어 죽겠어요 uses: 배고파 죽겠어요, 추워 죽겠어요, 피곤해 죽겠어요 — all everyday exaggerations.

Three traps: (1) avoiding 죽겠어요 as morbid — Koreans hear it as harmless venting; (2) writing 덥어 죽겠어요 — ㅂ-irregular means it's 더워, not 덥어; (3) using 더워요 for hot food/objects — ambient heat is 덥다, but a hot object or liquid is 뜨겁다 (뜨거워요). So hot soup is 뜨거워요, not 더워요.

entries.english: It's raining.
entries.shortExplanation: 비 와요 is a practical expression meaning "It's raining.".
entries.explanation: 비 와요 (bi wayo) = "It's raining.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 비 와요 ("it's raining"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: polite; stating or reporting the rain
반말; to a friend
rising tone to ask about the rain

usagePhrases.en: it looks like it's going to rain
usagePhrases.note: extension predicting rain from the sky

examples.ko: A: 밖에 비 와요? / B: 네, 꽤 많이 와요. 우산 꼭 챙기세요.
examples.romanization: A: bakke bi wayo? / B: ne, kkwae mani wayo. usan kkok chaenggiseyo.
examples.en: A: Is it raining outside? / B: Yes, quite a lot. Be sure to take an umbrella.
examples.note: practical A/B exchange — shows the question form and the caring natural follow-up

examples.ko: 갑자기 비 와요. 우산 없는데 어떡하죠?
examples.romanization: gapjagi bi wayo. usan eopsneunde eotteokajyo?
examples.en: It's suddenly raining. I don't have an umbrella, what should I do?
examples.note: real reaction to a surprise shower; shows how 비 와요 pairs naturally with practical concern

examples.ko: 하늘 보니까 곧 비 올 것 같아요. 우산 챙기는 거 잊지 마세요.
examples.romanization: haneul bonikka got bi ol geot gatayo. usan chaenggineun geo itji maseyo.
examples.en: Looking at the sky, it seems like it'll rain soon. Don't forget to take an umbrella.
examples.note: predicting from evidence with 올 것 같아요; contrast with 와요 for ongoing rain

entries.nuance: 비 와요 is the natural, idiomatic way to say 'it's raining' — Korean pairs 비 ('rain') with the verb 오다 ('to come'), so rain literally 'comes': 비가 와요 → 비 와요 in speech. This verb choice is the crux English speakers must learn. The near-synonym 비가 내려요 (from 내리다 'to fall/descend') is equally correct but leans slightly written or weather-report in feel; 와요 is the everyday spoken choice. Snow works identically: 눈 와요 ('it's snowing'). Dropping the particle (비 와요 vs 비가 와요) is natural in casual speech. For ongoing rain, use plain present (비 와요); Korean does not use a separate progressive. For a forecast, switch to 비 올 것 같아요 ('looks like rain') or 비 온대요 ('I heard it will rain'). The English-speaker traps: (1) calquing with 하다 (비 해요) or 있다 (비가 있어요) — both wrong; (2) forcing a progressive tense; (3) using 비 와요 for a future forecast instead of the right forms.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Calquing 'it rains' as 비 해요 or 비가 있어요 — rain 'comes' in Korean: 비 와요 (or 비가 내려요).
Using a forced progressive for current rain — plain present 비 와요 already means 'it's raining now'.
Saying 비 와요 for a forecast — for 'it'll rain' use 비 올 것 같아요 or 비 온대요.

structuredNuance.t: 비 ('rain') + 와요 ('comes', polite present of 오다). Literally 'rain comes.' Korean conceptualizes precipitation as coming toward you, so 비가 오다 / 눈이 오다 is the fixed grammatical pattern. There is no separate 'it rains' structure — 오다 IS the verb for falling precipitation.

Polite with -아요; casual is 비 와 or 비 온다. The subject particle 가 can be dropped in speech (비 와요) without any meaning change. Used for CURRENTLY falling rain only; for forecasts use 비 올 것 같아요 (inference from sky) or 비 온대요 (hearsay/forecast).

비가 내려요 (내리다 = to fall/descend) is equivalent but slightly more written/formal — heard in weather reports and songs. 비가 와요 is the everyday spoken verb. 비가 쏟아져요 ('rain is pouring') is a stronger intensity variant. For a drizzle: 비가 부슬부슬 와요.
비 온다! (casual exclamation), 비 많이 와요 ('it's raining a lot'), 비가 그쳤어요 ('the rain has stopped'), 비가 올 것 같아요 ('looks like it'll rain'). Snow is exactly parallel: 눈 와요, 눈 온다!, 눈이 많이 와요.

Two classic mistakes: (1) calquing 'it rains' as 비 해요 or 비가 있어요 — both wrong; use 오다 or 내리다; (2) using 비 와요 for a forecast — current rain is 와요, predicted rain is 비 올 것 같아요 or 비 온대요. Also don't use a progressive form — Korean plain present (비 와요) already means 'it's raining right now'.

entries.english: Take an umbrella (don't forget it).
entries.shortExplanation: 우산 챙기세요 is a practical expression meaning "Take an umbrella (don't forget it).".
entries.explanation: 우산 챙기세요 (usan chaenggiseyo) means "Take an umbrella (don't forget it).". Say it as one set phrase — for example 우산 챙기세요 ("take an umbrella"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: polite; caring reminder as someone leaves
반말; to a friend or family

usagePhrases.en: don't forget to take an umbrella
usagePhrases.note: fuller, more emphatic reminder

usagePhrases.en: be sure to take an umbrella
usagePhrases.note: with 꼭 to stress it

examples.ko: A: 나가려고요. / B: 오후에 비 온대요. 우산 꼭 챙기세요.
examples.romanization: A: nagaryeogoyo. / B: ohue bi ondaeyo. usan kkok chaenggiseyo.
examples.en: A: I'm heading out. / B: They say it'll rain in the afternoon. Be sure to take an umbrella.
examples.note: typical caring exchange before departure — shows 챙기세요 as a natural response to news of rain

examples.ko: 나갈 때 우산 챙겨. 하늘 좀 봐, 비 올 것 같아.
examples.romanization: nagal ttae usan chaenggyeo. haneul jom bwa, bi ol geot gata.
examples.en: Grab an umbrella when you go. Look at the sky — it looks like rain.
examples.note: casual parental or friend reminder with sensory evidence; shows 반말 form 챙겨

examples.ko: 일기예보 봤어요? 비 온대요. 우산 챙기는 거 잊지 마세요.
examples.romanization: ilgiyebo bwasseoyo? bi ondaeyo. usan chaenggineun geo itji maseyo.
examples.en: Did you check the forecast? They say it'll rain. Don't forget to take your umbrella.
examples.note: reminder grounded in a specific source; shows fuller form with 잊지 마세요

entries.nuance: 우산 챙기세요 is a small act of care that doubles as warm small talk — reminding someone to take an umbrella signals concern, parallel to 감기 조심하세요. The verb 챙기다 is central: it means 'to pack/gather/take along (and not forget)', carrying the 'remember to bring' nuance that separates it from the plain carrying verb 가져가다. You챙기다 your phone, your meals (밥 챙겨 먹어요 'make sure you eat'), your belongings — the verb always implies attentiveness and care. The nearest near-synonym is 우산 가져가세요 ('carry an umbrella with you'), which is grammatically fine but loses the caring 'don't forget' flavor; 챙기세요 is what Koreans actually say. Casual is 우산 챙겨; add 꼭 ('for sure/definitely') for emphasis. The English-speaker traps: (1) defaulting to 가져가세요 loses the caring nuance; (2) writing the honorific request as 챙기요 instead of 챙기세요 (챙기다 + -세요). Pair naturally with a reason: 비 온대요, 우산 챙기세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 우산 가져가세요 — fine, but 챙기다 adds the caring 'remember to bring' nuance Koreans use here.
Writing the request as 챙기요 — the honorific is 챙기세요 (챙기다 + -세요).
Using 챙기세요 only for objects — it also means 'make sure to' do something (밥 잘 챙겨 드세요).

structuredNuance.t: 우산 ('umbrella') + 챙기세요 ('please pack/take along', honorific request of 챙기다). Literally 'please take the umbrella along.' Real nuance: an act of care — 챙기다 implies mindful attentiveness ('don't forget'), making this a warmer reminder than a simple 'bring it.'
Polite caring reminder (-세요); to coworkers, family, seniors, anyone. Casual: 우산 챙겨. Strengthen with 꼭: 우산 꼭 챙기세요. Always more natural paired with a reason: 비 온대요 / 비 올 것 같아요, 우산 챙기세요.

우산 가져가세요 = 'carry an umbrella with you' — plain and functional, understood. 챙기세요 adds the caring 'remember to bring / don't forget' flavor. 우산 잊지 마세요 ('don't forget the umbrella') is direct about the forgetting risk. Koreans default to 챙기세요 for warm, socially rich reminders.

챙기다 is broadly useful: 밥 챙겨 먹어요 (make sure to eat), 짐 잘 챙겼어요? (did you pack everything?), 몸 챙기세요 (take care of yourself). The imperative chain: 챙겨라 (plain imperative, very direct) → 챙겨 (casual) → 챙기세요 (polite) → 챙기십시오 (formal).

Two traps: (1) defaulting to 우산 가져가세요 — grammatically fine but loses the caring 'don't forget' warmth that 챙기다 carries; (2) writing the honorific as 챙기요 — the honorific request form is 챙기세요 (챙기다 + -세요), never 챙기요.

entries.english: The fine dust is really bad.
entries.shortExplanation: 미세먼지 심하네요 is a practical expression meaning "The fine dust is really bad.".
entries.explanation: "The fine dust is really bad." — that is 미세먼지 심하네요 (misemeonji simhaneyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 미세먼지 심하네요 ("the fine dust is bad"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: polite; shared complaint about air quality
반말; to a friend

usagePhrases.en: the fine dust is really bad today
usagePhrases.note: with 진짜 for emphasis

usagePhrases.en: my throat feels scratchy from the fine dust
usagePhrases.note: extension naming a symptom

examples.ko: A: 오늘 미세먼지 심하네요. / B: 그러게요. 마스크 꼭 쓰고 나가세요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul misemeonji simhaneyo. / B: geureogeyo. maseukeu kkok sseugo nagaseyo.
examples.en: A: The fine dust is really bad today. / B: I know. Be sure to wear a mask when you go out.
examples.note: shared complaint with practical advice — the most natural flow of this small talk

examples.ko: 하늘이 뿌옇네요. 미세먼지 심한가 봐요.
examples.romanization: haneuri ppuyeonneyo. misemeonji simhanga bwayo.
examples.en: The sky's hazy. The fine dust must be bad.
examples.note: inferring bad air quality from a visible cue; shows 심한가 봐요 (soft conjecture)

examples.ko: 미세먼지가 너무 심해서 창문도 못 열겠어요.
examples.romanization: misemeonjiga neomu simhaeseo changmundo mot yeolgesseoyo.

examples.note: relatable daily-impact complaint; shows how 심하다 pairs with a result clause

entries.nuance: 미세먼지 심하네요 is everyday Korean small talk with no clean English equivalent — air quality (미세먼지 'fine dust', roughly PM10; 초미세먼지 'ultra-fine dust', PM2.5) is a constant Korean daily concern driven by pollution from the mainland, so commenting on it is as routine as commenting on rain. 심하다 means 'to be severe/intense (in degree)' and is the standard collocation for anything intense in degree: 미세먼지가 심하다, 교통이 심하다, 증상이 심하다. The sociable -네요 marks in-the-moment shared reaction. The nearest near-synonym phrase is 공기가 안 좋네요 ('the air's not good'), which is softer and less specific. The English-speaker traps: (1) translating with 나쁘다 ('bad' in quality sense) — 미세먼지 나빠요 sounds off because 심하다 ('severe in degree') is the natural verb for intensity, while 나쁘다 is moral/quality; (2) treating 미세먼지 as a verb — it's a noun, so it needs a predicate (심하다, 많다); (3) confusing 미세먼지 ('fine dust', everyday term) with 황사 ('yellow dust/sandstorm', a seasonal weather phenomenon from the Gobi Desert).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 미세먼지 나빠요 for intensity — Koreans use 심하다 (severe) or 안 좋아요; 나쁘다 is more moral/quality 'bad'.
Treating 미세먼지 as a verb — it's a noun; pair it with 심하다 or 많다 (미세먼지 많네요).
Confusing 미세먼지 (fine dust/PM10) with 황사 (yellow dust/sandstorm) — they're different; 미세먼지 is the everyday air-quality term.

structuredNuance.t: 미세먼지 ('fine dust/particulate matter') + 심하네요 ('is severe, isn't it' — fresh observation). Literally 'the fine dust is severe, I see.' Real use: routine Korean weather/environment small talk expressing shared concern over air quality, with no tidy English equivalent since Western weather talk rarely includes air quality.
Polite casual; everyone says it to everyone. Casual: 미세먼지 심하다. The complaint usually prompts practical advice: 마스크 쓰세요, 창문 닫으세요, 야외 활동 줄이세요 — naming a symptom (목이 칼칼해요, 눈이 따가워요) deepens the bond.

공기가 안 좋네요 ('the air's not good') is softer and more general. 미세먼지 많네요 ('there's a lot of fine dust') is also natural — 많다 (quantity) vs 심하다 (intensity). 황사 심하네요 is specific to yellow-dust sandstorm events (spring, Chinese/Mongolian origin), not everyday pollution.

미세먼지 수치가 높네요 ('the fine dust index is high', more precise), 오늘 나쁨이래요 ('they say it's in the 나쁨/bad category today', referencing the air quality index), 미세먼지 때문에 눈이 따가워요 ('my eyes sting from the fine dust').

Three traps: (1) saying 미세먼지 나빠요 — 나쁘다 is moral/quality 'bad'; Koreans say 심하다 (intense/severe) or 안 좋아요 for air quality; (2) treating 미세먼지 as a verb — it's a noun needing 심하다/많다; (3) confusing 미세먼지 (everyday fine particulates) with 황사 (yellow dust, a distinct seasonal storm phenomenon) — they require different forecasts and different responses.

entries.english: It must be because the seasons are changing.
entries.shortExplanation: 환절기라 그런가 봐요 is a practical expression meaning "It must be because the seasons are changing.".
entries.explanation: 환절기라 그런가 봐요 (hwanjeolgira geureonga bwayo) = "It must be because the seasons are changing.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 환절기라 그런가 봐요 ("must be because seasons are changing"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: must be because seasons are changing
usagePhrases.note: polite; explaining colds/fatigue in small talk

usagePhrases.en: must be the change of seasons (casual)
usagePhrases.note: 반말; to a friend

examples.ko: A: 요즘 계속 피곤하네요. / B: 환절기라 그런가 봐요. 몸 좀 챙기세요.
